I have to admit that I've played a lot of otomes with fairytale themes, but this one really shines. For a free game, I didn't expect much, but I'm on the third route so far and I'm very, very impressed. While each route is relatively short (for a quick reader), they're very detailed stories with very good storylines. Apart from the prologue, none have shared plots or scenes, so it's unique with each playthrough, the stories are interesting, well-written, and engrossing, and the characters are interesting, too. Each route is long enough that I can actually see the characters coming to care about one another/learn about themselves, it's not just a sudden "one day I'm in love with this person," which always feels hacked. The writers did a very good job of fitting each story to the fairytale from which it stems without making them obvious, and none feel too forced. The art is really good, too, and I love the character sprites.
15/10, would highly recommend. Will be interested in seeing more games from these guys!

Level design is the heart of a Sonic game, and the level designers for this game delivered. There are fewer Zones than a genesis-era Sonic, but each of the three acts of a zone has a clear identity. Difficult platforming segments that drop you into a bottomless pit do exist, but they are restricted to the short area between the last goal post and the end of an act, which gives the sense of a final exam on the act's particular design element. Bosses generally open by retreading a boss from either Sonic 1 or Sonic 2, but partway through a battle a phase 2 with new behavior will begin.
The final boss was very impressive. I died many times but playing normally though the game supplied me with an ample supply of extra lives and more often than not I felt that each try was a fair learning experience.
Artistically, the summary is: Looks like, but plays different. Splash Hill Zone looks like Green Hill Zone, but plays different. Casino Street Zone looks like Casino Night Zone. Lost Labyrinth Zone looks like Labyrinth Zone (but the resemblance here is more distant than in any other zone). Mad Gear Zone looks like Metropolis Zone. Special stages look like Sonic 1 special stages, but you control the rotation. And the final boss looks like the final boss of Sonic 2, but the play puts the simplistic battle from Sonic 2 to shame.
There are two sour notes. First, when jumping Sonic's momentum will die very quickly when directional input is neutral - this threw me off until I made a concious effort to figure out what was going on, and it never felt natural. Second, the third zone boss phase 2 uses a crushing attack that is an instant kill, following a lengthy phase 1.
Reading a story is not a game.

As a day one Sonic fan who played the original Genesis titles as soon as they came out. This is a really good Sonic game. The game took old concepts for levels and created something fresh and new. With platforming puzzles that would use old mechanics in a brand new and interesting way.
After 10-15 years of bare bones, turn your brain off Sonic gameplay. I feel the audience for Sonic just didn't want a game like this. Episode 1 will actually challenge you a little bit. You'll find platforming puzzles, because Sonic is a platformer. A shocker to some, I know. I feel that's the main reason why people preferred Episode2 over Ep1. Ep2 looks gorgeous and is completely brain dead.
Also it's worth noting, the nitpicks about the physics and earning speed are misguided. The physics are 90% the same and there's no meaningful difference between this and the classics. Earning speed is also a talking point parroted by people who didn't want to take the time to figure out what was really bothering them. For example, who complained the spindash in Sonic 2 took the 'earning speed' element out of the game? The real reason why it didn't feel like a Genesis Sonic game was the save system:
This game was designed to be played through once without having to replay levels. There's no muscle memory or memorization of level layouts, unlike there was in Sonic 1-2.

I bought this as part of the sonic hits collection and decided it to be a good idea to play these games in order from sonic one to sonic 4 episode 2. This has worked to a disadantage however in the sense that it just shows how much this isn't a classic sonic game, sure its 2D and there are a lot of nods to past games (and i mean a lot) but thats as far as it goes.
For those who are interested i am about to list reasons for this but for those who arent i will just say that it is a reasonable 2D sonic game but it certainly is not worthy of being called sonic the hedgehog 4. It was fun to play up until the last boss which i have been attempting to beat for the past ten minutes or so at the time of writing and still have not managed it. it is a nice nostalgia trip but not a great game in itself merely an ok sonic game and it really varys from peson to person as to whever or not it is what they are looking for.
Now for details
Positives
. It serves well as a nostalgia trip so for those who are looking for that kind of thing then yes this game has it in spades.
. Fun gameplay for what it is, it is nothing like the old games at all but it is not terrible and yes despite thinking that the game is not worthy to be called Sonic the Hedgehog 4, i still think it is fun
. Super Sonic is available in normal stages and the chaos emeralds can be collected from special stages which i always like to see. Collecting the Emeralds used to be the only reason i played sonic games when i was younger so i shall not complain about that.
Negatives
. The games physics are certainly not like past sonic games and it is most notable in the games speed. by this I mean that there is none, unless you hit a speed boost. this makes the game feel very artificial as whenever you start to move fast you know it is not because of your own actions (i.e. rolling into a ball on a slope like in sonics 1-3) some people may have no problem with this but having played this straight after the classic games it was a notable difference.
. The presentation of the game overall may look nice enough but it certainly has flaws. an example of this could be sonics animations, his slowest running speed is walking pace which makes the game feel incredibly slow as it takes so long for sonic to actually start to run. Also the music is forgettable except for tunes like the supersonic tune and boss battle music as they are so short and on a constant loop that the notes are carved into your very soul.
. There are so many nods to the past games that it really doesnt feel like it is even its own game, all stages are not inspired by previous games but actually feel like they have been taken from previous games and given a makeover, there really is not an original stage in the whole game (original gameplay ideas and puzzles yes but not a lot). this is the same for boss battles as well as they really are just taken from previous games and given new attacks to fight you with. Really not original in the slightest
. Final Point, This is a small nitpick of mine but i feel it is worth noting. the description claims that this game continues the story of the classic games, this really is not true. while the classics where light on story sonic 3 and sonic and knuckles has small scenes scattered throughout the game to give the player and idea of what is happening (like eggman betraying knuckles for the master emerald and knuckles then proceeding to help you) this game has none of that and as a result has no story. so how does it continue from the classic games if it gives the player no idea as to what is actually happening? like i said more of a nitpick but worth noting.
So my final thoughts are that if it is a nostalgia trip you are looking for or just a short and fun sonic game then yes pick it up. however if you are looking for "Sonic the Hedgehog 4" this is not it, it is nostalgia and no more and really fails to envoke the "style" if you will of the classic games. Sonic 4 episode 2 certainly fixes some issues of this game and i would reccomend that over this.

I bought one of these awhile back to stream my PC that was in the office to the 55" TV in the main room.  Do yourself a favor and just find a way to hard-wire an Ethernet cable to it.  WiFi is setting yourself up for disappointment, but still can work if you have a very good, strong, and clean wireless environment.  However, I use mine over a pair of PowerLine adapters and it works flawlessly.  Besides the ability to stream your desktop to a TV easily, I think a few things that are overlooked are:
- Streams your PC.  Just minimize Big Picture mode and you have access to your entire desktop, as long as the Steam app is still running on the PC.  This means you can run other applications and even use other apps / software on the remote connection like you were at your PC.  Need to check a website?  Look at a work document?  Even watch a movie in VLC or Kodi?  You can do it.
- Controller support:  This is the biggie for me.  This thing supports just about any controller that you throw at it and emulates an XBox 360 connection over Xinput.  This means that you can easily plug in controllers like an Logitech F310, or even use native DS4s via bluetooth without any special software or apps.  I've heard the DS3s work fine as well, though I have no tired them myself.  You also have the XBox 360 (with wireless adapter) that works as well.  My one minor grip with the box is that it will only support 4 controllers.  So, games that use more than 4 players (IE:  Screen Cheat, Gang Beats, Knight Squad, etc.) can't be done exclusively on the Link.  I've had to plug in additional controllers to the host PC to make these games work and luckily the PC was close enough that the controllers worked, but just a heads up there for any 4+ player games you plan to play.
- Streaming just WORKS:  Being a Nvidia Shield TV owner, I had my first stab at streaming through Nvidia's GameStream offering and found out that the stream aspect was kind of cool.  However, it was a constant gamble for each game:  Some games didn't support the Shield controller, others wouldn't work properly, often at times I had to try to use Moonlight instead, would lose connectivity during games, latency issues were present, etc.  I've never had any issues with the Link.  Games that didn't work on GameStream worked fine with the Shield and I've never had any controller problems at all and latency has been smooth as silk.  I never went back to streaming my games on the Shield.
- No Nvidia requirements:  I've used this thing with Intel video chipsets (though, not perfect, it does still work) and you're not locked in to having to use a higher-end Nvidia GTX video card to stream.   Love Nvidia (maybe even fan boy level...?) but the ability to stream without having to be locked into Nvidia's cards is nice for those that do not have them. Intel and AMD uses can feel the love here.
Over time, I ended up moving my desktop PC into the main living room, but my Link quickly found another home on the office PC and works extremely well when my son wants to play on the PC and I'm using the main TV for something else.
I was quite impressed with this box (and said it was the best $50 I had spent for a tech device at the time I got it) and even plunked down another $15 for the recent $5.00 sale to pick up 3 more.  At that price, they are almost giving them away!  If I ever add anymore TVs to the house, then I'll be ready to add more Links for more streaming destinations in the house.
Hats off to the team that brought us the Steam Link.  It's a great device that works VERY well for me.

Sonic the Hedgehog is such a simple concept, yet it's amazing that there are so many games starring the speedy rodent, that completely miss the mark. By now we're all familiar with legendary mis-steps like Sonic 2k6, Sonic Boom, and Shadow the Hedgehog: The Game. Then there are other games like Sonic Unleashed, Sonic & The Black Knight, Sonic Heroes, and so on and so forth. It's like Sega isn't interested in having Sonic games be about..well..just running fast and jumping on stuff. There needs to be a hundred dozen gimmicks, special abilities, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ friends(tm), and dramatic game-design changes.
I don't know what's best for Sonic, I just know what I like. My favorite games are the 16-bit titles, Sonic Generations, and bits & pieces of the other 3D games (haven't played enough of Colors to form an opinion on that). You're probably thinking: "He likes the earlier games, it must be nostalgia." Maybe it is. So what's a better way to play on my nostalgia than by making a Sonic 4? For starters, they should've just done nothing at all.
Episode 1 is comprised of 4 zones with three acts a-piece, 7 special stages, and five boss battles. It's a tad on the lean side I guess, but it overstays it's welcome very early on. The first thing that sticks out to me is the poor level-design. Splash Hill Zone is very messy, with a lot of walls, springs, and corridors. It feels awfully claustrophobic for a zone that supposedly takes place outside. Casino Street Zone is mostly just flashing lights and things to bounce off of. The second act features a ton of cards that can be flipped for bonus lives, that's all I can remember about it.
Lost Labyrinth Zone is where I was stunned to silence. Act 1 features silly boulder balancing and not much else. Act 2 has Sonic running around in near complete darkness, with only a torch to guide his way. There are also a couple cruddy mine cart sections. Why would Sonic Team create an act where players can't see much of anything? When the concept is thoroughly flawed, no implementation can save it. All I can remember of Act 3 is these weird rooms. Sonic is trapped underwater, and the room has to be tilted, but not too quickly or else he'll get impaled on spikes. This is just no good, no darn good.
Mad Gear Zone is a rip-off of Metropolis Zone. I knew I was going to be in for a good time, because Metropolis Zone is my least favorite in Sonic 2. Somehow Sonic Team managed to make it more annoying, with a bunch of mantis robots, exploding starfish, and grinding gears. By this time I just wanted it all to end.
The final zone is merely a boss-rush, followed by a climatic encounter straight out of Sonic 2. Eggman mixes it up a bit with the boss having a second form and a last ditch final attack. It's the hardest part of the game, though I probably died more times on the first act of Lost Labyrinth. Apparently you can't use the d-pad on the boulders, it's analog or fall off and die.
The special stages are supposedly based on Sonic 1, except with all of the simplistic wonderment and unique design stripped out. Ever play the arcade game Cameltry? You maneuver a ball by rotating a maze. It's a really fun game. Sonic 4's bonus stages are the same way, except with all the fun stripped out. Worst of all, there's this horrible lullaby that sounds like it came from an infant's toy. Sonic 4 suffers from uncharacteristically awful music, and the special stage tune is the cherry on top.
The most damning thing I can say about Sonic 4, is that all it does is poorly rip off its superior prequels. If you're familiar with those games you'll recognize everything that happens here. You're seeing all of the same stuff, except it's poorly arranged, with terrible physics, sloppy controls, while looking and sounding positively ghastly. This is a title specifically made to cash in on gamers like me, who are nostalgic for the early games, before ridiculous anime plots and half-baked concepts became the norm. Sega loves to sell their entire Sonic Steam library for a pittance, so you probably already own this game.
It's evil, don't touch it!

I was primarily excited about this game for the art style, which is definitely really nice.
I didn't realize however, that this game is primarily a shoot 'em up.  Based on the trailer, it kind of seems like it's equally divided between platformer and shmup gameplay, but it's not.  Since I'm not really a big shmup fan, this was a bit of a letdown.
Additionally, the platformer sections are really weakly executed.  The controls are clunky, and it's kind of a confusing, aimless experience.  You're thrown into it without any sense of direction or purpose. I liked the concept of switching between gameplay styles, but exploring felt like a chore (and I have a strong preference for platformer-style play).
In the shoot 'em up sections, I felt like the melee weapons were absurdly stronger than the shooting weapons... and working up to getting upgrades felt repetitive and not very rewarding.  Admittedly though, I didn't play very long, so I didn't explore many of the customization options, which seem to be one of the strengths of the game.
tl;dr- The art is as nice as advertised, but the gameplay felt too clunky and drawn out (haha) to be enjoyable for me.  If you like shmups, you'll probably still enjoy this game despite its flaws.

Ballpoint Universe is quirky at its finest. From the odd mix of 80% shootemup and 20% adventure platforming, the awkward controls that you need to get used to and the odd but cutely presented story and characters that come with it. My wife really liked the main character, but was questioning her nose. At the start it all is a bit confusing cause it’s not often you start a game like that, to be honest I think that was the 1st game of this kind I ever played to begin with and I really enjoyed the game as a whole. It's not too hard or easy, the weapon and ship upgrades are numerous and feel pretty unique (by design anyway). It's fun to see the uses for each item “even the crappy ones” and just start collecting everything while finishing the rather short storyline. Plenty of replay ability if you want to get each and every achievement, as long as you don't mind some repetitiveness. I think the story mode could have done with one or two more worlds though, but it's enough for its price (and budget, I presume). Just the pleasure of looking at all worlds which created the artist (developer) is worth it all.

I played the game for 31 hours, patched in full to 1.6, and played with/without DarthMod. Sorry to say: it is a buggy mess. I played all previous games except the first Shogun (played Shogun 2), all are stable after patches. The killer for Empire is the dreaded 'Ottoman bug' which ruins an otherwise fun and entertaining game (look up the bug yourself). I loved the action, the graphics, the encyclopedia of historical events, basically everything about the game - except the longgggg turn times. Some claim mods fixed the bug but I couldn't get it to work with mods and I've got technical knowledge and c++ background (tried vanilla and with DarthMod 8, 8.1). Turn times start out taking a few seconds, and within 30-40 turns it devolved into literally 8-10 minutes staring at the screen. I spend time between every turn playing guitar and staring at the screen...waiting. The bug is due to the Ottomans spamming multiple single unit armies near a certain land bridge, clogging up the AI because, for some reason, CA decided that even when AI units are not visible (and I check the box that said do not show AI movement) the AI still moves EVERY one of them, in a queue of first-in, first-out order. The bug exists in vanilla and patched. There are ways of changing the unit costs so that the Ottomans disband the units when they run out of cash, but as an adult my limited free time is to be spent actually playing games, not modding them to work as advertised. After 31 hours of play - the majority of it staring, waiting, and my frustration turned to irritation - I sadly have to call it quits. I recommend any previous CA title but this. (running on Win 7 64-bit w/GTH 970)

DDO is a great game filled with meticulous character planning, questing, leveling and even more character planning. Despite how it sounds, it's actually very pleasing. Overall gameplay experiences are positive and it's not bad on the eye either. DDO brings outstanding events (mabar, crystal cove, etc.), and I found these to be extremely rewarding.
However, I'm kind of sad to see DDO becoming less and less D&D in an attempt to please a more mainstream crowd. I greatly enjoyed playing it over the past years, but I find myself playing less for exactly that reason. Every update comes with it's own set of new bugs and support is sloppy. Every update seems to make the game more profit oriented, the gaming experience coming in second place. And I'll admit, I have spent my fair share of money, with no regrets.
PROs:
- Hours of fun. Find yourself a capable, well balanced party and you'll be having a good time.
- A variety of different locations, each with their own inhabitants, all equally eager to knock you down a peg.
- A very supportive community
CONs
- After hours of gameplay, going from TR to TR becomes quite a grind.
- "Incompetent" (By lack of a better word) parties will prolong a quest greatly. This is not always a problem, but can be quite aggrevating when it takes 3 hours to complete a seemingly simple raid.
- Bugs and poor fixes.
- Quest mechanics have been changed, making it next to impossible to do a quest solo.
TL;DR
DDO is still good, it just used to be better.

Bottom line (at the top): It's ok, I'd recommend it because I enjoy it, but you need to be able to see through the WoW-ification of a decent D&D game.
I've got mixed feelings about this game, perhaps that's why I keep coming back to it. Essentially what happens is every 2 or 3 months Turbine releases an update that either completely alters the gameplay experience or breaks 3 or 4 old quests (or both), and they slowly hotfix about 50-75% of it (I've seen a Level 2 quest that's been around since before I started playing being unavailable for an ENTIRE update period!), and then they release a new update. As for gameplay, it's ok as far as D&D-based TPHSMMORPGS's go.
Lack of proper support and lousy management decisions aside, the community is good, the fanbase is awesome and there's something to do for every non-epic level (1-20) without having to pay for anything.
If you like D&D-based games that have gone off-track a little (think in the direction of WoW), this may be the time sink you need. Otherwise, there's tons of other (more populated) MMO's that might suit your fancy.

Games Workshop's IP has been dragged through the gutter for years with very few highlights (Dawn of War being the only reasonable exception) and this is just another game in a long line of products with so much potential that is ultimately a let down. The art style in this game is quite an achievement of ugly looking people in proper dirty clothing and real life looking weapons for the most part,  contrary to the horrible color palette abuse and toyish designs most developers seem to follow (cartoon style, how I hate it). While the graphics themselves are not that great, the game itself looks good.
If you are buying this its not going to be for the graphics, but the gameplay.
The game has its fair share of flaws like I mentioned at the start, some of them being:
Rather poor animations that could use a lot of more work.
Limited variety of maps (4 maps if i recall correctly, and despite that every time you play the maps have different starting locations and random features such as blocked paths, holes in the walls and different routes, so all in all is not that bad).
On that regard some more map(s) could improve this lack of variety. Sewers and catacombs and underground tunnels connecting buildings would make such a great addition... even if it is in the already known maps.
Certain mission goals are a bit anal, such as the already discussed "steal the idol from the enemy cart, then place it in your own cart". Should not be enough to just steal it?.
On a personal level I would love to see some kind of weekly or even daily randomly generated special missions featuring some narrative and rpg elements allowing you to play with the dramatis personae of your warband (the dramatis personae is the npc which acts as your "boss" and gives you the campaign missions). Maybe even reusing some of the campaign maps (which btw are different from the usual maps you get when you play normal missions).
All in all, my best purchase from the previous year along with Space Hulk Ascension. Kinda funny that these small developer teams are making better turn based strategy games (and understand the concept) when compared to the big budget productions with lots of marketing and shiny graphics.
However if you have mental issues with losing, and expect a game to be fair towards the player, or this is just a casual interest because it belongs to the GW franchise or whatever, then save your money.
As a diamond in the rough it wont please everyone.

Simply one of the best fast-paced shooters I have ever played. Miscellaneous points:
* The physics are simply sublime. Moving through the game once you have gotten down some of the fundamental mechanics is like gliding through melted butter. I've never played any other game with such smooth movement. The air control leads to dynamic levels of control as you maneuver your way toward, around, and away from enemies as you engage them.
* The fast pace of the game lends itself to incredibly intense matches in organized play, and very fun, rapid matches during pub play. Rarely a dull moment.
* Strongly emphasizes teamwork in organized play (and in some cases, pub play).
* Massive selection of maps (well over 100, 200?). On top of that, many of these maps are skill-based maps that utilize the game's concussion grenades and rocket jump physics (think Quake 3 Defrag for all you Quake players out there).
* The game is 100% FREE for Christ's sake.
If you're yearning for a game reminiscent of TFC, or are looking for a great fast-paced team-based multiplayer FPS, I see no reason why you shouldn't give this game a go. It has sucked up many hundreds of hours of my time, and I'm sure it will suck up many hundreds more. The skill ceiling is infinite, the physics are the best I've ever encountered, the fast pace makes each competitive match intense, and the game lends itself well to teamwork in organized play.

I was disappointed in this purchase.     When compared to Transport Tycoon and Railroad Tycoon type of games it just doesn't compare very well.

Great at first! Gets VERY boring after a while.

I'm now on the last scenario of the first campaign - tens of hours in the game (offline).
The game is fun enough to keep you playing, although it could be so much better.
The scenarios are really boring with bad missions (e.g. long bus or tram routes that'll just ruin your reputation if you don't close them immediately after completing). The way you are forced to play the same cities over and over in campaign isn't very fun. You don't get to keep your stuff between scenarios. And the scenarios all end too soon. There's no way to lose - there's no due date on missions, and banks are willing to lend you money endlessly. You can even complete 'get X money' missions by borrowing from the bank!
While you get different ways of moving peeps around, there's no balance. Underground, while expensive, makes you a lot of money. Buses and trams cause traffic jams everywhere they go (btw, trams have as much capacity as buses for some weird reason). Helicopters don't have enough capacity to service a popular route and are too expensive for unpopular one, and boats… there aren't many good spots for boats.
Building interface isn't great either. With trams its just annoying. With metro it penalizes trying to optimize. Since every part of an underground line is so expensive, you can't really experiment with placements (for example you might think that building a short part of your line on the ground/elevated might be cheaper, but it requires so much trial and error to make it all fit, that it'll probably end up being more expensive).
Managing prices is really boring and needs to be done pretty often. Every now and then you have to adjust ~10 values to make them green/white/bright red and that's it.
Despite all this the game is playable and pretty fun. If you are done with Roller Coaster Tycoons, openttd and sim cities than sure, get this.

Absolver does a lot of things that so many other games wanted to do. For me, this game has everything I could want in a fighting game, and more. (BTW, the server's are fixed.)
-Gameplay-
Pros: The gameplay is what keeps me playing this game. The simple combo and deck building system is user friendly
and makes me think that Absolver did something that other games have failed to do. They give the player the freedom to create their own styles. It doesn't matter how you build your deck, it'll flow. The singleplayer was fun for me since I had never played a fighting game that had elements from MMO's and Dark Souls. The game drops you in leaving you with a sense of a wonder, and over time it becomes familiar. As you travel the map you can fight and learn the moves of the mobs spread across. Over time you'll get used to some of the bots and will probably spam most of them to death, but that's okay, because the real fun is in the boss fights. You beat them but it doesn't end there. Leveling up in multiplayer lets you come back to those boss fights to discover more of the myster in the world.
Cons: Some bots are pathetic and easy to learn quickly. The way the NPC works and responds was easy to figure out as well. You will encounter plenty of people who are cheesy as hell in multiplayer. I don't want to say there is a meta so much as types of fighting styles that are way lower risk higher reward when compared to other ones. The flip side to this is that if you're good enough you'll eventually crush people that spam and that is very satisfying. To learn more moves requires you to either grind against bots or go into multiplayer, and either way you're grinding. You can expodite this process by taking up a School at a certain level, if that's your cup of tea.
Story:
Pros: For me I love it when I'm left to wonder and fill in the blanks of a world. A movie that did this recently was John Wick 2 which only shows you what other people show they know in the world. There is no unneccesarry exposition that feels unnatural. The dialogue from the boss fights to your character both give you answers while leaving you with more questions, giving you more of a reason to level up and train besides cosmetic wear and max rank decks. It adds another level of depth for those enjoy this sort of subte story telling.
Cons: You have to spend some time running from one boss to another as well as gridning through multiplayer to get more of the story. You can always watch it online but if your old school with that sort of thing this gets frustrating.
Art: The art is such a pleasure for the eye. The animations are fluid and satisfying while the very design of the world is charming in its origniality. Absolver took the feel you get from the Mystical Swords Man from Kungfu Movie's and turns that into an art design for the game.
Overall: I find myself getting frustrated the most with how the camera can ♥♥♥♥ around with you when against walls, when bots run train on you, and when people cheese. But these are all things that are normal in games. I think people are giving this game too much of a hard time. There's a lot to enjoy here and almost always something for you to do. Want a new experience? Turn the games music off, play your own. Train against mobs or players online. Tag up with people in coop to fight boss's. Join schools and just keep getting better.
If you like fighting games you'll probably likes this game too. Personally, I love it.
Absolver is a great game. You can team with a friend, or just solo. The players are usually friendly, either that or they're scared of me. >:D I joke, anyway. I highly recommend this game.

I'll start by saying that I love this game, I've played it for almost 120 hours as of 10/12/2017 (The time of this review.) I have every achievement, including every move, and almost all the gear obtainable through PvE, I'm rank 160 Combat Trials, and I've provided more information on how to get items to the wiki than probably anyone. My point is I know this game, and I know it better than most people, even though I love the game I know its flaws and strengths in and out. Also play the game with a controller, I don't play it with a keyboard, I haven't tried, so I don't know the issues with that but I hear it's... to say the least not good.
Combat 8/10: The combat construction is unique, satisfying, and diverse. It's by far the most in-depth fighting game in that aspect that I've ever played. Getting good at it takes some work though, In addition to creating your own deck of moves, which there are MANY to choose from, you have to pay close attention to the moves, and attack chains of enemies and other players so you can counter them. You can't just jump in and be a "God."
Now you may be wondering why not give the combat a straight 10/10? And l'd really love to but the problem is while individually (1v1) the combat is amazing... you're often pinned against groups of enemies and the mechanics for that aren't exactly stellar. There are a few reasons for this but the main reason I'd say is the targetting system, you'll constently find yourself not targetting the right person and the fact that the camera doesn't automatically target the enemy you're attacking will anger and frusturate a lot of players, including myself. Hopefully the devs rework the system, but as of now fighting groups can be a real pain even for the best of players.
Enemies 6/10: The enemy NPCs in the game can all have as extensive move sets as you, making them often very difficult to fight and counter. Though I wouldn't consider that a problem since you learn moves by blocking and parrying IAbsorbing/Dodging/etc. the different styles) them. The problem lies with what they're doing when they're not fighting you and their placement within the world. They don't spawn consistently. The amounts of enemies in an area, especially a small one, can greatly vary everytime you die or re-enter that area. When you're not engaging them in combat they'll just be standing around doing absolutely nothing or running in clumps/into walls. Basically what l'm saying is they're boring and stupid when you're not fighting them. Luckily you're mostly fighting them.
World 7.5/10: The artstyle in Absolver is amazing, and the enviroments are beautiful. It's all nice to look at and mostly non-linear but even so the enviroments have their problems as well. For example you'll often find yourself falling to your death because of a swarm of enemies in an area of the map where there's not sufficient room to fight them.
The world's navigation is almost non-existence besides a crude map with no sense of direction in certain 'checkpoint' areas or shrines, while some players might find this annoying, in my opinion it serves to give the game a feeling of mystery and loneliness. I think the developers did a great job of that. The designs of NPCs are unique looking and colorful as well, nothing is an eye-sore.
Story N/A: I can't exactly rate the 'story' in a one out of ten sense because it doesn't really have one but it also isn't really trying to have a traditional story. Your character is a 'prospect,' who's goal is to become an Absolver. You do that by beating mini bosses and three major bosses that include cutscenes, and that's pretty much it. You're not supposed to be a "character," you never see your 'character's' face or hear them speak but the game is supposed to feel lonely and cryptic, it's more about the world, the enviroments, and the uncertainty of why or if there's even a point to what you're doing and it really does a good job making you feel that way. You really feel isolated and I understand why a lot of people may not like that but I mean that in the best possible way.
Online Connection 4/10: The connection is HORRIBLE, not Dead by Daylight initial release horrible but bad. When playing online (The same as single-player, except other players will show up and fight you or progress in their 'story.' along side you) you'll constently find yourself teleporting all over the place, occassionally getting into infinite loading screens, and not having enemies in world areas spawning at all. This is easily the biggest problem with the game in my opinion. Luckily the developers are working hard to make it better and it has improved a reasonable amount since release.
Gear/Drops/DLC 5/10: As of now there's no DLC or in-game purchases. The game is in NO WAY pay-to-win which anyone who has any patience will love and the developers intend to keep it that way. Gear isn't purely cosmetic but none of it is inherently way better, so if you want to look a certain way it won't punish you for it. Currently there are generally two ways of acquiring items; RNG based rewards from Combat Trials (PvP) and drops from enemy NPS. The reward system for combat trials is god awful. There is no way to guarentee you'll get anything you want, especially masks, you'll generally find yourself getting twenty of the same belt and maybe one or two good pieces of gear. I've known people who've grinded PvP for over 200 ranks and still haven't gotten a single mask, meanwhile some newbie gets the mask they want at Combat Trials rank 4. As for the drops from the enemy NPCS, what you get is RNG based, and you can get more than one of the same item, although most enemy NPCs can drop everything they're wearing, including the color variation of that particular gear, don't get me wrong... it can be frusturating although it's nice to have enemies actually drop the gear you see them wearing.
In conclusion, if you're a fan of the art style and you want a fighting game where you can make your own move sets and have them flow well then this is your game, the game's combat makes you feel in control, you get to decide what you want to do, and you don't have to worry about messing up some combo because of your timing with the joysticks, the move strings are easily executed. The devs are extremely dedicated and are constently working to improve the game. Though if you're too worried about the connection issues you can always wait to buy it when the connection is sorted out.

This is a beautiful and unique horizontal shooter/platformer. All the art looks like it was drawn by hand, doodles brought to life. The style is beautiful, and the story is silly and convoluted.  The Horizontal Shooter portions are great fun, and fairly easy (I was able to earn gold on all of them).  The platforming sections are 2D with depth switches, and are interesting but not particularly a focus of the game.
There are two issues I had:
1) Controls are either Keyboard or Mouse or Gamepad - you can't use both at once.  Mouse works great for the shooter sections, but is not good for the platforming. Keyboard is the opposite. I found myself having to switch back and forth between controls depending on what portion of the game I'm playing.
2) The cost for new weapons and shields on your ship seem really high - even after finishing the game, I've only been able to afford maybe a quarter of the options.
The ability to upgrade the ship allows for lots of replayability, and the beautiful environment and skewed story all combine to make for a very enjoyable experience.

The world the game created was well worth the purchase though.

is my favorite shmup to date.  I normally hate shmups.  Make of that what you will.
It can set a bad first impression, though, since it also has platforming sections with wonky physics.  Fortunately, you can change your control method in the pause menu, so you don't have to move with the mouse during these parts.
Platforming is certainly the weakest point, but thankfully not the main one.  The shooter levels are much better.  There is mouse control, which is basically vital to this genre IMO, and it follows the bullet hell formula, so there's plenty of precise dodging.  Most bosses are comprised of several parts, and it's satisfying to break them down piece by piece.  You get five lives per stage with extra rewards for finishing with more remaining, so it's not super punishing but still rewards you for doing well.
There's a good selection of weapons, including strong melee weapons to reward high risk strategies and shields to absorb and reflect oncoming bullets.  You buy and upgrade items with ink from defeated enemies.  Each purchase contributes toward unlocking satellite allies, so upgrades to weaker items are not wasted.
The ballpoint pen artstyle is nice to look at without being too busy.  I felt like I had a clear view of what to avoid.  The music is also pleasant and the sound effects offer a decent sense of feedback.
I'd say this game is worth a try.  Just don't let the platforming segments put you off and it should prove to be enjoyable overall.

At first, I thought that this game was also programmed with a ballpoint. It's very awkward to control, there's too much acceleration going on everywhere, you have to change control modes constantly and the physics feel that everything is about to collapse at any second.
But I persevered, and after getting used to it's controls, I found myself liking it a lot. I love arcade shmups, and after figuring out how to buy weapons and equiping them, shooting sections very fun, although I found them too easy at first, I was having a blast in the later sections. There's no way you'll have enough ink to buy all weapons and try them without grinding, so I stuck to the ones I know I would liked and upgraded them to the max. Also, ♥♥♥♥ kamikazes, one touch and you lose a life, no matter how much you have.
Personally, I would've liked a score system, which also could have alleviated the frustration of losing a life trying to get a gold by gaining one after hitting certain number. It would be a nicer bonus for your skill than having a star that makes a short blast of bullets.
Also, the graphics are very unique and cool, but sometimes I feel this game is kind of egotistical, shoving them in your face. This is really a problem with a boss that shows up in front of the camera and blocks your view of the enemies, I dont mind it too much in the overworld, but it can be annoying. The opnly other graphical problem is in the last level, when all the objects being white becomes a problem, there were times that I didnt know where I was, what was attacking me and where it came from.
And lastly, I think that the game would be better if it had less focus on the overworld, specially platforming in there, and different music. My god, I had the game on mute 80% of the time, I was so sick of hearing the same thing over and over.
TL;DR: Like Skyrim on paper 420/666

Let me start by saying I played no vanilla whatsoever, I launched the game once and then immediately set up Darthmod, and yet the features I found most astonishing and pleasant compared to other Total War instalments are unrelated to the improvements Darthmod applied. However, if what I found to be positive in the game pertains to the vanilla, so do many of the negative points I could of come across in a vanilla game, which were addressed in Darthmod. So, ultimately, indeed my review is not based on the overall quality of the product as downloaded from Steam.
Like mentioned above, I consider Empire to be superior to games such as Attila or Rome II, both of which were my very first Total War games (sadly, I didn’t start with the good ol’ ones). Compared to the latter, it seems to have more interesting technologies, meaningful historical events and campaign objectives, as well as an intriguing unit variety. These superior features, so far allowed me to fully enjoy a 50 hours long campaign run, and I’m only at the 45% of it, still fighting and struggling and most importantly enjoying the game. Unlike some most recent TW’s I feel Empire is really
.
Before we delve into this, let me assure you I am not discrediting Attila and Rome II because of their theme and period. I am not just a gamer but first and foremost a scholar of the whole medieval period, from 400 to 1450 AD
. What I love of Attila is in fact the time period, as I know many of the tribes and civilisations included in the game, and I have studied their migrations and customs during the Völkerwanderung. Back to the subject, compared to the stuff we have here, I find Attila’s Tech tree really uninteresting, bland, shallow. I don’t remember a single remarkable upgrade that was stuck in my head as something amazing I couldn’t wait getting my hands on. The opposite feelings I have for Empire’s tree: multiple improvements on bayonet types, on formations, or even new infantry technology (rifles in the mid-late game); then we see through the campaign an exciting development of our and other nations’ artillery, both in the engines themselves and the ammo types too. And that is just the military tree… Which on Attila I find is the most delusional one. The changes and improvements applied by the other two trees are very appealing.
Short point really. What keeps me going and going on conquering without losing interest for my campaigns is that they match with historical events and conflicts that actually occurred and had an impact on how the world looks now. It’s not just random wandering and slaughtering, which some may like, and I do too, but which gets a tad boring after you run out of fantasy. ETW gives you several possible campaign ‘missions’ as you walk your path to reconstruct a historical empire or something even greater – changing the curse of history. (e.g. Austria winning the 7 years’ war, the British maintaining control over the colonies, etc). I think in this case the fault is not the most recent titles of the Total War franchise are shallow, but that the periods treated in the games are missing some relevant background for several of the factions. Maybe it’s just me, but even sailing to Britannia and making it Englaland with my Saxon spears didn’t feel to rewarding – not as much as defeating the Ottomans with Austria (see the Austro-ottoman wars for further reference). Again, it’s just my feelings and my opinion as for this point, and I can’t blame anyone or anything.
I have always been concerned by the extent of unit variety in strategy games, and I must say seldom have I been fully satisfied. Empire Total War is one of these very few cases. Playing as Austria, I haven’t a handful of basic units which then upgrade from “generic♥♥♥♥♥♥tier warband” to “mid tier warband” and then further on. I have detailed regiments, which vary depending on the region. I can muster basic line infantry, grenadiers both basic and Hungarian, and the list goes on with line infantry units, first pandurs then grenzers and further on jaegers. (Darthmod mainly adds regional versions of these units, giving some more variety). Of artillery and cavalry units there are many and all work in a different way, although cavalry diversity in Attila was proper enough and siege does not much fit the setting. However as for ETW, I am amazed at the beauty of my army composition, whereas Attila has very bland unit trees for the “barbarian” factions. If I can tell I have been impressed of some units in that game it’s the Lombards’, and unsurprisingly that faction is in a paid DLC. ;)
All in all, this is just how I feel about it, and I have no wish to bother putting down numbers and making comparisons as in who has the most units and whose variety and uniqueness is superior between the two games.
What I can add is that I’ve seen literally dozens of modders doing the developers’ work on the units Attila, Rome 2 and TW Warhammer contain, whereas even the biggest mods I have come across for Empire added but a handful of units.
That’s really all I had to say, hope my review proves useful to someone.
Thanks for reading.

I went into Sonic 4 episode 1 expecting to hate it. At first I did. I saw all the nostalgia they're trying to recreate the feeling old Sonic levels with new technology and graphics. It felt like there was nothing new. The more I played, the more it felt like there was a freshness to the old 2D platforming of Sonic. For those who have never played the old Sonic games, they are labyrinth levels that you need to make it to the end. Along the way you collect rings. These rings let you take damage without dying. The rings go spraying everywhere when you get hit. If you have no rings, you will die when you get hit. The game is single player only and offers controller or keyboard support that you setup out of game.
It feels the same as the original games and not much has changed control wise. There is still one button controls. The one button will make you jump while you're standing or running. If you hold down and push the jump button you will perform a spin dash when you let go of the down. When you are running, you can press down to roll into a ball to kill enemies. New to the series is what I feel is a game changer. A mid air lock on dash. Just hit the jump button in mid air and Sonic will immediately dart to whatever he has targeted. Usually the closest enemy, spring board or item box. This is a game changer because it adds constant momentum that is easy and more efficient than a spin dash that takes a second or so. Just jump and dart in mid air. Its easy and efficient. Not just that, but attacking enemies in the air turns into platforming. It feels like a lot less time wasted gaining momentum. With this new mechanic, I can see why Tails wasn't included in this first episode.
The game looks great. It has detailed backgrounds and bright vibrant colors. There are four main areas, each with three levels and a boss fight. Each area has a theme from a previous Sonic game. There is no new territory. Consider it a best of rather than a new album. With that said, Sonic 4 takes them in interesting new directions every so often unique to Sonic 4. One level features a lot of cannons that Sonic can hop in and control where he shoots out. Another level has Sonic in a mine cart and keeping his balance on rolling boulders. You'll see Sonic in the dark carrying a torch, lighting things on the wall to open doors and activate platforms. It all feels fresh, even if it steps away from the Genesis. There are still classic Sonic tropes like using pinball flippers, bouncing off bumpers, going through loops, swinging from vines, using zip lines (Sonic Advance) and so on.  There are a few moments of going underwater. While underwater, Sonic just moves slower. He can't actually swim.
The items feel limited to the ones found in Sonic 1 and 2. You can get temporary invincibility, ten rings, an extra life, super speed shoes and a bubble shield that lets Sonic take an extra hit.
Even with only 4 areas to visit, there are still 13 levels (not including boss fights). Each level is around five minutes to complete. I hate to say it, but it feels like a full length Sonic game, even if this is only episode 1. It runs around the three hour mark. The boss fights evoke nostalgia. Their patterns are like the original games, but they add new twists.
Sonic 4 does a good job of utilizing Sonic's speed. A lot of the previous 2D games had you go at your own pace, but Sonic 4 has you chased by boulders, crushing walls, running after Dr. Robotnik in boss fights. These reasons for Sonic to run feel engaging more than typical exploring the levels. It offers a variety.
Since you are collecting rings, if you complete the level and have more than 50 rings, you'll see a giant ring to jump into that sends you to the bonus stage. Even the bonus stage feels good. Its a take off of the original Sonic 1 bonus stage, but this time you get to control the rotation of the level while Sonic is just stuck in a ball. There are barriers that need coins to pass through. At the end of each bonus stage is a chaos emerald.
As you progress, you will unlock levels and areas as you progress. So if you get stuck on a level, you can skip it. After each level it gives you a choice to jump to the next unfinished level. That just feels odd. While its helpful to have level selection, I'd much rather progress to the next level instead of getting asked.
While this might be a departure from the old Sonic games, it adds new life to what was a stale franchise if you include the Genesis and Gameboy Advance platformers. The challenge feels good, its more difficult than the other old school games.

I don't understand how (since the unfortunate and untimely demise of SWG), anyone can play any other MMORPG.  I mean, in all fairness, other titles might have the advantage of being a venerable title (WOW), or have a massive fan following (either FF XI/XIV), but when it all comes down to style, playability, and taking full advantage of the MMO perks, by incorporating them into the games construction, DDO, has done exactly what it set out to do...Emulate the adventures of the pen & paper game that has reached critical acclaim from loyal fans the world over.
All the versatility of the tabletop format is right here at your fingertips.  You want to customize your stats and feats to build the most critical to form shield & sword knight, emphasizing value of honor and virtue, or become a shadow walker with deft fingers and mythic ability?  You can.  In fact, you can be both at the same time!
Multiclass?  Yes, please!  I found myself easily bored by other MMO's and their linearal ability trees; maxing out my characters to get a taste of their potential, only to wish that there was more I was capable of doing.
WOW?  Pffft... not if the game paid me!  DDO is the closest experience to the tabletop format as you can possibly get, without actually drawing up a world yourself.
And trust me, if you enjoy this game for even a minute, do yourself a favour, go pick up some dice.  When you experience all that D&D can be, you'll never turn your back.  It's the ultimate high.

Third mission - A Rat Ogre tears off my best archers right arm.  Not willing to pay for his recovery, the man suffers for a few days and dies alone in the ruins of Mordheim.
The city is both capricious and cruel. Not only does it make you fear the consequences of every misstep, it gleefully punishes you for each one.  There is no "save-and-quit, try again".  There is no mercy in Mordheim; expect none and give none.  The true god of the setting, the RNG (or Tzeentch for the knowledgeable), is fickle and treacherous.  Trust not in the 95% chance hit, for it is a lie.  All is a lie - there is only Warpstone, and gold.  Glory, truth, honor, chivalry - leave these at home, for the city will drink your tears if strive for them.  There is only survival.
This game is really fun.  I've never quite played a game with this degree of difficulty.  It's the Dark Souls of tactical RPGs, but at least Dark Souls has save points,  This might sound like its not for you, but trust me.  Every victory is all the sweeter when it came at the cost of one of your henchmen's eyes and a harrowing, intense battle amidst the insanity of Mordheim.

One the best games out there if you are into turn based games and or Warhammer fantasy world setting.
The average person will get about 200 hours out of this game along with the DLC already available. And you will want the DLC. With witchunters, the smuggler, and the poison globe skaven being my favorites. Even if you dont buy the DLC's they will still show up in your game as enemies. So really its all free unless you want to play them yourself.
This game is unforgiving and brutal. The learning curve will have you swearing and pulling out your hair. You can not manually save and if you screw up, your warband will pay for it in crippled or dead troops. You can manually cheat and save your games, but id suggest not as you risk corrupting the save file and losing it all. If you are used to save scumming and just taking back all your mistakes, then you will be rather annoyed with this game. AT least until you learn its generally ok to take a beating and unless you totally bite it three times in a row, then you can recover from a bad round or two.
Some quick hints for new players:
Keep your band together, dont try to one on one fight the enemies. Choose missions where your warband all starts around your wagon.
Choose early on to what defense type you will use, being either dodge or parry type and seek out skills you can learn later on that allow you to use these defenses twice in a turn.
Its ok to skip a day to let your team heal from injuries or train skills. Its not the end of the world to skip a day.
Story missions are impossibly hard, well so it may seem. Make sure you are ready before diving in.
This game has a good selection of warbands right now, but it really could use more. And hopefully there will be more ASAP. The table top version has so many options and in comparison the PC version feels a bit lacking. But 7 like the game has now is a decent enough selection of warbands. And they all have different play styles which makes it even better. But personally i wouldn't mind 14 of them, with each main warband re-skinned in a slightly different variant.
The leveling system is addicting. The loot is just varied enough to be addicting, though i wish there were more to choose from on some warbands. Some warbands use rather specialized gear and it can be hard sometimes to find upgraded versions of it from all the random drops. The wolf priest being the prime example, i have never once found an upgraded version of his enhanced weapon of ulric.
All in all this game will give you your monies worth. And hopefully in the future DLCs will up the ante even more. Its a total buy and if you find this game on sale and dont buy it, THEN SLAP YOURSELF! cause youre making a huge mistake not getting it.

So this is the finished state, the Devs have moved on to the next project presumably taking the good bits from this into their design and hopefully reworking the bits that didn't really work. As a day 1 of early access purchaser, the final game is quite a bit different to how I would have originally expected, in the following ways:
- Fewer warbands than expected for a now finished game, expected the variation to be at the core of the gameplay
- Hero DLC characters for hire disproportionately powerful
- Metagame quite good, although many many of the skills are completely useless and I expected they would at some point be rebalanced to get to the stage where the choices were between genuinely comparable skills, instead it is a few good ones and lots of complete rubbish
- Ultimately because of high hit point pools requiring multi hits to kill, the game boils down to outnumbering opponent in combats, so grouping up is much more effective, whereas in the tabletop lone gang members could pull off some very useful results with a little luck. Big hit point pools mean that the bit of luck needed for 1vs2 to win becomes a huge amount of luck
- As mentioned by others games come down to exploiting the mechanics and AI quality, rather than it playing at it feels like it should. If something looks like it should work, it usually doesn't
- Scenery looks nice, feels like it should be really important, isnt
- RNG, everyone talks about it, one day you are going along fine, the next day 2 heros can be killed from injuries in a battle that looked like all the others and you were well on top of
- Cash flow comes and goes, not well balanced, skills for henchmen much less valuable but cost the same
So in the end I have a few hours in this and enjoy the first few hours of a warband quite well, but overall as the final product which will not be improved past this, its very neutral. Hard to strongly recommend given the state it is left in, a little unfair on the good content to downvote.

This has the potential to be something really great. I've spent nearly 90 hours playing this game. Where this games faults lie, is in the fact that there is not nearly enough content. Game mechanics work great, fighting is engaging and fun, intuitive and encourages experimentation. However, the superb combat system isn't coupled with any real reward or end game.
The developers released this game way too early, with too little content. Once you've learned all of the moves and fought in combat trials endlessly and gotten a set up with your character you like, there really doesn't seem to be any incentive to continue playing. There aren't any global rankings for fighting, there is one Combat Trial mode (1v1). The single player/co-op experience is so unbelievably bland it's almost not worth doing. The map isn't nearly large enough to hold anyone's attention past 20 hours, and there simply aren't enough different enemy types OR bosses to keep interest once you've mastered the combat system.
This game comes off more as a tech demo for a unique and very well executed fighting system than a full game. I really love the aesthetic, the sound, the style, the feel, and the movement of Absolver. It plays very well - when the p2p connections aren't absolute♥♥♥♥♥- which brings up another point. The development team for this game doesn't seem capable of ever fixing their server/connection issues. The hit registration is some of the worst I've seen in a game when it does go bad. The net code seems to need a complete overhaul and I don't think Sloclap is at all capable of delivering on this front. Absolver, while an amazingly interesting game and concept, just doesn't stand the test of time and really isn't going to provide any real long term satisfaction. Again, I really enjoy the combat system, however, it definitely left me wanting more. A LOT more.
I wouldn't recommend this game for it's current asking price because it's fairly clear this was rushed out the door as a cash grab and I'm almost certain there aren't any real intentions to add new Combat Trail modes (even though the padlocks at the top would imply there are at least 3 other modes coming).
Updates did not come quick enough and it completely and utterly destroyed this game's fanbase. Hooked an audience but the bait wasn't sufficient enough to keep us from jumping ship.

tl;dr: This is ABSOLUTELY worth two bucks.
The thing about a casual puzzle game is that the gameplay matters so much more than the production values. Hellscape Games is clearly a very small studio (I'm betting a single person created this in his spare time), and Intergalactic Bubbles's strengths dovetail perfectly with that.
The gameplay is excellent. Imagine Puzzle de Pon and a physics engine had a baby, and you've got the idea. You fire bubbles into an ever-advancing array, trying to match groups of three to remove them and clear the board. As pieces are removed, extra pieces retain their remaining connections to the main group, but can start to wiggle around quite a bit. This creates a wonderful emergent gameplay style that complements the main puzzle beautifully. It's a genuine rush to detach a group of bubbles and send them flying into a separate group, causing a chain reaction that destroys dozens of piece in one fell swoop. The tension of seeing a large group at the end of a long thin chain of pieces and desperately trying to break that section off is captivating and nail-biting.
The pacing is... less than excellent. Hellscape has confused length with depth and that puts a big damper on the festivities. It would be a lot easier to go through 250 levels of very slowly increasing complexity if those levels were more carefully designed, rather than randomly generated. If the game had half as many levels, with upgrades costing half as much, it'd feel like much less of a slog. (Even better would be a simple, more customizable settings screen instead of an awkward list of levels, but that's a much bigger change.) As it stands, this is a game I play for about an hour every six months before I get bored.
The production values aren't good. They get the job done, and do very little else. That said, this is a puzzle game; you don't come here for the graphics or the sound.
All in all, I'd call this game a great idea, but unpolished. That said, its current sale price is two bucks, and it's absolutely worth that. It's a lot of fun, just in smaller doses than the game seems to encourage. Keep it installed on your system, and play it just a little once in a while. You'll have a great time.

Cities in Motion is one of those games you just cant help but enjoy playing.  Its got a lot of positives going for it and then.... inevitability the longer you play it, the more frustation creeps in.  In the end it will wave goodbye to all that goodwill that it built up in the many hours of previous play.
The game tries to be at its core a simplified mass-transit simulator.   You take control of a company looking to build several transport routes across a number of recreated cities in the hopes of gaining enough money to expand the network and eventually complete a number of mission objectives.  All the while you have to deal with maintaining the infrastructure and vehicles, keeping your public reputation as high as possible and generating a profit to pay your workers.
There are 2 campaigns.  I only completed the first, which consisted of 12 scenarios, each of them stand-a-lone so you are not penalized when you begin the next one.  Objectives come in the form of petitions, which tend number around 12-18 per scenario.  Their content is a variation upon a theme, such as; build x number of lines, build a line from a to b, keep your vehicles maintained above y, transport z passengers, increase or decrease prices, remove n number of stops, stop a line for x weeks, etc.  For the most part these are all fairly easy to carry out and you are only restricted by money, at least at the start.
There are five types of transport lines which you can use to carry passengers around the city: bus (road), trams (lines), metro (underground), ferry (water) and heliports (air).  Each has several (around 35) vehicles in total with their own strengths and weakeness such as; carry capacity, reliability, speed, attractiveness, which provide benefits and weaknesses to your strategy.
Add to this the need to tinker with prices as an abstracted economy rises and falls, the ability to finance through bank loans your next big project and you get the picture.  Take all of these ingredients and you get what is a fun, enjoyable and not to difficult game to play.  For the most part the game works.   However... as you play more and more you get to see that the game isnt exactly well designed.  Or built.
You can essentially perform gamey actions to circumvent the restrictions that the developers have in store for you, allowing you to build up cash reserves quickly without any bad effects.  Once youve completed the first few maps there is little to tax anyone looking for something with a harder challenge.   The first campaign maps encompass four cities; Berlin, Amsterdam, Vienna & Helsinki but, once you have figured out the best strategy for each one, you can re-apply the same strategy over and over, despite the different starting circumstances.
The biggest let-down has to be the bugged campaign scenario 2 petiton that never triggers.  This means you can never complete the associated achievement, unless you find a user-made editor, that allows you to access the relevant file and edit one word in the code.  One word!!  Thats unforgiveable given that many patches were released for this game and this major fault is still not fixed!  The other major issue (if you are an achievement hunter) is that another achievement requires purchase of 34 base game vehicles.  Of which I have attempted to acquire twice.   The base game even includes more than 34 vehicles.  Unfortunately the counter stops at 15 for me.  I know others have had the same problem.
Despite having many, many dlcs, you do not need any of them to get all the achievements.  The fact that the developers (and publisher) do not force you to buy all the extra dlcs they made to get 100% achievements would have otherwise been a great plus for this game.... but alas no..... I highly suspect  that you will need to purchase at least some other dlcs (with extra vehicles in them) to get this "all vehicles" achievement.
Its really disappointing... because if not for these core issues I would say that overall Cities in Motion is an above average, if slightly lightweight mass-transit simulator.  One that I would have recommended to those of you interested in the genre or looking for something non-violent.  As it is all that good work was undone on the final straight.
* If the developers ever fix these two achievement issue I will happily change this to a YES recommendation.
** The Complete Collection achievement can be triggered by downloading a MOD (of all the vehicles reworked)  For some reason in their unpacked form they register.

Beyond: Light Advent Collector’s Edition:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
From a young age, Diana has been mesmerised every time she looks up at the stars. The bright shiny sparkles that light up this infinite canvas at night was like bliss to her eyes. During the day, she raved to her imaginary friend, Nix, about the spectacle she saw every night and vowed to become an astronomer as soon as possible. Many moons passed and Diana kept her promise and indeed became a spy of the Milky Way. One incredible night at the observatory, she and her colleague identified a meteor on a weird trajectory; it was definitely destined to crash into Earth! Could it be her breakthrough or something sinister? You are about to find out in Beyond Light Advent!
Beyond: Light Advent Collector’s Edition is a casual / adventure / hidden objects game where you play an astronomer named Diana. She will embark on a journey to save the earth against Nor, an alien World Eater.
Before you start the game you must choose between four levels of difficulty; from having access to a tutorial and hints button to help you if you have never played this type of game, to no help whatsoever for the people who know what to expect in this genre.
The story is well written and will keep you entertained all the way throughout the game, which has six chapters including a bonus. Cut-scenes are well done and fit perfectly within the story. In a nutshell, and without giving too much away, Diana will have to activate three towers to save the earth. Early on, Diana will discover an alien bracelet which she will be able to use to blink (teleport) to different locations. This artefact will give her access to memories from characters from the planet IRIDESSA which was also attacked by the World Eaters in another galaxy. However she’ll need the right crystal to do so. These sessions will give Diana a better understanding of the connection between IRIDESSA and planet earth.
Plenty of collectables to gather in this game; try to find the spaceship in each of the locations you visit. I had to take the magnifying glasses on some occasions, despite wearing my own specks! The hidden objects sequences are well done. All objects are generally well-blended within these sessions but they are relatively easy to find. In a few parts of the story, Diana will have to evade the military. Here, Diana will have three paths to choose from to in order to evade detection from the military flashlights. It’s like a mini game. In regards to the puzzles, they are quite easy, too
Graphically Beyond: Light Advent looks good and the soundtrack is fun. Pretty good voice acting all the way through. There are achievements within the game but not on Steam, and there are no trading cards to gather.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice graphics
-	Good story
-	Good cut-scenes
-	Nice voice acting
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No Steam achievements or trading cards
-	Puzzles need to be a bit harder
Beyond: Light Advent is entertaining with fun mini games, hidden objects sessions and easy puzzles.
7/10

Procedural levels and items, challenging technical platforming action RPG. Inspiration drawn from some of my favorite games; Symphony of the Night, NetHack, Spelunky, Dark Souls.
For those unfamiliar with Roguelikes, this game has that beautiful duality of being incredibly relentless and at the same time incredibly rewarding. You die, and rage at yourself for whatever mistake it was that you made, and at the same time feel "okay, well now I know never to do THAT again." You'll be violently and permanently punished for your mistakes, but you'll learn, and you'll be back with a vengeance. It will challenge your gaming abilities on every level.
On the plus, the levels can compensate you for your intelligent use of strategy as well as your twitch reflexes. There are many ways to approach the game and the classes have a lot of contrast between them. It is extremely replayable.
The game already feels rich and nearly feature-complete in its current state, so why not jump in for the reasonable price? the value is already there, and the game will only get better over time. Enjoyable both for couch co-op and solo play. I recommend a gamepad.

It's funny to think how Indie games have stolen my soul these past few years. Only L4D2 and DMC3 managed to get over the 100 hours, the first because most of my friends play it and revel in it's chaos, and the later because I'm a freaking SSS maniac obsessed with perfect ranks. Dark souls is different, it's a game for real mans, it knows it's not a casual AAA game.
But every other single big titles can consider themselves lucky to be even played through. And I mean, I try, sometimes I even hope it gets good, but it often fails to deliver. Even DmC was baaaaad, hell, EVEN XCOM: Enemy Unknown failed to get a second playthrough. And it's X-COM material.
But games like The Binding of Isaac? Xenonauts? Dungeons of Dredmor and Don't Starve? Terraria, Starbound, you name it. These games captivates me so much. Maybe it's because they don't treat me like a child or an idiot. Maybe they don't feel bad about beating me to the ground. Maybe they think I like it, want more, thirst for vengeance and have a chance to show the game who's behind the controller. Maybe their mojo captured my mind, their music trapping my brain...
Plus these games are well made. The hundreds of items in Isaac, the 70+ classes of Dredmor, the random levels, the effect of surprise always being present, everything from the colors to the little details...How could you not love this?
Well, Vagante is among these. Right in the tutorials it shows you what's up by killing you twice. There. Now you know what's gonna get you. And the first couple of runs are tough, maybe even unfair and infuriating. But then you kill your first boss. Open your first great chest. Equip that fat loot. And break your first statue.
...I shouldn't have done that, I should not have done that!
But if it was only about the rad difficulty then I'd play Real-Life: The Game. Vagante has a beautiful aesthetic to it, it has an enchanting charm when you first select your characters (via tarot cards, that's pretty neatto). From there, all you see is a gaping hole in the wall daring you to go inside. The warmth of the torches begging you to stay, the vines over the remains of decaying structures saying you shouldn't be there and that little bug just minding it's own business. The game feels alive. It is a beast baiting you with items, pieces of gold, dangers and rewards. The music and the sound effects are all suiting, the characters are easily recognizable. How could you resist? So you hop in. The gap behind you shutting down, only one way to go. You brace yourself, as the environments around you changed from last time's attempt. And you know you have high chances of kicking the bucket. Yet you go stab that slime, it deserves it. Stupid slimes.
Vagante is not a complete game, yet it already does so much. If you think you want to try it out based on that I wrote, then you should give it a proper try. I know, from the feels of it, that I will play it for hours and hours.

It's obvious that a lot of love was put in this game, and it has immense amounts of potential.
Overall, I'm very impressed, and from the amount of time I put into it and the enjoyment I got in return, I feel like it being free to play is doing the developers a disservice.
"Cinderella Phenomenon" deals with the grim subject of emotional child abuse in a surprisingly clever and sensitive way (dare I say, much better than I had expected, and much more openly than many big budget AAA games) that is so subtle, that if you were only to play one route, one could easily blink and miss it. On the surface it's rather lighthearted, reminiscent of classic, good-vs-evil stories, but it is precisely that simplicity that invites further exploration, which then unfolds a surprisingly complex and well-thought out story throughout the different routes.
Cloaking such a heavy story in something as benign as a fantasy fairytale provides a very stark, very striking contrast as well, which, while not exactly a unique idea with how many fairytale adaptations have been popping up lately, is a refreshing take on an old subject. The art is quite beautiful, the characters are mostly all very charming (you know, different strokes), and the game as a whole is very well-done.
I would also like to mention that after a while I found it a touch uncomfortable that almost all (not all, but enough for it to be noticeable) the characters of color in the end turned out to be either morally grey, or antagonists in some way, while the protagonists (or those wearing the facade of positivity) were almost all white. It's most noticeable in the discrepancy between the skintone of the protagonist and the mother (that was a bit of a "yikes" moment for me) or in the battles when multiple characters appear on screen at the same time, and while I'm almost sure it wasn't conscious, I would recommend keeping this in mind for future endeavors.
It definitely has some ways to go (maybe a skilled beta reader could have helped tie it all together a bit more tightly, remove or tweak some extra lines of dialogue that make some parts feel a bit clunky, and clean up something that is so full of ideas and obvious passion from the team), but overall, it is definitely worth your time.
