Ballpoint Universe is quirkiness at its finest. From the odd mix of 80% shootemup and 20% adventure platforming, the beermat doodles brought to live in a beermat doodle world, the awkward controls that you need to get used to and the odd but cutely presented story and characters that come with it.
I didn't like it first time around, but at a second glance I suddenly got into it and I really enjoyed the game as a whole. It's not too hard or easy, the weapon and ship upgrades are numerous and feel pretty unique (by design anyway). It's fun to see the uses for each item -even the crappy ones- and just start collecting everything while finishing the rather short storyline. Plenty of replayability if you want to get each and every achievement, as long as you don't mind some repetitiveness. I think the story mode could have done with one or two more worlds though, but it's enough for its price (and budget, I presume).
So yeah, it's worth the 4 euros that it's currently at, but you can also wait for a discount if you're in doubt. I like quirk.

Recommended, but with slight caution.
Ballpoint Universe is a side-scrolling shmup with adventure-y platforming between missions.  The art style, obviously, is the most notable and unique aspect of the game.  It's consistently good (and weird) throughout the game and, along with the music, adds a ton of atmosphere.  The "ideas vs logicians" story fits in perfectly.  There are a wide variety of upgrades to acquire for your ship, including some genuinely useful melee weapons.
Here's the biggest issue: the controls.  Do not expect precise movement like most shooters.  The platforming segments are better with the keyboard, or maybe controller, but the movement and physics feel wonky no matter what.  It's doable, but prepare for some frustration.
The flying missions should be played with the mouse.  It's highly unusual, but because the ship moves as fast as you can move the cursor, it seems as though the game was meant to be played like this.  That advantage will be required on the harder missions.
Control schemes must be switched manually by going into the menu, unless there's a shortcut I missed.
Control issues are often a death sentence for this kind of game, but once I stopped resisting the mouse, and bought some better equipment, the good started to outweigh the bad.  The developers appear to have been confident about going their own way here, and the result is a game that's fresh and worthwhile.  Some mental effort on the player's part may be required to see that, however.

I've greatly enjoyed the game, as much for the thematic elements of the warbands of undead, mutants, witch hunters (and so forth) as for the warband campaign and progression system. Fighting around mordheim, completing faction quests  and leveling up and customizing my warband is a lot of fun. I would recommend buying this game! (On sale of course...only ever buy games on sale). My only complaint is that its a little too easy. More on that below. But first, add on about 20 hours to the amount of time I've played; I spent a lot of time playing disconnected from steam, and even when I resynced the hours played didnt update. Go figure.
So I dont get people complaining about this game being too hard. Sure, my first warband got wrecked, but after that it got alot easier. Maybe its because I'm an over-cautious player (doing whatever I can to keep my precious, customized, stylized warband from dying), but with my current warbands I win about, um, 100% of the engagements (vs. AI mind you).
Yes there is a perma death/injury system, yes there are the wyrdstone deliveries, but they arent crazy difficult if you PLAN around that aspect and position/group your troops accordingly.
To those complaining about RNG; no such problem on my end. Sure there are untimely enemy crits, and terrible misses from your party, but nothing about that shouts out "broken RNG!!" to me. All to be expected.
My only complaint would be that the enemy warband setups are too predictable; in order to have an easier time balancing the strength of your warband vs. the random skirmishing AI warband the developers made it so that your oppsoing enemy will take the EXACT SAME unit slots at you.
So if you take 2 heroes, 1 impressive and 3 henchmen, guess what your enemy will bring? 2 heroes, 1 impressive and 3 henchmen. O____O
It takes ALOT of strategy out of the game. No large mobs vs small elite forces. Its always large mobs vs. large mobs, or small elite forces vs. small elite forces.
It would make my day if the developers released a patch that changed that. Right now the predictability makes the game too easy.
Also, if the developers ever put out a full set of customization options for your warband (like different heads, armor appearances, etc) I would totally get behind that!

I got this game because it seemed fun and simple; match three bubbles, get rid of bubbles, win. As I played it, I quickly realized that it was just that simple, yet somehow, so much more. I frothed, I raved, I swore. I was able to create inexplicable combinations, yet the most basic of shots elluded me. Perplexed, I vowed to never again feel that bitter sting of defeat. Not to these bubbles. And thus, I began to hone my skills.
As I began to take this spiritual journey deep within the confines of that digital arena, egged on by soothing music reminiscent of puzzle games from my childhood, time seemed to slow. Nay, it seemed to halt for me alone. I could vaguely hear my family calling my cell phone, my boss to inquire of me as it had been three days of my absence, and it was unlike me. I could hear weeping, but was it myself, or the ones I loved?
My family grew older, and larger, friends mourned for me, and yet I remained transfixed by this game, untouched by the hands of time. I lost my job yesterday, or was it perhaps ten years ago? The concept of hours, days, even years has become lost to me as I still hone myself, becoming a master of the bubbles. They called to me, speaking promises of glory and victory, and I refused to deny myself that which I so dearly desired. I would never bow to these colorful orbs as I had once in my youth.
Youth? What did that even mean anymore? I have been here centuries now, unhindered by the pains of old age, frozen in my prime, learning the ways of the bubbles. Even death itself has forgotten me as I remain transfixed by this game. My family that I knew had passed on, leaving me alone, yet astoundingly without resentment; the woman they had known had been gone all of these millenia.
And now, this very day, I stepped out of that plane of existance changed; born anew in the fires of reds, greens, and blues. My life as I had known it is forever gone, and I alone, save for the holy knowledge that the bubbles have bestowed upon me, remained. I shall go forth, and conquer.
TLDR; Really addicting game. I totally recommend, but only if you are willing to lose your day to playing it.

As a fan of the puzzle platformer genre, I couldn't figure out what rubbed me the wrong way about this game. Many major design elements are well done. There are optional puzzles requiring more innovative solutions that result in their own achievements. There's also a steady build in your abilities as you advance. Yet I stopped playing about a third of the way through, and I didn't have much of a desire to continue.
The missing element is player ingenuity. I'm not personally a fan of entirely linear puzzles. I like games where I can develop a strategy on the fly. Some of my favorites in this genre are Mark of the Ninja, Trine 1/2 and Gunpoint. Those games are characterized by an ability of the player character which the game does not guide you in how to use. It only makes opportunities to use it available. I like the lego set mentality of game design. "Here's a really cool thing with something you could build, but do whatever you want with it."
To me, a magic marker that changes the play environment promises a whole lot of player experimentation, but there isn't any. Every puzzle, every movement you make, is completely linear. It's pre-determined, and there's no alternate way to solve it. The abilities can only be used on pre-marked 'ability areas' that provide the solution to the puzzle. The puzzles are not difficult. I found myself fighting the controls more often than an intellectual challenge. In the end, it's like playing an FPS where every really cool kill you get automatically switched your weapon, highlighted your target, and all you had to do was click. The rest of the time you just proceed where the directional arrow tells you to.
I think the game doesn't deliver on its promise of a magic marker in that respect. There's still quite a bit to be enjoyed here if the completely linear aspect doesn't bother you. The animation is great. I found the controls a little clunky but hardly unusable. Some of the puzzles are entertaining even if not hard, and the story is almost worth playing through in itself. Gameplay is king though, and I wanted something that would beg for a second playthrough just so I could change things a different way the next time.

Ballpoint Universe is half adventure-platformer and half level-based horizontal shooter, both halves have some glaring problems sapping the fun.
You walk around a hand-drawn environment, finding new character to help so that you can unlock the next area. Helping a character involves playing a level in the horizontal shooter.
There's a plot in this half, and it's not that bad actually. The Doodles are in a war with the geometrical Logicians and it is your job to find out what's going on with the Logicians and how to stop the war.
The main gripe with this segment is that the controls are very, very weird. With three control schemes available (keyboard, mouse and controller. Mouse being the default) you'd think there was something in there for everyone's tastes.
Jumping is floaty to the point where it's almost impossible to accurately steer where your little doodle guy is going. This isn't such a big deal at first, but for some reason the developers decided that precision platforming is exactly what would make the second half better.
The first impression here is a lot better, which is good since this is the meat of the game.
You fly around in a little ship with 4 customizable parts (2 weapons, a hull and a type of special weapon with limited uses) destroying or dodging all enemies until you get to the boss of the level, that you then have to defeat. You then get Ink to spend on getting new parts and upgrading existing parts (Ink can also be earned in the platformer half, but has no use there).
Pricing on new gear is very high though, so you'll need to fly a lot of missions before you're able to get that heat seeking missile pod (not the ultimate weapon, just my personal favourite).
There's some finesse where some enemies have armour that can only be bypassed with melee weapons, so it's generally a good idea to bring one gun and one melee weapon.
What frustrated me here is a minor detail, but one that I couldn't exclude here. The heat seeker missiles I mentioned are excellent when they work as intended, and are even capable of getting around those pesky melee-only shields. However, the targeting on them is way off. Missed enemies that are by now far behind you and out view, scenery, enemies that haven't spawned yet, everything gets targeted by it. This is more apparent on some levels than on others, but especially since it's such a late-game weapon where players will have had to save up Ink for dozens of missions, it just reeks of poor design and/or testing.
Ballpoint Universe isn't a bad game, but beyond the distinctive graphics there just isn't anything exceptional there.
You can enjoy it, but the same can be said more so of a lot of other games on offer.

A platformer/shoot 'em up hybrid with a unique, if not beautiful aesthetic. "Intriguing", you may say, much as I did. Well unfortunately, that is where the pros end and the cons begins because Ballpoint Universe is a complete and utter mess beyond those two qualities.
Let's start with the default button mapping: frankly, it's a joke. There are three control schemes available and not a one of them is configured in such a way to mirror the standardized control schemes of any certified staples in either the platforming or shoot'em up genres. Sure, you can remap them (only through the launch menu like other Unity-based titles, though), but it begs the question: have the developers played anything other than their own work? Well, let this be a foreshadowing for what's to come.
The side scrolling segments more or less make for a glorified map screen; you can talk to various characters, acquire some of the golden sketches and locate available shooting stages to play. To navigate through the game world with the mouse or a gamepad is practically unfeasible, though a logically configured keyboard is at least serviceable and other than the jerky movement of our protagonist, there's not much to complain about here. Sure, the puzzle solving is mindless, but it is functional.
Where I really lose my patience is when the game switches to a shoot' em up. Movement with the keyboard causes your ship to fly all over the screen at the slightest tap making it a worthless input method. Only here does the mouse shine, but Tyrian this isn't; Ballpoint Universe is bottom of the barrel, indie shoot 'em up garbage. There appear to be a number of optional pieces for building your ship, though as of six lengthy stages in, I have yet to find anything other than the freebies given at the start. The defaults can each be upgraded by three levels by spending ink, the game's currency, though this does little to improve their viability. On the positive, the trash mobs have little variety and never move with more than one pattern making upgrades pointless, anyway. On the down side, this makes for an incredibly dull, uneventful outing, causing the player to die almost exclusively from a monotonous lack of engaging stimulation as opposed to genuine challenge. Disorientation caused by both the screen shake effect and nauseating parallax scrolling (particularly on 'Brethren') don't help out much, either.
Honestly, this is one of the most baffling games I've played and for all the wrong reasons. It's as if Arachnid Games have deliberately created something that completely misses the point as to why anyone would play a platformer
shoot 'em up in the first place... broken controls, dreadful gameplay and an intellectually insulting waste of immaculate hand-drawn art all make Ballpoint Universe of the worst games I've ever had the misfortune of adding to my Steam library, case closed.

Can't speak for gamepad though. Fortunately they're not the focus and you'll only have to deal with them every so often, the focus is on the shooter parts and that's probably for the better.
The genre's never been one of my favorites but it's fun enough here, plenty of variety in enemies in their movements and attack patterns and a variety of upgrades available to the ship. Though the shotgun, which is one of the earlier weapons, was never beaten in effectiveness for me, for whatever reason, though I did not unlock any of the highest tier of weapons. Because the game a little too grindy if you want to pull off everything in it. Playing through the story once is still certainly enjoyable enough though. The game's certainly worth its rather low price. I have no clue how it fares as a shmup since, as I said, I don't really play these often, but I found it fun enough.

This game is a frankenstein abomination of different Sonic games and really has no business being called Sonic 4. If you're looking for a good Sonic game to play or a new 2D platformer, skip this one and head straight for Episode 2.
is a much better game. If you're looking for a good nostalgia trip, grab Sonic Generations. If you're still on the fence about this one, read on.
Sonic 4 Episode 1 is the first part of an episodic approach to returning to Sonic the Hedgehog's roots, riding the 2D revival bandwagon started by games like New Super Mario Bros. There is nothing wrong with the idea, but Sega put absolutely no effort into preserving their most important mascot's heritage. Sonic 4 was outsourced to Dimps, which makes its complete failure even more baffling, as Dimps has made several decent to good handheld Sonic games over the years.  They must have let the janitorial staff take over for this project, because it's clear no one understood what makes a good game, let alone a good Sonic game.
The graphics are garish with a prerendered art style that isn't evocative of any Sonic game except maybe 3D Blast (which no one wanted to be reminded of). The music sounds like it's coming out of a bootleg Genesis/Megadrive; the compositions aren't necessarily bad, but the sound is very unappealing. The level design is bottom-tier Sonic but still modeled after actual Sonic games, but the borked physics result in bizarre situations like Sonic moonwalking in slowmotion on a ceiling, or just stopping on a dime.
For a game called Sonic 4, it takes several steps back and uses its predecessors as crutches. As such, its truncated level selection gives us such wonderful, original zones as
Splash Hill Zone, Casino
Street Zone,
Labyrinth Zone,
Mad Gear Zone, and
EGG Station Zone. So to sum it up, we have an inferior rehash with half the content of a typical Sonic game due to its episodic nature. Someone at Sega must have wised up because Episode 2 is such a big step up over this and I can't recommend someone put up with it when you can get far better Sonic experiences on Steam.

The spin dash as a form of acceleration is useless, it doesn't even get you to max speed. Using the homing attack, instead, gets you at max speed in less than a second without having to charge it. However, using the homing attack as an attack is useless and is often the slowest option to move across an enemy laden screen. The homing attack is also a burden to use when the reticle decides to not track an enemy as long as it occasionally does.
The physics, oh god... They're terrible and unintuitive and inconsistent. It feels like you're walking through six inches of mud, and you stumble into corners of ledges. Sometimes you don't stay in a ball long enough in the air, which proves problematic when anything aerial is hard to control in the first place and there are enemies you
hit, but have hit you instead. Sometimes you walk up the wall 30 feet, backwards, with no input, and sometimes you struggle to hop up a small incline. Suffice to say, precision is not this game's strong suit.
There are miscellaneous strange choices involved in this game's creation, too. Why do acts' title screens look like the Chilean flag? Why does the mouse cursor stay visible in fullscreen mode when there are no mouse controls? Why are pictures of required inputs on menus not replaced with whatever you're really supposed to press, as opposed to the colored rectangles that represent whatever controller's buttons this game originally played with? How does a 2D game have camera issues?
It's a mediocre port of a cousin of a Sonic game. The art's ok, the music is middling, the character animations are student level, the 3D models are mildly unsettling. It's frustrating and unsatisfying, especially the achievement to beat the final area with no hits taken. Buy Sonic Generations instead.
The physics are really wonky but the levels are fun and the graphics look pretty good, buy it if you're a sonic fan, if you're not a sonic fan there are better sonic games than this.

I really like this entry in the franchise, but it has a few weak spots.
The setting: The move to a primarily firearm based era makes this Total War different from the others. While at first it is a refreshing change, it gets a little old after a while. This style of warfare relies a lot more on standing around and blasting each other with artillery and a lot less on charging into melee. Most battles play out in a similar fashion.
Naval combat: While the first addition of naval combat is exciting, it is rather slow placed. It can be tough to get the hang of, but is still fun to watch!
Campaign: This is where the game excels. The grand campaign in this iteration offers lots of new options, like rebellions, protectorates that actually do something, and a more intricate trade system. No real downsides here!
Overall, a good game. Still crashes to the desktop occasionally, so get used to hitting quicksave.
One last pet peeve. The implementation of forts is completely broken, making them a liability more than a bonus.
Empire: TotalWar is definitely far from a perfect game. But overall its a fun little game to speand your time on while not really doing much at all.

This game is amazing. I've been playing the original Mordheim since it came out. It's not exactly like the table top version, but it does a great job of capturing the atmosphere. The campaign is open enough to allow limitless street skirmishes and build your warband the way you want. Character customization is spectacular. And I love the risk in every mission. You can spend 20 missions building up a hero just to have him criippled or killed by a skaven hiding in a closet.
The best part to me is the city itself. At a glance, it doesn't look like much, but on the ground, it's a labrynth. Climbing to the top of a ruined house in search of wyrdstone or treasure, hiding in doorways to ambush enemies. It's just like I imagined playing the tabletop.

Releasing only 3 out of around 20 factions with the initial game, then drip-releasing the rest as expensive DLC leaves a bad taste in the mouth. I really think something out to be done about this current trend of releasing a half-finished game at full price and then making people pay extra for features which should have been included in the first place.
That said still a very good game, done a very good job of making the tabletop game into a viable and fun video game.

This game is many things... it is thoughtful, deep, steeped with lore from one of the most amazing fantasy settings ever created since it is warhammer, among many things.. But i think the most important part of this game, and what makes it different from almost every other game out there, is the emotional context.
there are NO saves other than the one you have. EVERY time you choose a mission and your crew, there is a very real possibility for failure and death. I have succeeded on the hardest "brutal" missions and wiped on the normal rated ones. The game is so emotional because there is a sense of accomplishment and loss that isn't present in other games simply because other games give you the option of iron man mode which most never take, and this one just forces it upon you because that is life in warhammer. Brutal, short, and only the strongest survive and flourish.
If you want a complex, deep, immersive experience where you must consider every move, because each move can mean triumph or disaster, then get this game. I've raged quit screamed and yelled at the RNG but i think it is actually pretty fair. It doesn't cheat as some say, it is just what it is. If you have played xcom or any other rng heavy product you will understand. The only difference with this game is that on several unlucky rolls in a row you may lose a character you have spent months developing, and there is no scum saving like xcom. You have to deal with the consequences of a harsh existence, which is what the WARHAMMER universe is all about.
So if anyone cares i absolutely recommend this game. There are many things i would like to see implemented as far as the campaign goes and not getting pretty much the mirror image of youur warband to face, and maybe revenge missions where you get to face the band that wiped you previously, but maybe they will come and there will be more diversity in the campaign. either way if you are on the fence, do yourself a favor and try it! especially for the sale price it is now you cant beat it.

The reason this game has mixed user reviews is due to (rightfully) misguided expectations. It is billed as an open world action-RPG while it should be treated as a PvP fighting game with a bonus open world to explore. The game will take about 3-4 hours to beat afterwhich you can explore the world collecting the ~160 different moves in the game. The AI however does not require you to make this effort so the only reason for doing so is either completion or for competition within PvP. Most of your time in this game will be improving your deck (the combination of moves that make up your fighting style) and improving yourself in PvP. If that thought does not interest you, you should turn away as that is what you will mostly be doing.

TL;DR if you enjoy well animated and satisfying kung fu, enjoy having control over every facet of your character and their kung fu, and you also enjoy 1 vs 1, player vs player combat, you may enjoy Absolver. The servers work now, and the game isn't dead like some people have said. Since they fixed the servers, I have never had to wait more than 10 seconds to find a match.
You have likely heard of this game and the customizability of your moveset, and while that sounds fine on its own, the real entertainment comes from comparing your own setup to the people you fight in the matchmaking queue. There's something very satisfying about meeting a new opponent, learning his tools and what moves he has put together, and trying to match your own against his. When you win, it's easy to see what the other player was doing wrong, where the holes in his gameplan are and where he failed to execute. On the other hand, when you lose, it's similarly easy to tell where your own improvements should be made, and so back to the moveset editor you go, to keep optimizing and make sure you have an answer for whatever you just lost to. Every player is totally unique, yourself included. It's likely that no one out there has the same set of attacks as you, even if you based your list on someone else's, since everyone is constantly making these little adjustments trying to find their perfect fit. To me, this makes the 1 vs 1 queue very addictive. I'm always trying to see what I can learn from the next match. Finding someone who has come up with an effective or novel idea within the confines of the moveset editor that I've never seen before is an amazing feeling. Combine all this with the immensely satisfying attacks filled with visual and audio feedback (you can practically feel the weight behind all of the heavy hitting moves, and the sound design is top notch), and you can imagine why it never gets old to roundhouse kick new opponents.
Most of the above falls under nebulous "game feel" territory though, so lets lay out some facts. There is very little single player content. The game is made for playing against other people, so if you're looking for a large world to explore or a deep story, you will not find anything like that here. It's a PVP focused game, plain and simple. The single player content that exists is not bad, but it's not great either, it mostly serves as a backdrop for building your character and your moveset.
The next fact is that it is an online game. That is, no local play. If you live in a country with poor internet (or simply have poor internet wherever you are), you will probably not enjoy the game very much, as your interactions with other players will be laggy. While the majority of the matches I've played did not have issues, I have had matches with teleporting players, attacks registering multiple seconds late, or animations speeding up or not playing at all. If you've ever tried to play a fighting game with a bad connection, you'll understand why this is no fun.
The last fact I think is most important to mention is that the servers are not broken anymore. This game had an infamously messy launch with more server downtime than uptime for most players, myself included. The developers have fixed these connectivity issues among others, and for me personally it's been smooth sailing since they did. If you had server problems with this game before, or were on the fence because you heard of how terrible the connection issues were (and they were pretty terrible), I'd recommend you give it another shot now.
While I've mostly been singing praises so far, Absolver is not without flaws. There's been a rare save corrupting bug since launch that hasn't been fixed yet, so if you end up playing, remember to back up your save and use Steam cloud. In addition, some people have found the controls and mechanics to be unintuitive. Personally, I think that if you've played fighting games or third person action games (think God Hand or anything Platinum Games has made) , you won't have any lasting problems adjusting here, but it's still something to keep in mind. You should also keep in mind that since the game is pretty much just fighting other players, it can get repetitive. If you don't get hooked right away by the gameplay and mechanics, you probably won't get hooked later, as the core gameplay loop does not really change, only your playstyle as you get better.
To wrap this up, Absolver is not a game for everyone. You have to really enjoy the actual minute to minute fighting to feel like coming back to it again and again, but if the game does hook you, or if you've been looking for an accessible fighting game that has depth and customization, or even just a unique change of pace to your usual PVP tastes, there isn't anything else like it on the market. Even at the relatively steep $30 price tag, I think it's worth a try. You'll know pretty quickly if you want to invest more time into the game, quick enough that running out your refund clock shouldn't be a problem. I find myself loading it up at least once a day for a few matches. With proper expectations, I recommend it whole heartedly.

First off, the Mac client has some serious technical problems. It wouldn't even install on my system (OS X 10.9.5), apparently due to some problems with the third-party downloader...which I don't see a reason for even including, given that Steam downloads all 8 GB worth of game content anway. So I haven't been able to run it at all in Steam, but the Windows version runs fine in Wineskin.
GOOD:
- The game captures a surprising amount of the feel of actually playing D&D. There's DM narration during quests, a lot of the mechanics from the tabletop game are included, and you have to do more than just kill monsters. There are spot checks to find hidden doors, traps to avoid, NPCs to bluff and even some puzzles to solve.
- Soloing is supported more than in most MMOs.
- Most of the game content is instanced: the only public areas are the towns, and most of the quests take place in instanced areas with a linear narrative. As a result, there are way fewer "kill 20 zebras" or "collect 10 rocks" quests than you might expect in an MMO.
- It's free, so if you hate it, you're not out anything more than the couple hours it takes to download.
- There are a TON of options for building a character (three trees per class and multiclassing), although several classes are behind pay walls.
BAD:
- The graphics and interface are really dated, and the voice acting is pretty bad.
- The player base is small.
- The downside of the character customization freedom and the jillions of different numbers brought over from the tabletop game is that the mechanics are really complicated. I imagine (I haven't gotten anywhere near endgame) that optimizing a character for raiding would be REALLY hard.
- There's a lot of pay-wall stuff that pops up right out of the gate. Want to have more than two characters? Pay up. Want to play a monk? Pay up. Want to res after you die? Pay up.

I hope that 74 hours alongside some very good and enamored friends was enough to give this game a fair shake, but ultimately I just can't really recommend it.
The game is an attempt to be a semi-faithful recreation of the 3.5 D&D experience, although unlike, say, the old Neverwinter Nights, the game adds some concessions to MMO playability between things like talent trees and the fact that you get Spell Points instead of myriad slots. The concept is set in Eberron, which is a kind of high-magic crystal-punk sort of setting, and the game is played almost entirely through instanced dungeon work.
There are reasons that D&D is not played in realtime, and this game demonstrates exactly why. An instant save-or-die death spell on the tabletop can have a dramatic buildup leading the clattering of that 20-sided die; in a realtime game, you just die suddenly for no readily apparent reason, which engenders neither tension nor "what could I have done better" counterplay thoughts so much as it simply engenders stunned contempt. The same can go for high end blast spells and traps, many of which can kill characters instantly.
They'll often do so with little more than a 'klick,' too, because the sound assets in this game are the poorest I've heard outside bad indie games. Your mighty two-handed sword will do little more than sort of lightly 'dink' while it slices a devastating critical hit through a gnoll; your entire team can be killed by a sonic trap that strongly reminds one of a rather shy doorbell, while, conversely, the discovery of secret doors leads to a deafening CLUNK that overshadows the din of any battle. The upshot is that there's no feel of impact to pitched melee battles. The music has been added to in the many expansions, but never replaced, meaning the early-game music is poor and repetitive.
Between that and lacklustre animations, the combat - which is what you will be spending the overarching majority of your time in Stormreach doing, this being a fantasy MMO - feels weak and ephemeral. By aiming for a more quasirealistic if colorful fantasy look, the character art assets might have been good in 2006, but have not aged wonderfully. While I hate to contrast to WoW, WoW's cartoonier style certainly helped preserve its original, dated models for a longer functional time; these assets currently sleep at the bottom of the uncanny valley.
The dungeons are pains to navigate, the quest UI is poor to nonfunctional, power (even if not strictly necessary power) is sold via the game's microtransaction system in the form of stat-boosting Tomes and field self-revives.
Is there anything positive to say? A little. The game does, unlike many MMOs, have more comprehensible mechanics to those experienced with the D&D 3.5 system, and so it's easier to see what's going on under the hood. The game also manages to successfully break the Holy Trinity (tank/healer/DPS) so prevalent in many other MMOs with a very fluid and diverse class system. Character customizability always was a strength of D&D 3.0/3.5, and that’s unquestionably present.  The Dungeon Master, a voice who narrates things your character is ostensibly experiencing, is a welcome nod to the tabletop.
Outside of that, though, it’s hard to recommend it, even to fans of the D&D 3.5 system. Fantasy adventures are not in short supply at the moment, and it’s probably best to seek them elsewhere.

"stay close to the edge, don't go into the middle of the floor...", rapidly types our Cleric as we approach an apparently harmless room. But i read it to late. I've seen the sparkling chest nestled enticingly in an alcolve directly opposite our position and i rush towards it. Stupid. The floor collapses and i fall into the misty chamber below. There are bones strewn around the room and then suddenly an elite level scorpian erupts from the ground and immediately attacks me. The rest of my group - my guild mates - leap heroically into the chamber and we engage the beast together and manage to bring it down. "we can't get that chest now, there is no way back up", says the same Cleric. "sorry" i say, and imagine my character, head hung in shame, shuffling his feet. "no problem :)" says the Cleric. My Ranger searches the room and finds the lever that opens the chamber. A gloomy tunnel stretches into the distance. We heal up then move on.
This is what D&D Online is all about and when it is at its best. The game has a number of large open hub areas but the missions will almost certainly lead you underground into a dark cavern or muggy sewer. In the hubs you can find group members, hire mercernary's, prurchase healing scrolls and potions, and upgrade gear and equipment, before venturing into the dangers below. Some quests ask you to clear out an infestation of spiders/kobolds/etc, normlly with  larger, more dangerous boss type near the end, whilst others may ask you to rescue a merchant's daughter or find a precious artifact. Throughout these dungeons there is the possibility of finding rare monsters with epic loot, normally only found by finding a hidden door or secret area, but only if you or one of your group has the riht skills. This is a game that rewards exploration, that encourages group play, and grabs wholeheartdly at that inner fantasy nerd that exists in so many of us.
As a solo experience this is a lesser game. You can clear same level content no problem, even an elite dungeon or two with the right equipment and merc's, but the exprience feels lonely and more shallow on your own.
The game truely shines as a multiplayer experience, which, to be fair, is exactly how the game is intended to be.
I can over look the aged graphics and tired engine for the wonderful frill of descending into the deaths of an undead crypt with a group of likeminded advnturers. Most stuff is decided on invisible dice rolls and armor/will saves just like (almost) the tabletop game, but the combat has a degree of twitch and you can dodge incoming attacks with a well timed double tap. When you find a loot chest automtic rolls take place and loot is devidied up accordingly but you can transfer items to another group member if you want to.
The community is very friendly and I was soon in a really helpful high level guild (this brings loads of perks to experience gains and buffs) and there nevr seems to be shortage of people to go questing with.
Much like LOTRO the whole game is F2P with the need to buy quest packs for additonal content or unlocks for certain race/class types. It is fair to say that you will likely need to pnd a few quid t some point to advance th whole experience but the good thing is this can be done at your leisure and if you done wan to then, well, dont.
I for one applaud this style of F2P model and for  a game that provides this much AAA fun I had not issue with spending money on it - i just purchased all of the DLC for just over £14 in the sale and thats good value by any standard.
If you like D&D, fantasy, and group style play then i can highly recommend this game. If you don't or are looking for another WOW style experience then keep looking. D&D online isnt trying to be WOW or Guildwars and I am glad of that.
As an fantasy adventure maker this game is top notch and you should certainly give it a whirl - 8.8/10

Intergalactic Bubbles is a bubble puzzler with a simple gameplay. They are some bubbles on the top of the screen and you have to shoot new bubbles while you make sure the colors are matching together. If you hit at least 3 bubbles with the same color, the bubble chain breaks and the bubbles disappear. When all the bubbles are gone you've won the game.
To make the game a bit more exciting, there are also some features like power-ups and 5 different galaxies with a different amount of colorized bubbles. Every galaxy has 50 levels, so there are 250 levels to solve in this game.
But even with the high amount of levels and some specials like power-ups, the game gets boring after a while. One reason for that is maybe the level design. All levels in all different galaxies look almost the same. The graphics do not look good in general and there are also some bugs / glitches and a miserable translation.
But even with all this cons, regarding the fact that this game is a low priced game which you can buy for some cents on steam sales, it's one of the better games for some cents.

Savant - Ascent is a sort of twin stick shooter bullet hell type game. You are essentially rooted to two spots on each level, you can roll between them to avoid enemies, jump up and down, and that's it - although this sounds like it is restricting, you soon realize that it's all you need, and you probably don't need an extra thing to think about, so having just two positions is quite a good idea.
The art style is very nice. A lot of games are taking on this graphic style, and rightfully still as it does look good. The sprites of the main character and all the enemies look awesome too. Now, the music, if you are into electro/dubstep music, you may just have stumbled upon a gold mine. The sound track to Savant is amazing, there are about six different tracks to unlock and each of them is probably one of the best soundtracks you'll ever hear. I am surprised they haven't released the sound track as its own download to be honest!
Each of the levels is presented very well; the aim is to just kill everything on screen for a number of minutes, nothing too complex. The game does get increasingly difficult though, it will probably take you a few tries on each level before you get to grips with what you have to do. The last two stages probably had me raging more than any other game I've played. That brings me onto game length, the game is very short, I managed to finish the story in just about an hour, while this is short, there are two other game modes that will keep the replayability going. I can see some people have over 100 hours in this game purely from these modes bringing them back for more.
I would say Savant - Ascent has a place in most people's library, it's short and sweet and for £1, 59, you can't really go wrong can you?

It befuddles me just why this game gets so much flack. People complain that it plays like a Genesis game.... which isn't that the point?? Lets be honest, Sonic the Hedgehog is a title that should have been retired in the 90's. The moment this franchise hit the 3D consoles, it began to suck more than a gay porn star. Yet Sega loves to double down on terrible 3D Sonic games, pumping them out like rabbits, and for an equally bizarre reason there is a section of the fan base that eats it up. In fact, the worse the game, the more these people defend it, "Cuz its da SAWNIK!"
So when I heard that someone at Sega green lit a throwback title, I was ecstatic! And this game hits the mark right on the head. If you loved the well built, simplistic style of the very original Sonic title, then this game is a true homage to it.
RIGHT: Obviously, someone did their homework here, because this game is everything that the original Sonic was, just with a nice 3D rendered facade. You play as just big Blue himself against Robotnik in four worlds broken up into four stages just like the original title. (3 stages + Boss Stage) Run the three levels, grab some "emwoads", trash Robotnik at the end, hit the canister, and let the little creatures out. Pure, simple, and classic. And while Sonic halls haunch just like he did in the original, he maintains a good pace, rather than flying around the screen like an ADD three year old on a sugar high. Bonus rounds are also a throwback to the first game, with the rotating maze except now you can control the maps rotation rather than hitting speed up and slow down buttons. Super sonic also makes an appearance unlike the original, but doesn't break the game play like he did in other titles. Level design, music, and even some of the boss designs are all taken from the first game with great care and detail.
WRONG: While everything in this game is a delightful trip down memory lane, for some reason the developers decided not make Sonic also look traditional.... No we get the current incarnation Sonic, complete with his long hair, bracelets, green eyes and "hip hop" attitude. Though to be fair, he thankfully doesn't pepper you with insipid banter like he does in recent games, but it still irked me they decided to keep that awful design. This also extends to Robotnik, who is once again called "Eggman" because we simply MUST comply with the Japanese who think naming people after food items is just the END of comedy, and is also packed into the ugly red track suit that looks like a Richard Simmons yard sale leftover. And why? Was anyone seriously thinking that if they didn't keep the crappy current designs that we weren’t going to recognize them? Or more likely it was a pathetic ploy to try and gain a few "SAWNIK" fans to download it.
Regardless, this game is very much worth a download if, like me, you grew up playing the classic Sonic titles. It gets everything right from the original, lush backgrounds, great music, classic looking enemies, rings, loops, springs, and of course "SAWNIK"!

For the record: This isn't a bad game because it's not a true classic sonic game. It's a bad game on its own merits.
Though it certainly is insanely far from a true classic series game. I mean, when every stage in the game is a rehash of a Sonic 1 or 2 zone (and thus entirely unoriginal, something the original series was not) then obviously it's playing off nostalgia fuel. But it doesn't play like those games. It relies on gimmicks instead of level design. Literally every single act barring the first is built around a gimmick. The physics are also all wrong, too; not remotely similar to the classic games, and playing more like the 2D bits of the modern sonic stages in Generations (see the problem there?).
But I wouldn't care if the game was any good by itself. But... it's not. There's an out of nowhere difficulty spike at the second act of the second zone (and only near the end). Which would matter if you didn't already have 50 lives by that point because the game showers you in them, removing any sense of difficulty. Dying becomes annoying and tedious more than anything. Some of the gimmicks, also, are pretty bad. Mad Gear Act 3's, especially. Since a lot of it requires you to learn where to jump since screwing up once = instant death. Yup. Good job with that one.
And let's not get started on the boss design. Well for one every single boss is a carbon copy of a Sonic 1/2 boss, or at least starts out that way. And the newly added bits to the later three are all awful. No, instant-death crusher traps in a sonic boss are not good. No, a sonic advance 2 styled running boss with the occasional impossible to dodge attack is not cool. And no, making Sonic 2's final boss even more tedious and unfair is not cool. Seriously, that thing has broken hitboxes and takes a bloody eternity.
The game doesn't have particularly good presentation, either. A lot of the graphical elements clash, and the music is the first time I've ever found a sonic soundtrack actively bad. It's just... horrible music. Truly terrible.
There's... nothing really to recommend here, at all. I didn't expect a great game but I didn't even get a decent one.

Man, I really wanted to like this game because, yeah, I like Sonic.  He's really only worked in 2d, though (I didn't care for Sonic Adventures, personally).  When I saw this a few years ago I was like oh man, exciting!  A new, potentially good sonic game!  And then all of the disappointment.
The two biggest factors as to why I don't recommend this game: the engine and the level design.  Graphics are a close third.
The engine is just kind of meh.  Sonic feels very bulky, heavy and slow in this game.  More than once I've stood on a hill and, after losing momentum, could not actually finish climbing said hill.  I had to go back, get a running start and then run up.  It didn't feel very sonic like and it very much breaks pacing/immersion/fun.
However, the level design is what kept me from wanting to finish.  It's just kind of meh overall, like a  bland cut/copy/paste of what a marketing person thinks a sonic game should look like, having looked at the statistics and level design of previous games.  It feels very soulless, much like the New Super Mario brothers series.  Sure, it looks similar to the original Sonic games but it lacks it's own character or creativity.  You can usually safely call where a spike trap will be, for example, because  the placements are so obvious.  That's not bad, necessarily -- you should be able to tell where the pitfalls are going to come up -- but they're predictable in the way that makes the game boring.
What really broke my spirits, though, was the third level: the ♥♥♥♥ing water level.  Water levels always kind of suck in Sonic, but in the past I at least appreciated their unique-ness as they did some cool things.  This one doesn't.  One stage has a massive pain in the♥♥♥♥♥puzzle where you light specific torches at specific times in order to make platforms rise and fall, but the torches burn out so quickly that Sonic's slow, impercise♥♥♥♥♥can't easily get onto these ledges before they disappear.  I personally was stuck on one part of a stage for a good 5-10 minutes just trying to get Sonic to do what I wanted him to do.  That's not a good game.  Worse still is the boss fight for that stage, which is a race to catch and damage Robotnik.  Except, you know, the race involves very specific jumps while water is rising.  Of course the water slows you down, and at that point why even bother?
No, I had a pretty bad time with this game and I wouldn't recommend it to anyone unless you really wanted to see how to ♥♥♥♥ up a 2d sonic game.  It just doesn't do much right.  Even Sonic Colors -- a game I also do not like -- was designed better than this.  I really want to like it, but it's just not very good.  If you want a good Sonic game, go check out Sonic Generations instead.

I have played Mordheim since before it was released, and then I am talking about Games Workshop miniature tabletop game, so I have followed the Mordheim franchise since they posted a trail version in an old White Dwarf magazine.
So when I first saw this game on Alpha, it was an instant buy for me. Sadly, my first experiences of the game made me doubt if that was money well spent. So after having tested that beta for about half an hour I shut down and decided not to poke it before it was released. And now, almost a year after it left its alpha and beta stage, I wonder why I ever doubted Mordheim back then.
So what do I think of the game? I love it! It's a wonderful, turnbased stratergy game with some light RPG elements to it as it includes a few story missions for each faction.
Are the rule systems the same? Does the computer game use six-sided dice? Does character progression work the same way? The skills? All the various heroes and henchmen? Spells? Items? NO! No, they are not the same.
Does the computer game capture the essence of the original miniature tabletop game...? <Insert curseword> YES! Yes, it certainly does and more.
So no, you won't be able to play the exact same game here that you would if you play with your miniatures, and my opinion is that it's a good thing for once. This game offers you, in some ways, more and different options that you lack when you play with your models.
The only true downsides with the game is that the core game only had four races (they have added two more with dlc now - which I don't mind, but others do), grinding missions might get a little repetative if done for hours and hours without a break and some seem to think the game is hard, but I generally have never had a problem with it, except maybe the first mission at times. Just.. don't be afraid of someone dying! Except if it is your leader, then you might have problems..

Reviewing this game is kind of hard, because it's about two things I really like: the lore of Mordheim and the Warhammer Fantasy universe, and turn-based squad combat.
However, I can't recommend this game, and that is painful. The reason to why is simple, but there is more to it:
The graphics is sub-par, and I'm running a high-end rig that can push the limits, and what did I get? something that looked like it cane from mid 00's. Thanks for that.
It's hard to get a good overview of what's happening, and the map gets a lot of use since navigation is a nightmare. Not even the ruin-iest parts of the Fallout universe are this bad.
Customisation of the soldiers is... lacking. One type of face, four types of hair and hair color, four types of facial hair... Come on, the denizens of Reikland aren't that conformed.
Missions are at best ok, but what really kills the game is the random number generator. When you fail to climb a wall three times in a row with a guy without any armour, then something is wrong.
But the main reason to why I have to give this a thumbs down is this:
It's not fun. I can't get immersed in a game that I think lacks so much, and its a damn shame, because if the game had been given some more time, it could really have been something. I have been following the game for quite some time and was onthe fence fo much of it, and then finally I decided to try it out. It was a mistake.
And since the game is this bad, I have found a reason to reinstall X-Com 2 and play it through a bazillionth time.
I recommend you do the same.

A water-colored, Kung-fu style PvP with a deep combat system and NPC brawls that hurt just as hard as other players. While you can play for the PvE, Absolver is a PvP at its heart, done right with an excellent community resembling masters and their disciples fighting to the top.
(This is a long one so, TL;DR: there’s a Drunken Master stance that makes me appreciate this game for more than its great community or martial arts mechanics, so you should at least try it if you enjoy online fighters.)
Play as a prospect thrown into a lost Empire world, punching up the ladder to become an Absolver. While the story is primarily a backdrop in this game, it provides a sort of creative freedom for the gamer to personalize their character as their own.
Absolver is very much a mute-colored Wind Waker, each setting like a water-colored background laced with bullies wearing tattered clothes and armor. Every so often, you’ll come across the Big Boss wearing fur-collared, regal apparel that matches the forsaken landscape. These chieftains stand out in comparison to the drab prospect NPCs laid out across each of the four zones.
As far as sound design goes, ambient noise accompanies your trek between areas while a tense guitar introduces boss battles. The game’s overall aesthetic interplays with each variable, and it works well whether it’s an intense fight to the death or a campfire meditation.
I prefer playing this game with a controller for two main reasons: (1) I’ve always kind of tenaciously associated fighting games as best played with a controller or game pad, and (2) Absolver’s combat is highly dexterous, dependent on fighting stance, fluidity of combos and some intermittent power-up abilities such as heals or shockwaves.
To give you the rundown, there are three combat styles to choose from in the beginning with a fourth one (Stagger Stance a.k.a. Drunken Master Jackie Chan) becoming unlocked once you’ve obtained all the moves from beating enemies. Your character has four directional stances that can have a maximum of four moves for each stance (three moves that combo together and typically a strong attack that can shortcut a combo to the next stance).
In short, while reaching max level might provide the preferred attacks and combos for higher-level PvP, the entire combat system in and of itself is deep, complex and ripe for experimentation. This provides a substantial learning curve for new players, and – to top it all off – there isn’t a level restriction when queuing up for a 1v1. For some, this might be discouraging when you’re Level 15 and your opponent is Jet Li Level 60.
Luckily, there are a few options to get started. First, the community is particularly helpful with aiding new players in their grind for moves. Invite someone to co-op, Steam message them and usually people are pretty willing to farm for and trade moves. Second, fighting schools are available after reaching a certain level in PvP so that this first process can be accelerated. Finally, if you enjoy the NPC and boss combat enough, you could also traditionally grind for moves, but it’s much quicker when linking up with a friend or a random person.
Overall, this fashionable martial arts title is definitely worth a try as compared to something like For Honor and Dark Souls. Though I believe it requires a few hours of gameplay to separate Absolver from these comparisons; it really is an inspirational draw from those games, but it is one of a kind.

This is a casual game, or well...Kung-fu Simulator.
The combat system is pretty fun; there's not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ grappel spam system like For Honor, or a super easy to abuse parry system like Dark Souls, but other than than the combat, that's kinda all there is to the game.
It feels very much like it was intended to be a DS or Switch game though.
It's also Dark Soul-ish in the sense that you start and are given no direction/purpose, you're supposed to find the "Lore" on your own, and some idiot at the first main "Checkpoint" gives you crytpic message about your objective.
The "Story" is literally about 5 minutes long, but padded with lots of walking and trying to figure out where the hell you're supposed to go or killing the same things over and over again.
The "End game" from what I've seen so far is to grind duels forever.  Every 2-5 duels depending on your performance will unlock about 3-5% progress toward the "Creating your own fight school" feature.
As far as challenge, this isnt really challenging, I beat it in the "5 hours" without ever changing the starting skills, going AFK for real life aggro several times, and only realy putting on armor that I thought looked cool.
The hardest part for me was figuring out how to read the map and where to go to find who you're supposed to kill.
I'd wait for it to drop to a about $15-$20, but It's a decent game to play when you're waiting on something else to download, or want to play something that you can walk away from at any time.

The problem is that the leveling system is top heavy so you don't get much of anything from it from run to run, and you can only level up once per floor.
This game suffers heavily from almost relying entirely on its procedural elements.
The handling isn't terrible, but it often wont do exactly what it is that you want, magic requires mana but almost every spell is nearly useless outside of special situations (except for things like Heal) and any of the advanced elements of the game are going to require a lot of personal testing or research outside of the game.
If it interests you, keep an eye on it, but unless you're totally fine with things that aren't final products, save your money.

Ballpoint Universe - Infine is a small indie game with a beautiful artstyle, as you can see from any screenshot.
It has 2 components. First and foremost, it is a shoot 'em up game. Its story, however, is told through a 2D platformer, between the shooting sections.
Overall, I think it fits the price, as a game. Despite being beautiful, its mechanics aren't too noteworthy (although not at all bad), and it has a few technical and design issues. On the other hand, it looks amazing, and it does a good job of entertaining you for a few hours.
Let's start with its
.
Everything in this game is
. It has a
style to it, even
, at times. But it fits the theme.
The texture work is impressive, with the weird patterns fitting all together, and the NPC and Boss design is also great! Everything seems out of this world and yet beautiful.
This is all well and good, but it has a few issues. First off, and this comes to the scale of this game, is the fact that some textures look low res, there are a few conflicts that lead to graphical bugs, and the fact that everything is a plane gives it a very fragile feel, at times. Just a little bit of depth (like cardboard) would have helped it.
But it still looks very good! And the issues are most likely because of its budget, so I don't want to be too harsh on it.
All that was regarding the platformer side. On the shoot 'em up side, the only issue I've had is the fact that the enemies explode into some very obstructive textures. This means that when you're surrounded by enemies, you'll often get killed by something that you literally can not see, and it's annoying, at times.
But that's my main issue with it. There's a very clear distiction between the background and foreground, and the levels look quite good.
Another minor thing is that the enemies have some parts of their body that do damage to you, and other that don't. Unfortunately, there's no visual distinction between these, which is a problem, specially with Boss Fights, whenever you need to get closer.
Also, despite the player having a small hitbox, it usually blends with the rest of the ship, making it very hard to do some tight dodges. Simply giving it a different color would have helped a lot. But hey, it didn't detract too much from the game.
didn't really do much for the game, in my opinion. They weren't bad, but I think they should've gone one step further with it. They felt a bit generic, and did very little to enchance the very surreal sense of the art style, in my opinion.
There's also the lack of separate audio sliders. It's just lazy.
Before going over the gameplay itself, let's talk about the
.
The
was pretty simple, but was surprisingly good. Whenever you paused the game, you would have a lot of info at hand right away, regarding missions, collectibles, changing the controls, going into infinite mode (more on that later), etc. Everything was a click away, so good job on that!
The
, on the other hand, were a really big issue. This game has some of the weirdest control schemes I think I've seen in a while.
You have 3 options: Mouse, Keyboard, or Gamepad. The Gamepad felt like the Mouse, and made it even harder to navigate the menus.
Mouse and Keyboard were good and serviceable, on 2 separate parts. For the platforming sections, the mouse is almost impossible. Know how you pan out the screen in a RTS, or MOBA? Well, it's the same here. You drag the mouse to move the character, and click to jump/interact. It doesn't work. At all. It's so imprecise... I have no clue why this is here. It makes no sense. For this section, the keyboard is significantly better, although the character still bounces around a lot, and the platforming hitbox is dodgy. The moving platforms also interact very weirdly with the character, everything feels just... awkward and bad. And that's unfortunate. But,
, the developers were aware of this fact, and kept platforming to a minimum.
For the shmup part, the mouse works really well. Simple move it to move your ship, and click to shoot. Simple and effective. The keyboard however, doesn't work very well. Because of this, you'll be constantly switching between control schemes... And this issue hasn't been fixed at all, so beware.
Alright,
then!
There's not much to be said regarding the platforming. It's mostly just a vehicle for the story, and to show you how beautiful their art is. There are Golden Sketches scattered around the world that you may want to collect (for compeltionist's sake), but other than that, you're there to look around, and talk to the different characters, learning more about the world and its people. The story was pretty straightforward and wacky, but in a good way.
For the most part, there's barely any platforming, unless you're looking for the sketches. To reach some, there's some more precise platforming. And that way is okay. It still feels really bad, but it's not in the way. Unfortunately, in the later sections of the game, there is some more obligatory platforming. And it shows how bad it is! There are some bad physics interactions, you'll get stuck several times, etc, etc. It's bad. And I don't know why they decided to go back with their design choice and put platforming into it!
.
The shooting is far more interesting. You have an infinite mode (with 60 balanced waves, after that is just madness), and you have the story missions.
It did
enjoy the infinite mode. The story missions were pretty fun, though.
By completing missions and destroying enemies, you'll collect Ink. You'll use this to buy more parts for your ship, and also upgrade them. This is shared between the 2 modes. The missions rewards you for your performance (perfection will also get you a Golden Sketch). And these are the best way of getting said Ink. The missions are far more rewarding, and let you experiment quite a lot with the parts.
The infinite mode, however, doesn't reward you with much, so you're just playing the same thing over and over. (You can spend a special coin to start out from the place you died, and you get these by defeating bosses, so you'll progress quite quickly, which avoids repetition)
The missions, on the other hand, feel far more different from one another, both visually, and gameplay-wise. Some are just defeating waves of enemies, while others have environmental hazards that require timing to avoid. I really enjoyed completing the missions and getting all the rewards.
You have 2 weapon slots, a body, and a special move. There are melee, ranged, and also shields, as weapons. The body provides more health, and one of 4 different effects. The special move is like a finisher.
The melee is far riskier, but also deals heavy damage, and destroyes shield. This was my favourite playstyle, and it felt different from most shmups because of it! Some blades did forward damage, some damage all around the ship, wide arcs, etc. There's good variety here! And the same with the guns. Unfortunately, the game doesn't get to show you everything before feeling very grindy and unrewarding, which is a huge issue for me.
While doing the story, it's great! You'll try out 3-4 combinations. After that, however, the ink payment is very low, and you're not pushed into trying out the different weapons, which would have been the joy of discovery in this game! Well, but it isn't. And that's very unfortunate.
Enemy and Boss variety is really great as well. Lots of different bullet patterns, some will try to melee you... more variety than I expected!
Overall, give it a go! It has lots of issues, but its incredible visuals are worth the price tag. It's a great example of a small indie idea enhanced a bit to make it a full game!

This is a beautiful game. I must admit I am sometimes amazed how some of the free-to-play games outshine some of the games priced at $30 or more. This one definitely fits that description. You play a Princess cursed with the Cinderella curse, a curse that can only be broken if you do three good deeds. The Fairytale Curse itself is the creation of her mother (though she is unaware of that at first), for when the Grimm tales first appeared it caused a Witch Hunt that nearly killed the Witches, of which the former queen was the chief.
That behind us, there are five choices for you to pursue, other cursed individuals. At first, you only have the ability to choose three of them, but after completing two of those three, the other two will unlock. The suggested path is Rod, Karma, Rumpel, Fritz and Waltz; the first three of which are the original choices. Through your choices and actions, you can end up with either the bad or good ending for said individual.
It is a fun game, and twists some of the fairy tales involved.

Mordheim is a great game, but also can be brutally punishing. If you don't like games that make you suffer for your mistakes (also this has a perma-ironman mode so all decisions are final, thus, no chance of save scumming), then this will not be for you.
As true to the tabletop game, there is perma-death, there are injuries, and they can happen at the most unexpected of times.
The start of the game is arguably one of the more difficult parts, you will have a severe lack of money, you'll lack skills and decent equipment. The AI is always matched to your overall exp level, which helps to provide some balance for the game, but early on this can be deadly, as they'll have had the chance to level up skills which you probably cannot even afford, and even if you could, you may not have days to spare to invest in skills.
Over time though the game gets easier, and subsequent playthroughs have also felt easier (I started as Skaven after playing the tutorial and found it challenging, but my second playthrough was as the sisters and this was significantly easier as I knew what I was doing). The best way to play is to take your time and think, this is a turn based stratergy game after all...If you go charging in, you're probably walking out missing a limb.
TL;DR: This game is meant to be challenging and punishing, if you don't like that idea, or ironman based games in general, this isn't for you. If you want a game which has a satisfying level of difficulty, but also gives you a slap to the face for making mistakes, this is perfect.

I had previously written a review for this when it was in Early Access.  Now that it is in full release I figured I'd better get with the program.
Mordheim is a turn-based strategy game based on the Game Workshop Mordheim setting.  Four different warbands (six if you get the DLC) square off against one another in a ruined city, competing for control of the city and the resources it contains.  It is difficult, unforgiving, and I love every second of it.
One of the things that stands out most to me is the way the gameplay functions.  When a unit takes their turn, instead of relying on any sort of grid, they are free to move around in a third person free roaming mode, limited to their movement range.  This gives the game a very open and exploratory feel, and really feels like a skirmish instead of a board game with pretty graphics.
Each army is unique and favors different playstyles.  They have their own unique skills, equipment, stat limitations, and unit types.  This provides a huge range of options with which to customize your playstyle.  On that subject you'd better get good at the playstyle as well, because the game will punish you if you don't.
One of the core principles of this game is that choices matter.  If one of your units falls in battle, they may suffer injuries that will affect their stats, lose equipment, or even die and have to be replaced.  If you do well, they will be rewarded with experience points that level their stats, provide skill points, and increase their health.
The PVP is a solid experience, though sometimes bugs get in the way.  Occasionally there will be issues causing you and your opponents games to "desync," causing different outcomes for checks.  This could mean that sometimes a unit falls out of action for you, but not your opponent.  It's a problem.  Most of the time though it works just fine, and battles against a skilled opponent are still very rewarding.  It works well enough, that I've done some one off games on my YouTube channel, and even joined six other YouTubers and participated in a PVP league that ran for at least 16 battles.  My point here is don't let the occasional bug scare you off.
Another benefit to this game is the DLC.  Since release they have added two additional factions.  The Witch Hunters, and the Undead provide very different styles of play from the other four, and I still don't feel like any faction inherently rises above all the others.  In addition to this, they added a Hired Swords DLC that added another four units to the game that can be usable by the original factions.  This includes the Poison Wind Globadier, Smuggler, Worf Priest of Ulric, and the Doomsayer.  The Globadier and Doomsayer can be hired by the chaotic aligned factions while the Wolf Priest, and Smuggler are hired by the order factions.  It's a great way to mix up your war band and through an unexpected wrench at your opponent.
All said and done I would highly recommend this game.  The great support from the development team, the wonderful art style and game features, and the originality in the maps and warbands combines to make a very memorable and enjoyable experience.

Written for the benefit of TF2 players who take interest.
If i were to describe this game in one phrase, it would be: Team Fortress Classic: Source
Fortress Forever is where Team Fortress would have gone if not for the massive gameplay changes made in TF2. (Not that TF2 is bad, but it's certainly a completely different game)
FF retains the old quirky Quake-esque movement system, with some minor adjustments from its predecessor.
FF treats bunnyhopping as a game mechanic rather than an exploit. You can auto Bhop by just holding the spacebar, no more practicing precise timings and all this other insanity in order to compete. The addition of auto-BH lets the player focus on learning the fun parts of the movement system, rather than struggling with the timings of traditional hopping.
No longer can an especially skilled BHopper simply cruise at mach speeds around the map, there's a hard coded speed limit set for each class for the sake of balance.
The weapons are a bit less fantastical than in TF2 in many regards, but they're suitable to the environment in which they are used. All the classes you know and love are in there, and they're similar but at the same time quite different from their TF2 counterparts. The medic is a combat offensive class, for instance. The Heavy in FF can move a good bit faster than his TF2 counterpart due to bunnyhopping or help from his teammates!
As a new player to this game one thing will likely strike you as absolte BS. The grenades.
Grenades in FF take some getting used to, they're offhand so you can toss them at any time without warning! Your opponent may be shooting you but he could also be cooking a grenade to airblast your face! Each class gets different grenades, some unique and some not.
There's lots of gamemodes in FF that are possible due to its unique movement system and the inventiveness of the team fortress community. There is a Civillian class included which mapmakers can use for escort missions and such, and there are a GREEN and YELLOW team who can be put in for up to 4 sides of insanity!

Fortress Forever not only pays an excellent homage to the old TF games, but also distinguishes itself from its predecessors in small but important ways. FF greatly emphasizes individual competence, a refreshing experience for anyone frustrated at the teamwork mechanics of a game like TF2. Though this could be a turn-off for people looking for more direct co-operative gameplay, for anyone interested in jumping into a game and showing off your skills, this is it.
The gameplay of FF is very balanced. The creators went to great lengths to make the game enjoyable and fair. For example, their replacement of the Soldier's Nail Grenade with a more effective and less spam-y Laser Grenade will come as a welcome change to anyone who was on the receiving end of a Nail Grenade in TFC. (The devs' notes on the game are a good read, if you're so inclined.) One of the only weapons that made raise my eyebrows was the Demoman's Detpack, which can be used to terrifying effect on maps with lots of chokepoints. That aside, FF sports fair and smooth gameplay that is generally enjoyable.
On the note of the community for this game, I found them to be generally helpful, even to members of the other team. The people who still play FF are generally interested in the community's survival and they don't often turn people away just for being new to it. As long as you exhibit a basic understanding of the game and don't go out of your way to make it frustrating for your teammates, there's a place for you here.
