This game is... well... let me explain.
I essentially "grew up" playing Team Fortress Classic (TFC). God, I wasted several hours of my life on that game, staying up until 2:00 am, "conc jumping" across the map, "emp jumping" to far places to setup a sentry, etc. The game was a blast!
Then, in 2008, TF2 came out and I jumped on that, buying the Orange Box prior to its release (Primeval Warrior) if I remember right, is my title in that game. That game became everything I could hope for. Everything still had the TFC feel, but was more advanced. The graphics were updated, the sounds, animation... everything was an advance over TFC.
I forgot how many hours I logged in that game (under my old Steam account years ago and my newer one here). Hundreds... thousands?
Now, Fortress Forever made its way into my spotlight and I have to say... progress is a good thing. Unfortunately, this game shows just the opposite.
This game takes a step back from the advancements made in TF2 and goes for more of a TFC feel but... it's 2015. Back 16 years ago I may have thought this game was amazing, especially for a community mod project. But here, in 2015, this game just falls flat.
There's nothing actually wrong with it... in fact, I can say it's a lot like TFC. Perhaps that's what's wrong with it though? TF2 improved upon everything TFC offered... before they got obsessed with the stupid hat gimmicks and unlockables. Now, if FF went for more of a "classic" TF2 feel, I would be doing nothing but singing its praises right about now, but they didn't.
There are a few things that do feel more or less updated. The graphics, effects and animations, for instance, feel more in-line with 2005 than 1999. I give the Source engine credit for that mostly. Some of the things that fall short though are:
The lack of detail in maps - this is what feels more like a TFC throwback, than a TF2 remake. It's the little thing... miscellaneous crates laying on the side, barrels littering the landscape, rubble piled in corners. The maps look like something taken out of the original Half Life text book and pasted into this game.
Stiff animations - says it all really. No real body movement that makes the other players feel "alive" so to speak. It's like shooting BBs at plastic bottles. Which brings us to...
Lack of detail in player models - same as the maps, but even more so. I'm not a big blood and gore fan, but it still looked funny to shoot people and see bloody parts flying across the map in TF2. This, again, is more like TFC though - not much detail in the "gibs" area, very little blood and it isn't as persistent as TF2. So again, it just feels like shooting plastic player-shaped-bottles.
It's not a bad game overall, but we've come so far in 15 years, it's a shame to throw it all aside for the sake of nostaligia.

This game is one of the most cleverly designed competitive games ever.  Almost perfectly balanced from launch (amazing!)
The deck system turns the game from purely reaction/mechanics based into much more of a thinking-person's competition.  You know how in most fighting games there are two phases, the first where the players are still learning the mechanics and combos, and the second where the mindgames begin?  This game skips the first phase and goes straight to the second.
Not only does it go straight to mindgames, but you have to PLAN your mindgames out beforehand by building decks with specific strategies.  The depth on the level of strategy is huge, while the mechanics are dead simple, and that's why this game is an instant classic.
The mixed reviews are due to bugs and lack of singleplayer content.  If you come into the singleplayer thinking it is anything more than a tutorial for a 1v1 online 3D fighter, you'll be somewhat disappointed.  As far as bugs, there have been 3 patches in the first month, and the devs actively listen to concerns.
Sale or no sale, you cannot go wrong with this game.

Before I say anything name a game in your head where you play as a graffiti artist who tags his name across everything as he makes his reputation be known to a highly opressive government. Can you think of any besides Jet Set Radio? Well whatever the case you have to admit that this kind of game really unique in that feature.
Marc Ecko's Getting Up is a game primarily made by a guy who said gamers should get up off their butts and buy his games, where you play as a 20-something year old male named Trane who wants to tag his name everywhere across the city just for the sake of getting his name up. All while he is doing this he faces a dangerous graffiti gang called the Vandals of New Radius and an opressive regime of "peace-keepers" called the CCK which is lead by the government to stop vandalism and defacement of property to build a better and clean way of life in the city of New Radius.
Sounds cool right? Fighting your way to become the best graff writer in town while dealing with not only a rival graff gang but the government itself sounds like an alright idea yeah? How could they possibly make this a frustrating game with so many flaws it can't even really be called a gem? Well... they managed to somehow make it that way.
See Trane moves like a 20 year old noodle with the brains of a 2 year old, he really is unlikable due to being so rowdy to control, and it doesn't help that the camera messes with you all the time even with a mouse. The graffiti system is just awkward to use and if you're playing with a mouse then the controls will really start to mess with you, but it does require skill and mastery which makes it tolerable and actually kinda fun.
The story is good at best and mildly interesting somewhere in the half-way point but at the end it all just closes up so quickly leaving you confused at the end searching for possible answers. Besides being one of the most rushed endings I've seen in a game, it leaves you with absolutely no reward for finally beating the game, which makes it all seem kinda pointless leaving you with the words "What the f**k was that" in your mind.
Trane also stupidly upholds his completely fake philosophy of "not killing" but in the actual game you can throw people off buildings, push them into oncoming high-speed traffic or trains, or even  burn them ALIVE, and so on, which makes no sense since no matter what you're practically gonna do this at one point or another since these instant kill moves are pretty much required for later enemies. "We ain't out to hurt nobody!" is one of the lines he says later in the game, even though you will see someone die by your hands beforehand at least once, which while being stupidly hilarious, just doesn't make his character feel truly authentic.
Some characters don't even have that much character to them, most notably being a certain story-related asian woman you meet near the end of the game, purely being there for the sake of being there without being touched on at all, in fact you only get about one line of dialogue from her that only slightly tells you who she is. While the voice acting is decent and at times pretty good for this type of game, some lines of dialogue are inaudible because either something louder is playing or another line of dialogue is playing at the same exact time as it is.
There are some objectives and levels that are just extremely frustrating to do and just aren't that much fun. Other than being frustrating, certain levels can also just be boring. This port is also terrible and it is probably the worst port for the PC I have seen, and I found myself sometimes having to do some background stuff to get the game working again multiple times.
This port in comparison to the original PS2 version also brings an inconcievable amount of lighting and texture glitches which can rip you from the immersion, and some of these glitches don't ever leave for the some of the levels near the end.
There's also a whole bunch of other cons that destroy the game's likeness, making it an extremely flawed game that had so much potential, limitless potential even to be the best graffiti game on the market.
But for some unearthly reason I still love it goddamnit. It is likely due to nostalgia from playing it on the PS2 long ago but for some reason it is still fun to play when I feel like playing it, and a lot of the missions are actually really fun to go through, especially the first few levels and a few ones at the end, and for being a graffiti game in a genre that's not really explored especially nowadays it is pretty decent when you get down to it. The hip-hop soundtrack is simply incredible and really fits the theme of the game perfectly (RJD2 is in this for you hip-hop fans). The cheat codes are also really cool and are just a little extra treat when you might've finished the game.
Besides the pros mentioned above, the story, while not that well developed when you look at it, still never fails to immerse you, at least that was the case for me.
In the end, I'm going to have to reccomend it. Pick this up on a sale try not to bother with full payment since it might not be worth it, and if you do happen to have a console then PLAY IT ON THAT INSTEAD, since this PC port is really bad and full of technical issues. If you don't have a console, no worries, just find one of the guides in the community on how to play with an Xbox controller.
While I don't know why, I just love this game for what it is even if it is massively flawed, and it remains my tenth favorite game of all time to this day.

Unique art style, very intricate and often clever designs. I'd say about 90% of your time is spent playing the main course of the game, the side-scrolling shmup portions. The difficulty level is surprisingly not punishing, which is very different from the shmups I'm used to where you have to practice until perfect to make any progress. Ballpoint Universe takes a more forgiving approach by allowing you to gain points for levels via fallen enemies, you keep those even if you die and can upgrade offensive and defensive maneuvers. The variety and customization is quite nice though I find there are too many largely ineffectual types of bullet patterns/weapons. The keyboard controls aren't good, the mouse controls are much better. Gamepad seems like it would be ideal for this type of game. The levels themselves are pleasing, a variety of enemy types to learn, distinctive music to listen to, and often beautiful visuals. Typical for this genre but definitely no slouch here.
Another thing I really like is the other 10% of the game where you're in this side-scrolling adventure game portion. You can talk to other creatures, find collectibles on your journey, and have a bit of non-linear choice in stages. If you're doing poorly at a particular stage for example it's often possible to seek out alternate paths and come back later.
To bring up some complaints though, navigation during this phase is dreadful with the mouse configuration so I often switch to KB config and back to M again for battle phases. It's a hassle. Also, the graphics could be crisper and higher resolution. The paper-like textures are not as convincing on a larger display.
To sum it up, this is extremely good for the asking price. Recommended.

There are many hidden traps that are impossible to avoid unless you already know the levels and it doesn't in any way encourage you to build up speed, particularly in levels where the entire screen is dark except a small area around Sonic which are just frustrating.
The game itself feels slow. Despite the fact that the whole selling point of Sonic is his speed, his plodding acceleration in this makes it feel significantly slower than other platformers like Mario or Super Meat Boy.
There is still an annoying "life" system, even though this hasn't been relevant in any game outside of an arcade ever.
The graphics are not good. Sonic is a weird sort of cell shaded 3D that clashes horribly with the backdrops and enemies. If this came out on PS2 or from a one-person indie developer I would have complained about it looking bad. Considering it came out in the HD generation and is the flagship franchise of one of the biggest game studios in the world there's no excuse for this.

I am sure with 100's of reviews you can get a good feel playing a Workshop Videos if this game is for you. It is a board tactical turn based game based on the classic Mordheim board miniatures with a lot to like and a lot not to like. It will infuriate you and challenge you, and rewards great strategy and knowing when to equip the right items. However, since failure is deadly in this game, especially in story campaign, many will give up, especially the novice or inter. player in that their hard work doesn't pay off. You count on luck, not skill, especially early in the game.
If you adore strategy games, turn base games, there is a lot graphically to like, but I caution the cons.
PROS
•	A: Like X-com wonderful camera perspective in this game. It is in your face graphics and terrific action finishing sequences. The right in your face view makes it more fun.
•	B: Simple puzzle solving and map planning, with up to 9v9 battles.
•	C: PC controller friendly with instant switching from mouse to controller
•	D: Nice customization, terrific warband factions with DLC additional heroes and warbands you can add.
•	E: Fun story modes for all factions
•	F: Two type multi players modes that allow leagues, and friendly players customizations
CONS
•	A: Your faction continues like it or not. You don't get do overs. You will get death, dismemberment and cruel ailments if you fall. Now inter. and expert gamers may love this, but novice gamers, may not. There is a learning curve. Really up to your style. A novice player will get extremely frustrated because he will feel unrewarded for properly distributing skills, armors and positioning. It is all dice rolls.
•	B: It is simple Stratego Flag positioning, Rock, Paper, Scissors and luck. Despite percentage hit rates it really comes down to specific attributes. Remember when you play in multi-player or single an AI is deciding your die rolls. This could turn off players.
•	C: One of my biggest issues is armors can be useless, because of Armor Penetration and again you’re not always rewarded at all for armors.
•	D: Heavy Weapons which can do so much damage, have too many negatives to warrant use.
•	E: Early your range members are awful. Some may view that as a negative.
•	F:  The game needed more completion in its choices, A Diplomacy section, Proper Medical Section where u can interact and have strategic value to it, strategized goals or have great scenes of resolvment to the character you invested in. In faction character interactions, treason, more inventive skill choices etc. Adding more player choices, would have enhanced the core or rock, paper, scissors. It honors the board game, but it is stuck in that mechanic. Game lacked in game depth.
•	G: Another killer is the objectives in missions can be pointless in any battle. Collecting material mid battle is a waste since all you must do is let them collect them and kill them to get the goals. AI does not always make logical choices. See? makes no sense. However, player vs player different story.
•	H: Skirmishes PVP, can get one sided quickly. Novice players may feel inferior at times.
OVERALL: I can only give my take on it. There is a wonderful beginner’s tutorial in workshop and if you wanted to try it see the VIDEO in discussions to get a good feel of the game before buying. If you love Mordheim, then you will adore this game. I found the battles to get too redundant, and even as the party grows, it is all gang up warfare. However, a very addictive game and it served its purpose in honoring the original content. It lacks in game depth, like more end action animation sequences, more warbands and even think more scope in game item uses, like mounts, more diverse traps and pits, multiple warband melees like 2 v2. I do think they were limited in their development either by license or imitations in their development. Mordheim is a wonderful first try for this developer who will get better. I do think this game will be improved upon in either another version or additions. It is possible they add some missing mechanics and elements. Also follow the system requirements, lower older machines may not handle the game well. Mordheim is a great start.
MY SCORE: 3.4 of 5 stars

Mordheim is pretty impressive I have to say. A wonderful turn based strategy game, where you build up a warband of adventurers. Taking to the streets of this doomed city in pursuit of the ultimate treasure; Wyrdstones. A mystical magical element that is somewhat of a byproduct from a cataclysmic event. A bit like Aspertame being pooped from E.coli. That sort of thing.
As a paper and pencil RPGer (in my youth) and having to deal with stats upon stats. This is a veritable wet dream of numbers and calculations. All required just to make sure you don't trip up over your boot laces while swinging heavy chunks of sharpened (or just blatantly heavy), metal around. Usually in the direction of something nasty. And there are plenty of bad guys to go around. Though this is a Warhammer based game, so who is good and who is bad is usually down to how many different shades of grey you are willing to tolerate. Each of the four factions (plus some more available as DLC), have their own agendas and each will be pitted against you one at a time as you rummage through the ruined city, seeking your fortune and glory.
But beware, Mordheim is not an easy game. It is no doubt as harsh as it's tabletop counterpart and just as unforgiving. I  started my first campaign with the Sisters of Sigmar. A sect of violent battle NUNS with big hammers and even bigger thighs. And by the end of the second mission, three out of my five starting units had been hospitalised. My Hero unit had been laid up with internal bleeding. Then I had one lesser unit down with a shattered jaw. Good thing she wasn't a magic user, as she won't be uttering any incantations any time soon, if ever. And finally one poor lass got her leg chopped off and is now hobbling around with a broomstick shoved where only an orthopaedic surgeon would dare to go. And that was just the first TWO days (gametime), of their campaign. However, a few hours of gametime later. My nearly dead one-legged zealot (Oussia"Peggy"Praseck), has grown to be become one of my strongest units. And can dodge around on her up ended broomstick, faster than any other unit in the field. Like some sort of crazed holy paralympic ninja.... With a hammer !
I didn't hold out much hope for a successful outcome during the first few hours. It all seemed so hopeless and against all the odds, yet I had a total blast with it. and stuck with it.  The strategy elements are functional enough and it's about as near to any tabletop simulation that as you can get. And although excessively tough on beginners. Once you have some gear and more warriors to field. The more smoothed out and even, the gameplay structure becomes.
The background simulation is completely RNG based and as a result you have to prepare yourself for a beating. Though to be fair, the game does warn you regularly that it's more about how you cope with one atrocious situation after another. As opposed to being a total wargod and beating everything, all the time. Winning is a luxury and Mordheim reminds you of this constantly. With the high price of blood, sweat and tears that it takes, just to get the smallest of victories. However, if you are patient, keep your squad together and play smart. There is quite a bit that you can do to lessen the impact of injuries and fatalities. Neither of which are an absolute certainty, should any of your team come a cropper and be knocked out of the game. You can get lucky and have some just walk away from the ordeal with minor cuts and bruises. Again, this will be randomly decided at the end of the match. And is something you will be hoping for, considering the alternatives (Broken bones, severed limbs, amnesia or even permanent brain damage etc..). Which will result in that particular unit being forever handicapped in some way. Sometimes to the point of being rendered completely useless. But it's OK. Should this happen, you can always fire your crippled units as any decent humanitarian commander would.
It could do with a little more "oomph" in the graphics department (Though I did come to this straight from playing DOOM. Which as you may or may not know, is glorious to look at. Even if the game itself is a bit rubbish). So Mordheim may appear to lack a bit of polish on that front, but it looks well enough and does feature some well designed characters / monsters. Other than that, it's just a really good game. With stacks of options and an excellent selection of customisation for each individual unit. If turn based strategy is your thing. And you want a challenging TBRPG that would give even The Darkest Dungeon a run for its money in toughness. You won't go far wrong with this one.

Instead, you see what your active player sees, which improves the immersion.
Bad - Improving your gang (warband) members has no meaning.  As your gang gets stronger, the AI will automatically match them.  As your gang gets bigger, the AI will automatically match that, too.  Add a big guy to your gang - you'll be seeing those on the other teams, too.  GW games have this approach in table top games so that anyone can sit down, play a game with someone they just met, and things are balanced between the two players - even if one has a much stronger team.  In the PC games, it kills all sense of progression and meaning.  If everything around you scales to match you as you progress, you never really feel any sense of accomplishment.  This kills the game and actually only increases the penalties for failure.  Losing a strong team member and replacing them with a basic new member weakens the entire team and that individual can't really contribute.  You'll see people online trying to find workarounds - such as never levelling anyone up or having gangs split up into an experienced set and inexperienced set.  Ultimately, you'll eventually feel like there's no point, though.

I want to like this game. Actually, I want to love this game. But it is too strategically limited, too slow, and just too random. Let me explain...
On the plus side, the game evokes the Warhammer feel very well, and the ruined city idea means the developers have been able to create environments which are tactically interesting without seeming contrived. So I keep wanting play it - to dive into the evocative ruins, in a brutal, scrappy series of skirmishes where the risk of permadeath gives extra weight to every decision. That’s really appealing!
But....
First off, as lots of peoples' reviews have noted, as a player you are often victim of the random number generator. And this can be spectacularly random. (As an extreme example, consider that if you cast a spell there is a random chance of something bad happening; one of those things is that the character can lose all his hitpoints; if a character loses all his hitpoints, there is a random chance of permanent death. So, on one occasion I had my fully-healthy leader lose all his hit points as a random result of casting a healing spell – and I could have lost him entirely. Seriously.) Now, some will say "ah but Warhammer is always strongly random." And that’s true. But that doesn't change the problem that there is a basic disjointedness between actions and consequences - if your main character can be killed because you decide to cast a healing spell, or if a glass-canon or scout-type character can be killed because a random set-up put him/her right next to a pack of enemies, this is not rewarding or fun. It's just dis-empowering.
Secondly, this game is slow. Really, really slow. You wait while each enemy warrior moves even if you can't see him/her. The user interface takes a little while to go through, so your own turns aren’t uick. And then at the end of each turn you even have to sit through a message saying that the game is processing a move for each of the already dead enemies. So, even if you take a direct approach to hunting out your enemies it can take a while to finish a mission. And if you decide to try hit-and-run tactics, or lay traps and goad the enemy, etc., then it takes even longer. (The last mission I played it took 3 hours just to kill off four enemy mooks.) And of course because it is so slow you often won't bother trying different tactics - it's much less frustrating to just use a direct approach.
And the same problem of pacing that bedevils the tactical game also impacts the strategic arc. Upgrades to troops are earned slowly, and don't often seem to have much real impact. A typical upgrade might give you a bonus of a few percent to some skill or other. (So, after X hours of grinding a character, what do I have to show for it? +4% to something or other? Hmm.)
This leads to the third point - that there just isn't much room for experimenting with different strategies. After 20 hours my main warband was basically doing the same stuff it was doing at the outset, but with slightly higher stats. Nor is my strategy even really one I've chosen - it's just the strategy that seems to work best across all warbands. (I tried developing a hit-and-run style, I tried a missile-weapon-based warband that lured enemies into murder zones... nope, those strategies just aren't as viable as what appears to be the expected strategy.) And trying different warbands opened up no apparent strategic options, as each band (with a few minor variations, like the Sisters not having many missile troops) basically behaves the same way. By comparison, in the XCOM or Shadowrun games, as examples, having different combinations of characters allows you to approach missions in very different ways, and as the characters level up this opens up new playing styles and tactical options; in Mordheim, however, the slowly granted bonuses are really just allowing the characters to do the same stuff that they did before (perhaps with a little more specialization).
So, I really want to love this game. I enjoy the feeling of the cities, and am enticed by the idea of delving into the chaos-riddled ruins. But unless you're a die-hard Warhammer fan you may find that there is only so much fun to be had from ploddingly repeating the same tactics over and over and hoping that the random number generator doesn't do anything too crazy.

I purchased Vagante after having played version 8 from their website. Here are my thoughts.
tl;dr - Yes. Vagante is worth the purchase.
Pros:
~ Fairly unique. You can compare Vagante to both Spelunky and Rogue Legacy, but for me Vagante leans more toward Rogue Legacy.
~ Large replay value.
~ Unlockable traits. Playing the game you will unlock several traits that allow your new characters certain benefits.
~ Four classes. (Knight, Rogue, Mage, and "???" - of which we'll call her universal.) Each has their own unique playing style and starting equipment.
~ Addictive. The game may cause you to mini-ragequit when you first start, but you'll start it right back up a few minutes later.
~ Updates. This is an Early Access, but it is one of the few in which the developers actually come out w/ regular updates. I encourage you to download the version 8 edition for free from the developers main site and then purchase version 11 later. You will see a vast improvement between the two editions.
Cons:
~ Lack of instructions. It's a very simple game to play and you will learn quickly how to do things. However, you will not learn certain things right off the bat. (I was 15 hours in before I realized what some of the altars do and how to use them.)
~ No use for funds after a certain point. If you choose a certain trait, gold serves no purpose other than for a certain altar; which could be a game changer if you are lucky enough.
~ Vast superiority in certain weapons over others. (You will find that you will end up using certain weapons more than others due to how they work.
~ Organization. A little one, but still valid. You have a rather small inventory. When you equip something it "stays" in your inventory, rather than being linked to a character grid. Over time, you've got a full set of gear and almost no room to carry anything else. (Melee weapon, Ranged weapon, arrows/quiver/both, head, chest, feet, two rings, hands, neck/face, 5 total potions, 5 total scrolls.)
At this point I do not see why this game has so little success. Of all the garbage in Early Access of right now, Vagante is a diamond in the rough.

Over the past few years there have been a lot of 8-bit revival indie games. Some just have the appearance of a game from that era, others fit the mold perfectly and feel like they belong on cartridge (i.e. Shovel Knight, Undertow, Cave Story). Enter Tribute Games, who pride themselves in creating pixel art games based on the 8-bit and 16-bit era. I’ve been a fan of these guys prior to them becoming Tribute Games with XBLA & PSN release of Scott Pilgrim vs. The World: The Game from Ubisoft and their first official Tribute game Wizorb. They later brought the Metal Slug/Contra metroidvania Mercenary Kings to PC and PlayStation consoles and followed up the next year with the arcade style 8-bit survival beat em up, Curses N’ Chaos. So of course I was excited for the release of their next title, Ninja Senki DX. Much like Scott Pilgrim, the original Ninja Senki was a pre-Tribute game and was created by Tribute co-founder Jonathan Lavigne and released on PC as freeware back in 2010. So to celebrate the 5th anniversary of the game, Tribute decided to re-release the game on PC, PlayStation 4 and Vita and included an arranged soundtrack, a challenge mode, 2 secret modes, multiple endings and more.
Ninja Senki DX at it’s core is an old school platformer that feels like something out of the Famicom/Nintendo Entertainment System era regarding gameplay and difficulty. You play as Hayate a ninja set on revenge after his lady friend, Kinuhime was killed by a ninja demon. Simple enough, right? The game has you go through 16 stages filled with enemies that you take out with your Mega Bus….I mean Shurikens and various death traps which pretty much feels like a Mega Man game mixed with the fast action pace of the original Ninja Gaiden Trilogy. Much like those games, the controls are super tight and at times take precision to avoid certain death or to strategically take out your enemies. That’s pretty much it gameplay wise. There are no secret powers you obtain or anything like that, it’s a straight forward playthrough the stage and try to collect all Korban (coins) and kill all enemies as fast as you can for the best score. You have a boss fight every now and then but it’s nothing special but that’s okay. As simple as the game seems, it’s challenging as hell and trust me, it will cause you to rage in certain areas of the game. (Especially the last boss fight)
It’s definitely a title geared towards hardcore retro game fans and speed runners. Aside from replaying the main story at harder difficulty (hardcore mode), the only other replayability the game provides is the challenge mode and the 2 secret modes Ronin mode which allows you to play the story as one of the samurai enemies (Musashi) and boss rush. But comparing all that content to the price point ($5) it seems like a steal.
In closing, if you are looking for something to get your old school gaming or speed running fix ,especially if you are a fan of Mega Man, pick this one up. Ninja Senki DX is an awesome plate of retro goodness as well as the rest of Tribute’s catalog. Ninja Senki DX is available for PC via Steam, PS4 and PS Vita. You can also download the original freeware here.

Believe it or not, Jamestown is a Bullet Hell game that isn't completely about Bullet Hell. Jamestown is a beautiful top-down arcade SHMUP that can be picked up and played by anyone, a casual gamer or a Touhou veteran. There are five different difficulty levels with each level adding more and more bullets that can riddle your ship (but not kill you unless it hits the middle). The downside if you're a casual player is that you only have three levels, the other three levels require you to be playing on the harder difficulties, cutting the experience in half.
If you're willing to put your neck out there and aim for the skies, Jamestown is an experience you'd be foolish to pass up.
If you aren't willing, well, the game's still pretty damn awesome.

I've been on steam for several years and this is the first time I'm writing a review. The only reason I'm doing that is to support developers.  I spent about 60 hours on this game so far, so I might know a tiny little bit more about the game compared to people with ~10-15 hrs of gameplay.
There are still problems with connection quality in some region and devs have been working on it. Other than that, the game is amazing, with great balance (if you are willing to learn instead of smashing you keyboard/gamepad) and unprecedented communication between player base and developers. For me this is one of the best games I've ever played.

Only being 10 hours into the actual game, I've spent at least double the time searching the web for tips and tricks, and about a dozen hours into figuring out how anything even works. This game is not friendly to new players in the slightest.
Personally, I LOVE THE GAME. The concept, the artstyle, not to mention the (broken)freeflowing combat system.
The "singleplayer campaign" was short, maybe even unnecessary, but it was merged smoothly into the sandbox.
I love walking around as a nameless fighter, struggling to be the best. I get easily immersed, and seamless encounters with other players tries to fill the otherwise empty feeling the enviorment gives you. You get the opportunity to both team up with, or fight (un)lucky players should they cross your path. There are no communication methods besides simple body language, and there are about 10 different things to express.
The PVP is where it's at. Imagine fighting someone you don't know to the death with sick moves straight outta the Matrix. You can choose between SOO many unique moves, and they are going to keep adding more. Just the thought should've made this game a hit, but apparently it's not.
When it comes to the PVP combat, there are meta plays. That's the last thing a game built entirely on user defined customization needs. What's makes this system even worse is that new moves are often unlocked by fighting against them, which takes time, something newer players just don't have. I have personally beaten players twice my level when I was at 15, but also lost to players around level 10 when I was in the early 20's. This confuses not just me, but many players.
The game left me wanting more, which is both good and bad. It's good in the sense that I will definitely stay updated on its future. It's bad in the sense that it didn't feel like I played a full game to begin with.
All in all I will continue to play this game, however probably rarely simply because there's nothing to do for me but PVP at this stage. I don't think I need to explain why when there's a whole paragraph about it an inch further up in the review.

Mordheim: City of the Damned is a tactical, turn based strategy game inspired by Game Workshop's tabletop minataure game of the same name.
The game itself is beautiful, in as much as any game based in a city torn apart by plague, cthulu-esque dark gods and magic, and skirmishing adventurers can be beautiful. The designs for the maps and the members of each warband are well designed and suit the 'feel' of each unit type.
The A.I. whilst at time prone to bugs and occasionally being incredibly derpy is for the most part well rounded and intelligent. Each unit has it's own specific feel and then is reflected in the A.I. with Skaven swarming as much as possible and often retreating incrdibly early. Chaos are glass canons, hitting hard and constantly coming at your band with very little self survival instinct but dying fairly quickly compartively. Mercenarys are from the little I've experienced long range specialists with a good well rounded unit structure and the Sisters of Sigmar are tanky, with large amounts of hit points and heavy armour- charging into battle and hitting like frieght trains, but falling underneath swarm tactics fairly quickly.
All in all the difference in unit types, attitudes, playstyles and structure mix in to create a well rounded and appealing game.
The mechanics themselves are interesting and certianly appealing, if at times being a little slow to react. But considering the map sizes, the warbands avaliable at the fact the number generator for everything is a true random number generator I can forgive a few misinterprated actions and slow load times here and there.
The only advice I would give to anyone considering is buy it, choose a faction based on your specific style and if a skirmish or campaign takes more than 3 minutes to load close the game and restart it.

The bosses are a real challenge when you face them, whether you dodge & take potshots or get up in their face, two screw ups & you will be in a very dangerous position. However, I have a few qualms.
Both the Mage & the hidden character have little to no purpose to play as. The mage is physically weak & since most enemies rush you down, the only thing to do is use up a precious wand charge or run away & use Magic Missile. Running haphazardly in Vagante either leads you being cornered or dead via spikes & boulders. A skill that can cause him to levitate would aid with reversing rushing enemies.
The hidden character is an unarmed fighter, which isn't an issue, it's that she is bland. The aspect that makes Vagante fun from my standpoint is the unique abilities of each character, she has none. I believe this can be resolved is to have her gain more affinities the higher their level. Such as, every 2-3 levels is a new skill set for her. Unarmed skills would make her more exciting, such as a combo or directional attacks.
Verdict: As it stands Vagante is an addicting game with satisfying gameplay, even though it is not finished, I am awaiting the later updates with much anticipation.

What a strange yet fun game. Ballpoint Universe: Infinite centers around you being a doodle and fighting a vague logic based enemy. You fight using a customizable ship that lets you purchase and upgrade 2 weapons (swords, shields or guns), a nosepiece that controls super attacks and a body that gives health and other bonuses. You fight the Logic enemy in a side scrolling shooter and at the end of each section fight a boss with various destructible parts. The enemies in these sections are varied and it is always fun to replay them for the perfect rank. The art style is unique creating a world from something as simple as paper sketches. The only complaint I have is the platforming which involves you only using the mouse. This is only emphasized in 2-3 sections and all are near the middle or end of the game so it is not a deal breaker. However it does feel lazy that they couldn’t give alternate controls for these sections because these 2D sections are how you navigate the world outside of missions. You can also collect golden stickers in this section which may or may not do something if you get them all. Overall if you have been craving a game with customizable ships with swords don't pass Ballpoint Universe: Infinite up.

Ballpoint Universe is a very unique game taking after scrolling shooter games like Raiden.  The game's graphics are almost entirely hand-drawn with, like the name says, a ballpoint pen.  This gives the game a very unique look and the lore of the game is designed around that as well.  I greatly enjoyed this aspect of the game, though I think the story could have been fleshed out better.
The gameplay is pretty standard sidescrolling shooter fare but features an upgradable ship with a good variety of weapons and hull upgrades that provide different bonuses.  It even features melee weapons which are extremely powerful but obviously dangerous to use and shields to protect your ship.  I haven't played a similar game with permanent upgrades or melee weapons and it's a nice change of pace.
The game is pretty easy with enemies not posing much of a challenge if you have decent upgrades on your ship.  There is a lot of enemy variety however and they are all very creative, being very different from what I've seen in other games.  It makes the game much more enjoyable than a standard side-scrolling shooter with equivalent difficulty.
My main criticism of the game is the overworld.  Outside of the ship missions the game plays like a 2D platformer with the player exploring the game world to find information about the story and new missions.  Unfortunately the platforming controls don't work particularly well, especially jumping which completely kills your momentum with even a small bump against an object and makes climbing stairs much more difficult than it should be.  The areas are quite large and can be confusing to navigate, especially since there is no map function than I have been able to find.  Near the end of the game you need to jump across moving platforms which makes the poor controls even more of an issue.
This is only a small mark on the game however.  The platforming is only required to play through the story and endless mode is available from the start.  The rest of the game is very enjoyable and if you're the type of person who wants greater difficulty, endless mode increases difficulty as you progress through the waves, moving towards a full fledged bullet hell game later on.

When I first heard about this game's development I was understandably excited. Like many, I grew up with Sonic and his adventures on the Mega Drive. So an old-style 2D Sonic game with modern graphics sounded just the ticket. This does not feel like an old-style Sonic game. It feels like a less-than-average platformer that would've been only slightly impressive back in the 16-bit era. The physics are appaling for a Sonic title. Any kind of momentum you might build up, whether on land or in air, is lost the instant you release the direction button; kind of strange for the fastest mascot in the world.
It makes me wonder who exactly tested this game and if they ever even played any of the original 2D titles. It amazes me that somebody actually thought, "okay, this game is finished and plays perfectly, we can't improve on this in any way." Well, they were wrong.
For newcomers, this is a pretty average side-scrolling 2.5D platformer and you will probably get some enjoyment from it, if you can tolerate the physics. For those trying to find some nostalgia, you will find it most definitely in the soundtrack and the level design, but most definitely not from the handling.
It's novel, if nothing else. Episode II is far, far better with its nicer visuals, slightly more original soundtrack, creative level design and, most importantly, a gameplay style closer to that classic mid-90s Sonic feel than anything within the last 15 years, easily. Buy that instead.

I... don't really know what to say or where to start. Of the otome I've played, this might actually be my favourite. Every storyline is different, no cutscenes are identical once you actually get started on a route even though some events happen in all five storylines, all five of the men are interesting and unique in their own ways but I found none of them distasteful, and the protagonist's journey to obtain three good deeds is constructed in a way so her character development is believable. It's like a really good book you just can't put down, but I don't think that description does it justice.
I will say though, Peter Pan isn't a fairy tale in the way the other four are (that is, it's not a short story, it's a full-on book AND a play), but frankly I don't mind since I'm a huge fan of Peter Pan and Waltz's story might have been my favourite of the five. Also that's not really a complaint, it's a logic flaw.
I went in the recommended order (Rod, Karma, Rumpel, Fritz, Waltz) by sheer coincidence, and it's the order I think it works best in having cleared all five of them. You could switch Fritz and Waltz, if you're concerned about being spoiled on how to break Waltz's curse, though, because how it's done is spoiled in Fritz's storyline, but Waltz's storyline also spoils Fritz's curse and Waltz tells you pretty early on how to break his, so either way you're going to have one of them spoiled.

The act of not copy-pasting identical events between storylines might seem a small thing, but I appreciate that though this scene happens in all five stories, it's different in all five of them. I really enjoyed the concept itself. I just want more, I suppose, and I'm kind of disappointed I finished all five storylines already, haha.

I've never been one to really play Otome/Visual Novel games but I found this one was free and decided it might be a nice way to explore a different kind of gaming.
I will start off with the art style, which is the first thing that I noticed immediately. The art is gorgeous from the splash screen, to the sprites, and finally all the way to the backgrounds and the closeups. You can tell how much work the devs put into this and it definitely shows. The art style is what I would call a typical anime style, but that doesn't make it bad.
Next, the music was beautiful. It wasn't super over the top and in your face, but it was exactly where it needed to be. It added the perfect amount of ambiance to set the mood for each scene. My only complaint would be that it could get repetitive, but really it's to be expected when you're trying to read through scenes over and over. It's a miniscule complaint really.
The storyline was well done. I enjoyed how every Fairytale curse has a slight twist, making the story more interesting while remaining similar to actual fairytales. This  would seem predictable,  but it allows the player to piece things together while still remaining in the dark, while simultaneously having an idea of what might possibly happen. I especially enjoyed each of the endings (for good endings) where there was still an almost bittersweetness to it all.
(Here comes the fortune cookie bit) After all, life isn't 100% happy ending, there's going to be some sour with the good.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys some good fluff and good graphics. Even better, this game is free, so really there's nothing to lose.

Normally, I don't play otome/visual games because I see the usual tropes and very overused stereotypes that makes the characters seem like cardboard cut-outs of each other. This game I came on a chance when I watched a YouTuber play it. And I'm glad to say that this is one of the rare visiual/otome games I genuinely liked.
First, I was instantly intrigued by the MC. She wasn't anything I've seen in a visual novel, where usually the MC is dense to a point where she lacks any character development at all. The MC was the oposite of what I expected from the usual. Her flaws were the best part about her, and it made her relatable. An unlikeable character, in my opinion, is better than some Mary-Sue. That being said,  my absolute FAVORITE parts of the game was the character development and writing style. It was realistic. Lucette didn't change overnight. She slowly became a better person through her actions and choices.
Most importantly, she stood up for herself. She didn't let herself get mistreated or pushed around by anyone, even if they were the love interests. The MC helped herself and others become a better person. Yes, the game did use stereotypes, but it was well-done. It gave distinct traits that made characters unique and a three-dimensional person. I'm also very impressed that, while the game was fairly low-budget, the developers managed to weave a well-written story with depth and intrigue. The graphics weren't the highest of quality, but, again, even otome games with beautiful animation can have the crappiest plot and characters.
Very long rant, but there was just much to say about the game!

1) First of all, a lot of players think this is like a “souls-like” game, but it isn’t, so if you are looking for that kind of experience, avoid it.
2) Now, while this game is labeled as a fighting game, it has and hasn’t elements, which could be pointing to its current problem: the amazing variety of attacks on Absolver dooms itself to the “meta” and it doesn’t appeal to its own description of “construct your own deck”). It has a false sense of freedom, which clearly isn’t.
3) Maybe the most important thing about it all: the playerbase. Many “pro” players tend to lecture the newbies because they don’t learn or understand the mechanics of the game, ergo, they are bad or don’t deserve to be in this game (they use “logical” words to say it, the “hardcore mentality” if you will). Those pro gamers don’t understand that if a product doesn’t appeal and isn’t easy to get in by your market by default, it means is failing. Remember that if a game can only be played in ALL its mechanics by the 10% of your market, CLEARLY is a problem, and you should be addressing it by your 90% of the possible players, not the 10% that doesn’t contribute to your sales or image in the world. The number of players in-game is criticized as “not showing the true playerbase”, but people don’t understand how these tools work in business. Have all this in mind.
In the end I can recommend it to certain market, but in the long term, there are other multiplayer and PvP experiences that will eventually get your attention… just see how LoL, Overwatch, WoW and FFXIV have established their own niche in its own genre… I was expecting Absolver to define its own place in its genre.

Too dark and terrible camera positioning. The maps for the Combat Trials are horrible and randomized so you either get too dark or too small. I'll elaborate on what's wrong with this game.
Too dark: The essence Mining or Tower Adal are the worst locations for anyone playing this game who doesn't set their Shadow to low. Play it on high or Ultra and the game is pure darkness and chances are you'll be fighting blind unless you change your settings. There's no in-game slider or modifier for Brightness or Gamma. Essence Mining is a horrible offender of this though not as dark as Adal. Essentially you'll fall off a ledge or two if you don't put your Shadow settings to low. That's open world stages.
Combat Trial - Get rid of Adalian Columbary and Imperial Quarters (Library). Those are the worst offenders on the list. You have a map with stairs where your attacks can and will whiff if someone's height is even slightly more elevated than you, and this is hilariously true of thrust moves of most kinds (jumping). The map is insanely dark and bad. Most players on this map prefer to fight in the small little circular flat surfaces either at the top or bottom, and these areas are ridiculously small and dark. Guns, Gore & Cannoli: A side scrolling shoot-em-up that actually tries to look and play different and does so with aplomb.
The Steam eperience in recent years is a flood of derivitive games with the same easy hooks that succer money out of people. "Open world survival", "Metroidvania", "Retro insipred" and so many other buzzwords that are flung around like toys in the hands of a spoiled child. And what Guns, Gore & Cannoli does different is put forth some real effort into graphics, art styles and voice acting to make a stellar side scroller that doesn't rely on dated "8-bit" graphics.
The story is cheesy and entertaining, and comedic in the same way that the names of the characters in Airplane! were. You are Vince Cannoli, a local mob enforcer sent to Thugtown to do your job. However once you arrive, you find the whole town is in the thick of a zombie outbreak released during St. Patrick's Day. With a gun, a lot of one-liners and a desire to see his job through, Vince goes through the town trying to figure out why the hell this is all happening.
Gameplay is fairly rudimentary, basic movement and weapons with little variation but easy to understand without going into elaborate details. The Graphics and Artstyle are the game's trick card, because they're stellar for what it is. While it is 2D, the basic look is comic inspired. And I don't mean "Telltale's lazy shading" I mean actually comic book inspired, like♥♥♥♥♥♥Tracy or The Shadow. Character features are slightly exaggerated while detail is still taken. Every gun can be positively ID'd, there's some intriquite detail behind both backgrounds and the various enemy types in the game and there are moments where I did go "This is some impressive looking♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;.
So if you want a side scrolling shooter that isn't knee deep in 8 or 16 bit art style with a fun main character, solid gameplay, great graphics and options for local co-op, here you go. Guns, Gore & Cannoli is enjoyable as hell to play, and I'll applaud the devs for actually trying to make an interesting and different game in a marketplace filled with generic similar crud.

Ninja Senki DX is essentially a remaster of the original Ninja Senki freeware game by Tribute Games, now on Steam, PS4, and PS Vita.  I've included my full thoughts about the game in video format here:
Taking the role of the ninja Hayate, you must traverse 16 stages to avenge the death of Princess Kinuhime!
Ninja Senki DX is a tough-as-nails action-platformer with a focus on perfection in execution and memorization.  While it's possible to sight-read levels to get through them, collecting all of the coins, killing all of the enemies, or completing a level within the 'speedrun' time limit definitely requires practice.
There's a lot of intentionally-NES-style design here.  Enemy placements are such that they'll catch you offguard the first time almost every time. Jumps are tight, leaps of faith are not always marked.  I would call this a negative for most games, but Ninja Senki has been built with this style in mind.  Instead of being frustrated by unfair design, I found myself wanting to take another shot at it and perfect my technique.
The DX version includes a completely remastered soundtrack that is *exceptional*, along with the charming 8-bit style graphics, and tight controls, Ninja Senki DX ends up being a pretty satisfying platformer in the $5 range.

The 'time played' figure, currently showing as 0.8 hours, is out by a factor of... tens of thousands. At least. That's because this is the latest version of a classic that I've been playing for forty years.

Think of them as a tribute to its past, and don't worry about them becasue the 'turn based strategy' game play is the thing.
One of the very first 4X games (it's where Sid Meier's Civilization got half its ideas from), you can play it like the simple and elegant 1980s 'Empire: Wargame of the Century' or get more complicated. Quite a lot has been added, but it's a strong enough game to cope with the extra weight and if you don't like it, it's all optional and editable.
Here's to the next 80,000 hours.

Such a fantastic mod! A must have for Team Fortress Classic fans!
Coming from a guy who wasn't a fan on TFC compared to TF2, I was a bit "eh" on this mod. I mean the idea of it was interesting, but I thought nothing of it. After playing about 3 matches I can tell you this mod is fantastic. This mod gave me a reason to fully appreciate TFC. It's fun, challenging, and giant learning curve for me.
This is NOTHING like TF2 which I can understand. This mod was made by fans of TFC that wanted to bring back the community and re-imagine TFC like never before. They did just that. After playing this mod, I see why many people prefer TFC over TF2 and how a lot of people say FF is what TF2 should've been!
For the game itself, the graphics are about the same as Half-Life 2. Nothing extremely good like CS:GO and nothing extremely stylized like TF2. Gameplay wise, it's basically the same as TFC, but running of the Source engine. All the clases have a huge learning curve and is hard to master which keeps the game fun and challenging.
One thing I appreciate the devs for is the tutorial. It definetely teaches you everything you need to know about TFC which helps a lot. Unlike most tutorials in other games, FF actually teaches you EVERYTHING you need to know.
I can't be for certain I'll play Fortress Forever forever (heh. Get it?), but this is one hell of a mod! I absolutely recomend it fans of TFC and maybe even TF2! If you have Half-Life 2, GET THIS MOD NOW!

Too dark and terrible camera positioning. The maps for the Combat Trials are horrible and randomized so you either get too dark or too small. I'll elaborate on what's wrong with this game.
Too dark: The essence Mining or Tower Adal are the worst locations for anyone playing this game who doesn't set their Shadow to low. Play it on high or Ultra and the game is pure darkness and chances are you'll be fighting blind unless you change your settings. There's no in-game slider or modifier for Brightness or Gamma. Essence Mining is a horrible offender of this though not as dark as Adal. Essentially you'll fall off a ledge or two if you don't put your Shadow settings to low. That's open world stages.
Combat Trial - Get rid of Adalian Columbary and Imperial Quarters (Library). Those are the worst offenders on the list. You have a map with stairs where your attacks can and will whiff if someone's height is even slightly more elevated than you, and this is hilariously true of thrust moves of most kinds (jumping). The map is insanely dark and bad. Most players on this map prefer to fight in the small little circular flat surfaces either at the top or bottom, and these areas are ridiculously small and dark. Cramped spaces have its own slew of issues involving the stupid and poor camera of this game when dealing with players in corners or walls. Adalian Columbary is more or less the same and unless you want to be cheesed into a corner where it's dark and the camera will pan vertical on your head it isn't worth fighting on.
Speaking of the camera: fix the camera. Why does the camera go over the head of the player? Why not have the camera behind the enemy player when someone is pressed to the corner or wall? For a game that relies on directional precision you'd think the developers would anticipate or even have the foresight to adjust proper camera alignment. When someone has you cornered there's no way around being defensive at this point. When you play Windfall, for example, you cannot truly read which direction an attack is coming from if you can only see the top of player's heads forcing you to either spam your fastest attack or turtle until your guard is broken. I've been lucky to have a mix of players who back up once this occurs probably because they realize how terrible the camera in this game is. Combine this with the darkness and you'll be lucky to even fight out of any corner you are in. Earthquake can only do so much and if you do not have it equip for these specific maps then you're going to be punished.

I am a competitive player and combat mechanics are extremely important to me.
Absolver has a deep combat system but may seem over shadowed by spamming abilities.
Sadly its easier to spam and leave it to chance than to take an effort in using your combat style (parry, evade); especially trying to parry or evade an attack move which starts on one side but decides to come from another. Or that one attack move where the guy defies gravity to bend his back over just to throw a punch. So sometimes the game suggests you rather not waste time reading these kinda moves, just spam quick attacks and interrupt the opponents' attacks instead.
The only 1v1 duels that I truly enjoyed where against players that bother to learn footwork/positioning, mind game timing, the over shadowed combat system instead of practicing their fidget spinner spamming capability. Its 2017 and you can't even rebind your stance/target-switch/evade/parry keys, please add this option. However; extremely beautiful art direction and animations.
I don't really regret spending 30 bucks; it’s a good price for what it has to offer but I just find it disappointing; for here is another game that has massive potential and hopefully in due time it gets better and not worse. If devs are reading this review, here is a possible solution; try lowering the attack speed cap of the fastest moves till you find a sweet spot. With this it is less beneficial to spam as it is easily parried/evaded therefore feints will come into play; encouraging skilled combat only. Or anything revolving around making it less beneficial to spammers such as additional exhaustion; you get the idea. You can even do it the other way where skilled players who parry/evade catch thier target off guard and maby do critical damage. If not maby have the stun effect from evade/parries longer so as to be able in pulling off one of thoese slow but strong attacks.
Edit:
Game made me frustrated sometimes but every time I leave, this game just calls me back. Absolver is a very unique game. The animations are amazing and so is the art style with so much mystery to absolver’s lore. Today I was lucky enough to 1v1 non-spammers a bit more often and it was just amazing. We were throwing feints and the mind games where just next level sure I lost a couple but dayume it was so satisfying. I also enjoy how you take a break from queuing in 1v1s to look around the world for a particular combat move for your deck. So, to stop having fast-chain spamming trolls take this experience away from me, I decided to sit down and think about how to deal with them as I am sure to come across in match-making.
I try to get better at my craft; I try to stay calm, be positive and respect the fast chain spam as a form of fighting style. As I pushed myself to analyse every move to out play, looking for openings and what not, I started to see how deep the natural mechanics of combat is. I believe the frustration comes when you do not see a quick solution, but through failure you see opportunities. Sure, enough I did come across a fast spammer in match-making; I don’t have a direct easy solution but I started to notice subtle things like listening to the rhythm of the hits. These intervals between the spamming attacks where little windows of opportunity. You are right, these windows are very small since their attacks are fast chains; but theoretically spammers are giving you more windows of opportunity. As compared for them, if you turtle in normal block and get stunned where they only get one or two hits in, right after you start to turtle up again. Obviously, I’m not a big fan of turtling but you get the idea of squeezing a quick attack in between these rhythmic intervals.
Yeah so, it’s a lot of pressure fighting spammers but maybe this game requires a high skill level from us and you can imagine victory is not an equal thing; in the sense that everyone has their own unique fighting style timing that you are required to improvise to. So, to win every 1v1, the game requires you to be a master at the personal attribute of improvisation.
Having an open mind and fighting fast spammers subconsciously made me aware to be more familiar with their move animations and hit timings. So, I guess at the current state Absolver has an extremely high skilled game requirement. I am sure the majority of people who give bad reviews where those unlucky enough to fight troll spammers non-stop. Clearly the solution to wining spammers is not an obvious one so people get angry like me. I have tried to come up with some possible solutions for how to defeat them.
1.	You could use attacks that carry the parry bonus, attacks that also evade, or that charging attack where you take a hit but get to land yours eventually.
2.	It’s good to have at least 1 opening fast attack or chain; this is the attack you use to squeeze in-between their fast chain spams.
3.	Another solution I use for kick spammers now is to dodge back between the intervals and do a kick attack (long range) knowing he would eventually land into mine when he throws his next spamming attack. But this back dodge is only more possible on the “Fast” mobility setting. Also, to note the back dodge is a better option as compared to dodging sideways. This is because side dodges won’t work against spammers that use that fast floor spinning kicks instead; unless you’re really good at using the windfall jumping/ducking evades.
4.	Normal blocking against troll spammers. So not all their attacks are equally fast; though some of these spammers just stick to throwing out only the fast ones and not all, but the idea is to wait in normal block for them to use up their fast ones and their next one is not going to be as fast; one where you are able to react to.
5.	Classic stuff like being able to pull off a guard breaking attack which kills their stamina is nice too.
6.	Finally, as you can see all the solutions seem to converge in having a combat deck that is able to improvise to many fighting styles.
Instead of the whole “can’t beat them join them” attitude I have been playing the polar-opposite where I use extremely slow but strong attacks. This play style forces me to calm down and be as precise as possible when deciding to launch an attack.  I would also like to note that I personally had a better chance at using the windfall combat style as compared to my previous style as forsaken. So since I am able to evade more I get my stamina back; that is probably the bonus Absolver has given us against fighting spammers since this keeps us at a higher stamina advantage from being exhausted, as compared to our fast chain spamming opponent.
Even with these solutions though I may get a couple of hits in, I would still lose to them as the game is expected of us to play at our best performance consistently. But yeah it kinda worries me to see not many people get to experience the awesome side of what the game has to offer and may just quit playing in the early stages. Maby absolver can come up with tutorial videos of how to defeat such a fighting style and remind them the game is of high difficulty; as now everyone is most likely to blame the game as “badly-designed” instead of challenging themselves to find a solution.
For the developers to create a complex combat system is not easy, not forgetting the beautiful animations and atmosphere. With all this for just 30 bucks we honestly should not hate on the game. Sure, the game may have its flaws but I realized we should be thankful for a group of people that got together to make this game even happen in the first place. The game is still new and I was too quick to judge, there is something very unique about Absolver and in time extremely good players will stand out to show the rest of us how the game is meant to be played. Until then let’s stay calm, have an open mind and embrace the challenge to being a better player.

TL;DR - gorgeous graphics, wonderful story, immersive world, engaging characters, no major problems or shortcomings, and I can't believe IT'S FREE so go ahead and play it already!
At time of writing I've only finished the first route, Rod's, so this will be based on that.
First off, that intro video swept me away! I wasn't expecting vocals so when those kicked in it became 10x more interesting! And the video itself was really well put together. The title screen looks lovely, in fact all of the art and UI look incredible - so much so that I can't believe this game is free! Now when I started playing all I could do was groan at the MC's awful attitude and horrible people skills. She's an awful person to start out with, and I could not sympathize with her in the least. This made me worried for how well the story was going to go and how much I'd enjoy it, but surprisingly (or maybe not? seems a little tropish) she does get better and eventually learns her lesson. In fact, watching her grow as a person was one of the most interesting parts of the game. I wasn't able to relate to her, but I enjoy her as a character.
I was surprised to find out that you choose your route as an explicit option. No guessing the right responses to the right people to get the route you wanted; they are presented in a pretty list and you simply select one. You still have to get all of the right responses to get the good ending for that route, but that was to be expected. Speaking of that, the right choice indicator didn't work how I expected at all. If it's your first time through a route it'll make a small sound at some point after you made your choice (if it's right). If you've gotten the bad ending, it unlocks the fast forward feature which skips to the next choice, and the right choice indicator becomes a sound and a purple crystal in the top right. I think it would be nicer to have it indicate the right choice BEFORE you make it, not after, but it's not a big deal. Saving and loading is incredibly fast.
The story is incredible. Once I got to about Chapter 2 or 3 (can't remember), when things really start picking up as the MC meets some new people and is taken to a new place, I got sucked in. The characters are all interesting, and I was immediately curious as to everyone's backstories and why they act the way they do. After choosing Rod's route (I've decided to follow the recommended order), things pick up again and I started to really care about him and his problems. The partnership between him and the MC is a rocky road, but it seems to bring out the best in both of them and I loved that! A lot of plot points were fairly obvious and easy to figure out, but I still teared up at that bad end and felt the love with the good end :3 Now I'm eager to do the other routes to find out what thier issues are and how to resolve them. I'm not so much interested in dating them anymore, because Rod is best boy <3
Oh and there's cool visual treats like a simple bowing animation (yeah the portraits just bob up and down but it looks like bowing/curtseying!) or a special effect when magic is casted. I also like the inclusion of the MC's portrait in the corner when she's talking, and the super fancy font for names - so pretty! The game is unbelievable gorgeous and for that alone I wouldn't mind paying something for it, not to mention the incredible story is worth more on top of that!
I only have a few nitpicks: there's a couple of typos and grammar errors, not many so far though so it's not a big deal. In fact, again, it is very well written! And I also wish there was a borderless window feature, as I was trying to talk to a friend while playing it and it was kind of frustrating, even with a second monitor. That's about all I can think of..
I would definitely recommend this if you like visual novels/otome, fairy tales, and the subversion of fairy tale tropes!
PS: I'd love an instrumental version of that theme song ;)

The game is a lovely Turn Based Strategy with a couple of flaws in the execution only.  Often the characters themselves appear as if they can fit through something, but they cannot when you try.  Also there are times when enemy units have immunities to various mechanics, and it does not show this on the buff/debuff menus when you inspect an enemy unit prior to attacking.  That being said, this game does not show mercy or cut you any slack, but that is part of the appeal.  It is a very tactical and thinking man's game, where you can easily lose a character mid-mission, and they end up being useless or near useless afterwards, and you are counting the days until you can buy a replacement.  It is a beautiful application of a masochistic strategy game, that makes you feel reaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaly good when you out-maneuver your enemy, and leave them in a horrid position to fight from, while you overwhelm them with debuffs and swarm tactics.

I picked it up during the Steam Summer Sale and got the expansions and DLC.  It can be really daunting at first but it's an amazing game.  It's my favorite game that I have played since Dark Souls 2.  I highly recommend it for anyone who likes turn based strategy games.

Ballpoint Universe is a mostly competant shoot-em-up that relies heavily upon a unique and wonderful hand-drawn art style to keep you interested. The game itself feels very Jekyll and Hyde. On the one hand you have the shmup half of the gameplay that feels solid, albeit nothing spectacular. It starts to lose a lot of its challenge once you begin to upgrade your ship beyond your original parts, but I still had a fair amount of fun with it thanks largely to its highly detailed art design and a decent soundtrack.
When you aren't playing through the shmup portion of the game, though, you'll be struggling with the platforming portion. I say without hyperbole that these are probably the worst platforming controls I've ever experienced in any game. Even the simplest of jumps can start to feel like monumental efforts. The end of the game in particular features some sequences that are far more difficult and frustrating than they have any right to be.
If Ballpoint Universe was just a shmup I'd have no problem recommending it. It's a basic shooter but the art style alone is worth experiencing. The platforming simply cannot be ignored, though. It's atrocious and nearly ruins the game. I'd probably give the game a "thumbs middle" if that were an option.

My favorite of all the available MMOs after playing these games for about five years now.  Much closer to pencil and paper D&D than Neverwinter Online and a much better game as well.
PROs
* Extensive content after eight years of updates and expansions (since 2006) with two major D&D campaigns: Eberron and the Forgotten Realms.
* The original quests are focused on group play and are similar in layout and tone to pencil and paper D&D modules.
* More detailed character customization than any MMO that I know of.  You can play a halfing ninja assassin (dark monk), a drow elf wizard / fighter, or a warforged artificer / ranger, among many other combinations.
* True Reincarnation system which allows a single character to start again at level one with a new class and/or race and become more powerful each time.  Indepth replay ability for this reason.
* A mature, dedicated player community that wants to expand the community.
CONs
* Ongoing bugs / exploits that are being slowly addressed by Turbine - but this doesn't make the game unplayable.
* The graphics and some other features are aging when compared to very new MMOs.

TL;DR:  it's a bullet hell shmup, which is the only deciding factor as to whether you'll like this game.
If you dislike flying a widdle ship through a maze of deadly glowing balls, you won't like Jamestown.  But if you're at least open to possibly enjoying such a game, you'll like, even love Jamestown.
Its only real flaw is that its premise and story are a bit overdone (Walter Raleigh flees the Spanish in the seventeenth century by escaping to the New World, except the New World is Mars), but the execution is masterful, from the beautiful eight-bit sprites to the solid mechanics to the surprisingly superb soundtrack.
There's unlockable challenge strages, multiple ships with different secondary firing modes, a ramping difficulty to keep you improving, and even DLC with three more ships (including a fourth that randomly mimics one of the other seven).  And seriously, that music.  Kinda freakin' awesome.

Jamestown is a wonderful homage to the genre, up there with Locomalito's Hydorah, and features a setting that quickly became one of my favorites - a 17th century alternate history that repositions "the New World" in the literal sense, while avoiding steampunk cliches. The music is fantastic, reminding me of the best of PS1 era orchestration in games like Final Fantasy Tactics, the pixel art is pretty much spot on, though a bit messy-seeming in places, and I only wish I had some people here in front of my macbook to play 4P with.
Jamestown is retro-graphicked pattern shooter that adds a lot of the fun factor that most pattern shooters lack.

Fun Factor: 4.5 / 5.0 : A wonderful game that'll have you play over and over again.  Every level up point is very rewarding. Choice of weapons could help add to customability in the beginning with the game, as the sword can be a frustrating first weapon.

And later a double-barrel.
And later a tommygun.
And later a revolver.
And even later a pump-action, a flamethrower, a bazooka, and at this point the zombies might as well re-kill themselves, save you the trouble.
Unless you're a masochist like me and played this game on Hard, in which case get ready for a shooter experience wherein 5 different things could be moving at once and unless you get the gist of the enemies you face, you will die. A lot. Only really got frustrating on the final boss, where the only thing that could help is the bazooka, as I couldn't stand still long enough to get more than a few shots off and I only lasted a minute at a time, if I was lucky.
My only other complaint is that once you've done the main story, there's not much left to do for single-player. When I saw the trailer for this game, I imagined something akin to This War of Mine, with the hub base that you return to between missions or the like. I feel that a hub would've extend the game's play time and made it much more worth the price. But, that's clearly not the game the producers wanted, and here's hoping they make a sequel.
