Mordheim is essentially a  turn based action strategy game that tries to reduce the feeling of turn based action, and by that I mean that the game removes more traditional elements like grids square moves etc, your movement, for example, is just like you would move in an action game save the distance and actions you take are limited and create almost a checkpoint system where you can back track your movement...so long as nothing happens during that movement.
It is set in a city that is basically hell on earth, where demons roam and everything is trying to kill you while you collect little green rocks called wyrdstone that serve as your main currency generator, which incidentally is also trying its best to make sure you die by debuffing you with magic radiation. The fish on the walls spray junk on you to debuff you, traps are everywhere and any corner could have a very angry woman with a hammer or a giant rat with big claws to maim, kill or eat you and then loot your corpse.
Surviving Mordheim is like surviving the game of thrones… don’t get too attached to any one character as it will die, lose a leg, arm or eye when you least expect it. There is no save scumming and you get what you get. Which is thematically accurate and well Mordheim.
There are moments in this game that are brilliantly funny, like seeing the enemy caster blow him or herself up… it's not so funny when it happens to you. The luck gods are fickle creatures and they do not like you. And that is the core of this game, managing and minimizing luck and risk.  If you can manage your risks well and understand what and why things happen, you will do fine.. ish. However, there are times when you will out right get bent over and torn to shreds, and you will pay for your mistakes. Which to me is part of the challenge of the game
The AI is not brilliant and sometimes the enemy will sit their licking the walls if it gets stuck on something..like their wagon, though overall the AI acts in a more or less intelligent fashion with the scripted missions being better about it, the AI is exploitable. I once trapped half the enemy force on my own wagon due to its inability to “see” or register some objects and I threw bombs on them until they died..or switched to range and got out of its hole to shoot me. However, this level of ridiculous exploitation is a bit rare and normally one or two enemy AI will get stuck like this every few missions..so don’t count on it.
The AI also tends to “prey on the weak” meaning your new hero is going to be target number 1 more often then not..so be aware.
Common complaint: other then the AI is regarding impressive..personally I don’t use them all that often as they cost me 2 hero slots and I lose versatility for raw power but here is the thing, as others point out when you 1st get your impressions as you will always be facing an impressive that out levels you own until late game “ie L7-10”. This is true and often frustrates people who play, fair enough, but the trick is until you impressive beefs up, don’t ever have it go head to head with other impressive instead treat him like any other new member, protect it have it beat on weaker opponents and use it as a tool to support the warband, don’t think “raaahg kill!” and send it running off on its own…its just going to die.
This game can be a great deal of fun and for me it is…likewise it can be an exercise in frustration as it will punish you, but the sense of reward when you do manage to complete a few chapters is that much more worth it, because unlike other games that just kinda had you victory with a simple reload, you haved, to earn it here..through a mix of strategy, luck and occasionally balls. For some people that is an awesome thing for others not so much

Morheim: City of the Damned is a turn based game where each character takes their turn based on their stats. The game is based off of a table top game so a lot of the percentages that decide outcomes are based on dice roles.
Each of the four factions in the game, well five with the dlc, all have their own strengths and weaknesses. Even the fifth faction plays different enough than the other factions where if you are enjoying the game and want something new it is worth getting. The other DLC so far are additional characters that can completely change how you run your warband. The reason I bring up the DLC is that even before I got the DLC I had to fight against the DLC warband. An interesting feature in the game is that any of the warbands you can make you will have to fight in the game. With how many ways there are to build a warband that makes a variety of things you can run into in the game. Also if you see an opponent in the game with an interesting build that you like it is possible to make a build similar to it regardless of whether it is a player or AI's warband.
Cons i have heard are that people enter the game thinking of it as a character management game but it is a warband management game. The reason it is not a character management game is if a character gets taken out in combat at the end they can either get a minor injury, major injury, killed, or a combination if you are really having bad luck. Injuries in the game effect a characters overall stats so sometimes you have to decide whether to keep a charcter or hire a new guy to replace it. This makes it where you sometimes you have to risk the possibility of loosing a guy permaneantly for the better of your warband. In one of my warbands i had a guy loose his arm so he can only loose one-handed weapons but it increased his dodge rate. This is just one way of how a permaneant injury effected one of my characters. Also never in the game click abandon match no matter how bad things are going wait till you can either retreat or don't care about the consequences of what happens. If you click abandon the match every single one of your characters has to make the injury rolls and anything can happen.
So far I have mainly been playing against the AI but have been enjoying the game the whole time. I actually enjoyed the fact that the game gave major penalties for trying to abandon matches if you didn't like what was happening. Luckily in multiplayer you pick whether you want a friendly match or competitive (not sure what actual titles are called). In a competitive match if you loose you can get the permaneant injuries or have your gear taken while in friendly no injuries and no gear taken. If you like challenging games and can handle loosing a character permaneantly that you have had since the beginning of the game I would recommend this game.

I was pleasantly surprised by how much fun I had with this. I'd heard that it was a great looking game that was kind of meh in the gameplay department, but I thought it was a fairly competent shmup. There's nothing particularly novel in terms of mechanics or level/enemy design, but there are enough different loadout options to let you make it suit any playstyle, and that's where the aesthetics kick in to keep it interesting too.
It's definitely on the easy side, so I took advantage of the loadout system to set a self-imposed challenge for myself and decided to see if I could play through a shmup without shooting/using any active abilities. The melee weapons are all auto-triggered when you're close enough to be within range, and I just ignored the special abilities entirely that require you to push a button to activate them. It turns out the weapons and other equipment in the game are balanced well enough that it's entirely possible to do that and play through the game using nothing other than movement, so good on them for that.
Although speaking of movement, that's one of the problems with the game. Between stages in campaign mode (there's also infinite arcade mode) there are minor platforming segments to get to the next level where you can talk to NPCs and find out more about the story and retry levels and whatnot. The platforming is COMPLETE BALLS no matter what input device you're using. The collision detection is kinda broken (just try jumping while standing next to a wall), you will flop over and slide off moving platforms when you jump onto them (have fun at the end of the game), and so on. I sincerely hope they never make a platform game.
Definitely recommend a controller for it, but if not, at least use your keyboard for the platforming bits. The main shmup part is playable with whatever you're comfortable with, but the platforming is awkward with a controller, quite annoying with a keyboard, and borderline impossible with a mouse.

Well, this one really caught me by surprise. When I first saw Ballpoint Universe - Infinite on Steam Greenlight it didn't really caught my attention but the more I saw it on several youtube videos and some gaming website news the more I got fond of the artstyle, slowly I started developing a certain "appreciation" for the fact that everything on the game was hand drawn. Then when I got the game and finally played I was completely blown away by it, the way that the 2D sprites that were completely hand drawn and the way the animations were made really fitted the world and the background and everything felt really smooth. You can say that Ballpoint Universe is both a platformer and a sidescrolling shooter, like something like Syder Arcade. You control your little doll with the mouse, and let me warn you, it is kinda frustrating at the begining because your character moves towards where you have the cursor so in certain parts where high precision platforming is required you might fail a few times until you get the hang of it. Now, the shooting part is where you'll spend most of your time probably, at the begining of each stage you get to equip, upgrade or buy parts for your ship. Your ship has 4 slots, one on the top which starts out with a blade that activates when you're next to an enemy, one on the bottom which at first has a machine gun that fires in short bursts, one which is the hull of the ship and the last one is your active ability which you can use after you kill a certain number of enemies and you "build" up your star counter, it basicly works like a combo system. By upgrading your weapons you get increased range, bigger spread, bigger magazines / faster reload time, by upgrading your hull you can get various benefits such as increased health, homing missiles etc and by upgrading your active ability I believe it only improves the performance of that ability. These upgrades and new parts can be acquired by spending ink which is the game currency and you can get it by killing enemies, destroying obstacles and achieving a higher rank on a mission. Each mission has 3 ranks which you can get by completing them, if you don't die a single time during that mission or if you recover a life you'll end the mission with 5 lifes and that will give you the gold rank, having atleast lifes by the end of the mission will grant you the silver rank and 1 life will grant you the bronze rank. If I recall correctly the bronze rank gives you 100 ink while the silver rank gives you 200 ink and the gold rank gives you a collectible, which as the name indicates, you can collect either by getting gold rank on all the missions and by finding some hidden in the levels.  The shooting gameplay is fairly standard but yet really satisfying, your melee weapon triggers as soon as you get in range of an enemy or obstacle and by left clicking you trigger your ranged weapon and eventually when you build up your star meter the middle mouse button will trigger your special ability, usually by the end of the mission you will fight a boss and as the game progresses the game throws at you more and more enemies which you can either kill or completly avoid. Overall I think that where the game really shines is it's graphical presentation, the soundtrack (which is really good, dare I say Electronic Super Joy level of awesomeness) and the plot. I do realize that the plot might not be that interesting for some people because it's really kind of weird but I do believe that given the graphic style chosen by the developer it makes sense and it really fits together. That said I honestly think this is a very good game which surprised me alot, I wasn't really expecting this to be this polished and really well put together, it certainly is a must play for indie games fans and art enthusiasts.

Fortress Forever was originally created since there would be no Team Fortress 2 but, as you all know, Valve still developed TF2.
The developers of Fortress Forever still continued working this mod and it even launched 1 month prior to TF2. Obviously, most attention went to Valve's Team Fortress 2 and most people forgot about Fortress Forever, untill now.
So why would you play this Team Fortress mod?
-First of all, Fortress Forever pretty much sticks to the TF classic formula. There are some changes in weaponry but for the most part it's basically the same.
-More balance. All the new weapons etc. in TF2 are very fun but with that they also lost the balance, in my opinion.
-Better graphics and more players than TFclassic. Obviously, TF2's graphics still look a lot better than Fortress Forever but if you're a TFclassic veteran, you probably like FF's graphics.
-It's free. So why not just give it a try?

Before you turn around and say "0/10 This is some rip-off of TF2!" I recommend you take a peek at Team Fortress Classic.  This game is a source engine homage to TFC, and in my opinon a more refined and balanced version.   The unique movement style is smooth once you get used to it. (Play the tutorial if you aren't familar with movement techniques like bunnyhopping and air-strafing.)  And the matches are a little more fun now that there are newbies mixed in with the vets. This game has been around a LONG time and a few of us hipsters played it before it was cool, so you might have a little trouble going against some of the older players, but most of us are nice and will try to help you, so stick at it!  So glad this is getting some the recognition it deserves.  Keep fraggin' on, fellas.  And for the rest of you newbloods, welcome to the jungle.

i'm gonna summarize this review a bit. across america is very arcade-like for a truck sim, and all the "big cities" are actually really small industrial areas packed together in an area that would be realistically barely the size of ohio.
there's also always something in me that really loves driving around in average american middle class neighborhoods in the early 2000s with america-defining vehicles roaming the road such as chevy camaros, mustangs, 90s station wagons, and late 1990s dodge rams.
also i couldn't help to notice the first semi truck you get in the game literally has the acceleration of a fully modified 2008 mercedes s550 amg, and if you fully modify the first truck's power to the max it can legit go from 0-70 in about 4.5 seconds lmfao.
the steering controls are very sensitive which i kind of like, and the turning of the truck and the physics of the truck and trailer are superb, and the shocks for the semi truck are pretty realistic.
i also like how the game points out little but realistic things like how if you don't turn on your headlights at night you'll get pulled over by a police officer and get fined 1000 dollars. implimentations such as these make this game from 2003 comparable to a game nowadays.
in all this game has a nostalgic touch in me, it reminds me of the old and simpler times where whenever i wasn't hanging out with my popular group of friends and i wasn't skating or dirt biking in my upper class neighborhood back in the early 2000s i would sit down and download demos of this game and similar truck sims (which did contain the actual demo but had malware) and i would end up infecting my parents' $6000 fully customized compaq with a top of the line geforce mx2 gpu with a computer-crashing malware virus. good times lmao. the amount of fun this game gave me back in my glory days (when i was like 6-7 years old) will always make me a fan of the 18 wheels franchise, especially the earlier games.

This review is for the Alpha version 10b and will be updated has the game is updated. I will not give a number score anywhere in this review.
Vagante is a 2d rogue-lite platformer that is also a RPG. Each level is randomly generated and as of now levels are not seeded, so you cannot replay a run. This game can be played solo or up to 4 players locally (I have only played it by myself so far so I have nothing to say about the local co-op). It consists of some elements from Spelunky: arrow traps, spike pits, and the shop somewhat works like the shop in Spelunky. Currently you start off with three available characters/classes and one is unlockable. Weapons and armor are not class locked and you can find spell books, swords, tunics, and other loot in random chests through each level. Gear is also not locked off by stat requirements but you should be cautious when equipping anything since it may take away stats when it is equipped or it may be a cursed item which leads to the item being stuck on your person until the curse is removed from it via a scroll. Scrolls and potions are randomized every run like how pills are randomized in The Binding of Isaac. Everytime you start a run you start with one affinity point which you can put into an affinity (unless you are the unlockable class) or stats. There are no repeating affinities on any of the classes.
I personally found the artstyle and aesthetic of Vagante to be very colorful yet still dark with the color palette. Everything looks really nice and does not blend in unless it seems to be necessary.
Thank you for reading my review, if you have any criticisms about this review please comment so I can improve it.

I'll admit it--I bought this game purely for the looks, but once I actually started playing it, I ended up enjoying it quite a bit. The game is a shooter, with some platforming/exploring bits in between areas.
Ballpoint Universe would be a bit on the easy side for shooter fans, but as a shooter-unsavvy gamer, the difficulty was about right for me.  The levels are fairly short, which makes dying and having to restart a level non-frustrating.  Overall, even with a few deaths per level, I made steady progress and never felt a level was unfair.
You can upgrade and customize your ship using Ink that you collect from destroyed enemies. The different weapons feel varied, and for some levels it makes sense to perhaps not use your usual kit, and change it up (eg. I found it useful on occasion to equip two melee weapons instead of melee + gun. I never bothered with shields, but that's another option if you like playing in that style).  The grind was minimal in terms of getting good enough equipment to finish the game, but if you want to upgrade EVERYTHING, you'll be in the game quite a while.
In addition to the story mode, there's an Infinite mode where you can see how long you can last. Also, once you pass a level in Story mode you can revisit that level any time from the Start screen and try to do better. There's enough there to keep you busy.
On the other hand, I found the platforming fairly frustrating due to the weird controls and collision-detection. Luckily here's no consequence for dying by falling off edges, otherwise I might have given up early on. I found using the mouse nigh-impossible for the platform parts, and ended up using an XBox 360 controller (which I recommend for both the platformer and shooter parts).
As mentioned before, the game is beautiful (and prompted me to whip out the F12 button for the first time on Steam ;) ). As an illustrator/game dev myself, my kudos to the artist for creating such a lovely-looking gameworld. The music is also very good and fits the game perfectly.
If you're looking for a casual shooter you can dip into to have a short game once in a while, you can't go wrong with $4 for Ballpoint Universe.

When you go into the game, go in without expectations and above all, don't keep trying to compare it to the previous three.  Especially in terms of the physics and control. As long as you stick to this, you'll find a fairly enjoyable game. It's pretty good, but not truly the real Sonic 4 it could have been. The reasons for this notably boils down to three issues in particular: Use nostalgia, progression, and level design.
First off is the appeal of nostalgia, it was unfortunately far too heavily use. With too much borrowing from previous games with the Sonic 1 style bonus stages, and nearly every boss being a rehash with minor tweaks at critical health. The level themes were all very close too in style to previous games, which made it felt more of a reimaging than a sequel.
Hand in hand with the nostalgia overload, the game was extremely conservative in the progression department. The bosses as mentioned above were a certainly a major notable case. However, lots of finer details are also affected by this as well. Gone are items introduced in Sonic 2 and 3, leaving only basic ones introduced in Sonic 1… namely just Shields, Power Sneakers, Ring and 1-Up monitors. Although not exactly bad simplifying things to focus on gameplay, it definitely is odd to have the first three progress in complexity and item count to have it go back to square one…
Alongside this, the game doesn’t really introduce anything new to the series to give it that “Sonic 4” feel. The only new aspect added was the homing attack, which certainly met with mixed reactions. Though it does at least give it that new feel and gives it a progression between the classic series and the modern series putting in the homing attack.
Finally, the level design in the game is often quite questionable at parts. The first level is fantastic, along with the third… but just about every level after these two has quirks with them. Often you’ll find horribly booby trapped, cheap tricks, or heavily gimmicked sections RIGHT before the signpost… which means if you need rings for the bonus stage you can pretty much forget it unless you have the level memorized like the back of your hand. Now that’s not bad to put a challenge for the player right before the exit… but there are good ways to do it and then there are bad ways to do it.
And if the traps before the signpost weren’t enough to keep your mind busy, you’ll likely have noticed how many times you came across cheaply placed enemies that offer not a challenge, but instead only frustration. Jumping on a spring or running through a speed booster shouldn’t result in an immediate collision with an enemy for instance.
Then we have Mad Gear 3…  certainly an experience.
However despite these shortcomings, I still find myself coming back to the game from time to time. It’s enjoyable, and is simple fun like a classic game should be. It has enjoyable graphics (though the shading is a bit of an unusual choice for the characters compared to the scenery), is challenging, and is a lot of fun to be Super Sonic again in a game instead of it being a story element. It may take a little to get used to it initially, but definitely worth a look into if you want a classic game experience.

First of all,
is not a bad game. It was perceived as being bad likely because it changed the formula of the classic
games and people didn't like that. Had it not been titled "Sonic 4," a lot of the negative reception would be diminished considerably, since many simply didn't think it was a worthy successor to the classic games. You have to look at a game both as part of a series and individually in order to have a valid opinion of it, and that's exactly what I plan to do in this review.
To begin with, I like the visuals and art style (although cel-shaded Sonic looks a bit odd). The music is enjoyable, despite what some have said, and the level design is definitely on par with the classic games, albeit slightly more linear. Of course, one of the major additions this time around is the Homing Attack, a move that many felt didn't work in a classic-style 2D
game. In my opinion, it's just as well-implemented as in many of the other recent 2D games, like the Rush series and Generations on 3DS. Now onto the physics. Literally EVERY REVIEW I have seen of
mentions the physics being poor or "floaty." I myself didn't have any issues with the physics, as they work well with the level design and benefit the player in most cases just as they did in the Rush series, whereas the physics in the classic
games would often lead to frustrating and unnecessary hits or deaths.
Moving on, the bosses are generally pretty easy, although the final boss is relentlessly difficult. The Special Stages are all ♥♥♥♥ing insane, and the last one is quite possibly the cheapest, most unforgiving Special Stage I have ever had the misfortune to play in a
game. I've tried again and again with no luck, so if anyone has some incredible strategy to beat it, please let me know. Anyway, the Zones themselves are actually pretty creative (especially Casino Street, with the various playing card elements) despite being mainly based on level tropes from the classic
games, but aren't really memorable, with the exception of Mad Gear Zone. That♥♥♥♥♥♥is epic.
Of course, as with the classic games, there are a few cheap deaths and unfair tricks in the game that can become incredibly frustrating, but nothing too big besides the aforementioned final boss and Special Stages. Overall, it's actually a decent game. Maybe it's not a real sequel to the classic
games, and maybe it's flawed, but it's still enjoyable and holds up as an individual game. If you want a true
, go buy
, but if this review hasn't convinced you to at least give this game the credit it deserves, then I don't know what will.

Sega, what is wrong with you? This game is an utter miserable pile of dump. It shouldn't be considered the 4th entry in the legendary Sonic 1,2,3&K series.
Why is this game terrible?
The graphics. Sega. What is wrong with 16 bit? Why didn't you follow in Capcom's footsteps and give Sonic the Megaman 9 nad 10 treatment? The graphics are so bland. It'd have been 100% better if the game was faithful to it's older Genesis series. The resolution is much too zoomed into sonic, too. The Genesis graphics in sonic 123 were beautiful and awe inspiring! This game includes ♥♥♥♥♥♥ rehashes of old Sonic levels, and not done well at that.
The music. You can tell it was inspired by the older games, and you can hear them trying to work the Genesis' gritty soundchip into the game. But it falls flat on it's face. It's possible to emulate a Genesis soundchip on something that isn't a Genesis, and it can be done very well, too. Sonic 4 Ep 1 fails to deliver any memorable music at all. Each act has it's own variation, I'll give them credit for not being lazy in that aspect, but it still doesn't sound catchy, or even good. The soundtrack is a shame to it's predecesors.
The control is halfway decent, and it feels clunky at times. The level design is literally just ripped from older 2D Sonic games but warped in such a way that makes the game slow paced and not fun to play. Don't buy this terrible game. Instead, go cleanse yourself with the Genesis versions. Or if you are looking for a newer Sonic game that is actually amazing, check out Sonic Generations.

It's better than Sonic 06. That is about it.

Though many rules are different from the original tabletop "Mordheim", the game is excellent.  You can feel the atmosphere of the City of the Damned in every corner, as you don't know exactly where your enemy is.

As a longtime fan and player of the tabletop game, I was thrilled to see Mordheim was being made into a computer game. My old computer didn't meet the minimum specs, but after buying an ASUS ROG rig on clearance at Best Buy this spring, I have to say Rogue Factor did not disappoint! This is a fantastic conversion, with four of the iconic warbands included, and now a fifth -- Witch Hunters -- available as DLC, as well as several hired swords. Keep it coming, devs!
Like the tabletop version, the gameplay is highly tactical. Ganging up on lone enemies, while preventing the enemy from ganging up on you, is the key to victory. Yes, you will lose warriors from time to time -- get used to it, it's Mordheim! Keep your heavy hitters in front, while your weaker members grab wyrdstone and loot until they're strong enough to fight. Hire a reserve leader so you don't miss days when your primary leader gets injured -- make those wyrdstone shipments to your sponsor on time! That keeps the gold flowing and lets you build up your warband. Now, my Level 10 Ogre is a killing machine!
No, the game isn't perfect -- there are occasional spots in some maps where you should be able to move but a small obstacle blocks your path. And the AI does get hung up once in a while, especially with the large monsters unable to find a path or blocked by a wagon. Also, the persistent arrows after you get shot really need to go away -- having your warriors running around fighting with an arrow right between the eyes or through their skulls looks pretty dumb. So those glitches still need to be ironed out.
But overall, this is a great game of Mordheim. The visuals are spot-on, the story missions are fun, and you don't even have to paint your warband. Now let's get that Undead warband into the game!
And then, Necromunda...

As a first impression you cannot help to compare this with bust-a-move, and you'll probably only see the bad points:
* A total lack of asthetics. (Biggest problem with this game.)
* Poor graphics and sound.
* Some buggy physics
Then after a few hours you perhaps get into it. (If you are exhausted enough, or relaxed enough, or high enough I suppose.) And you'll find that the ball physics brings some pretty interesting mechanics. Such as strings of bubbles swinging around, tension and weight of bubbles-branches,  and snipping a few bubbles here or there might snap away a branch of bubbles in another direction. It's rather subtle but interesting. Sadly it's all the game has to offer.
If you add a few dozen more hours you'll find that:
*All the levels are identical, with a gradial ramp up in bubbles per level, falldown speed and number of colours. (It never gets very difficult)
* The stars progression and talents are all very bland. There are a few situational elements to the skills but really nothing to write home about.
* The game is far too long for the content it has to offer.
It's not a horrible game, but it needs at least a month or so of polish before it can pass the barrier from non-recommend to reccomend. Maybe something like arkaniod-style levels (where each level has a designed layout) to not make 30 hours of gameplay seem like the same 5 minutes repeated over and over again could be an idea..
It took me 30 ish hours to get 100% achievments, and if I weren't such a sucker for achievements it would never have lasted that long. This is a $1 or $2 game for people listening to audiobooks while playing or are on mind numbing meds and can't think.

I did not write a simple review strongly criticizing this game. I wrote a declaration of war against it and anyone who likes it. This is my opinion and if you have something against it then I dare you to express it competently so I can get the chance to burn all of your words down! With this mentioned let us begin.
I would also like to mention that I might have a little of a bias against Absolver. I do not like to think of video games as simple mechanical nightmares that are only designed to frustrate and satisfy one's needs to destroy other's self esteem, that is why I probably did not like this game. The games that mainly gave me this opinion were games like Fallout 1, Dark Souls 3, Portal 2 or Dota 2. Those games allowed me to channel my inner feelings into something more then pure hatred. They allowed me to immerse myself into worlds full of curiousities, wonders and mysteries. They gave me problems to solve, things to think about as if they were designed to keep me entertained. Unlike this fighting game.
Absolver does not have that many flaws believe me but because of its size those flaws become much apparent and frustrating with every single hour of gameplay. There I was at the start thinking of this game as ethreal, calming. I gazed at its wonderful mechanics that allowed someone not only to express their creativity but also share it with others. I loved it all, I was as naive as to even think that this may be the first fighting game that I'll play and I will not furiously scream because of. Well, I was wrong. So horribly wrong.
Let's start with simple things. There is lag. Constant undeniable lag that makes the gameplay that relies so heavily on proper timing a chore. You want to know why "Player Unknown's Battlegrounds" was such a huge success? It was beacause the developer took an idea that was being rolled over for the last billion years and did it actually decently. Look at their success! All they had to was take all the mistakes of the previous games of this newly established genre and just do not make them. Now they have lots of money and a really bright future ahead of them. Unlike this game. Take this for example, after seeing entire series of Dark Souls having unbearable multiplayer because of constant lag and For Honor having an extremely painful launch due to unreliable game connection you would think that Absolver devs would focus on actually making their game not laggy, right!? NOT AT ALL. Instead they launched with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ servers, had all the players dissapointed and saw probably a huge money loss due to the fact that everyone decided to refund the game because it did not work! Good job. Good ♥♥♥♥ing job. You can just tell how mad I am at the incomptence of these devs. They had such a great concept, great idea. They dedicated so much time and work into it and they would dedicate much more but they accidently shoot themselves in both of their legs and now will probably never see their game grow to a proper size. Good job. Good ♥♥♥♥ing job. Now we'll all be stuck with a miniature community until the devs finally realize how much time all of us have wasted here. Unless, I dunno they would re-re-re-release the game or something. Maybe then someone would actually notice this product.
Speaking of community. Have you ever wondered why is everyone so mean in fighting games? Well, it's because the game they are usually playing is so bloody frustrating it makes them rip off their bloody hair and Absolver just might be too that kind of a game. There are two types of attacks in this game. Quick annoying ♥♥♥♥♥♥ one, long annoying strong one. You would think that there is more depth to it, there isn't. You have diffrent dodges, diffrent things that your punches can do like increase poise, decrease someone else's poise, interrupt someone's poise. You know all of the things that would hide the game's simplicity. In the end it all comes down to one thing. Which player makes a more broken combo.
In strategy games players fight constantly on the field of both physical and psychological plain. They create strategies that counter other strategies. They raise armies only to see them burn and to build new armies. They basically get a chance to express their knowledge, intelligence and skill into the game they are playing. Here on the other hand you can mash buttons, two of them. You have 4 stances, 2 buttons. "Stances change randomly sometimes, depending if the enemy player has moved few inches to your left or right it makes you change your stance and all of your attacks with it. Your stance is also set by your previous attack. That is why you make your attacks loop your stance to keep it all under control. Otherwise you will end up with an upredictable but easily counterable mess that does not fit for multiplayer. Now that you know that you can design a moveset. It can be a fast annoying combo that keeps your opponent stunlocked for the rest of his playthrough beacause if you won't do that he'll do exacly the same thing to you." There, whole moveset making process described. When I played this game I felt like creativity was being punished. I was constantly being beaten by drunk people who looped the same move. The same exact one I am not kidding. It was a worm punch and a quick spin, worm punch, quick spin and every single class has a simiular broken combo. Why? Because stunlock. Why make a flexible deck of attacks that will allow you to put yourself into every kind of situation and come out at least somewhat successful, when there is only one type of situation in the multiplayer? Being stunlocked while button mashing. Just find the most annoying moves in the game and loop them. Occasionally holding your guard and sometimes blocking an attack. I swear to god that does not exist, was it really that hard guys? To make a game that does not spin around stunning your opponent to death or do you just enjoy seeing people in this state of basically feeling cheated?
I'm tired. I'm sad and I'm in extreme pain. I wrote this entire review as an act of vengance against all of the evil phantoms that patrol this game. This is not fun to play, for us, for them or anyone. This is all about being frustrated or sharing frustration. The skill is worthless because you will never do anything positive with it. You will never have friends in this game because the only way you can express your friendly intentions towards them is by bowing before brutally murdering them. You will never have romantic long battles in this game because your opponent can not react whilst being constantly punched in the face by nuclear powered teenagers. I have tried to find deeper meaning in it all. I seeked strategy in the deck building, I looked for the magic of duels in the multiplayer and I only found ash of what the game could be. There is nothing to come here for, nothing to fight here for. Just a bunch of skinny teenagers fighting in the ruins.
I wish I could enjoy this game. I wish I was not so frustrated because of it. I also wished it had more reliable connection and enemies with less stamina but well this is the game. You got what you asked for or in my case didn't.

ARMA: Cold War Assault (or Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis as known until Codemasters gave up rights to Bohemia Interactive) is a delicate game that takes you back too 1985 where the US and Russia's relations are at a breaking point. That is, until Russia mounts an invasion on the fictional neutral Island of Everon. The story will get more intense overtime. The gameplay may not be at its finest at today's terms, however this game shows that the ARMA franchise had built off of the following mechanics in this game leading to ARMA 3.
I find this game intriguing, as there is a long and exciting campaign (As stated above) and single player scenarios that will place you in the boots of many unique soliders in various factions with many different objectives.
And finally there is the mission editor, which will allow you to create a mission in anyway you'd possibly like.

Unfortunately the game does not deserve the complement of its predecessors as for the most part the game insults the classic era of the franchise with a mediocre game that has a inferiority complex - trash can't disguise itself amongst gold.
The level design does not complement the momentum and even the momentum mechanics of the game are poor or rather broken and don't hold their own to the older brothers which will leave you with nothing but a sigh as the game spoonfeeds you dash panels so that you don't earn your speed and you're not punished for mistakes.
The developers don't understand that earning your momentum gives you a fresh experience when you replay the level and you understand the layout well enough not to crash into Badniks or spikes which is why the ring system is there in the first place; so you can fail multiple times, learn from your mistakes instead of punishing you downright so once you finally learn you're allowed to hold the reins of speed and all its goodness.
Taking that away devalues what made the classic games in the first place. The game also introduces the homing attack that is forced on you and drops every bit of speed you've gained so far.
Despite what has been said about the level design, Zone 4 takes a few steps towards the right direction but it doesn't stop the game from falling on its face, you also have the terrible floaty physics and the poor (re-)designed bosses to also thank for that.
The music however is great and with the beautiful visuals are very reminiscent of the classic Sonic games are by far the strongest points of this product which thankfully don't collapse with the disappointment of the game. Even the 2.5D models are great other than Sonic's model itself oddly enough.
What makes this game bearable is the fact that it's a average platformer game when you don't compare it to its far superior prequels, the length is very great for its price and the online time attack where you can compete against other players that can have you playing for hours to see who can break and exploit the game to the finish line the fastest.
The game is by all means worth the £6 but you're better off spending a bit more of that money to buy games like DuckTales Remastered and/or Sonic 4 Episode 2, despite them having lower scores on gaming review sites they're superior in everyway.

Sonic the Hedgehog 4 Episode 1 is a game that had its work cut out for it,
and sadly, it falls a bit short.
The game, rather than expanding on the ideas of Sonic 3 & K's
multiple characters, shields and storyline integration,
is visually a rehash of the zones, bells and whistles of Sonic 1 and 2.
That's not to say the game doesn't do original ideas,
in fact, every act is flavored with an unique gimmick of one sort or another,
and it actually generally work really well.
The control on the other hand, imagine Sonic Rush, Colors or Generations' modern stages.
Now take away the boost and what you're left with is one rather clunky Sonic.
This game is perhaps the worst example of Dimps' level design as well,
with bubble-chains, speed-boosters and bottomless pits looming below the end of several acts
as if it somehow constitutes for challenge, made even more frustrating knowing that contrary to popular beliefs, Dimps can make great Sonic games.
Still, the game is a fairly decent little romp,
but I can't with a good conscience recommend this
when there are so many great alternatives readily available on Steam.

Being a fan of the tabletop game, I really wanted to like this version of Mordheim.  Sadly, I don't.
The game does a number of things well, starting with presentation.  The graphics style matches what I always imagined Mordheim to look like, and the music and sound mesh with the art very well.  And at the tactical level, the actions your characters can perform are varied and useful enough to keep things interesting -- stuff like climbing walls to gain elevation advantage, intercepting enemies who enter your AO, providing overwatch, and so on.
That said, this game has significant issues.  Some of the more minor ones include camera positioning that ranges from awkward to actively infuriating, a clumsy and unintuitive control scheme, data feedback that misrepresents the true gameplay mechanics, and AI that's a lot bigger on the "A" than the "I".
All of the above problems are small enough to be forgivable if it wasn't for the hot mess they made of the strategic level gameplay and multiplayer aspects of the game.  Where the original Mordheim was a skirmish-focused game with some RPG elements, the devs have chosen to place the cart before the horse and create a game where the battles are just a chore you muddle through to drive the ridiculously extended character progression and loot collection.  Gone are varied victory conditions that might reward creative play and create memorable matches; now every fight revolves around grouping your warband into one giant mass and rolling it at the enemy until they rout.  Which you'll be doing A LOT of, because the pace of campaigns has been slowed down drastically to account for the CRPG tropes that were shoehorned into a game that didn't need or benefit from them.
But the most astouding failure of all is that there is no support whatsoever for multiplayer campaigns.  Let me say that again: THERE IS NO SUPPORT WHATSOEVER FOR MULTIPLAYER CAMPAIGNS.  IN A GAME THAT CALLS ITSELF MORDHEIM.  All you get are one-shot battles where you use the same warband that you spent 60 games grinding against the crappy AI with.  Ugh, I'm done.

Soundtrack compliments the art style sufficiently - it's sci-fi but fits the doodle world with mixes of heavy overlays to chirpy switch ups.
There is low involvement when it comes to a story but we are taking a break from all the deep plots at the moment. You basically are a doodle in a doodle world, with doodle ships in a doodle war.
My only real gripe about it is the achievement system not unlocking properly at the moment. Whether it's my own internet connection that's the problem or something on the game's end, I can't really say right now.
Overall I do recommend getting this game, as a leisurely break from all the complicated titles out there. The visuals are a dreamy landscape to say the least, and the simple shoot 'em up gets very tripped out.

Unlike all of my other reviews which were just joke reviews, this is an actual one.
You have all of the classes of the original game (Scout, Soldier, Pyro, Heavy, Demoman, Engineer, Medic, Sniper and Spy) and unlike TF2 where you have unlock weapons: There is no unlocks. Savant - Ascent is an attempt to mesh an awesome series of soundtracks with arcade twin stick shooter action! so what could go wrong?
Except the camera, not a lot actually because the game is pretty rad.
But the camera, that ♥♥♥♥ing camera, ruins everything.
You see in Savant you don't move in the traditional sense. Rather like a "game and watch" you are fixed on screen with only 3 options, dodge left or right or jump. Baddies charge at you and you need to get out the way; this gets tricker as the game goes on and is great stuff.
This all falls apart due to one fatal flaw which is the moving camera, you see the camera moves in the direction you are shooting in so you are blind sided from every direction except the one you are shooting. To make matters worse, moving prevents shooting, so you can't just hop around to avoid getting hit otherwise too many enemies will appear and you will die.
Everything about the game is either good or great. The art direction the various soundtracks (yes you can pick different soundtracks as you play!) the controls (although admittedly they are limited and simple) are good but the whole challenge of the game is dodging enemy attacks or enemies altogether so its a huge, huge promblem that you can hardly see where the enemies are coming from in order to dodge them.
It's a handicap that ruins what is otherwise an amazing gaming experience and while progress in the game will unlock ways to help deal with this, it is clear it was a design intention but sadly a misguided one because games like Contra are hard; like Metal Slug are challenging but those are great games! No will look down on you for copying the tried and tested method of making a run and gun game!

Ah yes, this game. The game that caused the Fanbase to blow up like an Atom Bomb. They were so outraged by this that they even resorted to do stupid things, like try and boycott SEGA by buying multiple copies of the first Sonic game when this one came out, and we all know how that went down. The Boycott was a complete failure, SEGA got more money then they were expecting, and the fanbase failed to realize how a boycott REALLY works. I'm not into goverment, yet I know the proper way of how to boycott something. Well anyway, here's Sonic 4 Episode 1, the long awaited sequel to the classic sonic games. It takes place a few years after the events of Sonic and Knuckles, Robotnik is back to doing his usual routine, kidnapping animale critters and using them to power his badniks and only Sonic can stop him once again. The game pretty much goes back to the old days where Sonic runs around, freeing small critters and so on. The only new thing that they've added to the gameplay is the homing attack which can be useful in some cases. I guess you could say this is when Sonic started learning this move before leading up to events of Sonic Adventure, but then again SEGA does a poor job with knowing what's canon to what. There are 4 Locations, Splash Hill Zone, Casino Street Zone, Lost Labryinth Zone and Mad Gear Zone, each of them looking very similar to levels in Sonic 1 and 2. And it can't be a classic sonic game without collectiong 50 Rings in order to access the Special Zone to retrive a Chaos Emerald. Yep, those stages are back, and the worst enemies to deal with in those levels are the bumpers. They keep bouncing you around all over the place in the harder levels and this just adds stress to it cause there's a time limit to all 7 of them. The controls took me awhilt to get used to, I just find it odd how there are like 4 buttons tha do different things instead of just using 1. Guess I'm more comfortable with the Wii Version. Out of all the levels in the game, the one that pisses me off the most is Lost Labrynth Zone Act 2, where Sonic carries a torch to light the way. There's a segment where you have to light these holders in a specific way to activate the bridges to the exit. It's so frustrating and annoying that it took me bloody ages to figure out a pattern. I've also heard people complaining about the Physics Engine but I really had no issues with the physics, not even in the Wii Version. All I could hear about it is that apperantly Sonic glues to the the ramp during the midpoint section. I never tried this since I never had this happen or even attempted to do a pointless trick. Not only are the levels similar to the past Sonic games, but enemies and bosses are brought back from Sonic 1 and 2. If this is supposedto be a sequel to Sonic and Knuckles, shouldn't Robotnik have come up with newer designs instead of rehashing his failed models? Nostalgia is one thing but this is ridiculous. Guess this game was forshadowing the crap that we would get in the recent Sonic games. (aka Sonic Colors and Lost World) One final note is that the Final Boss is okay. It starts off with an endurance round wit bosses from the different  stages, then it leads up to a rematch with Robotnik in his Egg Destroyer Battlesuit, or the "Death Egg Robot" if you want to call it by it's lazy and uncreative name. Even though these bosses are how they were in the past, they do tend to throw in some twists to make them more interesting. So unless your one of those saps that took part of that failure of a boycott, you might like this game. It's full of nostalgia!  It's obviously not the all time best Sonic game ever created, but it's not really the worst sonic game either. I'd fancy playing this game than having to sit through the awful writting in Colors and Lost Worlds any day. In a nutshell, Episode 1 is more of a throwback to the classics with some familer enemies and locations just with a few new tricks thrown in here and there. The game is still fun to play as how the classic sonic games were fun to play. I have seen some footages of Episode 2 looking more original with it's designs, unfortunantly I don't have Episode 2 as of yet. Oh well, I'm happy I got to play this game whether it be on the Wii or on Steam.

This game is exactly what you'd get if you wanted to make a roguelike 2D platformer. While it lacks the turn-based and top-down gameplay that define the genre, pretty much every other aspect of the genre is retained. The procedural generation of levels is executed perfectly, as the levels are challenging and look good. Loot is randomly generated in true roguelike fashion, where nothing is identified until you use it, or if you cast from an identification scroll. This goes for potions as well, of which the color never indicates what type of potion you find between runs.
Itemization so far has been pretty great. The items not only offer random stat upgrades, some of them also offer platforming assistance (to some extent) and other abilities. For instance, it is possible to find gloves that allow you to grab hold of walls, boots that allow you to bounce around or leave a trail of fire, a grappling hook, and even items that allow you to phase through walls and floors. If you're a dumbass like myself, you'll find yourself phasing through the edge of the level by accident, killing yourself in the process. There are many more items like this, and I haven't even gotten that far into the game.
The fact that there's more to items than just numbers makes itemization in this game a LOT more interesting.
The game controls feel a lot like spelunky, which makes it a bit clunky in combat. The clunkiness, however, is rather charming. While I personally opted not to play a knight as the rogue's dagger is much faster (and thus hits the opponent when I press the button, not half a second later), once you get used to the controls the game should feel natural to play.
The controls can be rebound from the menu, and it's possible to use a controller (which I would recommend for this game, although it is certainly not necessary).
The fact that this game has local co-op makes it all that much better. I have only seen co-op in videos, as I haven't yet had the chance to play this game with friends. The videos show that if one of the players dies, he is 'resurrected' as a skeleton, with some chances to return back to life as a player. This means that dead players can still help, but would much rather be alive since living characters have more to offer.
The game is quite difficult. At the very beginning you lack the gear to withstand a lot of punishment. Each level contains a boss, and if you can't find a way to cheese the boss, they can be quite a challenge. Difficulty also hinges a lot on the item drops you get. Getting health potions early on helps a lot, as well as items giving you higher defense, or more attack power.
This game is an absolute recommendation for those enjoying 2D platformers with a mean streak. It also has co-op! What else could you wish for? The co-op is still limited only to local, but on the discussion board the developer mentioned making online co-op. The fact that this game is still early access is fantastic, because it means from here on out it will only get better.

An amazing mix of Spelunky's gameplay and randomly generated terrain with all the difficulty and depth of Dark Souls. They started up a Kickstarter that sadly failed so I'm really glad to see it finally up on Steam. I originally backed it and was super hyped about it so I'm more than happy to support the development of this game. I absolutely recommend this game for any fans of Spelunky, roguelikes, or just enjoy a nice difficult game. Would I recommend it for it's current price? Probably not. I don't think it has enough features to necessitate a $15 price tag. Why did I buy it? Purely because I want to support it's development. They also have a free demo on their site if you want to give that a look. I recommend trying that out before buying it to see if you'll truly enjoy it.
Gameplay is great. If you've played Spelunky then you'll get a hang of the controls just fine. Has really good controller support too which I highly recommend using. Each class you choose from pretty much handles the same at the start. There's three to begin with (knight, rogue, mage) and you can unlock more as you play. I'm not sure how much there is currently in the unlockables department but I really hope they just load the hell out of this game with them because this is the perfect type of game for it. You can even unlock different backgrounds. I unlocked Deprived which starts you off with no items at all (a nod to Dark Souls I'd imagine).
Basically you go through randomly generated areas slaying monsters with a pretty diverse arsenal of weaponry and spells to gain levels and loot. To gain levels it's almost mandatory that you kill the boss in each area but you only level up once you transition to the next floor which will allow you to distribute a point in either a new ability or into one of your stats. Along with loads of xp the boss also drops a key that'll allow you to unlock a super chest tucked away somewhere on each level. There's a decent amount of crates to smash and chests to loot but there's also a shop very similar to Spelunky's.
The difficulty is fair and makes the game challenging enough that it'll keep you hooked. Easy mechanics that are difficult to master. There's quite a few things that can kill you in one hit. Mostly spike traps. It may take you a while before you're used to how to handle areas with spike traps but don't give up.
They also plan on adding in online multiplayer to go along with the local multiplayer they already have. They've already changed up the gameplay to facilitate multiplayer so I assume now they're just adding in netcode which is a huge thing.
I tried really hard to think of something I don't like about this game. I think my only real gripe is that all the monsters are just generic fantasy creatures. You got slimes, goblins, bats etc. I can understand why they would make it this way though. They do fit into the theme really well. I'd also like to have sounds play when a creature is defeated. In Dark Souls when you kill something they play a really satisfying slashy noise but in this they don't really make a sound. This is early access so maybe they'll add it in at some point.

As a fan of Games Workshop I was looking forward to playing this game.  Positives first it looks great, has not lagged, crashed or frozen on me once.  Sounds great and does a dame good job is emulating the table top game it is based on.  The reasons why I am not recommending this game boil down to the combat.  To be fair to Rogue Factor they have done a good job in merging the rolls to hit, wound and save into one single action but however there are some major problems.
First the percentage chance show when about to hit an opponent is just wrong.  It only shows your chance of hitting after your characters modifiers are taken into account, but not the enemies.  The community keeps pointing out that the opponent’s modifiers are shown; they are just not included in the calculations for hitting.  This is especially frustrating when despite being told you have a 95% chance to hit, you miss four times in a row.  Second and perhaps the biggest the range for the RNG used in this game is too high.  When turning a table top game that requires dice to play into a computer game using an RNG is a good way of measuring the dice rolls.  In this case however Rogue Factor have taken a game that uses dice numbered between 1-6 and ups it to 1-100.  This is a major issue as it greatly increases the chances of missing and failing to repel attacks.  The worst one of these I experienced was having a single Novice from the Sisters of Sigmar kill two of my henchmen and my war band leader on her own because I could not roll a single hit.
I would suggest you play Bloodbowl instead as Cyanide has done a far better job at converting a tabletop game into a computer game.

Whilst its quite unpolished with clunky UI, its an excelent strategy game that manages to be challenging and rewarding.
I cannot stress enough that it is VERY challenging, you might get on a winning streak for a while, but one bad loss can leave your veteran soldiers permenently dead or with debilitating wounds.
Whilst that sounds frustrating (and is!) it creates a brilliant atmosphere where you have to constantly judge the risk and reward of each mission, often encouraging you to use new recruits as meatshields whilst your elite troops look for safer opportunities to attack.
Thankfully the game comes with a progression system so that even if your entire warband gets killed, you will have earned a bunch of bonuses to any new warbands you create which helps the difficulty not feel too opressive.
in short:
-A challenging game of calculated risk taking, it is not a game of certainties but rather of adapting to misfortune.
-Somewhat unpolished, UI is poor and controls are unintuitive.
-Fairly repetetive gameplay, there are story missions with unique objectives but the bulk of the game is within familiar streets of the city fighting against roughly equal forces.
-consistently creates interesting strategic situations without clear 'best' solutions.

This bubble breaker game is a rigged bingo machine.
Firstly, the bubbles have magnetic physics, which although sound helpful are actually frustrating, since each bubble's magnetic field is painfully small. This mean that sometimes you end up "missing" that massive combo chain of two chains because the magnetism has decided to teeter towards one chain rather than both of them, although sometimes this magnetism works in your favo(u)r, making the game basically play itself for you at least a few combos before all is still again. However, such mechanic is very annoying due to its unreliable nature, especially when you are trying to complete a level in the fewest moves possible.
It also doesn't help that the camera is placed in a "at the side of the table" perspective, which makes it hard to see which balls are connected to each other by their weak magnetic fields.
There are also power ups that should help you destroy a bunch of bubbles per use, which I haven't even been able to use because the energy recharge rate is too slow to get a power up before I end up completing a level. (You can upgrade the power ups and your energy's recharge rate etc. but you don't even need them due to how the game tends to play itself often, eliminating the need for power ups in the first place!)
Overall, I have not enjoyed this game very much due to its unpredictable nature.
I do not recommend this game at all, even on sale or in a bundle; You can play countless better bubble breakers online for absolutely free!

This game looks so neat. It's artwork isn't "beautiful" but still charming and occasionally complicatedly pretty. It's all sketchy and papery. Real cool. A lot of stylized designs like Monty Python animation or different cartoony styles.
Ahem, anyways. This is a SHMUP. But it's really interesting. You run around in a 2D platforming area, occasionally finding collectables, but mostly just talking to people and accepting missions. Once you accept a mission, you launch up to a brief (or long) SHMUP section, collecting ink, that ends in a boss and are graded and rewarded based on how many lives you have at the end of it (1 is Bronze, 3 is Silver, 5 is Gold). There is also an "Endless Space" area you can go to at any time as long as you have the units of payment for it and it's pretty much a place to collect ink for upgrades. You start where you left off or died last time in neverending waves of enemies.
The upgrades and combat is where it actually is a bit different than standard SHMUP fare. You have a top and a bottom weapon, a nose which determines your overload ability which you get by killing enemies without being hit for an extended period, and a body which determines health and passives your ship has. What's cool is that a lot of the weapons aren't standard fare. There are three main types; projectiles, melee and shields.
Projectiles are your bullet weapons and are actually quite varied. There's one that fires in diagonals, one that fires a buckshot cluster that spreads as it gets further away, one that fires a slow shot that pierces and so on. They really vary it up a lot.
Melee is where the game gets really interesting. Melee attacks mean you have to get your ship close to the enemies. They are generally much stronger than projectiles, but as a result are more risky to use. There are enemies that can only be damaged by melee so it pays to have one equipped. Likewise, there are lots of types. Swords that slash near it in an arc, a spear that shoots in front with greater range and hits enemies on coming back but doesn't hit above or below you, a blade that simply circles your ship, a chainsaw and so on. They are really cool and fun to use.
Last is shields, which are fairly simple; they block attacks. They are likewise varied in how they are used, some reflecting shots but having less strength, some a wider area, some spiky so they do damage if you hit with them. They can be real life savers on certain bullety bosses.
There are a couple annoyances in the platforming part with how...odd your character moves and sometimes the screen can get so cluttered it's hard to see shots coming for you (and your hitbox is...indeterminate most of the time) but honestly any bad parts to this game are easily washed away by how fun it is to get right into the swing of things and how quick the levels play out. Getting a perfect on each level sure is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥in a fun way.
And that's pretty much it. You're a little squiggly doodle who comes out of the Idea Spring and is immediately conscripted into the war against the Logiticians or whatever they're called which are trying to oppress you with their straight lines and harsh angles. You just gotta be free and squiggly!
The game is cheap and mad fun. It's on Steam too with a bajillion cards and achievements.

I have been playing this game for over 20 hours and I'm very surprised at how much I like it.  At first I thought this was going to be sort of like Batman (Arkham series) meets Tekken, but it's actually much more than that.  The combat deck building is incredibly engaging, and switching up your move sequences can have a huge impact on your ability to face certain enemies.  The game is mostly well-balanced (with a few exceptions where you can aggro 5+ enemies at a time), and I lose just often enough to push me to get better.  Dying has no real consequence and only serves to make you want to run back and finish the fight.
One really positive thing for me is that playing with a controller seems very natural and comfortable.  I enjoy sitting back and pretending I own a console.
There are some flaws.  Buggy camera position in close quarters, lag makes it look like you're punching straight through enemies some times, and the inventory management is atrocious.  They have already released some early fixes, and I'm hopeful patches will continue to come.

For a game titled to pay homage to its classical era, it fails to live up to its name:
> The physics for the game is terrible, I usually find myself stuck on a wall or flung in the air when I don't want and not flung high enough when I do need to go that high.
> Counter-intuitive and extremely bland stage design with various mechanics that can be extremely frustrating and seemingly without pattern which ends up causing your death and make you feel like it was the game's fault and not your own.
> They based the Special Stages off of the ones from Sonic 2. Normally, that would be okay, especially since the entire game is based off of the first three Sonic games, however Sonic 2 had the worst Special Stages out of the three, imo.
> Almost unpredictable bosses that spontaneously switch attack patterns causing you to die much more times than neccessary for your first playthrough.
> The final boss is probably THE most frustratingly tedious and repetitive thing in the entire franchise, let alone the game itself.
I don't usually like to judge a game for it's graphical qualities so it doesn't really factor in my opinion, but I'd like to just point it out incase you might.
> Character models are super bloomed and look like plastic.
> Foreground scenery and on-stage objects look like cardboard, with the exception of the waterfalls in Splash Hill Zone...
That all being said, I think the only redeemable factor in this game is that the music, although not the best, definitely fits with what the game is trying to be.

After an exceedingly popular public alpha that captured the attention of roguelike and platformer fans  alike, Vagante makes its much needed appearance on Steam.
Vagante is an action platformer with procedurally generated stages and perma-deaths , making this absolutely imperative for any enthusiast of games with roguelike elements. The game is very akin to Spelunky in terms of its random maze-like passages sprinkled with difficult enemies, and its maiden rescuing side objectives. The controls and platforming are smooth, combat is simple and fun, and your skills and equipment actually have a noticeable impact on your current run.
Your consecutive runs will be incredibly difficult with narrow and claustrophobic corridors trapping you between numbers of varied monsters. As challenging as it is on the surface there is a slew of options available for your survival from leveling up important life-saving skills and abilities to finding or buying very useful equipment from the merchant which keep the game increasingly addictive in its progression, exploration and discovery.
The level and character designs in Vagante are stunning while retaining a simple indie game charm and the very well-done character portraits of the distinctly different classes you can choose in particular are reminiscent to me of the most memorable mid-to-late 90s era JRPG designs, with lovely organic background art in the eye-catching title screen almost akin to series like Secret of Mana/Seiken Densetsu.
The music also follows the same attractively unique yet familiar territory into RPG classics, the natural wood and string instruments sounding to me almost like tracks you would expect out of the likes of Yasunori Mitsuda's Chrono Cross soundtrack. Long story short, even in its earliest form Vagante already has the makings of a classic.
Vagante is in an alpha state currently, and is already very hard to find any faults with other than the fact that it's early and still has lots more incredible content to come. With the nostalgic visuals and music combined with fun, precise and easy to pick up but challenging to master randomized gameplay this is a title I'm certain could become the next 'big' roguelite. I already know it is for me, at least.

If you enjoy other roguelikes or like being challenged, I would recommend checking this title out.

Really wasn't expecting much of anything from this title at all.
I bought it on sale figuring it'd make a nice mindless game for my 6 year old son.  As it turned out, it made a nice mindless game for Dad - LOL.  No kidding, I love it!
Waves and waves of progressively harder enemy armored cars, tanks, and planes attempt to navigate the maze of defensive measures you place to stop them.  You start off each battle with a set amount of cash to buy pre-positioned guns.  As you kill the enemy tanks and planes, you get more cash to buy new guns or upgrade existing ones.
There is nothing to the manning of the emplacements (they fire by themselves)... the skill comes with what type of gun to buy, when to get it, where to put it, and in what sequence.  A sole gun in the right (or wrong)  place at the right (or wrong) time can make the difference between plastering the enemy before he gets his steam up, or getting overrun by the hun.
The music is a blend of cheesy bravado-style muscle pumping arcade noise - that somehow meshes perfectly with the action (I wouldn't change it).  The interface is remarkably easy (took me all of 10 seconds to figure it out - with no manual), and the entertainment value is undeniable.  For those who would complain about the graphics, I say they are perfect for what it is.  For those who would call the game too repetitive, I would guess they were not around decades ago to enjoy the genre of arcade games like Pacman, Asteroids, or Space Invaders.
1 out of 10 if you're looking for Company of Heroes or Men at War; 10 out of 10 if you're looking for a few hours to kill ("just one more turn" anyone? - LOL)

I've been playing Team Fortress since 1996, from Quakeworld Team Fortress to Team Fortress Classic to Quake 3 Fortress to Enemy Territory Fortress to Team Fortress 2, and even weird versions like Weapons Factory, Unreal Fortress, or ones that never saw release like Fortress Extreme, Wolf Fortress or Quake 4 Fortress... and Fortress Forever has become my favorite iteration of the TF genre. After having almost two decades of nostalgia rooted in the aforementioned games, that's a pretty surprising thing to hear myself say.

This game is a Source Engine remake of the Goldsrc remake of the Quake mod Team Fortress. It's free so you should try it if you're interested, but I definitely wouldn't recommend it.
Problems I have with the game after playing for an hour and a half (some more important than others):
- Bullet weapons (shotguns, nail guns, etc) do very little damage. I've shot at a soldier at point blank range four times with a super shotgun without killing him.
- It's hard to know how much damage you're actually doing since there's no damage numbers, etc
- Calling for a medic/ammo is clunky, as you need to hold down a button and move your mouse over an icon. The standard key then number would work just fine (especially since there are only three options)
- Health is difficult to find, as you need to search for a green backpack which may or may not have health
- This could only be a problem on some maps (all of the maps I played), but there is no equivalent of a resupply locker, making you need to go looking for a green backpack or a nice medic
- The voice in the tutorial is grating and repeats itself too much when you mess something up
- The air strafing mechanic explained in the tutorial straight up doesn't make any sense to me (I just might be dumb) and I didn't find it needed in the actual game at all
- Game crashes
- Lack of appealing/coherent graphics style (or really any style at all)
- Weapons don't feel meaty, powerful, or fun to use. They just feel weak, like something I'd download and then delete in Garry's Mod
- Demoman's grenades and pipes look the same for both teams, leading to unnecessary confusion. Grenades and pipes are colored different to differentiate each other apart when they should just be separate models with the team color.
- Classes have too many identical weapons. Almost every class has at least one shotgun (why does a class need two different ones?) and a crowbar
- Classes look too similar at a distance
- Most fights turn into rocket and grenade spam
- Every class has the same voice
Community related:
- Elitist community (e.x. "this is real team fortress," "man, hat fortress sucks now")
- Not enough populated servers
The worst part about all of these issues is that they probably will never be fixed. The mod was originally released in 2007. As a remake of Team Fortress Classic, however, they have done a decent job. That game has most of the same issues, almost all of which were fixed in Team Fortress 2.
Closing: If you like Team Fortress Classic, you'll probably like it. If you like Team Fortress 2, this will serve as a sort of history lesson (if you don't want to pay $4.99 for Team Fortress Classic).
