An easy and nice game to spend a few hours with. Dynamics and tricks are quite simple and intuitive; background music and sounds are very nice. The special weapons and combinations added a new layer to an old-type game.
PROs:
- Commands and dynamics are really easy to grasp. You likely won't need the step-by-step introduction - but it's there, neverthless, if you need it.
- Music and sounds. Like I said, they did a great job with it. They can be easily muted and regulated through the game, too.
- Special weapons and their combinations. Nothing is as viscerally satisfying as being able to get the whole table to explode with just one move.
CONs:
- The level of simplicity. Really, the whole game is almost too easy. You get almost at once the right, intuitive combination of exploding bubbles and special weapons needed to pass the harder levels. Conversely, the last sector is literally impossible to win with full stars and without special weapons; you'd need to try and try and try again until you get a lucky screen.
- The colours. Blue, green and red, all right. But, add the yellow one to the mix and it gets really hard to pick them apart - and I'm not even vaguely color-blind. (And then comes the orange... no, really. There were moments when I had to stop and look at them a second time.)
Going just by genre, I'd say 8/10. As a more general vote, a nice 7/10. I'll be likely re-playing this sometimes soon and I've already suggested it to other players.

Red Crow Mysteries is a key finding simulator disguised as a strange hidden object/point ‘n’ click game. It is also a secret weapon to bore the players to death with its dullness.
Red Crow Mysteries: Legion is an irregular hidden object game with a large focus on casual point ‘n’ click mechanics. It is also, almost objectively, boring as hell, because we spend almost the entire game looking for an endless stream of same-looking keys. These keys then unlock either some barely-described objects or the occasional weird puzzle minigame—all of which reward us with, what else, even more keys.
In theory, there is a story; in practise, it is more of a set of drab monologues about a young woman, who one evening awakens to the revelation that she has some mystical powers and has to stop something called Legion.
This is the entire plot, by the way, not the premise: the ending, where she prepares for the fight, is likely some sequel bait, but the series thankfully died here, before polluting the HOG scene even more.

DDO is probably the most underratred MMO out there. I wish more games in the genre would use modular content like this one does. It allows you to solo and make groups on the fly while still enjoying the content, and you never feel like you have to twiddle your thumbs waiting for a "healer" or "tank" to show up. It's an altogether better system than the traditional MMO in many ways.
The free account is limited in that you can only create two characters and they will be removed if you don't log on for a while - which makes me sad, because I really play this as kind of a pick-up-and-go game and I don't like to pay subscription fees for MMOs. That said, the game itself is definitely worth your time if you're looking for a free to play MMORPG that actually has some depth to it.
It can be difficult to find other players to group with because the player base is small. It's still a very enjoyable game, and if you're even vaguely familiar with D&D 3.5 rules you'll get into it pretty easily. I only know the very basic gameplay and I was able to jump into this without too many issues. The leveling system is more complex and robust than a typical mmo, but the game has features that allow you to select a goal. The game then builds toward that goal for you. It's a fun game to play causally. I would play more often if I had a regular group to play with.

There has been a serious dumbing down in the difficulty of content such that most PUGs are with individuals who feel entitled to a win without working for it.  Strategy?  Unknown.  Entitlement?  Yes, now.  While that description by no means encompasses every player it fairly describes such a prevelant sentiment that the enjoyment of the game is in a steady decline and has been so for a quite some time.  Also, the last year or so has seen Pay-To-Win options introduced on their store, further degrading the player base and removing motivators for continued play while lining the pockets of Turbine.  Gear is handed out like candy, through duping or otherwise.  With no real motivators to be better, skill declines.  Unless you're the kind of player who likes easy walks in the park and readily accessible gear for all, then this is not the game for you.
What once was good now needs a burial plot at the nearest cemetary.
R.I.P. DDO

This game is amazing. It's graphics and combat give it a classic feel, and even though it looks old, it is updated regularly and has a large amount of players. The quests and dungeons are interesting and immersive.
There are large "Wilderness" areas filled with monsters and places to explore, and they even have a few rare named monsters! The dungeons are exceedingly fun, with many different monsters and 4 different difficulty settings that effect XP earned. Choose Casual and go through it lone wolf, or go Elite and bring a few friends along to conquer all those who oppose you! Grouping in this game is fun, as you learn to depend on one-another when in danger.
The crafting system is a little boring, but it is absolutely rewarding. Armor and Weapon designs are cool and flashy, with multiple different armor sets for diversity.

Combat is fun, with weapons having hitboxes and a certain reach based on their weapon type. There are somewhere around 15 classes, all of which are interesting and fun to play. The game features a multiclass system, so you can make your character exactly what you want it to be. Whether you're a mage with a huge greataxe, a stealthy tank, or a magical rogue, whatever you want to be is entirely up to you.

War in a Box: Paper Tanks is a plain vanilla TD game that feels rushed.  It's like the developer had some good ideas that were hard to implement and when he got them working, he didn't do much with them.  Like the tower views.  That is all it is…  One view from a chosen turret.  No shooting or even turning the turret.  It's just a camera view.
The game is okay, but it's basic to the point of not really wanting to play it again once you get the 3 stars and 100%.  There are only 5 towers with 3 upgrade levels and 24 small maps.  You can only build towers on predesignated platforms and there are not very many of them scattered throughout the small maps, so you must choose your towers wisely!  Like only 5 - 7!  Once you figure out the correct combonation of towers to use and placement, there is no challenge anymore.  Also, once you place all of your towers and upgrade them, you just sit and watch the battle.  There's nothing left to do...
It's also got one bad design choice IMO.  The enemies don't explode or disappear from the track fast enough and this can cause unpredictable problems. Sometimes shots get blocked, making you lose the level and have to restart the mission over from the beginning.  If you are going for 3 stars, you'll need to start over sometimes.  It's not that bad and doesn't happen all the time, but when it does, it's frustrating.
Animations are stiff, but the enemy are supposed to be made out of paper, so it fits the game style I guess.  The sounds are okay and fit the game well.  It's not a bad or broken game.  It's just very basic and at times, unpredictable.  Hey it runs in the highest settings on both of my Mac's so I give it a huge plus for that alone! :-)
I "only" recommend this game to diehard TD fans looking for something new!!!  Get it on sale like I did or you might regret it...  There are so many better TD games out there for much LE$$!

But there is where all the 'key selling points' of this game end and a fairly generic game begins. You got waves, you can upgrade your towers, you have levels, it all scales up. Downside is the missed chance to do something nice with the game mechanics or animations because we are playing with paper. When a tank is destroyed, it disintegrates... why not unfold or disperse into paper pieces? Ballistics are nice round balls. Why not paper darts or crumpled papers? Why not let a tank burn to the ground? Why can't you destroy a tree that is in the way? Missed chances to make this game stand out a bit more.
Upgrading is also not mouse-frienly, and geared towards touch (where the origins lay I suppose). You have to click the unit, then a menu appears on the left side of the screen, you have to move the mouse and click the upgrade twice. RSI guaranteed.
In the end it is fun for a few round until you yearn again for a good round of OTTTD, Shad'O or Defense Grid.

War in a Box is a basic tower defense game. The graphical style is pretty inspired -- everything looks like it's made out of cardboard and paper and the levels look like a child's playset. You can move the camera just about anywhere and there's also an option to see the game from a tower's perspective (watching it fire at enemy units). The art is definitely top notch.
On the flip side, the gameplay mechanics are not very sophisticated. The tower defense genre has dozens of titles that have innovative twists and interesting mechanics. This game is a bit lacking in that department. Towers are placed in a few fixed positions and have 3 levels of upgrades. Towers and upgrades are instant and there aren't any extra buttons to press. There are no end of level stats or bonuses for leftover money, and while upgraded towers do more damage I couldn't see numbers anywhere.
One mechanic of the game that is somewhat interesting is that each unit, tower, and bullet fired is modelled in the physics engine. This means that trees and destroyed units can block the trajectory of your tower's bullets, and sometimes units go flying off the screen when they are destroyed. It also adds some randomness, since some tower shots may be blocked and this throws off the timing for a wave.
All in all, though, the game is too simplistic for my taste. The art style is cool. But tower defense as a genre is a bit played out and this game adds nothing innovative to keep me interested.

If you would have asked me several days ago if I thought I would recommend this game, I would have said yes. Now however the answer is a resounding no. I was willing to forgive the absolutely horrid launch state of the game server wise, I was even willing to forgive rng loot drops as a reward for pvp to keep people playing in order to achieve there desired "fashion". I looked past alot of bugs and the like because I understand that Sloclap, despite having the big name of Devolver backing them, is still a small studio. There comes a point however when it's too much.
The combat, as most reviews have mentioned, is excellent. It's exactly what I had hoped for. I had some issues with some of the maps in the pvp rotation (specifically the prominence of ledges in them) but for the most part that was fine as well. The controls are excellent for gamepad, which is of course the way a game like this is meant to be played, and I feel that giving it a negative review because of the kbm controls is unnecessary given the type of game this is. The story is a bit lackluster, with just enough lore sprinklings to keep me interested at least. It is short however, so do not buy in expecting a full blown RPG. The dark souls comparisons I've seen from time to time I also think are inaccurate (although anything with even a moderate amount of skill required is "like dark souls" these days according to many) mainly because aside from a relatively connected central hub similar to firelink and an obscured story picked up in bits here and there, there are no real similarities.
Up to this point my review may seem to be positive despite my negative recommendation, but we're getting to that. See, the problem is that although they are a small studio the game has been out for weeks now and there are still bugs that are absolutely gamebreaking. Today the game crashed not just itself but my whole computer. When I relaunched, my saves were gone. All of them. Eighty-four hours worth of progress. Nearly every unarmed move in the game learned. All schools save Khalt unlocked, story beaten, level 200-ish in combat trials, and gear that I had grinded out long and hard to get from that aforementioned rng, gone. This kinda thing happening this long after release is unacceptable. The devs are either incompetent, or just don't actually care. And why should they? The launch was huge, the money's there and they're now free to take it and run. The only real effort they've made to fix save corruption is a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt to back up player's saves in game that is obviously ineffective given that all of my saves are now gone, not just the last one I played.
In conclusion, in it's current state I cannot recommend this game. You should only purchase it at this point if you are okay with all of your progress disappearing at a moment's notice. It's pretty fun, but I'll never get those 84 hours back and I don't think I wanna sink anymore into it knowing it could all go up in smoke again.

Making combos and smiting fools is fun. The story is intriguing, but relies largely on the equipment you find, and a few snippets of dialogue. The game itself is mostly intended as a PVP fighting game. You can co-op with people well enough, but the entire game is aimed towards getting you ready for the end game of PVP. So far, there are a number of planned features that aren't released yet, but the devs seem fairly active in terms of community and patch work.

To start out with, this was given to me as a gift, but I'd have bought it myself knowing what it is now. The game is solid. Yeah, the story is short, but in my opinion the game isn't supposed to be based on the story, but supplement the PvP. The story gives you NPCs that you can learn moves from by using your style's special counter to learn their special moves, which is where the PVE comes in. After you block or evade these moves enough, you can use them yourself. Half the game is building move sets that you can move through seemlessly and change at a moments notice to throw your opponent off guard, which took me a little bit to figure out but was very rewarding. The other half is PVP, where you still learn moves by dodging and blocking the enemy.
People also seem to think that the Drunken Fist style is OP and I have to say it's not as bad as people make it out to be. I don't know the name of the style I use, but I'm able to parry. With the parry ability, I'm able to hold my own against high level people and tend to mop the floor with the Drunken Fist people closer to my level. It's just about having the proper move set and once you learn to parry it's very easy to handle a lot of things.
I will say though that if you're playing with a keyboard and mouse you're at a severe disadvantage. Parrying and other style special dodges are harder and being evasive is even harder. If you don't have a controller you can still have fun but you will have a hard time keeping up unless you play a lot of fighting games with only a keyboard. Which means you have to shell out another 20 bucks or so to be able to keep up with higher levels or more experienced players. Luckily, I already had a controller.
I've not played for a week or two now, been busy as of writing this and playing other games, but the game did go offline frequently but it never really bothered me or my friends. We would just go do PvE and level up our skills and learn new ones, exploring for better equipment. It's not like it was the end of the world when the server went down like others make it out to be.
Like I said in my opening statement, the game is solid. I'd highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys fighting games, but would suggest you invest in a controller to play this at your best, which is the only real downside to this game.

Onto the PC version: I'd heard bad things, but I'm happy to report it worked great for me.  The game is written in Java and doesn't support the Steam overlay for some reason, but it has standard Xinput support so your 360 controller will work perfectly, and it ran at a nice smooth 60 fps on my computer.  There is one bug with the PC version, however: The Enemy Hunter achievement counter apparently resets when you quit the game, so you have to do it in one sitting.

Savant - Ascent has to have been my best 79 pence I have spent all year. As a fan of Dubstep and the man himself since he released ISM, its amazing to see him rise to prominence, even if it includes a video game.
The simplicity of the game bedazzles me, basically its an Arcade/Action style shooter, where you fend off hoards of enemies whilst on either two available platforms, or an elevator of some kind. Some enemies in this game will offer CD pieces when destroyed, and can be collected to form full CD's that offer 1. Sweet music from Savant's previous albums and 2. Exclusive powers to give you an advantage during play.
The game offers limited controls, Left, Right, Mouse Control for aim and Space for Jumping. This makes it a simple game to play for anyone who wishes to reminisce over old arcade shooters. Like myself.
The music you collect through CD's can be selected at will, they are offered as Savant's old songs from his previous albums, they are Ascent, Bach To The Phuture from the Ninur album, ISM from the ISM album, Kali 47 and Butterfly from the Cult album, Fat Cat Shuffle and Melody Circus from the Alchemist album, Organismical from his recent Orakel album and Vario 64 from his Overkill Album.
Overall, I love this game not because I am a fan of Savant, but because this sort of game is so challenging it makes me want to bash my computer in with a Sledgehammer (No pun intended)

I tried the game during a free weekend.
I'm not a casual gamer, i started playing turn-based games since the very first X-Com in 1993 and tried most of the famous titles. Never thought i'd write a negative review on such a game, but i seriuosly can't recommend it to most of the people. The game is hard, and it's achieved not by some tactical advanatages or clever AI, but through crazy random.
80% chance to hit? You'll miss. Twice. 73% chance to climb? You'll fall. Twice. The game is an offence to the theory of probability itself.
That's not to mention quite complicated controls, uninformative map, lack of normal grid, being unable to save at least once during the mission and several other issues that make the game uncomfortable to play.
The devs tried to reinvent a bicycle, and in my opinion they failed. And all the nice features, like interesting tactical moves, character customization and progress and warband management are killed by the rest of the negative things.
Some people might find the game interesting, and i even might buy it myself, if there will be at least 80% discount on a bundle with all the DLCs, but until then - not recommended.

I'm giving this a qualified recommendation.
All the criticisms in other posts are mostly on-point. You live and die by the RNG, but that's also very much like the tabletop game where a series of sub-par rolls will kill you. If living and dying by the dice isn't your thing, then stay away. The optional victory conditions are unnecessarily difficult because one side or the other usually routes before they can be fulfilled. Unlike the tabletop game, finding chests isn't easy, and in the early game isn't even all that rewarding. The graphics are subpar for a game where the meat of the experience takes place in first-person, and animations are lack-luster at best to the point of reminding of the Seinfeld episode where Raquel Welch was revealed to walk without moving her arms.
That said, it's a reasonably accurate translation of the boardgame, and it is fun. When the game is on sale for 60% off, it's worth the money for tbs fans looking for something a little different. At full price ($39.99 at the time of this writing) it's only worth it for dedicated fans of the original tabletop game.
Also, unlike the base game, the dlc is worth the asking price, sale or no.
It's a difficult game, but very fun and heavily focused in strategy. All in all, it's a beautiful gameand well designed.

★☆☆☆☆
Take turns moving and attacking units.
A painfully bad version of XCOM.
Way too slow, not fun, not intuitive.
Maybe this game gets amazing at some point, but the first battle was so mind numbingly boring that I was ready to uninstall before combat even got started, and that combat was no better (see recap below).
- Slow
- Text Walls
- Unintuitive
- No strategy
- Weak Graphics
- Drawn intro movie
- Unappealing factions
- Can't see enemy turns
- Click twice to confirm everything
- Tutorials aren't integrated or dynamic
- Manual upkeep payments, and even to your own character?
- No map or way to locate units (edit: apparently there is a map)
:
- First off, there's the party screen, which is one of the most overcomplicated unintuitive things ever.  There are huge walls of useless text everywhere.  You can't click directly on heroes to edit them, you have to find their little icon at the bottom, which hardly even matches the locations they're standing in.  Things vary between being able to hover over them or having to click on them.  Every part of this menu system is just awfully designed.
- Then we get into the actual "battle", which for the first 5-10 minutes, is not an actual battle.  You can't see the enemy, so you blindly walk around, looking for them, I guess?  XCOM does a similar thing, but it is meaningful and functional, both as a lore aspect and through gameplay.  You arrive and are looking for aliens.  You get audio clues as of which direction the enemy are in, so you know where to go, and you want to approach them slowly and via cover, because if they get the jump on you they'll have an advantage.  Mordheim does none of that, just walk around lost and confused until you get a lucky spot.
- On top of those 5-10 minutes of walking around lost and confused being a frustrating waste of time, its made even worse because enemy turns are not shown to you, but they also aren't skipped, so you can spend several minutes in a row sitting there idle as the game does literally nothing on your end.  Again, XCOM fast forwards though these invisible turns, so it doesn't waste 3 minutes of your time on a long chain of invisible enemy turns.
-  Finally found an enemy!  Woo!  Time for super tactics and meaningful combat?  Nope.  Just faceroll directly at them, get inside their red circle, and spam the default attack.  Quality tactical turn based gameplay design right there.  Again, in XCOM, we've got cover, flanking, abilities, classes, AoEs, heals, and so much more.
- Once I found those enemies, my party was split up, and I had no idea where they were in relation to eachother, because theres no map or any other useful information anywhere in this game, so half of my team spent the match blindly wandering around while the others fought.
-  Then there's the actual combat input itself.  You can freely move around with WASD within set circles, I don't have too many problems with this, though its not especially great.  To end your turn, or input any combat command, however, you have to click once to select it, and then again to confirm it.  Why?  There isn't any additional information provided, its not like you would click on accident.  By this game's design logic, this could be an infinite chain of confirmations.  Are you sure you want to confirm that confirmation?  Are you sure you clicked to click to confirm that confirmation confirmation? etc.  In Final Fantasy Tactics, for example, once you select an attack, it shows you the predicted damage, % to hit, and any additional effects like maybe a counter attack.  That gives the additional confirmation meaning.
- Also, the way you select abilities is idiotic.  It only shows you one at a time, and you cycle through them with Q and E, not sure that could be handled any worse.  Most of the time you just use the default one available anyway.  XCOM, again, has a simple and standard hotbar for you to select abilities from.  Not that any of Mordheim's abilities are even relevant or optional, you just faceroll into an enemy and spam attack.

I am not a fan of the bullet hell genre. I AM a fan of Jamestown. Unlike when playing other bullet hell shmups, I never felt like Jamestown was difficult for the sake of difficulty or taunting my failure to finish a level in some ultra-niche genre. Instead, the Vaunt mechanism, the level design, and the overall tone of the game always seemed to suggest, "You can do it! Try again!" The risk/reward design philosophy behind Vaunt is simple yet brilliant, allowing players to focus on survival or gaining points or a balance between. Perhaps most importantly, the game just /feels/ good to play. Few modern games are this much fun. And don't let the lack of online co-op dissuade you; the single-player experience is fantastic, replay value is great, and the game truly shines when you get one, two, or three friends to play with you on the same screen. There's nothing quite like the rush of victory when you and two buddies narrowly clear a level on Divine difficulty after the third or fourth try.
This is a GREAT return for the franchise!

While I personally can't compare Jamestown to the entire Touhou Project as I've only played a couple titles from the series, this game is a fantastic bullet-hell shooter on the high difficulties, and an enjoyable vertical shooter on the lower difficulties. It's the most fun I've had since Ikaruga and Gigawing 2. If you're a fan of Raiden, Raptor: Call of the Shadows, or even Gradius, I highly suggest you pick this one up and give it a shot.
There are several levels, a couple dozen challenge levels, eight different ships with two firing modes each, and a combo system that encourages skillful movement, positioning, and awareness. If you're a real master at bullet-hell games, I'll admit that Jamestown might be too easy for your liking to get through - but mastering the combo system takes time, patience, and is very rewarding once you can tie together a huge string of hits.
It's available in the Humble Indie Bundle 4 if you want more bang for your buck, but it stands alone quite nicely.

I really want to like this game. I do recommend it, but I ended up refunding it because it wasn't quite what I liked.
+ Interesting concept. I like management games and most of the time it's farming. It's a definite upgrade on the standard tycoon games.
+ Informative tutorial.There are so many things you can manage and the tutorial does a good job covering most of them.
+ Cute dialogue. I didn't play long enough to see real personality, but the brief quips felt less two-dimensional than a bunch of slightly-animated pictures.
+ Low price point. Full price is $6.69 CAD. Can't complain.
The low cost, however, leads to some of the downsides.
- Cut and paste graphics. Honestly it reminded me of Big Fish Games kind of game, just classier. For the low price point I really shouldn't have expected much.
- Lack of a strong soundtrack. Again, low price point. But it would've been nice to switch soundtracks to the genre of music you were producing in, for example.
- Clunky map interface. When preparing for a concert I would've liked to be able to view my songs by genre/popularity. Instead I was using generic titles like "POP LOVE SONG" to remind me what it was. Selecting venues themselves was a bit difficult - being able to roll over each one to see what genres it prefered, setting up a set list for each venue specifically so I didn't have to check every time I changed it, or even just putting their names on the map instead of me waving my mouse in a desperate attempt to find it, would've eased this a lot.
- Grinding. This was why I stopped playing and asked for a refund. After getting out of the pit of debt creep (first 15 minutes) it became "write songs whenever I'm not playing a concert". I'm not sure if I expected more out of the game than this but at 116 minutes I started losing interest. I probably could have tolerated it if the game had been dressed up a little more.
Maybe I'll come back to it. The game does have lots of ways to improve characters, get boosts, etc. so it's not a straight-up grind. The packaging on the outside, however, leaves me wanting a bit more.

This is a game I call a spiral, it basically just ramps up the rewards and costs without any real change in play approach,
The Good:
A fun concept.  I really like the idea of managing a band and was glad to see someone develop a game around it
Play is mostly intuitive and doesn't have a high learning curve
The Not so Good:
Game has no documentation (see note above) and only a basic tutorial.  Many features are not really explained
There are many issues with the game currently.  Dollar amounts reported without formatting, negative numbers, scientific notation, etc.
It doesn't seem possible to win an award even when you have the top two albums and singles in the nomination
The manager mini games are in such broken English as to usually not make any sense but they seem to just be basic outcomes regardless of the choice.  Really should work on translations or with a Native Speaker to improve these to at least make sense
The developers have never apparently seen a map of the world (cities are not in the right places) and apparently the real world size of the cities is not reflected in the touring etc.
Things which should be fixed
There is no ability to change the band's clothes, style, etc or even the characters (just the looks gets boring after a while)
Bad jokes which often make little sense in English or are extremely sexist, misogynistic in nature.
Performance shots are the same regardless of a club with 100 people or a stadium with 100,000
Drop all the racist and sexist stuff please
Not sure about why the band is often involved in criminal activity to make money (and there is little penalty).  This is not reflective of the real world and to me, is not a choice I will make (bribes, swindles, etc. are not typical of bands)
Revamp the performances so they change with the level
Fix the maps so they are at least somewhat like reality
Make some different models for band members
How about some accounting so you can actually track what is going on financially.  The limited reports make no sense much of the time (negative numbers for income etc.).  I really enjoy the management but without data, management is just guesswork.
Wrap Up
A thin game with little content.  It is a casual game for sure and could be great but needs a lot of development, consultation, to improve the content if it is to be a signifcant game with repeat playability. It's a really great game, but for a niche group of gamers. To sum my experiences with this game:
- PvP.
There isn't really much story to the game, and if you find the NPCs difficult to fight, then this game is probably not for you. Very refined combat system. Not talking about the balancing, the devs are working hard on that, just the hit registration and everything is very fluid, especially with the new server stability patch. Devs have said they have been working on more PvP modes beside 1v1, and I'm looking foward to that. For now, allow me to review the game at its current state.
- Technicality.
This game is VERY TECHNICAL, deceptively so. Even in it's early stages, as a fan of fighting games, I can tell this game requires time, patience and practice, even in the deck building, which isn't even the fighting part yet. Feinting, Gold-linking and Delaying, Step-cancelling, Trait-buffering, if you dive deep into the possibilities of the mechanics, it's very diverse and complicated, which may admittedly fustrate some players. Which bring me to my next point.
- Balance.
I briefly mentioned earlier that the devs are working hard to manage the slight balancing issues, and I say slight despite some controversy for a few reasons. Personally, I feel most of the complaints by the average gamer are justified, but do not invalidate this game's fun and complex experience. Again. this is a very technical game, and I spent hours and hours just trying to create a deck that can deal with as many playstyles as possible, let alone actually using it in actual PvP (I'm a perfectionist, what can I say). If you're the kind of player that just wants to fight strangers and whack them with cool or fast combos without considering that there is a meta involved that you might need to work around, adapting playstyles and be thinking on your feet all the time, you will be disappointed.This game's fun comes only when you respect it for everything that it is and put in the effort to be good at it. And I feel that the devs have thought this game through enough to give you enough tools to deal with certain metas. Any regional server issues will definitely be addressed by the devs. The passion and effort such a small team (6 PEOPLE!) put into developing this game is really inspiring.
- Grinding / Learning curve.
A bit of tediousness in things like learning new styles and moves, but I feel this, and the complicated combat system, do help to narrow the scope of players down to a niche enough, but not too obscure group that makes PvP fun so you don't run into mindless whackers/cheese strats all the time (In my experiences anyway. Also, the point on balance above to address the cheese thing) Most of the grinding is PvE, which helps to refine your basic mechanics/fighting game concepts with simple NPC logic patterns, smoothening out the learning curve just enough to familiarise players to the core concepts of the game, all while hiding the intricacies to prevent the average player from getting overwhelmed, leaving those curious enough to discover.
Overall, this game has been exactly what I've been looking for in a fighting game, and I see massive potential for this game, given the devs insight and dedication, and really hope this game grows big. Do give it a try, and if you don't like it, I can perfectly understand. This game is not for everyone, even some of you who are familiar with fighting games. But do consider what I have said before giving a negative review with a one-liner, especially if it's about things that are not part of the core concept of the game like server stability or balancing. Good reviews, patience with the devs, and constructive feedback help game developers learn from their mistakes/complacencies and motivate them to enhance a game's experience as much as possible.

This was a reddit post I made and was encouraged to post it as a review. ANY NEGATIVE REVIEWS, are due to the games launch connection issues that they've already patched once and are about to patch again for stability. THE OTHER BAD REVIEWS come from those too impatient to learn the intricacies of a mechanically deep fighting game...now to the post:

To start: I LOVE THIS GAME. I am addicted.
The art style is beautiful. The combat mechanics are, while a little intimidating to master, some of the best I've ever seen from a fighting game. Be it benevolently intervening whenever I see a fellow player who has bitten off more NPC action than he/she can chew, or picking fights with everyone I meet, the open world aspect of this game is amazing. The Combat Trials (PVP) mode is equally fantastic. I get my butt handed to me just about as often as I am the one doing the handing. Building my own unique set of fighting moves is fun, but something I've honestly not touched ever since unlocking the Stagger style and Rakkio's combat deck. Drunken Master FTW.
However, as with any game, this one is not without its drawbacks. I'm sure if you're reading this, you've heard of the connectivity issues that have plagued it since release. The first week, I could scarcely connect to an online server for sometimes literally days at a time. BUT - the devs have been working as best they can to fix these issues, and I have seen a vast improvement. The past week, every time I start the game up, the little green "Online" indicator is there to greet me. I do still experience lag, to a sometimes match-ruining extent, but it is by far not enough to deter me from playing.
Online, Absolver has decent replayability. Each free-roam session can be totally different if you choose. Team up with others to take on Marked Ones and their lackeys, join a player-owned school and learn some new moves, or pick random passers-by and start beating the ever-loving tar out of them for no reason. There are a number of "boss" NPCs, whose fights start with a cinematic. You can fight each one three times, but after the first time for each, you'll have to do some grinding in Combat Trials before you can face him/her again.
Combat Trials mode, I feel, is the real star of the show here. Once you've built your combat deck to your liking, bring it to bear against other hopefuls in 1v1 PVP matches. Kill your opponent 3 times and you win the match! This mode constantly offers new challenges as each player has his/her own unique play style and combat deck, and you must learn to adapt and find a different way to beat each one.
Offline, replayability is somewhat limited. Sure, once you've beaten all the named NPCs and have been granted the title of "Absolver," you can continue to run about the world, repeatedly ruining the day of the Marked Ones all the other NPCs you come across. You cannot, however, return to the other cinematic-inducing bosses if you're not able to play online, as you must level up in Combat Trials to face them again.
Overall, the game feels like it needs more substance in the way of an actual plot. The fighting mechanics are easy to lose yourself in, and that is great, but it still leaves me wanting more.
If you can only play offline, well, you may find yourself wanting MUCH more.
However, I would still recommend this game to anyone who has the ability to play online, as I CANNOT STOP PLAYING.
If you read this review in its entirety, I salute you.
See you in Adal.

I've never experienced combat like this in any other game. The number of combos you can create with your deck are endless and every opponent I have fought until now had a unique fighting style. Fighting an evenly matched opponent feels amazing, it tests your ability to combo, your reaction time, your ability to adapt to your opponent's fighting style and dodge their barrage of attacks. The controls feel smooth and the game is responsive immediately, it feels like a real fast-paced hand-to-hand duel between you and your enemy in real time. I log on every day just to experience that thrill of overcoming an experienced opponent in a battle of speed, quick thinking and intelligent use of abilties. The weapons system is seamless having smooth swordplay and only allowing the use of a weapon for a limited time as an ability before switching back to hand-to-hand combat, making them a valuable commodity to be used carefully and made the most of as your opponent can knock your weapon out of your hands with the right number of attacks.
The artstyle fits the game perfectly and the sound design and number of cosmetics come together to make for a very enjoyable atmosphere with every Absolver sporting different masks, robes and other clothing items with color variations. I hope the studio will expand upon the number of cosmetics and fine-tune the distribution system through PvP as it motivates most players to engage in PvP duels.
The length of the campain seems to be the dealbreaker for most people, however I didn't feel the abscence of more bosses and areas significantly changed my experience as the main attraction of the game has been the combat mechanic and PvP duels for me. However, if the studio further expanded on the singleplayer elements through more bosses, regions and worldbuilding, I'm sure the reception would improve. There is a lot of potetial in the singleplayer campaign to become a vast souls/journey-like experience and I hope we will see this improvement in the future.
I'm really enjoying this game thus far and would love to see future updates expanding on both singleplayer and PvP elements. I'm hoping the studio doesn't abandon this game, it has so much potential to be more. It's great, but it could be amazing.

Empire Total War is comparable to an outdated grandparent, an old dusty yet beloved teddy bear stashed away in the closet, or your one and only soul mate, who may thoroughly anger you, yet you still love them with every beating ounce of your heart. Empire Total War is just that; although the game may be annoying, outdated, and frusturating, one can simply not resist to love the game, which, in its own way, is quite the masterpiece.
For those readers who do not know, the Total War series is a well established set of games in which the player controls a nation, its politics, trade, finance, and of course, its military conflicts. Now, do not rush to quickly classify Empire as a boring tactical game void of action, this is where the Total War games, especially Empire, truly surpass other games of the same genre. The player experiences two seperate "gaming styles/points of view", the first being the campaign map, where the player may see their entire nation, select cities, construct buildings, develop trade networks, and move one's troops around the map to face enemy forces or conquer cities. The player can also move navies around the ocean to establish trade and face enemy fleets in naval warfare. Now this is where the Total War games really put the "Total" in the phrase; the player controls one's forces in the actual battles! In the battles the player can micro manage his or her forces, telling them when to go, what to do, who to shoot or charge, and so on. The naval aspect is quite similair, the main difference being... it's on water, duh. The greatest aspect of the battles is that they are comparable to actual battles that took place at that time. Meaning, the battles are "actual size" and a player can have thousands of troops on screen fighting it out as if watching a line battle from a front row seat in the 1700's. Silly reader, you won't be watching, you will be the one commanding the forces.
Empire has a significant amount of glitches that truly drain from the overall experience in many cases. The game also was not, in my opinion, developed to its full potential. Make no mistake, the game's sweeping and vast campaign map, numerous playable factions, and unique controllable units are truly capable of blowing the player away. There is just so much to conquer and gaze at! Despite the game's several draw backs, Empire: Total War is truly a "Must Buy".
It should be taken into consideration that Empire: Total War was released in 2009. Thus, the graphics aren't mind blowing. On the highest graphics setting, the game can truly be quite appealing to the eye. Unfortunately however, the "Ultra" setting requires a considerably decent computer to have the graphics and still have the game run smoothly. I personally do not have the best gaming computer, but she definitelty "gets me by" with this game. On the weaker computers, the lowest graphics setting is the player's most probable safe bet. However, the player should note that he or she would be sacrificing the overall asthetic appeal of the game. Animations are not affected on the lower settings, however your experience will be more like of that of a one good eyed 93 year old with 10/20 vision.(Don't quote me on the vision statistic, I believe that's quite low however.) The in-game troops will look quite commical with petrifyingly lowly detailed faces. However, it must be noted that there are thousands of said ugly gentle fellows. That leads me to another topic, there are a select number of female units, huzzah! Anyways, the main point being, don't expect to see beautiful graphics on a weaker computer running the lower graphic settings. Keep in mind however, the game does look quite appealing on the higher graphics settings.
Now, I will attempt to remain as well mannered as possible throughout this paragraph, the reason being: the AI can in some instances (if not a considerable amount) be plain stupid! On both the campaign map and in battles the AI troops rarely fail at aggravating the player to the extent of doing his or her own bayonet stab at the screen. This game is mostly looked up by fans of the oh so glorious Transport Tycoon and Traffic Giant, because nowadays, it is quite rare to find transportation games made.

CiM is definitely more Traffic Giant than Transport Tycoon. You manage a citiy's public transportation network, including buses, trams, subways, helicopters and boats. The gameplay is definitely comparable to TG, but it seems slightly less professional. For example, you can't let buses and trams stop at one station. Buses only pick up passengers at designated bus stops, and trams need their own stop, too. Other minor cosmetic details the game lacks are the ability to place (longer) train stations diagonally, which makes it sometimes difficult to efficiently place elevated tracks and stations in cities with a round shape.

These minor things are however almost entirely neglected by the fact that the AI (e.g. the city's inhabitants) are far superior. They don't need a tram and a bus to stop at one specific station. They get off the bus, look around, see a tram station not far and they will go there by foot and then take the tram. This allows for realistic, central traffic hubs with a subway exit which people leave, then cross the street to get to the bus stop to continue their journey.

In general, the game looks great. Graphics are VERY detailed, I've spent at least 40-50% of my playtime doing nothing but watching my trains and trams going around town, picking up passengers, fighting their way through the (sometimes intense) car traffic and all the other little things you can observe.

There are 4 maps in the game, which you can play in a period of 100 years. In this time period, cities grow and change, just like the cars and vehicles you can use change. The managment of your business is not super deep, you can set the maintenance percentage of stations and vehicles, but not much more. You can get loans, but these things are somewhat simple, too. For example, after taking three loans of each 100 million $ from three different banks, the fourth bank is totally fine with giving you a fourth, giant credit wihtout even asking. So, the economic structures are there, but they are kept somewhat simple. Which is fine by me.
Slight issue with this: atm chaning ticket prices doesn't seem to affect anything. You still have 300 people waiting in your metro stations. Maybe this will be fixed later. Nothing serious, though.

In general, this is not Sim City, it's not complex and deep and superior in any possibly way, but it is a very fun game for people interested in the subject. And for 20€/$/whatnot really worth its money.

I love Bust-a-move, so Intergalactic Bubbles is the sort of game that would get my attention quite quickly. On a simple level, this is taking the classic Bust-a-Move game style and putting it in a 3d situation. It does do that, and for the price, I'd say it's definitely worth the money, but I do have to say that there's some missteps with the game.
First of all, Bust-a-Move had a lot of interesting level design, something that's entirely absent here. There's 5 'worlds' of 50 levels each, and each new world adds an extra color into the mix. However, within a world, every single level is basically the same, you have solid rows of bubbles and higher levels simply have more rows. As the number of rows increments slowly, this means that every single level in a world feels basically the same as the one before it. It ends up feeling very monotonous and repetitive, and even a handful of change-ups in there would make it more engaging. The other issue in this vein is the power-up system. There's really too many options in the power-ups, and it somewhat bothers me that having beaten the game, I can't unlock everything on the power-up tree. There is also that by having the right power-ups, the game goes from very challenging, to beating every level in about half the required shots. I flew through about the last 20 levels because of the right power-up combination making this, imo, too easy.
There's also a few issues with the rendering. The shots that take advantage of the 3rd dimension seem to have a nasty habit of getting stuck somewhere slightly earlier than what the arrow would indicate, which is really frustrating. There is also that the bubbles don't always handle occupying the same space well, and you can have a chain reaction of glitches virtually clear the board sometimes. I beat levels in only about 10 shots a few times because a glitch would happen in one corner, and take out the entire field. It basically finishes the level for you, so on one hand, that's sort of convenient and it's a bit harder to get made about it, but on the other hand it's a bit frustrating and it sometimes meant that I had to restart the game to get the controls working normally again.
Overall, while there's a few interesting mechanics on top of the classic Bust-a-move (such as using momentum of bubbles to make connections), it's a bit lacking, but still good entertainment for the price (a buck or two)

Intergalactic Bubbles is hardly an original game design; it's one of those simple games that get cloned ad nauseam, like Arcanoid or Tetris. Nevertheless, such clones are invariably entertaining because their core idea is so good, and if they manage to give it some nice twist, they can expect some real popularity.
This is exactly what Intergalactic Bubbles does: by taking the concept of "put balls of the same colour together to make them disappear" and adding real physics, as well as some special moves and buyable upgrades, it provides a surprisingly good gaming experience. Yes, each level is virtually the same, but it's just this kind of game - it's pointless to expect anything else from it. It is what it is, and the repetitiveness is a feature like any other, not a shortcoming. What matter is that it's fun to shoot the balls, look for combinations, buy new skills and watch the balls swing quasi-realistically (hopefully with unexpected combos).
The game has no major weak points, but the graphics aren't exactly pretty, which is a shame for this kind of game (especially visible on Steam cards, which I've melted to crystals as soon as possible just to get them out of my sight). I also have some reservations regarding balance of power-ups (for example, bomb costs more energy despite being less useful than multi-coloured ball), but it has very little impact on the actual gameplay.
To sum up: Intergalactic Bubbles is a game for many, many evenings, but only if you don't mind doing the same thing over and over. But it never hurts to try, especially since the game is addictive as hell.

This is a Warhammer tabletop game conversion into a video game. And it is amazing. Hailing form GamesWorkshop. Into the grim dark Warhammer world, this game really immerses and sets the enviromental/atmosphere of the tabletop and fantasy world. I don't think they could of done better with that aspect. The music is eerie and the maps of Mordheim itself are rather halloween gone dark.  Nothing is happy and yay, but grim, dark and pulsing chaos mutations growing on the walls kinda thing. ITS GREAT. With buildings and walkways all over the maps, it really does feel like a city gone to ghost town and believable. Choose to make a warband out of 5 possible factions. Chaos, Skaven, Empire, Sisters of Sigmar and Witchhunters.  Within each warband you get characters to make thus warband. Choose a hero and a leader that will be the mainstay and backbone of your army. You only get one of each and this is where you can really design what your warband will be capable of or designed to do in game. ( If you are going kinda ranged or melee or spellcasting )Then you get henchman. Henchman are the simple guys that you get more out of their numbers then your ''one man army'' characters. You do get to custimize names and outfits and really make the warband personal, so dont be afraid to! Also the RPG aspect of the game of leveling your warband as individauals and as a warband is there. Equipment is important and make sure you got your warband in tip top shape before you venture out!  So in Mordheim; CIty of the Damned,  you have the  controlling your warband- leveling them up , equiping them and learning skills and paying the henchmen, a shop- to buy/sell equipment for your warband, Skirmish -where you can do fights against other online warbands, Vetern-where your compiled expereince and acheivments and such, from all your warbands lets you spend and upgrade points that all your warbands gain access too. Then the two big points is the campign and your shipments. The whole point of the game and your warband is to steal, pillage plunder wyrdstone. The missions are played in tactical turn based combat style. It's extremely unforgiving and you need to make some tough dicisions. There is alot fo rolling dice going on with the attacks and defence. Extreme luck and randomness happens. Magic? HAHA well remember that things dont always happen the way you want to... Map awareness is to be learned and your warband to work together as a team. Cliche? yes, but men stay dead when they die and loot can be more vauable then life! Wyrdstone is what your fighting over and killing/stealing from the other warbands from in missions in the campign mode. All the missions are about gaining these goods so you can make shipments to your supreme leader/god/king. Making shipments and doing missions is good for your warband and the'll level up and equipment and your warbands numbers will grow. FAILURE to get your hands on the green rocks and dying in combat, makes perminant injurys to your warband and will make life harder for you to complete more missions. After failing to ship out the wyrdstone up to 4 times, your warbands and your life is forfit and die. GRIM? Well its Warhammer. The game is to be hard, and to experince the stress and toll pillaging and killing can be. For good or bad, its a tough life. SO, can you keep your warband together? Think you have the leadership to be succesful in the pit, deseased rotten Mordheim ? With creepy music and lots of screaming/blood animations in combat, this game is as dark as it goes. Referances to Dunes '' The spice must flow'' comes to mind while playing this game...

Crazy Monkey Studios knocks it out of the park with its freshman effort, Guns, Gore & Cannoli. GG&C is a sidescrolling action game in the vein of the Shank games, but much better executed in my eyes. GG&C wonderfully mixes accessibility with fun and excited gameplay that looks great to boot.
Like Shank, the first thing most people will notice with GG&C is the fantastic art direction. I really liked the ripped-from-a-comic-book aesthetic that the game presents and it fits perfectly with its 20’s era gangster vibe. The animations pair quite nicely with the art and are satisfyingly fluid and responsive. The visual layout that Crazy Monkey went with here was very smart, as the action is never muddled and it’s always clear what is background and what is foreground, which not every game does well. These characteristics carry over to the enemies as well as there is good enemy variety and each one has a distinct silhouette and is instantly recognizable. The enemy animation is quite nice as well, as I found shooting the chef and watching him pop like a bloated blood balloon particularly satisfying.
The gameplay itself is quite tight with just the right amount of float (which I’m usually not a fan of, but it works well here). You are progressively given more guns to use and each feels like an incremental upgrade over the prior one without making the previous guns obsolete. One of my biggest complaints with Shank was that when you were hit or knocked down, your character was locked into an animation of them getting up which, if you were swarmed, would lead to an infinite loop causing you to be unable to escape and eventually dying. Klei usually makes very good design choices but that was certainly not one of them. Thankfully, Crazy Monkey does not make this cardinal sin. When you are hit you slow down a bit, but it is easy enough to recover and gives you a chance to escape.
The story is also better than it has any right to be, honestly. While not the deepest of plots, I was engaged enough to care about character’s motivations and it’s clear the team over at Crazy Monkey loves themselves some gangster movies. It’s a simple narrative, but charming all the same.
While I played through the four hour campaign solo, (and loved it) GG&C can be played with up to four players coop, and I imagine it’s even more of a blast there. For me, the game was just the right difficulty when played solo but I’m not sure how enemy scaling works when played with more people. In addition, there is also a versus mode where players can face off against each other. Again, I did not try this mode.
I had my eye on Guns, Gore & Cannoli for quite some time and I’m glad that when I came around to picking it up, it surpassed my expectations. This is definitely in the upper echelon of sidescrollers that I have played and would love to see Crazy Monkey Studios do another. Whether playing it solo or couch coop there is plenty of fun to be had here and it’s definitely a game that deserves your time and attention.

If I were to describe Spheritis in a single word, I would probably call it "hopeful". I would also be inclined to call it "convoluted", which is unfourtunately the word that stands out to me.
Spheritis is a game in the same vein as Ballance, Aerox, Monkey Ball and a good number of others. In these games you roll a ball around a stage, solving puzzles and watching as the natural flow of the level either provides the feeling of speeding along rolling hills or the curves of a racetrack, or sends you off the side and into oblivion. Most games of this ball-rolling genre have one or the other, but more often they are a mix.
Currently, Spheritis is halfway there, by which I mean it's slow. No matter which type of ball you're using, the control always feels like it's giving into the terrain more than your keyboard, and I often find them sliding further than I wanted them to even when I don't have to deal with ice, as if they're all made of heavy stone. Granted, this isn't all that much of a problem in the end, but it can be annoying.
Next, the levels, and this is where "convoluted" comes into it. In each level you are required to press a number of switches that will open the exit portal, avoiding traps and other hazards along the way. To do this you are afforded six different powerups - so far I have found Jump, Speed, Levitate and Shrink. Might edit this review once I find the other two - that will help you reach those switches. At first it doesn't sound like a problem, but having to go back and forth across the level, finding the wood ball workshop to be light enough to boost over the gap to get the shrink powerup to then get that button at the other end of the map but oh wait... crushy trap in the way. I need to go back to change to a steel ball in order to get through.
Convoluted. That word is the bane of many games, but this type I feel suffers more from it. Ball-rolling (or whatever the actual name for the genre is) games need to have a certain flow to them in order to stay fun. Ballance did this perfectly, which each part of the level leading onto the next. The puzzles still needed to be solved, but it really felt like you were getting somewhere once you did so. In its current state, Spheritis will have you backtracking again and again, looking for where you left that stone ball workshop so that the spikes won't kill you. There are also bonus stars to find in each level, though right now I don't really see what they add other then something to have an achievement for.
Now for the "hopeful" side. Spheritis looks like it has potential, definitely. While the level designs could do with some more imagination, and the mechanics given a few tweaks here or there, I do think some of the groundwork and developer skill is evident so far. Especially given the fact that this is just one person who has made this entire game so far. I... wouldn't say buy it just yet - although at just £5.00, that's pretty cheap to be fair - but keep an eye on it. It could be a worthy addition to the genre given time.

[TL;DR] KBM controls are horrible, recommend only to players used to using gamepads.
After playing a while now, I've found that Absolver has the potential of a great fighting game.
The art style, music, and a few gorgeous sights overall create a pleasant and enjoyable atmosphere. The unique level design, and the fact that there is no minimap, contribute greatly to the sense of mystery already perpetuated by (or lack thereof) a rudimentary story.
The animations are smooth and good-looking and flow nicely.
There is, however, a major flaw in the gameplay.
While the combat looks incredible, and is very, very satisfying, the Keyboard and Mouse controls are abysmal. Especially controls for Block, Dodge, and Absorb, which are bound to various mouse movements. While there is full gamepad support, and one may easily switch to one, such flaws in a 30$ game simply should not exist. The controls are clunky and at times feel unresponsive, and even the developers themselves advise using a gamepad, meaning that they are fully aware of the horrendous state KBM controls are in.
In the early stages of the game one might not notice the awkwardness of KBM controls, however in late game 1v1 PVP modes, the weird, stragenly unresponsive controls start to put KBM players at a major disadvantage. The above metioned Block, Dodge, and Absorb abilities are very unreliable to use, but are a major part of combat, as each respective ability may stop and turn the tide of the match.
Aside from KBM controls, the occurences of infinite loading screens and black screens in PVP contribute greatly to the (non-existing) immersion, in that you have to restart the game after every second match or so.

Few points to make:
1. Absolver's netcode is so bad that they purposely dont allow players to check their ping or to filter whom they're matched with (probably so the players dont realise that they've foregone regional servers for peer-to-peer $$$ savings).
2. The singleplayer 'campaign' (Its actually more of a tech demo) takes just enough time to complete (4ish hours) so that you cant refund xdddd.
3. The gronks in question, Sloclap, managed to slither their way through Valve's remarkably low game standards and masquerade their early access tech demo as a full featured product.
4. Developers overtly mention, after release, that the sole purpose of the PvE map is as a lobby for their PvP content (of which, only 1v1 duels are avaliable) - and that apart from tweaking cosmetics and adding the odd new AI that they won't be further addressing the widespread networking issues.

So for the uninitiated who are curious, M.A.X. is a simultaneous turn or turn-based strategy / RTS hybrid... Wonder how that works?
Well imagine playing the classic Dune 2 / Command & Conquer with all the RTS mechanics in place as a turn based strategy game. Quite simply it was an innovative risk by developers Interplay that actually paid off! As a result, the game was very highly praised by critics back in the day, and is widely regarded by those who have played it to be one of the greatest Turn based games of all time. It's a game which unlike the RTS games of the day, was never copied or cloned. So to this day still remains rather unique!
Whilst the graphics have indeed aged (some would say rather well for a game released in 1996), the core gameplay, its mechanics and the whole package still holds up today. It is a testament to the quality of M.A.X. and if you have any interest in the Strategy genre, because you missed it first time around, or simply was too young or not even born back then, this is well worth picking up! Be aware though, this game is not like an RTS, you cannot rush your opponent and expect to live. This game will crush you if you try. Careful planning, and even planning turns ahead is a key to victory. War in M.A.X. is never easy!
But....
However there are a few cons. This is due to the game and its age worth noting. Whilst this game is regarded a masterpiece, it is a diamond in the rough. The game is a little unpolished and still in some instances buggy. From what I can tell, this Steam version is just a re-release and hasn't been updated beyond what fixes existed for the time, so you may run into a crash here or there and/or experience a few live wires. But it doesn't detract from the game too much.
Also...
This game is old. MS-DOS 1996 old. Whilst we have the miracle of DOSBOX,, Some compiled games run with DOS4GW .bat executables. This has been known to cause issues on modern machines with some older games. M.A.X. is no exception, and there have been reports of the game freezing up and crashing at 100+ turns due to a Memory Stack Overflow bug. Considering certain missions and multiplayer games can go upwards of 300-400 turns, this is a problem if you do experience it.
However, all is not lost if you do experience this issue, and all that is required is a bit of manual tinkering. You simply need to convert the DOS4GW executable to DOS32A... How to do that you ask??? The answer is here:
Overall though. If you can get past a few potential issues with an "As is" game that has stood the test of time. You are in for a treat. This is still one incredible game and is very much welcome on Steam. At the price-point, it's a steal in my book!

If you don't have at least 6GB+ of VRAM you may experience stutters and low framerates on Ultra Quality, try to reduce some settings, but first try to reduce Texture Quality, and turn off Shadow Cache if you still have low framerates, it doesn't make a lot of difference and plays way smoother, optionally I'd suggest to turn off Depth of Field (optional), Blur, Chromatic aberration (hate it) and Lens Flare (eyes are not cameras), for cleaner image quality.

I played Getting Up a long time ago, but I remembered that there was not a game like this one. It is a quite unique mixture of platforming/climbing + fighting the enemies using your combos and weapons + graffiti + some stealth actions.
Pluses:
+ very interesting story. You play as Trane who wants to become famous, to get up, but later you get into political intrigues and scandals and become a rebel!
+ Graffiti! There are lots of styles to choose from.
+ Atmosphere of anti-utopian city. There are guards and patrols who will shoot or try to apprehend you as soon as they spot you.
+ Music! It is one of the best soundtracks I have ever heard. Songs vary from hip-hop to hard rock!
+ CGI cutscenes. There aren't many of them, but they are very well done.
+ Voice actors. Rosario Dawson, Giovanni Ribisi, Brittany Murphy and many other famous people gave their voices to different characters.
Minuses:
- Not very comfortable controls. Your character sometimes just doesn't want to do what you want him to do. And yes, use gamepad. It's just better.
- Stealth. I love stealth games such as Splinter Cell and Deus Ex, but here it is just poorly executed. It is not obligatory, but you won't survive otherwise.
All in all, solid 9 out of 10! Try it.

TL;DR, game is boring because the combat just isn't that satisfying after a handful of hours.
I haven't written a review before, but I feel this is something other people aren't saying. I really wanted to like Absolver, and even got to combat level 50 on the second day. I didn't lose a single pvp match before getting the hundred win achievement or whatever it is. As it is, I've lost maybe ten of the few hundred fights I've had. The reason is that the combat system isn't "deep" like advertised or talked about. It boils down to find a fast chain with built-in crushes and a couple of slow but high damaging moves to throw in when they start parrying. Other than that, just pay attention. Essentially every attack but the fastest jabs are parriable on reaction. If the opponent starts throwing in feints, just jab until they reliably parry the string and throw in some heavy attacks. Feinting is almost pointless considering the recovery time on parries is juuuust long enough to land spinning high kick or your damage move of choice if they expect a jab or the normal string ender. The combat isn't so much "chess" like many people are calling it; it's more like the most basic mixups in literally any fighting game, with a ridiculously easy parry mechanic that makes fighting boring pretty quickly. I've had fights drag on and on and on because of back-and-forth parries. The only reason there isn't a defensive meta is because the parries aren't really rewarding due to the servers: you basically just get stamina and reset the neutral, with no real guaranteed punishes. Regardless, this game's combat gets stale in a spectacularly short amount of time, and I don't really see how that could change in the future.

I've tested it during 3 day free trial.
TLDR: Good idea for a game, balanced mechanics, but with some frustrating little inconsistancies, bugs, and too little content per race. Try it, for a few warband levels, if you like it, buy it, if not, you probably won't like it in the future.
Pros:
+ tutorial explains the basics, however there are some rare situations, when I find myself wondering what will happen if XYZ... and those situations are unexplained...
+ combat mechanics are good, well balanced (except 2x1H weapons:( - they should change that for sure), charge, ambush, dodge, parry stances are all OK, however they should add a contant reminder for begginers, what costs what, so you can plan ahead, instead I've found myself lacking 1 movement or attack point, that could be spared if I knew it beforehand...
+ looting, equipement and RPG elements for every one single unit is very good, XP gains are slow, but not too slow. you get points to distribute, when you get each 1/4 of a level.
+ each of the unit, have many stats, that are clearly explained, so you know what you must do, to get better at what you want.
+ game offers a decent challange regarding difficulty... some missions are harder, some easier, some you can win without losing a single unit
+ good number of maps (12 i think is the number now), that have numerous types of deployment rules, with random wyrmstone gems and chests to scavenge for. Also i think there are seperate maps for campaign special quests but im not sure. also the side quests, are quite interesting and valuable
Cons:
- you cannot change armor/weapon proficientcies for any unit, so if you want to make an archer from a meelee fighter, you can't... also you can't for example use hammers for warrior that uses maces. so you're stuck with those weapons that devs set up for this specific unit.
- there are for every faction only: 1 leader, 3 hero units, 2 henchmans, and 1 giant unit (counts as 2) to choose from... so it lacks diversity in regards to units (not factions). At one time, you can only have 10 units on the battlefield, and thats a good number, not too high, not to low.
- skills are too expensive, so for the first 20~ games, youre stuck with generic units, even if you got ability points to spend. you will lack money, or you will not want to waste precious warrior in next few battles, to instead learn a new skill in X days.
- equipement picked up, and then dropped by your dying unit, dissapears after winning game, unless you pick it up, by some other unit... wich is quite annoying. also you only get a very small percentage of whole loot on the map, after winning, so sometimes you find yourself stalling, and scavenging instead of killing the enemy right away.
- some sidequests in campaign are very hard to do, and others are very prefered. you always get 2XP plus additional 3XP for sidequests, where for a win, you get only 2XP. so a mission without a completed sidequest is worth 1/2 of the other one... again you sometimes have to stall to get the side objective done
- there are some UI issues, that should be handled... it feels like a console game with control scheme and hints. however there should be some options added that would help to orientate, for example: overhead unit icons, and maybe custom icons for each unit... also scavenge and wyrmstone sites are marked on map, but when its inside a 3 story building, you must run thru whole of it, to find it. mark it clearly OR just disable those markings, and add more of those points to collect, so you must find it yourself, but its easier. also only recently I've found out how to check, wich specific unit is in the initiative queue next (shift and then E/Q)

Music Awards Manager. . .wait. . .Music Awards Tycoon. It's one of those. But it doesn't matter, because neither of them are accurate. You are not managing music awards, but rather a band.
There's not a lot to do in Music Awards Manger Tycoon. You can rehearse, you can buy your band members new instruments, play shows to get fans, write song, record songs, and do odd jobs to get the money to pay your bills.
There's really no challenge in the game. Every week you need to have a certain amount of money for your bills. If you don't have that money. . .maybe something happens? There's no reason you shouldn't have the money, because working gives you a very generous payout (sometimes it can be as much as four times what you need to pay your bills) and doesn't take a lot of time.
And that is the only thing you have to watch out for. Your band members don't get tired or stressed or sick or unhappy or anything. They're always good, so they can always work, perform, record, whatever. So, all you have to do is work enough to pay your bills, buy studio time, or upgrades. Then, just do whatever. Play shows, get more fans to unlock new venues, play shows there, get more fans, repeat.
Write a new song every so often. No much goes in to that. Pick a genre. Pick a theme, that doesn't really matter except you'll get a bonus if it's popular at the moment or if your band has items that increase the quality. Pick what effects you want to add on to the song. Pro-Tip: Add them all. There's no reason not to. It takes more time, but time seems to be meaningless. Then, figure out how you want to mix the song and give it a title.
Record your songs, so the quality can drop significantly. Why does this happen? I don't know. But it does. Record enough songs and you can release an album.
And then you just keep repeating all of this. Again and again. It gets old fairly quick. But if you love repetitive action and naming songs, then Music Awards Manager Tycoon Sim is a great choice.

Had a lot of fun playing this game completely blind, and trying to solve all the puzzles independently on Senior Detective mode. Although the game is made by HER Interactive, I believe some male gamers might still enjoy the challenge the game presents in using one's brain to fit hints and pieces of the story together, and ultimately solve the mystery.  As a kid I was a fan of reading the Nancy Drew novels, so there was a bit of the nostalgia factor at work for me, but really if you're just the type of person whom enjoys a decently concocted plot, as well as the mystery genre, you'll probably find enjoyment in this title. If you aren't into solving puzzles, or have very little patience, best to avoid as such things ARE a requirement here. In summary:
Pros:
+ Creative puzzle designs and decent graphics for it's time
+ Outdated graphics still hold a certain charm in their aesthetic, as does the period music
+ Good voice acting. Nancy Drew's voice in particular is quite memorable and occasionally pops into my head when reading lines from other leading female detectives in novels
+ Good character variety with a believable setting
+ There are some very genuinely funny and cute things that give the game a human flair; like the quack hypnotist guy owning a cat you briefly interact with, smatterings of relevant real world literature, and the money earning sidequests leading you to dialogues with various quirky small townsfolk
+ Nancy herself is a well-developed protagonist, and the phone/radio conversations she had with her father, friends, and random strangers were some of the best. She has some sass and fire when the situation calls for it, but isn't rude, and has a thirst for exploration & knowledge that makes her relatable
Neutrals/Cons:
- A few of the puzzles were annoyingly chance based, or difficult based on controls
- Although most of the puzzle rewards and clues end up pointing you in the right direction, I still personally ran into a couple of moments where I couldn't figure out where to go next without looking it up
- Backtracking. Lots of backtracking
- The sewing machine game. Accounted for 90% of my frustration
Overall:
8 out of 10

I very rarely had to use guides, and that may feel simplistic to some more hardcore puzzle solvers, but I liked the easier flow. The driving wasn't great, and I do admit the whole telegram/gas/money endeavor was a bit annoying, but only minutely to me. I enjoyed the characters, the fun twist ending, and the story a great deal. It's not one of the absolute best ND games, but it was definitely one I personally enjoyed.

This was my first Nancy Drew game, and I was surprised by how challenging it was! Every detail is significant - I recommend keeping your own notes in addition to the one Nancy keeps for you. The puzzles were great and the story was entertaining, if a little hokey.

As someone who has never been great at moving characters or objects skillfully on a computer screen, I found these both frustrating and time consuming.
But overall, very fun - I'm looking forward to playing more Nancy Drew games!
