First off I'll say I enjoy this game though it has many obvious flaws. There are quite a few things it does right like the pvp and enconter system and I loved both. But through my journey which took no more than about 6 hours for me to complete I experienced a lot of bugs at least 9 times I was just walking down a main pathway and I just fell through the map and died. Along with phasing through objects and walls along with the bosses which would often multiply(more than certain the same boss shouldnt be in the same area like 2 of the same boss and 2 other enemies which are often stuck in their running animation prior to your arrival). But its a solid fighting game especially its community ive yet too meet any players who refuse to start off a battle with a friendly bow along with people often being happy to cooperate with randoms. I like how this game also rewards practice and skill In 1 v 1 duels the winner will almost always be the better player of course there are spammers and those who try to abuse armored abilities ( basically only Charged Haymaker) but there isnt a massive amount of them at least from my personal experience. I also have come accross bugs within the school system which keeps me from gaining experience in it. In short the system allows you to learn attacks and the defensive abilities of another class like if you start one of the 3 starters (Khalt , Forsaken , Windfall) you can learn the stagger style which though is fun is very irritating to fight. Out of the 4 combat styles I personally have enjoyed windfall the most fluent precise and fast but there is a lot of inconsitency with pvp like the tracking on some moves is just stupid and will follow you and your dodge no matter which direction you go.And the forsaken classes defensive ability parry is exceptionally hard to time so its not recommended for a beginner( didnt read the explanation at the beginning telling of its difficulty suffered later due to this ).  In the end through all its bugs and minor inconviences I'd still recommend this game. Its fun and has a good pace a little dissapointed in the story though didnt really expand much on the lore and overall importance of important characters ( I could also be very ignorant or its hidden 50/50 chance I'd say) but its a great game which succeeds where other games like it failed ( R.I.P For Honor ).

The best MMORPG game I've played (and I've played a lot of different ones).
It's got it's fair share of bugs, and it can be laggy in some situations. It's not very well opimised so people with slow hard drives, and not very powerful computers might have issues.
But despite this, it's still kept my interest for many years.
It's got great character customisation (although sadly not as much cosmetic customisation as I would like), and lots of interesting quests.
The only down side is that while it is technecally a free to play game, and you can infact play it for free. Getting past level 14 or so becomes very hard due to there being few free to play quests after that point. You can unlock more quests by earning pay for money in game, but it's very time consuming to do so, and becomes easier the more content you have unlocked (so it's harder to do to start with).
It lets you really try the game out though, and I would recomend anyone who likes the game to spend at least a bit of money in order to change their account from free to play to a premium account (unlocks permanently after you spend any amount of money on the game). Doing so lifts a lot of restrictions on your account.
Other than that, the only thing that I can think to say is that the comunity created wiki for the game is your friend in this game.

Guns, Gore & Cannoli puts you in the stylish shoes of mobster Vinnie Cannoli. Residing in Thugtown during the 1920's, Vinnie soon finds himself in the middle of not only a zombie apocalypse, but a war between two mafia families. The game is a 2D side-scrolling shooter that is promised to be packed with action. The real question here, is whether or not this title is worth your time and money.
The hand-drawn graphics have a great comic style to them, and they're very pleasing to look at. There are vibrant colors abound, which off-set the overall noir style and tone of the game. Completing the 1920's gangster era vibe, the jazzy music is a classy touch that completes the overall immersion of the setting. However, there are relatively few enemies that you will encounter; although Vinnie does make a quip about this from time to time, noting that it feels like he's killing the same people over and over again. Oddly enough, the lack of foes does not hinder the game much, as the backgrounds and foregrounds are consistently changing to something new and fresh. That, and the amount of fire, bullets, and explosions pretty well cover up the bad guys anyway.
When it comes to gamplay, Guns, Gore & Cannoli is pretty straightforward. There are copious amounts of weapons that you will acquire throughout the game; a shotgun, mini-gun, flamethrower, rocket launcher, and a magnum are just a very small amount of the large arsenal that you will come across. Likewise, not only do you have grenades at your disposal, but the ever-so-handy Molotov as well. All ammunition, with the exception of your starting handgun, is limited and you must be conservative of your bullets. Like your bullets, your health can also deplete rather quickly in a large swarm of zombies, and you can only heal by gobbling up delicious cannoli that is scattered throughout the levels; usually after a well placed checkpoint.
The game only clocks in at roughly 2 hours in the longevity department, and this is if you take your time to explore and kill as many enemies during your first run through as possible. This time frame is pretty well to be expected for most run-and-gun types, just be forewarned that this is not a title that will keep you entertained beyond one or two playthroughs at the most. The good thing is, is that there are multiple difficulties to try, and a very handy level selection menu in case you want to try out that new laser weapon at an earlier point in the game.
All in all, Guns, Gore & Cannoli is a fairly decent side-scrolling shooter. It takes a unique twist on the over-saturated zombie market of today, by throwing in some Italian gangsters, humor, and a nice plot twist at the end. For the two hours of play time, I wouldn't recommend grabbing this title at its full price, but on sale it's a definite steal. I didn't get the chance to check out the 4 player local co-op, but if you have some friends over they could make this game even more fun.

A rather old game, but it is still amazing. Does it stack well against the new entries of Hearts of Iron? Maybe, maybe not, but from my own experience, Darkest Hour has given me more hours of content than Hearts of Iron III. For what it is, it's an amazing WWII game where you can play different scenarios, from the Great War to the onset of the Cold War. While it does a great job keeping you immersed in the nation you're playing, it does a better on the combat. Hearts of Iron has always had a very complex combat system, and it doesn't help that the tutorials of these games are always horrible, so you have to learn from YouTube videos and experience. From what I've heard and played, the newest installment of Hearts of Irons, Hearts of Iron 4 streamlines the game into a much easier game, which could be appealing to newcomers, but a lot of veterans were extremely disappointed in the new direction. The same veterans praise Hearts of Iron III, with it being a game that requires meticulous micromanaging, but is much harder to grasp. Darkest Hour does a great job of being in between: not too hard to learn, and with not too much micromanaging in combat, but not too easy and streamlined. While the base game is great, it is not where the main fun is.
Why? Because of the mods.
90% of my playtime has been spent on a single mod: Kaiserreich. If you don't know what it is, it's an alternate-historical mod on what if Germany won the Great War (excuse me... the Weltkrieg). In the aftermath, Germany becomes a world power and inherits most of the Entente's colonies, but becomes troubled with Black Monday, which is essentially the Great Depression of the alternatate timeline. The Entente becomes extremely unstable, with Britain and France having syndicalist revolutions and their original governments in exile. Russia's Revolution fails because of the German intervention, and becomes a failed state where multiple factions are eager to fight for power. America, on the other hand, never joined the Weltkrieg, but heavily supplied the Entente. Since they lost, America was put in a more miserable Great Depression. There are many more changes to the world the mod makes, such as the balkanization of Asia and the exile and native conflicts in Africa that you can follow.
What makes the mod so great is how no two playthroughs are ever alike, and practically each nation has its own pathways. You could play as one of the American factions during its second civil war, emerge victorious and change the New World, or decide to prevent it from happening, and avoid the Second Civil War with careful decisions. You could also play as a smaller nation, like Poland, and become anything on the political spectrum.  And with all of this, other AI nations are making their own choices and creating their own paths. Russia could become the Soviet Union as we know it in our timeline, or become literal Nazis. When it comes down to the inevitable Second Weltkrieg between the Commune of France and German Empire, the end result is usually unpredictable: sometimes France wins, others Germany does. There are just so many paths for every nation, that the only nation you can predict its path is the nation you control.
Kaiserreich is not the only great mod. There are other excellent mods, such as the Fallout Doomsday mod, where you can play as nations from the Fallout universe, or the Communist Germany mod, another alternate-history mod where the KPD or Communist party comes in power instead of the Nazis.
I could go on and on and the great mods that this game offers, but I think I made my point: the game is already excellent, but when compared to other games in the franchise, nothing beats this on the sheer scale of mod excellence.
EDIT: I know I sound a bit harsh and pretentious against those who enjoy HOI3, but I am not (or at least try not to sound like I am). I played a bit of HOI3, and I am glad to say that it is a great game for those looking into a more detailed WWII. It's just not for me.

Savant - Ascent may have a killer soundtrack, but that's not the only good thing about it.
This game is a simple 2D shoot-'em-up, played mainly with the mouse. Savant, your character, is stationed at the center of the screen, on one of two platforms, and your goal is to survive the hordes of enemies around you. You can "dodge" by quickly switching platforms, which will keep you alive much longer if used correctly. Power-ups, unlocked by collecting CD pieces dropped by certain enemies, make the the game a little more interesting, and the levels get more difficult, but the basic gameplay remains the same.
It's fun blasting away enemies, having to decide which enemies to target, how best to use your abilities to defeat them. But the pixel graphics and the amazing soundtrack by Savant (no, that's not a coincidence) aren't enough to conceal the repetitiveness of the gameplay. This game is more of a score attack than a constantly evolving experience, since most of the replay value comes from attempting to beat previous scores. That having been said, it's probably a good thing that the game is short, otherwise it would drag out and lose its entertainment value, which it currently has a lot of.
Savant - Ascent is definitely short, but it's awesome, and I'd say the low price tag was worth it.

I bought the boxed version of this game on a whim when it came out, I can't remember why because I wasn't much of a gamer then and had seen no reviews etc. I really enjoyed it but it was subsequently lost so I was happy to see it appear here on Steam all those years later. It's something I would recommend to fans of classic point n' click adventure games. It's like a cheaper, less funny version of Curse Of Monkey Island, similar cartoony style and dialogue/inventory-based puzzles.
PROS:
- lots of inventory items to collect
- lots of characters with fun dialogue
- lots of areas to explore
- many clever and mostly fair puzzles
- wide range of good voice acting
- it is LOOOONG
CONS:
- probably too much dialogue overall, even if it is often amusing
- voice acting probably a bit too diverse (North American, Scottish, English, Middle-Eastern, Spanish, etc. makes things a bit too bizarre at times)
- also, the main character's voice acting can be very annoying (at least if you're British, like me!)
- bit of a stupid plot
- some puzzles are not intuitive at all
But overall, it's a game I don't think that many adventure-game fans are familiar with, it's always fun to play a little-known game, and it's definitely worth a play if you're a fan of this genre, at least to say you have. Almost certainly you should snap it up in a sale if the chance arises!

I never would have bought this game were it not included in the Humble Indie Bundle, and I must say that it would have been my horrific loss.  I had thought that, like denim overalls, top-down shooters were out of date and I had outgrown them.  Not so.  Jamestown brings back the top-down shooter in an incredibly engaging way.  There is no shortage of enemies to destroy, and when each one explodes in a shower of coins it gives a particular feeling of satisfacction.  Not to say it will be easy - they swarm and their firing patterns mean some artful dodging is required if you want to reach the final boss with enough lives intact.  Though the single player is spectacular enough, the multiplayer just pushes it over the top.  Though there is no online play, crowding around a computer with your friends and screaming at the screen has its own unique charm.
Good shmup!

Between the large numbers of FPS games, and the RPGs, Bullet Hell shooters are sadly under-represented on Steam, and in fact, in Western gaming in general.
Jamestown is one such example of a Bullet Hell shooter. It gives you a variety of ships that you can use to pummel through a variety of enemies, while at the same time trying to avoid getting pummeled yourself. It's very lenient on lives, and the levels are short, so if you can get used to levels one at a time it's not a particularly difficult bullet hell, but it serves its purpose well and is highly recommended if you're a fan of scrolling shooter type games, or perhaps are looking for something in a genre you have not had any chance to play yet.
It's very inexpensive, so worth a buy.

Without any real strategy the AI can run up to you and win every single combat it enters, the only time I was able to win close combat was when I had two or more men attacking a single enemy. Note: I only played for the free weekend.
Negatives:
- The game plays at such a slow pace, that I'm typing this between turns. Sometimes there's a long block of enemy turns till my next unit moves and it takes forever to wait.
- There's a lot of loading, which coupled with the above point makes the game feel unbearable. Fighting 1 battle and returning to camp can be 30-60 minutes.
- Climbing and jumping down have a success rate. Fail the former and you stay low and take damage, fail the latter and it's just damage. It makes sense in practice, but seeing cloth-wearing warriors fail to climb makes me VERY angry.
- Non-story missions are repetitive. You have 1 of 3 bonus objectives, but all battles boil down to knock out enough of the enemy and force them to retreat. The one story mission I did play (First Sisters Mission) was agonizingly long. I killed the opposition, but I had to run a sister all over the map just to tag locations. I had the match won and they artificially increased the length by 5-10 turns.
- BUGS. On 2 occasions I found my soldiers transported to different locations, On one map, my soldier was transported through a cart that was blocking an alleyway with no exit and no means of returning to the group. The other happened while trying to climb a chapel wall outside, and next turn magically found herself inside.
Positives:
- Challenge. The game feels difficult and you have to learn how to properly play. Going into a risky mission feels risky. The inability to save scum allows me to really feel the jeopardy and think strategically.
Random Thoughts:
- When RNG works against you it hurts. A LOT. Remember, even if you have 95% chance, that means 5 attacks will miss out of 100.
- I want prettier Sisters model. Vain, I know. But I want to lead an army of heavy armored supermodels.
Overall, I can't give this a positive review. Too many flaws for too little benefit.
(This review was made while waiting 5 extra turns for Sister Selma Holtzman to run up to the god damn chapel to bless the god damn bell.)

Played this over the free weekend and I gotta say my feelings are mixed. The tactics and bones of the game are good but oh my god is it slow, and punishing so very very punishing. Some of my issues with the game can be explained away by taking into account a multiplayer focused experience but still.
The AI takes as long as a player would during its turn, up to about 25 seconds per unit assuming it attacks twice, and you must sit through every animation with no options to speed it up. The overhead map is ugly and has no indications as to height or depth of objects or persons.
The game is very difficult and a few loses can easily put you in a tail spin of loss after loss, with ever decreasing unit abilities due to injury, and the ticking time bomb of Wyrdstone deliveries and gold via unit upkeep and medical costs.
The warriors I had when I started the game looked and played the same as when I quit the game. I usually enjoy a challenge but what you gain seems so miniscule compared to the time and effort invested. It takes about 6 hours and some luck to make headway, and it aint much.
And yet the game is enthralling, well voiced, interesting mythos, with somewhat varied factions doubtless more varied  after extensive play. It's fairly easy to lose hours playing it, but you spend every enemy turn wishing it wasn't so many minutes waiting tied up in those hours.
Thanks for reading, have a good one.

I have played almost all of the Nancy Drew games. This one has been my favorite so far. I loved that it was set back in time and the mini games were not irritating like some of the games.

Nancy Drew: Secret of the Old Clock
A game very loosely based off Nancy Drew's very first mystery. I was greatly anticipating how the storyline and villain could have been changed but found myself greatly disappointed with the choices that the writers decided upon. Although not perfect, the original mystery had a certain charm to it and had great memorable characters. What I have found in place of these remarkable people and events that took place were shadows of their former selves. I will not spoil too much of the game but I feel that the mystery could have been told in a different way and through out game play I've found myself continuously shouting at my laptop: "Oh come on!" over and over again.
I did not expect the game to copy the story word per word but what I DID expect was a well told storyline instead of what I got.
The mini games were quite annoying, but the story overall was pretty fun.

It's Nancy Drew, what more can I say?
If you love Nancy Drew, PLAY THIS OF COURSE. The puzzles aren't too difficult and the characters aren't the best but for one of the first games it's still pretty fun.
If you don't know who Nancy Drew is and you're looking to try out one of the games, maybe try a different one first? It really depends on if you want to play an AMAZING one and then come back to say you've beaten them all, or play a pretty good one and then move on to the better ones.

Now, for this, I'm going to try and maintain as much of a calm demeanor as possible for a game that has angered me so much in so many ways and not in a good way. Arcane Raise is nothing more than a shoddy, low effort waste of time and money.
I'm going to structure things slightly differently in this review of mine since there are aspects of this game that I want to talk about that I wouldn't normally cover and so I'm adapting a more freeform writing layout for this one as I don't really think my usual one will really effectively get across the main issues with the game, and I'll instead be giving a list of what is wrong with the game and then further elaborating off of it, and I'll only be focusing on the cons as frankly, I can only see cons in this game and there are no pros and nothing working for the game.
Before I get onto doing that, let me just first describe the premise of the game, just so you can get a better picture. In Arcane Raise, you play as three RPG Maker VX Ace assets, who play through a world made out of RPG Maker VX Ace assets where you need to enter random encounters to level up enough to face off against the boss.
With that premise being set, let's get into what I greatly hate about the game.
The gameplay, to put it simply, is boring and repetitive. With the whole goal being set on just leveling up enough times to face off against a boss, the game is literally just a grind. Usually, when there's just a small portion of the game that is grinding where you have to level up enough to get to a specific goal, this game bases it's self around grinding to simply reach that goal.
As I said earlier, the game is built up entirely out of stock RPG Maker VX Ace assets and includes no original work, and I'll be frank with this, the RPG Maker VX Ace asset environment and just design overall (at least the way it's used in this game) is completely bland, messy and plays in a stretched 4:3 screen, which may be where the problem lies.
Now, as I stated earlier, the game is nothing more than a grind, but I was additionally at a later date upon receiving a copy of the game from the developer able to get a hold of a couple of the game's DLC, these DLC packages being the booster pack and the Male #2 DLC.
The DLC greatly reduce the amount of time you spend grinding and just overall playing the game, as the booster pack spawns in a chest in the starting area, and when you open it, it automatically levels your characters up to level 15 and the Male 1 & 2 DLC and Female 1 & 2 add a new slave slot to your game that includes that character in your party and adds another guy/gal to deal extra blows to your enemies. You can't play with 7 characters if that's what you were wondering, you can only play with a maximum of 4 which means if for some reason you end up getting this game, don't buy all the character DLC as you won't get them all at once, you can instead simply choose between them before you start a new playthrough, and all characters are literally given no personality so there isn't even differentiation there. All I really saw the characters as were a bunch of stats and attacks in battles. The DLC overall is you paying for a head start in the game, and is basically the embodiment of an admittance that the game is just one big grind, as you can cut down on the amount you can do by coughing up extra cash. I'll give you a different recommendation, if you don't buy the game, then you won't have to grind at all.
So, if the whole game is building up to one boss fight, you might be wondering how is the boss battle? I'm going to say that after facing this boss around twenty times, I have never beaten him. Now, with me saying that, you might think the boss battle is deep, intricate and complex and requires a lot of figuring out, but no, I'd rather go with the fight being unfair. Now, before people start screaming at me to "git gud", there are a few things that I want to say about why the boss battle is unfair and has been made I'm willing to throw out and say almost impossible to beat.
1) Unlike a lot of other RPGs, you only have one form of attack that deals a predetermined range of damage on the boss, and regardless of level, every hit will be minuscule to the boss' overall health (which you don't see the total amount/remaining health of an enemy.) As a result, if you want to deal damage, you can only carry out this one default movement or a magic move called life drain that deals even less damage for little actual result overall besides you losing MP.
2) Magic is useless. By the time you reach the boss, you'll need to have stacked up on potions, herbs etc. and since the whole game overall is a grind, you won't really be caring too much about getting your character's health too much if the goal is just to go out and level up when you can just take a short walk back to the haven area where you can rest at no cost. Additionally, magic is useless, to begin with as very little health or anything at all is regenerated, to begin with, and barely any damage is dealt with either.
3) The boss is defaulted to attack twice, whereas your team can only attack once. Even with any of the character DLC, the boss will thrash your team up quickly in a few swings because for some reason he can attack you twice, whereas each team member of yours only gets one hit in each. Meaning the boss can enter a state of paralyzing all of your team and attacking them, paralyzing and attacking, rendering them useless right from the beginning of the fight regardless of level and then going on to take away all of their health, killing all of them before they can even lay an attack in.
4) The potions will torment you more than help you. As I said in my previous point, the boss can end up putting you in that kind of endless loop but in the few occasions where you are able to reverse the effects of this through herbs to getting rid of your paralysis and potions to regain back lost health, there will be at least two teammates dead as a result of this, which makes it more complicated if you had no DLC. You will b drinking potions which allow your team to be resurrected, but then when you've drunk that your turn it up without you having landed a hit in and no matter what you do your allies always come back to life with the only 1HP. This means that on the next turn there's a good 80% chance your boss will have an attack ready and the only times he doesn't is if he's trying to blind your team to make the likelihood of hitting him lower or he paralyzing you again, requiring more herbs still with downed teammates. So if the boss lands another hit in then your resurrected teammate will go down again. So then, you're stuck in an endless cycle of trying to resurrect your teammates, getting lucky enough for the boss to not lay an attack on you the turn after and then filling that teammate up with a full health potion....but then you have to do it again for the other characters.
Essentially, Arcane Raise is nothing more than a huge grind with no pay off except a boss that is way too hard for you to actually beat, meaning there isn't even a pay off for your incessant grinding. I would make this longer but this is what happens when a game gives you nothing more to really talk about besides grinding and a boss fight. Oh, but there is the fact that the rat enemies are misspelled as "Rate."
Final verdict: 1/10

It's not bad, but it's not good. It's an average game made in RPG Maker. Let me break it down so you understand though. There is no story other than you are fighting the final boss because you want to rather than because you need to. The gameplay is repetitive and dull, but some things I found made it a less boring experience overall. The soundtrack is okay, but it's nothing I wouldn't listen to outside of the game. It's just a boring game, so if you do have a lot of patience, I would recommend to finish the game thoroughly to say you did it. I wouldn't recommend this for any other reason except for the easy achieves and the free cards. The achievements aren't very complex as you get them all from just walking to the right on a certain screen, but they do make me want more as it didn't feel very good to earn them. The cards are a plus, but it isn't too much better otherwise. It's steps up from stuff like Vickinachi, but doesn't reach the perfection for stuff like Lotia.
Pros:
-Free achievements and trading cards practically.
-It's standard, so if you've played other RPG Maker Games, you'd know how to beat this one.
-Hardly any bugs and glitches as far as I can tell.
Cons:
-The gameplay is repetitive as far as I can tell. You beat at enemies until their health drops to 0. Not bad, but it's stale and boring to go through.
-There is almost no story. You walk around until you are strong enough to beat the Darkness.
-The soundtrack sounds like standard music to an RPG Maker. It isn't the worse I've heard, but it does leave some wanting for more.
Overall: I'd give it a 4/10 or 5/10.

I like that you have cards and that it has very few as it only takes 5 to finish the set, and its achievements are all easy to obtain, but it is done lazily and not with much effort. It's not the worst that I've seen in a game in achievements, but I wish I could had obtained them like I earned them rather than just walking to the right.

This game is a story-driven beat-em-up with stealth elements, although most of your time will be spent "going over" the graffiti of others. At its core, it has a fun concept. There is even a pretty wide variety of graffiti (your designs get more elaborate and varied with each chapter) to keep you going through the graffiti process. But there are three fatal flaws which bring this game down. First, the "freeform challenges" require you to write marker tags on things. They're boring as hell, and there is literally no reason to vary your tags. But you get reputation from it which is required to unlock things, so you feel obligated to do them. Second, there is a mixture between action, stealth, and platforming (reminiscent of prince of persia) which really isn't bad overall; however, there is a disproportionate amount of required stealth at certain points in the game with controls and interface that aren't designed for stealth. It's frustrating when you have no indication that someone will or will not see you and a good portion of the game is based on this. The final issue is the camera. It glitches around frequently. By frequently I mean pretty much all the time. As soon as you approach a surface the image will stop popping in and out, the camera will start shaking, or suddenly you will be looking in the complete opposite direction. There is camera control, but it doesn't work for some reason when you're near things.
The final straw for me was doing a series of jumps with a group of guards below me when my character suddenly began walking off to the side and getting off the platform. I corrected this, at which point he immediately jumped into a wall and stayed there where the guards (who now saw him) could not kill him with their taser arrow things. Yeah I don't know what those are.
TL;DR It's glitchy as hell.

It seems the "revolution" in Resident Evil happened mostly in the Capcom press release. While the game introduces first person camera for a fresh experience, it cuts down on pretty much everything else. Hardly inspired storyline draws deeply from cult pop horror elements and prefers jumpscares to deliver emotion. Dialog is often bland or illogical, and the otherwise high quality audio tends to be overused for random house creaks, with some truly outlandish sounds for footsteps and environmental objects. Compared to the complexity of previous installments, the game is almost linear with barely any depth to the environment or actors aside the visuals. It still feels like Resident Evil and you will be swapping shotguns on a piedestal, but the experience leaves you expecting more game and less F.E.A.R./Silent Hill meets Evil Dead B-movie.

After a painful lack of quality in the series, Resident Evil 7 finally brings back some former glory.  Merging ideas from Rob Zombie classics such as The Devils Rejects and House of 1000 Corpses, Resident Evil 7 creates its own unique take on southern gothic horror. Playing out in the swamps of a derelict mansion, RE7 reinvents itself as an FPS. Merged with old-school aspects of the series such as save rooms, puzzles, resource management and (intentional) clunky movement. Playing like a survival action game with moments of cat and mouse similar to Amnesia and Outlast, Resident Evil 7 should satisfy both appetites of horror and action fans. However, RE7 it is not without flaws. Outside of the fantastic Baker family cast the enemy variety is awfully lacking, leaving some diversity to be desired. Also the game begins to run out steam making the last quarter a slog to get through. But considering the massive jump in quality from previous installments, Resident Evil 7 gives the series a much needed nudge in the right direction.

A bullet-hell game. Normally, most people just hear the words and move away from anything related to the genre. But Jamestown is easily an exception to that instinctive behaviour.
If you're old enough to remember those games where you had a plane or a ship flying on a vertically-scrolling background and tanks/turrets/monsters/something evil appeared and lobbed a red ball of death towards your vessel, Jamestown doesn't fall very far from that tree. What you need to know is that, much like most of those games, enemies spawn at the exact same place every time you run the exact same level (that is, the level itself associated with a difficulty). Unlike those games, however, you get the chance to select the difficulty.
Jamestown is nice enough to players new to the bullet-hell genre by having multiple difficulties. "How is that nice?" you're thinking. The easiest difficulty is easy enough for someone that never played any game in his life to learn patterns, which in turn make them develop a sense of where to be and where not to be given the properties of the ship they're using. And each step in the difficulty curve is acceptable at the point where the player can reliably clear a level without dying more than once; it's a proof of skill from the player's part. That said, most people won't be able to clear all levels at the highest difficulty the game offers, and possibly not even the one before that. If you're in it for the "100%", you better be prepared to invest a good time of your life here.
But achievement nuts aside, Jamestown is full of strong points. The controls are responsive as you'd expect a game of the genre, the music is like someone tossed you a thousand dollars and said "keep it, no strings attached", the visual style is undoubitably gorgeous. It even has an unusual backstory in a strange futuristic-pastlike-future for a game with no reason to have a story, if you care about those things. It also has a sort of "challenge mode" where you try to complete hard tasks in a preset course; think of it as this game's minigames. You have an activatable invulnerability shield on certain conditions as a base game mechanic related to scoring points. You also get to have four different ships to blast the baddies, each very different in gameplay from the others, so you can specialize in one that best suits you or try to master all of them for added replayability. And of course, you have a "gauntlet mode" where even reaching its end is like getting a free pat in the back and a bucket of your favourite drink.
If you're looking for weak points, the only things that come to mind is the extra ships dlc (because you either love them and use them or end up sticking to only one or non-at-all since you already love one of the base game's ships) and the inherent what-you-see-is-what-you-get replayability that's associated with fixed levels and how high the skill barrier is for you. If you're a master of the bullet-hell genre, the hardest difficulty may be less challenging than you'd hope.
Also, one can not stress this enough: the music of this game is amazing. The soundtrack's extra cost? If you play the game and like it, I recommend you buy it to hear it outside the game; supposedly the money goes to the composer, which needs to eat just like you.
All in all, Jamestown is a great game. A solid 8 out of 10 easily, maybe even more. If you consider the game a little costy, wait for a discount; if the music is also at a discount, make sure you also buy it if you liked it in-game. As for the dlc ships, hit or miss: if you like the game, and want to say you like the people that put their heart making it, buy; otherwise my opinion is avoid unless at a good discount.

Whoever decided to allow free weekend access to Mordheim needs a good smack, because this seems to be specifically designed to make your first several hours' play as frustrating and annoying as possible. It may well be that once you get into hours 10-20 it gets really enjoyable, but that's unlikely to happen in one free weekend, and the only people who are likely to power through a dozen or so hours of screen-punching are people who have paid full price and are invested in the game. Anyone given a few hours to try it out is likely to come away with the impression that the last thing they want to do is play any more of that annoying nightmare.
It comes down to design, which has presumably been fixed in order to ramp up difficulty and make the game more "hard core". The trouble is, whilst most gamers enjoy a tough challenge, what really pisses us off are stupid/illogical game mechanics that have obviously been introduced simply to make success harder. Looting, mission objectives and combat mechanics all conspire to make it impossible to get a good result from a mission. Here's why:
You take control of a warband of your chosen faction, a bunch of 5 newbie toons who, in good RPG tradition, you expect to start levelling up and improving. The leader of your faction puts in an order for wyrdstones, and you need to get X stones within Y days or you'll fail: 4 fails and it's game over. You enter Mordheim seeking wyrdstones and other loot. So far, so good. At the start of a mission you see there are, for example, 20 wyrdstones and 15 scavenging points around the city, so you examine the map and think OK, I'll send a couple of guys this way, another couple over there, maybe one to hang back and guard our cart.
First off, movement is incredibly slow. It may take you 2 or 3 turns to reach that pile of wyrdstones. Secondly, your inventory is ridiculously tiny - 3 items total?? Forget about carrying potions or buffs! Of course, you can dump stuff in your cart then head back out, but that takes twice the time. And if you get to the stones and there are 4+, you're going to need 2 people (40% of your entire force) or 2 trips (4-6 turns, which is an eternity) to get them.
None of which would be a problem if time wasn't such a huge issue, but it is because of how combat works. Within 2 rounds, maybe 3 at most, you're going to run into the opposition. Now, being outnumbered is a real problem in Mordheim, because if you are you have to face an "All Alone" roll every turn, and if you fail you flee. And you can very easily get outnumbered because as soon as one of the opposing warband engages one of your guys, EVERY OTHER ENEMY RUSHES IN TO JOIN THE FIGHT. Fights aren't quick, one-shot affairs either, it'll take your newbs several turns to eliminate any enemy, and in those turns all his mates arrive. If you don't immediately start rushing all your own men to the fight, your guys are going to get overwhelmed and killed or forced to flee.
What this all boils down to is this: you may think you have a bit of time to explore, wander round collecting the stuff you need to not fail and end the game, but in actual fact what happens is that within about 2 turns a fight will start, and you then have to rush all your men to fight all the enemies and see who wins. No exploration, no gathering, no tactics, just a quick rush into an all-out brawl.
And even that wouldn't necessarily be too bad if you could then get back to collecting the very stones you'd come to collect (assuming you won the fight), but no! Once you've won the fight, it's mission over! What do you mean, you didn't explore any scavenge points? What do you mean you didn't go and pick up that pile of stones 20 yards away? It doesn't matter! The last enemy's dead, so poof, it's back to base IMMEDIATELY! And yes, leave all that gear and loot that's LITERALLY RIGHT AT YOUR FEET!
It's so frustrating, because you can see how this could have been such a great game, but sadly the devs have decided that they need to make this game "hard core", so they've just introduced really stupid and illogical mechanics to achieve that regardless of how much that pisses players off. I'd love to explore Mordheim, roaming around in what looks like a fascinating setting, but in reality all that happens is that you and the enemy locate each other pretty quickly, an all-in melee ensues, and at the end the mission's over. They may as well just have made this an arena brawler. Shame.

I usually wait until I 100% a game to review but mastering all moves will take me a while, so here it goes.
Absolver is a pve/pvp fighting game with very fluid and rewarding combat, a gorgeous art style/sound track, and a surprisingly honorable community. Upon launch you choose one of three styles (Forsaken, Windfall, Kahlt) based on various real life fighting styles. You're then thrown into the world with little to no context other than "beat these bosses move on" and while not having a very present story may be a turn off to some, it allows people to create their own lore and background for their character. The combat deck system is a very interesting one. You learn moves by successfully absorbing/parrying/avoiding/guarding moves and then have to beat your opponent to solidify that experience. While this does create a grind, it encourages you to seek out new opponents and explore new areas. The actual combat is very fluid and well animated, and depending on how you build your combat deck you can easily master your moves to be as effective as possible. The main bosses themselves aren't all that hard (I beat Risryn, Cargal/Kilnor, and Kuretz on the first try) the marked ones put up a slightly tougher fight. The ai in this game is bipolar, however, sometimes they're braindead punching bags who go down with little to no resistance, and other times they're god like kung-fu masters. The other Absolvers (actual players) you meet along the way tend to be very friendly and will assist you in your fights, or just stay back and watch out of respect. The PvP is very fluid and besides launch day I've had almost no connection issues. A couple of the PvP maps are annoying (The Oratian Quarters, The Adal Tower) with their ledges that people can knock you off of in a couple of hits. Lastly, as much as I love the game, the loot system is god awful. There is almost no rhyme or reason as to what drops at any moment, and you're going to be getting a lot of duplicate starter/low tier clothes. The devs have addressed this and said they will be adding a rarity/coloring system and improvements to the drop system, but until those patches are pushed through this part of the review will stay.
tl:dr - Absolver is a must buy if you like PvP focused combat that allows for full customization in how you fight
While the PvE content is limited at the moment (devs will continue to add content) the PvP has potentially limitless content as you keep improving your skills and tweaking your deck.

This is an excellently designed game with a ruinously bad control sceme.
In keyboard mode, it is nearly impossible to trigger your block/dodge/absorb consistently, because it is bound to mouse movement and cannot, under any circumstances, be changed.  Response to a particular mouse movement is unpredictable, and may do nothing or activate the wrong move, even when performed in an identical manner.
In controler mode, the block works fine, but stance change and free dodge (both of which are tied to joystick + button push) have similar consistency problems.  Again, it is impossible to remap the joystick assignments for stance change or free dodge (although you can change the keybind, that does not help).
In a game that depends on precise timing for its (otherwise elegant) combat system to work, this is an unforgiveable sin.
Wait 6 months before buying, and make sure they fix the control scheme before laying out money for this game.

Arcane Raise is, without a doubt, one of the absolute worst JRPGs on Steam. Much more effort went into devising obscure forms of monetization for this game (DLC characters! A Compile Heart-style cheat item pack! Tradeable Steam marketplace items that look to have been made from stock art which do absolutely nothing!) than the game, which has no original assets, almost no story, a bare minimum of mechanics (3 characters in fixed classes, all items available from the shop at the beginning of the game), and is less than an hour long when using the "Booster Pack."
Basically, since I can sum up the entire game easily: after a tutorial featuring mechanics that don't actually exist in the game (e.g. potential punishment for retreating from fights, vehicles), you are dumped in town, with a glitchy-appearance NPC you can talk to in order to fight the final boss at any point, shops selling all of the items in the game, and four portals to one-map dungeons full of obnoxiously-high-rate random encounters and treasure chests full of potions and gold. Go grab all the chests, then buy +attack items at 200 a pop / 99 for 19800, enjoy the sound of consuming items 99 times in a row. Then hit the final boss for 11000 damage in one hit. Now you are not a Shade, but a Shade Alpha, a term that might be explained in the lorebook, but which there's no reason to care about what it means. Also you can uninstall the game now.
Oh and you get 37 achievements, probably also all stock art, for starting the game. Just make sure you start the game normally if you want that, instead of loading one of the "DLC character" savegames.
In conclusion, no. Irredeemable.

After two disappointing installments in this franchise, RE has (finally) bounced back. It’s almost as if they read my reviews of RE5 and RE6. They are finally trying something new without any linkage to previous games. “New”, is a curious way to to describe this game though. Sure, the first-person gameplay is new to the RE franchise (unless you are including Resident Evil Survivor or Dead Aim, I’m NOT!!), but Capcom is definitely capitalizing on the successes of the Outlast, Amnesia and Alien Isolation franchises. That’s all perfectly fine. It works in this environment and the story they tell.
The gameplay is well done; players use a combination of running and hiding, shooting and puzzling solving (just like the original games). There’s very little cut scenes, which means the player is playing more and there’s a few throw backs to some of the original mansion puzzles. Remember the crank?
The game succeeds by making ammo scarce, with the exception of the game’s finale, which forces players to choose wisely when to spend that last bullet. The eeriness of the house’s layout adds to the ambiance in addition to the stellar sounds effects and music queues.
Sure, there’s some jump scares. And this element of the game I found most depressing. There’s no need to have enemies teleport near the player for a cheap jumps care. This happens on two or three occasions involving two of the game’s antagonists Marguerite and Jack.
The boss battles are clever, and the ending Boss battle is reminiscent of Dead Space.
Above when I said there was no linkage to past games; that’s not entirely true. Towards the end of the game there’s a newspaper reference of Racoon City, Chris Redfield makes an appearance as he saves Ethan at the very end, and the placard on the side of the helicopter says “Umbrella Corporation”. So it’s a soft-reboot. I for one welcome it. It’s 10 years too late and I’m excited to see where they go from here as well as the incorporation of VR.

I completed RE7's main story in 12 hours on normal difficulty, I had one issue with a recurring crash referencing DX11 <something> .cpp, this was resolved by putting my GPU (GTX 1080) back to its original speeds. Other than the OC'd GPU crash, the game performed extremely well and I didn't experience any odd bugs.
I've been playing Resident Evil for at least 20 years now and I feel that RE7 is very good at returning the game to its roots; what separates RE7 from earlier games is 1) first-person perspective, which gives the game a more in-your-face feeling, and 2) better voice acting. The action elements that were present in RE 4, 5, and 6 have been significantly toned down, there will be some jump scares, most of which are encounters with the main characters, but the other enemies are often foreseeable and can be ran from. Capcom doesn't put you in any bad situations that leave you helpless, I made an effort to use ammo wisely, sometimes thought I'd get stuck with no ammo, but ended up doing fine (normal difficulty); you may need to repeat a boss fight several times, but nothing is grind-y about this game.
As far as the story goes, it's very good and typical of a Resident Evil game, so be sure to read documents you find. You can clear areas and then have all the freedom you need to read through documents, so I advise doing that to get the entire story.
Definitely a good game, there is one reason to replay it but I might not (I need to finish many other games), I'm definitely going to play the DLC. I recommend it.

At first I was surprised by the simplicity of moving the character.  The only places he can be at is to a left and right position.  There is no walking on platforms.  But despite this straightforwardness, the game is insanely fun.  You control a Savant who not only can output a barrage of damage to wipe out enemies but also quickly evade enemy attacks by switching positions by either jumping or rolling.  It's fairly hard at first but as you collect these in-game objects that are CD pieces and complete them to become full CD's, you unlock powers that makes the Savant stronger, such as shooting missiles after rolling.  Not only that but completing each CD unlocks a new soundtrack to listen to and every soundtrack is awesome and matches the hectic pace of the game.  It's a fairly short game but considering the price and replayability, it's very well worth it.  If there was any wish I had about the game, it would be for the developers to sell the soundtrack as well.

At first glance, this game reminded me so much of a roleplaying game called “Popmundo” which is a web based game in which you have to develop a music career to make your living, improve your skills and form a succesful band or an artist persona. In this game, similarly your goal is to develop your career by writing songs, recording them, giving concerts and so on. However in this game you have the control of a whole band and  by micromanaging each member you strive to make them reach to the ultimate goal of their lives.
When you start the game you get to choose in which genre you want to specialize. There are four genres consisting of pop, rock, hiphop and electro. This choice affects the overall skills of your members. Later on, the game gives you the ability to name your band and the vocalist of this band. So that you can feel a bit more attached to your band. From here on out, you can write a song and start your career. To write a song, you choose a theme first and then you’re able adjust special effects and instruments used taking song’s theme into account. All affect the quality of the song and the time it takes to write. This impacts the overall quality of the song as well. For instance, let’s say you’re writing a song that has a sad theme, the game prompts you to use guitar solo since it’s more convenient for this theme.
Every song takes time to write. With each song, the members of your band gain XP and they improve their skills. Also, there’s a way you can upgrade each member’s equipment with the money you’ve earned and the best way to earn money is to give concerts. In order to give a concert, you have to pick a place that will accept your band, depending on your fame. You can choose which songs you want to play in your concert. Don’t forget though, quality of your songs affect your concert performance and if it’s successful you’re able to sell more tickets and make more profit and gain new fans.
Besides giving concerts, you’re able to record the songs you’ve written. You get to choose which studio you can work with, again it depends on your fame and more quality studios won’t work with you at first. Recording might increase or decrease your songs final quality so it won’t stay same as before. Later on in the game you’re able to record and sell albums. Another way to make money is to do side-jobs. These usually take time and has a risk value. The more risk of failing it has the more profit you can make. Doing these take time as well, like any other thing in this game. There are works available not only to make money but also improve your skills. For instance you can “Practice Guitar Hero” and improve your stats or you can go “Hang Posters” and earn money. As you earn more and more money you can hire managers, that manages your public relations which affects a variety of things. Besides buying equipments, paying for fees etc, you can invest your money in loot boxes from which you can pick an item to use on your characters to improve them. It’s definitely well-balanced though, since they’re not overpowered and you’re forced to choose them wisely since there are limited slots you can use.
I like the general way of things look in terms of user-interface, even though texts saying “tap to continue” and big buttons make it look like a mobile game. Not to mention that this game is very lightweight and it’ll probably work on a potato.
Overally, It’s fun being able to have a complete control of things and this game is going to make you feel accomplished for your success. As you develop, you’re going to feel that you’re turning into a giant and you are going to want to compare yourself to real world singers and bands in the “Charts” section, which is an immersive and a fun detail. Taking its low price into account, it’s definitely worth buying. If you are a fan of the management genre, you’re going to be immersed and addicted.

Personally i thought this was a good although very difficult game when i started, but i found despite the few issues and UI the game was actually quite good.
If you are looking for another casual turn based game where you can just pick some classes and tank up then I would recommend avoiding this game. Every mistake you make will come back an haunt you at a later date including avoiding some side objectives,
I think it would be easier if i gave a basic description of the pros and cons for this game...
Camera: The camera is a 3rd person camera that locks onto the unit you are meant to be moving that turn, Doesn't allow free roaming with the camera and makes seeing around corners and in buildings a little more difficult when trying to avoid ambushes.
Movement: This caught me off guard at first.. Using the standard movement keys WASD to navigate was a bit odd for a turn based game but once I figured out the blue circles were something akin to movement areas, you would only lose a movement point when changing to a different ring giving you free movement within your Movement points.
Actions: This i found a little off at first but every action has a reaction.. Firing a gun means it needs you to use a reload action, gives you arm fatigue for the rest of the turn lowering accuracy.  Climbing walls needs at the jump points Isn't always guaranteed with a chance of a sprain if you are very unlucky ect. Usually it is best to prepare for the consequences for most actions.
UI: I agree with most people... It is a little clunky and not the best.. But when you look past most of its appearance you mostly use Q & E to change action instead of a menu. Regardless it shows everything you need.
Ok now for a simple list:
Pros:
On High graphics settings it looks good
AI is hard and sometimes unforgiving (Well good in my opinion)
Soundtrack is fitting
Open maps in most levels
Excellent customization
Consequences for loosing affect appearance of units
Randomly generated map placements
Some replay ability
Unlocks persist through multiple play through
Ways to deal with enemy vary based on your preferred tactics
Cons:
AI is hard but can predict how they act based on the game mode
Very few game modes
UI is a bit clunky
Maps look a bit samish even if they are randomly generated
On low graphics looks appalling compared to most modern games
Don't always get chance to loot stuff
The game is hard, fun but at times frustrating when it goes from bad to worse. Not always the end of the world but makes progression harder.  Worth it if you like difficult games that seek to destroy you in as many ways as you can.. until you figure out AI tactics but even then still easy to die.
I'd give this game a 7 out of 10.. Despite its flaws it has some merit and room to improve.

Do this for each level and thats the end of the game.
The hardest part is waiting for the mana so you can build the ground. If it wasn't for the forced mana & minion regen you could finish the game in under 30 minutes.

So, you can beat it in a day, or an afternoon if you're more hardcore than me. You probably won't pick it up again unless you want to try for the steam achievements, or you've got another afternoon to kill to see if you can beat your high scores...soley for the sake of beating your high scores. Some people are into that. I'm probably done with it.
Thats why I'm recommending it. For <$5 you can buy, finish, and beat a game. No dailies. No weekly event. No life sucking eternal online micro transaction angst. Sometimes thats nice.
However, because its an afternoon jaunt, the entire game felt like the tutorial for something bigger. And maybe it was-because there are bonus missions that I just don't have the stamina to attrition to a win. If I had spent more time or actually needed to learn a "strategy" at any point during the campaign, maybe I would find them to be the challenge, but I find them obnoxious. The whole campaign was "ok, baby step me through how this works, ok cool! I win. I like winning." and then you get to the "you've defeated the greatest evil! but wait...something is lurkiing..." and its instant hard mode/you're the underdog/we made these for the hardcore guy who reviewed the game and said it was too easy and/or childish.
So yes, its pretty easy (minus the bonus missions) and pretty short, and its also pretty cute and I liked the interface and think this model for "god games" could make its way to tablet or phones pretty easily, and I would buy something similar on those platforms. I wish there were more "god games" out there, that aren't part of the play-to-progress or pay-to-win or login-everyday-till-eternity-and-maybe-you'll-get-somewhere sorts.

I came to Absolver after being disappointed by For Honor, which I wanted to love but couldn't. For Honor had many structural problems (netcode issues, stability issues, matchmaking issues), mechanical issues (character balance, constantly patched meta that ended up only making things worse, repetitive heroes), as well as consumer issues (non-cosmetic loot crates) that finally ended up driving me away even though For Honor had a unique type of gameplay that at its core I loved.
I see a fair amount of negative reviews for Absolver based on stability and connectivity problems, and to some extent they're fair, I've had the game crash on me a few times in my 30 hours, and sometimes my matches are laggy as hell, but overall my experience has been great.  Matchmaking is quick and the rounds are short, letting you quickly leave behind a bad match for a new one. The core mechanic of building a deck of moves and executing on them is great fun, and you're never locked into a specific moveset for longer than a match, building and trying new decks is fun in and of itself.
If you're the sort of person that used to play For Honor in primarily 1v1, this is your game.
The worst thing I can say about it is that there is a slight lack of content, in terms of items, you get duplicate drops and inventory management sucks. I'd love for there to be more rad armor for my character to dress up in, and to be able to sort and hide items, but I'll wait and see what they drop in patches (they've promised more items and UI QoL changes) before making a final judgement there.

If there was ever a game needing a "neutral" button for reviews...this one would be it.
First: I was very much aware of all the things I criticise in my review and will not complain about buying the game. To get it out of the system...yes, it is fun and nice to look at and I do not regret paying cash to the devs at all. Yes, including that the single player campaign sucks harder than a hoover and the fact you cannot practice against bots with own decks.
I will start with what made  my thumb turn down:
1. Weapons are styles..wait not really...or are they? They are. You can use a weapon and make a deck, but you need to summon the weapons with shards you need to heal and cc in a fight. So noone in MP will use them unless for fun. That is SUCH a wasted potential.
Instead of giving weapons damage through guarding, make them permanent and let people have fun with them.  Without that shortsighted decision, one could add MOUNTAINS of weapons...without making them OP, but giving players a way to mix up their styles. And yes...there would be a chance for weapons to be an ending to the 'lets all have 10 moves or you will lose'.
The weapon desaster is one of the bigger reasons I will not recommend the game.
2. Move grinding...really? You need to grind moves by blocking/evading enemy moves you do not know. What a nice idea...for the singleplayer. One can argue that you build skill by "achieving" moves...there is no achievement. And no skill involved either. I gave one of my chars a bit more endurance and just perma-guarded until an enemy had "taught" me all his new moves, then i kick his butt. Moves learned...yeah.
Sounds like no fun at all? Because it isn't. Now I bought this for the MP part...and only for that. Still, I need to grind all the moves.  Doing that will not increase my skill against human opponents at all, so the point I should practice with the npcs is moot, they always use the same moves. Why not separate sp and mp and give mp "characters" the full set of moves. Does not change the skill level in the slightest....but they decided against such an easy way. Schools would have been able to teach 'special' moves...oh well, they didn't.
That decision  makes the experience tedious. And if I want tedium, I can go to work.
3. "Matchmaking" is not a thing, apparently. I started MP as early as possible ... but when I found out that I would be matched with people 20 or 30 levels above me, I started to chuckle. Now..if I pull off a full combo and don't even get the guard down to 3/4 of their stamina, I just idle or jump down a cliff. Saves me time.
If a game is so dependent on MP since the SP aspect is not really a selling point...the for all that is holy, make a good matchmaker. It is no rocket science, actually. They did not.
4. Balance of speed vs. skill. Has been discussed to death and is  a negative point. You can argue as much as you like, but if a windfall's slow is not enough to squeeze a straight punch through against an opponent built for speed, you might need to think again. I actually had fights where a successful evade with a follow-up punch was worse than just guarding until the enemy runs out of stamina.
That is actually a minor point as I think it will be balanced over time and only slightly turned my thumb.
5. No "free fighting". That locking business drives me nuts. Even if I was confined to 1/4 stances while fighting freely, I would love to see that. Shifting stances would just be another skill...but that locking stuff...gah. Maybe a personal matter of taste. Is on the "bad" side but would not have caused a thumbs down.
6. Fighting is not rewarded: In MP, if  I face a superior opponent (levels, skill..whatever..), there is no reward for me trying for 2-4 minutes to break his guard, outsmart him or actually trying to hit him. Once I find out that I will not be able to beat him (not easy..but at all..), I get exactly the same reward for trying or for jumping down a cliff or just let them beat me up.
There should be a 'participation' reward. And that reward should be greater, the greater the gap in level/k-d ratio/whaterver metric they would choose is.
Now the good stuff:
1. Like the graphics and the animations. They really give you the impression of fighting. Weapons too..cannot wait for the staff or other MA-weapons...but see above. Grinding those will be next to impossible outside of a school. Which is fine with me tbh...
2. Schools. Great idea. You found a school and people can 'learn' your moves by equipping the 'school'. Works  with the grind I hate. But still the good outweighs that.
3. Decks. Even though I am no fan of it (has been done before, the mere idea sucks imho..) it is as nicely executed as you can execute a fundametally bad idea.  Not going to discuss it, my opinion. And it is nice enough to push it to the good side, but just barely.
In conclusion: Is the game fun? Yes. Is it fun enough? Maybe...but there is no maybe in steam. Currently, in my opinion, there is more polish needed, more balancing and maybe a lessening of that horrid grind.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Earth Liberation is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was the latest as of the date of this review (20161226): Version 0.5.
Earth Liberation is a combat-oriented Real-Time Strategy game from new indie developer, PoRovoz Studios.
In Earth Liberation you play a commander of the Human Resistance, fighting back against the invading reptilian aliens. What that means, in essence, is that you're the person who sends countless waves of human soldiers to crash relentlessly against the alien hordes, in an endless tide of bullets, rockets, and mortar shells.
Graphics - The first thing you'll notice about the graphics is the title screen, which has a very nicely modelled alien space ship. The in-game units are nicely modelled and animated, as well.
The introduction falls a bit flat after the 'wow' factor of the title screen, but it's functional and looks okay. You'll probably only ever watch it once, anyway.
Other than the normal resolution and full screen / windowed setting, graphics options are limited to a single detail selection: low, medium, or high. I ran in 1920x1080 on 'high' on my new gaming laptop and didn't experience any issues with performance.
Sound - The first thing you'll notice about the sound is the title screen music: there isn't any! There's also no sound or music through the introduction and the whole thing felt very weird being in absolute silence. I assume music will be added to both of these sometime before the game's release.
In-game music is very nice: a sort of atmospheric chill electronic track that reminds me a bit of Jean Michel Jarre. I found my foot tapping and my head nodding to the beat on occasion.
Game sound effects are okay, but limited to weapon sounds. There are no unit acknowledgements or movement sounds, which seemed a bit strange, particularly at the start of the game. These would be a good addition to the game before it leaves Early Access.
Interface sound effects seem a bit loud in comparison to the game sounds and music. A bit of volume normalisation might be in order.
Gameplay - Earth Liberation plays like an older RTS game, similar to the early Command and Conquer titles. There's a focus on training/building and deploying troops, rather than on resource gathering and base improvements, and because of this the levels are relatively quick to play. You won't often find yourself playing one level for hours on end. The only resource is money, which you earn at a steady rate as you play. You'll also receive some 'free' drops on some missions, which give you a boost to begin with. There don't seem to be any building or unit upgrades, either.
Unfortunately this focus on combat means that most levels quickly degenerate into a cycle of building as many troops as you can before the next alien wave and, after taking out any aliens you find, sacrificing your nameless marines on suicide runs against the enemy turrets and buildings.
Controls are a bit fiddly. The game uses keyboard and mouse, but for some reason introduces the use of the 'A' key and left clicking to attack, rather than just right-clicking like basically any other RTS game. Right-clicking does work against buildings, but against enemies your troops will usually end up running into the fray rather than attacking. The old shift-click doesn't work to attack while remaining in place, either; it has to be 'A'. There's no way to rotate the view, and even panning only works with arrow keys or moving the mouse to the screen edges; WASD can't be used.
Pathfinding is a bit rubbish, too, making your troops need far more babysitting than they should. Strangely it seems worse when using the A-click for attacking than when just right-click moving, although one would think the pathfinding algorithm would be the same either way. Given the focus on combat, controlling large groups of troops is something you'll need to do often, but when you have to navigate around any corners or terrain obstructions, you'll often find stragglers being left behind; they seem to just give up and stand still until you select them individually and tell them to move again. There's no way to set waypoints or see what path will be taken to a destination, either.
Another annoyance is that there's no grouping of units, so once you receive airborne troops it becomes a nightmare trying to separate them from the ground units so you can send them off to do their own thing. The developers need to add grouping by selection as well as quick select by unit type to remove these frustrations. But the game is still in Early Access, so I'm hoping these features will be added before final release.
The story is nothing new: powerful alien species invades Earth and wipes out most of the defence forces, leaving bands of resistance fighters left to try to win back the planet. It's done reasonably well, but the in-game text has a number of errors in it and could do with some editing.
There are a few little bugs, too. The worst are the poor pathfinding and units that just stop and stand around while their buddies are dying in numbers around them, but I also found that ground units can attack raised buildings by shooting rockets through the terrain (see one of the screenshots in my profile for an example). They're not game-breaking problems, but now is the time for the developers to address them, while the game is still in EA.
Pros:
+ Great unit graphics and animations
+ Excellent in-game music
Cons:
- Poor unit AI: pathfinding and reaction to enemies needs attention
- No music in the intro or on the title screen
- Needs some unit response sounds, movement sounds, etc.
- The story text needs some work
- Very limited options for strategy
I'm not a big fan of RTS games, and Earth Liberation is a good example of why: it always seems to me that the 'strategy' part of the genre should be in quotation marks, since in games like this the only viable way to win is to build hordes of units and go kamikaze on the enemy. That aside, though, Earth Liberation knows what it wants to do and, mostly, does a pretty good job of it. If the developers can fix the pathfinding and unit AI so that your marines always go where they're told and actually do something useful once they get there, this will be a pretty fun game. And the price is about right, too.

My Thoughts:

I want to like this game, but it's too slow for the pay off.  Being a roguelike game, there are obviously frustrating moments, like getting to level four only to discover that apparently some enemies can blast you against the wall at nearly full health and insta kill you.  Well, FTL and Don't Starve have those moments too, but at least they don't seem as slow as this game.
I don't have a problem with turn based games--original XCOM is one of my favorie games, and some of those turns can be quite long.  The problem here is, that it just isn't as fun for me.  This isn't really objective, as some reviewers don't mind it.  What I really find frustrating is that when you loot sarcophagi it can take you a full turn to equip the item, unless it's the first item.  For example, if you loot a shield and you didn't have one before, it's automatically equipped.  If you already had a shield, you now have to choose to spend a whole turn equipping it.  The problem is the turn based system for this game.  It's the whole design.  It seems to be built around initiative, so you get our speed up and it seems you get more turns, but it still just takes way too long.
I really like all the different equipment and spells you can get: armor, helmets, amulets, defensive/offensive spells, and weapons.  Probably my favorite spell is the vampire spell which allows you to take half an enemie's life.
There is a lot of thought put into this game, for sure, and I do enjoy trying to figure out the mechanics myself.   Some enemies you kill will turn into white bat-like creatures that you can heal yourself with, or they may heal or kill certain enemies.  There are also black bat-like creatures that can heal or harm you and enemies.  There are certain conditions for that which you have to figure out.  You can knock enemies into walls, each other, and various items and have completely different reactions.  It can be quite dangerous figuring out what new spells do, as they can hurt you.  There are different kinds of traps: acid/gas, fire, freeze, spikes, etc. and each level is random.  There are a lot of different things going on each turn, and you can't stick around too long in the levels as enemies spawn in from the left, and you really don't want to face all of them.
I like a lot of things about this game, but it's just so slow.  I may play it again, but I really can't recommend it, because I know a lot of people aren't going to like this aspect.

Guns, Gore & Cannoli is a 2d side screen scroller action shooter in a mobster/mafia/ post apocalyptic zombie world. The music does an excellent job of connecting all the aspects of this game together, and tailors each section very well to what is happening on the screen. The theme of the game is less about the zombies, and more about a mafia gangster from that era in history, and you feel like a badass hitman striving to complete your mission. One thing to note is that while the game does offer a co-op option, there is no ease of access in how to add a player; there is no interface via steam, an no friends list. It's not as simplistic as it should be, which is a shame.
The weapons that you play with have weight behind them, with each weapon having strengths and weaknesses depending upon the enemy you are facing. There are also Molotov cocktails, flame throwers, and rocket launchers for more specialized attacks. I go over each individual weapon in the video summary, if you are interested in more details. The only issue I had with the weapons would be if the game offered upgrades to weapons to increase damage, accuracy, or reload time, which would encourage replay-ability.
The platforming is more basic, but not disrespectful to your time. The different elements within the world and the different themes of the maps fit in perfectly with what you were being asked to do. There are a multitude of save points and health so that you don't lose much progress when you die. Enemies will come from behind you, but nothing randomly or continuously spawns in, so you do feel a sense of progression. There is no fall damage, which can be beneficial when you fall, so you don't die, but also can be detrimental to the game, as when you knock a zombie off a building for example, you don't get to see them go 'splat'!
The story in the game is surprising; the cut-scenes and aesthetic does a good job of connecting you to the character. The voice acting as well does a good job of making you feel like a badass mafia enforcer who goes in to get the tough jobs done. It conveys a good sense of purpose with what you are doing.
The game give you action at a steady stream.The story isn't award winning, but is entertaining. The platforming and the weapons both give you a feeling of accomplishment and progression. The game does an excellent job of providing and excelling at what they promised, and it's an easy recommend.

The Virtual Villagers series has always been one my favorites since I was a kid. If you want a casual/simulation game that requires some puzzle-solving and villager care, this game is it. However, this game is not for everyone.
Pros
+Four music tracks
+Game progresses at selected rates even when the game is not running: paused, slow, normal and fast.
+Customize villager outfits (after building the required shack).
+16 unique puzzles to solve.
+Endless replayability (game will never end unless you start over or every villager dies).
+Multiple save files (tribes).
Cons
-Beginning of the game is very tough, villagers are inexperienced, there is a lack of food resources, and only a few villagers are able to work.
-Villagers can/will die even if the game is left off for so long.
-Villagers need to be manually taught how to do things, like building and farming.
-A villager must be 14 years old before they're able to do a lot of things.
-Game can be extremely boring once everything is completed: puzzles, steady food supply, all tech upgrades, etc.

Prism Collider is an action puzzle game with the objective to maneuver your way through a maze while avoiding enemies, and collecting chips which sometimes unlock areas which were not accessible before. The maze is designed with two layers - a white one and a red one, and you can switch between them only at designated points. You move around by using the arrows on the keyboard. Purple teleporters allow you to become impervious to all walls, so you can travel to another purple teleporter, and continue from there.
Some levels are easy, while some are more challenging. The harder levels are hard enough to cause frustration, but if you keep trying, you will prevail. The enemies can only go so fast, so its a just a matter of keeping on your toes.
Visuals are simple, but the game is a fun experience at a cheap price. There are 30 levels included.

Prism Collider is a fairly straightforward navigation puzzler. I came in expecting shovelware. I definitely did not get shovelware. This easily justifies $1 and it's a game I can actually see myself coming back to.
