Ok, but quite basic. This isn't really a competitor to Photoshop or Paint Shop Pro, it is a mixed bag of features in a sometimes questionable user interface. Instead of using the traditional menu bar which has always been in Photoshop/Paint Shop Pro (and other photo editing software such as Corel Draw) they have put some of these menus into tools. At first I was a bit shocked by this as it looked like there were hardly any features at all. However, I have later discovered that some of these features like the effects section (which seemed to be absent at first) hidden away in an effects tool. I can see how this makes the UI neater but really it's a bit disconcerting to start with.
To be quite fair some of the features are quite good, such as the panorama tool which puts up to 8 pictures together in a bigger panorama. I have been finding this quite useful and most of the panoramas I have made are completely seamless. The shadow and 3d tools are also quite nice because they can be used very neatly on text.
They have included an online content catalogue which is nice to have and has some great ideas (such as editable charts and logo designs). However, they have put the filter presets in this catalogue which is a bit too difficult to use as it doesn't let you see previews of your picture with the different presets. Instead, it shows you pictures of a woman’s face with the different filters and you have to guess from that which one will suit your picture. There also doesn't seem to be any control of the filters once you have applied them. It would have been a lot easier to have a separate tool with previews/controls as I am still using the filters in the windows photo viewer and this is something that is now included on most other apps/programs.
Overall, I'd probably give it around 50%. It's good for the discount price I paid (£29.99) and very useful to have something on Steam (as I will be able to install it without having to look for a cd somewhere next time I get a new computer) but for the full price of £49.99 I'd consider looking at paying a bit extra for Photoshop Elements or Paint Shop Pro.

This review covers all 4 of the East Tower games in one. Simply put, the game isn't very good. The art has occasional good moments but most of it is pretty bad. The story is set up in such a way that it could lend itself to an interesting discussion of gender identity and digital sexuality but it instead chooses to do cliché "oops, I tripped and grabbed your boob" moments. There are dialog options but the game is still very linear; you either die instantly, find a solution, or pick a solution that gives you a bit of extra dialog.
I would not recommend any of these games except for Kurenai (which was admittedly pretty good). However, there are parts of the Kurenai story that won't make any sense without playing at least a bit of the other ones.
The game is also way too expensive. I bought them all as a set with 40% off ($18 total) and I feel ripped-off. There are much better VNs available for much less. Takashi, Kuon, and Akio were each only about 1.5 hours of play time, which is not a great value.
Finally, every time you finish a section (and there are at least 7 sections per game) the game tries to get you to post to social media. That really pisses me off. It takes me out of the moment to try to get me to advertise for a game that I paid for. Dear game devs, please don't do that!

This game was fairly interesting at first.  As the tutorial walks you through your new powers, I was feeling like this would have a fun level of complexity to it.
However, the game quickly becomes repetative and tedious with the end game of each level taking an inordinately long time to finish.
The game strategy is basically choosing what order to build your 5 types of units in, most with a hard cap on the total amount you can have, and managing when to use your mana, as in using a cheap power now, or saving for a more powerful attack.  You have no control over the placement of your buildings or actions of your workers and very limited control over your soldiers.
The game is also fairly short, I beat it in about 5 hours, maybe less.  About a third of this time was spent more or less just waiting for my soldiers to finish taking out the enemy's town with virtually no resistance.
There is a sandbox mode once you are finished, but other than using my earthmoving powers to draw a few funny shapes into the dirt, it got boring very quickly.
This is not a bad game, but I would not recommend buying it.

Not the kind of person who normally writes reviews but I am making an exception in this case because I think a lot of the reviews here are a bit unfair or maybe they don't fully understand all of the mechanics. Make sure you go to practice mode and read all of the tips in there and you'd have a lot of information to dismiss most of these negative reviews. Let me address a couple of the common complaints i see:
1. People are saying things like spamming is encouraged or that they can't handle when npcs or people gang up on them. At the risk of sounding like a Dark Souls a$$hole, Git Gud... you can block attacks and counter if you are fast and pay attention to where the attack is coming from. Every game like this (dark souls or for honor) have metas, just roll with it and learn to counter different playstyles.
2. Story. Who cares? The world and the ambience really works here and what story there is works well enough.
3. Lag/Bugs. I can only speak to my experience here but I have only had the game disconnect once and not let me out of a pvp round once and also had it crash once. I have only had lag when running between zones. I know tripple A titles that have more problems at launch. Not saying this is OK, but my experience hasn't been game breaking.
All in all, I quite like this fighting game. I am a big Dark Souls and fighting game fan so this works for me. Would recommend right now for fans of dark souls and fighting games that are challanging, if you aren't maybe wait till the price comes down or they make improvements. Keep in mind this is half the price of a full title. For the level of customization and control over fighting style this offers, it was good for me. Right now there is only open world and 1v1 pvp and a sort of short story. I really hope that they add extra story, challanges, combat deck cards, balancing, bug fixes, pvp options etc. If they did one or two of these I could recommend to everyone.

The concept of the game itself is great, but from the red thumbs down I'm sure you can tell that I didn't find the execution satisfactory.
As a speed reader I've gotten through three of the four scenarios in my forty five minute play time, and thus I'm going to imagine it would have taken me an hour to gotten through all of them.  So it's President for a Day but only Gameplay for an Hour.  But it's a little more than $4 at the time of the sale, so I didn't expect there to be a lot of content itself.
That being said, time does have a large factor as to why I didn't enjoy myself.  You see the game has a score system that ranks how you did in the little more than a dozen turns you're given, and I felt it actually hurt the game more than it helped it.  Why?  Because at the start you choose which leader you play as, with some buff attributed to them as well as a goal which gives 250 points should you complete it.  To give a comparison, score from other sources (as far as I'm aware from my three scenarios) more often than not amounts to less than a hundred, and I'd guess that's if you do really well in other categories.  With that I feel as though I'm playing Quidditch.  Sure, I -could- do other things to help raise the score up, but ultimately it comes down to that goal.
A lot of people will probably think that it doesn't have any influence on the game itself so I shouldn't complain, and I can't fault them.  That being said there were other problems I had.  If I pandered to a group as hard as possible, if I agreed with everything the rich and the military say, I obtained support in the 60s region, which only provides the first buff, though that is still useful.  I don't even know if there's any buff from raising it higher than that because again, the game length is fairly low.
And that's what it comes down to.  This isn't a bad game, it's just a short game that leaves me feeling unsatisfied.  I didn't feel a lot of weight to my actions, but maybe that's the point, life is hard in Africa and there's only so much one man can do to change things up.  Anyway, it's $5 when the sale ends, you might find more enjoyment than I did, and feel it was a worthwhile experience.  But I'd first reccomend getting an emulator to play Hidden Agenda on.
(I encourage people to add comments, either in favor or even if you disagree with me, and if I have any extra tidbits to say about the game I'll probably add it to the comment section so that the review itself isn't a huge wall of text on what I would or would not add to the game)

A brilliant return to form for a series that desperately needed it. Much like Resident Evil 4, Capcom have taken the series and turned it on it's head, while maintaining many of the small details that make a Resident Evil game FEEL like a Resident Evil game. The best writing the series has had (which isn't saying much, admitedly, but the story is actually geniunely enjoyable), a spooky atmosphere to rival even the scariest of "pure horror" games, and boss characters that are incredibly memorable combine to make RE7 one of the best in the series.
It's not perfect, the last third of the game is pretty lackluster and forgettable, and the presence of the regular zombies honestly detracts from the awesome atmosphere the first part of the game set up, as they tend to show up in areas where you're expecting something more significant. RE7 maintains some of the "action-horror" aspects of the earlier RE games, but it is absolutely not a FPS that you play for the gunplay or weapon variety.
Overall, RE7 is a great horror game, a great Resident Evil game, and an okay action game.

I bought this game based on the number of “very positive reviews” and regretted it deeply, after playing for more or less 4 hours I am requesting a refund. It looks like the typical CAPCON scamming that made the developer so infamous.
There is so many issues but what really bothered me are the following…
It felt not scary or tense to me. It was doing okay creating a suspense/murder setting until the first enemy appears. Then the game turns it self in a really poor minded, unfunny and tedious joke about rednecks e B terror films. And keeps repeating those to the point that I wonder if the game is trying to satirize a genre that is already so difficult to take seriously.
But the technical issues are the worst part... I am really sorry to say that but the game was released in January and it still feels like it belongs to the early access category. The developer really made a lazy shameless job in the PC version, how very CAPCON-ish, the graphics are not really good and it’s configurations options are extremely limited. BUT there is at least one truly a horrifying thing in this horror game, the anti-aliasing filter(s). They look like from generations ago! It is so bad that I suspected that was a graphic card issue and googled it, it’s not. There is a lot of complains on the subject.
Then comes the worst, for me, the movement. I don’t consider myself a fan of RE but I’m not a strange to it either. I played enough (specially the 2, 3 and 4) to know that there is a characteristic type of movement in the series and it takes a while to get used to. And, as I dragged myself through the corridors feeling like was trying to escape from a retirement home while carrying the nurse on my back, I again though that there was a technical issue with the game. Then I searched and again found tons of complains that the thing is just that bad! You can’t fix it. The protagonist is so very slow and often get stuck in corners and objects that are not supposed to be in your way. The weird first person camera is no help either because it makes your character seems to be way narrow than he is, so you keep hitting objects in the sides and getting stuck. You can hit the run button like crazy but it barely makes any difference. Wait… it does, the screen gets bouncier... It’s really the worst movement that I met in a RE game and one of the worst I have ever seen! I does not improve the terror setting and neither is addition to the difficulty or challenge, it just makes you repeat stuff again and again. It’s by far the most annoying and frustrating thing in the game, after a couple of hours it feels that RE7 is just trying to win by boring you to the point of giving up.
And there are others minor issues that I’m not listing. I can’t understand why there is so many good reviews, because in my experience it was the worst game I played in this year. I can’t imagine people enjoying it even in a “masochistic” way. Maybe it got some merits further on but I am not willing to put my time on it.
It really feels like the game is on beta or maybe alpha, I’m serious, feels like the game was stuck in its development; it needed a lot more testing and feedback, and was released anyway. And that was eleven months ago but the developer did not bothered patching up anything. I don’t recommend it, it’s a half made game that will not be fixed. Stay away.

I bought this in the latest 'Hidden Gems 4' bundle from Bundle Stars. It's a little like the old arcade game 'Bombjack' with no enemies, but with a more modern Meatboy feel. Style-wise, I think this game harks back to GBA-ere games, with a bold Japanese aesthetic and chirpy chiptune music. The game focuses on a finding one of a limited number of time-limited routes through the colour-coded buttons and pick-ups, for which you'll die many times trying to find.
Some levels are very difficult to make out where the platforms are, and death is 'rewarded' with a five or so second pause to endure before being able to start the level again. This is exactly the sort of game you want to get straight back into before you forget the route you have just started to learn. If the developer can allow a button-press to skip this and get back to the game, it would be less frustrating to play.
Personally, I gave up after the first 20 or 30 levels, finding it unrewarding.
Bearing in mind the above, if you like this sort of puzzle-platformer game you should like this.

I'm reluctant to thumbs-down this because there are some very cool elements to this game. I dig the character building to an extent, but it's pretty rudimentary. There's so many skills on display, but you can't access them. Overall, there's so much depth to the game, and yet it feels so shallow--why? I want to like this game. I really do. Even though I'm not a huge fan of the muddled universe that is Warhammer, the concept of this game is great.
That being said, it's just too poorly executed. Mordheim suffers from a similar problem that XCOM 2 has, where the AI not only takes far too long to make a decision, but it always ends up doing the most obvious lemming-esque choice. If you're just gonna keep auto-attacking, why do you need more than a couple seconds to figure it out? To top it off, while the animations *do* look nice, they have this weird ending lag where the characters are just kind of awkwardly staring at each other after one just bashed the other in the face with a flail.
Everything just takes too damn long. You know it's a problem when you feel more relieved being out of combat not because you achieved a victory, but because you're bored.
In sum, though, I'll say this:
PROS:
* Character customization, building your own team is always fun.
* Solid animation.
* Cool art overall, as one would expect from Warhammer, it's a dark universe.
* Playable with both KBM and controller, button callouts change as you swap between them.
* Decent soundtrack and voice acting.
CONS:
* AI takes too long.
* So much to learn, but so little to do with it.
* Environments are fairly bland, but hey, it's Warhammer.
* Witch Hunters are DLC, yet they stand prominently in character select, dead center, and highlighted as if they're playable. That's kind of an insult to gamers. Like, if I were to boot up Diablo 3 or something, go to make a new character, and, say, I wanna make a Witch Doctor or something--nope, sorry, you have to pay $2.99 first! That's a super special DLC character! Why stop there? Make every character/warband/what-have-you DLC!
All in all, if this is your cup of tea, try it and see if you like it. The game is *almost* mechanically sound, and has some redeeming qualities, but I'll pass on this snooze-fest.

There's a lot to like about Mordheim, but not enough to recommend it. The visuals are solid: graphics are good, aesthetic customization is satisfyingly deep, and the ruined city, forgive the expression, comes alive. Though some have criticized the gameplay, I really liked the combat system, and had a lot of fun in the actual fights.
However:
The campaign becomes extremely unfun pretty quickly because of how the game compensatses for the poor fighting skills of the AI, namely, massive, massive bonuses. You can see it in the description of the difficulty of a given mission, but what isn't clear is how the game "balances" the strength of your warband as you level up. Enemy warbands will have a rating similar to yours, but will have /all/ their members leveled. In addition to this, they'll have a composition similar to yours, so if you have six members, they have six members. If you have one of your special heroes, they'll have one of their special heroes. One of the biggest frustrations I experienced was leveling up my Cult warband until I could, FINALLY, hire the Possessed. Once I fielded him, though, I found myself up against a fully leveled and upgraded Augur that handed his♥♥♥♥♥to him. Read some guides, found out that people that Possessed heroes were underpowered, so I ditched him, and started leveling up for the Spawn. Got the Spawn, and then faced a fully leveled and upgraded Rat Ogre. That was when I stopped playing.
Maybe I'd like it better in multiplayer, but the campaign became just incredinly unfun to play after a while. The only way to win those kinds of match is to get lucky in the set up, and then exploit the very poor AI strategy. Which, by the way, is to just run straight at you along whatever road is closest. I have never seen the AI go after objectives, which also makes it hard, bordering on impossible, for you to do the same. Unless you get REALLY lucky, expect most skirmishes to devolve into a scrum, which is why the best and only strategy is to keep your whole warband together at all times.
But it on sale, maybe, but I'd give it a pass. It's more frustrating than fun.

Honestly, this game is great. It successfully combined the compulsive, frame counting, competitive side of fighting games with the role-playing and feel of a kung-fu movie. If you're a fan of martial arts and lament the way they've been either ignored or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized by modern games. Please check this game out.
These developers set out with a simple mission, with simple goals, and simply achieved them with upmost integrity. They didn't cut corners or give into corporate greed. The aesthetics are simple BUT graceful. The atmosphere is simple BUT absorbing. The gameplay is simple BUT smooth as butter. etc...I'd be tempted to give Devolver D all the credit, but I feel Sloclap was just as honorable and determined.
Speaking of determination, the game is all about the grind. STAY WITH ME HERE. The game is essentially a bare-bones kung-fu movie story with slight mystical elements. One is simply told "prove yourself"and put into a world with thousands of others that are your equal at worst and a roflstomping Bruce Lee and best. You go about the rather small BUT well crafted world and are constantly thrown into combat against others proving their worth. You will fight, and fight, and fight, and fight until you have learned more moves than Jagger and are good enough to defeat the "story" bosses.
The fighting system is Phenomenal. It offers a high skill ceiling with a very low skill floor. 2 attack buttons, 1 block, 2 evades, and 4 stances. THAT'S IT. Within that simple framework is an extreme amount of customization and instant familiarity. The moveset itself is determined by a "combat deck" which one can swap moves in and out of. You learn moves from fighting NPCs, joining a school (a cross between a MMO guild and an online tutorial), or fighting other players.
Here comes the most disputed and experimental aspect of the game. The world itself, with all it's story, art, and dangers, is simply an online lobby. PvP is built into the game from the ground up and is introduced at the very beginning. You will constantly encounter other players and through the streamlined emote system (or just pure aggression) cooperate with them to take down tough enemies, ignore them, or fight them in a unusually nice and respectful competitive community. Fights between players can break out often, and will offer an insane challenge increase when you least expect it. More than once, I've teamed up with a dude to lay the smack down on a "marked one" only to have an honorable duel afterward. The endgame itself (other than fashion, whose loot are ALL RNG drops) is about combat trials: just straight up 1v1 (and hopefully more modes soon) duels with other players. This is a great system because it not awards you others to fight as your (hopefully) equals, but also rewards with exp, loot, and ranks. The combat trial ranks actually reflected in the game world by giving you access to tougher boss trials and (in my experience) populating the world with much tougher NPCs with more exotic moves.
This game gave me a journey that I haven't felt since my first playthough of Dark Souls.

This is a great Fighting/Arena game.
It is not, however, an action/adventure game or a MMORPG.
If you are expecting the latter, you will be disappointed.  The "story," plays more like a guided tutorial.  A short romp across the PvE map designed to show you a variety of fighting styles and moves which you can then learn to build your own customized deck/set of moves.
Once you've done that and hit max level (60), which doesn't take too long, the game becomes mainly about queuing up to fight other people online.
And that's it.
And for 30 bucks that's enough, because they really have built an amazing and pretty balanced fighting engine.  If you're a fighting game fan that always wished you could build your own character, this will probably scratch that itch.  An arena fighter with a touch of RPG stats + equipment.  You can spend hours customizing move sets, hunting for new ones both in PvE and PvP), or just farming for gear.
But if you're looking for an adventure game to "beat," or a big open world to explore with big boss fights and a story that ends....you'll definitely be disappointed.

Given the fact that East Tower: Akio and East Tower: Takashi are more or less the same game apart that Sakuya is teaming up with Takashi instead of Akio, nearly whole of the review is a copy/paste of the one I did for Akio.
Sakuya is a woman wishing to be a man since an incident in her childhood. She makes everything in her power to look like one. Her cousin Daiki works for Dreamworld and needs her help to try a new virtual attraction called West Tower, reserved for women. However, Sakuya managed to convince him to let her try the East Tower, reserved for men. She ends with four other testers, trapped in the virtual world, though she's happy to see that she's a man in it...
This is the same beginning in each Each Tower game. Once in the virtual world, Sakuya will team up with one of the guys. In the first of the series, she's Akio's partner, whose virtual form is a child. East Tower is an attraction that will confront everyone to their own insecurities and fears.
I will go straight the point: this is a visual novel, where you have choices to make. Each stage must be cleared to advance in the story, you don't have any skills or relationships to improve/destroy. However, choices are mattering: you can get a bad ending immediately where you have to begin the stage again (not the entire story), a best friend ending (by scoring A on each stage) and a romance ending (by clearing each stage with a S). If you follow the romance route, you'll end up with an extra chapter. However, some stages don't have a A rank, only a S one - in that case, for the best friend route, it's considered as if it was a A.
Choices are generally made during the challenges proposed for the team. It's much rare to see them outside of them, before or after them. True, without skills or anything to worry, the game is easier than any other visuel novel I've already played (apart Shan Gui, which is more an interactive book), even the first Heileen was more complex and even Blue Rose was more complicated. I don't mind at all this lack of difficulty.
I find very interesting the fact that the guy will be your best friend at the end, as the bad ending isn't a "you're alone", "you're killed", etc.. However, should you choose to pursue him, it means that your character is also evolving and accepting herself more.
Let's speak about Takashi. He's a sensible young man, that admires his older sister, who seems way more stronger than him and that's why he wished to be her and that he adopted her appearance. Takashi is also the typical comical teenager boy, a side more developed in the romance route: he's hit often by Sakuya, he's slow to understand that she's a real girl and he has every corny line to deliver. However, given the fact that he's very sensible, he's wishing to be strong and the only time he did, well, he managed to get his footh in the mouth because the girl he protected was believing that she didn't need any protection. In the end, the fact the team was a girl wishing to be a boy for escaping some stereotypes and a boy that is wishing to be strong like his sister is very interesting. I largerly prefer Akio than Takashi but well, Takashi can be mature if he wants. Besides, his voice isn't as charming as Akio.
Indeed, the visual novel has voice acting... in Japanese. I don't understand a thing but as the subtitles are in English, I could follow the story. The only character not voiced is you. However, I find it really good. It's always fun to hear something in a foreign language, it's reminding me some good memories with some anime.
As for the style, it's really in a manga style, reminding me of The Rose of Versailles or anything directed to girls - because it's clearly stated in the official website that it's a visual novel for them (but everyone is welcome to play it). I loved it. I also loved the HUD, kinda hi-tech and with a good shade of green.
The music is very good too, very adapted to each scene. I really liked it. And with Takashi being comical, you bet that you heard more the funny music than anything else.
East Tower: Takashi is a little good moment I've spent, though I wished that it was a little more serious as in Akio, without having to think too much. It's not the best visual novel out there, I admit that, however, it's still worthy of a purchase and you'll learn more about Sakuya's past in this game.

The East Tower series is a set of otome visual novels that are different than your standard Japanese otome game. If this review peaks your interest, I would recommend buying the whole bundle as it is cheaper than buying each one individually. The 4 games together give 15+ hours of game play.
Note: If you read my reviews on any of the other games (Akio,Takashi, Kuon, Kurenai) aren't terribly different
I was surprised at how much I ended up liking game. I think a lot of that has to do as a Otome game addict I was getting a little burnt out on the mobile games. (When I say burnt out, I think I have played the main story line of more than 80 characters on mobile otome games.) East Tower Takashi is the second installment the series. The order which the game is recommended is Akio, Takashi, Kuon then Kurenai. I would recommend this game even to just VN fans (not necessarily otome fans) because it explores interesting themes and has a great overarching plot.
The story is what got me hooked on this game, I love a different story than your more standard otome game that ET has. I liked the Takashi route, but I would say it is my least favorite of all the characters. -Not to say that you shouldn't buy it-. It reveals a little more about the underlying story, but not much more than Akio.  I especially like how this game explores gender related sexuality in a very interesting way. Gender fluidity is something much different to be explored in a VN/Otome game, especially for a Japanese market. Sakuya (the MC, name changeable) bends the standard female protagonist role, rebelling against the female stereotype, actually starts the virtual game as a male character.
The voice acting is very nice for an indie game. I liked some of the unique voices in the game (Daiki specifically). I wouldn't say that there is any blaring miscasts in the voice acting. Of course this being an indie game, there aren't the big shot seiyuus (voice actors) to really make the voice acting really shine.
I was not big on the art style that ET has, but I grew attached to the characters anyway, which is a good sign as the likeability of the character is not just based on the art. I would say the thing that bothers me the most is the roundness of the faces, especially the young versions of the characters. I think of all the VN/Otome games ET has to take the cake on roundness of faces. There are more CGs than I was expecting for an indie game. The backgrounds in ET are interesting, I really like how the game world is portrayed. I would really say that the only (slight) drawback to this game is the art style, but it is still nice in its own way.

Oh, how I wanted to recommend it.  On the plus side, it’s a god game that lets you reshape the land so that your furlings can construct their own structures as well as cast powers like earthquakes and volcanoes (similar to Populous).  On the surface, this sounds great!  On the other, there are some really odd things about this game that make me scratch my head in wonder as to what the developers were thinking.  There are no time controls, no WASD or arrow key camera movement, no zooming (there is a fixed bird’s eye view), holding in right mouse click and moving the mouse up and down (not left or right oddly) rotates the camera, no HP bars above buildings, your score decreases as you play (rushing you into beating it more quickly), and more.  As far as I can tell, there are eight levels on the campaign menu and no skirmish modes.  The inclusion of the latter would have given the game some replay value and could have made it worth $20 despite these short-sided gameplay mechanics.  As it stands, it just doesn't do enough to justify that price tag (in my opinion).

+ Terrain control
+ Cute, but not annoyingly so, characters
- Poor sound. VO sounds like someone had some awful series of accidents in audacity.
- Poor camera (and camera controls). Feels like a poorly adapted port from a mobile game; no zoom, quite clunky in general.
- Lack of variety. Limited missions, characters, powers, and reasons to actually play.
More or less feels like a dodgy phone adaptation of Black & White without any of the qualities that made B&W engaging, fun, or challenging.

I love the game, but in the state is in right now I simply cannot recommend it.  Connection issues, bugs, and a lack of things to do make loving a game that deserves to be loved unnecessarily difficult.
But behind all of these launch issues that are only really to be expected for an Early Access game is a beautiful stance fighter that borrows the transient online interactions of Dark Souls to create stories of self improvement through respectful competition.  Up to two other players can be in the same area as you, and if you meet them the game is open PvP... but you'll usually find people are quite friendly and more often than not will cooperate with you to help you progress through the game. Even the ocassional ganker will usually pick you right up off the ground after beating you up - you don't lose anything by dying except maybe a few seconds and you're brought right back to full HP.  The interactions you see grow out of these simple rules are just amazing and it makes being a part of the community surprisingly a positive experience.
The PvE content unfortunately is incredibly short and fairly dull.  NPC's do little more than turn their head while text scrolls by underneath them, no gesticulations or hints about how that NPC feels about what theyr'e saying.  The story might as well not exist except for the few voiced boss fights that actually lend a bit of intrigue to what's happening.  Environments are beautiful but hard to navigate, with lots of invisible walls and knee-high unscalable obstacles making the whole thing feel like a bunch of gussied-up corridors that look too similar within each area to make it clear which direction you're going (the forest areas in particular are notably nondescript and it's easy to spend lots of time running around in circles).  And the map in this game is hard to parse, making finding your next objective a pain as you stop randomly stumbling into bosses and start needing to hunt down the one you haven't found yet.
But when you do finally meet one of the three actual boss fights, they're a real treat.  They're convincingly voiced and their delivery makes the tidbits of lore they reveal actually interesting and they can be surprisingly tough but fair.  At least until you've figured out the deck system and figure out what three-hit combo you can spam endlessly at them to kill them easily even on their hardest iterations, but up until that point they're fun fights.
But to play those later iterations, you have to first game levels in Combat Trials, the dedicated PvP portion of the game where you duel other players 1v1 in a best of 5 match.  The game is inarguably a PvP-first game, but that there isn't even the option to continue progressing through the game through PvE is quite annoying.  I'm saying this as a very PvP-focused player, there is only one PvP mode and doing that one mode over and over and over again gets old and I wish there were other ways to gain these combat trial levels so I can take a break once in a while.
But good
, the fights.  The combat system in Absolver isn't mechanically very demanding, using only two buttons for regular attacks and alternate attacks (moves you can do in place of your normal attack to mix things up) and generally not requiring godlike reflexes. But by doing this, the game immediately thrusts you directly into the best bit of fighting games, the mindgames.  Understanding what combos your opponent uses for their bread and butter, throwing out a ducking move to duck under the high kick you think is going to come next only to be surprised when they
you would catch on and instead throw out their axe kick to smack you in the noggin.  Your opponent starts parrying your attacks because you got a little braindead and just started spamming attacks, so now you start intentionally doing imperfect timings so that they miss their parry, throw out feints so they parry thin air and then get smacked in the face by a quick follow up punch.  It's incredibly satisfying to play for how accessible it is, it feels like the perfect answer for any Dark Souls or For Honor player that is tired by the antics of the respective developers seeming to ignore their competitive communities.
As the store page will tell you, you put your attacks together in a "deck" of attacks, stringing from one to the other automatically unless you use one of your four alternate attacks to change things up.  This brings a lot of expressiveness to fights in addition to the fashion choices and different combat styles (three which you can choose from the start, one secret you can discover in the game).  Through the course of a match you can feel like you're getting to understand your opponent, predict what they're going to do next, what kind of person they are.  It's endlessly entertaining.
But the grim reality is that the game's connections and bugs disrupt this beautifully choreographed dance far too often.  My opponents and I not too infrequently will start teleporting around, sometimes straight off a cliff for an instant death which will likely decide the whole match.  It feels like one out of every five matches my opponent will just disconnect right at the start.  Hackers seem to be a common occurance already, and that's only when they're being obvious - more subtle cheaters seem to be using stuff like infinite shards to spam abilities in a way that you might just chalk up to extra investment in the Will stat.  And you can't even 1v1 someone in the dedicated 1v1 mode yet through an invite, making the community's tournaments hard to organize.
The game just is not ready to be put up for sale yet despite its underlying genius, and the disappearing playerbase seems to be proof of that.  This game deserved a far better launch.  I'm hoping that in a month or two I can turn this into a recommendation, but I'm afraid there might not be people to play with by then.

A turn-based tactical game featuring no manual save, a Warhammer fantasy setting, heavy combat RNG, and an obnoxious inventory/side objective system.
The RNG can really make this frustrating, even if you escape an ecounter with a win it can feel more like a loss when a lot of your soldiers end up heavily wounded in need of a few days resting period and money to get him that medical help.
I can forgive the RNG and no manual save because the title advertises itself as extremelly cruel and punishing, but what i'm not sure I can get used to is the side objectives that I mentioned earlier, having to stall fights to send troops running around the map just to collect a bit of loot is beyond annoying, and from what i've seen (please correct me if i'm wrong) I couldn't stack Wyrdstone so you have to send someone who's inventory isn't already full and most of the characters i've gotten have about 3-4 slots to fill.
Some plus sides:
Great audio and visuals, the music and environments blend well with the grim dark setting of Warhammer.
Lot of skills/attributes for your warband troops with a bit of customization looks wise.
If there was a middle ground review option I would go with that but for right now, i'll recommend it on sale to masochists and lovers of Warhammer.

Sadly I cannot recommend this as the controls and interface are not a good choice, and not nice to use. You have to constantly navigate between a barely helpful map and a third-person view. In a game where placement and even orientation seem to be paramount, that you have to manoeuver in third-person is beyond me. I did not find the same feeling I had when playing the boardgame.
The warband setup part is quite fun, and the atmosphere is excellent. But why so few warbands, and the less famous ones at that? The combat can get rewarding at times, but mostly you'll see your guys fail and the CPU success. CPU turns also take a long time.
I looted some items but never understood how to actually equip them; I'm guessing they had requirements as I could equip some others, but I never saw it explicited. The loot after you win/lose is also quite ridiculous, as others stated if you didn't pick everything you wanted before the other band routs, bad luck, it's lost.
I also personally miss an auto-resolve option for the encounters, so I could focus on the warband management and campaign part, but that might be just me.
Overall not a bad game, but the investment on time and energy is too heavy for the return on fun.

My Let's Play:
Quick Impressions: Idol Hands is a God Game that features terrain deformation as a requirement for growing your village of Furlings as well as being used offensively/defensively (whichever way works best strategically) against the opposing God/village.
Easily the Terrain Deformation is the stand-out feature in this game and is handled remarkably well and is graphically impressive. You'll need to use these powers to level land so that you're farmers can cultivate crops and feed your population so that you can produce more workers (wood/metal/priests) and warriors to protect your village. As you level the land around you, the border of your colony will slowly grow larger as your workers build new buildings automatically.
Another plus that I really enjoyed but doesn't really change much of the game was clicking on the minimap and zooming out super far and you are presented with a landscape that is very reminiscent of the view enjoyed in Act Raiser. Again, not the biggest thing but I really liked it.
The big negatives that I have for the game is the SUPER long mandatory tutorial sections (1+ hour(s)) and the inability to speed up the game. Everything in the game runs at 1x speed, always. So the early part of the game is rather boring because you don't even have all of your spells yet.
Overall though, the game is very charming and family friendly.

Pros:
- The music
- The block design & variety, don't know if the shapes are proper random but there are at least more than Tetris & that was nice & annoying because I wasn't expecting to need to make space for a + symbol.
- Line explosion graphics are satisfying as is getting the | block on the side where you've set a channel for it.
- I will probably assist my spatial thinking if I can get my head around remembering 4 board layouts at once.
Cons:
- I never realised how awkward keyboard only menus were until this.
- The pieces auto-lock when they touch another one, so you can't do the just-in-time slide across the board that produces many heart stopping saves in Tetris. It basically renders the top 4-6 lines of the board useless in the later stages as the piece will drop in & you have basically zero time to adjust.
- The pacing in the early levels is very slow due to essentially playing 4 games of Tetris at once, for the first 5 minutes of my first game it felt like the most boring game I'd played in a while; that goes away by level 6 or so of your first game when the speed of gameplay heats up & you know what to expect for future games, but I feel it needs addressing.
- White background with a slightly shinier white grid is an odd choice. The grid is hard to see when you need to make some fast channel decisions & bright white is annoying for long periods. It doesn't need to be dazzlingly colourful experience in the background like I guess Neon Drive or even Lumines, but...something to not blind me when games run 15+ minutes.
- 'Fixate' the game mode where you can't rotate the pieces feels like something you could do in other games of this type, but wouldn't.
- I do hope we get a 'Piece Hold' function, seems like it'd provide some good strategy.

Quatros Origins provides a refreshing twist on a 2D block puzzle game we all know and love. By manipulating tetromino and pentomino blocks in an effort to clear filled horizontal lines, Quatros takes things to a new level by rotating the build stage by ninety degrees every time a piece is set. Even though this game is fantastic on its own, local multiplayer support ensures that 3 other people in the room can join in on the fun.
There are currently 4 different game modes, single or local multiplayer supported, to play in Quatros Origins, described below. There is also a leaderboard for each mode (global and against friends).
In every game mode, the build stage will rotate 90 degrees to the left (clockwise if viewed from the top) after each piece is placed. The pieces will affect every side of the build area. With extremely careful planning, quick thinking and impeccable foresight, it is possible to maneuver undesirable pieces in such a way to create a favorable grid (after stage rotation) for the next piece.
In addition to the recognizable tetrominoes, pentominoes are also included, greatly varying any strategy you may have developed if you happen to be only familiar with playing Tetris. In case you may be wondering, the familiar 7 one-sided tetrominoes are copyrighted/trademarked, so removing the pentominoes may get too uncomfortably close to infringement. These pentomino pieces can be described as: T, U, V, Z shapes (not to be confused with T, Z tetromino shapes).
This review does not follow a general structure due to Quatros Origins’ relatively straightforward/friendly nature. What you see in the Store page’s trailer and screenshots is exactly what you get. Several random observations are presented below to provide a little bit of insight into playing the game.
Controllers were clearly designed to be the preferred method of playing for Quatros, as seen by the lack of multiplayer support on a single keyboard. Although the Store page lists support for NES/SNES controllers, it is still unsure as to whether classic arcade sticks are supported. It may also be important for hardcore/veteran players to know that Quatros Origins indeed supports the option to rebind key bindings/reconfigure the controller mapping (for the Primary and Secondary players). Although I personally do not have an issue with the default layout, a major complaint in many of the negative reviews of Tetris Ultimate is with regards to a lack of controller configuration (among other issues). It is very fortunate that Quatros does not make this mistake.
Advanced controller options also include the ability to customize the Delay and Repeat Rate. For those that may be interested, the Delay controls how long it takes for a piece to start sliding once you hold left or right. The Repeat Rate controls how fast the pieces slide left and right.
Quatros is already at a polished and relatively complete state. There are, however, a few suggestions that may improve the gameplay listed below.
Quatros Origins is a great and addictively fun product. Its unique stage rotation, sleek aesthetics, and assortment of game modes earn it a recommendation for any fan of block puzzle/casual games or retro arcade/score attack games. With such a lack of similar games in this genre, especially on Steam, Quatros Origins definitely shines above the rest and deserves a chance to be in your library.

Alright, this was a fun game that definitely shows its fondness for the Metal Slug series.
As far as this game itself, it was over the top silly, with super exaggerated voice acting that was at times hilarious. The story was actually pretty cool such as it is, and was a pretty unique take on how a zombie outbreak might begin. You play as a hitman/enforcer, Vinnie Cannoli, sent by your boss to pick up a dude named Frankie who is held by a rival gangster family.♥♥♥♥♥♥just gets out of hand from there, lol.
The graphics were really cool looking. Very cartoon and gangster Noire all at once, with vivid colors and striking landscapes, minimalist as they were.
The enemy variety is fairly limited, but the game isnt long enough for that to really matter. You basically have a couple different types of a few different enemies (zombies, zombie rats, gangsters, and military).
The gameplay was pretty fast and furious, with an assortment of cool weapons that you find along the way and can scroll between on the fly. Ammo isn't generally scarce although you will have some barely eked by with not much ammo left moments. Also, health packs are in the form of cannoli, lol, which Vinnie seems to love and comments on pretty much every time. This alternates between funny and annoying depending on how many times you here it in a short span of time (such as if there is a cannoli at the start of a boss battle which you keep dying in). Speaking of boss battles, there are pretty much three of them, although the last has several parts to it.
What else? Lots of jumping around and blowing stuff up. Some platforming mixed in.
Oh, and the script was strictly followed by the voice actors. They embellished a lot, as is evidenced by the fact that the subtitles wont necessarily match what is being said. It works though. You can tell they had a lot of fun with it, and that is a theme that carries through all the aspects of this game. Just the right length to keep you interested and allow you to appreciate the labor of love which was created here.

Although the music doesn't stand out, the sound design is actually quite effective in an understated way. The little scribbling and scruffling sounds are unsung heroes in creating the illusion that you're sitting in a posh office filling out orders, brooding, scheming...
The gameplay fits well with the theme, despite feeling a little basic. Some additional mechanical depth or challenge modes would have increased the game's longevity -- as it stands, you'll probably be playing nearly optimally after your first full run. The different character routes and options save it from being a one-play-only game, but it relies on unfamiliar content for its full effect, and while it's got a very respectable amount, it's inevitably finite.

I expected text. I expected numbers. I expected complexity and I even expected difficulty. I cannot recommend this game.
The setting is good. The intro-cinematic sets the scene brilliantly and left me eager to dive into the mysterious city of the damned. The graphics are good and the atmosphere is created through them, even if the musical score is somewhat repetitive. Unfortunately, the illusion started to wear thin on the race-selection screen and, after several missions, the complete lack of any form of story was quite apparent. Without a story to speak of, all that remained was the strategy game-play itself and, sadly, it is awful.
The strategy game-play is scuppered by the user interface which is abominable. Text flashes on the screen, containing vital feedback and numbers, and even though the game is a turn-based one, you still miss things because it disappears before you can read it - most noticeably when effects and spells trigger or during your opponent's turn! This is simply inexcusable - a scrollable text console of past dice-roll outcomes and effect numbers would have been more functional than the fleeting semi-transparent U.I. overlays that Mordheim relies upon.
The controls are also pathetic. There are no mouse-and-keyboard controls at all – the left and right mouse buttons act only as pseudo-buttons, keyboard keys as more buttons and, together, these basically replicate a console controller. The mouse pointer, itself, is hardly utilised. Expect console-style inventory management and lists and lists and lists. To select a parry action, for example, you do not click a parry button or press a parry key. Instead, you use Q or E to scroll through all available actions until you get to "parry" and press the single action button. You have to scroll all the way, every time. To find out whether you have an "Aim" action available, you have to scroll through every available action, reading each one, to see if it is in the list. It's hopeless.
Additionally, on the user-interaction side, the concept of a party-based strategy game with over-the-shoulder third-person movement is simply laughable. To see an overview of the situation - vital for any sort of strategic planning - you have to open a map view in which everything is represented symbolically, the height-levels of the terrain are inscrutable and no commands can be issued. To issue commands, you return to the over-the-shoulder perspective in which you can't see much at all and the game controls like a regular third-person game. This is extremely awkward to use, accurately. Why the developers thought this was preferable to a click-to-move, click-to-select scheme with a proper pannable and zoomable camera has only one possible explanation: can't click with a controller!
Mordheim's penultimate failing is its complete lack of respect for the player's time and patience. I appreciate slow games and long games and games that reward a time-investment. I do not appreciate games that consist more of waiting than of playing and, in Mordheim, you spend well over 50% of your play-time staring at the message: "Waiting for opponent's turn." Why can't the opponent's turn be simulated near-instantly, as fast as my CPU can do so, when I can't even see the opponent-character that's acting? Time is also wasted by pointless animation for non-actions - for instance, the silly one that plays every time you select "Overwatch" - something that should be instant because it only has an effect in the next turn, if at all.
Ultimately, however, Morheim fails to answer the most important question of all: "Why should I care?" After playing for a few hours, I realised that I simply didn't have any attachment to my warband or to the goals of the mission or to the gear I had scavenged or to the future of the game - the game simply neglected to make me care... certainly, it didn't make me care enough to see past the abominable U.I. and pathetic controls, or to invest the boredom-time waiting for my opponent's turn.

My "not recommended" review should not be mistaken to mean this is not a good game, if this is the genre you're into. If you thoroughly enjoy strategic RPG, are really into turn based strategy because RTS is just too simplistic, love multiple-week-long campaigns of tabletop gaming, and like action/combat/mass battle movies like 300 but think the battle scenes should be a few dozen hours longer as each blow is calculated for where it should land...  Then this may be for you.
That said, I'm glad it was free for a weekend so I got to try it out.  It's a game I'd rather watch than play, so as a game I wouldn't generally recommend it.  Other reviews will do a better job than I at explaining what this game truly is.  I can simply say it's a bit tedious and unforgiving, from the intro paragraphs of text vaguely explaining what you're getting into (that players of the tabletop series undoubtedly already have embedded in their brains), to the pummelling my characters took while missing their attacks repeatedly, (I can only assume because I didn't know to do something strategically correct, but maybe it's just that hard).  If this is your sort of game, you already know you're going to spend a lot of time getting good at it.

An X-Com esque soldier manager with a bit more depth to the character skills/stats.  Mordheim is a pretty damned unrelenting game.  Expect to lose the first few warbands you create while you're getting familiarized with the interface/UI and the different soldiers you can hire and what their strengths and weaknesses are.  The actual combat has a tendency to be nerve racking as you need to concentrate on both attacking whoever happens to be your enemy that round and collecting wyrdstone or loot from the battlefield so that you can continue to fund your warband.  And in order to collect anything off the battlefield your soldiers need to be standing at the end of the match, as any loot on KO'd units isn't collected.  This mechanic adds a lot of the stress and tension to the combat, as you'll find yourself cussing at the screen trying to find a possible way to save your one footsoldier with a full inventory mid match.  If you're a fan of the Warhammer franchise or turn based strategy games I think its worth checking out.  Just dont expect to master it within an hour.

Utterly, massively, unplayably based on RNG which can and WILL destroy all your best-laid plans for victory.
I would compare it to classic XCom, but that's not an apt comparison. In XCom, your technology gradually improved, allowing even your rookies to have half a chance of hurting what they hit and surviving being flicked by a wet towel. Furthermore, you had a ton of warm bodies to throw into the meat-grinder. In Mordheim however, you have a very small band and your tech in the end-game is going to be largely the same as what you started with. Instead, you're expected to nurture and grow your little warband into a team of elite fighting badasses who can pick their teeth with the business end of a bloodthirster's battleaxe.
The problem with this is that the costs of keeping your team alive and in the fight are astronomical and the odds of being downed in a matter of moments are heavily against you. Your team never survives long enough to become even halfway reliable, without a shower of shooting stars over a field of four-leaf clovers and quadruple-amputee white rabbits! Your enemies will always seem to hit you on a 60%+ chance, while you struggle to land half your blows on 80% or higher. The game is entirely based around chance and simply cannot be beaten by anything less than a professtional Russian Roulette player!
But I suppose if you're the kind of masochist who enjoys having a game feed you your own elbows in literally every encounter, then have fun, you lunatic. Personally though, I'd save your £30 and go punch a biker instead.

Brilliant, if slightly flawed game that will have anybody that is use to ‘board games’ delighted. Yes, things can go wrong, that is the nature of dice rolls. The sheer amount of customization and character development can be a bit overwhelming to those that come to the game blind, and normally I would not recommend this, but watching a ‘You tuber’ play this game before attempting a play though will be of use to mitigate some of the complexity. This may be a bit of flaw of the game, but once these idiocrasies are overcome what lies beneath is deeply tactical (and in the context of the game, i.e. as a turn based board game, extremely pretty). A more forgiving introduction to the game with a deeper tutorial may have helped get this game the recognition it truly deserves, and it truly does deserve more recognition.  This game reminds me of the more unforgiving and harsh games of the past, which in my opinion is a good thing, as a caveat of course your mileage may vary.
Recommended to those of us that are willing to truly roleplay, and accept that things do not always go to plan, we may just have a bad day…. but I also understand that it is truly a niche concept in the world in where the majority expect to ‘win’. Be prepared for frustration, as well as joyous victory’s against the odds, as is the path in all game that use RND For me personally the ‘wins’ out way the frustration. This type of game is what makes the PC game platform truly unique, great stuff, long may the company support such truly unique experiences!

Welcome to the family, son!
After the abysmal reception and sales of Resident Evil 6 in 2012, Capcom changed the course of the beloved horror franchise for the better. Resident Evil 7 is a reboot and the return to form which RE aficionados and horror fans have been waiting for years.
Resident Evil 7 opens up with a man named Ethan who is looking for his long-lost wife, Mia. After 3 years a mysterious video clip emerges in which Mia asks her husband not to look for her. Mia's traces lead to Dulvey, Louisiana where a towering mansion rests deep in the bayou. Once inside, Ethan is captured and forced to fight for his life against the Baker family who would make Leatherface himself feel right at home. Ethan needs to manage dwindling resources, tight inventory management, and keep a keen eye at all times to survive the trip.
The game is played from the first person perspective which works surprisingly well. The gameplay compliments this new addition to the series by giving players more freedom to search every nook and cranny, but also to take in the horribly beautiful visuals. The game looks absolutely gorgeous even on lower settings with a lot of attention to detail and environment. The Baker household looks like someone has actually lived there with shuffled piles of papers and books, refridgerators full of maggots and intestines, and wear and tear on surfaces and furniture. The ambient sound design and voice acting are great, as well, and deserve a special mention in how they serve the purpose of utmost immersion.
During the course of the game Ethan finds your typical RE arsenal of weapons, including handguns, shotguns, a grenade launcher, and a machinegun. On normal difficulty munitions and herbs are plentiful enough. On RE 7 you won't find gold lying around, but instead antique coins which are well hidden. With enough coins, Ethan can upgrade his abilities or acquire better weapons. Weapons themselves cannot be upgraded. After the first playthrough, a set of unlockables is granted, with them a new difficulty setting. There is no mercenaries mode or any other extra content available after the main campaign. The free extra-dlc "Not a Hero" is available to everyone who have purchased the game, but needs to be downloaded separately.
RE 7 hits the rights targets on many things, but certain foibles still exist. Enemy variety is one of such niggles. Sadly, there are only few enemy types in the game, and since this is Resident Evil, one would expect an armada of different types of monsters. The "Molded" which make an appearance early in the game lose their scary-factor quite fast as the game progresses. Another thing is the sheer lenght. For the full asking price, RE 7 is NOT worth the price of admission. The content on the base game is around 8-9 hours (+ Not a Hero). Consider buying the game during a sale.
Resident Evil 7 is an entertaining haunted house simulator, but do consider picking it up during a sale.

Guns, Gore & Cannoli is a a side scrolling action shooter with the welcome addition of zombies. This game was released in April 2015 and has actually got a surprisingly low number of owners given how awesome it is. You play the role of a gangster named Vinnie. You are thrown into Thugtown to find another gangster who has gone missing. You soon find the town has been overrun by zombies as you wade your way through streets, buildings, sewers and urban America.
This is one of the best side scroller games of this type; it's action packed and face paced. Gunplay is a key factor, with about 8 or 9 different weapons which you will eventually find, you have plenty in your arsenal. Whilst working your way through the levels, you will find health packs in the form of Cannoli and tons of ammo to keep you rolling. All of the weapons have their own feel and different uses and none of them feel useless.  There are a couple of jumping type puzzles in the latter levels, but the platforming element of the game is very limited.
The art style in Guns, Gore & Cannoli is gorgeous. The cartoon magazine style look really works well with the setting and story. Not to mention all of the animations are perfectly done too. I often find problems with games that have a generic cartoon look, but this is easily one of the best games to pull it off.
Guns, Gore & Cannoli also has some very nicely recorded voice acting; the American/Italian accent feels like it has just come straight off the streets of New York. Hats off to these devs who put in the extra work for the voice acting, as they could of quite easily just put in text instead, for me it made the game so much more enjoyable.
This game has a very gentle difficulty curve, I only really struggled with the last couple of levels of the game, but was able to push on through once the best weapon was chosen for the scenario. The end boss is also quite challenging too which is a refreshing change compared to other games nowadays.  At some points trying to kill everything on site is not always the best option too; sometimes you just need to run and hope that there is a checkpoint near by because you are just being overrun - keep that in mind.
Length wise, I completed the game in just under three hours on single player. Whilst there is no real need to replay it again, there are also plenty of achievements for you to go back and hunt, and this can be done easily though the Chapter select option. Guns, Gore & Cannoli also has a local co-op feature too, I have yet to try it out but have watched a couple of Youtube videos of it; and it looks so much fun. This is going to be one of those games that I sit down and play with my partner and finish it for a second time.
I had one technical issue whilst playing; sometimes the game would freeze for half a second. This seems to happen especially when reaching save points; but also happens at random points too. This is a known problem with the game and has been reported to the devs. It seems to point to an issue with the fact that the game records lots of stats, such as headshots etc.
In conclusion; Guns, Gore & Cannoli is a really nicely put together game, and one that needs to be experienced by more people than it already has. For the none sale price of £6,99, this is a bargain to pick up especially if you have friends to play with.

A simulation-style VN where you lead the Student Council into solving cases while something brews in the background. Each day you assign your followers to actions that work towards solving a problem. Cases increase in amount and difficulty, new things are uncovered, and you try your best to deal with it. And as a cherry on top, one of your followers is a traitor who will try to work against you. Decent graphics and story, characters and situation were interesting enough for me.
There are four stats used for activities, Social, Intimidation, Observation, and Stealth. Each action you take is a contest between the best stats of the people you send and those of the target. For example, an Investigate action may put your Observation against their Stealth. Whatever the numbers are, both sides add a D20 roll (and whatever item bonuses you use) and if it's 10+ better than the opponent's score it's a success. Otherwise it's 'Too close to call' (sometimes good enough) or an outright failure.
There are other stats that impact the game: Loyalty, Stress, Reputation and Karma. Loyalty serves as stress maximum and is affected by story events. Followers gain stress from doing actions or events. You lose stress by not acting that day (or being forced to take a day off from hitting the max cap). The school loses reputation as you fail missions or do inappropriate things. The student council loses karma as you do underhanded actions or push things harder than necessary. If either reputation or karma hits 0 the game ends.
You're graded on each case on 3 criteria: How many days it took, how much karma you've lost, and how much reputation you've lost. The higher your grade, the more stat points you earn to boost the stats of a follower. When spending stat points it seems best to sharpen their strengths instead of help their weaknesses because if you don't have a high enough stat, you'll have to rely on the D20 roll or be lucky in getting the right items for stat bonuses.
However, it's pretty important to note that not every case can be completed for a perfect grade. Some are false alarms (you let time run out and nothing happens), sometimes the suspect is a big threat (suspension doesn't change their attitude so expulsion is the only answer which stains the school reputation), and some you might not want to do for other reasons. They are randomly generated cases but the solution to each case changes; you figure out what you need to do as you investigate.
There should be a way to more easily scroll through the case files. Either click-and-drag or arrow keys could be nice. Alternatively, it would be nice to 'minimize' the folder or to have an option to use a more compact UI that shows everything on one screen. As it is, you have to click on the arrow buttons.
You ideally want two people with high enough stats for each category. One should be the main person (because there are certain cases you can't solve without especially high stats unless you take time to find multiple items) and the other a backup in case something happens or if you want two similar actions done on the same day.
There are girl-girl love/friendship scenes but you can easily avoid going into it if it's not your thing and skipping text is always an option.
Worth a look if you like games like This is the Police, where you assign people to tasks as you play through the story with something dark looming in the background that may come to light later.

People in here OF COURSE are likely to tell you to buy it. I say now, but i'll say this:
Combat: 9.5/10 Great and the real meat of the game. The chess matches you can have if you actually learn to play the game and build your style accordingly are great. Extremely fun, and rewarding when you win. Creating a school is a very exciting prospect to be sure. The game absolutely excels with regard to combat.
Balance: 8/10 Game is decently balanced in the sense that everyone can get the same moves and everything has a counter. The only downsides are that some styles are easier to use/have greater advantages while many moves have bonus effects which make many of the other moves completely miss them. This can be countered but can also be exploited. Nothing too bad (in my experience) though.
And here's where the problems start to lie.
Conenctivity: 6/10 A few issues besides some lag here and there. I know I'm one of the lucky ones though. De-Syncing leading to death however, has happened frequently.
Game Stability: 3/10 Buggy. Very very buggy. I've ran into areas only to die instantly, which was funny the first 2 times it's happened. I've been trying on gear and have the game literally freeze and have to reset my computer. I've been editing my style and i've found my game locking up because I went to back out and reset my current style because I removed moves from slots.
If I have to restart my computer because your game freezes and it does it more than once, that doesn't sit well with me.
Gear Drops: 2/10 RNG is severly flawed in this game, as you can get starter gear from very significant loot drops which is a brainless design decision if I ever saw one (and they say that may not change). While gear isn't super important, this is worth pointing out.
Story: 2/10 While there isn't much at all, there is some there so regardless of people saying "LOL it's a PvP game" the story is there and you must explore and open up areas so it is a valid aspect of the game to judge.
Immersion/Environment: 7/10 I'm referring to the game sucking you in, not so much getting sucked into the lore. The environment has an enjoyable artstyle and is well-done if a bit simplistic, but that is a strength in this case. Fighting will absorb all of your attention.
Amount of PvE Content: 2/10 This may or may not matter to you and that's fine, but buyer beware: It is very short and very limited. Locking story progression behind PvP is honestly one of the most counter-productive decisions i've ever seen in a game.
Overall: I'd say it's the best 4.5/10 i've ever played (no I didn't average my scores, I just gave it one I felt it deserved, the avg is 4.8125 if you're wondering), because everything outside of combat and the landscape feels lazily done by people who are great at making combat fun, but terrible at overall design and progression choices. I feel they completely ignored player fatigue because it is largely a PvP game. Problem is that it is a PvP centric game with a mandatory PvE component to experience PvP to the fullest and vice-versa
The fact that they baked in some of these horrendous and easy to avoid design choices (mainly PvP to progress story and gear RNG, poor planning for server load as if they expected to fail) is pretty dissapointing.
Verdict: Get it on sale or at least wait till more patches go out, if there's even a playerbase for you to PvP to progress the story/create a school by then.
