Black Closet, the latest from Hanako Games (Long Live the Queen, Magical Diary) is part visual novel, part detective RPG. You play as student council president Elsa Jackson, who is tasked with quashing scandals and keeping up appearances in a sophisticated all-girls' high school. Also on the Council to assist you are your minions: popular flirt Althea, her stubborn and opinionated sister Thaïs, naive newcomer Mallory, unusually competent Vice President Vonne, and antisocial Rowan.
Each week, you receive a couple of cases and have to assign your minions to various tasks, such as questioning witnesses or searching crime scenes. The girls have different stats that will determine their success or failure when executing their assignments. In the background, you also have some overarcing plot cases to solve; one of your minions is a traitor, and you have a limited amount of time to figure out which girl it is and deal with her in one way or another. And then there are the outside enemies that your advisor, Miss Talmage, alludes to, such as a mysterious group called the Red Mask that seem to know lots of things they shouldn't, such as where you sleep.
It's a rather difficult game, difficult enough at times that you can tell it's made by the same developer as Long Live the Queen, but there are tricks to learn that make it easier, and the game also includes an easy mode (which was not included when I initially played waaaaay back in the pre-Steam days, but am happy to play with now). The mysteries are interesting, and your fellow council members are all well-developed. Elsa is somewhat unique in that you get to choose everything she says (from a visual novel list of options, of course), and what you pick will affect her characterization and what your minions think of you, especially if you're on a romance path.
And the art and soundtrack are both beautiful. You actually get two art sets to choose from, the original art set and a new one that was added in later versions of the beta. Truthfully, I prefer the first one and am not sure why the second one gets all the focus in screenshots, but both have their merits. (And you have to earn CGs in both art sets, so you'll be seeing a lot of them either way.)
Upon completing the game you unlock custom minion mode, which lets you create your own council and is rather fun to play around with. You also get the ability to choose who the aforementioned traitor is at the beginning of a normal game, which makes things easy for completionists.
All in all, another excellent Hanako Games title and well worth your money to pick up.

Black Closet is an intriguing game that piqued my interest because in addition to solving mini-mysteries throughout the week you have one major overall case to solve in order to figure out who is sabotaging your Senior year.  The characters are  well-written.  Your minions may seem like game tools at first (you use their special skills to question, harass, stalk, inspect witnesses, suspects and locations), but each one really has a background story with depth.  You can romance them to flesh out their full story line or just stay friends.
There's also a secret society and your college applications to worry about along with your love life.
Like "Long Live the Queen", it did take me several play throughs before I successfully graduated and found out the saboteur.  There can be a lot of things to juggle at one time which can be overwhelming at first. And like LLTQ I was interested in the story line enough to want to replay to get all the CGs and achievements.
There are 2 art modes to choose between.  There are 3 difficulty levels.  After completing the game once you can choose a more customized game or play a shortened version of the game solving cases with random minions.

Black Closet is a game about solving mysteries. But not just one or two mysteries; Dozens of tiny mysteries in each playthrough. Every week new cases hit your desk, and using your wits and skills of your faithful council members you must put together the clues and solve the cases before something terrible happens... or maybe it's all a red herring. Only by solving it will you be able to tell. Along the way you can make friends with your classmates, find romance, and uncover the darkest mysteries of the school.
Quick Look:
+Wide variety of case variants mean it's possible to play an entire game without repeating a case outcome
+Solid writing and diverse and interesting characters
+Easy to understand pass/fail check mechanics
+-Art is usually great, but some assets are a bit rough
Each case is a tiny story within itself with it's own cast of randomly generated charaters. While there are a set number of case types there are a large number of variations in the solutions to each case, so that you canplay an entire game without seeing a case variant repeat. Even once you've managed to learn all the different case variants there is no way to tell which variant youre dealing with until you begin investigating, making each case a race against the clock to solve it.
The cast is diverse and interesting and each route is different from the last. Each of the characters come with their own motivations and desires and the plots never fall into the predictable or cliche. There's hours of gameplay to be found in exploring all the different story paths. Once you've done that, there's also an unlockable freeplay mode where you can create a custom council of your very own and solve cases without the distractions of the plot.
Overall, Hanako has delivered a solid and enjoyable game yet again and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys  tabletop inspired mechanics with a good story and enjoyable writing.

The 1920's setting is extremely fun, and I've always enjoyed shows, movies, and games set in the period. Guns, Gore & Cannoli is no exception.
The narration is done rather well, with comments being thrown about mid fight from the protagonist Vinne; which only adds to the atmosphere of the game and your current situation.
When it comes to weapons you have everything the 1920's was known for; from the world famous Tommy Gun with drum magazine to molotov cocktails and magnum revolvers. Each extremely satisfying to use in their own right. Not every enemy can be effectively taken out with any weapon, and finding the right tool for the job can be messy if you're suddenly overwhelmed by a small horde of face ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
Even so I've been really enjoying the game and would easily recommend it. It starts off well, and keeps the awesome flowing.

When you start playing this game you will find out you only can shoot left or right most game I played in the ‘90 this can be weird in some way when you try to shoot some enemies that will attack you from the sky.

as I cover this game vigorusly!
-------------------------------------------
Pros:
High replayability - it is almost impossible to have two missions that are the same with the randomized maps and variation in the warbands. There are also a ton of different ways you can skill up your warriors making different builds that suit your playstyle.
Exciting gameplay - you will find yourself in situations where you need to make difficult descisions and that descision will mean life or death of your warriors.
Great atmosphere - The city really feels like Mordheim, just beware of traps and daemons ;)
Story missions - if you want to explore the Dramatis Persona's stories you can do that. They are well written with voice acting to accompany them and brings a completely new aspect to the regular missions that you face. Just be aware that these missions are usually tougher and you should prepare accordingly!
------------------------------------
Cons:
I'm not oblivious to the problems that the game has, so here are a couple of things.
Sometimes the AI will act really weird or get stuck on things - which is due to horrible pathing issues. Sometimes this saves the life of your warband and can feel a bit like cheating.
The graphics are not the prettiest - but then again nor is life in Mordheim. I feel that more work could have gone into the models to make them look truly amazing.
PvP is hard to setup with the lack of a matchmaking system - but there are steam groups that are dedicated to bringing people together to setup matches, just like in the TT.
-------------------------------------------
Remember going into this that it is a video game adaptation - not a direct port - of the tabletop game. This means that some things are different, will feel different - but I asure you that this is Mordheim in it's finest form.
Thanks for reading buddy - I hope you will find your way into Mordheim

Spoiler free review
Pros:
-Beautiful atmosphere, everything in the environments are finely detailed and very atmospheric, the re engine does a great job of making RE7 stand out as a true AAA horror game
-While not too complicated, the story has much depth too it and lossely ties in with past resident evil games (I have not played 4, 5, or 6) but I have noticed throughout the game some loose connections with past re titles.
-The main antagonists, the Bakers, are scary, charming, and completely insane, they're what makes this game truly shine among past RE titles, I loved listening to their dialog and seeing how each one had their own specail quirks and personalities and different motivations for wanting to kill you.
-While the first-person perspective is a little jarring to get used to at first, it can really add to the immersion, I found the first person angle to be a nice change from the original formula. (again not counting 4 5 and 6 since I haven't played those).
Cons:
-I'm a little hypocritical for saying this since since I put nearly 50 hours into this game so far, but the overall experience is a bit short. My first playthrough, I was able to finish the game in about 8 hours, and while this doesn't bother me because I love these types of games, for some people this may not be worth the full 60 dollars.
-Besides the Bakers, the enemies (while scary) are a bit bland, there just isn't much veriaty in enemies in this game. Other than the Bakers, there is really only one type of enemy (comparable to the regular zombies of previous games), and while they do come in a few variations, even having something familiar like a cerberus would have been nice instead of the one repetetive bullet fodder enemy.
-The main character Ethan is a little bland, his reactions to some situations are a little akward and simply unrealistic, which can sometimes break the immersion. While I do like that we get to play as a new character, I can't deny that resident evil's past history with corny dialog is kept alive through Ethan.
Conclusion:
Overall great game 9/10. I had a really fun time with it, but I wouldn't say its worth the 60 dollars. I paid 30 for RE7 during the halloween sale, and I gotta say, for about that price it's worth every penny, but for most players, 60 is just a bit too much, I highly reccomend waiting for it to go on sale.

I decided to pick the game up again after refunding my original purchase... They had fixed my main complaints about the game, but it's still buggy. I've had a few instances where I had to force-quit the game and reload due to characters getting stuck in their actions (which becomes a serious problem if the game map won't load up again).
The AI is pretty awful and all too often you'll find them running into a wall every turn.
The game is ironman mode only, so if you can't load a battle, you'll have to suffer a complete defeat just to load the warband. This is usually a game ender as your warband will be injured (which is costly and the units are unusable).
EDIT:
After more playtime, my advice is to stick to XCOM... Better yet, grab the Long War mod for XCOM. This game is a bit too buggy (crashes, corrupted saves, deadlocks) and it's lacking in content. You'll play the same levels and the same enemies, it'll never get better as you progress. Sure, there's the new Witch Hunter warband... but it doesn't feel that different from the other warbands. The levels are all still the same, and you'll play through the variety rather quickly. The most interesting levels are only slightly better, but they put you at a crippling disadvantage.
Most users will have trouble getting beyond the first few levels. The chances of a new player simply failing are high. Even as you progress, your odds don't get much better. A lot of the game boils down to focusing on the most effective strategies, there's no room for "trial and error".
The game relies a little too much on dice rolls to create difficulty. Even if you have a sound strategy, you can easily be foiled by some random numbers. Most everything you do boils down to dice being rolled... Many actions involve multiple dice rolls to succeed.
Basically, the game relies on dice rolls and enhancements to the opposing team to create a sense of difficulty. Unfortunately, this ends up being frustrating and tedious.

Get it for the combat.
The stance system takes some getting used to, but it creates a flow that's completely different from any other fighter or action game out there. There's a lot of move properties - speed, reach, and thrust vs sweeping motions really matter because the hitboxes are accurate and they mostly avoided iframes as a defensive mechanism, and on top of that you get moves that dodge high/low/thrust, super armor for 1 hit, double-hits, break super armor, break guard/absorb...and that's without getting to what stances it can start in and what stance it'll end in. Stance changing is huge because it dictates what moves you can chain together, but also lets you create all sorts of mid-combo mixups because your alternate attack changes with the temporary stance changes in your combo strings. Games pay lip service to "endless combinations" a lot, but with Absolver, it's not such an exaggeration.
I've already gotten at least 7 hours out of the PvE playing offline up to beating the "final boss" - 10 or more if you count the hours I sank into messing with different styles before I settled on my main. There's still more to do - finding higher level NPCs online for more moves, unlocking the 4th style - and there's still a ton to learn and improve in PvP, but it's a decent benchmark.
My playtime might be longer than others' since I took the time to learn every new move I encountered. The "sparring" against NPCs to learn moves is a bit of a grind, but it didn't feel like an artificial time-sink to me. It encourages you to practice observing combo strings and timing your special defense, which is key to beating bosses and players alike - and it teaches you a thing or two about what works against that new move and what doesn't. The exp comes in real quick once you can defend against it reliably. And all that defense practice really came in handy when I tried out PvP.
PvP has been a lot of fun so far. Observing and learning your opponent's deck, their habits, and using the cards in your deck to open them up. You can get pummeled for 2/3 lives, then come back and beat them 3 times for the win once it all clicks. And you can rematch as many times as you both want - rematches are well worth it, since it gives both players more time to keep adapting to each other's approaches, and that can easily change the outcome in this game.
As an aside, the launch server issues seem to have been fixed already. It's the weekend but I still connected to the servers quickly and played a whole bunch of PvP matches and ran around in PvE a bit without any noticeable lag issues. Honestly, I enjoyed the offline PvE more than online PvE since you can grind moves without interruptions and enemies have less of a tendency to attack in groups.
All in all, I can strongly recommend Absolver if you enjoy games for good combat. The game can be rough around the edges in terms of QoL features and the raw volume of PvE content, but that's because they really put everything into the combat, and it shows. Personally, I enjoyed the character customization and exploration too (the areas are dynamic and varied, and some are quite beautiful), but the main selling point is still going to be the core combat.

After a short time one can start to combine the different weapons, wings and cases of the plane, this adds another layer to the game. I'm looking foreward to be able to figure out more different playstyles in the future.
However, it's still an Early Access game and should be treated as such. The controls in the workshop-menu are klonky, and here and there are little bugs. Also the progress could be made more visible by changing the visual representation of the different Layers more intense. The D-Pad Down to land is quite hard to find out, even with the small banner telling to press it when you're almost dead (in that situation I'm not reading anything and am just trying to survive ;-)). But what in my opinion needs changing the most, is the missing Fog. If you reach the upper Layers it's getting hard to read the screen because of the colors and objects of the lower layers which make identifying enemies really hard, a Fog on the lower layers would fix that quiet easy.
All in all AIRHEART is a good game and fun to play. I can totally recommend it.

I do not need to write this.  We all know this game is terrible and that the only reason you own it is for trading cards.  This review is just an expelling of demons I acquired while playing it for the easy achievements.  If anything, I was entertained for the first 5 minutes just from sheer awe and shock of what I was seeing.
I have nearly 7 hours of game play, but almost all of it was from a failed card idle.  I got this game from a BundleStars $2 bundle.
-Christmas Themed Music:  I have no idea why this is here.  You will hear various holiday songs done in the style of nightcore and what I can only ignorantly describe as “happy EDM”.  If you check out the developers YouTube channel, shown during every launch of the game, you will see he is quite the anime dweeb.  While that explains the genre… I still don’t get the Christmas music?  Nothing else about this game seems Christmas themed. The release date isn’t even close to December, and I could make something like this from a Blender tutorial in a few hours at the most.
-Graphics:  Ugly as sin.  All objects are made of fundamental 3D objects like cylinders and spheres.  Lighting effects are entirely 2D, and can be noticed as such when the music cuts out, more info on that in Audio.  I can’t really tell the perspective of whats happening on screen.  I want to imagine the ball is climbing a tower, but the perspective of the camera seems to suggest its just a flat cylinder.
-Audio: The aforementioned holiday songs and a single collision sound is all there is.  No menu sounds, no distinct sounds between hitting an obstacle and collecting a power up.  The music will randomly cut out and require a restart to come back.  The music has a visualizer effect on the textures/lighting, but does nothing to any actual game play.  You can add your own music, so I assume this is just a weird music visualizer project gone terribly wrong.  If for some god forsaken reason you want to go for a high score, you should load a steady house song that lasts for a long time.  No audio = darkness; it can make it difficult to see upcoming hazards as the game speeds up.
-Controls: I cannot fathom how you can ♥♥♥♥ this up so bad.. the game is just a simple infinite runner where the only dodging directions are left and right.  However, your ball will randomly continue in the direction you left it, while other times coming to a complete stop.  While grinding out 90 deaths for the last achievement(Play/Die 100 times), I tried my best to find a logical game mechanic or explanation for why it did this, but came up with nothing.  Best guess I can make is the game is♥♥♥♥♥♥and the developer didn’t care.  You can also jump, but…
Gameplay: Its not worth it.  There are no obstacles which you can gain enough height to jump over.  You sometimes have to jump to reach power ups, but said power ups will usually end up getting you hit if you try going for them.  Ever.  They aren’t even worth anything.  One is a healing kit that takes about 3 kits to heal from one hit(3 hits will kill you).  The other is a slow down which will keep you from speeding up constantly.  Neither of these will make too big of an impact on your score, as the game is balls easy anyway.  The obstacles hitboxes are bigger than the objects themselves, but power ups seemingly have the opposite problem of the hitboxes being smaller than they appear.
-Side Note: As you can tell by screenshots and the trailer, this game is headache inducing levels of bright flashing colors.  But for something spectacularly awful; anytime you hit an obstacle while moving that ends up killing you, the players ball will sometimes spin around the tube faster than the player can ever make it move.  Seriously, I’ve tried, I cannot manage to make the ball spin that fast without dying.  The only reason its worth mentioning is because it is especially nauseating and hard to look at.
So those of you who read this, you are probably wondering; “Why did you write this all out?  Its obviously♥♥♥♥♥♥ and we all know this is a trading card shame.  Do you not have a life?”
To the last question, writing about garbage is a hobby, but its a very small part of my existence.  Secondly, I just want to stress something here. this review might come off as nit-picky for something so plainly bad, but look at it the other way..
There is not a single good thing I could say about this game.  There is nothing I could pick out, by itself, and say was even remotely okay.  Don’t buy this for cards.  They are nearly worthless, just go form the badge from market sales.  Do not buy this for achievements.  Not even achievement hunters will care.

Steam does well enough with the game description so, here is a biased review.
DUNGEONS OF CHAOS
The pros:
Don`t let the primitive graphics fool you, the mood is quite well set and very efficient. There are some places where I literally stopped and just went Whoa...
The music, for the most part, delivers adequately. The chaos rift music is just epic.
You can build the party you want. Yes, you can be uber, yes you can gimp yourself. You can spend HOURS rolling your stats (I LOVE doing that), you can make a tree hugging barbarian, an electric monk, heck, your rogue can even be a presidential candidate. (Don't ask, just do it). Speaking of Rogues, there are NO necessary classes in the game, there are enough classes and skills to allow you to go around just any and every problem, providing you have enough craft and imagination.

The NPC dialogue is rich, varied and entertaining. The occasional humor is just perfect. The quests are fun. The goats give awesome advice. (No they don't, but one can wish...)
LEGIONS of equipment items to keep you busy outfitting your party. Lost of inventory slots by character. This is not your usual "One Weapon, One armor, One accessory" game.  Be prepared to manage LOTS of AWESOME gear.  From your Inferior Broken Warhammer of Sluggishness to your Infinitely Glorious Moonsword of Goblin Displacement, it's ALL there.
Interesting classes that have clearly defined strengths and weaknesses. Mages have tons of spells.  Melees have fun skills to use. Rangers summon wolves, barbarians rage and druids all come with their secret stash of... well, we're not allowed to tell you if you don't have the game yet.
A Facebook community that is alive, helpful, thriving and generally fun to be around. Yes, with a game like this, this is a HUGE perk. We even have the occasional troll.  (In the game, silly...)
A game dev that participates to this community, who talks to the players, who listens to them and who implements many good idea given. (And tell you if your idea sucks)
The achievement system offers some very interesting challenges and adds insane replay value. And by insane replay value, I mean people going "VOLKER WHY DID YOU MAKE THIS CHALLENGE GAWD DAMMIT IT'S JUST IMPOSSIBLE ARRRGH!!!" *Five days go by* "Well I did it, was fun! Can't wait for the next one!"
Lots of configuration options! 9 pages of choices that allow you to customize your game experience in just out any way you like.  Like an auto run system that I discovered after 100 hours of play.  Don't judge me.
The cons:
Though some areas are exciting to visit, exploration often means plodding through extremely vast and empty landscapes.  No, caves don't have to be filled to the brim with vampire lords to be interesting, four or five of them are enough, but if I didn't need three different methods of mass transit to reach every one of them, it would be just as awesome.
The difficulty system can get confusing as it not only influences combat difficulty, it influences experience obtained from battles (which is fine, really),  leveling bonuses (this gets annoying), item drop chances but not their quality (a confusing point but you get used to it).  The fact is you can change the difficulty as much and as often as you like so it "makes sense" to take the lowest difficulty possible when you level your characters to get the best bonuses but you'll also want to crank it up when fighting a monster that has a chance to drop nice items.  All in all, it quickly becomes an annoying process. You don't HAVE to do it, but let's face it, most people who play a game like Dungeons of Chaos love to play with their numbers. (It's not innuendo, GAWSH get your mind out of the gutter!)
The many easy battles VS the auto-battle system.  In some old RPGS like say, Might and Magic 4-5-6 and up, You faced just as many monsters but they were in your face and just a few clicks was all you needed to get it done. One click = one mace to the face.  Easy.  In Dungeons of Chaos, EVERY battle plays out on a rather large combat screen and in EVERY battle, you have to manually move your melees all the way to the mobs unless you have enough offensive casting to do it remotely. Which you should. Because wizards are awesome and nothing says you mean business like A FIREBALL TO THE FACE. This is where the AUTO BATTLE shines. The auto-battle system is really well done for your typical trash mob encounter. Set it to max speed and see your warrior and your barbarian ZIP through ¾ of the distance between you and your enemies before your mage explodes them anyways.  The auto-battle system is a blessing when dealing with the legions of easy things and in some of the dungeons, legions IS what you will encounter.  But if you abuse it, your daily skills will never go up and you'll never understand how to really use your characters when manually playing them against a hard boss.
Conclusion: If you do not have this game, you are doing something wrong with your life.

Railroad Tycoon 3 is an excellent railroading business sim that has rock-solid gameplay and aging 3D graphics.  This is a classic game that could have easily been a game-of-the-year candidate at the time had the designers not made a few flawed decisions.  That said I find myself actually enjoying it more than Railroad Tycoon 2 because it corrects some of its predecessor's mistakes and is without doubt one of the best business simulations ever made.
Major improvements
Some features the designers added were sorely missing in its predecessor.  You can now mass replace locomotives via a set of conditions or just replace one.  This is a huge time and hassle saver versus RRT2 when you're dealing with hundreds of trains.  The game adds a critical "un-do" button to track-laying, saving you from mistakes that would have ruined a game in RRT2.  It also lets you build overpasses and tunnels, both of which were sorely missing in its predecessor.  The only aggravation with track-laying is it is sometimes awkward to place tracks and it's far harder to lay parallel tracks like you could in its predecessor.  The game also does a far better job with running your rail empire by automatically prioritizing which trains stop and which proceed by whichever has the higher value cargo, negating the need to micro-manage train priorities for hundreds of trains.  Thanks to this feature along with the addition of larger maps, trains, tunnels, overpasses and easy mass locomotive replacement, you don't have to micromange to build larger rail empires with far less congestion.  However if you do want to micro-manage, this is made easier by the much-improved record-keeping this game offers.
Railroad Tycoon 3's biggest improvement is its economics system.  Passenger and freight revenue is no longer driven by distance but by the laws of supply and demand, which makes success in this game harder but more satisfying.  No longer can you have all of the passengers picked up in New York City sent to to Chicago for fortunes.  Instead only a portion of the passengers will want to travel there, and prices they are willing to pay will vary with demand and your supply of trains.  Initial success instead depends on building a hub-and-spoke network of rails and building from there.  Being able to build industry instead of just buying it also makes that part of the game more rewarding.  Like in RRT2, you can play in the stock market as an individual or both the stock market and bond market as your railroad company.  One fun aspect to this game is you sometimes don't even have to build a train empire to make money.
Mixed Changes
Managing carloads is an area where the game both improves and regresses at the same time.  This game's carload management system will automatically select the most profitable carloads to haul, which cuts a lot of micro-management.  You can set it to haul both freight and passengers/mail, freight only or passengers/mail only, or even set it to haul specific carloads.  However when setting up a multi-city route, you can't keep a load on the train until there's demand at a stop for it like in its predecessor.  Nor can you haul unprofitable loads to a station and store them them until another train comes along.  However the system will no longer haul empty carloads--instead the worst that will happen is you'll haul a half carload of passengers or freight when demand is low.  Given its improvements and regressions it's debatable as to whether RRT3 or RRT2 has the better system for managing cargo and routing.
Negatives
The AI in this game are somehow less competent at running a train network than in its predecessor.  The only things the AI are good at is playing the stock market and buying industry.  One thing this game is sorely lacking are the managers from RRT2, whose selection could make or break rail empires based on their positive and negative attributes.  You can also no longer build additional properties at your stations like roundhouses and hotels.  This is most annoying at major hubs, where train loading and unloading can no longer be sped up by building telegraph or telephone lines.  The game designers also made the decision to require trains to stop for maintenance as well as water/sand at 2 different buildings on the track, which while partially adding accuracy (for steam engines) also adds a lot of unnecessary congestion.  Although almost any system can handle this game with ease now, that's only when your rail empire has only a couple hundred locomotives running.  Be warned that building a rail empire with 500+ locomotives will slow lesser systems down to a crawl with this game!
I absolutely recommend this classic game to anyone who enjoys business sims or other Railroad Tycoon games despite a few blemishes.  If however you're looking for a simplistic train game, you're likely better off playing Railroad Tycoon 2.

For the rest of us, it's perhaps enjoyable enough to play a level or two at a time, before finding something decidedly more engaging to do with our evening and/or lives. A sincere effort on the behalf of the devs, just the same.
I shouldn't complain, really. If I'd grown up in a different era, it might've been ME who found himself traversing a deadly mine, rather than a cute robot avatar. We really are a privileged, smarmy pack of lazy brats, aren't we? "Oh, woe is me, this video game isn't QUITE as good as some of the fifty other games I've forced myself to play in the past six months..."
TRY SWEEPING OUT A CHIMNEY SOME TIME, YOU SPOILED LITTLE TURD!!

Bad End Review
[Spoiler-Free]
If you want to spend an easy evening with a quick playthrough of a game, this is an excellent choice.  There's not much I can say in a review without spoiling it as it's all story-based.  Basically there's a guy in high school who gets hold of a game that's been making the rounds online for its infamous ability to kill its players (the "if you die in the game you die for real" cliche).  So it's a game about a game that's within this game.  Got that?
While you, through your own character, play this game, there are multiple bad endings.  These basically serve as the achievements.  After making the right choices through trail and error you will eventually find the one true ending which is cannon to the plot.  One good feature is that the game autosaves right before you make your wrong choice, so you don't need to worry about saving after each dialoge screen.
Characters are the typical "I swear I'm a normal Japanese student who ponderously eats lunch on the roof" type.  Nothing you haven't seen before.  In fact the whole concept seems outdated, even for the two years ago that it was released.  If you just want some quick achievements, it'll satisfy you.  The art has the "fake anime" look... I'm not saying it looks bad, but you can just tell from the colors and shading that it's not professional anime (particulary with facial features, eyes overlapping hair and clothing is too detailed).  This is normally where I'd conclude it wasn't from an actual Japanese developer, but you have the option to play in Japanese, and the credits display Japanese names so I guess I'm wrong.
I'm done spilling my thoughts about this game.  If you have any interest you'll probably like it.

BAD END isn’t absolutely awful and for its price it isn’t an eyesore in your library but there are far better choices out there. However if you care about achievements, this should be an easy way to get another 100%.
+ Short
+ Fascinating premise
+ ‘Skip’ works flawlessly
- Dumb protagonist
-  Cliche, unoriginal twists
☆☆☆☆☆☆☆★★★
3/10 - Bad
This visual novel simply didn’t live up to the interesting premise it set up so I’m forced to give a bad rating to BAD END. While it wasn’t completely awful to sit through, there simply isn’t anything too engaging or memorable about the whole experience.
The protagonist is so unrelatably idiotic in getting himself into the mess that it’s just hard to care about him surviving through all of it and it becomes more fun to see how many ways is there for him to die.
It needs to be mentioned that the player is presented with choices to make the protagonist less dumb but these bring the story to an end and thus are not correct choices. It is understandable that with a premise like this there needs to be something driving the protagonist to go through with it, but in this case it feels too feeble of a reason what is given to work here.
The story offers no surprises and the supposed big twist is painfully obvious. The characters are uninteresting and it feels strange that some seem to have been inserted just to create an illusion of bigger cast.
On a more positive side, the art is okay and BAD END plays well, it’s very easy to go through it multiple times since the ‘Skip’ function makes it effortless. There are several choices and they (for the most part) lead to different types of outcomes, but it seems like there should’ve been more “real” endings rather than just a ton of dead ends. But with a name like BAD END, what else would I expect?

Albert and Otto: The Adventure Begins is a dark puzzle platformer that reminds me of Limbo with it's graphics style, and linear story line.
You play as Albert. You are armed with a gun, and a stuffed rabbit, named Otto. While Otto is on you, you have special abilities like levitate, double jump, and a shock. You can also place Otto down, and use the abilities remotely to help solve your way through the levels. Both Albert and Otto must survive and stay together to progress.
I prefer the puzzle aspects over the timing platformer type of gameplay, but it was still an enjoyable game, and a great start to the series. I died quite a bit on a few levels, so the game took me about 3 hours to complete, but I can't see replaying it unless you want achievements.

The gameplay itself is pretty fun and does a decent job capturing the feel of a tabletop game for the most part. Unfortunately it's bogged down by a grind oriented campaign that has you doing the same thing over and over and over. There are a few different scenarios, but that merely changes how you deploy, not the objective which is to eliminate or route the opposing team. Story missions change it up a bit, but not enough to make it feel fresh. And while there is a pvp component that ought to be fun, it's just more of the same. It lacks the fun social element of a tabletop experience. Also playing the pvp mode that enables injuries and looting is a huge risk considering the intensive grind that goes into getting decent units, and the safe mode is without risk or reason to play, though you may learn a trick or two.
I like the hardcore element, but leveling up is far too arduous. I think the most frustrating element is that you can rarely complete secondary objectives for their xp boost because the enemy team routes and essentially ends the round. Thus any unclaimed salvage, unclaimed loot, and unclaimed wyrdstone dissapears. Sure you get a few bones for a victory, but it's pitance in comparison. Furthermore this makes no sense. If they ran away, why not let me get everything? What's stopping me? Why make me game the system and spend three hours emptying a map only to realize that doing so is insane and a total bore. Fixing this issue alone might go a long way towards making the game feel less like a grind.
The game needs some fresh ideas and a strong multiplayer component if it wants to have any real staying power, right now it's one of those titles you buy on sale, play for a week or two and then forget about. It's a real shame too because this game does have potential. The underlying mechanics are sound for the most part, but everything built off of them needs to be reconsidered.
Bottom line: If you are interested in this title and enjoy turn based gameplay then snag it next time it drops below $20. However you'll most likely regret spending anything more than that.

I really wanted to like this game, and I am sure it is great if you are willing to invest a lot of time into learning it. Unfortunately, the difficulty level - at least for noobs with no experience of the TT game - is insane. Now for some people, that will be the appeal, and I say good luck to them. To other people - count me among them - if a game is too difficult, especially when starting out, it's a massive turn-off. I want to feel like I am progressing and learning the game while also feeling like I have a chance to win. With Mordheim, I never once felt like there was a chance that I was going to win a battle (I got totally wiped out each time I tried), and never once did I feel in control over the way things were going.
I am sure that you
influcence events once you have got into the swing of things and learn how to exploit the AI's deficiencies. The question you need to ask yourself is: are you ever going to get to that point in the game? If you want ironman challenge from the start, and don't mind starting a new game every half an hour or so, then ignore this review and buy the game if it sounds like your thing. If you prefer a gradual progression and the ability to ramp up the difficulty later once you have a grasp of the basic mechanics, steer well clear. Chances are high that you will ragequit and not come back.
The reason I asked for a refund is not because I hate difficult games, or have an issue with no save-scumming and permadeath (I've been playing nethack et al since before most of you were born), or don't like complex games. I do, but I like them to draw me in and give me the feeling of progression and an ability to influence events. Mordheim failed to do either of those for me. It ticks all the boxes for me, but just didn't click.
So this thumbs down isn't so much a "OMFG this game S|_|XX0R" but a warning to other players who may be on the fence about whether to purchase it or not. You want to be sure that this is really your cup of tea. I also appreciate that with <2 hours of playtime, my opinion is hardly well formed, but that's the cut off period for steam refunds and I don't feel like I am going to come back to this one.

Only have time for a short session tonight and since there isn't much feedback for the game yet I thought I should give a quick impression. (I ended up going back to the game for another hour and a half)
The game is a very charming twin stick shooter. I keep getting too greedy and dying instead of retreating so I haven't progressed past the third level (now fourth), but I was having fun the whole time.
Game play is basically flying around gathering flying fish for oil and blowing up enemy planes and gathering crafting items to build up your plane, the number of plane parts is still pretty shallow but it just entered early access. Flying up to a new level whenever you feel like you are ready for a difficulty jump. You can return to base with a diving mechanic to return with your loot. If you are shot down you have a chance to try to guide your burning plane back to your landing pad, it takes a bit of practice. If you do the crash landing you lose all of your currently equiped plane parts and all the loot you are carrying, if you fail the landing you need to start a new game.
There are a couple control rough edges that I am sure will be cleaned up soon. Keyboard/Mouse control with 2 monitors led me to clicking outside the game area causing the game to lose focus. With the controller the starting gun is single shot and fire is bound to the right trigger, I found it quite hard to spam fire since you must fully release to fire again. The other guns I tried all had auto fire, but I didn't get to try them all yet. Both problems are easily fixable.
I am guilty of playing alot of games once and then letting them rot in my library but I will definately return to this one when I want some light action. Pretty sure this will be a "Just one more try" game when I should be going to bed. (It already happened, see above. :) I am looking forward to where further development heads.

A Terrifyingly Fun Experience
WARNING: This article contains spoilers for Resident Evil 7 (sort of).
After over 7 years, I finally played a new Resident Evil game I enjoyed, Resident Evil 7. I can’t really make any comment that hasn’t been made before; the game goes back to its roots with survival horror instead of action, and the first person perspective is a significant change but it works really well. What I can comment on is my own experience playing the game.
First thing first, I played the game on Easy difficulty and have no plans on playing it on Normal or Madhouse. The reason I chose this was because I wanted to enjoy the game for its atmosphere rather than have it be a frustrating challenge that I give up on half way through. I felt very uneasy during the first half of the game, and could only play for 15-20 minutes at a time. After each iteration I had to take a break for at least 2 hours, which meant that I usually played it once a night (on weeknights). The game starts you off with limited ammo, so I only took a shot when it was absolutely necessary. Several reviews I read suggested that in order to preserve ammo it might be better to shoot the Molded in the leg and run, but I preferred to take them on one at a time and defensively stab them to death. This allowed me to roam the cleared areas freely, thanks to no re-spawns. I didn’t even use the Chem Fluids, herbs, and gunpowder until I was completely out of handgun bullets or First Aid Meds. Half way through the game I found that I was doing pretty good on resources, and started to get a bit freer with them. However, I rarely used the Flamethrower and the Grenade Launcher. When I picked up the shotgun I didn’t feel as helpless anymore and thus the game was less unsettling. The shotgun has been my favourite weapon in all of the previous Resident Evil games I played. By the time I got near the end game, I had a lot of resources stashed in the trunk. I could have been fairly liberal with the resources throughout the whole game. I never fired the magnum, I wish I did.
The one place I felt that the game was lacking was regarding the puzzles. The previous Resident Evil games had some interesting puzzles, but there were only the shadow puzzles here, which were fairly easy to solve.
The scariest part of the game was the Grandma. She kept showing up in random places, and always watching you. She doesn’t say anything, she doesn’t move, but she keeps showing up where you have to go.
All in all, I enjoyed this game very much. I beat the game in a little over 8 hours so it felt pretty short, however it is still a complete game. I’m happy I played through it.

Resident Evil 7 is a fantastic throwback to the survival horror of RE1 and RE2. It has the soul of those games with the exterior of a modern AAA title. The shift to first-person perspective is brilliantly executed, accentuating the tension and abject terror of the game as well as its very tight gunplay. The various locales are nicely detailed and thick in atmosphere – this game just exudes anxiety, and item management & ammo conservation add to the survival horror feel. There are many cinematic set pieces that would feel right at home in a great horror film, and despite a relatively weak third act, RE7 is well-written, featuring memorable characters and a story shrouded in dark mystery and moody intrigue. While it often borrows a little too much from previous Resident Evil titles (two sections in particular are very similar in layout to RE1’s mansion and RE5’s boat), it separates itself from them with its largely self-contained story, variety of cinematic influences (including Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Deliverance, Ringu, Saw, and The Blair Witch Project), and new first-person POV and gameplay mechanics. I was skeptical about Capcom’s ability to pull off a good sequel to the abysmal RE6, but they really surprised me – this is a true Resident Evil game for the current generation. One of my favorite games of the year and worth picking up not only for the excellent, highly replayable campaign but for the free Not A Hero DLC which takes place after the events of the main game and ties it into the Resident Evil universe. What is Dungeons of Chaos? It is one man's dream about the question what would a game play like if it was a mixture of Ultima, Wizardry and throwing in the Birth signs or feats of something like Daggerfall or Skyrim. Now this was a iPad game first so the graphics are old school, but this really fits for the type of game DoC aspires to be.
You have several starter classes and these classes can be upgraded to advanced classes. You barbarian can master his rage and become a beserker. Your puny mage can become a wizard or even an archmage etc. Let's say you choose an intellect birth feat. Well, your barbarian wouldn't benefit much but it would make all the difference in the world for your mage! Give that Barbarian a birth feat that matches his class. Make him have Troll blood and he'll regenerate hit points and have tons of them too.
Quests are pretty straight forward. You'll talk to town members and they'll send you to clear out the monsters close by. They're reward you with goodies, perhaps a nice axe for the Barbarian or a cool spell book for the Mage. Maybe they'll have a nice dagger for your rogue/assassin.
There are dozens of possible build options and even more once you start unlocking achievements. This game truly rewards unlocking the achievements because it opens up new styles of play for new game+ modes. You may start out as just a rat slayer but you may achieve Dragon Lord status if you stick with it.
My only negative would be the lack of save game options. You can tell this is a mobile port. You have one save for each party though you can make 4 backups. It is not user friendly at all, so I'd suggest manually backing up your save directory every so often.
Note that I have not finished the game. This is just a review of the steam version from my 30 hours played. I still have a long, fun way to go to reach the end.

I originally bought this game for Android, and happily bought it again when it came out on Steam, it really is that good. This is a glorious reminder of the days when games couldn't hide behind shiny graphics, but instead were forced to actually create interesting gameplay and deep mechanics. Meaning, if you're the type that just HAS to have great, or even good, graphics, you can keep scrolling, this game wasn't made for you. However! If you're the sort who can remember the classic RPG's of the 80's and early 90's, and remembers them fondly, then this game IS made specifically for you!
Deep class/skill system, certain character creation options unlocked by achievements, enough variety of equipment to sift thru to do a remake of Diablo, tons of little hidden surprises to reward exploring the vast world, a very well implemented spell system...to name a few of this game's many charms. All presented without any of the handholding that has become so endemic in modern games. A huge part of the fun is discovering how things work for yourself, and developing a strategy from your own hard won understanding of game mechanics. All done by a lone...and very attentive and dedicated...developer. Community suggested features are often added within days if they fit the vision of the game. This is old school RPG at its absolute finest!
Seriously, if you're considering buying it, go for it. It would be a bargain at twice the price. This is truly a gem of gaming that deserves far more attention! Give it a try, you got nothing to lose...aside from the hours and hours of your free time that this old school RPG crown jewel will soak up!

I REALLY wanted to like this game, and for periods I would have quite a bit of fun with it.  It mixes several things I really like: (1) Turn-based combat; (2) good graphics; and (3) a 3D Map.  But I'm about to uninstall.
My primary issue is COMBAT:
- You want victories to be as clean as possible, meaning that none of your troops get put out of action (lose all their HP).  That's fine, but the "strategy" required to avoid such ruins the game.
- The RNG of whether you (or an enemy) hits or misses a swing is far too important.  I don't mind an unforgiving game (where its very possible to lose characters or die) but when the unforgiving element is tied heavily to RNG, that's a problem.
- The enemy often has more (or stronger) troops that you do.  They will swarm on you really quickly once they find you.  So if you go out and try to collect loot on the map (fun) you expose your troops to getting pounced upon and dying (not fun).  The best tactic is often to ignore loot and set up a very defensive position and simply wait until the enemy finds you (not fun).
- Some maps force your units to be split apart from each other, either randomly or by choice.  In any event, its quite frequent for some of your troops to be separated near an enemy.  Once they jump on you, you can't really effectively run away.
I think those are enough points to give you my general impression.

Early review, I think this is worthwhile at this point as I believe those who purchase this game should be aware that the learning curve just to get started is very steep.  If you are looking for a game you can just drop right in and play, stop, drop and roll on by, this is not the game you are looking for.  The tutorial system is a mess; they would benefit greatly by creating the tutorial as a chain rather than pick a topic and jump in.  This is one of those games that is not hard to play, but it is difficult to master.
As for the play of the game it took a few tries to actually win the first mission without losing my entire Warband, there is no lead in to the Campaign, which gives you a few light and fluffy engagements to win. It is kill or be killed.  You learn very quickly that if you separate a member of a Warband the AI is relentless and will gang up quickly and single a member out.  But the good news is that tactic works for you as well.  You can also exploit the environment to some extent with LOS, and Height advantages.
Game play is not to bad once you get over the initial OMG what the heck am I doing here.  As I stated before took me three tries before I won a match and only lost one instead of the entire band.  Losses in this game are just that, a member of your Warband dies, he is dead.  He may not die, and in one case he lost a limb, which may or may not be causation to be fired, but you still pay his healthcare.
There are game guides out there, I am just looking at those know, as I think a few tries and you can start to put together some questions on the mechanics.  This genre is specific to either the Warhammer crowd, or for those who like very micro managed man to man tactical games.  Was the game worth the money, that remains to be seen, but I will be playing it again as I like this type of game, though would have liked it a whole lot more with an easy lead in to teach the game mechanics.

I pre-ordered Absolver after finding it in my steam queue a while back but I didn't follow it exclusively and wasn't aware of any pre-launch hype. I was excited for the game but didn't concern myself with expectations. I came back to write this after seeing that it's recieved mixed reviews because I'm the type that would normally pass over a game with mixed reviews and Absolver is certainly not a game I would want to have missed.
First, the pros:
-An incredible world design with a beautiful artstyle that is a breath of fresh air. (The world isn't large and it's paths are fairly linear but it is interconnected in a way that it feels like a maze when you first enter,)
-Amazing combat. I won't go into detail as there are numerous and more well-versed reviews and videos demonstrating this. Complex, fluid, and intuitive.
The cons:
-Unstable servers on launch. While I've only had a dozen or so execeptionally laggy games, one of the biggest issues players have right now seems to be the lag. The devs are working on it (and it has improved since launch day) but it still needs to be mentioned.
-A lack of PvE. This isn't a con for some, and this isn't a con for me, but if you're not looking for a competitive Player versus Player game, then Absolver might not be for you. PvP is required and it is the core of the gameplay. PvE is present but it's more like a tutorial than anything else. It took me 2-3 hours to complete after I got the hang of things but you will spend a moderate amount of time move grinding.
Ultimately Absolver is a PvP game and I feel like a lot of people wanted to be a martial badass but didn't want to fight other players, hence some of the negative reviews. Heck, even I was too timid to start fighting others for the first two days but after I finally did I haven't been able to put the game down. Of course, as is with pvp there are ways to cheese other players but the majority of gameplay is skill based. (Cheesing essentially boils down to if you fight in a map with ledges or not- all other types of spamming or moves have their own way of being punished once you know what you're doing.)
The last thing I want to mention is that the fighting might make you really mad. I rarely if not ever find myself raging in a pvp game, but I've had moments in this game where I've been quite frustrated, whether it be from an annoying opponent or my own lack of skill.
Needless to say, Absolver is a PvP game and you need to go into it with a PvP mentality. If you are this type of player, then more likely than not you will find Absolver to be an incredible game.

An outstanding game. Unlike any game I've played, while sharing the best attributes from many of my favorites- and innovating by mixing several genres together with an unprecidented, almost overwhelmingly complex-yet fluid combat system that asks you to make full use of your ability to react, predict, decieve as well as strategize before, during, and after every fight.
Absolver is understandably confusing, and misunderstood judging by reviews I've seen, as coming in fresh, when the credits roll, many feel mislead or shortchanged, and too often 'lack of content' means length of story. The short story mode is indeed not long, but that is by design, because that is only a fraction of what Absolver's bigger picture is. If you are coming in for the story, and not the multiplayer, this may not be for you. If you want an endlessly challenging multiplayer experience post-ascension quest from 'Prospect' to 'Absolver', you'll find that in one-on-one, 3v3, or roaming the open world with the omnipresence of others, making for threat-or-alliance circumstances and unique encounters, this game delivers. No, you won't spend more than ten hours in the story mode but frankly by no means is that a negative if you have the willingness to understand Absolver in it's entirety, and the endless nature of what the game's PVP focus asks from you and rewards you with in turn. When you 'beat the game', congratulations, you've only begun Absolver. When the credits roll, you've basically earned your yellow belt. More on that below.
First, though, it should be noted for prospective buyers that Absolver is in a big way an endurance test and an exercise in revision and redevelopment. For those who have the patience to learn from losing, which is the only absolute in Absolver, will find themselves perpetually rewarded for their efforts to experiment, re-learn, and try again.
With 96+ hard-earned hand to hand moves to collect, (not including the two-soon-to-be-three weapon sets), and four styles to master, and the opportunity to order them in an infinite number of ways, utilizing as many as 13, or as few as one, even with 900+ hours in, it's a constant re-shuffling of every stat point, move ordering, number of moves per deck, defensive style, and piece of gear going into the combat trials.
The main complaint about the story mode being short is valid if you are expecting a rich solo-experience. However, as pretty as Absolver's world is, and though the 'story mode' may have bosses, loot drops, enemies as well as random encounters, this space and construction is understandably confusing for players upon entry- and when the credits roll six-ish hours in, you've only just begun. The open world is in a metaphor, the most elaborate and decorated training stage in any fighting game ever, with the bonus of bosses and cutscenes thrown in for flavoring. That's going to confuse many, and dissapoint others who have been told the game is 'dark souls with kung fu', as that seems to be the most popular description, but is in entirety only skimming the surface of Absolver's PVP based depth post game- where your ranking depends on how you utilize an expanding knowledge of how/when to use any move, to play mind games on an opponent, and earn your wins by knowing what moves you have in your deck, and what they have in theirs. The story mode is there to help you get a handle on how to play, from beginning to end- in essence, the entire story mode is a tutorial, a very rich and innovative cooperative tutorial that tells a story to keep you interested as you learn to cross the base skill threshold you'll need to enter the real meat of the game; Combat Trials.
The open world is always there, and you can challenge main bosses for XP, and high level gear, but the Combat Trials are the heart of the game, and are where you will get your butt kicked back into the deck editor to cover weak aspects of your moveset, or method of play. You earn more XP in combat trials per-match than any open-world encounter, and your rewards pre-and-post game in the form of 'coins' or 'disks' that contain common-to-rare-items as well as 'crystals' for emotes, and crystal fragments, the game's only currency, to customize/color/repair your gear. Cosmetics and superficial rewards aside, I haven't played a fighting game that asks you to fundamentally be flexible as popularized trends of play come and go- opponents playing entirely new 'meta' decks with new strategies by the day, that require you to refine and redefine what you consider your 'best' deck, or approach to a win. There is no 'winning deck', no 'best style' or stat allocation, everything is a toss up from player to player, and every experimental risk taken has it's potential reward, and because that's omnipresent for every player, it requires you to adapt every single match you play. Failure, and the patience to learn from it, is something many gamers simply won't have patience for. But for those who do have an attitude that isn't shaken from loss, it's an opportunity that refreshes the game almost infinitely, as you have an infinite number of ways to re-shape your style of play, adapting to metas, trends that come and go, and inventing your own ways to cover weaknesses, or over-power with strengths. If you're coming in with a big ego, prepare to be humbled at any time, over and over.
It's completely up to you and your ability to learn and adapt, in a completely unique way from other fighting games. With a 3v3 mode, an additional world area, a fifth style and ***FREE*** content updates by the truckload each month, this game is endlessly playable. For the open world, you can be a school mentor and help new players through their first story run, or grief to your heart's content, earn loot from drops and get rich enough to buy the prestige items from the in-game gear shop. For those who understand Absolver, and are patient and humbled to learn from their losses, and want a game that delivers endless challenge, the Combat Trials will perpetually ask you to evolve and fine tune your method of play, making for an endlessly replayable game with no skill cieling, or 'perfect' deck/formula. Everything can be countered, nothing is invulnerable, even the best players have weak points you can find as you learn what to look for.
It's up to you to customize your Absolver, in a realistically paced martial arts PVP simulation, from the blows you deal, the defenses you choose, all the way down to the gear that you wear, and that is something you cannot 'master', and because of that, Absolver is truly an endlessly playable and perpetually evolving game, with a community unlike any other, on steam and on discord, and for fifteen dollars I cannot reccomend any other game in my library more highly than Absolver.

Now onto the detailed version for the literary ones :

(This game has been gifted to me courtesy of Artificial Raven.  Thanks, bro!)
Do you enjoy button matching?  Do you enjoy achievements raining down upon your profile?  If so, then this game is just for you (otherwise, move along).
is essentially as I just said.  A game about pressing the right buttons in the right order and getting achievements.  You can play a variety of modes including:  Match-the-shape-line-to-the-outline mode, pressing-the-letters-in-order mode, pressing-the-numbers-in-order mode, press-the-letters-in-order-as-they-spin-and-move-around mode, press-the-numbers-in-order-as-they-spin-and-move-around mode, and finally press-the-numbers-AND-letters-in-order mode.  Aside from that explanation, there's not too much that can be said for
outside of it being a simplistic game with some decent music.
Sadly, this game has a low replayability after completion (which is a little grindy).  That seems to be the only downside to playing this game.  That and it does get a bit boring after a while.  You simply press the buttons before time runs out and you recover a little more time as you press the right buttons faster.  Keep in mind that button mashing will punish you by reducing your available play time.  Simply put, "Faster you press right buttons, more time you get.  Press wrong buttons, lose your time."
If you want to buy this game, you can expect me to say "wait for a sale" and this time is no different.  $1 is a bit pricey for what you're getting.  Wait for a sale and it'll most likely be 50% off.  After gathering all the achievements, I doubt that you'll return to this title.  And of course, there are card drops, so you do get a slight refund from purchasing this game.
6/10  A nice experience, though the scope of the project is rather limited.  Don't expect much other than achievement rain.

Double Dragon: Neon really does hit every sweet spot and any other nostalgic spot you may have from this and other similar genres of its time in history. The level select screen looks like its from Super Mario Bros 3. The sprites look exactly like the ones from Double Dragon 1 on the NES.
The story is super simple: Rescue girlfriend from powerful "evil" person. Where this game ascends from "good" to "great" is the superb effort put into the writing, voice acting, and little tongue-in-cheek jokes sprinkled throughout the game. The only thing this game got wrong was Abobo's design. Abobo (mainly the arcade and NES versions) traditionally has a large torso, massive head, short legs, and a comically thick black mustache.
The main characters have a menu of special abilities in the form of cassette tape tracks (Side A for fighting, Side B for passive effects) they can have "playing" in the background. While some of these abilities were creative, I found that only one or two were useful. Primarily the "Dragon" ability and the life recovery. The other abilities either seemed too weak, or the risk was too high vs the reward I would get. I would've preferred seeing abilities that borrowed more inspiration from Golden Axe. Like, you could summon a barrage of Tornado Kicks all across the map or rain fire on all enemies. Or even a humiliation move that made everyone's pants accidentally fall down and embarrass them! (debuff for the win!)
Anyway, I had a BLAST playing this game. I highly recommend Double Dragon: Neon!

Cool game. I actually played through it a month or so ago off Steam and it's a lot of fun. Originally released as Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis, this is a tactical Cold War shooter. It hasn't aged that well and the voice acting is quite wonky but it has an excellent campaign which is the main reason why I picked it up. It's more of a thinking man's shooter, and after a few missions you'll be put in charge of a squad which you can order around. I was really surprised at how well the squad mechanics worked, it's not just a worthless gimmick. It was quite fun playing this game in contrast to ArmA 3 and seeing how the series got started and has evolved. Unlike the ArmA 3 campaign this one featured a greater variety of missions, there's stealth missions, tank missions, heli missions, even one where you fly the A-10. While the outdated graphics place a lot of limits on how large scale the battles are, the game still has pretty good draw distance for its time which makes tank battles really feel like tank missions (after the first tank mission I hated them, by the last tank mission I loved them). If you're a fan of Cold War stuff there is a lot in here, you'll be running from BMPs loaded with Soviet troops, supported by HINDs and T80s rolling around destroying everything while the SHILKA denies friendly air support. This is all accompanied by a great original soundtrack which I feel was a little hampered by the poorly chosen licensed music. The difficulty picked up significantly during the last few missions (I actually had to resort GameFaqs, something I haven't done in a while) but overall the game is very playable aside from a couple crashes and bugs. So in conclusion it's not perfect, but still a great tactical Cold War shooter that's worth picking up for free.

While I haven't finished the story yet, I've enjoyed this game immensely. It has a robust combat system, and while it has a few weak points, these are things that can be resolved with time and patches, rather than being critical errors to the core of the game.
The apparent weak points at the moment are: sometimes there is lag. Sometimes this isn't a huge problem, because it's like playing in slow motion. Other times you and the npcs start rubber banding around and it becomes rather frustrating to try and do anything. The other problem I've had is that the tutorial is kind of spread out across the map, with guys in fancy masks dispensing a single piece of advice each. The problem being that I didn't learn you had to block/dodge (or whatever) to learn moves until hours into the game.
Those problems aside, the game has a pretty steady difficulty and generally will punish you if you try to flail your way through with thoughtless button mashing.
Overall, I would give it an 8.5/10. I hope to see more out of it (more moves, more combat styles, more storyline, etc). It's already got a strong foundation from which to build.

I enjoy this game quite a lot. The PVP combat is very fun most of the time you're doing it in free-roam, i've already met a bunch of guys i really enjoy messing around with and fighting. The customization is very impactful and well done, and the base controls are very responsive,
However, for me, there are a number of glaring issues that I feel some of which need to be assessed before I can in good conscience recommend people spend $30 on it:
-the meta is as follows:
A: light attack light attack light attack light attack light attack light attack light attack light attack light attack maybe a guard break and 4 hyperarmors (note that some light attack chains cannot even be parried while being hit by them)
B: all the hyperarmors 1 light attack chain and 2 heavy attacks (and there aren't enough charge breaks in the world to chain to stop it)
-Almost everyone in the combat trials just builds these decks because they can only find enjoyment in winning, not playing the game, but winning every match because they have annoying decks that could only lose if they're absolute garbage at the game. This has already been heavily reinforced by the pre-launch testing having the same results as the post-launch on the matter so it's essentially set in stone until the devs make some changes.
-For myself personally I had better connection quality before the new stability update, currently i'm now being hit with phantom range (for those who have not played dark souls i'm being hit by attacks i shouldn't because the servers think my character is somewhere else)
-They are missing content on-release that we were promised for the combat trials (2v2, etc)
-The game lacks LAN offline play which worries me for the possibly squandered competitive play this game might have seen.
-The abilities are poorly balanced, more than half of them are completely useless in general, and a couple are just flat out broken
This is not to say that there isn't enough content to enjoy the game for quite some time, it's just that there is a lost potential due to many problems this game has in balancing and oversight.

Tobe's Vertical Adventure is one of those games that makes me long for a ~Meh~ option for steam reviews.
Right, right, so what've we got here? Well, Tobe's Vertical Adventure is a Side-Scrolling... Er, Up-n'-Down-Scrolling(?) platformer where the idea is to get from the top of a cave to the bottom and then make your escape back to the entrance, all while collecting gems and animals as you descend/ascend. It offers two different playable characters for singleplayer and multiplayer story modes across four different worlds, each with four levels. So lets get started shall we?
First of all I'd like to mention the presentation. The majority of the game is represented in the form of sprites, with some art slides that are used as cutscenes and such. The style of the art is nice; it's a simplistic style where everything is gratuitously round for some reason or another. I'm being told it's cute, but something about the hips of both characters being twice the size of their heads puts me off... Anyway, it works, but it's nothing I can say is spectacular. The in-game sprites also look okay and have decent animation to them, but I noticed that a fair few of them were blurry or lacked sharpness, specifically the character sprites. Overall, it's a quaint artstyle, but it's nothing to write home about.
Audio is also just okay. Not a lot of music to listen to; There's the menu music, one track for each world, and then some cutscene music. Once again, none of it is /really/ good, just kinda okay. I suppose I liked the 1st and 3rd world's music the best, seeing as I remember them the most, but it's still all... Whatever y'know? Sound effects as well, which really wouldn't even be noted in this review if it wasn't for the fact that many sound effects occuring at the same time will cause the sound to increase in volume exponentially. Collecting gems becomes a little less fun when you start hearing "ding, Ding, DING, DDDIIIINNNGGG" as you pick them up in groups.
Put hey, as long as the gameplay if fun, right?... Er, well, it's okay. That's the word of the day folks. As previously mentioned, you start at the top of the level and must make your way down to a chest at the bottom. You'll encounter stage-specific traps and collect power-ups such as balloons and ropes... Which is to say those are the only items you collect. Balloons allow you to float down for a short period of time and ropes can be thrown to the ceiling where they'll hang down and you can climb them. In all honesty though, I never really /needed/ these items. Aside from using balloons to break my fall simply so I could go down a vertical shaft a little more quickly for my own convenience, everything can be done almost, if not just as easily without these items. They /can/ occasionally be used to make speedruns easier, but speedrunning, while encouraged, is not the main focus of the game.
The worlds don't have a whole lot of diference in them either. The first one is just a cave; there are some enemies that walk back and forth, nothing really special. The second world is an ice world that introduces horizontally positioned ropes, and has invisible blocks as one of it's level gimmicks. There's also a trap that's, like, an impossible-to-see fake wall that'll drop on you from the background, but it only appears twice and it's where you'll be running so fast that you'll pass them without a second thought. Third world is the lava world, so there's lava and stuff. This world has these bubbles that'll pop and bounce you up when you land on them, which make the platforming a little more interesting. Thing is, these bubbles reform waaayy too fast, so you'll encounter vertical shafts with unavoidable bubbles in them so that you can quickly ascend, but on the way down will only bounce you up and reform before you fall beyond them. Lastly there's the pyramid island. There's some shooty traps, there are some annoying spike traps, and some crushers. Nothing entirely notable really.
What IS kinda cool about this game is the escape bit of the levels. Once you get to the bottom, you have to unlock a chest which causes the cave to crumble while you make your escape. You have a limited amount of time, which can be extended by 10 or 15 seconds depending on how well you do on the chest unlocking QTE. At this point in time, the level changes, destroying certain walls and platforms to allow for certain shortcuts and various hazards. It can also make getting the collectibles easier, but you also have a time limit, so you kinda have a risk/reward thing goin' on there. You can even see what blocks will be destroyed when the cave crumbles, so you can semi-plan your escape route on your way down!
Finally, lets talk about the characters. There's not a whole lot to say about them; both can grab ledges, wall-jump, and roll. Tobe, the yellow one, is faster and can do a short wall-run. The controls for the wall-run are fairly clunky and imprecise though, so I'd always screw it up at vital points in time. Nana, the pink one, on the other hand is slower, has less health, but has a double jump. This double jump allows her to make ascend quickly, break a long fall, take short cuts, and basically wall-climb. She is by far the easier character of the two, as reflected by the stricter speedrun times in the achievement sections. The game was short enough as it is, but even after clearing the game 100%, Nana got me through it in a little under a half hour.
And that's kinda the whole problem with the game. It's pretty short, and what little there is of it has a lack of substance. Playing through the game as both characters was probably an hour's work, and that's with doing the previously mentioned 100% completion. And that's not even mentioning the various glitches I've come across, including but not limited to being clipped inside of a wall consistantly after being hit on a particular level, or stuttering scrolling during co-op play. Match that with head-scratching desgin choices like unnoticable but sparsley placed wall traps, or quickly respawning bubbles, and this game is a short, unpolished, substance-lacking "meh" of a game.
The one place where this game shines to it's fullest though is it's co-op, which is still flawed in a way thanks to the lack of duo-controller support and the fact that it's local-only. Still, in co-op, there are some extra moves you can pull off such as head bouncing or pulling the other player up a ledge, which made for some interesting multiplayer-specific shortcuts. Two players also collect gems and animals more quickly and efficiently, making the experience a touch more streamlined.  Good luck finding someone who'll play it with you though, even if it would only be a half-hour.
But hey, that's all just my opinion. Cross reference mine with others and determine if this is a game for you. Though personally, there's juuuust enough wrong with the game to lean it towards the negative side of meh, and I really wouldn't pick it up unless it was on sale or something.
