VERY HIGHLY RECOMMEND : 92% (Awesome Replayability, Deep RPG, Great Combat Mechanics)
Initially, I did not notice this game, because of the poor graphics. However, once I started playing the game, I am hooked on it and have been playing 120+ hours non stop. I have not even completed a single playthrough of the game, and I know I will be doing many playthrough to get all the achievements.  Let me give a detail breakdown of the strengths and weaknesses of this wonderful game.
The Strengths
1. Awesome Replayability - Although I have spent 120+ hours and have barely completed a single playthrough, I know that I will be playing this game a great many times to get all the achievements. You can select your team of 6 members, from a variety of starting classes. Each class can advance into a number of specialize classes as well, like a Fighter can advance into a Warrior, a Knight or a Samurai. Some classes can also advance multiple times, like a Mage can become a Wizard and then become an Archmage. Each of these advancement will unlock new skills and spells, and might require you to adopt different strategies to play them. In the end there are many class-specific achievements for many of the advance classes, which you can only get through multiple playthroughs.
2. Deep RPG - Each character can get a single, radically different BIRTH FEAT during creation time. This birth feat will make your character play differently because you will get some special abilities or advantages that you can use since level 1. There are also many birth feats that are unlock only when you accomplish a series of related achievements in the game. For example, you unlock a birth feat if you finish the game with 0 deaths, or if you finish Chapter 2 with 0 purchases. Some birth feats like the Dark Lord, is extremely difficult to get and you can only unlock it if you finish the game. Interestingly enough, there is also an achievement if you finish the game with a character that has a Dark Lord birth feat. This will mean that you have to unlock the Dark Lord birth feat first, by finishing the game with a whole string of achievements. After that you need to restart the game, and keep rolling for a starting character until you find one with the newly unlocked Dark Lord birth feat, which will grant you many advance super powers at level 1. Note that with super powers, you might also get super weaknesses for some birth feats, so you might still have to consider a totally different play style when you are engaged in fights.
3. Great Combat Mechanics -I simply love the combat mechanics of this game. There is so much to learn as the game has a highly complex skills and spells system. It took me many hours of steep learning to understand how to successfully do combat in this game. Furthermore, there is also a highly complex AUTO-COMBAT system, which allow you to customize and control what type of skills, spells and strategies each of your team member need to do. Once you fine-tune the strategy for each fight, you can just run auto-combat for several hundred moves. This is because monsters are INTELLIGENT and can also heal, or summon allies, or develop a strategy for the fight as well. Since monsters have different weakness, you might have to change gears, skills and spells whenever you go to a different area of the dungeon with different type of monsters. However, the auto combat does make it much easier to execute several hundred moves and make it a must for grinding and farming.
The Weakness
1, No Fancy Graphics - Unlike expensive PC games like the Witcher series which have awesome graphics, this game only have very simple, tile-based graphics.
2. Simple Layout for iPhone - There are also no complex, high resolution layouts that are made for PCs because this game was originally made for iPhone.
For the extremely low price, I HIGHLY recommend this game to any old school RPG games out there who love to immerse themselves into many hours of interesting game play. Furthermore, the game is also on sale this week. I bought the game where there was no sale, but even so I still feel that this game is more than worth its weight in gold !! This is a fantastic game.

If, like me, you grew up playing 1980s RPGs like Wizardy, Ultima, and Bard's Tale, you'll find this game familiar. While not a direct descendent of any of them, it blends aspects of all of them and combines them in a fresh way with minor nods to some more modern RPG concepts.

Definitely not going to rival Obsidian in story. And the UI is certainly a bit clunky. But, if you're like me, these minor quibbles won't get in the way. This game definitely scratched an itch that I've had for a decade or so. Fun, easy to understand but somewhat deep mechanics, tactical turn-based combat, and multiple character build progressions are all integral to the success of this game. Recommend this to anyone who enjoyed 80s RPGs. If they're not your cup of tea, you're probably going to have a hard time overlooking the UI and story.

All in all, perhaps my favorite Steam purchase since Terraria.

Quick background there was once upon a time a D&D game for my favorite console the Turbo Grafx 16. The game was Order of the Griffon and it was unlike other D&D games in that the combat was like turn based strategy. When I saw this game on
I was super curious. I watched a few videos and was sold.
Since I've been playing I've found the learning curve a bit strange. There is a mix of UI based on 8/16bit era games while trying to make things function on mobile touch devices as well as us computer players. It's a tad strange at first but I'm getting the hang of it and the dev has been writing guides. All in all despite the quirks it's oddly satisfying.
Anyone that knows me know I'm pretty crotchety about games these days. I loved the classic 8bit NES RPG's but struggled to replay them due to bad interface and other issues. Strangely this game embraces those awkward UI tropes but it works.
The story so far is laden with silly dialog but I find myself interested in getting things done, exploring and managing gear in ways other games in the past made feel like work. While there is plenty of vendor fodder there is also lots of little unique things and the lack of new age polish makes keeping an eye on stats important. Normally this would bug me but again some how it works with this game. The vendor fodder in say Diablo 3 just drove me mad.
There are a few clunky aspects of the UI like how I want to click and drag the maps or wish I could zoom in and out the game is over all oddly fun. If you like classic console RPG's I'd wager you will like this game. While being basic in some areas there is a lot of complexity in the stats, management and strategy. Interestingly on the note of strategy the auto fighting helps you zip through repetitive things while letting you disable it for more complex battles for a more TBS game which I love...it's the whole reason I got it and why I loved Order of the Griffon. All these years later I love seeing this idea revisited and I'm enjoying the hell out of this title right now. However it's beyond detrimental to my productivity.

BAD END is a love/hate for me.
GOOD STUFFS:
It is a visual novel that revolves around a game where if you get a BAD END you die. It's basically a visual novel inside a visual novel.
The idea is really cool. The plot and story is in my opinion great and at some points a little surprising. Gameplay wise its a visual novel meaning you read and select choices. Not much more complicated than that.
The characters are well drawn while the environments seem a little bit generic. The music suits the game in most cases.
The spelling can be a little bit rough at times but still understandable and doesn't brake the game's feel much.
The BAD ENDS are great. I recommend doing them all as some of the deaths are pretty well written.
HOWEVER:
To get to that good plot, pacing and investigation you need to survive about 40 minutes of PURE NOTHINGNESS. The first 40 minutes of the game is the introduction to the environment, scene and characters which is WAY TOO LONG for an introduction. They could have easily condensed this into 10 minutes MAX. This is mostly because the dialogue keeps repeating how you might die for real if you die in the game. Yes we get it for like the 15th time.
I understand why a lot of people dislke or frown upon this game. It's because it takes way too long to get to the good stuff. The first 40 minutes are boring. Nothing else.
VERDICT:
I think this is a great visual novel with great plot and awesome mystery elements but gets dragged down by the stupid 40 minute intro that most people not bother with going through because its really boring.
8/10

It's a fine little mystery / horror story based around an urban legend - the story and it's style is a genuine pulp-horror story. Nothing fancy, nothing outstanding, just the really typical twists for the genre. The game will kill you if you die in it!  Online hype about it, mysteriously stopping diaries about playing it, people not believing that it could happen, but *gasp* it does!
The gameplay is a standard visual novel, text speed can be set up from slow reading to instant text, nicely working text log, no voiceacting, and thankfully a skip function in case you die and have to repeat sections. The story is a little bit weird  in style as you follow the hero of the game who'll download the BAD END game ingame, and plays the game, inside of the game. The gameplay is really fair, unlimited saves and the skip text feature makes correcting mistakes / bad choices fixable in a matter if minute, and a really nice user called Jedo wrote a for all endings ( I like VN's stories, but not really fond of actually looking for endings, to it was a godbless)
So, all in all, a cheap VN-horror story about an urban legend being just as cheesy as it should be, while having no holdups in the gameplay. Playing for story, for endings, or just to getting all achivements are all doable with ease, so everyone can find what's looking for in the game easily.

Really enjoyed this game, especially considering the price. You do get some replay value due to the multiple endings. You could get a few hours of gameplay before you finish it in its entirety. I'm a fast reader, so I got through it pretty quickly. I just went back and tried to find all the endings. You do get what you pay for though, but it's worth the buy. :)

I was stoked to learn that RE7 was returning the franchise back to its horror roots, as the series had, in my humble opinion, devolved into an interactive action/adventure movie with the random quick time event.  The gameplay itself had become sporadic and stale, the storyline mundane, the characters were steadily losing their charm.
RE7 is the breath of fresh air the series desperately needed.
It is legitimately scary, featuring deliciously unsettling sfx ambience and a thoroughly creepy atmosphere; and while jumpscares abound it doesn't depend on them to the point of feeling cheap.  The storyline is somewhat predictable (It's RE afterall) but it differs enough from previous installments to keep you alert and interested.  The boss battles are fun and intense,  and the Baker family proved to be superbly sinister and unhinged.
RE7 sits comfortably on my list of favorite horror games, although the early Silent Hill installments still reign supreme.  (I'm still upset over PT getting axed.)
Now, that all being said, I do have a bit of a grievance with it: the dlc - specifically "Not a Hero".  The previous dlcs were released fairly quickly and while there was some silliness (Jack's 55th Birthday for example), there were also some heart racing minigames as well (such as Bedroom and Nightmare).  Overall, those dlcs were enjoyable and fleshed out the base game's backstory quite well.
Now here's where it gets a little bit spoilery:
The hype was real.  I think RE fans, in general, were excited about this revelation.  The dlc was coming soon!  No wait,  it's coming later, the devs said.  Much later. They want to give it the attention it deserves so that it lives up to the quality of the base game.  Okay, fair enough.
Well, it's nearly a year later and that dlc
dropped.  I just finished it.  I have to wonder if I let the hype train speed me along to the land of unreasonable expectations because I feel as though the dlc did
live up to the quality of the base game.  It felt generic and lackluster.  There was a smidgen of storyline and a wee plot twist, but it didn't feel as if it were some masterfully handcrafted dlc that had taken almost a full year to produce.
**Edited to add that the dlc in question "Not a Hero" is FREE and while that in itself is a bit of a redeeming quality, I still stand by my original assessment that it fails to live up to the hype surrounding it.**
That little disappointment aside, RE7 is a solid game that stands on its own within the horror genre and the series itself.  With its financial success and almost universal praise from the playerbase,  I hope the devs continue to guide the series along its current path.

A review in retrospect.
Resident Evil 7 is a strong entry into the series. The main reason? It's a fine blend of new and classic RE elements.
The first person view makes for a more immersive experience, especially when you're running away from Jack Baker. Combat is fairly fun, since you have to balance attacking and defending. That being said, there isn't a lot of enemy variety at all.
Storywise, RE7 definitely relies on more emotion and pathos. The Baker's story is a tragic one, and there's one scene in particular with Jack that is heartbreaking.
All in all, this is a worthy entry into the RE series.

“When you thought red bunnies were just the color of red. I am afraid there is more to the story because this red bunny encloses magical abilities” - CutieRoo
The first thought that came to mind when I first laid eyes on this gem-of-a-game was *oh great another indie game that is similar to Limbo…*but I was wrong! The game in itself brings its own charm and heart. Nothing of the sort of limbo’s design and style that has been introduced. While playing Albert and Otto, I noticed some of the ideas that were implemented were their own and that helps separate itself from the other indie games out there. Such as, the ability to use a magical bunny that gives you powers in order to help solve the obstacles you come across. The other positive thing I noticed is despite some of the puzzles being a bit repetitive, the achievement of completing the puzzle is always different leaving you feel accomplished and interested.
As I mentioned before, a few things that stood out for me that helped make Albert and Otto its own game is the cute-little-red-magical-bunny and the ability to use a shotgun. Now these two items will be used throughout, and will be necessary to progress forward. With each puzzle you come across, you will be using your little furry friend to aid you in solving them; giving the game an appealing twist compared to some of the other puzzle platformers I have played. Plus, the shotgun puts an enjoyable influence on the game *Plus! It helps to eliminate any foe that comes your way*. However, this is the only weapon provided to you, and no other weapons will be given *for now*.
In terms of story-line for Albert and Otto, I found it to rather intriguing through the way it was told. As you progress, the story-line unfolds when you visit your mail box and read the mail inside. Now this doesn’t implement cut scenes. It’s just a letter you focus on and learn more about what is happening with drawings that the mysterious girl sends.
In addition, the next thing that I wanted to discuss are the graphics and artistic style of the game. The quality of graphics was taken into a new direction compared to most indie games that try. In this case, they do catch your attention and was a great idea to try because it succeeded in how it did stand out. The artistic design almost follows the path of Limbo but has more attention to detail that gives it a very tasteful style. It ties in well with the obscurity and gloomy design, but not as ominous as Limbo where you don’t know what is going to come out to kill you next. I feel like the music helped in aiding this very well to help contradict that dark and scary vibe.
There was a drawback for me when it came to playing and that was the contrasting between white and black. There would be moments where I would be playing and the character would blend into the white color and completely disappear or make it very hard to see him.
Another one of the pleasant moments of playing Albert and Otto was the music they created for it. It was very pleasant to my ears, and flowed very nicely to each changing environment or situation that may happen as you progress.
In conclusion, I found Albert and Otto to be a very delightful and creative game even though it was rather short leaving me with wanting more. Fret not though, this is only episode one of the Albert and Otto series and more is set to come in the future. KBros has made a well-rounded game that is full of potential to become even greater than it is now. I am beyond excited to see what is in store from them with current development of this series and other games in the future from KBros. If you are a fan of the puzzle platform style games, this is a game that I definitely recommend to add to your list to play when going through the vast collection of Steam games available.

I really wanted to like this game.  The aesthetics, the music, and being a genre that I enjoy very much should have made this a highly enjoyable experience.  Unfortunately a lack of polish, harsh check-pointing and a punitive learn-by-dying approach to game design has soured the positives.
The lack of polish is most noticeable with the platforming and levitation system.  Getting stuck on geometry is frustrating at the best of time but when - especially in the latter river sections - demand a high level of timing it's less forgivable. In may other punishing timing intensive platformers (Super Meat Boy, Rayman Origins, etc) I've always known that the issue has been with my ability to learn the required process, not with factors that seem outside of my control.  Which brings me to the checkpoints in the game. Playing minutes-long sections of a game to then die because of the glitching gets old, very quick.  In addition, many sections of the game face you with traps and enemies in a fashion that's highly unlikely you'll be able to react in time sufficiently the first time you encounter them, sending you way back to the beginning of the section.  I can handle learn-by-dying games but not when the polish is lacking and the checkpoint system doesn't support it.
Which is a shame because as I started out saying, the aesthetics and the music are absolutely wonderful.  And what they were trying to do with the gameplay is a solid idea, which should have meant a highly enjoyable game. If you can deal with the issues that I've mentioned and it's at a good price it's worth playing for the experience.  Just be prepared for frustration.

This game is a beautiful gem with some serious flaws. I should know it pretty well after about 600 hours of gameplay.
Flaws from the worst to the least:
PvP. It isn't well balanced, the turns are painful to wait through, and you never find matches anyway.
Moderate to difficult learning curve.
AI has major tactical faults, and it's still painful to wait through your opponents turn.
Time consuming. I spent more than 100 hours on each of my single player warbands, but at the time I am writing this I have not completed all of the campaigns.
Random number generators, usually have a bias. This one causes 1% chances to occur 25% of the time.
Looting wyrdstone to improve your faction reputations takes an investment beyond any reasonable effort.
Discovering the enchanting recipes is also random (many have no benefit).
The Value:
This emulates the feeling of table top games like warhammer, warmachines, and malifaux wonderfully.
You can make a list from your collection of mercenaries and kit them them in minutes. A full game should take less than an hour, and if both players act quickly can be over in less than 30 minutes.
Each of your models is highly customizable in both appearance and functionality.
There are persistent effects from inuries and mutations (chaos only). Often times this means you will have a completely unique warband.
The reserves allow you enough extra troops to be able to have a flexible fighting force. (You don't have to do the same thing every battle).
This game is challenging, and learning its intricacies is rewarding. More importantly information is attainable.

I'd give this game a neutral review but since Steam only allow for a thumbs up or thumbs down, ill have to lean towards negative. But only for one main reason: this game is not Mordheim.
If you have ever played tabletop Mordheim and were expecting this to be a direct translation, you'll be disappointed. In and of it self this game is an ok game for its genre, it's not a great game though. That's not to bash Rouge factor. Like tabletop Mordheim, Rouge Factor probably didnt get a lot of funding from Games Workshop.
TT Mordheim had simple skirmish combat system that made for great quick battles. And Half the fun of the game was the awesome leveling system they used. It was a very casual friendly game. TT wasnt perfect, and had some issues, but with a few house rules it was a great system.
Instead of making a translation from TT, Rouge factor (or GW) decided to make their own system based of the Mordhiem setting. Maybe they didnt think that space hulk or blood bowl sold enough (those games where more of a direct translation). The game mechanic system that rouge factor made seems overcomplicated for what it does, half my play time was spent trying to figure the system out. Where in tabletop you could level up almost every battle. In this game there is a lot more grind involved. When you level up in this game, a lot of the time its hard to notice any improvement. There doesnt seem to be a whole lot of game variations so it can get repetitive fairly quick.
Pros:
This city visuals are amazing. The cities really have the look and feel of Mordheim. Unless you had tons of dosh, and/or time and skill. You would not be able to get that on tabletop.
The Developers seem to actually read and respond on the forums far more than most game Devs do. So props for that.
Cons:
Way too much grind in this game. Its usually not a good thing if game develops substitute grind in place of content.
City movement is very restrictive and constrained. You can only climb/jump in certain spots, even though that ledge looks just as good as this one. Many times you'll find an area that looks like you can move no problem, too bad its impassable. Rotting paper thin door blocking your way? Nope cant kick it down. Trying to get into a locked “cell”(that only has two walled sides and no roof, with a grated door skaven could easily climb over) and you dont have a key? Too bad.
Lack of visual character customization. Im guessing that they had plans for lots of customization, but ran out of time and/or money. Some units have a few options, most have very little.
Too much focus on gathering wyrdstone during the battle. In TT this was mostly handled in the post battle sequence. It just gets too repetitive in this game. If they streamlined the system of picking it up, it would be much better.
I can appreciate and understand why the developers made their own game mechanic system instead of making a more direct translation from tabletop. But, to honest I much prefer the original.

First of all, I really wanted to enjoy this game. I recently replayed Limbo and Never Alone, and really wanted something similar to get immersed in. Unfortunately, this game does not have the stylistic low-graphic art style that Limbo does so well, or the genuine connection to the protagonist found in Never Alone. It's biggest downfall, however, lies within its gameplay mechanics.
The controls feel quite clunky, and for a puzzle-solving game, it is incredibly unintuitive. It also has its fair share of bugs. As it is pretty standard to die a number of times whilst solving a puzzle, it is really unhelpful when one of the cogs you're meant to be pushing somewhere decides to get stuck at an angle, or fly off altogether. Obviously, dying in games is all par for the course, so it shouldn't actively make you angry, but this game pulls it off in a way I've not experienced since the early Tomb Raiders (which gives Albert and Otto far too much credit). I have no problem in dying to learn how I'm meant to solve a puzzle, but when you decide to make a level insanely precisely timed and then give the player buggy, tempermental controls, which sometimes choose to just not work at all, and then punish the player by making them die repeatedly and reload in a far off checkpoint, then you are not designing games well.
I love indie games, and really appreciate what a tough industry it is, and I honestly wanted to enjoy this game, and stuck with it long after I had begun to lose my patience. Maybe, with some more work on the gameplay, it will achieve what it set out to do, but at the moment, I would recommend trying Limbo or Never Alone.
Also, being mysterious and telling a story through (honest to God) children's drawings is not compelling or new, it's just confusing af.

It’s like LIMBO, with guns. This is a comparison that I’ve seen a couple of times, and immediately thought of myself. In truth that’s a pretty encapsulating statement. The gameplay of Albert and Otto is almost exactly the same as LIMBO but with more intricate mechanics, i.e. a gun. I’d like to try and avoid the comparison to LIMBO but it’s such a strong resemblance in feel and theme that I had to double check to make sure it wasn’t some kind of sequel.
For the few of you who haven’t played LIMBO or at least don’t know anything about it, Albert and Otto is a puzzle platformer. Set in a mostly black and white world you play as a child with a ‘large head’. You move through the creepy landscape going after some abstract goal that you don’t necessarily understand and along the way, you die. Brutally.
The controls are for the most part very tight and easy to control and even in the places where time is short you rarely mess up a jump. You push and pull boxes, press switches and try and avoid falling on spiky things. So far, so standard. The way the Albert and Otto stands out is through the use of the titular Otto. Otto is a stuffed rabbit that you find fairly early on. Whilst you hold him you gain the ability to double jump and move objects telekinetically. However you can drop him which will allow him to be used as a long distance switch operator or as a weight on pressure pads. It’s these added mechanics which really allow for a varied puzzle experience that in my opinion surpasses that of LIMBO’s.
The game also features a couple of boss battles and both of these feel great, perhaps not as memorable as LIMBO’s infamous spider but still great. And what’s great is that neither of these rely on the gun you have. The game understands that it is a platformer and that your gun is just a tool rather than a weapon.
The game has a story, that much is clear. But as this is the first in what seems like will be a series nothing much is explained, and all you find are scattered across the world are hints and clues. It’s incredibly creepy and something bad is happening but you feel like you’ve only just scratched the surface. Wartime Germany is about the only thing I managed to figure out and I look forward to the next game so that I may find out more!
So where does it stand? If you enjoyed LIMBO you’ll love this game, it’s better in every just about every aspect and is about the same length (just under two hours). Thanks to the addition of more intricate mechanics there are far more options for the puzzles and despite the difficulty spike at the end I enjoyed it a lot and eagerly await the next game.

It's really difficult to rate this game since a simple thumbs up or down won't do it justice. The devs obviously have a lot of love for the genre and Double Dragon (even though the style they chose funny as it is, has little in common with DD which was never what the latest trend of Kung Fury/80s style parodies are doing now - so some hardcore fans of the original might find the shift questionable), there are some great ideas behind it, some work, some don't (not sure if grinding and rpg elements add depth or just drag it) but unfortunately it all comes down to the game's main problem which is the sluggish controls and combat.
Considering this is a Double Dragon game, you can understand how important this is. Everything feels slow, not very responsive - a thing that becomes even more noticeable and irritating in the few platforming segments - , limited movesets and even missing classic moves that have been the staple of the franchise forever (no hair pull/knee on face?!), some cheap difficulty and encounters where opponents and bosses have some iffy invincibilty at times, a bit of repetition with stage traps and worst of all: the weapons!
Yes, as strange as it sounds I never felt so dissapointed with weapons picking in a Double Dragon game, one of the most famous mechanics the game introduced. The animations drag, the hit detection is not always perfect and picking and using weapons felt less rewarding and more of a thing to avoid so you won't get easily hit.
And why no d-input support? At least for me the gamepads could not work with the game! :(
Another problem for some systems including mine was the eventual framedrops and stuttering that happens after a while, I guess due to memory problems?
Not everything is bad though, some stages have great art direction, the music is a blast to hear (what a great soundtrack, both new songs and homages and remixes to the classic ones!), and special mention has to be made for one of the funniest and greatest end credits in a game ever!
Of course I may sound as if the game is horrible, but it is not! There is enjoyment out of the game and if you sit and remember the past horrible shoddy ports and various awful games that have tarnished the brand in the past, this is definitely one of the better efforts. The game might not exactly feel like a Double Dragon and the controls are not that good, but at least it is playable (!!) and a fun little beat em up that pays homage to the genre.
It's just unfortunate that the devs could not repeat the fastness, fluidity and overall greatness of what I call "The definitive Double Dragon" of Double Dragon Advance, a game so many years older but - forgive me for the pun - so much more advanced than Neon.
Still an admirable effort!

It’s clear that
was made out of love for the classic originals, but while it’s presentation does an adorable job of capturing the essence of classic 80s beat-em-ups, this beat-em-up unfortunately takes just as much steps back in terms of it’s gameplay.
I am absolutely astonished just how hard it was for me to enjoy the game. While the presentation for the game is incredibly high-level, it feels like the gameplay bogs the entire experience down to a short, frustrating, and repetitive experience.
Double Dragon Neon takes a lot of it’s beat-em-up traits from the original classics, but the end result is something that feels incredibly slow compared to the originals. Punching feels incredibly sluggish and moving around is janky and clunky. Besides your simplistic combos and weapons that you can pick up, you also have both special buffs and special moves in the form of mixtapes. The Sonsetsu Mix-Tapes give you a generic, spammable ability that drains a bar and the stances change your stats, which is often quite useless. Leveling up these stances require a unwelcomingly long amount of grinding for what can be not that noticeable changes in yours tats..
Perhaps what’s even worse are the enemies and bosses you encounter throughout the game. Some of the enemies in this game are just poorly designed, with them often having cheap moves or having a certain mechanic to them that makes fighting them an absolute chore. Bosses are even worse, with some of them even having large one-hit KO moves that are often very difficult to avoid. And don’t even tell me that fair or even remotely acceptable game design: Because it isn’t.
So what does Double Dragon really do right? Well for one, the game looks visually pleasing to the eye (Although at the cost of some objects being difficult to tell from the background), has a really good soundtrack, and for the most part has a often goofy tone that is while cringey, incredibly adorable. The aesthetics look like a HD Remaster of an actual Double Dragon game, and the cartoony humor is an often weird but zany change that gives Neon it’s own identity.
But that identity just gets wasted on an overall frustrating and sluggish experience to go through. And it’s not necessarily a long one either, with the game only lasting a short, one-hour playthrough. And because of it’s gameplay I really don’t see a reason to come back on it’s even more frustrating and unbearable difficulties.
So ultimately, Double Dragon Neon isn’t certainly a complete mess. With it’s decent aesthetic it can be good fun with a friend, but that really depends if good fun = Clunky Gameplay, Cheap Levels and hilariously unbalanced battles by your standards. If you want to play a good beat-em-up, look elsewhere.

I WANT to get new moves and DO get better, but fighting the same enemies and same 1v1 fights over and over again gets me a bit bored.
That said, I'm looking forward to new features, enemies and areas to explore - because the gameplay itself brilliant and fun. It's just that after 20h it's a bit too repetitive for me without more things to explore. But I can definitely recommend Absolver as one of the best, or THE best fighting games I've ever played!
I meant what I said. You guys have tightened up, you took your hits, and I am incredibly happy to turn this review into a positive.

Let's get this out there now: I have not had server issues other than a very small handful of times where I had to retry one extra time to login to the server. I'm currently sitting on a PVP record of 76 wins 14 losses, just to show that I have at least played a decent amount. (Not impressive, it really isn't.)
When you look at if you should buy Absolver, be realistic with yourself. At the end of the day, although you may have fun, will you get your moneys worth? It's a FIGHTING game still, a genre not many people actually understand, and to break into the genre properly takes some effort and getting your sh*t kicked in before you figure out what to do and how to be good at the game.
For $30? Right now, I wouldn't. For $20 if you can get it on sale or cheaper, then I would definitely recommend this game.
Let's start with the negatives and look at this without bias.
- For PVE players, the world is at times confusing because the map that you are provided with (which is only at the game's equivalent to a Dark Souls bonfire or the "Guidance Bridge" is odd to understand because it's simply 3 grey squares with some dots put in them to show you where bosses are. No pathways, no detail, it's just a blank gray area with dots sprinkled around. The mobs scale the higher level your character is, so the combat becomes a bit trickier the stronger you become vs NPCs, they usually have insane stamina regen, but they pose almost no threat so long as you're not being ganked by 3 mobs or more. The PVE content runs out after you've beaten all the bosses, which only takes 3 hours usually, and that's with exploring around the world for items ect. There is almost no incentive to continue to PvE in this game after you've learned your moves and beaten the bosses, so if you're a PVE player this game is not for you.
- Network stability problems are a big complaint from a lot of people, I personally have not experienced them very often, but this can't be a one person problem if so many people are complaining about it in waves. This is not about framerate, "OH I GET 60 FPS YOUR PC IS BAD!" There are actual server lag problems. I have had a couple of times where I may be running around in the world to get to point A to point B and rubberband inbetween the route, but nothing major and nothing frequent.
- It's a fighting game. Why is this a negative? Every game genre is difficult to get into if you are truly unfamiliar with it, but fighting games are even more so difficult because you have to begin to understand the opponent, adapt, make educated guesses (reads) to try and cut your opponent off and be one step ahead, you have to do this actively and be aware of it as you're doing it, and even if you're thinking about it as hard as you can, someone will still mudstomp you with a deck you just can't adapt to, and that will discourage a LOT of people from playing this game. Nobody likes to lose over and over, but that's how fighting games go if you aren't used to them. Gotta get knocked down to get back up stronger than last time.
- Once you start to climb up the PVP ladder, you realize it's literally only a number saying "Combat Trial Level ___" There's no reward for being higher rank, you get item drops after each level up but 90% of the time it's an item you already own that will not mean anything or matter. Some masks which are some of the coolest in the game can only be unlocked through PVP combat trials, but it's not a static reward, it's just something you may or may never get so long as you play. Once you realize the only thing you can do is actually just go up in numbers without it changing anything other than playing against other higher number players, there is virtually no actual reward from climbing as of right now in PVP.
- Learning moves to use in your combat decks is a bit of a tedious process. In order to learn new moves, you must find an NPC that has the move in their arsenal or a player that has it, block or defend against this one particular move over and over (sometimes up to 12-14 times being hit by this one move) and then kill the mob/player to keep that XP, or else you lose the progress you gained during that fight. When you factor in there's around 60 non-sword combat moves and 20ish sword moves to learn, it's difficult to find NPCs that can fill out your movelist (especially sword moves, as NPCs do not spawn with swords typically), and it feels more like a chore than it feels rewarding for playing the game.
- Lack of diversity in stat builds means everyone runs 25 endurance, 25 vitality, and then 15 in either dexterity or strength, as these are the softcaps for the stats and nothing else will matter past those. Anyone who doesn't at least invest into stamina will be rushed down and overwhelmed very quickly, within seconds of the match.
- I skipped every story cutscene because they were an inconvenience and didn't offer anything to the game. Appreciated that there was an effort, but at the end of the day, I'm here to PVP and play a fighting game, and your story isn't strong enough to make me pay attention in the slightest.
Okay, let's get to the positives. (I promise, they're there)
- Beautiful world. Although it's confusing to navigate at times, it's given comparisons to Dark Souls for some of the ways the areas will wind into these lopsided spiral environments, almost all of the environments are some battle torn ruins or an ancient city, which helps with the Dark Souls comparisons. Colors pop out at you, you can immediately recognize what are you're in (you may not know your way around it but you'll know where you are), the world is also sprinkled with Cairns which are the equivalent to your treasures chests, althought they only hold specific clothing items.
- Clothing, masks, weapons, there is an okay amount of aesthetic customization to your character. Some items can drop in different colors by defeating mobs in the PVE world, but you get most of your items through PVP rewards for leveling up, which only takes 2 wins max to ever level up. Currently my guy looks like he belongs in Naruto as some Kage, but mixed with the Absolver world, you feel like your character fits and belongs in this world.
- Combat. Oh man. One of the funnest combat systems I've played with. It's For Honor within the sense of you use these 4 directions to play with, but that's as far as it goes basically. While althought retaining some features known across fighting games like Super Armor on some moves (Really powerful moves can block 1 move before you break them out of it, so double hit attacks are great at countering these. There are only about 4-5 moves in the game that have the armor though.) The general idea with combat is that you create a movelist for your character through moves you have acquired throughout playing, you are able to setup a 3 attack string attached to each of the 4 directions. Each of those attacks themselves can break off into other strings if you end it early or add in proper mixups, and the part that sucked me into the game is the addiction to tweaking your deck should you run into someone that beats you, you can immediately realize what went wrong or where you need to improve your style and begin adapting.
Should you buy it? I would say wait for a price sale, unless you actively enjoy combat games, then this is a very fun game to get into. If you're a regular gamer, you aren't particularly going "tryhard" at any specific genre or willing to put in the time or effort, then I would probably stay away from this game as it will more than likely become frustrating for you because of how punishing it can be when it comes to PVP (If you drop a hit versus a good player, expect a lot of damage and a fast combo)

Alien Breed: Impact is a game that, if I remember correctly, I purchased at (or shortly after) launch. I played about 20-30 minues 7 years ago, and forgot about it. Recently though, I decided to pick it up again as I wanted something that I could enjoy with a controller from the couch.
My experience with this game was average... at best.
It's by no means a BAD game, but by the time I had finished it after about 5 hours (on the Veteran difficulty) , it had overstayed it's welcome by about 2; the game is padded out to be longer than it has any right to be.
During the majority of each level, you make your way most of the way through, only to be told you have to backtrack half-way to the beginning to get an item to unlock the door to progress. Not to mention that. just about every point of interaction through the levels (opening lockers, searching bodies, using consoles, unlocking doors), takes a good 3-5 seconds on average to complete.
This happens many times throughout each level. So much backtracking.
Then we come to the enemies. While the designs are decent, there are about 4 or 5 different types, and (again) to pad out the level, you have to fight a horde of them in just about every other room. You run down a long hallway, and as you do about 20 enemies rush you from all angles. Then you make it into the next room to unlock that console that you were backtracking for, only to have another 20 enemies rush you as you spend 5 seconds holding "A" to activate it. Tnen another 20 enemies rush you as you run back down the hallway.
Just... why? It gets old pretty quickly.
While the game has a less than average graphics and decent gameplay even with the padding, it was still fun to play. The weapons you get to use are pretty cool and devastating (even more so after you upgrade them), and while the atmosphere and story are nothing to write home about, they are engrossing enough to keep you interested for at least a few hours.
Overall, the game has more going for it than against it, but unless you're looking for a mindless twin-stick-like shooter, I'd probably pass. I don't remember how much I paid for the game ~7 years ago, but If you are really into games like this and the good points seem to outweigh the bad, I'd try to catch it on a Steam sale at around $5 as that seems to be a good balance between price point and a few hours on the couch.

Same-ish looking, manga-inspired visual novels have been a bit dime-a-dozen on Steam of late; though in all fairness, this one was actually released a year ago, thereby beating a good number of them to the punch. It's also of greater interest than most to Yours Truly, given that it's in the horror genre, as opposed to the done-to-death "romantic" and/or perve-friendly territory which the majority of these games seem to occupy. So rather than reviewing this product from the perspective of a wet-panted teenager, I'm going to appraise it from the POV of a die-hard horror fan, which is to say: would I recommend this game to fellow horror gamers?
Hmmm. Kinda yes, and kinda no.
Is it "scary"? Lord no. Especially not to anyone accustomed to the horror genre. Is it..."interesting"? Um, well, yeah...the premise certainly is, though said premise is hardly original, if you're even remotely familiar with "Ring"-style tales of haunted videotapes and whatnot. This time out, it's a haunted mobile phone game, which allegedly kills anyone who plays it. If you find that basic idea interesting - which I certainly did - then sure, the devs explore the notion from some pretty interesting and varied angles, and create a scenario compelling enough to keep you interested, at least for a while.
Having said that, I've now played through to two of an apparent thirteen endings, and I wouldn't say that either variant of the story lived up to the full potential of the premise. Whether other story paths would impress me more, I'm unsure, but for now I'm going to give it a break and come back with a fresher mind in months or years to come. No doubt many of you out there probably favour the kooky antics of these manga-styled visual novels more than I do - early Resident Evil games are about as kooky and Asian as my tastes generally get - so the more serious-minded of us horror fans were in all fairness never the target audience for this game anyway. It's certainly good of its type, I'd say, so take that statement as you will...
Another obvious question: is it worth two dollars? Yeah, sure. Especially if you're going to play through to all thirteen endings. A single playthrough is well under an hour, but you could still get a good few hours out of this game, easy. So there's no issue with the price, far as I'm concerned. As long as you're prepared for what is, ultimately, a horror game aimed more at "young" adults than real ones, you shouldn't be too disappointed. Just don't get your hopes too high, and don't expect to have too much agency over events (choices being fairly few and far-between), and you should be sufficiently satisfied with your whopping great two buck investment.
You could do better, you could do worse. Simple as that.
Verdict: 6.5/10.

Albert and Otto - The Adventure Begins is a good to great puzzle platformer that unfortunately ends a little abruptly.
The art style/atmosphere and the puzzle design are the two things that really stand out in Albert and Otto. The style of the game is remiscent of Limbo but the game does a good job distinguishing itself. The best part of the game in my opinion was the puzzle design. While the puzzles aren't that hard, the game does a good job mixing the different mechanics in order to make interesting puzzles that don't seem like more of the same. The puzzles at the end of the game in particular are really well done.
The only significant problem I had with the game is the length. The game is only around three hours long and ends abruptly at the best part of the whole game. Since the game is just one chapter of a much larger story this isn't that surprising. The game ending abruptly did leave something to be desired with regards to the story though since the story so far in the game is not great.
If you like puzzle platformers I think you will really enjoy Albert and Otto. If you should buy it at full price or wait for a sale will probably depend on how important game length is to you. I know I am interested in seeing how the next chapter of the game turns out.

This is a game I really want to like. The art style, and even the puzzle elements, are pretty reminiscent of Limbo, but presented in a longer format that lends itself well to developing a deeper story. Yet, after the completion of Episode 1 (a 2.5 hour adventure) we know very little, if anything at all, about the story or the world it is set in.  I find myself with more questions than anything else, and not in that intriguing "oh man I can't wait to see what all this stuff is" sort of way, but in that "seriously why am I even here" manner.
Some of the physics needs help. Your ability to levitate objects has a massive yo-yo effect on said object, and it takes far too long for the object to stabilize.  This is not a big deal in situations where you're able to solve puzzles at your own pace, but in many segments you have a limited amount of time and one shot to get it correct.  This is easily the most consistently frustrating element of the game, as your success is no longer just dependent on your skill.  Knowing what you need to do and knowing how to execute it count for little if your crate is bouncing everywhere and you're waiting for it to settle down enough for you to be able to place it.
The checkpoint system needs a revisit, as after a number of both purposeful and accidental deaths I've found that some of them are so close together I don't see any reason for them both to exist, while other segments go far too long without one.  The puzzles are well done on a theoretical level, however many of them have too many elements strung together that all leave zero room for error that they feel like they're cheating the player.  A segment towards the end of Ep 1 is rife  with these, where if you fail it on the first shot you die, or if you don't complete it fast enough on the first shot you're stuck and have no way to escape the situation other than resetting to the last checkpoint (which of course is waaaaaaaay back at the very beginning of the sequence).
To add insult to injury, holy glitches Batman.  I believe I spent more time raging at the bugs than at the unforgiving death puzzles.  I actually had to complete the last segment of obnoxious puzzles I just talked about three different times, because the first two times I completed it the cut scene that is supposed to trigger didn't do so correctly, and the game thought I had died. Not only did it reset me to the beginning of the segment, but actually to the checkpoint BEFORE that, and somehow also simultaneously broke the physics. I had to completely exit out of the game to get the correct physics back, then do everything all over again.  And then again.
I want to like this game, and I'll probably play Episode 2 in the hopes that maybe the issues that plagued Episode 1 are a fluke, but as it stands I can't recommend this game.

Overall, I do recommend this game, but I have several reservations. It is at once the most frustrating game ever concieved and one of the most engaging that I've played in recent memory. Check out the full review at Fanboyplanet.

Slash It is a game made up of 6 modes of play. The modes of play challenge you to type letters or numbers, or both, in the order presented to you on the screen. The game begins with a Classic mode, which requires you to match shapes in a timely manner. This is quite challenging at the beginning, but my reflexes improved gradually as I became accustomed to the shapes appearing in large and small sizes. In addition, the colors are constantly changing regardless of the mode you play.
After reaching level 5 in Classic mode you can begin to unlock Numbers mode, Alphabet mode, Twisted Numbers mode, and Twisted Alphabet Mode and Insane Mode. The electronic music playing in the background adds to the entertaining and challenging gameplay. I think that Slash It can help improve your typing skills after reaching the minimum level required to unlock other modes. There are Steam leaderboards showing high scores if you are interested in seriously improving your typing skills and become part of the top 10.
Other rewards offered by this game include 300+ Steam achievements and Steam trading cards. The achievements are easy to attain if you continue to practice getting the letters and numbers in the correct order presented to you.
Just1337, the developer behind Asteroid Bounty Hunter and other indie games, did a good job making a game that challenges your typing reflexes. They also did a good job with the entertaining aspect of the game by changing colors quickly and implementing electronic music. Therefore, the game is not boring at all. I recommend this game to those who want to be entertained with matching shapes, typing letters, and typing numbers, in a never ending challenging to increase your score. If you are an achievement hunter you would have more reason to buy Slash It.

Absolver is like a beautiful cake, hand crafted decorations on the surface arranged perfectly... but then you bite in to find it's a vanilla sponge with no filling.
= The GOOD =
The fighting is fun but punishing and requires you to learn how your chosen style functions. Crafting your own move set is easy and lets you really choose how you want to play; fast with small jabs and kicks, big punishing haymakers, maybe a mix of both?
The locations have a consistent muted palette that looks great and makes identifying enemies easy. It's one of those games where when you stop and look, then yes, you can notice the lack of detail in the far-off background but it never becomes an issue, you're focussed too much on your surroundings.
Grouping with players online is easy and quick and most of the community seems quite happy to cooperate, I have only had one instance of a player outright attacking me in the open zones. I have personally had only small issues with lag recently despite being in Australia and it seems to be when players with a bad connection are in your zone, which can be fixed by leaving and re-entering usually.
= The DISAPPOINTING =
The world areas themselves are small and fairly uninspired design-wise. There are very few "secrets" apart from a couple of spots you can drop off a ledge to get an item. The tutorial area has you busting down doors and beating a mini-boss to progress and this NEVER happens again. I spent a good portion of my first few hours testing every door I came across to see if I could do it again.
Learning moves sometimes just involves holding block til they finish they're combo, letting go to get your stamina back, then repeating til you've got it. It would have been better to have had diminishing returns on this method of gaining abilities so that to finish the last ~20% off, you had to actually evade/absorb/parry the attack a number of times.
There is no obvious way to gauge the strength of your enemies. There are a few "higher level" ones that are obviously wearing more flashy clothing but other than punching them to see how much health they lose, the only indicator would be to memorise their fairly bland character models.
Adding to the previous point, the vast majority of enemies have the same Lost Prospects mask, which is disappointing. The item descriptions hint at all these clans and groups but you never see any extra mention of them, it would have been nice to have see a visible difference between the NPCs populating each area.
Enemy AI is predictable in one-on-one combat but in groups they don't "soften" at all. In multi-player this is fine but trying to play single player, it means a group of two or three enemies are often more challenging than the boss NPCs.
Customising your character requires finding enemies with the clothes you want and grinding them to get the drops. There is also no way to actually drop any items from your inventory, so you end up with multiples of items that you're never going to equip.
= The BAD =
The majority of Absolver's progression is locked behind online multiplayer. This would be fine, but even getting to the first tier of rewards to unlock a new style means a lengthy, boring grind. This effort is way out of proportion to the speed at which you unlock other things and feels like running into a brick wall.
The balance on moves is woeful. There is an immediate "meta" around using the fastest possible attacks and using shockwave to distance yourself from the enemy to regain stamina and repeating the process, getting glancing blows as your enemy tries to dodge to create an opening. I understand there are established counters to this strategy, but it's so pervasive that it makes duels boring and frustrating. I wanted to play an interesting fighting game, not "Button Mash to Victory; $30 edition"
The single player content is an afterthought and the story is non-existant. There are a couple fights that lead with an interesting cinematic but to access them again, you need to complete (you guessed it) more bland online duels. NPCs you encounter in the world have zero personality and are literally just there to spout information at you.
The map presented in-game is confusing at best, only giving you the absolute barest of ideas where you are. The majority of the "marked ones" you have to defeat are put in side areas, not in the way of progression so they're easily missed and they're indicated so vaguely on the map you can't be sure if there are more than one in a zone or if you need to try find another path somewhere (Hint; there is only one per area.)
=========================
Despite being reasonably enjoyable at the start, I found myself becoming increasingly disappointed with Absolver the more I played it. There is so much potential here but it feels so much like they had an art style and a framework for the fighting system and just phoned it in on the rest of the stuff, there are just too many small things that feel underdone to the point where they drag down the bits of the game that are actually satisfying.

Absolver is very similar to Dark Souls, but also kind of like a wrestling game. You create your character, give him the combos and set him off into the world. The world is pretty barren, and can be very punishing and frustrating, much like dark souls. But much like a wrestling game, it is very fun and satisfying to use your custom character to demolish everything.
Absolver leaves much to be desired in the PVE.
The PVP also leaves much to be desired.
But the game is very fun, and for the price that I paid for it, I definitely got my money's worth. I look forward to continuing to play Absolver, and hopefully the dev's continue to support it, Absolver has potential to be great. I have seen many a good game die young because of low player base and because of mistakes the dev's have made. I hope Absolver is not another one.
I would reccomend Absolver to anyone that may have played old WWE games like Day of Reckoning. Or enjoy the Dark Souls games. However, if a rich and interesting story is what you seek, Absolver is not the game for you. Absolver is purely about the gameplay, go into it with that mindset and you shouldn't be dissapointed.

Absolver is a very fun game, I would be lying if I said I didn't enjoy my time playing it, but at this current point in time I can't recommend this game at it's current sate.
I won't be mentioning the current server issues people are having since I personally have not had many issues and I wouldn't be able to add much to that.
So, the game play, it's very well done, it's probably the most well done thing in this game (As it should be in a fighting game)
Essentially the game has a deck building feature that allows the player to create their own movesets, similar to GodHand, and the moves that you use in your deck are learned by fighting NPCs or other players and defending their attacks, blocking the attacks gives you a small amount of XP for the attack blocked, dodging the attack gives a bit more and using your classes defensive ability (For example forsaken has a parry and windfall has a spot-dodge) gives you a great deal of XP.
Each move has different effects and scalings, some moves are better at breaking guards, some moves scale higher with Dex, and some with strength.
On top of all that there area different stances that give you access to different moves, and your moves put you in different stances and there is also goldlinking were if you press the attack button at the correct time it will come out much faster and cost less stamina.
Now on to the meat of the game the PvE and the PvP.
Now the singleplayer is not that great you can beat it in a few hours, it took me about 6 (Most of that time was spent lost) and it consists of 6 mini bosses and 3 main bosses, all of which can be pretty easily beaten once you have a grip on the game mechanics, but their is a pretty cool feature with the encounter system, when you enter a area online you have a chance to run into other players and if you want you can help them or fight them making the pretty stale single player pretty enjoyable. You can also fight the 3 main bosses more times to get more of their gear, but to fight them you are required to rank up in the combats trials.
Speaking of the combat trials they are were my issues with the game start coming up.
Currently their is only one PvP mode you can play and that is 1 v 1, (I'm sure they will add more but we will have to wait and see how well the devs handle updates) which if there is going to be only one game mode that is most definitely the best one to have, but it can get boring after a while (But it is always interesting to see what decks people have came up with) and the rewards are completely random, for example you can get some really good gear (Like a shiny new mask) or some really bad gear ( Like the starting equipment).
Now this is a little rant I'm going to go off on, I feel like the justification for the poor single player being "It's a PvP game" is a pretty poor one especially since, with a bit more work the single player could have been a BETTER online experience than the current multiplayer, now one of the main issues with the singleplayer is how short it is, but I feel like another issue is how little incentive is put on player to player interaction during the singleplayer, like you don't really get any rewards for attacking and killing other players or helping them, so most of the time people will just run right past eachother.
Encouraging interaction between players in the single player would make it far better, and possibly distract from how short the single player is, just some small things would be enough like maybe if you beat a player they have a chance to drop a degraded version of the gear they are using or helping them and being a team could make it so you start learning moves they use in combat while helping them, obviously there are issues with both these but they are just some examples.
And making the bosses tied to you online rank instead of you overall level wasn't to great a decision, it just seems a bit unnecessary.
But the biggest issue that I have with this game  is the lack of content, right now the game just feels really barren and empty.
I really hope that the devs keep the community in the know and not leave them in the dark, that will kill this game fast.
This game can be really great, if the devs keep their promises and make them in good time (things like dungeons and more weapon types) it CAN become great, but right now I don't think it's worth buying, but I would recommend that you keep up with the game and see what updates and what plans the devs have for it.

Disclaimer:  this is a review for people that are on the fence about this game.  If you like visual novels, you probably already have it.  If you hate visual novels, it doesn't matter what I say and this game is probably not for you.  That said, let's continue...
BAD END attempts to sell itself hard as a survival horror visual novel experience, but I'm not seeing it.  First of all, each choice, which usually occurs after a ridiculous amount of dialogue riddled with sophomoric spelling and grammatical errors, will result in either continuing to play the game or dying right out.  Since you can save whenever, this is rendered a somewhat neutered concept.
There don't seem to be any choices you can make that have long reaching consequences.  If it doesn't kill you, you keep playing.  Even in the event something different happens, it happens only in the effect of changing the next paragraph or so of dialogue and that's it.  Most of the deaths are pretty lame as well and in no way scary, interesting, or creepy.
The main story and characters are also fairly generic and uninteresting.  So why play it?  Well, if you're looking for something a little more on the dark side and you actually enjoy visual novels, you'll probably like this.  However, I remain unimpressed, especially after playing games that get this formula right such as Magical Diary and Long Live the Queen.  And if you don't have those, I would get them instead.
I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes this type of games! :D

[TL;DR]
I wish I could give a neutral review. As it stands, I'm forced to give a negative one. 3/10
Is this game worth the full price tag?
It's really not that expensive at £1.59 so if you are a HUGE fan of visual novels and are not exceptionally picky it may be alright. If not, wait until you find it in a bundle or it gets a discount. I have seen free-to-play games which do a better job, though admittedly not horror-based stories.
[Actual Review:]
[Writing] The writing isn't great in a technical sense. There are grammatical errors as well as strange word choice. The characters don't speak naturally either. I doubt you'd shout "Give me a break already!" when running for your life but perhaps that's just me. Fortunately there's a 'history' button in the menu so if the wooden tone has lost you, you can pick back up on what's been happening. I've certainly seen a lot worse from other cheap VNs.
[Plot] Have to admit, I wound up getting distracted and idling at first. I didn't manage to feel much for the main character's initial grief. It was almost mechanical. Other characters and situations were simply flat. The nod towards a few Japanese horror films might be enough to keep your attention although it's very goofy. Pacing feels off. Just when you think the game could be about to pick up, you have to click through some tedious nonsense.
[Choices] If you dare to choose disbelieve early on then the game simply ends. I guess that's supposed to be cute. You have to act like a superstitious twerp to continue and despite the fact that the protagonist is described as sceptical on this Steam page, he honestly seems easily led. It takes a while to get to the choices and they don't always make much sense. If you look at the achievements you'll see they are all for getting 'bad endings'. Wish I'd taken the time to learn this. The whole point of the game appears to be what I dislike about it.
[Music] I turned the music off after a short time. I found it distracting. While I think it would work for an arcade type game, it took away from any sense of unease I could get from the plot. There isn't any seperate ambient sound control and I feel some extra background effects would have livened up a few scenes.
[Visual] The few characters who actually get shown are quite well drawn and the backrounds are decent. Unfortunately the text and its box look clunky in comparison to the rest. A font colour difference between the characters might have helped me focus on who was talking at which precise moment. I don't always need that but for some reason I found it hard to concentrate with BAD END.
[Conclusion] It isn't completely terrible. It's certainly not enough to keep me going but others might enjoy it if they go in with realistic expectations.

Purchased in a pack which included all three Alien Breed games in the series, each coming out to around 1 USD.  At this price it would be hard to argue that this game is not worth it for any fan of the genre.  There's probably closer to $5 worth of game here, possibly $10 considering the multiplayer options and also depending on how much of a completionist you are and whether or not you like to retread the experience at a higher difficulty setting afterword.
If you like top-down shooters this is a decent one.  Nothing groundbreaking (other than the aliens that literally break through the ground).  What this game does well is simply execute on a simple concept without trying to do more than the studio could handle.  The result is smooth gameplay at a high framerate that is fairly well-paced.  In other words: the game never gets in the way of itself.
I am a huge fan of just about any game that does not have regenerating health.  HP must be refilled through the use of different sized healthpacks which can be found throughout the levels or bought with credits in a pinch, though at a steep price.  Said credits can also be spent on ammunition, which is fairly cheap.  If you manage to be more conservative with ammunition & healthpacks, you will be able to spend your credits on a very barebones but appreciated weapon and item upgrade system.
Two caveats:
1) I recommend keyboard & mouse for precision aiming, but the default control scheme is trash.  See the screenshot on my profile for the binding setup I used that felt most natural.
2) The default camera rotation system for this game is clunky.  By changing one instance of "false" to "true" within a config file, this is totally resolved and the camera will then point in whatever way you are aiming your weapon.  Look in the Discussions or Guides sections for details.

A game in which you adventure up and down, your name is Tobe. Nothing more to say about this game.

is a retro platformer built around modern ideas. As the titular Tobe and his would-be girlfriend Nana, you embark on a quest to loot every island you come across and making off with as much gold as you can carry. A simple plot for a simple game, it sets up Tobe's most interesting feature.
Each level is structured like that of a cave, starting you off at the top and forcing you to make your way down to the treasure somewhere at the bottom. When you finally get your prize, the cave begins to collapse opening new paths and sending you scrambling for the surface before time runs out and you are trapped under the rubble. It's a cool mechanic that I haven't seen other games do, and works well given the somewhat nonlinear level design that lets you choose from several different paths going both downwards and upwards. Being able to run off one side of the screen and pop out the other also allows for more creative traversal, which is the game's strongest asset.
But aside from this much of the game is rather clumsy, especially in terms of controls and movement. Essentially you move as a mix of Sonic 2's underwater levels with the original Prince of Persia's acrobatic hijinks. Tobe can run up walls, slide under gaps, and dangle from hanging branches, whereas Nana swaps the wall climb for a double jump. This sounds great on paper would work fantastically with the open level designs, if only the characters controlled with any consistency. Button presses register only part of the time, your jump is terribly weak which makes scaling walls frustratingly unpredictable, and movement as a whole feels like Sonic plodding through a muddy swamp.
The second problem is the game is alarmingly short. I completed all 16 levels in just over an hour, which for the price feels quite insufficient. Theoretically you could double this time if you plan to play through with both characters, but they play so similarly I don't believe it to be worth doing so.
All the while I was playing I couldn't help but think how much
feels like a flash game awkwardly dressed up as a full game and put up on Steam as if players wouldn't notice. If it wasn't for the terrible controls I could still recommend it at sale prices, but unfortunately they ruined my enjoyment of the game and I wouldn't feel right advising others to purchase it. I'm quite disappointed to have to say it too because the level designs, art and music are not half bad, but a platformer with bad controls is like a sandwich without bread. It just doesn't work.

Based on a puppetry play, It's Spring Again is a form of interactive education designed to teach young children the cycle of the seasons. A smiley landscape adorned with equally smiley trees and clouds and weird creatures representing the seasons, will act out the passage of time to show the order and effect of spring, summer, autumn and winter in a thoroughly charming manner.
Interaction is fairly minimal and kept to clicks on the changing elements of the scene, or the occasional dragging of an obscuring cloud, while the whole process is narrated in a warm, endearing fashion. Though if this is a little advanced for some children, there's also an autoplay option, essentially turning it into a short animation instead.
The whole thing can be experienced in about ten minutes, and while I'm sure an argument can be made about the merits of it needing to be a game or even having a price tag on it rather than merely being a YouTube video or something, I can't help but be enamoured by how cute and adorable the whole thing is and forgive it any such issues.
For its intended "2 and up" audience, I think this is joyous enough to earn its recommendation... maybe even for a few people stretching the "and up" part of that suggestion, like myself. Though, all that said, if you're from the southern hemisphere then all of this is just a massive middle finger to you and nothing but horrible northern propagandist lies and should be boycotted vehemently... So there's that, too, I guess.

So, when this game first released it was riddled with lag and connection issues. It was region locked and it had very little to do in the world. Now that the lag, server, and connection issues are fixed as of today, September 8th, the game is a lot more enjoyable.
So, here's the thing. If you're looking for a 1v1 fighter that's easy to pick up and learn but difficult to master, this game is your game. The ability to create your own unique fighting "deck" is the best part of this game. Slowly learning the moves and then implementing them into your character to create a unique fighter of your very own is the best part about this game. The fights are intense and highly skill based.
There are a few cons, such as region lock and small world, as well as content locked behind PvP. I recommend this game if you're looking for a PvP game, not PvE.

The game has some nice touches. I was a huge Limbo fan and with that I have high expectations for other platformers. The art style and graphic details are really impressive and I love the music. As another reviewer mentioned the music is very chilled at times. The relationship between Albert and Otto and the extra abilities Otto provides you are very well done. When ever I had to put the bunny down I felt incredibly weak.
However this isnt a game for Novice Platformers, it is very unforgiving in parts and doesnt handhold you at all through the numerous puzzles. I love platformers and am not pro by any means but I am stubborn. I did experience a bug or two along my journey but nothing that stopped me from progressing. There is a lot of trial and error with many of the sections where you have to die multiple times in order to figure out what to do. But I prefer this to a game that I could complete in a single playthrough without dying at all.
I played/streamed this for 4.5 hours yesterday and didnt quite finish episode 1 yet but I am close. Probably around 150-200 deaths during this time with close to half of them happening on one very long sequence that takes 3-4 minutes where you can not make 1 single mistake. During this section you also have the most chilled music playing in the background which made me wonder if it was intentional to soothe the rising frustration levels.
The main criticism I have would be for the game to have extra checkpoints (Especially during the above mentioned section I spent over an hour on). I can definitely see people rage quitting this game at points and this is just the first episode.
Overall I recommend the game to anyone who is an experienced fan of platformers knowing that the game is not a cake walk. I would suspect many players relatively new to platformers may not last an hour without giving up.
I am looking forward to completing the game tomorrow and waiting to see what upcoming episodes bring.

It has great combat system which mixes simple controls similar to those of Batman: Arkham games with the complexity of fighting games and actually brings out a lot of complexity and nuance.
I recommend it to anyone who likes both card games and fighting games - especially if you're the type of person that likes coming up with strategies vs other ppl and continuously improving them as you see new flaws while versing different opponents.
For everyone else, I recommend keeping an eye on it and buying when they introduce more content and do some quality of life fixes.

This game is average, but I mean that in a good way. I've seen a lot of shady, sub-par VNs for sale and this is not one of them. Don't go in expecting the Mona Lisa, but there's a solid story that grabs you and sucks you in for a few hours of VN bliss. For $2, it's a no-brainer. Buy this game.

This game isn't great, but for $2 it's pretty solid. The writing's kind of bland and all the deaths and "bad ends" are very similiar, but the art is very good and I didn't encounter any glitches (just a lot of typos) which is actually pretty surprising for an almost free VN.
It does get kind of repetitive though, even for its short playtime. Almost all of the "bad ends" are obtained the same way, and otherwise the game's so simple I had to actually TRY to get them. And while I admire the writer's attempt to describe the deaths differently, they all boil down to basically the same scene. Even the "true ending" felt like kind of an anticlimax to me.
Also, don't go into this expecting anything actually scary. The characters are too full of horror movie logic/terrible survival skills to really get invested in them, and more of the plot centers on high school drama than anything particularly spooky.
All that said, it was still $2. It's definitely worth its price if you're just wanting to kill a couple of hours on a not-hideously illustrated VN.

BAD END has simple controls that are very easy to use and many saving slots so if you wanted to save every choice spots in the game, you could. The artwork is very pretty and very enjoyable. The grammar in the game was good, it barely had anything wrong in it and there wasn't any complicated words that you would need to look up to find the meaning.
