Having originally reviewed this game when it was released, I felt it necessary to alter my opinion of the game.
In the beginning, this game is incredibly difficult to get going - the computer always has an advantage, you suffer losses whilst the computer cannot (because it matches your rating) and ultimately you are going to struggle out of the gate.
But eventually the pendulum begins to shift in your favour - where you can optimise characters with the best weapons, armour and skills the computer tends to pick rather randomly (nothing says fun like a heavily armoured darksoul... with a dagger.)
The game's movement system is exceptional in design and really helps you strategise, trying to eek out a way to charge for 5 minutes by manipulating the system. The RNG, while incredibly rough, does eventually tone itself down to the point where you can survive the bad luck with skill.
Overall I feel with the improvements to the game and a bit of perseverence passed the initial setup the game is definitely worth playing for those who enjoy X-Com and other turn-based strategy games.

This is quite the interesting game. I got it, seeing how I've shown some interest in ArmA, I have a low-end PC and the game itself was pretty cheap. Needless to say, I was far from disappointed.
But to prevent others from being disappointed, let me make one thing clear:  This game, in terms of realism and style, is nothing, and I mean
like Call of Duty or Battlefield. Those games try to be cinematic and intense, leaning on explosoins and special effects that almost trump Michael Bay in terms of how ridiculous and frequent they are. ArmA, at least this one, tries to approach genuine military simulation, and it shows.
For example, let's look at the damage model:  A shot to the legs, you can't walk, a shot to either arm, and you can't shoulder-fire your weapon, a shot to the head? Well, unless you're a courier stuck in a desert, let's just say you won't be stumblign back up. For most, it's two pops and you, your allies, or your targets are dead; none of this life bar that slowly regenerates which the newer Battlefield and CoD games do for whatever reason. If you're hurt, you need to call a medic, no easy way out.
Also, vehicles. You can't just hop into a tank by yourself and go and wreak havoc. You must get into a vehicle, and depending on the circumstances, you must crew it (If it's a multi-person vehicle), rearm it, repair it and refuel it, call it your Three R's. Like with a tank, while there *is* a manual fire option, I suggest not using it, as it only aims in the direction that the weapon is last fixed in. So you must have a commander tell the driver where to go, and the gunner where to shoot. Operating on a team is absolutely
to winning. Which means team participation and roles are imperative to the gameplay.
My only qualms lay in the graphics and the voice acting. I've seen some pretty impressive titles come out of the year 2001, (Does the name "Halo" ring a bell?) and the graphics are blocky, choppy and overall unpleasant to look at. I like that they tried to make character models more organic; not just a bunch of cardboard stiffs, but for some reason the design of their faces make them look perpetually stoned out of their minds. The environments can look a little dull at times, and I can't help but look at trees and bushes that behave almost like cardboard cutouts--like pieces of paper being flattened as you run over them. However, building and vehicle models are rather well done, and guns look pretty good too. The voice acting sounds a little...odd. The way some of the folks in campaign talk in ways that almost seem hammy, Koslowski being the most poignant display of this in my humble opinion. However, I don't mind this too much. Even if the graphics are lackluster, at least it can run on my PC, which has a rather outdated GPU (Has 256MB VRAM, substantially less than the norm)
So, if you're looking for a good first-person shooter you can hop into, maybe this shouldn't be your first choice. However, if you want a game that gives you a realistic simulation of the different theaters of combat, and you want to live out what it must've been like in 1985 to see everyone's hate of the USSR before the Iron Curtain fell, and just to overall enjoy yourself in a good first-person shooter that you don't need a top-notch PC to run, then ArmA:  Cold War Assault's your game.
The game that pioneered present-day computer gaming.

Alien Isolation......But with the Waltons!!
Yep, I have learned to wait for a sale, but I'm glad I did, so my review is based on Value as much as anything
While It is still unclear whether this is actually a complete reboot or not, and the debate Rages on through a Thousand forums in all it's Geeky Fury, I personally feel that RE7 retcon's the series cutting out the events of RE 5 & 6, which are not bad games in and of themselves, but the series had become far too silly to  recover and seriously be considered "Scary" again.  In the late stage of the game you find a note about "Raccoon City Sixteen Years Later " in an area that has been abandoned for a least three years which would place this game around 2004 - 2005.   Personally I think it was a wise move to remove 5 & 6 from the Cannon - in much the same way it was wise to remove Fate's Carnival and Sacred Grove from the Mystery Case Files Cannon - so this seemingly takes place either shortly before or alongside the events of RE 4.
WHAT IT DOES WELL -
The main game is divided into Two very separate and distinct halves including Two optional mini games via video tapes Two mandatory Video Tapes and a really good "SAW" level at the half way point.
As mentioned above the first half plays, and feels, very much like a Hillbilly version of Alien Isolation but is still completely recognizable as Resident Evil with the crazy Jack Baker playing the part of the Alien or perhaps a Nemesis type character that stalks around attacking you on sight.  There is very little to do here other than run, hide and try to escape the house.  As also with Alien Isolation there are secondary enemies in the basement that act in the same way as the Working Joe did which can either be fought or avoided to survive.  Make no mistake this does bring back the scares and the tension, perhaps not on the same level as Amnesia or Outlast, but still a very worthy return to form after the series went from it's Campy Beginnings to full horror to complete farce.  Evidently the recent Campaign from a very rich and very Orange Man with Small Hands and a Bad Wig to "MAKE RESIDENT EVIL SCARY AGAIN" has definitely paid off.......or am I thinking of something else?
After escaping the house the Tone of the game changes drastically and becomes a lot more action based, very much like Doom or Dead Space.  Fans should know though that this offering does not place much importance of Boss Fights as there are only Two "Bosses" really (three if you count the SAW TRAP), that being, Jack Baker, Margaret Baker with the final battle with ALMA....ahem....I mean...."Eveline" being more of a Set Piece rather than an actual Fight.   BTW it's pretty easy to figure out which member of the Baker Family ALMA really is in the early stages (no, it's not Zoe).

Playing this on very high settings (both with and without the Depth option) this can't really be called "Photo realistic" as is claimed by Capcom because there are many really bad textures and patchwork backgrounds, in fact the Graphics were actually better on the Demo "Beginning Hour" for some strange reason.  Nevertheless this is very well optimized and by toning down the brightness, combined with the Washed-Out look of the color pallet this will make the visuals perfect for this game rendering the graphical shortcomings largely unnoticeable.  I can play this through my NVIDIA 870m at maximum settings perfectly smoothly with the only shortcoming being a time lag between the voiceover and the speech animations. Also for people with low to mid range rigs setting the frame rate at 30-fps is perfectly adequate (yes I also tried it on my older Rig and was surprised at how well it performed).


THE "NOT EXACTLY BAD BUT SLIGHTLY ANNOYING" -
Your character "Ethan" is rather wishy-washy and bland, often speaking dialog that is meant to be camp and humorous but is completely out of sync with the dark atmosphere of the game.  (Why are so many heroes in  Video Games always called "Ethan" anyway?!)
The music is well done but massively underused with long periods of complete silence making the game often feel "Empty" very much like RE ZERO.
Escaping the House and completing the first half was somewhat of a let down as the Vaccine you have been risking your life for doesn't work anyway, even playing both of the "Choice" options (again feeling like one of the pointless tasks in Alien Isolation).
As others have mentioned this is a very short game, my first play through on Normal difficulty took me  Nine Hours Fourteen minutes to complete,  and that was taking things slowly being careful to explore every nook and cranny, collect all the coins, destroy all the Bobble heads  and being careful to find and read all the notes and Diaries.  This I will admit after waiting all these years annoyed me a little but as I got the sale price I can accept that.

The DLC

Just when I thought that CAPCOM had completely redeemed themselves they go and pull a stunt like this and I am rudely reminded why so many people tend to hate on them!  Suffice it to say that most of the DLC content has clearly been cut out of the main game forcing us to  "Buy it at a High Price" and it just isn't worth it.  The best offering is the room escape which is will please fans of HO Mystery Case Files type games (or fans of "The Room" series).  In fact CAPCOM are so greedy for money that they actually Retcon their own game with the "Daughters" DLC which completely contradicts the story of RE7.  I'm sorry if this annoys people but to Retcon it's own story is such an obvious cash grab and is completely unacceptable.

Despite this I the game pulls through with no need for the DLC as completion unlocks the "MADHOUSE" mode which is much more enjoyable and challenging making it's short duration worth the effort.

I've just completed the story - honestly this is one of the best games I've ever played.
I hear a lot of people saying this is the best Resident Evil title since 4, myself being a fan of the franchise I didn't think much of RE4 as I know a lot of other fans do (though I can't argue it is a good game), for me the first was my favourite - I speak for both the 1996 game and the remake, I loved the pure survival horror aspect of both games, and in terms of survival AND horror this is the closest Capcom has come to achieving that thrill from playing back in the day thoughout all of the other titles they have produced since.
Reading previous reviews before I baught this one, I noted that someone (or maybe a few people) complained that the story was too short, personally I did not feel this way, not from my first play through at least - there is an achievement for beating the game in under 4 hours (as you would expect from a RE game) though on my play through I completed the game in 11 hours, searching around for any ammunition, medicine or other valuable item (and believe me, they're valuable)!
Every battle and encounter is terrifying, and I'd say I died in the majority of them - it's scary, it's challenging, the character design is fantastic (for a change! Capcom seems to have struggled on this aspect in the latest releases I feel) the graphics are excellent, despite that fact I was running them on what seemed to be quite far from the maximum settings as I tried this in the first few minutes of playing but experiened some frame rate drop, probably due to my 7-year-old gaming PC. The story itself is one to remember, whether you too are an RE fan (and have still not got this game for whatever reason) or have never played an RE title in your life, or stand somewhere inbetween, I highly recommend this game to you!

The worst aspect of this game though, is the shared screen gameplay, its horrible and unnessicary.  Give us both our own screens, and tether our characters to a certain distance of each other.  That way when I look one direction, my camera shows that direction, while his camera shows whatever direction he's looking.  Its much more helpful this way.  Though I'd still prefer not needing to be tethered to them so we can both walk around a bit, however this is another story that'd need to be discussed in discussions if the devs wanted me to as I do have ideas but, game being 7 years old I doubt it matters.
I just can't recommend this for anyone who wants coop and to play with friends.

Short version: Broken Expansion, Broken Achievements, Dead Multiplayer, Overpriced
The game only seems to work if you disable expansions and use the same very limited amount of buildings over and over, If you try to load a multiplayer game with more buildings enabled it spits out a connection error and from what I could gather this issue doesn't seem uncommon either. Without the expansions however the game loses a lot of replay value as there's just barely any variation.
The interface is fiddly at times and the auto-assignment of animals gets irritating very quickly since you have to wait until it's your turn again before you can fix the bad decisions the AI makes for you.
Achievements don't work (with the exception of "noob" for trying out the game) which is a minor nitpick to people who don't care, but since I care I want to mention it anyway: They don't work. Maybe they work in ranked games but if so they are probably the worst achievement ideas ever (and given that most of them have really low completion rates, I assume I'm not alone in this either). Trying to get into 1000 ranked games is very idealistic, winning 1000.. well noone has ever done it before, so go figure. Let alone you can't set a time limit for people to react to your moves (it's either short or a whole day).
But honestly you wouldn't want to play this game a 1000 times or more against people you don't know as there's just not enough variety. It's not chess where there is a lot of variety in terms of approaches. It's a casual fun boardgame intended for two friends or playing. Playing against someone you neither know nor communicate with takes away huge aspects of what makes boardgames like this charming. It just becomes a dull and dragged out exercise very quickly.
They are way better, less broken and more satisfying ways to waste 10 bucks.

A fantastic, smooth, adaptation of an amazing board game with support for Linux, Mac, and Windows.
Agricola: All Creatures Big and Small is one of legendary designer Uwe Rosenburg's better known games, and is well worth repeated play. This adaptation is a perfect translation of the board game to the screen, and I couldn't be more impressed.
My only complaint is that these developers don't have the licence for the full Agricola game, and haven't (yet!) adapted some of his other classics. I'd love to see At the Gates of Loyang, Ora et Labora, Caverna, or Glass Road here.

Agricola is a very good two player game and I like it very much. It is a low priced game that could entertain you for hours and hours in competative game play or just a few minutes per game to beat the AI or your best friend. It´s up to you.
"Agricola: All Creatures Big and small" is a good port from the board game to the digital world. Digidiced did it well to stay close to the original board game from Uwe Rosenberg. The game introduce you in the famers life by build up stables and pastures to gather and breed different animals. All rescourses living and natural have to be chosen wisely step by step as there is an opponent farmer on the other side of the fence that will go for their own good or constrain you in your effort to get your farm up and running. Watch out carefully what he is doing on the other side or follow up our own plan to win the match.
The game itself is divided in 3 steps per round and 8 rounds per game where you are able to choose to pick from different rescourses like wood and stone and wool or grassland or animals for breeding. Just a few samples - there are more available - you will figure them out easilly by playing the game. If you are stuck you could as well read the tutorial.
It could be played against another player in ranking style or by free game just to enjoy it. Matches against other players could be played right away in direct play or asynchron what will give you the time to play it over the day in any break or by free time in between. I really like this possibility!
You could play as well against 1 of 3 different AI´s from easy to difficult. If you are a rookie in the game the difficult AI will challenge you in different ways and tactics. Watch out what it is doing.
The game is including the first addon what give you the possibility to play with more than a dozen different buildings (4 by each game which you could choose by pick upfront or randomly by surprise) to bring up new tactics and possibilities.
The upside down of the game could be this asynchron play type that you could choose. Some people would like the way to play a handfull or more games simultaneously and are able to do it that way others won´t. I don´t think that it interfere the quality of the game itself what is really high and very well.
Just my two cents. Hope this review help you and I see you around for a farmers challenge. :-)

A very good port of the 2-player Agricola board game focusing on animal management. This is a worker placement game in which you only have 3 workers and during a round each player takes turns choosing a market space to place one of their workers. Each market space can only be selected once during a round, so you need to weigh out what you need vs. what your opponent might need and sometimes it's a better strategy to deny your opponent a critical resource space rather than advance your own needs. At the end of a round there is a breeding phase and if you have enough farm space, you increase your livestock count. Any excess livestock that can't be accomodated, are lost.
Building your farm involves placing workers on market spaces that give you building abilities such as fencing in pastures and placing various building upgrades to hold more livestock. Scoring is based on the number and variety of animals and building types and pastures you have at the end of 8 rounds.
The game features multiple levels of AI, a tutorial, and online multiplayer. I started an online game and had an opponent in just a few minutes. The multiplayer utilizes steam turn notifications which makes running multiple online games a breeze.
The game comes with a free game dlc. Highly recommended for any Euro-style board game lover.

The tutorial is good. I also wanted to see the written rules, so I checked the board game manual on the net. For the moment, I'm still a beginner and I played against the AI (three levels of difficulty). The game is fun, not too difficult to learn, with interesting strategic possibilities. This adaptation is essentially the same than the mobile version (I think), including the extension.  I just have minor nitpicks: it's written "tap" on the first screen, and there are no tooltips for the first menu buttons (at the beginning, I was wondering how to continue a game in progress - second button on the right). The graphics are nice enough, close to the board game, and the music and sound effects fit well with the theme.

As someone who has been traditionally partial to medieval armour, weapons, and aesthetic, I originally didn't think style of warfare in the early modern period or the "Black Powder" style of warfare prominent in the 17th and 18th centuries was particularly fascinating and appealing. This was largely due to the inaccurate portrayal of the grim realities of warfare in contemporary period works at the time. however, as a history major who became acquainted with enthusiasts, connoiseurs, and aficionados of this style of warfare. it was their presence which inspired me to take the time to learn about the politics, warfare, society, and culture of the 17th and 18th centuries. it was through my studies that I came to understand how intense the aesthetic and experience of warfare was during the early modern period of european history. most artistic interpretations by the period of warfare's contemporaries as well as much of our modern interpretations of this style of warfare in both games and films make little effort in the way of expressing the visual, physical, and emotional brutality and intenseness that many young men and seasoned veterans had to face in the early modern period.
advancements in military technology such as those made in firearms and artillery transformed the face of warfare forever as opposed to the melee and armourcentric style of warfare that happened in the middle ages and the renaissance. Thus, with these new technological advancements came new, and might i argue, scarier and more visceral kinds of human cruelties and brutalities that made fighting and killing far in excess of the limits of the raw powers of the human body. The human element of warfare was also highly elevated in response to these new evolutions in the nature of warfare. with the advent of military drill and training, the physical and mental fitness and discipline of the soldiers of this period were arguably superior to the serjents, men at arms, archers, and crossbowmen who peopled the infantry of the medieval era. with the exception of the aristocratic knights who were trained from birth to be expert killers and equipped with the finest weapons, armour, and mounts. medieval infantry to the best of scholarly observation and research were fairely weaker and undiscplined in contrast to the line infantry and footmen of the early modern period, who were typically organized into a line of battle and were expected to depend on discipline and sheer individual courage to hold the line of battle in the face of opposing firepower.
However, the novelty that I came to appreciate most about the warfare and military aesthetic of this time period was the surprising amount of melee and close combat that was used in this battle, with the development of the lighter, more efficient flintlock muskets and the extinction of renaissance "Pike and Shot" formations in favour of the plug bayonets and their later innovations. regiments of line infantry would often resort to close combat or melee, which would remain strategically and tactically sound both as a means to save ammunition and fight on terrain where "The lne of fire" would be a strategically unfeasable means to fight an opponent, such as the narrow corridors of an urban settlement, strategic bottlenecks like the crossing of a bridge or the breach of a fortress, or even certain narrow and uneven terrain where froming a line of attack would be impossible due to the strategic limitations of the terrain. The other occasion where close combat and melee would also remain in a position of strategic and tactical importance in this age of warfare would be through the use of cavalry. while black powder warfare would influence the strategic and tactical use of cavalry with smaller firearms such as carbines and pistols, close combat cavalry charges with "cold steel" such as sabres and lances would continue to be the weapons and tactics of choice for many, if not most generals in the 17th and 18th centuries.
This understanding of the strategic and tactical importance of close combat and melee in early modern warfare would be enough to spark my enthusiasm for both the warfare and history of this time period. however, in coming to understand the aesthetic innacuracies of modern portrayals of medieval soldiers and warriors. i have come to realize that the rise of standard issue military uniforms is a novelty of early modern european warfare in this time period. and thus, military attire of this period was both aesthetically superior to all its predecessors from the medieval and classical periods, and would remain the alltime epitome and gold standard of military attire that would serve as the foundation and inspiration of later forms of military uniform.
Lastly, Through my personal understanding of the military expoits of the French Emperor and General Napoleon Bonaparte and his experiences leading french armies during the revolutionary and napoleonic wars. I have come to believe, taking into consideration napoleon's love for classical greek and roman military history as well as his mathematical expertise in understanding the nature of probability and calculated, strategic planning. That the individual tactics and overall military strategy of the black powder warfare of the 17th and 18th centuries centuries are largely inspired by scholarly research and understanding of military warfare as practiced by the ancient greeks and romans. The rennaissance, or the beginning of the early modern period in the 15th century was marked by an intense fascination and study of classical texts from ancient greece and rome. while originally preserved and interpreted by the literati of the roman catholic church, a growing secular interest and interpreation of these ancient texts was beginning to take prominence amongst the scholarly community of the renaissance onwards which would affect and improve all manner of life and society, and warfare and combat were no exceptions from this advancements made in the study of these antiquated texts. the organization, structure, tactics, and strategic docrines of the black powder warfare the 17th and 18th century were arguably inspired by scholarly research and interpration of greek and roman military treatises and manuscripts as well as the personal military exploits by classical greek and roman generals like Julius Caesar, Alexander the Great, and Leonidas. Both the Impact and influence such texts would have on the developments of early modern warfare would be epitomized in Napoleon's battles such as rigoli, austerlitz, and liepzig, and toulon where application of the principles behind Spartan, Macedonian, and Roman military tactics would would result in triumph for napoleon and the french empire that would result in france being the first european country to dominate europe since ancient rome. Due to the multitude and the genius of napoleon's many military victories, his battles and military exploits would continue to be studied in the presitigious setting of military academies to this very day, and the accounts of napoleons military triumphs and those of generals like him, as well as the treastises and manuscripts by military theorists of the time such as carl von clausewitz would serve as the foundational material for which all aspiring military officers to this very day continue to study as a means of developing a knowledge base for military thinking.
In conclusion to all my points. My studies of the politics, warfare, and military theory of the early modern period have opened me to chossing this game as my alltime favourite total war game. even moreso than medieval II total war, my traditional favourite of which I have spent 2000 or so hours on. For all of you who enjoy swords, armour, and melee, and hack and slash style rpg and action games, I wouldn't recommend this game to you unless you have the openness and curiousity to learn about and appreciate the political and military history of this time period.

Getting it out of the way right away, DD: N has a catastrophic bug that users seem to have pinned down to anyone playing on Windows 10 with an Nvidia graphics card. Due to what seems to be a memory leak issue, after a short while the game will crash to desktop. 3rd party programs attempt to fix this problem by increasing the amount of memory available to the program; this increases the time you can play before it crashes but cannot truly fix the problem. The longest I could play this game before crashing with a patch was about 1 hour 15 minutes. Without the patch, maybe 15-20 minutes at a time.
Outside of that issue, the gameplay is fairly standard fare for a Beat 'em Up. It might be my overall lukewarm opinion on the genre in general, but I find it incredibly boring because of the same uninteresting combos you use for the entirety of the game. Variety is attempted through constantly introducing new enemies and environments as you play, but you don't really handle them any different, so I don't know if it really matters. Final thoughts on gameplay is that it feels like a chore you go through to see the rest of the game, after the game crashes (always at the end of a level, of course) neither I nor the handful of people I've played it with feel any desire to replay the level.
Gameplay out of the way, though, and the game has a really nice feel to it. That "mock 80's retro" feel played up to 11 gives you something to smile about throughout the game and the soundtrack -- by the wonderful Jake Kaufman --  is a treat. I'm also a fan of the antagonist: Skullmageddon, an over the top Skeletor-like villain. I hear that the ending credits are simply amazing, but as I can't get the game working long enough to beat it I haven't actually seen them.
While the aesthetic is charming, the incredibly repetitive gameplay and horrific bug(s) that nobody thinks they need to fix make this game something I can't recommend.

BAD END is a short (about 90 minutes for completion, longer for all achievements) visual novel with horror themes and an emphasis on player choice. Something unique about BAD END is that you are playing a visual novel about a character playing a visual novel, and the visual novel they are playing is called BAD END. Failure in the game within a game not only ends with the protagonist dead, but the person controlling the protagonist dying in real life (and by real life, I mean in the story of BAD END.) Confusing, I know.
There are a large number of possible endings (at least 14, as far as I know) though admittedly, some of the endings are a bit samey. Unless you are using a guide, it will take you a few playthroughs to get the true ending to the game. When you do receive this ending, the game will then grade you on your performance in the first playthrough, and only the first playthrough.
Why exactly is a visual novel grading you in the first place, and why only on the first playthrough, during which you cannot possibly be expected to know what you are supposed to do? When you consider that most visual novels lack any type of scoring system, that only the first playthrough in an almost entirely luck-based game counts, and that you are not given any warning you are being graded until you reach the true ending, the idea is pointless and obnoxious at best, and a middle finger to the audience at worst.
The artwork is nice, with each character having two sets of clothing and a variety of facial expressions. Music is good. There is a CG Room and Music Room, though there are not a lot of CGs to collect. I would have liked the option to view the backgrounds from the game as well.
I wouldn't say the story was scary per se, though it was tense at times, especially when you are late in the game and are trying to avoid one of the titular bad endings. The story was interesting enough that I wanted to see it through to the end, and I was satisfied by the resolution. There is a bit of foreshadowing and a small sprinkling of red herrings, but overall the story is fairly straightforward. The English translation is solid, although there are a handful of typos it never got to the point that I could not understand what was going on.
For the game's price of $2, I can readily recommend this game to fans of visual novels. BAD END is not perfect, but it is worth playing.

This is my first review.
Mordheim is absolutely my very most favorite tabletop game of all time.  I love just about everything it has.  I love the feeling of scarcity.  I love the brutal, unforgiving nature of that terrible broken city.  I love how your heroes grow and develop only to eventualy succumb to wounds, madness or death.  It is dark, and it is amazing.
This rendition of it did get some things right, a lot when I truly consider it.  However, I can not recommend it.  It simply has no soul...  It is immediately a grind from the very beginning and nothing else.

Yes, you will get some new units unlocked and some slightly better gear.  Yes, your units will level up, get skills and improve.  Yay!
The game made it feel as if none of that really mattered.  You will never encounter the same warband you fought before.  They are all random.  You will never enter an engagement against anything other than a superior foe.
I like hard games, but I also like a game to make me feel something other than annoyance.
Here's what happened to me.  I made a whole bunch of different warbands.  I tried 'em all.   Started with the Skaven, but couldn't get them to work.  They were really fast and could kind of use that to determine where the battles took place but they just seemed too fragile to keep up with constantly superior foes. Chaos way too random.  Really liked Sisters of Sigmar, but seemed to get the furthest the Empire.  Had everybody in really heavy armor.
Ended up in a fight with the Sisters of Sigmar.  Did freaking great/  Didn't lose a single guy and filled up with a lot of wyrdstone.  Awesome!  Wait...  where is this last enemy? The leader?  I creaped around through a few buildings ready to fend off an ambush but nothing emerged.  The computer was thinking every turn, so I thhought the matriarch must be moving.
I found here in an attic right in front of the only ladder, too stupid to come down.  Because I had found them largely useless, none of my guys were packing ranged weapons and the only archer who could do something a little bit useful sometimes was wounded.
That left me with three choices:
1.  Accept every single one of my units as a casualty because I had not lost enough units to voluntarily rout.
2.  Start a new warband as the game does not allow for loading previous games.  I am totally fine with this concept.
3.  Quit the game because I didn't like the first two options.
I chose number three, and that is why I cannot recommend this game.

I know it's been 7 years since the release but after buying the whole trilogy mostly out of nostalgia I had to write a review even after all these years. This review goes for all three games despite that initially I only played ep2 (check it in my library if you don't believe me). I upgraded the whole trilogy recently because of the cheap price and because of the name.
I am a huge fan of the original Amiga games. I played the floppy disc versions so much that my discs stopped working and I had to get replacements from the store (yes - floppys could malfunction after being used a lot). I was hyped when a new one was announced finally but unfortunately it disappoints. Not because of core gameplay - that is okay. nothing exceptional but very solid. It disappoints because of lack of polish:
1. Sound and Music.
This is my biggest gripe with the game. Everything feels like it's placeholder for an unfinished product. Speech is emotionless and is queued in game (and cutscenes) without any sense for timing or drama, whatsoever. Some effects are over the top while others are way too quiet. All the sounds are super minimal. Music is completely absent. It feels like there was no budget left so things were handeled as cheap as possible.
This is the thing that keeps the player distanced the most because it never pulls you into the game into the first place.
2. Muddy to no accentuation in the environment
The art in general is absolutely fine. Animations are smooth, environment (especially for a low budget 7 year old title) are very detailed. The Unreal Engine 3 renders as crisp an with nice effects as one expects.
What doesn't work at all is that gameplay targets can't be made out in the environment without referring to the minimap. Terminals and interaction points blend into the uniform environemt so good that you have no choice but to walk near with help of the minimap and wait for the interaction text to appear when you get close to the target. This is no fun and it's bad design.
Gunshots feel solid until you shoot aliens. Then it feels like the shots are fired in the general direction and the enemies (like B-movie actors) just drop dead when they think they should be dead. Gunplay feels like it has no impact.
You shoot in a general direction while the laser pointer even shines ABOVE the aliens. So you actually feel like you shoot the air above small enemies. Still they just drop at some point.
3. Minor gameplay decissions that interrupt the flow.
Nearly all interactions need 1 or 2 seconds. You can't just explore and grab stuff. you need to stop to interact for everything that doesn't lie around in the open. And each interaction takes time. It's like the game couldn't decide if it wants to be a tactical game or an arcade shooter. Ultimately it fails at both.
Also there's only checkpoint/terminal savepoints.
On the other hand there are a lot of good things to be said as well:
1. Art and details
The art is really detailed. The environments are fleshed out and look superb for a 7 year old low budget title. The artists gave everything it seems.
2. controls are fluent and snappy. No sloppy, sliding things. Everything that needs to snap at angles snaps and everything that needs precission has enough precission. Switch between gamepad and mouse/keyboard works without any problems.
3. Local 2 Player coop. Not many games still have that today.
4. The levels are not only linear corridor runners like so many newer games. They are in a very similar style of the other games from the 90s even though the environment types aren't as varied.
5. It's a new and official Alien Breed! The core gameplay stays intact. Find money, shoot aliens, buy upgrades, search for keycards.
Ultimately the lack of polish drags the game down and keeps it from being fun.
I love you Team17 and I hope you do manage to release another one without these problems.
Ultimately I still cannot recommend it except for hardcore fans.

Slash It is a game made up of 6 modes of play. The modes of play challenge you to type letters or numbers, or both, in the order presented to you on the screen. The game begins with a Classic mode, which requires you to match shapes in a timely manner. This is quite challenging at the beginning, but my reflexes improved gradually as I became accustomed to the shapes appearing in large and small sizes. In addition, the colors are constantly changing regardless of the mode you play.
After reaching level 5 in Classic mode you can begin to unlock Numbers mode, Alphabet mode, Twisted Numbers mode, and Twisted Alphabet Mode and Insane Mode. The electronic music playing in the background adds to the entertaining and challenging gameplay. I think that Slash It can help improve your typing skills after reaching the minimum level required to unlock other modes. There are Steam leaderboards showing high scores if you are interested in seriously improving your typing skills and become part of the top 10.
Other rewards offered by this game include 300+ Steam achievements and Steam trading cards. The achievements are easy to attain if you continue to practice getting the letters and numbers in the correct order presented to you.
Just1337, the developer behind Asteroid Bounty Hunter and other indie games, did a good job making a game that challenges your typing reflexes. They also did a good job with the entertaining aspect of the game by changing colors quickly and implementing electronic music. Therefore, the game is not boring at all. I recommend this game to those who want to be entertained with matching shapes, typing letters, and typing numbers, in a never ending challenging to increase your score. If you are an achievement hunter you would have more reason to buy Slash It.
My Score: 8/10

Now then.  It started out well-adorable kid has a nice birthday with mommy, plays with a mildly disturbing talking teddy-nice way to do the tutorial, by the way-goes to bed with ONE BITE of cake!  NOOOO!!!!  Cue it was a dark and stormy night, and we're on our way.  The on-edge creepy feeling of being a 2 today year old during a thunderstorm was very nicely done. I adored the magic paitings.  Sound was used very well, and the storm!  I LOVE when a game has good storm effects!  I got about 3/4 of the way through-yes i got stuck, hence my long playtime-and then it just fell apart.  At the very end of the closet level, it just bugs out for me.  I could not get past the trench coat man, no matter what I tried.  It was a disappointing failure in an otherwise enjoyable game.  So, I never got to finish it.  That was the good.  Now the bad.

Many times I curse the fact that crawl is Crtl, which is right next to the Windows key, and therefore had me hitting it by mistake at the worst times.  There were some notable graphical fails, which had me falling through the floor of the world.  It was too dark, and I had to blast gamma to see anything at some points. Negative reviews: "lag, 0/10"
Positive reviews: "Brilliant game with an in-depth fighting system, highly recommended"
I played this game, as of writing, for about 30-40 minutes. Discovering that my discount, four-year-old off-brand controller didn't work with Absolver, I filed for a refund. While it went through, I figured I might as well play it a little bit. Perhaps the kb/m controls were decent.
And decent they were. Playable, at the very least, though the website explicitly states that it recommends a controller. After 40 minutes of playing through the starting area, I was hooked. Despite lag issues (caused by my weak PC and their servers in equal measure), odd mouse controls, and my own general lack of prowess in fighting games, I had a brilliant time. The fighting is very satisfying- each punch and kick landing with an audible thud that makes them feel weighty and powerful. The combat deck system rewards careful planning, and the wide variety of moves ensures that no two foes will fight the same. Sure, the single-player campaign is short, but the meat of this game is in the online (which, though it lags, is being worked on by the devs).
Ultimately, I'd recommend this game, but not without a few caveats. OCE servers are either nonexistent or horribly laggy, and server connection in general isn't the best (though the devs have repeatedly expressed that improved servers are currently their #1 priority, and are making progress towards better servers). Player count has dwindled from 18k peak on day 1 to about 2.5k peak as of this date (9/8/2017). But if the devs can pull the servers together, and the community supports this game, I can see it becoming something excellent.
I appeal to the developers of this game; if you do not want the game to die, improve it: release additional content, add donat (this is for your benefit to improve the game) and follow comments.

Most of the grievances are due to:
1. Server instability
2. Region Locks
3. Short Story
4. PvP centric game
Servers, the server stabilty has gotten better, you can connect and play with friends, do some online pvp but there are still issues that spring up. Disconnects don't happen as often, and you do get some rubberbanding occasionally. I can tell the staff is working hard to fix the issue and I am confident they will soon.
Region locks are going to stay as far as I know.
Short Story, yes it's a very short story. But alot of the fun in the game comes from the gameplay, the combat, refining your deck of moves, and mastering your craft against npcs and players. What at first seems completely out of your ability to control, later with a greater understanding of the nuances of the combat system reveals you can control alot more than you realize. So if you play games because you enjoy the gameplay, this game will keep you very busy. I've logged a decent amount of time well beyond what it takes to complete the story and I keep going back because it's fun and there is still alot to learn and master.
Beyond this, the staff does plan on expanding the amount of Absolver content in the near future.
PvP Centric game, because this is a pvp centric game there will always be alot of complaints and mixed reviews due to the nature of the PvP genre. It's difficult to satisfy a community centered around PvP, where most people just aren't able to compete or can't invest the time needed or won't invest the time needed in order to master the game. Few people can admit they just aren't good at something and chalk it up to the game, saying it's a bad design, or it requires no skill,  or it's just button mashing. But the truth is, they just couldn't compete and got tired of losing and didn't want to invest the time required in order to get better. You are going to die alot, you are going to lose alot, not everyone is honorable in their victories, or their defeats, sometimes they like to rub it in your face. That's just how people are, learn, grow,  adapt, and keep at it and you'll do better.
Overall I'd recommend this game for those of you who can not only see the potential this game represents, but also who enjoy pvp, who enjoy a good combat system, and those who want to truly master the game because you enjoy it. You will need to learn to weather defeat and grow stronger because of it. For those of you who don't have the patience or desire to do so, I would say move on to something else.

Bad End is a horror Visual Novel within a horror Visual Novel. You'll play as Kyuuhei, a boy who tries to uncover the mysteries behind his best friend sudden death. The only thing he knows is that his best friend played "Bad End" - a Visual Novel that is supposed to kill you in real life after you get a bad end in it - in his last night alive. Has the game anything to do with his death...? Are the rumors true or not?
This game is a short non-kinetic Visual Novel that's not frightening nor too exciting, but I still liked it. It's unintentionally funny and there are quite a few mistakes in the translation, but nothing too serious to affect the plot comprehension. You can get multiple "bad endings" and one "good ending" based on your choices. I recommend you to play it trying to get as less "bad endings" as possible before getting the good one, so it can be more challenging.
It was a short but pleasurable experience.

This is a good game for Japanese leaners. I got well over ten hours of fun reading practice for $2, and I still need to do another playthrough to fortify vocab. This seems to be aimed toward middle - high schoolers. (The hours count it shows for me isn't accurate because I left it running in the background a lot)
Pros:
-There is no automatically advancing text. All must be advanced manually.
-There is a dialog log that shows past dialog lines.
-If you have two monitors, you can have dictionaries and whatever else open on the other one, and you can move your mouse between the two. The game doesn't even minimize, just pauses.
Cons:
- Some hard Kanji usage. For example writing かわいそう as 可哀相. Who does that??
- They took a lot of liberties with the English translation. It's not very helpful to play the English and Japanese versions side-by-side. Sometimes it helps, but not often enough for me to bother with it.
I liked the story too, though the ending was kind of a letdown. There may be a better ending that I just didn't get. As for the horror aspect, it's pretty tame. It's a creepy idea, but not very likely to keep you up at night, and there aren't any gory scenes or such, none that I ran across anyway.

This doesn't seem to be a very popular game and with only 18 reviews (at the time of writing this), nearly half of them are negative. It seems that most of them are complaining about the unresponsive controls or glitches, which is a surprise to me because I never actually had a problem with either. I suppose there are a few minor bugs, like the options returning to default every time you open the game up again, but it's certainly nothing that interfered with my experiance. I did however have to re-map the keys. It wasn't much trouble to do, but it made the largest difference. The way the controls were originally set up made the game very difficult and hard to navigate the character. For anyone that may be having the same problem- I set it to the WASD keys for movement and J, K, L for running, jumping, and to use balloons/ropes. For me, this method worked perfectly.
Something I didn't like about the game the lack in variety between the two characters. You can play as Tobe, his girlfriend Nana, or have both of them at the same time as a sort of co-op if you have a friend in the room. This will be an impossible feat though unless one of you, if not both, have a controller. Many people in the other reviews very positively recommended Nana, and I don't understand why because although she can double jump, her controls are very clunky and over all, she just feels incredibly clumsy to handle and harder to navigate. She is much slower even when running, and therefore she has a has a harder time getting through timed gates and getting away from enemies. Although her double jump can reach places Tobe can not, I still didn't find Nana worth playing as because Tobe can just use a rope. On top of that he is much faster, more agile, and has wall run which is over all much more useful. Nana also had a very strong and strange weakness that caused a lot of deaths and added a difficulty to the game that it did not need. When she is hanging from a rope or a ledge and jumps, the first jump does absolutely nothing. She gains no vertical altitude from it what so ever and falls straight away. It is only the second jump that does anything, and it barely does much. It definately does not have the same effect that her double jump has when standing on a solid surface. So I would not recommend Nana, but Tobe is very acrobatic and acrobatic, and will quickly over come obstacles and climb things with a very stream lined feel.
I feel that I should also warn about the lack of depth in story. Although this won't bother everyone, some people like a more immersive story. You get a brief slide show about Nana wanting to look for treasure, forcing Tobe to go with her who just wants to stay home and play video games, and then upon completing each world you get a short scene each time that more or less says "The treasure isn't here. It's on another island" sort of thing like how Super Mario Brothers did with, "Your princess is in another castle." The way they did the story did feel natural to the game and fit in. I thought it was cute, but looking back on it, I do wish there was more to it but I guess with a simple retro style game as treasure hunting, you don't really need a complex story.
This game does not have much replay value, and it isn't some amazing experiance, but I do recommend it because it's still very enjoyable. The platforming is very fluid and fun, and it was a great feeling to just rush through the level without much of anything slowing me down after some practice.

The regular campaign missions have a number of small glitches/errors and can feel quite arbitrary. Said errors sometimes hamper you, sometimes the AI. It says something that for a while Sisters of Sigmar gangs caused me grief because I would have to fight their impressive warriors, whereas I normally relied on them being stuck in doors. Similarly, it helps to pretend certain other glitches are actually intentional - your best warrior spawns in a room with no exits? He obviously fell victim to a trap or similar etc etc (Incidentally, that happens quites rarely, and i'm not bitter, honest). Annoyingly, everytime an update has come out it seems to have brought at least one new glitch with it, but generally it's a pretty shiny game so i'll be quiet on that.
What makes me unreasonably angry and is going to lead to me walking away for a while (I'll probably come back, I'm a sucker, but i don't guarantee it) tends to be the story missions. As a rule of thumb I don't write reviews but, while I've never felt so euphoric I've been tempted to write a positive review for Mordheim, every other story mission has made me consider throwing the computer out the window and dancing around the ashes. Why? Sometimes it's the same glitches combined with the extra difficulty and the fact that failure nets you dead and mutilated party members but no material award. Mostly it's the extra special glitches they roll out just for the story missions - key items that don't spawn, or they don't register that the character has them, or the character is killed and no-one else can pick it up. I could go on, but the item issue is the one that crops up most often. I also take issue with not being to check who is carrying what, but that would just be convenient and I can at least overcome that with pen and paper.
As a final note, I will say that the glitches really are peculiarly evenhanded. In a previous storymission, tasked with setting free 2 sisters of sigmar to aid me in defeating an all powerful magic used protected from outside harm, said magic user  attempted a spell and was instant killed by a miscast about five minutes in. But just like I don't really want to beat other gangs because their impressive warrior gets confused by corners, I don't really want the occasional plot mission handed to me on a plate to counterbalance all the ones that are exercises in futility.

This is not a game. It is a stress and disappointment simulator. There are no tactics - only luck. There is no fun to be had, but by the time you realize that you will have too many hours of play* to get your money back from Steam.
*Play is used very loosely here. You will spend more time looking at load screens and waiting for the computer take its turn than you will spend actually doing anything. I would often get up and leave my computer while 'playing' this game because a 5 minute wait for my turn bored me.
The game often freezes up during the computer's turn, and the developers don't seem to respond to bug reports. After 3 patches the issue persists. The worst part about the bugs is that you have to force-close the game, and the game thinks you are cheating, and so when you load that save your characters all get permanent stat penalties (which is part of the game).
The controls are slow and not designed for computer. You can't click, you can't mouse over for information, you have to cycle through disorganized lists.
There are four warbands to choose from but they are not balanced. No matter which one you pick the result is the same: there is one enemy you will always win against, and one enemy you will always loose against.
The game is not tactical. If you go up against the warband that your warband is weak against you simply cannot win. If your character takes any amount of damage they may end up with a permanent disfigurement (loosing an arm and not being able to use weapons, loosing a leg and not being able to equip armor, loosing stats, loosing skills, etc). Your chance to deal damage to an enemy will hover around 50%, but even with 95% chance to hit I've had characters miss 5 times in a row and then die. You don't get control over troop deployment. You don't get to choose what type of mission you go on or what the objectives are. You can't see the whole map, and even what you can see is grainy and hard to decipher. When characters enter melee you cannot have them retreat - they must win the melee or die.
There are warbands designed for stealth, and there are character classes designed for stealth, but you can only win by killing every enemy - so any character that is not a fighter is pointless. There are characters locked behind a pay wall (DLC they say) but you will have to fight them even when playing single-player, and good luck doing that without the paid DLC to counter them.
The single most annoying part of the game is how your characters get punished as you play regardless of win/loose. Did you win the encounter? That's good. But did any of your characters take even 1 damage during the encounter? Yes? Then lets see what disfigurement they get! Turns out your archer lost an arm and can't use bows any more, your fighter lost a leg and can't use armor any more, and your mage took a permanent -5 to intelligence and can't use some of their skills until they level up. Congratulations on winning!

I think this is truly excellent game, with a unique, well thought out take on turn based combat.
Set in a rich (and slightly terrifying) environment that never seems to be the same map twice, thanks to the random(?) generation of traps, bridges and the destruction of structures.
The 4 factions are well balanced and allow for surprisingly different play styles, thanks largely to their standard passive and Warband specific abilities (when you create a warband you'll see what I mean). Also, the DLC warriors are great. They add a real dynamism to the Warband.
A word of warning though. This game is very unforgiving. You will make mistakes, you will overextend at some stage, hungry for Wyrdstone, your warriors will be permanently mutilated or die. Accept that. It is what makes winning a battle so exciting and losing so upsetting.
If I could give the old me advice (250 hours ago), it would be:
Never do maps where your Warband is scattered randomly - you are leaving them in the hands of the Gods
Wyrdstone is everything - try to do maps with the highest Wyrdstone rating possible, balancing difficulty.
Fill every slot - hire all the warriors you can and rotate them to gain experience. It may take a little longer but that way when one loses a leg or gets brain trauma or dies, you won't be too upset.
Be patient - Money is hard to come by and good gear doesn't begin to appear until at least level 4. That's fine. A time will come where you have all the money you want and can really invest in skills that suit your Warband and the gear you have.
Lastly, thanks to the devs of this game. You clearly care about the game and the lore of Warhammer. Very good job.

This is one of those games that I want to give a "Meh" or "So-so" review, a more neutral score.  For the sake of the fact that I enjoyed it more than I was bored with it I'm giving it a positive review, but for the most part this isn't necessarily reflective of my own opinion of the game.  I'm probably going to do an in-depth video review of this in the future, once I acquire the two sequel games.
Pros:
+ A decent twin-stick shooter
+ A budget game, you can get this on a college budget
+ A very smooth game, no bugs encountered beyond the intentional enemies
+ Fairly cool level aesthetics, especially with the final chapter
+ Short n' sweet, you're getting your money's worth.
Cons:
- Game gets repetitive up until the fifth chapter, most of the levels look similar despite each deck having its own "theme" to it
~ Enemy roster's far from perfect (though for a short game it's understandable, kinda)
- Way too much ammo lying around
- Flamethrower was best weapon when at damage upgrade, while ion spike was nowhere near as good (two shots from a default Ionspike could damage the boss, when only three were needed from a fully damage upgraded laser rifle, which is far from nominal)
~ Story was completely meh, though its presentation of comic-like cutscenes was okay-ish.  You aren't even given an explanation about why the aliens are there, though I presume this is explained in the later games.
Bonus Points:
+ You explore a space hulk at the end that's a derelict ship built by whatever company designed yours, so awesome.  This is why it's getting a thumbs up instead of a thumbs down, because Space Hulks are kind of my fetish fuel
+ Aliens look like giant-sized four-legged ticks, which actually looks really great IMO
+ Flamethrower's the best weapon on the game (PURGE THE XENOS!)
~ Pistol animation makes it look like you're holding a shotgun instead of a deagle, which is amusing
+ Has co-op, so if you have a low-budget friend you can play this with them too (haven't tested it yet)
For what's essentially a revision/remaster of an old title with modern graphics and engine design, Alien Breed: Impact is not that bad, though it isn't perfect either.  Fans of the old game might enjoy their time with this, and while fans of the twin-stick genre might find its controls appalling it's alright if you want a cheap 5-hour time waster.  However this is one of those games that I know I would have had much more fun with if it was an FPS.  If Team17 wanted to remake Alien Breed: 3D I would totally play it.

Alien Breed: Impact is the first part of a trilogy of top-down arcade style shooters that I got in a bundle who knows how long ago as "Alien Breed Trilogy." You can get it by itself for $10 from Steam, or you can get it along with its two sequels - Alien Breed 2: Assault and Alien Breed 3: Descent - for $23 as Alien Breed Trilogy.
For those of you who have played Alien Syndrome on the Wii, this was EXTREMELY reminiscent of that game, but it plays much better than the Alien Syndrome reboot in my opinion. You play as Connor, a generic space marine-turned-chief engineer on a ship that's going somewhere for some reason. They don't really tell you why you were doing whatever it was that you were doing prior to the events of the game because about 10 seconds into the opening scene (all of which are done in a really great comic book style), your alcoholic pilot crashes the ship into some monolithic "ghost ship" that's just drifting through space.
So anyway, after your idiot pilot crashes your ship into some ancient, derelict dreadnought, killing like 90% of the crew, you go off to see what's what. Oh, and your character is a racist against synths. Cheers.
You explore the ship, trying to get systems restored when OH CRAP there are bug alien things trying to eat you. You start off with just a pistol (unlimited ammo) and an assault rifle (very not unlimited ammo), but the first few aliens you encounter are just stupid little ankle biters that you can kick to death with one hit. You start to see the giant bug-aliens that want to use their spiky alien mandibles to butter up your fleshy human pooper real good.
One thing I do want to note is that this game plays MUCH better with a gamepad. You can totally play it with a mouse and keyboard, and I'm sure that there are those who prefer that control scheme, but I found that an Xbox One controller worked far better for this game than a traditional PC control setup. The controls are about what you would expect from an arcade style shooter. It's almost a twin stick shooter in that you move with the left stick (obviously) and aim in a two dimensional circle with the right stick, using the right trigger to fire and the left trigger to use an item (medkit, grenade, etc.). You use the left and right bumpers to change the camera perspective. There's also a co-op feature, supported by both local and online multiplayer, but I didn't play around with that.
This is not a complex game, nor is the story especially interesting until the end (in the last of the five chapters, there are some things that, if you pay attention, will make you say "Hmmm, why is that there?"). It's a whole bucket of alien-killing fun, though. You've got five weapons from which to choose - your pistol, an assault rifle, a shotgun, a laser rifle, and an ion gun. Oh, and a flamethrower, which is straight up sex. All of these weapons can be upgraded three times - one upgrade for fire rate, one upgrade for reload speed, and one upgrade for attack strength (which is the only one that I ever bothered spending credits on).
Now then...the flamethrower. Imagine, if you will, mixing the taste of your favorite food, the sound of a creek gently flowing over pebbles, and the sensation of vigorous fornication with your anime girl of choice, all blending into one euphoria. That euphoria is what you feel when you use the flamethrower in this game, ESPECIALLY after upgrading its firepower. It's just....bliss. Pure, unadulterated bliss.
So here's basically what it boils down to. Aliens, arcade shooters, co-op, and flamethrowers - if you like any of two of those things, then you need to get this game. Like, yesterday. It's really great, surprisingly so. It feels like one of those gems of a game that manages to use a low budget to hit the "sweet spot" of gameplay, atmosphere, and charm that no $100,000,000 AAA title could ever quite emulate.

I've played Alien Breed before. I have it on my XBOX 360. I picked it up because it was cheap and I rather enjoyed it. Controls are tight, graphics are fantastic on high resolution, and the tension is pretty palpable as you get deeper into the levels. Being a big fan of isometric shooters, I instantly dug this, but it's far from perfect. Alien Breed suffers from major pacing issues. Just when you feel like you're moving forward, you find yourself backtracking to activate security measures to get access to a room. There is a lot of backtracking in Alien Breed and it never feels necessary or really relevant to moving the game forward. It's just there to waste more time. The other thing that is slightly irritating is the camera movement. It's not smooth, its done in eigths by tapping the bumpers on the controller. I would have much preferred a smooth sweeping movement with the environment camera. That being said, I still really enjoy the Alien Breed games, and at the prices when they're on sale, they're a steal!

Remember why I've thumbed down the game? It was because I couldn't identify some nuances and because no color had a name somewhere to help whoever had color problems. Since then, the developer managed to correct that - he was very understanding of that and here's the result: the update I was waiting for.
However, there is still a warning: I've played
. Avoid this one. If you really want a digital color book, spend on your money on Discovering Colors - Animals.
So let's go change a few points.
Steam is opening itself to other customers and I can see that many educational games are also sold on it. While it's true that the platform isn't for all ages, parents are using their account to buy them and generally, they're keeping an eye on what the kid is doing. For a so young audience, I can point to It's Spring Again and Big Thinkers Kindergarten.
What's Discovering Colors - Animals?
It's a coloring "interactive" book. Indeed, the kid choose an animal, colors it with the pencils proposed and when they're done, an animation is triggered either automatically or manually - depending on the current mode.
Indeed, you can find three modes: coloring, free and painting. Sorry if it's not corresponding to the real English words but I've played it in French.

It means that if the kid begins with Painting, they can let their imagination run wild and then compare with the vision of the developers through Coloring.
But these creations can't be exported. If you want a trace of them, you need to take a screenshot (as advised in the info menu). If you don't, when exiting the drawing, everything will disappear.
There is also an editor where the kid can draw what they want, with all the pencils unlocked. Again, you can't save his creation. You need to take a screenshot (Steam allows you to take screenshots easily, luckily).
What does change now?
Apart that finally, an adult struggling with colors is now more at ease to identify them and to explain them to a child. There was a color I couldn't identify as being light brown or grey, now, I can say that it's brown. I could also be picky about some colors but I'm pretty sure that my mom will disagree with me, as she's more accurate for that than me.
Now, the title isn't misleading anymore: you can activate an option that will allow an audio file to play with the name of the color. Each time you're clicking on a pencil, the name will be played. I'm just a little disappointed that the voice is well-known as it's like being read by a computer. But hey, it's already better than nothing. And for the adult, it's a lifesaver there if (s)he had indeed problems to identify them.
The animals are easy to recognize though I'm wondering why there is an alien in them. The only missing thing here is probably the name of the animal (no need to have an audio file, however, the name to color could be nice). But well, if the aim of the developer is to let a maximum of freedom to the adult, I'll concede this point: it will be less confusing for them to recognize an animal than a color.
Now, while I do think that there are probably more opportunities to improve this PC/Mac version (like the animation in the end with a little story, little facts about the animals or the colors), the developer listened and managed to find some alternative to make sure that a larger public can play it.
Discovering Colors isn't expensive and can amuse a child. Right now, it has stepped up above a simple coloring book on paper. With the new option, it's making it more interactive. And despite the cold and metallic voice, the audio option, which will probably make some crazy if you switch too often in a short span of time, is really what was missing for me to provide a thumb up.
There is room to improve a game and the developer managed to see that: even the mobile version will be updated. I'm glad to have discussed with him - we didn't have a problem to discuss easily as we're both speaking French, the language being our native one.

By the time I reached the later difficulties my experience when playing the game was at its max. My character's stats were appropriate to the difficulty and the game became fair and less frustrating. Steam, we need a neutral button, for the love of Pete's sake.

But honestly it felt like they took what could have been a very interesting concept and watered it down into something else entirely.
One big issue I had with the gameplay was that once you die, you either start over completely from the beginning of the entire game and have to hold down your mouse for literal ages (and re-choose from previous dialogues), or you have to start from where you left off at the last save point. The latter of these options still consists of holding your mouse down for ages.
Speaking of the mouse thing, there is a LOT of dialogue. If you like reading, you might like it. I struggled with reading it all, but did, and while the story itself was okay, the scripts and playout in the end were not so much to my liking.
This really comes down to personal taste and by all means, if you think you'll like it, you just might. I'm really on the fence about saying yay or nay and just out of that experience I had I have to go nay. But it's not a concrete thing. The game reminds me of Hell Girl in a sense, and that's why I feel it would have done well as an anime. But as a game, it left me looking for closure. And things without closure are hard to enjoy for me personally.
It's not bad for what it is, it just isn't for everyone. I can't recommend it unless you're okay with a lot of reading, okay with backtracking when you fail, okay with holding down the mouse for long periods of time and repeating many scenes, or, alternatively, you're going for the achievements/cards/whatever and following a guide.

"BAD END" is a short Visual Novel with some Horror elements in it.
I certainly would not consider it to be an actual horror VN.

The spooky ghost villain is also pretty,

it's just a black creature who has the embodiment of a human.
I feel like this was merely done to make the work easier for the developers,
not having to create the actual monster.
There's also a huge lack of character models for side characters.
I also would like to point out how conceited the whole game feels. It's so self-aware.
First you're kinda okay with it but after a while it just gets weird..

The soundtrack is decent and artstyle is alright. Neither of those certainly aren't bad.

I was also positively surprised about the text barely having any spelling mistakes,

Characters aren't very likeable and their actions are pretty abnormal,
and reactions are unnatural and bizarre.

Artstyle is alright, but you might want to check some screenshots out before you purchase this.

Unlike other Games Workshop based games of recent years, this is not an attempt to translate the tabletop game directly into a videogame.  Some people who were hoping for that have been disappointed, but personally I think a direct translation would have been nearly impossible, and in the end probably less fun.  And it is fantastic fun.  Creating and customising a warband is very enjoyable, and the battles themselves are fairly short and sweet, so it's a good game to dip into for half an hour.  Each warrior will progress in both positive and negative ways as they accumulate experience and injuries, the horrors of Mordheim both hardening them and taking their toll on their minds and bodies.  That will mean that your warband will be unique in subtle ways, and you'll get to know each member.
The lore and atmosphere of Mordheim are lovingly recreated and you can tell there is a lot of love for the original here.  The cityscapes are absolutely beautiful and although scenery often gets in the way more than providing many strategic options, some maps change things up wonderfully with multi-floored indoor areas being a particular favourite of mine.
The game, they warn, is 'hardcore'.  Battles won't always be fair, and losing can have dire consequences.  For the most part this works well, though the sheer number of ways in which a character can be randomly screwed over, often permanently, sometimes makes you want to quit and start over.  Losing a limb, for example can make a character next to useless.  It would be awesome if there were some crazy ways to try and heal such wounds, say with erratic healing spells or mechanical prototypes with chances to add another level of random craziness to battles.
It was exciting to be a player of an early access game with regular updates and news, from a team who really listened to player feedback.  There's a lot more that could be added to the game, in fact it seems a waste not to develop further with such a deep and unique framework.  The product as it is is magnificent, but it is absolutely ripe for further add-on content especially additional warbands, as I think 4 is the absolute minimum they could have got away with.  It gives lots of variety as a player, and many strategic options in multiplayer, but it certainly gets repetitive seeing the same few bands of enemies in single player mode.  Perhaps an old-fashioned 'expansion pack' would be a better idea than small pieces of DLC, as lots would be willing to pay to expand the experience with any kind of new content.
In short, it's brilliant.  Maybe the best game ever made within the Warhammer universe.

However, once you get the hang of it it's pretty easy to keep your warband alive and thriving.
The customization is great, both visually and the way you can level up your heroes and henchmen to fit different roles. You're constantly leveling up your characters, finding new armor and weapons, and new runes/enchantments, which makes the grind of the game worth it.
