This is a semi-incomplete review as I've only recently started the game, but I've been impressed enough to comment on it so far.
A puzzle game? A find-it adventure? An extradimentional platformer? A fox-hunting extraviganza with seemingly no fox? I forgot, but I'm starting to get drugged looking at it.
This game is quite trippy, once I realized it started doing some... bizarre things... perspective tricks? Impossible rooms? Maybe the fox knows more about it? Ask him.
Who knew that a game about making disjointed polygon errors could be so intreaguing? And perhaps it's because it's consistent with the Japanese folklore of the bizarre world of the gods? Of course we are talking foxes here. There is nothing straightforward about them, and if you like their tricks?
They have plenty for you.
As far as my criticism on the game, I'd say the devs hit a home run on the art style. This game is ideal for a toaster regardless that it's 3D, but the color pallet really sell this extradimentional realm. (I sadly hate red to yellow color pallets, does Blue Fox have a blue temple I can go to sometime?)
Otherwise, the music is nice, but the eastern chant mock-ups get a bit old. Perhaps intentional because... madness? Again ask the fox, I don't know.
-------
Whatever else I figure out about this weird yet intreaguing gem of a game in the meantime will be down here in a log.
Update: I've now completed the game, and yes I can indeed say that this game is the trippiest thing I have ever played. It lacks a shiny coat of paint, but it's writing kept me laughing, gameplay kept me engaged, and surprises left me baffled.
I can say the music criticism remains. I like the blend of ... oddly Jamacan sounding chant with acoustic guitar. But of course, it will get boring to listen to after some time.
I kinda wish it would have had a dynamic tracking, such as a new track or instrument that plays when you do things right? Maybe when you pick up one of the red statues? Either way, it wasn't too bad.
There is no level editor, but the story is what is there. A level editor wouldn't really make the game last much longer. You'll probably take over 20 hours to complete the main part of the game if you take some time with figuring out puzzles? They can be quite time consuming. The ending was quite worth it, and the title screen credits song is awesome.
This game was quite an indie gem for a puzzler, and it's sad that it's semi-gloss polish is probably what keeps it from being more popular. The use of Japanese fox folklore sells this world though. Even though the voice felt budget, the writing made the monk believable. The fox's actions made him likeable. And I'd totally buy another game with this theme and writing that went into it. The further and further I played, I really felt as if the fox was watching and actively playing tricks on me with his oddball world.
Perhaps you should play a trick on him to save him from his madness?

FIRST IMPRESSIONS MATTER
(After struggling with the control scheme and overall repetitive, boring gameplay, I lost all desire to continue playing, hence the low play time.)
Early impressions are everything and unfortunately Phantom Halls could not deliver. After initially enjoying the paper-craft aesthetics, it became clear Phantom Halls still needed a lot of work at this point in Early Access; a risk of playing games in active development.
Boring, repetitive gameplay and clunky controls are at the heart of my overall sour experience. Navigating the halls of a randomly generated mansion feels the same every time as you fight the same enemies, search the same drawers, and open the same doors. The game supports active combat but feels cheap, light, and un-impactful.
Searching for gear is heavily RNG-based, which is fine, but standing even a small chance against certain enemies will require a fire-arm, and if you don't find one early on you might as well restart. The exploding bugs were the main cause of my frustration -- blowing up in your face within melee range forces you to take them out from a distance -- damn near impossible without a gun.
Still, it's early days and the developers could turn this around. As of the date of this review, it's merely a phantom of its own idea.

It is an excellent strategy game. As a warband within the walls of Mordheim you are tasked by superiors to retrieve a substance froma meteor that's all over the city, while combating rival bands and improving your troops.
It's strategy, so you'll move units around a battlefield and combat and pick up items and resources, pay tribute to your benifactor, and upgrade your team. However, given my complaints, it might be better to call it a rouge-like strategy.
Your higher ups will demand some wyrdstone, you will go out to complete the order, and get paid for it. RNG will kill your team. You will try to hire more people. You will run out of money. You will be stuck without money and without units and your superior will still demand more until game over. Over and over and over again. Plan to fail in the face of an awful system of routine pain and suffering if you want to get to the delicious center where all the excellent strategy and gameplay lie.
An auto save system keeps you from save scumming, which would be a mode in another game, allowing for a variety of people to enjoy the game any way they want. As it stands, it serves only to frusterate as men you pay to fight fail and fall over while trying to complete basic plans. A 90% chance to hit is closer to a 50 in the eyes of the RNG gods. Watch people you've put hours of work and skill into die because they were randomly put next to an ogre. Observe nights of effort put to the flame by lucky crit.
Some people are into that, and that's cool, this game will cater to you, and I can reccomend it. The rest of us are left kind of disappointed we spent money on this.

I have a love/hate relationship with this game, but I can't bring myself to rate negatively. I will, however, be leaving a lengthy review explaining my opinions of this game.
First of all its one of the best tabletop to video game conversions I have ever played. The play mechanics are superb and feel refreshing for a turn based strategy game, aside from the RNG.

The overall look and feel of the game are excellent, it is a great blend of horror and strategy. Great graphics, awesome artwork, cool noises, amazing voice acting, and genuinely creepy.
Yes the game can be immensely challenging and unforgiving, but that is one of the best parts. Real true consequences that you will be feeling the effects of for a long while to come, so play smart, be cautious.

The downside of the game is really that the AI, although incredibly tough, is incredibly stupid. Every match is basically a Zerg rush. The AI will throw everything it has at you (aside from one guy who will wander around aimlessly) right at the start of match.
The goal of the game almost entirely revolves around collecting this precious green crack called Wryd Stone. The AI is not at all interested in doing that. Instead they will mindlessly pursue you like ravenous zombies.
If they could improve the AI, wherein they actually cared about collecting the Wyrd Stone, as the game implies they should, and used some genuine strategy instead of 'walk straight at the closest enemy and kill' strategy it currently uses then this game would be huge win.
Another sore spot is the RNG. I suggest you keep a pillow close by to bite on because you will be getting royally ♥♥♥♥ed in the♥♥♥♥♥
The RNG seems to purposely want to cause you to smash your computer in complete rage. I have lost numerous battles, where I overwhelmingly had the tactical advantage, simply because my team would continually miss attack after attack and take every incoming hit right on the chin till they where all decimated.
There is little to nothing you can do about the RNG except pray and pray. It completely sucks the idea of 'being the smarter tactician' right out of the game. They should add in some fail safe so you can only miss so many times in a row or something along those lines because it seems no matter how likely your odds of landing a hit are its always a 3/10 chance you will actually land the hit... especially when you really really need to land that last freakin hit!
Lastly, I absolutely love the fact this game has multiplayer support. Although it is neigh impossible to find a match unless you join a community group that host pvp tournaments. It may have been the saving grace of the entire game if not for the fact that multiplayer is not balanced at all.
Every faction in multiplayer has some super cheezy tactic or advantage that will make them OP depending on what lvl your currently fighting at.
Early on the Skaven move so far and fast they can easily swarm, poison, and kill half your team before you even get to move. Later on the Sisters will drop comet after comet, after comet, after... you guessed it more comets on your head till you have two guys remaining that they quickly surround and flog to death. Late game the Mutants if played right, will have uber mutations giving them more strength and health than anyone making them a wall of flesh and claws that will pound your face, body, and soul into the ground.
If they where to improve AI, add a more forgiving RNG (so the game is more based on tactics than luck), and tweak the multiplayer balancing this game would be absolutely amazing. For now I suggest if you like tabletop games, turn based strategy, Warhammer, or are a masochist get this game next time its on sale.
I'll be looking forward to updates... if there are any.

Well, I went back and tried the game again to see if anything had been fixed.  It's still the same.  Unplayable.
There is a lot to like about this game:  atmosphere and graphics being the best selling points.
Unfortunately, there is an awful lot to dislike about this game:
1) the RNG is a joke.  The 2nd time I quit it was after 16 consecutive to hit rolls of over 90.  That's 16 in a row, people.  One of the biggest mstakes the dev team made was putting the actual die results on the screen. It simply allowed me to see EXACTLY how awful the RNG truly is.   Over the course of 5 games I tracked every die result for each type of action.  I saw very little difference between action types such as "to hit" vs. "climbing."  But I wanted to track if there was a difference.  After averaging my "to hit" rolls, I found an average roll of over 80.  That's not even an attempt at randomicity.  IF you are the kind of person who enjoys constant failure at easy tasks...then this game is for you!
2)  the variety of warbands is unacceptable.  I am a long time tabletop Mordheim player and loved the variety in the warbands. Here we get 4.  The Sisters have been solely relagated to a melee warband (they removed their sling option) and also removed perhaps the coolest aspect of the Sister...the steel chains.  Oh, well.    The Mercenary warband is one that wasn't even an actual warband in the original game, and here is just a watered down version of mish-mash of all of the other warbands that existed.  The possessed are unplayable becasue the mutations are random and one cannot actually plan/develop a warband because the random mutations ruin warband members so thoroughly that the only answer is to fire them and start over.
3)  skills are just a waste.  Pick a single attack and rank it.  Ranking more than one is a waste of time as you will never use it.  The passive skills are MUCH more useful.  Most skills are completely useless since you have limited slots for skills.  As a result, some skills that you may find quite useful ...such as helping you climb, will NEVER be taken becasue they are not worth the slot they use up.  A a result, at least half the skills could be removed from the game and it would have no significant effect on gameplay at all.
4) the compensation for a good AI is simply the fact that every warband you face is better than yours.  Generally, a lot better.  More hits, better damage, faster; everything.  As many have said in other reviews, the game has a steep learning curve, but is not as impossible (in general) as many here seem to feel.  BUT, the huge advantage the AI has in strength, makes this game a series of gambles more than anything...pull the lever and hope you win and aren't ambushed.  Which leads me to the next thing...
5) Ambush.  This breaks the game entirely.  When you are ambushed, the AI starts in range, usually goes first (due to the fact that they are simply better than your warband) and can take out 2-3 members of your warband before you even get to make an action.  This is essentially the game devs implementing a feature to knock the player down a few pegs by randomly killing some of their warband.  Such fun, let me tell you.   Spend hours upon hours building your warband only to be ambushed and  permanently lose 2-3 members of your warband before you even get to make an action.  Such awesomeness.    Which leads me to the SINGLE RNG factor that succeeds more than it fails...
6)  When your Warband is being utterly destroyed, you have a MUCH greater chance of making your route check than ANY OTHER ROLL YOU EVER TRY.  You will miss attack roll after attack roll and fail all of your ALL ALONE checks, but when it comes time to make that 20% chance to NOT route...you make it.  Thus ensuring you get to hang around for at least one more round and risk losing even more warband members.  The ONLY way I can explain this is that it is a purposeful inclusion in the game to ensure the utter destruction of your warband.
In conclusion, I think the devs are sadists.  I can only imagine them laughing themselves silly as players continually struggle against their plot to kill them at every turn.  They probably lay bets on how many players have launched their mouse against the wall in utter frustration. Additionally, I think they are lazy.  Dudes, just make a better AI...don't take the cheap way out and simply overpower the player with overpowered adversaries and rigged die rolls, that's such a chicken**** way out it makes me sick to my stomach.  You are expecting people to give you money for your product; have enough respect for your customer to put the work in that is needed to justify the money you are making.  If that's too much to ask, you should find a different line fo work.

TL;DR:
Mordheim is a good game for those who want the masochistic torture it offers, despite its clearly imbalanced nature. It can be immensely satisfying when victory is achieved and you come home with your pockets lined with Wyrdstone. It can also be bitterly frustrating in the moments when victory is stripped away from you. I've had a lot of fun with it, I'm just not sure how much torture I can take.

Among the Sleep has very little dialogue but manages to create a wonderfully frightening setting for you to play through.
You play as toddler and as you'd expect you'll find no shotguns or laser weapons to defend yourself. Just good old fashioned running and hiding. The world around you is big and scary as it would probably seem to a defenseless child without his parents and yet upon closer inspection you'll realize that appearances can be deceiving as nicely presented in the first moments of the game which will set the tone for what's to come.
From a gameplay perspective the game offers a short 2-3 hour run (including the free 'Prologue' DLC) but has a really nice and open to interpretation story to tell which I will not spoil here. The main focus of the gameplay is basic puzzle solving which range from easy to extremely easy. There's nothing really challenging here which in the context of the game feels like a natural expectation. In fact the hardest thing for me for the entirety of the game were the really awkward controls and handling of the main character, but again you'd not expect a toddler to be able to run and jump like a ninja so even here it fits within the theme of the game.
You are also accompanied by your talking teddy bear which will assist you through your journey. There were a few great moments between the toddler and teddy which make for more character development than I've seen in AAA titles with 10 times the gameplay duration.
Graphically the game is not something I'd praise; nonetheless it succeeds with the simplicity of the Unity engine to create a very fitting atmosphere to get lost into. Ambient sounds and music merge well with the gameplay and what little voice acting is there, is excellently done. I'll truly say that there are several moments in the game where you will feel scared and alone and that's something that is the result of the excellent work the developers did by intertwining several simplistic concepts.
Despite its short duration, lack of replayability (besides getting the collectibles) and how easy it is, Among the Sleep has charisma in its presentation and a fascinating albeit polarizing story for the player to interpret. A solid recommendation if you want to experience a couple of hours of a nicely made adventure/puzzle game.

TL;DR: VERY solid core with fun Souls-Like combat and exploration, but lacking in content that the developers say they will add in for free at a later date.
Absolver is another one of those "Souls-Like" games that keep cropping up every now and then on Steam, but I would say it's one of the better ripoffs... err... adaptations of the SoulsBorne formula.  In it, you play as a martial artist called a Prospect on a quest through a ruined kingdom to prove that you have what it takes to become an Absolver (which I believe is like a hybrid between a ninja and an Interpol officer).  The combat in this game is fluid, fun, and intense, and truly does make you feel like a bloody ninja as you punch, kick, chop, and elbow your opponents to death with perfectly timed combos that you can construct yourself (or find on the internet somewhere).
My only issues with this game are the connection issues (which are partly to do with the placement of a whole lot of wood, walls, and other crap between my rig and my router) and the huge lack of content, especially in the end-game.  It has the same problem as Destiny, where it feels like I'm paying $30 for the tutorial.  However, Absolver seems to have learned from that little Bungie blunder and has decided to make most - if not all - future DLC free.  I actually have an idea for a set of potential content additions.  I call them "Absolutions," and they're very similar to the strikes/raids from Destiny and World of Warcraft and the Chalice Dungeons from Bloodborne.  Basically, you (and for some, a number of friends or randoms) are called in by the guy who gives you the Absolver Cloak at the end, and you're tasked with completing a large mission.  This mission could have a premade map or a randomly generated one, but they will always involve exploration, puzzles, some dialog trees (maybe), and LOTS of combat, and would even have their own stories to flesh out the world of Absolver more.
Terrible match making.  Pros vs noobs all day.

Honestly, I was very skeptical about this game in the months leading up to its release. It's so satisfying to pull off a perfect dodge or parry and knock out an enemy with a huge right hook or roundhouse kick. Bosses can be intense and deliver that same sense of urgency you get when fighting a boss in a Souls game, and when you beat them it feels great. I know server issues have plagued this game from the start, but I'm confident they will sort them out. I hope the developer keeps adding content and sticks around with Absolver, it's some of the most fun I have had with a game this year.

I enjoy all of the games set in the world of The Dark Eye; except for this one.  Why?  Well, there is almost no story to speak of, and the game seems to be only superficially related to the world of Aventuria as far as I can tell, but the main problem with this game is the excessive degree of grinding required to reach the end.  By level 50 or so, you have to literally fight dozens upon dozens of battles which don't give you ANY experience (enemies 10 levels below your character don't offer experience), which wouldn't be so game-breaking if you the shopkeeper offered weapons that were anywhere near as good as the ones you find along the way.  You essentially have no way to improve your chances for later battles.
I can't count how many times I've fought through over 80 enemies (none of them giving me XP) only to face one or two that DO give XP and then die shortly thereafter to begin the grind again.  On my last run, I fought over 300 enemies without gaining experience!  This is unforgivable game design in my book.  It wouldn't be so bad if you could skip past the many experince-less battles to the enemies that you are "on par" with (who are all MUCH stronger than you), or if varying your strategy actually made a discernable different to the outcomes of battles.  I only held out as long as I did in hopes of getting the last achievement for Steam...
As much as I wanted to enjoy this, I can't recommend it.  Maybe if it's on sale for a huge discount and you're extremely bored...

Awesome 2d scrolling shooter/shmup. The art's pretty good and the old west theme works well. If you haven't heard of bullet hell or danmaku games, here's a good game to get acquainted with the genre. The basic premise is there's lots of bullets on screen and your ship's hitbox is a small circle in the center, which allows you to squeeze through bullet patterns. The scoring system is based on item collection chaining.
You have 4 ships to select from, with different main and special weapons. In addition, you have a "Vaunt" ability, which gives you a temporary shield on use, and 2x strength and points until the meter runs out. You can keep the meter going by grabbing gold that enemies drop, and the longer you keep it going, the more points you get once it runs out. If you need to live a little longer, you can Vaunt again, giving another shield but a smaller bonus.
There are 5 levels and 20 challenge levels, which makes the game perfect for both long sessions and quick bursts.

This is one of the most polished games I've ever seen. So much thought was put into how everything works. For the multi-player (local only, but that's ok) you can use pretty much any control setup you like. If you want to stick four separate mice on your computer and hand each one to a different person, the game has no problem with that. Or four keyboards, or gamepads, or any combination. I tried it with a keyboard, a trackball, a mouse, and a gamepad all at once, and Jamestown didn't mind one bit, it just worked.
The pixel art is excellent, and you have control over exactly how you want that to scale. The music is very good. The story is unique and interesting, crammed full of proper historical references stuffed into the alternate what-if timeline of 17th century colonial Mars. There appears to be a massive number of bonus levels, challenge levels, and multiple ships (and weapon systems) to choose from.
It's fun.
It's not Touhou (not even close), but it's beautiful, it has great music, and it's fun. Bring friends. Just beware that the game is very short.

This game manages to pack in a little something for everybody. While it's taken cues from common modern-day Flash games - including things like a shop with unlockables from points earned in-game, plus challenge levels and the like - it provides for the more hardcore shmup community as well with an arcade-style Gauntlet mode and enough points to unlock it right from the start. It also has a more classic difficulty progression, with some of the late-game stages only available to the higher difficulty levels.
Gameplay-wise, Final Form did their research before working on this. They followed the conventions of modern shoot-'em-ups and made sure to give it a polished feel. While there are a couple small things that bother me here and there (Dark Sector is quickly becoming That One Level for me), it's generally enjoyable all around no matter what kind of action experience you're into.

As an escape room aficionado in real life, I figured I'd try this one out. I have to say that the quality of the puzzles in this game rivals that of some real escape rooms I've done.
Some rooms were really easy for me, but as I advanced through the game, I started to struggle a bit. Some of the puzzles are cryptic, which might cause some frustration, but talking with your companions often leads to helpful clues. I did have to resort to a guide at a few points when I got stuck, and the answers all make logical sense, which makes me appreciate the amount of thought that went into the puzzles. Bravo.
The story offers multiple endings, but I won't say anything about them, other than that I still have questions about some of the characters. Being that the game is primarily puzzle-based, I'm not particularly turned off by not getting all of the answers in this regard.
Is it perfect? No - but it's a quality game that I enjoyed. I am happy to be amongst its initial supporters, and I hope it finds success!
EDIT: The developer has been vigilant in responding to questions, bugs, and requests. Mine was resolved within less than a day. Impressive customer service!

The game also has different paths you can take and different endings you can get. Saving, loading and such stuff is no problem, you can do that anytime before important choices.
I have finished the game, completed all secrets and hidden puzzles. The puzzles in the late-game were really difficult and i had a hard-time figuring them out. The puzzles are great and i definitely would buy this game again for them.
The big downside is the story though. It`s pretty... weeeird. The story concept is actually not that bad... but
thus making the story really mediocre. The dialogue is skippable, which is important for those kind of games (you don`t want to play twice through story sections to reach different endings without being able to skip :p)

I've been a bit on the fence about this game throughout yesterday and today. On sale the game costs £3.5 and I have 3.5 hours so far so I have my money's worth.
The game presents itself as an RPGMaker styled locked room/escape the room mystery. I've done a couple of these puzzles in real life and thought I'd give it a shot.
The gameplay is pretty much what you'd expect; hunt around the room for clues to solve the puzzles to find keys to open the door. That's all great, fun and challenging.
I came across a few issues while playing. The developer (in the comments below) has been great in responding to them and promising to work on some quality of life improvements. I'll leave these issues at the bottom as a reference.
However, overall my review is to recommend this game - this game has an active, engaged developer who is passionate about their game, who talks to the playerbase and tries to improve the experience for the players.
The experience is fun, quirky and as far as I know, unique. There are different endings dependent on your choices, the story is decent and the puzzles are intricate and challenging on the whole (various difficulty across the game of course). With some of the issues I describe below being sorted, and being informed that you need to manually save I have no major problems with the game. For the price you can definitely get your money's worth from the game, and a lot of enjoyment at the same time!
PREVIOUS REVIEW ISSUES - DEV COMMENTS BELOW ABOUT IMPROVEMENTS:
First of all the dialogue is frustrating in the sense that talking to one of the other people there requires a lot of clicking to progress through it. You'll find yourself talking to or interacting with the same items multiple times and seeing the same dialgoue, but without a way to skip it.
Secondly, I'm currently stuck in one room, where I've been left on my own in a dark maze. Usually when you get stuck the others will offer you clues and assistance. This room, being alone, I have no assistance. I solved the first part and then was presented with a 2nd section which seemingly has no solution - a 6 character and numeric code with only two sets of 4 numbers as options. No doubt it's my issue not figuring it out, but my issue is that there's no assistance to help you out when you're stuck. This could just halt my progress and enjoyment through the game.
There are also hidden puzzles to solve, but no real way to interact with them. You find a piece of paper for example with a riddle on it alluring to one of the people you're with being phoney/dodgy. It ends with "I wonder who it is?". I could guess, but there's no where to input your guess and see if you're right/wrong etc... so "completing" these for the clues seems impossible. Maybe you just have to find multiple hidden clues first.
The achievements seem very specific. I believe there's 5 rooms in any play through (of 7 total) and I'm on room 4 but have had no achievements yet. I'm guessing there's some extra hidden clues or alternative progressions to find in extra play throughs.
My biggest issue occurred when I reloaded the game. Despite the game appearing to save at every "checkpoint" save screen between rooms... I reload the game and it saved nothing of my progress.

Just completed my first playthrough on the first try. This game is extremely fun, and has a lot of potential. Basically, so far, you are given a mission that you have to complete by going through the mansion, picking up machine guns, rifles, shotguns, flare guns, and an assortment of other ranged and melee weapons. An interesting but hard to control mechanic is that you can 'rescue' two people in the house that will aid in your battle. The problem with this is that they follow close behind you but you cannot control their movement. This makes giving them a melee weapon basically useless, as they will take damage because they wont be able to move away. This means that you will end up giving them the guns and you having to slowly melee your way through the mansion, not that thats a big inconvenience. The monsters are classic: skeletons, bats, and zombies. Although they are basic they can be a pain to put down, especially with melee weapons. I would like to see scarier monsters in future update, and maybe some more movie tie-ins. Overall a fun that reminds me of old school slow paced survival horror like alone in the dark.

Quest successful, it's then a case of fighting a way back out of the haunted house (new monsters spawn) and done!

Muffled conversations between vaguely defined characters reveal early on that all is not well in this household. Soon you'll be on your own to explore a distorted version of this toddler's house and dream world, armed with your new Teddy as sole companion.
The developers obviously have no idea how a 2-year-old sounds like (hint: it's not a baby anymore) and they repeatedly make small realism mistakes that might briefly irk real parents, but controlling such a young character is decidedly refreshing and well done for the most part.
They added some nice touches, such as the inevitable stumbles when running for any length of time, or hugging Teddy for some comfort with the added benefit of producing enough light to partially see in the dark.
Moving chairs to reach higher places normally not accessible to a young child introduce simple puzzles, though interactions could have used more variety as a whole. These physics-based challenges would be infinitely complex for a toddler but are very simple for an adult, so breezing through the game is done with relative ease.
The game is only scary if you let it be. Your decidedly creepy talking Teddy keeps saying we should be quiet but there's absolutely no danger until the latter half of the game, when your toddler finally comes face to face with his nightmare in screeching distortion and static. A lot of tension rises from that moment, when you must rapidly crawl to safety under a table or bed to escape the hazy creature unseen.
Unfortunately, that tension soon dissipates once you realize your character always easily awakens a few meters away when caught, with any danger gone. It only temporarily halts gameplay and diminishes the fun in crawling to safety just in time to hide.
Collect memories as main story progression and optionally drawings for extra achievements. Beware that the game does not track progress of such collectibles, if you are into that sort of thing, nor do they add any value to the story or gameplay.
Progress does not save at all mid-chapter either, despite a very obvious mention of the game being saved at different checkpoints. The game does not inform you that progress will be lost when quitting.
Overall, Among the Sleep is a sympathetic little game with enough good qualities to recommend despite a large amount of noticeable imperfections.

Mordheim: City of the Damned is not for the faint of heart. It's tactical and relies on strategy and wit, but luck plays an important part, and it may not always be on your side. But if you're up for a gamble, then there's no denying it; Mordheim is one of my all-time favourite turn-based tactical rpg's.
Making good use of the Games Workshop franchise in terms of atmosphere and looks, the devs managed to create an extremely addictive and engaging game, which will gradually suck you in until there's no getting out. It's great fun to level up your soldiers and unlock skills that will offer whole new ways of approaching each match.
If you're a fan of games like X-Com (1 and 2), know that Mordheim does share a few similarities, but it's also very unique. It's much less forgiving of your mistakes, but it also feels much more rewarding when you are successful, as it really puts you to the test. If you're not afraid of trial & error, and occasionally getting your behind slapped by Lady Luck, then don't think twice and dive right in - this game is totally worth it.

Mordheim: City of the Damned is the first game I’ve played that has so much going on! I have to admit, I seriously underestimated the sheer amount of mechanics there are to think about when diving into the city of Mordheim.
Not only do you need to think about the units you’re hiring but you’ve also got to consider what types of weapons they can use, stats, paying for their upkeep, completing shipments to sponsoring groups and heaps more.
After being engaged in civil war for years, the Empire finds itself with no Emperor. Rivalling powers were in competition for control of the throne. In the Imperial year 1999, a twin tailed comet was sighted in the sky. This comet was believed to herald the return of Sigmar and bring in a new golden age.
Flocks of people travelled to Mordheim, filling the city to it’s brim. With a lack of law in the city, citizens of Mordheim degenerated to giving themselves over to personal worldly temptations. An increasing state of anarchy rose within the city and the situation became worse when even more made the journey to Mordheim. Soon, the city’s streets were plagued with demons. Chaos and corruption had long since claimed the souls of the thousands who now resided in Mordheim.
When the comet fell on New Years Eve, the coming of Sigmar everyone hoped for, did not happen. Instead the comet came crashing down into the city, killing all who gathered around it. Word spread that Sigmar had smitten those he judged unworthy. Mordheim was filled with fear and paranoia. But word got out that a mysterious stone had been discovered scattered throughout the city known as Wyrdstone. This stone had all sorts of qualities and vying factions would pay great deals of money for this precious stone. Soon warbands started travelling to Mordheim in hopes to make vast fortunes by finding and selling Wyrdstone.
To fully comprehend how to play Mordheim: City of the Damned, it’s a very good idea to start with the tutorial. At the time of writing this review there were twelve separate tutorials branching across how to do basic things such as moving around, ending your turn, and more advanced things like ambushing opponents or dodging/parrying attacks. The tutorial then goes into how to manage your warband.
Each character you hire costs an initial hiring fee and require upkeep to be paid in order for them to stay in your team. If you choose not to pay for upkeep or treatment for injuries (or can’t afford it), each day that passes in the game, interest will accrue and injuries will get progressively worse. So make sure you loot that gold!
Also in the warband management area is the option to customise each individual troop. You can change the look of their head gear, skin colour, armour style/colour and more. If you’re really into role-playing and coming up with your own story, there’s the option to give your characters new names and even write a biography for them. Unfortunately the biography can only be seen by you.
As you will learn in the tutorial, whilst you’re in a match, each character has their own turn and can be controlled by the ‘WASD’ keys. Movement is limited by the amount of movement points a character has and attacks are also limited to a character’s combat points.
There are so many ways to plan your attack on an opponent. If you have a ranged character, find an ideal position up high so you can fire down upon your enemy without running the risk of them coming over to you next turn and beating your♥♥♥♥♥♥down. Otherwise you can just run straight in and start pummelling an opposing unit as many times as you can.
Once your turn is over, depending on how many movement/combat points you have left, you can change to a dodge, parry or ambush position. Dodge will give you a higher chance to dodge, parry gives a higher chance to parry, and ambush will force your character to charge at an enemy who ends up within your ambush range. Be careful how you use the ambush range, as you could easily make up the extra gap between you and a horde of the opposition’s team, and ultimately lose a character.
When a troop dies, your team’s morale decreases. If your team’s morale falls below forty percent of it’s maximum, your team leader undergoes a leadership test. Should your leader be out of action, the test falls to your team’s hero. Henchmen cannot take the leadership test, therefore if your leader and hero are both OOA, the team will “route”. Routing basically means a loss for you.
If the leadership test is passed, you can continue fighting. Should it fail, your warband will route. With this in mind, if you prefer to deal as much damage as you can to the opposition, try to refrain from taking out the enemy leader or hero. Take out the henchmen first and then focus on the remaining troops who can undergo a leadership test.
Mordheim: City of the Damned combat relies heavily on RNG (random number generator). As everyone who has played a game with RNG mechanics knows, percentages aren’t necessarily something you should get excited or disappointed over. A ninety-five percent chance to successfully attack an opponent can miserably fail… quite often as well. But then again a five percent chance to parry an attack can very likely be a success. Of course it’s all down to luck, but then again sometimes it can feel like luck is always against you but completely on the side of your opposition.
RNGs can often be the difference between your team routing or winning a match, but other factors can also hinder you such as hidden traps. Scattered randomly among the procedurally generated stages are a number of hidden traps. These traps can be quite frustrating, especially if you end up running through an area that you know will most likely give you an annoying debuff, but forget, and end up doing it anyway.
Each member of your warband gains experience for doing different things. For example, performing the attack that puts an enemy out of action will net your troop an extra bit of XP. After reaching a set amount of XP your warband members will go up a level. Levelling up provides them with points to go towards attributes. There are quite a few attributes to build up which provides even more strategic planning.
Some stats might increase your chance to attack successfully, whilst others will increase your dodge or parry chance. Because of the vast range of stats to increase when levelling up your warband, you can have one troop specifically designed for long-range fighting whilst another can be decked out to become a supreme spell caster.
You’re probably thinking, “So what’s with this whole Wyrdstone business?”. Wyrdstones work as a currency to purchase certain things as well as a commodity to send to your “sponsors” or primary faction. Each warband has a primary faction that requires a certain weight of Wyrdstones to be delivered to them within a set period of time. Along with the primary faction are extra sponsors you can build your reputation with.
However, if you leave your primary faction wanting and miss a shipment, your warband will disband. All gone. Poof in a cloud of smoke. Start again. Essentially this is game over. Game over will also occur if your leader dies from injuries, so yet another reason to horde that gold.
If you think you’re ready to tackle an advanced game such as this, Mordheim: City of the Damned is a great investment. But if you’re new to intensely customisable strategy games, but are prepared to learn, Mordheim: City of the Damned also does a great job at taking you by the hand in it’s tutorials.

I don't tend to leave reviews, but there seem to be so many negative ones for Mordheim I felt I should post one...
The game relies heavily on RNG - which is fine by me.  Don't be fooled by people complaining about it; it may be unlikely that you'll fail lots of 95% actions in a row, but it's NOT IMPOSSIBLE - so it CAN happen, it doesn't mean the game is broken.  You don't see anyone moaning that they are making 30% chance attacks all the time.  The RNG works just fine.
It's a hard game too - you can exploit the AI, and it's easier once you have a few games and experience under your belt, but if you don't want or enjoy tough, unforgiving games, this isn't the game for you.
It's very unforgiving of mistakes and there are negative points - animations are very similar, there are only 4 warbands, the AI is dumb as a post and (like a lot of games, tbh) the information you'll get from the community makes up for the lack of documentation/obtuse menus.
Read the community guides for beginners, don't expect your first warband to do very well (or rather, expect later ones to be better built) and stack the odds in your favour (esp. when picking missions in the beginning) - and if you lose warriors to injuries, death, and amputations, well, that's part of the 'fun' (see Dwarf Fortress).
But overall, guiding a warband through the ups and downs of Mordheim is hard, rewarding and unpredictable - just like the boardgame, so, fine by me.
Will be nice to see more warbands and variety, but I personally think this game is a lot of fun, and recommend it to anyone wanting a challenge in the old Warhammer setting.

Let's start this off by saying I like this game, I may play it in the future if the DLC coming out for it looks good and they fix some of the balance problems.
Let's start with the good and the great.
-Level design
Good, the custom maps are great and the random maps are good except when the occasional glitch happens.
-Enviroment
Great, mutated corpses blowing bubbles of blood, giant mutated bodies suspending the roof of a tower, captures the atmosphere of Mordheim.
-Management
Really enjoyable management making and customizing a warband is great fun.
-RPG elements
Also great, in depth, with lots of build options, if the game was more balanced and less decided with a coin toss I could see myself spending hours making builds.
On to the negatives.
-RNG
The RNG is not right, this has been echoed and repeated by almost everyone, there are less then 20 people I have talked to who can defend the RNG.
You can test it yourself, get CoP there leader gets a spell with 85% to succeed. Cast it a hundred times, realize that it only works HALF THE TIME. Casting chance has no modifiers, int doesn't increase it, armor and weapon enchants doesn't increase it either.
Its the best way to test RNG.
-Implementation of the RNG.
This is my second problem, lets say I'm deluded, I'm just a bad player who makes bad rolls scapegoats. Even with the RNG working as it should the prevelance of it is unbearable.
Its random when you get a shipment, you can fulfill the shipment just to have once come in the very next day, usually demanding 50 pnds more.
Secondly the difficulty of the missions you go on AND the deployment is also random, so you can have 10 days to fulfill a shipment only to have awful rolls that makes it so 6/10 days you have are up against tough or brutal missions all with the chance for your group to be scattered.
Which means you will end up in a house with one of your units getting gangbanged before you ever get a chance to move.
Mutations are random as well which is fine MUTATIONS SHOULD BE RANDOM, however mutations should not be the saem for EVERY MUTANT.
The first Mutant you have excess to has 5 points in ballistic while only 3 in melee.
However you are almost gauranteed to get an arm mutation making any ranged weapons unusable so why the hell do we have a mutant that is your only hero option in the beginning with 2 extra points that could be anywhere else except ballistic?
The game is full of stuff like this but more on that later.
Ultimately with the RNG you will find yourself ♥♥♥♥ed regardless of how well you play, I have lost one match ONE! However I still often restart with a new warband because of being forced into a bad spot by the RNG.
For example I have had my leader unit roll Wrath of Tzeentech TWICE in two matches, both on casting WoD and wearing a blue amulet to avoid this.
First ended with a light wound rest for two days, the other a near death experience which takes 5 days.
My shipment was in 7 days so I had only two days to make the shipment.
So whatever I have only a couple more clusters to deliver to make my shipment.
So I check the missions, I have the choice of Brutal and Tough missions all with scattered deployment for one side or both sides.
With only two days I decide I have to take on so I choose the Tough mission, and surprise surprise my luck gets two of my units basically sorrounded by enemies that get taken out before their turns because of their lower initiave.
Which is the point I uninstalled the game.
-Balance
Good god the balance is so poorly figured out no wonder multiplayer is dead.
Skaven for example are king, they get 3 meters extra movement, which means they can outrange your charges and ambushes even when you have Bullcharge the AI still gets to ambush or charge you on even, you cannot do this.
CoP is the weakest group as they are based entirely on RNG and have weirdly built heroes.
I already brought up the weird mutant with pointless points in ballistic.
Now let me bring up the possessed, absolutely worthless unit, Fear checks are almost always passed by the AI meaning he rarely gets the buff that would make him usefull.
He has awful dodge unless points are sunk into it which gimps him in other ways. He is incredibly squishy, only clothing allowed.
He has incredibly low DPS, only two attacks on start because he is always dual wielding thanks to bracers/mutations only which means he is always going to cost another OP for an attack.
LOSING AN ARM MAKES HIM BETTER, honestly, if he gets his arm chopped off he gets a bonus in dodge, initiave bonus and can make three hits a turn.
So in summary to squishy to tank, not enough DPS to be a glass cannon.
-NPC handicaps
These are the worst.
Skaven which should be a squishy race with high movement is now a terror because the NPC get a large chunk of extra health often given more health then your own units!
Their leadership will also rival yours regardless of what your focusing on.
It completely skews the feeling of progression.
How am I a high leadership warband when EVERY warband has higher leadership regardless of stats invested?
Why do I invest into alertness when my units can't ever break ahead of the enemies initiave?
You will never have the option for Easy missions, Normal missions is you still facing enemies with higher stats, health, leadership and initiave.
In summary.
I'm at a loss with this game, I really like its mechanics, I really like how it plays.
However the poor balance that hasn't been fixed, the dead multiplayer, the boosted NPC enemies, the constant RNG ♥♥♥♥ery.
When I sit down and begin a match while the game loads I just think to myself, why don't I just flip a coin and leave it at that?

Aww man... I love the direction with where this game is going, but I feel like this is moreso a beta test than it is an actual final release.  But regardless, I think the game is fun.
Here are some things I like and don't like about the game so far (and this is talking about 22 hours+ into the game and promoting from Prospect to Absolver).
Likes:
-  Mostly customizable fighting styles.  I like how most fighting styles are like fingerprints.  No two fighting styles are exactly the same (between human players, that is), and the process of creating your own unique style is an adventure in and of itself.  It goes in tandem with the type of equipment and attributes you tote around, so the possibilities are endless.  Even if two players happen to have the same fight decks, they also have to put into account the type of equipment and attributes they have, which makes things incredibly interesting.  Questions come to mind like, "Why does that combo string work better for him instead of me?"
-  Sporatic and cut-throat.  As a first-timer, you might crash and burn a lot, BUT don't be discouraged!  In fact, I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the first time I played because I felt like the difficulty curve was too wide, but I kept with it and learned through trial and error.  And, I'm talking with just NPCs!  Just calm down because this game takes some patience.  But, once you get the hang of it, it turns into an incredibly fast-paced rock-paper-scissor game.  Each encounter keeps me guessing and makes me want more!  Circling back to the previous paragraph, I just love watching what combinations get thrown out (even if I lose).
-  Friendly fire.  I know it's weird, but I like the fact that you CAN hit your teammates.  HOWEVER, knowing this also helps you!  It's somewhat realistic in the sense that in a real life brawl, you might hit your friends.  Morbid, I know, but the magic is learning to NOT hit your friends.  I've recorded a session with a random player I just met and after playing with him/her for a while, we got around to learning each other's play styles and wove in and out of each other's attacks, and conquered our enemies as a single unit.  (You can watch it here:
and props to Charlie2-1.
Probably the best partner I've had so far!)  I'm thinking about making tutorials about how to approach multiple targets with or without a partner.
Dislikes:
-  The idea of having random players come in the area and not knowing if they're going to help you or kill you is thrilling.  But, the problem is that sometimes we run into players that don't have a good internet connection, then things get wonky.  As previously stated, I felt like this game is more beta for this reason, but not just this reason alone.  Most of the time, you're going to be arguing with the game, because sometimes your attack doesn't get thrown out right as soon as you press the button.  You will experience button lag, and, as a fighter, you know how important keeping lag to a minimum is.  On top of that, you're going to be teleporting back and forth all over the place and many times it's led me to the depths of the abyss or in the warm embrace of my enemies.  But, when the connection cooperates, the game works like a dream!
-  The storyline is short and it still makes me wonder why the world is the way it is.  After completing the quest of defeating the marked ones and ultimately promoting to Absolver, there really isn't much to do except gain new moves you haven't got yet, hit up the PvP mode, and constantly grind to max.  For now, it's alright for me, because I haven't maxed out and don't have all the moves yet.  But, I can imagine how boring it'll be once I get everything.  To make things a bit more grueling, you have to make level 10 or 30 on the PvP mode in order to progress through another couple instances in the game, which I yet have to do.
Mixed feelings:
-  You can't chat in-game, which I think is a little weird, but I also think that's what sets the vibe of the game.  The mysteriousness, not know who is friend or foe, is what intrigues me, but at the same time... I think it's a little weird.  I don't know how I feel about it, but for reasons, I like it, but otherwise, I just wish I could at least talk to teammates.
-  When you cooperate with someone, die, then revive, you suddenly aren't in cooperation with that person anymore.  That I think is weird, because what if I don't want to separate from these players after we all die?  Sometimes, you're going to team up with someone who came in from the other end of the area and that means your spawning spots are at complete opposites of the area.  Then, you're going to have to make that trek to find your teammate... that is if you're even in the same instance anymore....  But, on the other hand, I think it's a fun adventure to have to fight your way to your teammate.  (Kind of like Romeo and Juliet coming together.  Bah ha ha ha!)  That way, when you finally contain the situation, you can cybernetically high-five each other.
Anyway, that's my spiel.  I highly suggest getting the game if you don't mind exploring the many different combo strings available.  The game is centered around exploring, not the landscape, but your mind, maaaaannnn....

Skilltree Saga is certainly a game that played with my heart. Whenever I hear the word “Rogue” my heart skips a beat, and right on the Steam page it advertises itself as such. If done right, it could be an extremely immersive experience. There isn’t a thing in the world I love more than dwarves and magic. I’ve sung the virtues of scraping stats on many occasions. Those new pants aren’t just shiny, they’re soaked in endorphins. It’s not as gross as it sounds. Well, it is. But at least it feels good. Erm, anyway… Skilltree Saga capitalizes on this mechanic relatively well. Unfortunately, this alone was not enough to hold me for an extended period. While some people may enjoy the grind, I found progress extremely arduous. There is much to praise, but also quite a bit of honest criticism. Let’s check out Skilltree Saga.
The soundtrack in the game has an extremely massive feel to it. I found the sound effects are also quite good, if not a bit repetitive. Repetition is a recurring theme in this game. I’ll say it again. Repetition is a recurring theme in this game. The background and animations during combat are nice, but unfortunately there is no exploration. Each floor only contains one monster, and you don’t have to look for him. I feel the three character models are nicely rendered, however none of the armor you equip will change their appearance. What you see is what you get. Meanwhile, the enemy models vary widely. The wolves and hornets look nice, while the elementals look almost like a placeholder model. It clashes pretty hard, and breaks the aesthetic in my book. The story is quite serious, revolving around The Dark Eye board games, so being attacked by a bug-eyed golem or a teddy bear doesn’t do it any favors.
The combat in the game is round-based. You can set up to six skills which will be used during the combat round. Once the round starts, it will take six turns before you’re able to drink a potion or flee. This is quite confusing in the tutorial, as you only have one skill and generally only make it to the second or third turn. During the tutorial I was under the impression that you weren’t able to do anything in combat except for start the fight. It wasn’t until about 45 minutes in that I actually started seeing the round combat screen. This breaks the flow of the game terribly and requires some looking into, as I would not have spent 45 minutes to figure this out if I weren’t writing a review. Diamonds are used instead of gold to buy potions, to keep you from going too far too fast, but in a game where progress feels this slow a little extra speed would be a welcome addition.
Skilltree Saga needs a bit of help before I’d encourage people to drop $10 on it. The death animations don’t always execute. UI doesn’t seem thought out, as you can get to your inventory from the shop menu but getting back to the shop screen requires closing out to the main menu. The grind is quite lengthy, and progress seems based more on levels than on gear. Some enemies have attack patterns that can be countered with skills, which seems engaging until you have them all memorized. The spiders in the jungle act just like the reskinned spiders in the cave. There are multiple ways to replay through the game though, changing your race or picking different spells. If you enjoy a casual grind I’d recommend you catch it on sale.
Summary: Casual RPG featuring a round-based combat system and a tremendous soundtrack.
Final Score: 5/10 for sound and replayability.

Really not worth your time. I realize I have 12 hours into this game, but I wanted to write a detailed review to compel any reader not get this.
Where to begin.. Lets start with plot. There isn't one. Well there's something about a kidnapped princess and some wizard helping you, but that's it. Its so barebones to the point where there might as well not be one. Heck you can change to the plot to just about anything and it still wouldn't change anything. Someone kicked my dog and now I'm out for revenge with my friendly neighborhood GPS who is also a wizard and can help me do wizard things.
The game works as such, you and your opponent attack each over 6 turns in which you can do a single action like attacking or using a skill. You can fight multiple rounds, but this will rarely happen. You think this is where tactical gameplay might kick in,  but after a while I realized that tactics you employ is only temporary as you will only need certain skills until the point where you outlevel any boss and can simply kill them with 2 abilities. Which brings up the point of why this game is terrible. The RPG system is basically a giant noob trap. There are 6 attributes, strength, cleverness, courage, constitution, defense, resistance. Most of these stats are self describing, but for some of the amgious ones, cleverness is magic, courage is who attacks first, constitution is health, and resistance is magic armor.
The noob trap begins here because of the crappy RPG system in this game. You don't get assignable attribute points when you level up, so you rely entirely on armor to boost your stats. Armor gives you attribute bonuses to a max of 4, which is extremely rare. Most of the time you'll be lucky to get 3 attribute bonuses. With that limitation, it becomes rather obvious that only you can only build a character to use 3 attributes to use, but which ones you might ask yourself. Well it certainly isn't the defensive ones because even if you go full tank enemies will do eye opening amounts of damage by the end of the game which leaves two options, kill the enemies before they even get a chance to attack you or prevent the damage with skills, which I'll get to later.
Basically only strength,cleverness, courage are the  skills you should invest in. But each piece of armor is randomly generated to give 1-4 attributes, which means your chances of getting those 3 specifically is almost impossible. For the most part though as long as these attributes are high enough you can kill enemies before they get a chance to attack you.
Skills in this are laughable, there are about 8 good ones out of the possible 21, the rest are worthless. In particular the Damage Over Time skills screw over any semblance of balance because you use a skill like burning jab (which is one of the first skills) to get your opponent down to low hp and then they'll die the next turn because of DoT.  Earth shield is the one of the most OP skills earlier in the game because it can block up to two physical attacks which is far better than defense or resistance. I would mention all 8 good skills, but in reality you'll only need about 5 by the end because some of the skills you needed become obsolete because you can now 1 hit KO the boss that you needed to use that skill on.
Exploration is a joke, there are 3 areas, which are basically endurance arenas, kill 30,50,100 enemies in one go. This method of gameplay becomes enfuriating by the end due to the fact that you stop gain XP from enemies 10 levels below you. By the time you hit level 60 this means that you stop getting XP from over 50 levels of the last dungeon, let me ask the developers a question, WHY DO I NEED TO FIGHT 50 MONSTER IF THEY"RE NOT EVEN GONNA GRANT XP.
Some reviewers mentioned that it feels like a mobile game, which is entirely true due to the "gameplay", but mostly because the alternative currency called diamonds, seriously I expected a prompt to come up asking me to buy 10 of them for 5 bucks. You can use diamonds to buy potions (the only way to get them without having a monster randomly drop one) or trade them in for money. Potions are you're only guaranteed way of getting deeper into the dungeon in one go because they refill your health or mana. But I found them useless because generally you'll probably run away when you encounter a hard enemy that you know you can't kill, then restart the dungeon after visiting the only town.
You can chose between 3 races, but the reality is that the elf becomes the best choice because magic is OP as all hell. Dwarf gives a constitution bonus, but as I mentioned earlier, this one of the worst thing to get because defense stats are worthless. Every race has the same class of "elemental knight" so there's no variety and no reason to replay at all.
If this was a cheapo mobile game, I would say that this is a good attempt, but this is $10 steam game which blows my mind.
Some might say having the story set in the dark eye universe is cool, but like I said there's no plot and there's certainly nothing that made me think wow dark eye is such a deep and entrancing universe! No, now whenever I see anything with dark eye in the title I'll think back to this terrible game.

Not only is this a good game, it's a good Resident Evil game. It's full of ridiculous situations, nonsensical puzzles and magical shadow paintings. If Resident Evil didn't exist and the first one came out today it'd be this.
The biggest difference from the rest of the series and what I loved the most was the reliance on atmosphere as opposed to obnoxious jump scares in order to build tension. This Blair Witch-type of scary is true horror and it isn't used nearly as much as it should in games. Not knowing what might be in the house with you heightens the feeling of danger as you play the game and its pacing of building tension, cutting it with a jump scare or a fake out only to start building it up again is how I feel horror games should be like. In Resident Evil 6 I struggled to play for 10 minutes without getting bored of all the action and loud noises. With Resident Evil 7 I got so hooked I forgot to go to sleep.
While the first hour is very atmospheric and scary the game never manages to capture that mood again because as you progress you get more and more powerful and enemies become less intimidating. It reminds me of Doom 3 in that way because that started out as a survival horror game but slowly progressed into a full-fledged action fantasy. Granted, there is a section later on where you don't have all your weapons for a while but I feel that the lack of enemy variety undercuts the tension that section was supposed to create. A fear of the unknown is a cardinal rule of the horror genre and I think they missed the mark with The Molded being the only enemy type in the game.
But the worst part of Resident Evil 7 by far is that there's no achievement for popping all of the balloons during Lucas' party! I was really bummed. There isn't much about the game that's original but there isn't much about it that's bad either. Resident Evil 7 takes after some of the biggest trendsetters in the genre of the past few years and that's by no means a bad thing. It takes the best parts of those games and makes them its own and it proved to be a solid return for the franchise I love.

First off, TRI isn't for everyone, It's a puzzle platformer with
mechanics when compared to games like Portal.
Although it has nothing to do with programming, It is similar to Zacktronics puzzle games in terms of having high complexity, masochistically hard end-game difficulty, and multiple answers for the same puzzle/problem.  Some of you may not like that, but others will certainly love it! As do I!
Many of the puzzles consist of learning the uses and limitations of the game's central tool: The TRI.
The TRI lets you place the vertices of magical triangle platforms onto the environment, If you have ever messed around in Blender or 3Ds-Max, you may have in idea how that works, (and what it can do.) Once 3 points are placed, a triangle materializes. Yellow can be walked on, Red is too steep, and platform vertices can be placed on other platforms- these are just some of the things you will have to learn to progress in TRI.
After reading other reviews I should note that placing TRI platforms can be tedious for some players, but this seems to be mostly subjective, as I said- not for everyone.
The game only has 15 levels (minus the tutorial)
One minor gripe I have is there are not enough early-mid game levels for the player to get used to the TRI, after reading the developer commentary, it seems that there was not enough time to make more levels, so I guess it couldn't be helped, but it would have been nice.
The Idols are
an added challenge to find, and in  challenge mode you have the option to either speedrun, (shortest time) 100% (all idols), or optimize (minimum TRI platforms) the level with quicksaving disabled.
Ok, so that's the gameplay, but how does it look?
TRI is one of the most
and beautiful games I have ever played. Each level set has a piece of music and appearance that conveys an emotion. I just love it.
The story is minimal, cute, and perfect for this setting. And I totally-did-not get all sentimental and teary eyed at the end.
And the monk has just the kind of British voice you would take a road trip to kerbin's north pole with, and that's always good to have.
To sum up, the game has it's flaws, and it's not very intuitive at first, but it's still massively underrated and I love it. If you want a puzzle platformer that is slow paced, hard to master, and rewarding; Then TRI might be for you, but that's just my opinion, and you have the right to disagree with me if you want to. and, you should read other peoples reviews too!
EDIT: also the game has foxes, so if you like foxes, you're covered.

Did you become infected with the Dark Souls 2 PvP bug and felt let down by the flailing, rolling, healing snoozefest that was Dark Souls 3 PvP?
Well, here we are. We made it. Somebody made the game we wanted to play. And as far as I'm concerned, it came completely out of the blue.
On my first day I played fourteen hours, the vast majority being purely PvP based after finding out you can go directly into a 1v1 match-up with some random other player around your level. Sometimes you get matched with people twice or three times your level, but there's a steep learning curve and this only serves to cement your status as a clueless ...unfortunate.
Everyone is going to suck going into this game. I was fortunate enough to have a friend of mine explain how the deck works and how to make sense of the deck screen, so instead of having to engage my own brain I had it all explained when I arrived there to begin with, which is ideal as honestly I'd have struggled otherwise with the lack of a tutorial.
I hope you got on okay without a personal tutor, but if you can get a hold of one I recommend it because otherwise it's a nightmare which could very easily be rectified with a couple of vs bot tutorials or even a paragraph explaining the importance of learning new moves if you've any interest in playing against other people.
There are some very basic aspects of the game which go completely unemphasised. For instance, you need to have collected a sizeable portion of the many and impressively varied hand to hand martial arts moves before you can seriously start to appreciate the intricacies of this wonderful game.
Besides all that, this is clearly a labour of love. Your character feels responsive amidst the staggeringly lovely visuals of the game, it's obvious how much thought has gone into the combat system and it gives me a warm feeling in my heart to think that one day the connection issues, myriad of random bugs and save file corruption issues will be rectified so I can make the most out of this truly fantastic game.
Let's just avoid going the way of For Honour. Please. This game has so much potential.
(If any devs happen to read this, if you add a PvP ranking system for 1v1 and 2v2 Teams and fix the current bugs your game will be a huge success! Also it would be absolutely sick as hell man cmon)

Brilliant fps puzzle game.
- Unique mechanic. Tasteful design. Tranquil music. Solid lore and backstory.
- Straightforward main puzzles with rising difficulty.
- The collectibles are practically the hard mode, finding them takes patience and getting them all can be really challenging. (Most of them are tied to hidden achievements as well). So the player is free to choose how deeply to explore a level.
- Levels vary in their concept but all of them revolve around navigating spatial objects. Towers, pits, stairs, bridges, labirinths. It is great how all of them make use of the base mechanic of the game.
Which is by the way so sell designed. Limited but instinctive, pohished but with a little space left for cheesing some situations. And the puzzles themselves stumped me just the right amount before I realized a solution. Only a few  game can do this right. They usually put too much obstacle b/w finding the way and actually letting you get to it. Here the two comes hand in hand. This game never left me feel cheated or stupid. Finishing a chapter felt really satisfying. Grat for the devs for a great game.
Being able to walk on the walls and ceiling is an unusually rewarding puzzle mechanic. Also brute forcing things is pretty fun.

It is a turnbased, Squad based, Tactical Role Player set in the Fantasy/Pre industrial Era of Warhammer.
Pros
Challenging
Meaningful Strategy
Meaningful Character Building
Rich Environment
Captures essence of tabletop games
Cons
3 mission types
4 maps
4 factions
Not for the weak minded
a few Clunky game mechanics (looting/targeting)
It is actually a really good game for what it was designed to be. It tells your right at the main menu "Mordheim was designed to be a hardcore experience" I think it accomplishes this very well.
It is hard, it is suppose to be. Your hard earned soldiers are going to die and going to get hurt, and you will be sad. It gets easier as you learn more tactics and your charactera get stronger, but it never becomes trivial. I think this is what makes it so enjoyable. So many games today are easy and formulaic, but in this game you learn and adapt or die.
Before I try and convince you to dedicate the time needed to fully enjoy this game, let me tell you my only major criticisms. Once you do figure out how to be boss, and your characters are stronger you tend to use your soldiers in specific ways over and over again for only 3 major mission types, "gather, kill and steal" on seemingly 2 or 3 maps. Some of the targeting and looting mechanics require very specific positioning which is just stupid, but you learn how to deal with it....eventually.
It is still a very rewarding process despite its flaws, and even once you are da'boss it is still challenging and tactical because if you do not play to your designed strengths you will not do well. Additionally, there needs to be more factions. Right now there are 4 factions (Skaven, Chaos, Empire and Sisters of Sigmar). I think 4 is an appropiate starting number for the rich experience it provides, but I want more. I really hope more factions are available.I will gladly and eagerly purchase them.
It was designed around playing a tabletop miniatures game and again captures this feeling very well. I find the combat to be intense, the strategies to be very broad and in depth. Your troop positioning, skills, spells, and equipment really matter. Most importanly though, is the character building. You will grow attached to your characters, and will live/experience game of throne moments when they die, lol.
Environment and graphics capture the "hardcore" dungeon feel of the warhammer universe. The animations are well done really bringing your characters to life despite being turned based. There is enough gore to keep it realistic too. I anticipate a couple hundred hours of playtime, more with DLC.
BottomLine: Buy it if you like challenges and turnbased gameplay, anticipate a learning curve.

I want to like this game... I really do. I gave it a big chance, tried each warband, played it pretty hard.. But it's massively let down by terrible balancing and lack of saving... My game was ruined at Act 1 scene 4, after building a solid gang, I was progressing across the bridge when the Chaos Ogre on next to no health, Stunned the main story character then killed him in 2 blows from full health.. Mission over I lose? all my characters take wounds which ruins them, I lose all my magic equiptment... Seriously 3 BS Dice rolls in a row and may as well start over.. Why would you not give a save option? Seriously it's 2016.. you have an ok game with a terrible mechanic ruining it.
Add to this... Terrible balancing means camping/Turtleing is by far the best option, kite an enemy, kill them, rinse and repeat.
I await the downvotes from the insane hardcore lovers.. "oh you just don't get it" or some such nonsense.. Terrible mechanics don't equal hardcore they equal terrible design descions...
Edit - It's not even difficult for the developers to fix. Offer a single player mode (so saving can't be exploited for multiplayer) disable the multiplayer for warbands created for singleplayer, and allow the player to save the game, it's clearly saved after every single characters move.  Just add saving/loading in camp. Then people can re fight bad fights.. Suddenly the game is less merciless and enjoyable.
Balancing the battles however might take a bit more work. At present the AI seems ridiculously over powered in 1 on 1 situations.
