This game really wants to be Street Fighter 3 Third Strike, a game I think is vastly overrated. Yatagarasu uses 4 attack buttons (2 punches, 2 kicks, like in KOF), and... 2 buttons to Parry, high and low, which in my opinion, is really terrible and an annoying feature. I'm not particuarly a fan of parry mechanics in 2D fighters to begin with, especially when it involves a dedicated parry button, but Yatagarasu has to take it a step further by having 2 dedicated parry buttons, on top of being able to tap forward to parry like in Street Fighter 3 as well. Games like The Last Blade, which had a single dedicated button for the job, also had a whiff animation, that Yatagarasu lacks, which I think is major problem for a game with a parry button. There is an indicator below the lifebar to show when a parry is attempted, but I think it's a poorly thought out system.
The game uses your typical Street Fighter style commands, It's very easy to get into and start doing stuff. The damage output is extremely high in this game, but it gets even more extreme when counter hits are involved, especially if you try to super jump in on your opponent or you somehow fail a parry attempt, you take much more damage. Two good solid hits can easily wipe out 40-50% of your lifebar. This is very much an old school style fighting game where a single hit can determine the outcome of a match easily.
The characters in this game are all pretty boring and bland. You got two shoto clones, two katana wielding school girls, Dudley wannabe, Zangief wannabe, rekka character, etc. None of the characters in this game are very interesting, exciting or original, they play exactly like you'd expect them to with one glance at their moves. Most of the characters look like they don't even belong in the same game together for some reason. Only Hanzo really stands out, and that's because she's total fanservice, but then you just realize in terms of aesthistics, she's Angel from KOF designed to be a "ninja". Her crouch stance is terrible, I dunno what the designers of this game were thinking giving her that. For her standing stance her chest inflates and deflates, it just looks really silly.
Graphically, the game can't even compare to cream of the crop 90's arcade fighting games. There's not a whole lot of detail on character sprites, alot of them look very flat and the animation on them is pretty average, but worse off is the background art. Most stages look like they are just a single flat image, with little to no scrolling or animations going on, not even spectators (There's spectators in 1 stage, and they are pretty awful looking, some even displaced/overlapping).
Far as audio goes, most of the music in the game is pretty forgettable, not a single good theme in the game. Majority of character voices are whatever, they don't have much personality. Sound effects, again nothing special, average fighting game fare. Don't even get me started on the commentators. They are totally obnoxious and one of the worst things about this game, almost as bad as the Navigators from Persona 4 Arena. Thankfully you can turn them off, for the most part. I dunno, sometimes they would pop back up even though I toggled an option to disable them. I don't get it. Although I did laugh at UltraDavid's "Is there trip guard anti-air in this game?".
So yeah, Yatagarasu... It's just really dull, boring and lazy game design. It does nothing new or original. How did it take them so many years to get this game out? I mean there are a ton of other fighting games out there that do what Yatagarasu does, but way better. The main issue I have with the game is that even though it's supposed to be finished, it still feels very incomplete and like an Alpha. It completely lacks polish, it's a mess, characters in this game feel extremely shallow and limited. I really can't justify spending $15 on this game. You would be better off spending that money on something like The King Of Fighters '98 Ultimate Match Final Edition or 2002 Unlimited Match. Those games are way better designed, with much better gameplay mechanics than you'll find in Yatagarasu. This game's been in development limbo for years, and frankly, it was not worth the wait.

If you like horror games, this certainly isn't the scariest game I've played. What I like about this game, that most other horror games do wrong, is that there is mostly atmospheric horror on display. This isn't Outlast, where you need to run, hide, fail, and do it again. There aren't any jump scares (well, there's one, but even great horror films succumb to this trope). Most horror games have a lame gameplay loop that often feels like you're simply waiting for the scary bits to come to light. It's impossible to enjoy a horror game if the fear raised is higher than the players will to continue/enjoyment of the story. Among the Sleep is more like your classic Haunted Mansion ride at a carnival; thrilling but not spooky.
The main draw to this game (at least on the surface) is that you play as a toddler. The scale of the world really makes you feel small as you climb atop boxes, drawers, and more to navigate through the worlds. The emphasis on verticality (everything being bigger than you) gives the game a grand feel for such a linear game. The gameplay loop usually has you fetching certain items in the world in order to proceed forward in the story. The story, while vague, is absolutely dark.
Sound design is the tops. While the lighting and visual design immerse you in the world, the sound is what raises your hair on ends.
I'd defintely recommend this game if you're looking for a fresh perspective (literally) on the horror genre.

It is sort of like a survival horror game, even though half of the game is just horror and no survival part (unless you fall into the void). It looks beautiful and it is worked out quite well, except for one major flaw: The game wipes your progress in a level completely when you quit the game. Within the levels you have checkpoints and the game pretends to "auto save", but this is just as long as you do not stop playing it. It will simply punish you for stopping. Given the fact that the game has only about 5 levels it basically wipes up to 20% of your progress.

Do you like being scared? Are you tired of horror games that are nothing but jump scares? This could very well be the game for you! I, personally don't scare easily. I am jumpy, and jump scares generally don't do much besides, well, make me jump. No real fear, or adrenaline there. While playing this game, I found myself experience the closest thing to terror that I have ever felt. Chills raced up and down my spine, as my heart rate increased. My movement became less intentional, and more based on reflex, and panic began to take over.
It's like that dream where you're being chased by something, but you can't see what, and you try to scream but nothing happens, so do the only thing you can do: Run. If this kind of situation scares you, and you enjoy fear that isn't caused by real-life stress, then I would highly recommend you play this game.
Pros: Interesting puzzles, eerie atmosphere, terrifying antagonist, and real-life problems that are artistically displayed.
Cons: OK graphics (not good, but not bad), and only about 2 hours long.
Overall, if you like horror, then this is a good game to pick up on sale. I would not buy it full price, but then again I wouldn't buy most games at full price.

This is a really interesting exploration of childhood trauma in a couple of phases:
Initially you are exploring the house and new areas, solving simple puzzles with no particular peril - and to be honest, all that really kept me going were the cleverly designed and interesting areas to explore (put me in mind of the Void for sort of eerie). It then sort of evolves into an Amnesia style avoid the monster, with the identity and nature of the monster becoming clearer and clearer. It's not a very good 'jump scare' game (though I think it tries really really hard to be one) but I still enjoyed it once I got going, and at the end. It certainly made me feel and think.
I bought it on sale and that feels fair... I completed it in about 2 hours (having to redo an entire area because of annoying save system though...). If you're interested in the above, I recommend. I think reading the negative reviews, people perhaps missed the point of the game and the type of horror it represents.

Everything from crashing and making your driver pop out the window to play bowling, basketball, black jack, long jump, etc. Nice little extra.
The racing itself is where the meat is. Really easy to drive cars, with AI that is fair and challenging without cheating, or being cheap. Lots of chances to make your opponents crash like in the Burnout games. You'll race in dirt, on city streets, and on professional tracks. From the perspective of it's gameplay design, this is my personal game of the year. The combat is easy to understand and execute, but has an incredible level of depth and customization as you progress through it's incredibly engaging world. The aesthetic is simple, but extremely well animated and stylized, and the visual design of the environments is downright breathtaking at times. The PvE is well crafted, but once you have a solid grasp on the combat, you'll be able to burn through the single player offering very quickly, about 4-5 hours if you take your time. I've also had some of the most dynamic and interesting multiplayer experiences I've ever had just roaming the open world. The PvP is beyond excellent, the customizable move sets and variations in play style mean two fights rarely, if ever, feel identical, and it contains a fascinating post-PvE progression that give you a sense of reward/accomplishment even after losses. However, the game is plagued by a host of server side technical issues, so if you've completed the game's very short single-player offering, if you are greeted with a message in the main menu that you can't connect to a server, you're only meaningful option is to re-roll a new character (which I've still enjoyed doing, but definitely won't be for everyone). For how vital PvP is to the long-term experience of the game, I think for a lot of people this situation, as it stands currently, is kind of unacceptable. I've had a completely unforgettable time playing this game so far, but you may be better served waiting to see if the next few updates smooth out the server issues.

I just finished the game, and this will not contain any spoiler.
I discovered this game in the Portal 2 steam news thing. I watched the trailer. I loved it. The idea is pure genius. I played the demo later. I loved that too. I then waited patiently for the game to release, all the while playing the demo a lot. Then it was released. I was ecstatic. Now, enough about me, the game!
The game starts with an easy tutorial level, in which you are introduced to your "mentor", the Monk, and to the game's objective: finding his friend the Fox [if I remember correctly, in the alpha period of the game, the fox was evil and you had to look him the strange world]. You will also see "visions" of the Fox throughout the levels. You then go to the Odd God's world: a world mostly comprised of giant cubes filled with puzzles floating in the middle of emptiness. No wonder the Gods are called Odd! In the second level, you are introduced to this game's collectibles: the Idols of Unnessecary Knowldege. Just my type of thing [I love trivia]! The Idols unlock artwork, in-game commentary and info on the game while it was in developpment. Each level has a few Idols, and one super secret one. They are quite hard to find sometimes, and not mandatory to beating the game. The TRI is encountered in the third level, if I am not mistaken. It works really well. If the TRIs are yellow, you can walk on them, if red, you cannot. You also cannot place TRIs on wood [which has the beautiful meaning that TRIs can only be put on an eternal materials. Well, to me]. Later in the game you encounter the GraviTRI [not the official name], which gives each TRI it's own gravity: if you have a slanted TRI, your gravity will become slanted too when you walk on it. So you could make a chain of TRIs that lead to the ceiling and walk on the ceiling! I read some people had motion sickness, but I [thank the Odd Gods] did not. The games contains 16 levels, which seems short, but isn't. To finish a level, you must gather the 3 Fox Status and place them on an altar. The levels are beautiful, stunning and extremelly well-crafted and brain-melting at times. The music is just perfect. The game seems to be reparted in a few "sections", with each section having 3 music segments that loop. The music is so good that the looping is not a problem to me. The story is nice, simple and touching: a tale of friendship, madness, and Foxes. The game is fairly glitchless: the 2 glitches I encountered were fixed, and the last level had a slightly game-breaking glitch, but thankully Ratking told us how to fix it in the "stuck thread". The developper commentary is also a bit flawed: the music doesn't get less loud, unlike when you talk with the Monk: so you'll hear the the great music and  the devs talking about things at the same volume, which makes it hard to understand it at times.
Overall, this is a great game. I loved it. I strongly recommend this to any amateur of FPS puzzle- and exploration-games. And you can buy the soundtrack! What's not to like?
Thank you, Ratking entertainment, for making such a unique and exceptionnal game. I love you!
Edit:
The way death is handled is questionnable: if you fall in bottomless hole/void, you immediatly respawn at a predetermined point, which is nice. But if you touch a red lazer or acid, you die and have to choose a previous save. So make sure you save often.
Oh, and the TRIs are the magical triangle-platforms. When you create one, the world becomes grey, except for a coloured zone which indicates where you can place the next point. Maybe I should've mentionned that earlier...

I LOVE this game.  First of all, it's about foxes, and I love foxes more than anything in the universe.  Second of all, the game is a lot of fun, it's well designed, the art style suits it, the music is great, and the puzzles are very well designed.
What you do in this game is you use triangles to traverse areas and solve puzzles.  As the game progresses you get a few additional powers for the triangles which are used for later puzzles.  The puzzles slowly get more and more complex and challenging and are a lot of fun.
The game has a somewhat Portal feel (at least to me) in how you go about solving puzzles; especially later on in the game once you have all the powers and the puzzles require more thinking.  As well, the puzzles don't always obey they laws you expect them to obey, but you learn how they work fairly quickly (although most of them obey the same laws).
It's a fairly relaxed game in that you can't really die (but you sort of can).  If you fall into the void you're just reset (and you will fall into it quite a bit), but if you touch a red light beam or fall in acid you die and have to reload a save.  Those hazards aren't introduced until later though.  Either way, it's easy enough to not fall in, and if you come across a point where you see these hazards just save the game as you can save anywhere (the game does autosave as well at various check points just so you don't have to restart the whole level in the event of forgetting to save and dying).
You have to find three fox statues (called key statues) throughout each level and then bring them back to a certain area where you put them on pillars and they activate a portal to the next level.  There are various golden fox statues (called idols) hidden throughout the levels as well.  You don't need to collect these but they unlock bonus content (the bonus content seems to just be development notes and level commentaries; you also get achievements for collecting certain ones).  Some of them are hidden in fairly obvious places whereas others are hidden in extremely well hidden places (such as places where you would think you're not supposed to go).  Some are even hidden in plain sight but getting to them is very difficult.
I'm not sure what else to say about this game, but you should definitely buy it if you like puzzle games.
And it works on Windows, Mac, and Linux; which is really nice as I prefer to play games only on Linux.  :p

Transported to a world of colorful and almost paper-mâché-like surroundings, set to the eerie trip-hop beats of the melody playing and its mysterious sounding eastern strings weaving in and out of your eardrums; TRI is certainly a world of mystique and ancient mystery, and it bleeds with a style that stands out from the rest.
You find yourself in a peaceful garden of zen, a wise robed and masked figure greets and leads you through your relaxing surroundings to the base of a shrine. Here he explains the story of two foxes with a symbolic relationship obviously revered by the people of this temple. As the title suggests, the friendship of these two once playful spirits has been driven to madness and your spiritual guide requests your help in locating and finding out what really drove these two sacred beings apart from each other. As you step through the portal you've been led to, this is where the game takes a twist from the relaxing to the oddly enchanting and mystic world of the Odd Gods.
Your objective for each ancestral act of the game seems simple enough; collect the three shining fox statues scattered throughout each sprawling temple of dream-like obstacles and bring them to their pedestal to activate the strange portal. As you'll soon discover after only a couple short levels, these fox statues all seem to be out of reach. Luckily, you quickly come across the very free-form and useful triangle creating ability. This allows full creativity and endless possibilities with how you construct your spiraling walkway towards each out-of-reach goal.
As you move through through each esoteric structure that acts as a separate stage you'll come across your spiritual masked guide again who pushes you in the right direction and fills you in on the rich lore and history of the world you've become enshrouded by. Who is this masked entity though? He obviously feels very compelled to protect the friendship between the two main fox gods, but his motivation and identity remain decidedly unclear throughout the story.
It's easily the most entrancing and thought provoking setting I've seen for this kind of a game, and it's actually enjoyable to play through to the end which was a bit of a surprise considering my rough history with puzzle-oriented games. I loved the concept of Antichamber and it's ilk of mind-bending brain teasers but just could not get into it. The concept was a mind opening experience but it was soul crushingly challenging, games like that or Portal often times made me feel stupid, I love them to death but I just spent most of the time wishing I could keep going without getting stuck every other room and taking in the beautiful and mind-bending visuals around me.
TRI challenges you just enough but keeps you moving fluidly through its surreal and colorful world, the pacing is impeccable. Instead of making me feel slow and inadequate it causes me to feel crafty and wise like the ancients who roamed its hallways before me, these seemingly impossible to reach spaces become closer to reach as you craft your serpentine bridges and staircases of colorful triangles with ease and just a touch of contemplation.
Throughout the entire journey for the wise and playful Fox god new powers are being thrown at you, and they do a fine job of shaking things up and keeping the pace exciting. Most notable was the acquisition of the wall walking relic which allowed me to traverse the surface of any connected triangles of my creation, even while sideways or upside down. Within minutes I was constructing interweaving triangle stairs that spiraled up the side of walls and upside down against ceilings giving me a serious feeling of vertigo as I hung high from the tops of the palace.
The levels often times play tricks on your mind, and you can catch a glimpse of a fox sneaking by as you turn around and re-enter a room and notice everything has been completely turned upside down. Is it the elusive and playful fox god we give chase to that plays these tricks on us as we navigate the puzzles of the world of the Odd Gods?
This is exactly the kind of memorable sleeper hit I would expect Rising Star Games to take notice of and pick up, and having another strange, beautiful and otherworldly title in their growing library of classics is why they're at the top of my list of favorite publishers right now.

One of the better Total War games and the first to allow you to take direct control of naval combat, which is well realized. It's also a game that doesn't take that long - you could breeze through even a 'world domination' campaign in just a day or two with most of the playable factions.
The modding scene is very strong with numerous gameplay-tweaks and overhauls available to spice things up a bit. My main gripe is that, outside of the Shogun TW games, the unit rosters are among the least varied - most of the European factions have near-identical unit rosters, and their unique choices are all too often functionally identical to eachother. Only the Ottoman empire and the Maratha Confederacy really buck this trend significantly, though the Russians have a few gimmicks too.
The game offers a tangible way of winning without conquering absolutely everyone through prestige victory, which is nice in principle, but in reality is still best achieved by conquering everyone. It's nice if you want to role-play a bit though.
Excitingly, the game takes place in three theatres, Europe, the Americas, and India, which gives you multiple avenues of conquest.
My main gripes are that Agents don't seem to grow very much. Gentlemen don't become better scholars while they are researching in a school, missionaries don't seem to improve much while they are preaching. The diplomacy AI is maddeningly stupid and thinks it is winning wars even if it is being crushed, and will often refuse to aquiesce unless you have their final settlement under siege (and even then it might deny demands, or even requests for peace!). Lastly, there is too much bias on things playing out a certain way - in every campaign I've done Prussia ALWAYS stomps over central Europe. The Maratha Confederacy ALWAYS gains full control of India. The Thirteen Colonies NEVER rebel against British Rule. Part of the joy of Total war is creating and witnessing alternate history, and seeing the same things happening time after time gets a bit stale. Too much is engineered to happen or not happen. I'd love to see a game where the Mughal Empire actually manages to resist the Maratha Confederacy, or one where France and Spain actually do something over in the Americas.
That's not enough to really ruin my enjoyment of the game. There is something very majestic about watching regiments of line infantry shoot the living hell out of eachother. Watching cannonballs rip through cavalry units in slow motion never gets old, and nor does mowing down foot soldiers with cannister shot. This game also has the best research tree of any of the total war games that came after. I enjoyed the way that scholars worked with schools, allowing you to really take control over how research-focussed you wanted to be.
Overally I really enjoyed, and continue to enjoy, this game.

While it may not carry some features found in the classic trilogy up to the same standard in terms of number of locked rooms, interactive puzzles and complexity of the map design (though it does bring them back which is very welcome nonetheless), it makes up for it with its simple yet harrowing atmosphere as well as far more robust shooting mechanics with faster enemies to take advantage of the new system. It even brings more elements to the table (at least only compared to the classic trilogy) that are unique to this entry, such as secret items that are hidden much better than in previous entries to the point that they're very missable, some new intimidating villains which actively persue and harass the protagonist, and secretive optional puzzles that won't be that obvious unless you pay very close attention. The opposition is now far more conniving and malignant when compared to those of the classics' as well, alongside some of my favorite boss fights in the series (how many games let you
Yeah. Not a lot).
In terms of visuals, the game nails it with almost life-like character designs and animations. The more quasirealistic contributes to the game's unnerving and eerie atmosphere. Unfortunately, there are times where certain models feel less realistic and more cartoonish-looking, though the gore and viscera at display helps to distract you from it just a little bit. The game doesn't shy away from taking risks, with special segments that can be triggered in-game that only contribute to building up the Baker family as this malicious force even further. The game will surprise you with genuinely-unexpected moments, by remixing the enemies you run into as you move around the house. A crafting system is available in the same way one was available in Resident Evil 3, but unlike then where it felt like it easily broke the game, this time around the new crafting system here manages to keep things balanced to a fairly large degree, without detracting much from the main experience.
It breaks my heart, but there are some very apparent flaws with this game that need to be addressed. The new Molded enemies do leave a lot to be desired even if they do manage to do an okay job at filling in whenever the Baker family isn't after your buns. The tone of the game also takes an odd turn and has a more action-focused not-really-all-that-scary atmosphere somewhere around the third act, with the very last hour of the game especially feeling more like a drag rather than an actually-entertaining lead-up to the final showdown. Also, what's up with all the remote bombs in this game's third act? It keeps throwing so much at you in place of actual ammunition, so even if you decide not to use them, you've pretty much got your hands tied behind your back.
Four last minor gripes: cutscenes are unskippable due to how they're integrated into the game so speedrunning is going to be a bit problematic; the limited saves via this game's version of the ribbon ink is limited to the highest difficulty in the game, which is something I absolutely despise as it was a feature that added additional weight to the player's actions; there are only sixteen save slots for some reason, which is odd considering how Resident Evil 4 has a total of 20; this one is more related to the PC port itself and it's the CPU-throttling which causes various degrees of stuttering, depending on your hardware, through various points in the game which could render it unplayable (turning textures down to medium seems to solve this issue, and oddly enough the game's textures on characters look just as fine on medium as they do on ultra, most probably due to all the other effects, which I'm not entirely sure of, masking the textures' clarity).
Overall, Resident Evil 7 is a welcome return to form that returns to the original formula while also maintaining an identity of its own. It's certainly no Resident Evil Remake (or whichever one's your favorite), but it manages to do a wonderful job at delivering an experience reminiscent of the original survival horror classic it started out as. It's absolutely worth giving a try (unless you dislike first-person shooters) and hopefully a sign that Capcom is on the right track again with this franchise.

I've never played Mordheim the tabletop game, but I heard it was good. This isn't. All the nice looking set pieces and good voice acting can't save what is a very shallow turn based tactics game. Most TBS have some kind of tactics to them, certain troops being suited towards certain roles or certain weapons being good against some and weak against others. This game has none of that. Aside from being able to see further from higher up (I think) and being able to ambush around corners, there might as well be no terrain. Ranged characters seem like they'd be good as long as you protected them, but they only get 1 attack compared to the 2-3 a melee character gets. At first it seemed like you'd be able to set up little traps and things, but the AI is so brain dead it's better to just group your warband together and gang up on the enemy one at a time. The tutorials make a meal of explaining the simplest of concepts and indulge in large blocks of text for small amounts of information. It's never clear what characters can equip what until you try to equip it. I thought my captain would be allowed to equip a pistol for instance, nope. Why? No clue. Captains aren't capable of holding them I guess. Maybe there's a skill I can get or something, but it'd have been nice to know in advance.
The real let down is the lack of diversity in the warbands, maybe it imporves later, but to begin with you get your leader (always the same one), you can hire a hero (1 of 3 choices, you only have 1 choice to start with) and 3 henchemen (2 different kinds, ranged and not ranged). Leter on you unlock more slots including an "impressive" (basically a big guy for any bloodbowl fans) slot, there is 1 "impressive" choice for each race. You can use the skills to diversify the warband a bit and make more unique characters, but then if one dies, you have to go back to genericland and pick one of the faceless drones to take his place.
I was left with a pretty lame experience of Mordheim, and there are some who'll say I didn't give it a fair chance, but I want my refund, I don't want to be stuck hoping the game "might get good eventually". Glancing over the positive reviews makes me think you perhaps need to already love the tabletop game for this game to be worth getting.

TL;DR at the bottom!
The best way one could describe Yatagarasu would be if 3rd Strike and King Of Fighters had a child.
This child is a real throwback to the late 90's early 2000's for fighting games, with simple combos and confirms, gorgeous sprites, and a killer soundtrack.
You won't find any massive combos in here like you can find in games like Skullgirls and Marvel vs Capcom 3, instead this games primary focus is footsies, you need to be able to safely get in and get a hit to confirm into a small combo ending with either a special or a super, all while making sure you're not punished in the process. But tha also means you'll have to defend against people coming in at you, and you have multiple tools to do this. You have your standard anti-air attacks and blocks, but you also have a parry, something 3rd Strike players are very familiar with. But beware, if you miss this parry, you can eat a lot of damage from an incoming combo.
The netcode, while a bit scary at first, is very good, with adjustable inputs to to minimize lag and work with whatever ping you have. (I have heard a rumor, however, that it will eventually be getting GGPO, which will be prettier and easier to use, but comes with all the problems GGPO entails, i.e. frame skipping rather than lag).
With a cast of 11 characters that all play differently, there is variety in the cast.
There are also "commentators" in the match, these range from the in game characters to actual commentators in the FGC from both Japan and America, such as Tokido, James Chen, Ultra David, and Maximillian. This is a nice novelty, but eventually they all run out of quips to throw out, and get's old after a while.
One thing this game has the people may see as a problem is an intentionally low resolution, so it could better emulate the feel of the fighting games from the era it draws so much influence from, but the people who place a high importance on this should be warned.
The only real negative this game has is the unpolished UI, such as 2 different modes both being named "Arcade", text overlapping in the lobby select screen and while doing the challenges in training mode, but im sure this will be touched up in future patches, and is a negligble complaint as is.
TL;DR - Amazing fighting game, total throwback gameplay and visually, great netcode - if a bit intimidating, subpar UI, 8.5/10

What can I say? This is a love letter for kids of the 80's. I'd played Double Dragon I and II, thankfully not III from what I've heard about it. Double Dragon: Neon is heavily derived from those, and was intended to be a classic reboot. Since most 80's games made no real world sense, it relies on humor instead of trying to be serious, and it does a pretty good job. The game references 80's pop music, hard rock, hair metal, along with references to 80's television programs, including the very recognizable main villain.
This game introduces to the series 10 special attacks, though only one can be equipped at a time. Like all modern games feel like they must do, there's an arbitrary level up system for "stances" you equip, as well as these special attacks. There are a number of special attacks initiated through button combos, much like your typical beat-em-up and fighting genres. Because of this level up system, it creates somewhat parabolic difficulty as it starts off hard, gets easier fast, gets kind of wavy until you decide to get the repetition over with, then becomes hard again once you unlock Double Dragon difficulty. Honestly I wish they'd have stuck to more classic style difficulty scales, but "experience points" seems to be a box to check when it comes to modern game design.
A couple more universally agreeable flaws came pretty close to me giving this one a thumbs down, including:
- After about 3 full levels or so, performance seems to gradually decay. It could be specific to the GTX 670 or certain families of NVidia drivers (and mine are up-to-date), but what happens is over time, there'll be increasing frequencies of frame drops until it affects gameplay too much (especially with platforming in the later levels) and I ultimately restart the game.
- I've had the game crash, but it only happened once over 6 hours of split play sessions.
- There's so many logos at the start of the game, it almost seems like parody. You can't bypass them either. Seriously, forcing me to look at your logos for 20-30 seconds won't make me appreciate your companies at all.
- The ending also can't be bypassed even if you've seen it before.
- It's a little time consuming going to the shop and songsmith. Probably should have had its own level on the world map. (that world map that does absolutely nothing)
- It's going to take you some time to get used to control timing. Due to being tied to "realistic" animations, many actions like running and turning around are too sluggish for a video game.
That said, I found the game enjoyable. For the $10 game tier, it's right where it should be.

Fantastic Beat 'em up with a lot of awesome aesthetics.
It knows what it wants to be and it's hard not to get hooked in with the silliness of the humor, references and the music.
The music, by the way, is REALLY good, as per usual with Wayforward games.
The fighting mechanics are simple but great. It's not at all a button masher, which is something a lot of beat 'em ups unfortunately end up being.
Every move feels like it matters as you need to time your heavy attacks just right and dodge at the right time to increase your damage output.
Mashing the attack buttons will just get you killed quicker basically.
So the fighting mechanics are very welcomed as it feels very satisfying now that it's more difficult for all the right reasons... Well almost all.
See, this game also introduces very light RPG elements. You collect two types of music tapes: Special moves and Stances. The latter is what kinda rubs me the wrong way.
It undermines the importance of skill when fighting. If you have too few tapes of one stance, it's not worth it on the harder difficulties. Too many and it's a bit too easy.
I like the tape collecting, but I wish that stances wasn't a thing. Or at least that they wouldn't increase or decrease stats with more tapes like like the special moves.
It's not that bad, but it's a slight annoyance when you realize that getting 10 more tapes for "Balance" made the harder difficulties much easier.
In conclusion: Awesome game which I think is the best in the series. Even if you're not a fan of Double Dragon, it doesn't matter. Helps to be a fan of Beat 'em ups though...

I write this for those who are looking for a co-op game to play with their young child (age ~6+). This may well be the game for you.
I'm godfather to a 6-y/o boy. He loves games, and so do I, but there aren't that many games that we can play *together*. And there are fewer games still that hit that sweet spot. For example, he likes to play Metal Slug with me, but has trouble with the platforming elements (very minor in this game), and there generally isn't much I can do for him when we play, other than kill all the enemies quickly. The ideal game is one where I can help him out but he still feels like he's pulling his weight. And that's exactly where this game had us. With me playing just a little better than average, the two of us were able to finish the game together. You can share health and life points in fun but easy ways (in-game high-fives, he loves it). You can forgo taking any of the power-ups yourself. You can choose 1 special move (which you can then power up using in-game money, which is also shareable) and you can also choose 1 passive buff. In that way, you can find a combination that makes up for your kid's weaknesses. Give him extra health and defense, or an invulnerable spin kick. We had a lot of success with the combination of magic gambit (extra magic power) and the dragon swarm, which makes a giant dragon appear on the screen and hits all the enemies no matter what (but takes up a lot of magic power, hence the magic gambit) special. He loved doing this. We finished the game together on normal mode, and went a good distance into hard mode already.
If you want to have a good time playing with a young one that has a decent understanding of how different buttons consistently produce different actions, then this could be the game for you. I do recommend buying it during a sale, as I think it is worth closer to $7.5 than it is to $15. The pc version has crashed on me a few times during the final boss battle and ending scene, but that may have been caused by the latest nvidia driver, which was giving me some other problems as well. Seems resolved now.

Charming and uniquely stylish first-person puzzler with fantastic soundtrack. Blends the challenge of puzzle solving with the Zen of exploration and treasure hunting, with a core gameplay that is playful, creative and provides an unusual amount of freedom to the player. Navigating the world of TRI is almost an artistic process in its own right. A must play for any fan of games like Portal, Q.U.B.E, Qbeh, Magrunner, FRACT or puzzle gaming in general.

Tri is a very very good game. It is a puzzle-exploration game. In each level there is a locked teleporter, which require three keys to open. Your task in each is the find the keys, find the teleporter and continue to the next level. Off course things do get complicated as you go along. To help you navigate the levels, you get the "Tri" - an artifact capable of producing triangle. The triangles can be created anywhere, as long as each corner is anchored somehow, and they are not too large. As you go along, the "Tri" can be used in more or less three ways - to create platforms, to be used to walked on walls and ceilings (dont ask...) and to bend light. The use of the "Tri" is fundamental to complete the levels.
There are in total 16 levels in the game, and if you know exactly where you are going and doing, some of them can be beaten in 10 min or so, though others require 20 min just to walk from start to exit through mazes. However, this is if you know the puzzles already, your first play through expect to spend 20-60 min on levels just to solve them. Added to this, there are an  x number of idols hidden on each level, some of them very devious. These are not required to finish the game, but you unlock concept art and such by finding them. Finding all will take a lot of time searching and head-scratching.
The game in not "trippy" as such, it is in fact quite serene. The mood of the game is peaceful, and it is much more cerebral than twitchy. The puzzles are logical, and the physics are 'real', so do not expect any subversive puzzles like Antichamber. The game is very highly recommend.

That game is a truly unique experience, which is only possible on a PC (probably a Wii U, too), because it needs good first person controls and benefits from a precise but fast pointing device like a mouse.
The game play is innovative. You may be reminded of other games but using triangles to solve puzzles permits you to do it with a lot of freedom. And the puzzles are challenging and diversified, so the game performs as a flagship of its genre.
Furthermore the beautiful artistic style and soundtrack cover so much individuality that I am able to assign it to the game instantly, when I see or hear a piece of it.

I've always been a fan of first person puzzle games ever since Portal. Since then, I've tried to play all of them from titles like Qbeh-1 to Path to Thalimus and I have to say, TRI has impressed me a lot more than most. The story line is pretty decent but the thing that really impressed me the most were the puzzles. You get to create these triangle sheilds that can be used as many things from platforms to mirrors that reflect light, all adding several possibilites to completing most the temples(Test Chambers) and finding all the secrets, and if you're into these types of games, I'm sure you're gonna want to find all the secrets and the exploration really makes you use your imagination when it comes to completing a temple 100%. There is also scores for best times and least triangles used, a great feature that adds to the replayability of the game. I remember playing portal and trying to get the least amount of portals as I could and the hours I spent doing it. I'm sure that will follow with this game as well. The only feature that I think could make this any better would be some type of 2 player online coop, but even without it, it's great fun. I definitely recommend picking this up if you're into these types of games, you won't be dissapointed. Oh and did I mention the graphics feel like a magical cell shaded deep space minecraft :)

Another in the long line of indie horror games that never gets going, has an interesting concept that's quickly abandoned with left-field developments, all filled out with a clichéd and predictable plot.
For the horror aspect, well it's best to say: even I wasn't scared by this game. I don't play many horror games, I'm easily scared by their shenanigans, but this one never really tried. It was certainly unsettling, but that's only down to you and how long it takes you to realise you can run around and make as much noise as you like when no demons come out to get you.
The concept seemed to be that you're roaming a hunted house or being attacked by demons, but with the killer twist that you're just a baby. This concept is explored for all of 20 minutes, after which you enter alternate worlds (the classic MC Escher-inspired linear platforming, toddler style). It doesn't help that you'll likely guess the ending and major plot points in the first 10 minutes. The characters say or do a couple of things at the start which appear to be hinting and foreshadowing, only for it to turn out they were just saying random crap you shouldn't have analysed.

Bought it on sale, but honestly it wasn't really worth the time or money I spent. Not scary at all, not creepy at all and they used no method to force the player to actually care about what happens. You basically just run around just to fall down and crawl and then stand up again all the time. Hardly any game mechanics to speak of, it's just one of those games you can play in around two hours, but if you could actually walk without falling down all the time and move a bit smoother, it would take around 30minutes to run through this game(yeah, I know it's meant to be like this, you're a baby after all, just putting it out there that it's short with almost no content). I like to look around and find items or funny things, but there is hardly anything of that either, just a few childrens paintings to pick up. Extremely easy, not even once did I have to stop and think "what should I do to proceed?", everything was obvious and you just picked up everything you needed on the way forward. The only good thing is that I didn't notice any real bugs, it flows on fairly well. But no real story to speak of whatsoever.
If you're really, really, really, REALLY bored and can get this on a sale and you have nothing else to do whatsoever, give this a try and it might help you burn 2-3 hours. I guess it gives what it says it does, you're a baby with super problem solving powers(for a toddler) crawling through a house while seeing illusions created by an infants mind, and I guess it could be considered somewhat creepy, but it's not scary in any way, every time a monster showed up I just ignored it and went on my merry way, when the monsters finally started chasing after you, everything you had to do was hide under a table or something, and usually you didn't even have to care even then as you could just crawl to your goal without minding the "monster", as it hardly aimed at you anyway, while disappearing in just a few seconds.
I respect the idea of this game, but I just found it really boring in the end, there is absolutely nothing to keep you hooked and care what happens, as there is really nothing much that happens anyway, way too linear, you just walk through everything and solve a few ridiculously simple puzzles that are so obvious that a toddler could realize what to do instantly. Do yourself a favour and find something else to play, please, anything is better than this, read a book, watch a movie, play another game, this is absolutely not worth your money nor your time, unless you're into linear games with a screwed up atmosphere and no story where you just mindlessly charge through. Even if you get it for free, just play something else and let this game rot in your library, it's way slower than it should have been with the content given, just a waste of time. I have a feeling that most of the people that upvoted this is either one of those people that are "neutral" and thinks it's neither good nor extremely bad and therefore went for thumbs up, or the guys that are total pansies and get scared when they hear cracking in their house, or the people that upvoted it for being "acceptable for the price" or maybe those that didn't like it but thought that it was better than some other games. If this was a free game, I might upvote it due to similar reasons, but even 1 dollar/euro is too much for this.

As from my experience it's good, but it has some flaws that I can see so far in PvE. However keep in mind this is a PvP based game, and not PvE. So, here are my pros and cons about the game so far. I'll start with PvE first. But before we get into my review, let me tell you guys what Absolver is. It's a love child of For Honor, as far as PvP combat (in a sense) with the Dark Souls difficulty against NPCs and overall aesthetic. However calling it that would honestly lessen what the game actually is. Apart from that, here's my review of the game.
PvE is fun, the story is nice and interesting enough to continue on and play through. Enemies aren't too difficult at the beginning when you start out with little moves, however some of the cons I've seen is that at the later stages of the story that they start doing something called input reading, which means they start reading your inputs and moves in your combat deck and abuse their ability to dodge, absorb or parry your attacks. This is especially in the area just before the final boss. However as the developers said PvE should be experienced with other players and friends. The community in itself is nice, with the occasional bad apple. The story is also quite story, it isn't a very story driven game, but the story you get is, like I mentioned, interesting enough. Moves are learned through PvE or PvP through different foes, and can be troubling to unlock if the foe you're fighting is particularly difficult, but if your friend has the move you want, it's easily enough farmed like through that blocking or your special ability.
As for the PvP it's fun, thrilling and really addictive fighting against other players, especially if they're knowledgable with their special ability and combat deck. I've had many close calls, many perfect wins and many perfect defeats, and I can honestly say that whenever I lost, I knew I lost because my deck wasn't on the same level of his, my ability was off at the wrong timings, or overall my skill level was less than the person I fought. However I always knew what I did wrong, and improved on that. That's what Absolver does. It makes you improve the things you lack in, be it your combat deck, your usage of your ability, or special powers. Biggest flaws I've seen in PvP, or overall the game, is the lag that it occasionally has, but the developers are working hard to improve that for the experience of the player.
Overall the game has more pros than cons in my opinion, it's PvP is fun and addictive, it's story short and sweet, with the occasional frustration and difficulty through input reading, but overall it's a game meant to be played with or against other players. Overall I'd give the game a solid 8/10. There are some flaws that need to be worked out, but if done right, with updates on the way with potential new moves, new styles and even new gear, I can see Absolver eventually even becoming an Esports game, much like For Honor will be.

Tri Of Friendship And Madness is yet another puzzle game shown from a first person perspective. I love these kind of games.  But is it as memorable as the Portal games or Q.U.B.E. ? Maybe. Let’s find out.
Tri drops you into the world of the Odd Gods where you have to complete 16 stages in order to find out what happened to two of the foxes that once inhabited the world. You’re being guided by a ghostly figure that gives you cryptic advice and messages. In each of the levels presented your goal is to collect the three hidden fox statues and to put them on their pedestal. Once all three statues have been placed on the pedestal you’ll be able to exit the current level and progress to the next one.
The game has a soothing and relaxing atmosphere. You can take your time; there’s no rush, but if you want you can beat your previous ‘records’ by replaying a level as quickly as possible, by collecting all of the hidden idols or by using the minimum amount of triangles. These triangles are an important part of the gameplay, so let me tell you a little more about it.
Your character carries a device that allows him to create triangular platforms. You can do this by pointing and clicking the mouse. The game will automatically complete the platform once three points have been placed but you have to take into account that there are many rules that make it impossible to ‘just’ create a platform. No, that would be too easy. For example, you can’t create platforms on wood. You also can’t create platforms in ‘corrupted’ spaces, and since the platforms created are in 2D (remember that you can only place a maximum of 3 ‘entry’ points) there’s no real depth or thickness in them. There are more factors to take into account, but I’m not going too far into this. It’s something you’ll experience and see for yourself.
Each level also has an amount of golden idols to collect. These are usually hidden in places you normally can’t reach so you have to carefully set up your platforms in order to be able to collect these. They don’t add anything to the experience, but it’s a fun side activity nevertheless.
A new ‘power’ will also unlock every couple of levels. The first one obviously allows you to create the platforms themselves, but the second one will allow you to walk on walls by carefully placing your triangles. There’s also a power that will let you redirect light and teleport.
The first couple of levels are very simple and can be finished in a matter of minutes. Halfway through the game becomes a bit harder and completing a level can then take anywhere between 15-60 minutes. Since you’re able to walk on walls after just a few hours of playing you can imagine it can get quite complicated; the camera will rotate often and some people might experience motion sickness because of it.
The puzzles are actually very fun - and sometimes also very challenging – to solve. You can’t die, so you can experiment as much as you want. You won’t fall to your death and you won’t get killed by enemies (because there are none). The mysterious story and characters make you want to keep playing, just to see what might’ve happened. The story isn’t 'in-your-face'; you have to think for yourself here, so it makes for a good incentive. A job well done, if you ask me.
The graphics are simple with relatively basic geometry. Graphically it reminded me of the game Kairo; it uses the same kind of soft graphics. But there certainly are more colors to be found in the world of Tri. Some of the levels also have a Japanese atmosphere, because of the lighting, use of colors and some of the objects in it (like lanterns). The visuals won’t blow your mind, but they definitely get the job done.
And the music: well, the music is… different. I thought that there were a lot of ‘world music’ influences in the game, with music similar to African and Japanese ‘tunes’. It’s subtle and not ‘in-your-face’, but it’s definitely something you’ll notice while playing. There are practically no sounds, with just a ‘hnnng’ sound for jumping and sounds for creating triangles. It’s all very basic stuff.
The voice acting is also limited (so far) to only one character. But this person does quite a decent job at pulling off a convincing, yet mysterious, character.
The length depends on your skill and intelligence. Some might finish it in 10 hours I think, others (like me) might take a little longer. Some levels are harder than you might think, and even though I’ve been stuck on the same puzzle for a few hours now I’m still enjoying it. Maybe because there’s no time limit or the fact that I can do what I want, trying to figure things out at my own pace. In any case, it’s a good sign. The length is perfectly fine for a game with this price.
Yes, yes; Tri is yet another game that can be added to the list of already excellent first person puzzle games like Portal and Q.U.B.E.  It introduces a new gameplay mechanic that’s original and one that works surprisingly well, even in puzzle format. The mysterious atmosphere makes you want to keep playing and the increasingly difficult puzzles are(mostly) fun to solve.
All in all this is a great game for puzzle enthusiasts.
[Rating: 82/100]

set in the Warhammer Fantasy universe, where the goal is to survive a hellish landscape in order to gather a rare, and dangerous, material known as Wyrdstone, known for its chaotic influence and ability to enhance magic. Being set in the more turbulent era of Warhammer Fantasy history, there is an abundance of weapons to use that are unique, magic with consequences, strict limitations and possible firing zones with ranged weapons (of which there are bows and firearms), and mythical races of characters. While this game does not have all of the races from the older Mordheim, the four chosen are very different and give a very accurate (read: grimdark) feel for the setting.
in CotD are the Empire Mercenaries, Skaven, Cult of the Possessed, and the Sisters of Sigmar. These races are divided into Warbands, consisting of (as time goes on) one Leader unit, up to three Hero units, one Impressive unit, and five Henchmen units. Following will be a generalization of each race, their purpose, and then a general playstyle (though this game is nearly limitless with how you create your Warband, and how you play them, especially with injuries being added into the mix). An interesting little game. The rather goofy, "totally radical" general aesthetic and Saturday morning cartoon plot (not that I mind these things much) belies an actually quite sophisticated, if also slightly unintuitive, set of fighting mechanics. Compared to the fast paced arcade beat 'em ups of Capcom and Konami days of yore, Double Dragon Neon is much slower and more deliberate in its approach, with slower attack animations and what has to be the largest input buffer of any fighting game I've ever played.
To explain what I mean: An input buffer is a mechanic, usually seen in vs. fighting games, where the game allows you to enter the input for your next move within a certain window of frames before it's actually ready to come out, instead "buffering" it to automatically be used on the first available active frame. The Virtua Fighter series is well-known for this mechanic, using the buffer to make the game less "execution-heavy" by giving you some breathing room to make your inputs rather than require frame-perfect timing. Double Dragon: Neon also uses an input buffer, but at something in the area of 30 frames, half a second when running at 60 FPS, this buffer is positively cavernous by fighting game standards. This severely punishes button-mashing playstyles typical of the genre, as you'll often keep throwing out attacks after you wanted to stop due to this, which conspires with the generally slow pace of moves to make it easy for enemies to counter you, and forces you to be careful in committing to any particular action.
This can make the game feel sluggish and unresponsive, but with some pacing allows for near-effortless dialing in of some rather deep combos, something not typically associated with beat 'em ups. This melds well with the evasion/gleam mechanic of the game, ensuring you can readily dish out highly damaging combos without worrying about precise execution thereof, and even adds some strategy to larger fights, such as using enemies that are easier to gleam off of to give you extra attack power for a combo against harder opponents like Abobos. Enemies and stages in general are also well-designed around this slower paced system, and it rarely feels like you're put into situations that require more maneuverability than what the game allows for as long as you aren't mashing buttons recklessly. If I could have added anything, it probably would have been more aerial combo potential, as there's one jetpack-equipped enemy (Roxy) which I felt the system didn't have enough viable moves against. Speeding up the pace of combat and reducing the input buffer might also have been nice to make the game more friendly to button-mashers, but isn't as big a deal relative to that.
As a rather straightforward game beyond that with only 10 levels there isn't too much else to say. The mixtape system has some customization potential, but feels a bit grindy at times, and generally speaking once you max out your preferred tapes there isn't much of a reason to switch. The soundtrack is pretty spectacular, especially its original songs, but that's going to depend on how much you like 80s throwbacks. One place I would fault Double Dragon: Neon in particular though, is its netcode. I've only had a few connectivity issues with it, but the bigger issue is that the second player experiences the game with a large amount of input lag even in optimal conditions, making it a lot harder to play the online multiplayer as player 2. I usually let my friends host the game so that they don't have to put up with that, but there really isn't a good excuse for it to have been this bad.
All in all, Double Dragon: Neon blends a very strong, if also rather subjective, audio-visual aesthetic with some actually rather deep fighting mechanics for the beat 'em up genre. It feels rough at times, but also very deliberate, requiring more thinking ahead and anticipation reminiscent of vs. fighters rather than the classically more straightforward arcade beat 'em ups of yesteryear. While bad netcode for online multiplayer is a let-down, the game isn't so hard as to make it unplayable, so I'm willing to overlook this flaw for the price. Fans of the genre's younger days may be disappointed by the reduced capacity for mindless fun, but for those who find the throwback aesthetic charming and are interested in the idea of a thinking man's beat 'em up, Double Dragon: Neon is worth the buy.

as a long-time fan of the Alien Breed franchise (at least the top-down ones) since the Amiga days, I was more than just a bit reluctant of seeing these new iterations of the games that I played and loved/hated during my youth (they were and still are among the most challenging games I've played, even in two-player)
but I was pleasantly surprised by this game - it truly does 'feel' and [play] like an 'updated version' of a classic game [should be]
sure it's not nearly as challenging, [mainly] due to the fact that you can actually [save your progress], but the 'feel' is there and it doesn't just 'look like a prettier version' of the classic, but rather what it sets out to be - an updated version of a classic
I am certain that if I was to analyze the game on a deeper level and compare it to other titles of the time of its release, I would certainly be able to find flaws and quirks, [but] this is a good ol' fashioned arcade-style shooter with upgradable weapons and a great atmosphere
my only gripe is that the multiplayer part still takes place on 'the same screen' (i.e. the players are unable to move outside of each-other's viewing range)
apart from that, I'd say that other companies from the era should look at this as a prime example of how to update your old classics in a way that stays true to its roots and at the same time adding nothing more but the necessities of keeping up with the times.

This game was my first Total War experience, and I must say, I was quite lost at the start of my journey. The grand strategy and RTS genres were probably the ones I had the least experience with, but playing around with this for 340+ hours was both an enlightening and rewarding experience. Even though this game is old and outdated by todays standards, that doesn't mean it isn't worth trying. I have completed around five grand campaigns, and as expected, are very similar to one another. The three 'superpowers' of the time period (Britain, France and Spain) are the only factions that have missions, one for each of them. The game does little to encourage more playtime apart from these three faction specfic missions and the initial goals of conquering a set amount of regions, making the mid-game quite tedious. One thing that needs to be addressed (and probably never will be by CA) is the fact that the Maratha Confederacy is ridiculously unbalenced. I've seen them field between 10-15 armies (a few of them full stacks) just in one region. I'm not sure if they're supposed to act as an invasionary force much like the Chaos Warriors in the newly released Total War: Warhammer, but if they are, it hasn't been done right. I've noticed that the aggressiveness of the Confederacy may be due to a patch made by CA due to complaints about factions not being offensive enough and is frequently mentioned in old posts found on the Total War Forums for this game.
Apart from this, the battles are entertaining and sometimes (perhaps rarely) even challenging, depending on the troops you field (to this day, I still haven't mastered Cavalry units). The siege variant of these battle can be boring, unless you take the fight straight to the enemy, unlike the historical methods of these situations. Sea battles are initially confusing, but are actually quite simple and easy to master. I recall that there is a guide someone wrote regarding this.
Overall, the game stands as a great acheivement and a welcome first step into the world of the RTS and grand strategy. It may trip over its own feet at times, but the entertainment value found in the game is ultimately up to the player.
Edit: Also, the Warpath Campaign is hard for the Iroquois, and the Austrian Army barely stands a chance against the Prussians from the get go. Very-Hard difficulty is insane, and combat bonuses for the enemy are ridiculous. Keep it to normal or if you want a challenge, hard for decent enjoyment.

I generally like to wait until I have a handful of hours in a game before I make any sort of recommendations. But sometimes you don't have to bother waiting when there are glaring problems.
This is easily Top 10 one of the laziest ports ever made. You play this with the keyboard and mouse (arrow keys to move, mouse to aim) and no option to change that those key bindings. I don't know about you but when I'm using the mouse for aiming I'm more comfortable using WASD for movement. But here's the really fun part! You have to use the R key to dodge. Just stop and thing about this for one second. Your left hand is on the arrow keys, your right hand is on the mouse, HOW EXACTLY are you supposed to reach that R key?! And to add insult to injury you can't simply just press R to dodge, you need to R+direction in which you wish to dodge.
So! You take your left hand off the arrow keys and move it to the R button and you take your hand off your mouse and move it over to the arrow keys, and presto you can dodge! For something like an on-rail twitch shooter dodging is an essentially core gameplay mechanic. This is broken, the controls in this game are broken.
I kinda want to like this game, I'll probably play it a few more times, but until they patch this up and let you customize your key bindings I can't help to tell you all to stay away from this. I can see why this went for $0.99 during the sale.

I am usually not a fan of "horror". I don't llike scary movies and I thought the same would go for games, but I was wrong! This is my first experience with a game tagged as "horror" and I was pleasantly surprised by the storyline. So, let me get into what I liked about the game.
PROS:
- unique perspective (as the two-year-old)
- you really aren't sure what the truth is until you finish the game.
- great "worlds" that you explore to find pieces of a puzzle that are childlike and at the same time creepy
- not enough to severely scare you, in my opinion (this might be a con for some, but for me it was good as my very first horror game), but there are some startling/creepy moments
- the subject matter is deep, which is refreshing, and the ending is surprising
- music and visuals let you know when you are in danger
CONS:
- The only con I could think of was that I really wanted the game to be longer! It only took a couple of hours. I mean, the length was good with the storyline, but I just wanted more! I'd be interested to see if they make more games like this from a child's perspective.
OVERALL:
9/10 (minus one point because of the game length)

This game is really fun if you're willing to put in the time. I have already beaten it but I am still very eager to learn more moves and become better than I am now! This game is worth the buy if you've played a few other fighting games such as DragonBall Xenoverse and others.

Intro:
Absolver came to us at the beginning as an inovating idea for a game, offering the player the freedom to create his/her own fighting style with the many many moves that the game has in store for you. Having 3 special abilities for each "class" and some special moves caused by some stones owned by the player. These can also summon weapons (A sword or wargloves) which also have a very personalized moveset. Having that said the main focus of the game is simply the PVP which does hurt the game a bit in terms of lifespan.
What's good about absolver?
-As previously stated, it brings great diversity and a breath of fresh air to us gamers and fighting game enthusiasts, with its unique fighting mechanics and costumization on each of the 4 stances you have as you fight.
-Brings a story mode that is very simple and straightforward that has you explore the basics of the game, and the entire map you'll have to live/fight in.
-Filled with NPC for you to learn new moves from, while fighting them.
-Allows you to find random players on your travels to fight, team up with, or learn from if they belong to a school of martial arts.
-Weapons that are fun to use and a decent leveling up system.
What about the downsides?
-Despite all the creativity it brings, since each move can only be assigned to certain stances, at the start it will take you a very long time until you can get the moves you want and even then it will feel very short as you may not exactly get what you seek in the fighting style you want to create.
-The hidden and fourth fighting style stagger is quite strong compared to the others and may get frustrating to deal at first. Perhaps even more.
-The servers are unstable and online can be chaotic at times due to that.
-Despite simple, the story mode feels lacky and with the whole map to explore, all the time you lose is trying to find your way rather than fight and explore interesting stuff. The map is very bland and not the epic fighting scenario you'd expect, unless in very specific zones.
- You can only have 2 more people on your world. Its understandeable so the servers don't overload or a player starts lagging out too much, but this still feels very unsatisfying in my opinion.
-NPC always spawn back, and if you wish to travel the world and perhaps just fight some friends on certain areas, those are all limited as NPC will always be there to annoy any player that comes to their path. If we could explore the world where all we find are actual players and NPC are turned off, that would be far better for those who do not seek any more EXP or new moves.
-NPC read your inputs at times and attack accordingly which can be very frustrating. Not to mention they come in groups of 2 or 3 and gank you a lot.
-The game only brings 2 types of weapons. Swords and Wargloves. It falls short but I guess they are already sort of fun if it wasnt for the fact that Wargloves have the exact same moves as you do on your barehand. Altho you can make it just a different moveset.
-Feels very incomplete.
Over all the game is great and a breath of fresh air but a lot of flaws prevent the game from being even better. Since its still too early to determine that, we can just hope that future updates fix some of these flaws and make the game even better than what it already is.
Would I recommend it despite all of it? Yes I would. It is fun and a great unique experience. You can lose a lot of time here either grinding, having a lot of fun or even being somewhat frustrated at some fights that do not go your way but finally after altering your fighting style, it starts to work. Well, that or just use Drunken style. Its easy.
So get the game during its early days because if the devs do not update it at all, this game might die in a matter of months.
My rating? 6.5/10

The game is good beyond a few early bugs here and there. For example I've fallen off a ledge had an enemy follow me off only for the enemy to fly off across the zone and get stuck still alive ontop of a tree you can't reach at all that said this glitch only seems possible to do with the miniboss in the arena.
Combat in the game is great once you get used to it and I love the art style they've used.
That said there are also huge flaws...
To start with while the PvE aspect is great most of the time when you are online the minibosses tend to spawn with extra mobs around them (In some cases I've seen multiple minibosses spawn which I think is a glitch but I am not sure) making the already hard fight impossible for new players by themselves and hard for solo players who don't want to group up and cooperate with people.
Next up the bosses. They're great to fight each having their own different battle tactics... one spawns endless waves of pathetically weak mobs until he draws his weapon, one boss is two seperate bosses that you fight at the same time, and then there's the one who's alone has nothing really different about them but they are far more powerful than the others.
That said there is a problem here... once you've beaten a boss you can't fight it again until you do enough PvP to get up to 10, 20, and 30 (For the second encounters)...then that level required rises again if you beat them again. Admitedly these are second ecounters and third encounters your character has with these bosses, they have different cutscenes... the boss is harder to beat... so on and so forth, but personally I find the fact I can't face that boss again at the level it was at to be annoying...the boss fights are enjoyable and they are the only good taste of combat in PvE where you can fight a single enemy (Most other PvE ends up with you fighting two, three ...sometimes even four enemies at once in combat that seems designed for 1 on 1 but I'll cover that later on) making them in some sense a good way to practice for PvP.
And on that note... PvP. Generally whenever you get an opponent of equal skill in the PvP the fight can be good fun and enjoyable the combat system in the game works BEST with only 1 enemy staring you down after all. That said there are problems with the PvP that I've found for example how it matches you to an opponent which is that it just doesn't match you to the opponent it just grabs the first other person it can find also queueing and going 'Here's a person! Fight this guy' not paying any attention to how it just put a completely new person who just found the PvP of the game with a guy who has been playing this since before release and has way more experience and moves... this ends with the newbie being crushed of all hope to improve as they probably have no chance of even beating the player it just dropped them with. Then you have the fact that PvE content is locked behind this awful 'matchmaking' and hey presto... a way to make PvE content impossible for anyone who isn't immediately skilled at the game after starting.
When it comes to getting combat trial levels in the game, which is necessary to unlock boss fights as mentioned, you need to get 5 stars to level up (this doesn't change ever) you get 3 stars for a win, 2 for a loss with 2 rounds to you, and 1 for a loss with one or no rounds won. Balanced and fair ... except that means someone who is hopeless at PvP but enjoys the PvE content has to suffer through 50 rounds or less of mostly straight losses to fight one boss again... then have to repeat that again to get another boss and again to get another boss. I don't know about you but only a serious masochist would enjoy losing hundreds of times in a game mode they can't stand just to continue doing what they like about the game.
Next up learning moves. You learn moves by blocking and evading moves you haven't learned yet naturally this sounds easy enough. block moves... dodge moves... counter moves and learn the move! sounds simple enough doesn't it? Well once you've filled up learning the move you have to then defeat the enemy and if you get killed the progress you gained from that enemy goes poof completely, no mercy all of that progress gone to waste. I mean sure the game is designed to be merciless and difficult but when you're ganged up on by 4 enemies at once trying to learn a move is the last thing on your mind as you frantically try to beat them all while they try to do the same to you. Personally I'd like it if you retained some of that experience on death... 1/4 of what you earned perhaps making fully learning the move only possible when you beat an enemy using that move.
Now onto that PvE problem I mentioned earlier in this review. The combat in the game is clearly designed with 1 v 1 in mind most moves will hit in an arc making 'friendly fire' an inevitability if you and another player attack the same target that said this also applies to the npcs as you can dodge only for an enemy behind you to get walloped instead by his friend. That said the main issue I find in the PvE is when you get thrown 3+ enemies at once ... at this point the combat system stops working effectively as they launch an endless tide of attacks some hitting each other as they do so but mostly making it impossible for you to block their attacks and they tend to surround making evading one attack the same as leaping into the way of another attack making combat very unfriendly when outnumbered by NPCs.
There's also a lovely annoying feature to the six minibosses in the game where when online... in a zone with multiple other people in it which tends to be the case minibosses spawn with two friends around them. Pulling any of them pulls the boss as well making the fight go from already difficult to outright impossible for a lone person to do.
In summary while the game in general is great fun the content is also heavily oriented towards PvP as most of the story is literally locked behind doing PvP so I wouldn't recommend it for anyone who doesn't like to PvP ...at least until they add more PvP modes than what the game currently has which is just 1v1.

Red Comrades Save the Galaxy: Reloaded is a remaster of a classic RU point and click adventure, the very first big(ger) budget one, which was so influential it essentially borne a new sub-genre of typified "Russian quests" ("quest" being how "adventure" genre was known due to Sierra series) - wacky pop culture heavy parody adventure games. And yet, despite always having a soft spot for adventure titles, this was my first ever time playing it, simple due to how incredibly pop-culture reference and cheap comedy reliance, which is not something I ever liked.
As a glimpse on what late 90s post-soviet parody/humor could be, it's a great history piece. And it's also a surprisingly well put together, quite well animated and relatively well paced game in its own right - it doesn't feel "cheap", rather - intentionally ugly, but with a lot of polish and thought underneath. That said, given that a lot of its humor is based on racial, gender and historical stereotypes and typical jokes of late-/post-soviet times, you might not get it or find it funny. Personally, I wouldn't find it particularly funny even in the late 90s, but I'm still glad I went with this experience and finally played the game.
