-Airmech Strike-
Airmech. A game that blends tower defense with RTS. A great combo, but there have been some issues over the years. A lot of experimentation has been done. Some for the better, some for the worse - but hey! That's what Alpha & Beta testing is for. While it is still in Early Access, the game is undergoing what we call The Big Split. What this essentially means is that Airmech Strike becomes the PvP focused portion of the game. No parts. Just pure player versus player. There are no co-pilots, so no stat differences on that part either.
Where-as the upcoming Airmech Wastelands will contain the PvE content as it's focus.
"But what about my stuff!?" you may ask. The answer to that is: You will gain access to your inventory in both versions of the game. In Strike, however - you will not see things will parts, where-as in Wastelands, you will still be able to see your parts, Co-pilots, etc.
"I'm VIP, why can't I play Wastelands!?". Well, the reason for that is that Wastelands is not currently ready even for VIPs to test. Much work needs to be done, so that we can enjoy the game.
"Is Airmech worth playing?" Yes. It's free, there's a pretty decent community. The gameplay is fun.
"There are some things I don't like. Will those things always be there?" Well, depending on what it is that you do not like, there may yet be a few changes here & there to balance the game out. Feel free to drop by the Airmech forums.
"What do you think of the gameplay?". Personally, I rather enjoy it. It's fun to see the changes. It's been a long ride for thise game, but it is ar from over. Will I continue to be here a few years from now & even still play the game? Ofcourse!
Fun to see ideas pitched on how to balance or fix things, as long as those suggestions, or bug reports are in a constructive manner.
So overall:
*Great community
*Great dev team
*Fun gameplay
*Sweet Soundtrack by Front Line Assembly
*Not super active players in-game 24/7, but one has to take it for what it is. A game with potential & it's getting there. There will always be a few hours of silence during certain parts of the day.
*No Pay-To-Win, only Pay-to-Pretty. Doesn't hurt that one can earn diamonds in-game to boot.So even non-VIPs can earn enough to get a few shiny things over time, should they want a re-skin, or a replacement head, or even wanting to pimp out their Mech with a new look. Heck, even pets.

Unlike the first couple of Choice of Games series I tried, this one is actually well-written and evocative of place and character. I'll be continuing the story.

It's interesting enough, plenty of action and weirdness, but it's written like some history textbook. No humor (which I find to be the centerpiece of anything I read, watch, or do, and if it's not funny I automatically like it less).
Another problem is that if you die - which I did - you have to start everything again. Also, I'm not sure if your choices have a long-term effect on the outcome. It seems that your choice will only affect what happens immediately afterwards, or maybe the course of one chapter. So basically, whatever you choose has no effect except whether you die.
Now, after being a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by starting with only the bad things, let's move to the boring part - the good things: the story was interesting, I liked the villain (sadly, not for her personality - only because she's really cool), the setting was nice (medieval Britain -who doesn't love it?), and my character was someone important, which is a nice change of pace from real life.
It's pretty long - It took me 2.7 hours, and as I mentoned, I died. So I probably had, like, half an hour left minimum. I personally think that's a good thing, but you may have your own interpretation.

Pendragon is a decent game and a very good introdcution into text-based rpg games. The game had me hooked from start to finish, and immersed me into a roller coaster ride of tough choices, interrupted with comical moments. I found that the more I played, the less I looked back on those hard choices made. Despite not ending up on the path to becoming the traditional Arthur, my experience felt richer and equally satisfying. Cons: Wished that there was more development of character relationships, reminiscent of BG I & II. Also, I just wish that the game didn't end so abruptly.
I would like to have seen the Pendragon story continue for many sagas covering the whole life of Arthur.
8/10
The second time I played through, "The End" page did not appear to go with the story. It mentioned characters that were not in the story and made no sense.

I wanted to like this game, because I've played a fair number of text based games I enjoy from this company, but the stat system got too frustrating and quite honestly just take me out of the immersion. There's simply no clarity to what each action will lead to and at times make me feel like I am being punished for the choices I make. Face all my opponents singlehandedly and take them out? Does nothing for my close combat stats. Responding to an event with a shred of humility gives me a huge penalty to my warrior abilities. Okay? I guess the warrior stat is affected by more than just combat then. That's actually pretty creative.
Few scenes later, make the smart decisions and plan ahead for an attack, rally my warriors and lead the charge. Somehow decreases my warrior abilities. Why? Because I had to charge off on my own apparently. The fact that I asked one of my battlesworn friends to assist me somehow made me worse of a fighter. There's no consistency to what actions affect which stats in which way. And the thing is that I don't have a problem with ability decreases in these games because they usually mean that another ability will get an increase. Which is the case here too for 3/6 of them. On the others, you get an increase or a decrease and no increasing one does not mean increasing the other, at least not consistently.
With the cons out of the way, I suppose it's only fair I move onto the pros.
In truth, the stat system has me extremely frustrated and the main reason for that is because it takes away the immersion and enjoyment of a story I actually enjoyed. I might have rolled my eyes on a few scenes, but ultimately I found the concept intriguing. It's a rendition that tries to appeal to chronological accuracy of the saxon invasion of Briton while at the same time keeping some of the mythology and mystery that make the Arthurian legends so fascinating.
At times you must rely on the advanced medicinal knowledge of scholars trained in Rome while at other times you must rely on the native druids and their knowledge of the land. At times you must approach a mystery from a rational perspective, while at others that which seems like superstition is actually the better option. I really enjoy that, especially because most games (text-based or high budget) I've come across just do one or the other. Embarrass the silly priests with the wonders of science or silence the unbelievers with displays of magic. This game doesn't go for either direction and plays on the setting that both could have value. As I mentioned earlier, there are some moments where I rolled my eyes, mostly due to events that were no doubt meant to be shocking feeling predictable and clichéd, but I enjoyed the writing overall. I liked the pacing and the characters and I could immerse myself in their internal struggles. But the stat system just feels broken and prevents me from completing the game.

A very engaging take on the Arthurian legend that focuses more on King Arthur's ascension to power rather than the tales of him and the Round Table. Pendragon Rising frames the legend by having Arthur (or, should you choose, Arta) be involved in political intrigue in a time of war. Each character you meet is relatable and bears significant weight whether it be in that very moment or in the grand scheme of things. The story presented by Ian Thomas is well-crafted - it's told in such a manner that it does its best to avoid stepping on the toes of Arthurian historians while making it accessible to those who have no prior knowledge of King Arthur or the history of the Britons and the Saxons.
Pendragon Rising differs from other "Choice Of..." text-based choose-your-own adventures in that it's more concerned with telling a story rather than asking you, the reader, "what would you do in this situation?" Rather than explore myriad choices and possibilities, Pendragon Rising asks you instead to be the best Arthur/Arta you can be. There are choices to explore and options to be had, but ultimately some choices are better than others. It's similar to a Japanese visual novel in that there are certain events you need to trigger for certain sequences to play out optimally - otherwise you find yourself at a game over screen.
Overall, Ian Thomas's story is enjoyable and well worth the price. For those of you interested in text-based games, this is a very good addition to any collection. For those who are not but are looking for a good way to pass the time, I would still recommend Pendragon Rising for those interested in a medieval fantasy setting that incorporates magical elements.
I enjoyed it a lot. It focuses on war and gaining support from other kingdoms rather than romance. For now, it's my favourite from the games made by this studio. Will definitely replay this.

Have you ever read a book and wished the character chose differently, or maybe taken a different path entirely? Are you a fan of reading in general? Then maybe this is for you!
It's rather straight forward, you got a written story that you read like a book and ocasionally the "game" will stop and let you chose what happens next. The story will change depending on your choices, this is an idea we have seen a lot of recently, however, since this is a purely text based game it is much easier to make the story REALLY change since you don't need to change any graphics or voice acting.
I can't however personally vouche for how much the story changes in this case since I only finished it once - but I did get the distinct feeling that things could have been quite different, especially after reading other peoples experiences with the story.
The story itself is interesting and well written, I got the same feeling I used to get when reading fantasy novels as a teenager. Is it worth the price? If you go by the old 1$/€ per hour formula, yes, it's currently 3,99€  as I type this and I got it at sale for less than half that - and I got at least a solid 5 hours of entertainment out of it and an interesting fresh experience.
I had ONE problem with Pendragon Rising and I do not know if it's title specific or common to the genre as it's the only text based game on steam that I have tried, but I did not feel like I got a conclusive ending because I did not make the right choices. The game ended on a rather bitter note and I felt like it was basically telling me "Game over, try again" if I wanted the REAL ending.
Since I don't know where I went wrong a second attempt would probably mean I took all the same actions  as I felt all of them were the ideal ones, and i'd change one or two things only in order to see if I could get a better ending which is by no means a guarantee, this basically means i'd spend hours rereading the same content multiple times trying to fish for the best ending which does not sound like much fun, and using a guide feels kind of pointless as i might as well just read a book in that case.
In the end I had to be happy with my lackluster ending and move on. So will I recommend it? Im not sure as im typing this, I would definetely recommend text based games, and Pendragon Rising has a good story - but the issue it has is a big one to me.
I will give it a thumbs up, it's good for what it is and it did provide me with an ending, albeit a lackluster one - i'd suggest to look at other text simulators before settling on this one to see if they have the same issue.

This game is by Team 6 Studios, who also brought you Glacier 3: The Meltdown, another terrible game that bears many of the same hallmarks as this one. Not only does it not give you the option to change the controls, it doesn't even tell you what they

From what I understand both these games are ported from the Wii, where a digital manual is available from the Home screen at any time, but frankly that's no excuse for at the very least making that information available in some form. The game is locked at a very low resolution, and the store screenshots look much nicer than anything you'll ever see in-game.
As far as gameplay, I came hoping for Star Fox, but got nothing of the sort. Bland enemies,
flight physics, uninteresting levels, and the requirement to both move the plane and aim the gun (which I imagine was originally designed to work with the Wii's pointer functionality) just doesn't do the game any favors. This game was my first Total War experience, and I must say, I was quite lost at the start of my journey. The grand strategy and RTS genres were probably the ones I had the least experience with, but playing around with this for 340+ hours was both an enlightening and rewarding experience. Even though this game is old and outdated by todays standards, that doesn't mean it isn't worth trying. I have completed around five grand campaigns, and as expected, are very similar to one another. The three 'superpowers' of the time period (Britain, France and Spain) are the only factions that have missions, one for each of them. The game does little to encourage more playtime apart from these three faction specfic missions and the initial goals of conquering a set amount of regions, making the mid-game quite tedious. One thing that needs to be addressed (and probably never will be by CA) is the fact that the Maratha Confederacy is ridiculously unbalenced. I've seen them field between 10-15 armies (a few of them full stacks) just in one region. I'm not sure if they're supposed to act as an invasionary force much like the Chaos Warriors in the newly released Total War: Warhammer, but if they are, it hasn't been done right. I've noticed that the aggressiveness of the Confederacy may be due to a patch made by CA due to complaints about factions not being offensive enough and is frequently mentioned in old posts found on the Total War Forums for this game.
Apart from this, the battles are entertaining and sometimes (perhaps rarely) even challenging, depending on the troops you field (to this day, I still haven't mastered Cavalry units). The siege variant of these battle can be boring, unless you take the fight straight to the enemy, unlike the historical methods of these situations. Sea battles are initially confusing, but are actually quite simple and easy to master. I recall that there is a guide someone wrote regarding this.
Overall, the game stands as a great acheivement and a welcome first step into the world of the RTS and grand strategy. It may trip over its own feet at times, but the entertainment value found in the game is ultimately up to the player.
Edit: Also, the Warpath Campaign is hard for the Iroquois, and the Austrian Army barely stands a chance against the Prussians from the get go. Very-Hard difficulty is insane, and combat bonuses for the enemy are ridiculous. Keep it to normal or if you want a challenge, hard for decent enjoyment.

Double Dragon Neon revitalizes the classic franchise, but a few missteps derail the silly fun.
What would a magical skeleton want with an ordinary woman? The answer isn't important (and is most likely pretty gross), but the rescue mission that follows this kidnapping sure is fun. Double Dragon Neon is a smart update to the arcade classic from decades ago. By melding the iconic characters and traditional beat-'em-up structure from the original Double Dragon with an overhauled combat system that rewards precise defensive counters and clever skill manipulation, Neon is much more than a merry trip down nostalgia lane. Billy and Jimmy Lee do occasionally stumble on their way to vanquishing Skullmageddon, but Double Dragon Neon overcomes that clumsiness with style.
The opening scene sends shivers down your spine. The sultry Marian walks alone down a dark alley, only to be greeted by a gang of lowly street toughs. With one punch to the stomach, she passes out in pain, and the trio of miscreants march away with their prize slung over one shoulder. A garage door opens, and out walk Billy and Jimmy Lee, searching for vengeance. For anyone who has played the original Double Dragon, this situation should be familiar, and the remixed music ties into the 1980s hit. By the time you square off against whip-wielding Linda and the abnormally large Abobo a few minutes into your adventure, you might think that you have a good idea of how this game is going to play out.
But you'd be wrong. Although Neon makes many references to the original game, it doesn't take long for it to forge its own path. It's a side-scrolling beat-'em-up, so the basic left-to-right kickathon is kept intact, but the combat has layers of depth that make it exciting for anyone itching for a challenge. Your basic moves are punches and kicks, and you dole out flashy combos by alternating between these standard techniques. Once you pound enemies in the head a few times, they become stunned, and their vulnerability is your gain. Toss them into a group of enemies or into a bottomless pit if you wish, or you can deliver a crushing uppercut that suspends them in midair long enough for you to juggle them like a hacky sack.
Don't leave me hanging, bro!
Making smart use of these core mechanics leads to satisfying encounters. A half dozen or more enemies often flood the screen, and you need to attack with precision if you're going to keep the crowd at bay. Mashing buttons delivers jaw-breaking attacks, but you won't get far if you ignore your defensive maneuvers. The Lee brothers have a handy duck technique that becomes the foundation for your success as the difficulty ramps up. By hitting the ground right as an enemy attacks, you avoid damage and you gain a gleam bonus. This makes you twice as strong for a few seconds. Mastering the gleam makes even the toughest bosses pushovers, but it takes practice to get the timing down. Sadly, finicky collision detection sometimes means you get hit even if you moved well in advance. Also, you earn the gleam bonus only by ducking. If you roll or jump out of the way, you still avoid pain, but there's less incentive without the temporary strength boost.
The avoid-and-attack rhythm of combat is strengthened by perks you unlock as you play. Called songs, these add passive and special abilities to your repertoire. If you're dying too quickly, you may want to imbue your character with more health, or you could add damage bonuses when you land successive attacks. Super attacks are just as specialized. A screen-clearing, flaming dragon deals out a ton of damage but drains your magic bar, whereas the one-inch punch doesn't deplete as much health, but you can pull it off more often.
As rewarding as it is to mix and match the perfect abilities for your style, the leveling-up aspect drags the adventure down. Extra songs can be purchased at stores or collected from defeated enemies, and the more you have, the more potent the ability. But unlocking the full potential of these buffs demands tedious grinding. You need to kill bosses to earn the precious currency needed to raise the limit of how many songs you can carry, so you have to repeatedly play through levels to make your character strong enough to survive. This isn't a huge problem in the default difficulty because ducking at the right time and then laying the smack down is enough to defeat anyone, but things become significantly more challenging on the harder difficulty settings. When only one or two hits can take you down, you need your abilities maxed out, and that takes hours of tedious busywork.
Bimmy and Jimmy never looked better.
If you want to conquer Neon, you need to spend a lot of time punching fools, but just having fun doesn't take any investment. The over-the-top atmosphere not only taps into your happy memories, but introduces a layer of ridiculousness that wasn't present in the original game. Billy and Jimmy Lee are unabashedly bro, and they wear that distinction with style. They dole out manly high fives, shout outdated catchphrases like they mean them ("Tubular!"), and wear skin-tight T-shirts that accentuate their PED-defined abs. When Jimmy smacks a goon with a baseball bat, he shouts "Touchdown!" without the slightest hint of irony. Neon is consistently funny and doesn't shy away from crazy situations. From a helicopter that hovers upside down, to the weaker enemies referred to as "cartwheeling cannon fodder," Neon is happy to make fun of itself.
Double Dragon Neon is a good update to the arcade classic precisely because it's not handcuffed to what the original started. By shifting the tone from serious to crazy and making the combat system rewarding for the most dedicated players, this is a beat-'em-up that fits alongside modern games. The downsides are noticeable. Grinding turns even the brightest games dull, and local-only co-op means you have to invite your friends to your house rather than partake in online shenanigans. But for the few hours it takes to reach the end, Neon is a satisfying brawler that's as deep as it is humorous. Double Dragon Neon doesn't quite live up to its prestigious heritage, but it's a well-made game nonetheless.

A true Resident Evil game.
As a huge fan of the original four games (RE 1 thru Code Veronica) as well as RE0 and the Remake I was incredibly surprised to see this came returning to its roots. Resident Evil 4 has always been the turning point in the series for me when it abandoned much of its survival horror for action horror segments. I never made it to RE6 because by then it looked more like a wannabe Call of Duty game. It plays more like the original Resident Evil than any others.
What returns is real survival horror, crafting, item boxes, items procured on site, puzzles, and of course clausterphobic mansions. I felt that the first person view and the slower movement of your character added to the suspense as well. The game definitely takes some queues from Outlast.
I don't fault the game for its main character who isn't really all that interesting and is knd of just mediocre or for the story because Resident Evil never really had a great story to begin with and only got more convoluted with time anyway. In addition the original RE characters were B movie cheesy. It's not Metal Gear Solid writing.
I really only have three complaints with the game. The first one is that the final area of the game felt kind of rushed and ncredibly linear compared to the rest. The second being that the final boss is underwhelming and half baked. Again it felt kind of rushed as if they ran out of time and just wanted to release the game.
One complaint I had was the lack of variety in enemies. Most of the enemies are these molded creatures and even though there is some variety in them it's subtle. In RE1 there were 16 unique enemies (including bosses). In RE 7 there are only 11. And of that 11, there are only three varieties of core enemies that you typically fight.
Regardless the game was a fun ride and I highly recommend it if you want to feel nostalgia for the earlier RE games.

In Resident Evil 7, the player controls a new character, Ethan, who has travelled to a spooky house deep in the swamps of Louisiana in search of his missing girlfriend, Mia.
It won’t surprise you to learn that there are things living inside the house that aren’t friendly, and that want to kill you, although it clearly surprised Ethan, because he didn’t bring any weapons with him. Fortunately there are plenty of weapons to find including 2 varieties of knife, 3 different 9mm handguns, a magnum, a shotgun, a machinegun, a flamethrower, a grenade launcher and some remotely detonated bombs.
I like that most of these weapons are hidden behind puzzles, not exactly complicated to solve, but they reward exploration. Its entirely possible that some players could complete the game without finding everything.
RE7 has changed to a first person perspective, after the other main games were mostly third person. This is definitely a massive improvement, as the environments are more immersive and the combat is more enjoyable. Most of the weapons are fun to use, the only one that I didn’t really like was the flamethrower. Outside of one boss encounter, it seemed to be quite weak.
Its good that most of the weapons are strong, because Ethan moves really slowly, kinda like Isaac Clarke in Dead Space. I guess its designed to make the player feel vulnerable, but when you also factor in the level design, which is often quite narrow and cramped, especially inside the house, you won’t be running away from many enemies. There’s a lot of backtracking through previously cleared areas too, so in the long run its better to kill whatever you see.
Thankfully I was never really in danger of running out of ammo. There’s a useful crafting system, where you can combine chemicals with either herbs to make healing items, or gunpowder to make ammo. You can also take some drugs that temporarily allow you to see hidden items. Plus, playing on PC with mouse aim, I didn’t waste many bullets (although there is this one annoying enemy who has a habit of jerking its head from side to side just as you’re about to fire).
The enemies are the weakest part of the game in my opinion. While trying to avoid spoilers, there are Human bosses, where Ethan’s slow movement speed mean you’ll inevitably get hit even when you’ve learned the attack pattern of the boss (you can block to reduce damage). There are four types of “molded”, that are basically monsters made of a black ooze, and some flying insects. Their visual designs and their attack patterns (run towards player and attempt to melee) are all too similar. The game really needed more enemy variety.
The story is probably the best of any Resident Evil game. Plenty of the usual elements are present –
– but its told in a way that feels more believable and easy to understand. The game is good from a technical point of view – I didn’t crash at all, and I could easily maintain a consistent 60 fps. Controls are fully rebindable.
I’d probably rank this as my third favourite Resident Evil, behind RE1 and Revelations 2, so if you’re a fan of the series, RE7 is definitely worth playing. It would also be a good place to start if you’ve never played a Resident Evil before, as the story doesn’t link to any of the other games. However it only took me 11 hours to finish the game, so the standard purchase price is excessive, and I’d recommend waiting for a 50% sale.

To give you a bit of background, Yatagarasu Attack on Cataclysm is a 2d fighter made by 3 ex-SNK developers. It’s slightly surprising then that Yatagarasu feels far more Street Fighter, and with the inclusion of a parry system, it’s easy to see the inspiration.
Straight off the bat let me say that Yatagarasu is fast. It’s more restrained than a VS game, but so much snappier than a traditional SNK game, with moves just rolling in to each other. It feels great, really on point, and ultra responsive. That said it may be a little too responsive, while it’s nice that specials and combos are easy to pull off, it’s also a little too easy to accidentally throw out your super to end a combo.
The character roster isn’t huge. Granted there’s the argument that fighting games wrongly take the ‘more is more’ approach to their line-ups, but Yatagarasu feels like it doesn’t quite cater for everyone. That said there’s a decent mix, if you like your Ryu’s and Ken’s then there’s a couple of characters there for you, there’s a boxer, a wrestler, even a charge character. As a fan of Garou and King of Fighters, I’d have liked to have seen the ex-SNK devs throw in a few more SNK inspired characters, but perhaps those movesets wouldn’t work at this pace, perhaps they just wanted to get away from that. Either way, there’s no point complaining about what the game isn’t, especially when what it is plays so well.
That said, as a package it doesn’t really deliver on the promise of the core game. A game made by a small team is always going to feel a little rough, but at the time of release (and I held back the review to play some games on release day), the online isn’t where it should be. There’s supposed to be fixes coming, but I’ve struggled to get in non-ranked lobbies. To play online I’ve stuck to ranked matches, which hasn’t exactly done wonders for my ego, but even when I’ve managed to get a game it’s been heavy with lag. It’s hard to know how much of that is because I’m playing against people on the other side of the world, but still, it needs improving. It’s also the reason I can’t really comment on how balanced the roster is, certainly there’s characters I prefer, and characters I’m awful with, but without lots of varied match ups, played at a decent lick, it’s hard to really see their strengths and weaknesses.
The story mode is an odd one. There’s 2 arcade modes, one with more story than the other. The various stories aren’t particularly great if I’m honest, and the presentation of them is the definition of bare bones. The cpu will give you a bit of a match on the normal difficulty, it’s not impossible to beat, and it will leave itself wide open, but it will also parry you and counter. It’s a shame there isn’t a bit more meat there to make up for the currently stuttering online mode, but it’s better than the bare minimum. Offline though you do at least get to see what the game is capable of,perhaps playing online against a not too distant friend will work well enough, but if you can get someone in the same room then all the better.
The training mode is a mix of far more options than you’ll ever really need, and far too little information to make the most of it. It’s not noob-friendly, certainly not if you want more than to just jump in and unleash on something that won’t fight back. You can command the AI to perform certain moves, so it’s not a bad way to practice your parrying, and you can set challenges, but the language used means you need to experiment to see what exactly is being asked of you. Which is indicative of the training mode really. There’s nothing in the game to tell you there’s parrying, or how to do it (it’s a high/low button selection rather than directional like Street Fighter 3), nor about the guard crush, etc. It’s a game that could have done with an instruction book.
This is all starting to sound a little negative, so let’s finish on a positive. While the graphics options are limited to ‘Do you want full screen or not?’, understandable due to the 2D nature of the game, but still a shame that the default resolution isn’t higher, the actual art is great. The characters are animated well, flowing nicely with a chunky 2D look. The backgrounds steal the show though, some are almost abstract watercolours, almost all of them would make fantastic wallpapers if they were a higher resolution. The music is great too, cheesey but great.
It’s a shame then that Yatagarasu’s package isn’t better. Ignoring the clunky arcade mode, there’s also the online settings being outside the game, with no real instructions on how best to set it all up. If you can get it working though, or can play against a friend, Yatagarasu is a great old-school beat-em up, fast paced and fun.

A mix between 3rd Strike and King of Fighters, Yatagarasu: Attack on Cataclysm brings a modern take on classic fighting games. The game's netcode is probably the best delay-based netcode that I've played in recent memory and the mechanics allow for a very honest experience that demands solid play.
The only problems I can see with this game are the lack of keyboard rebinding and how the online lobbies work. Port forwarding is needed in order for players to join your lobby (which could be problematic if you've never done it before), however those with experience with the GGPO client will have no issues, seeing as GGPO needed ports to be opened for it to function.
There's also been complaints about the look of the HUD, launcher, and the lack of resolution options but personally, I don't have an issue with that and I hope that doesn't keep players from enjoying this game.
Do I recommend it? Yes.

All that you read about the broken and biased RNG is true and then some.
Warband characters who have 80%+ chance to hit miss 80%+ of the time. Whilst AI characters hit your characters 80%+ of the time and a high percentage of these hits are critical kills or stuns. Your hits do minimal damage, with very few criticals.

In the 92 hours I played so far I have formed and deleted over 100 warbands, most of them during the first or second mission, because they were put out of action so easily by the AI warband, with resultant loss of items, and treatment costs and cost of replacing items and characters which were out of action or died.

Chances of beating them latter in the game increase, but only slightly. They have high level spells, and multiple high damage hits with weapons.
Out of action characters get wounds which need treatment. This treatment is expensive and far out weighs any loot or gold gained from a mission. On the subject of costs, the costs of training a character are prohibitive. On the one occasion where I did get a warband to a decent level I had characters with 6 skill points which could not be used as the costs were unaffordable. Most charcters had got to their maximum stats too as it took so many missions to get anywhere.
In the end this warband was deleted at the library mission still in the first chapter, as charaters were either so badly injured, lost limbs or died that continuing was not possible.
At high levels the costs of replacing characters who die is so expensive as to be pretty much impossible. This means you can only get low level replacemants who are put out of action the first mission they enter.

Game load times are appaling. Go make a drink, finish it and go make another. If you are lucky the mission may have loaded. Deployment and AI movemnt also gets increasingly lengthy as the warband members increase in numbers.
I will probably continue playing in the hope that the RNG issues are fixed, but I won't hold my breath on that score having seen the number of comments on this area without improvemnts being made.

As a tldr; I can’t recommend this game. If you are mature enough not to be triggered by this and slam that downvote button then keep reading below and I’ll explain. And no, it isn’t about the RNG.
Mordheim is a semi-faithful digital recreation of the table top game of the same name, many of the mechanics of the board game is also present in this one. There is a strong link in terms of aesthetic and lore of the Warhammer fantasy universe and this one is no different – it is highly immersive and the soundtrack isn’t bad either. Not “listen to when I’m at work or at the gym” good but not “Jesus Christ where are the sound settings” bad. Just “meh”.
The lore, what little there is of it, is true to the universe as well and it seems a lot of research has been done on it, which is more than I can say for Deathwing. The game boasts a full 5 factions including Chaos (undivided), Sisters of Sigmar, Mercenaries (empire), Witch hunters [DLC], Vampire counts/undead [DLC] and Skaven. Each of these factions supports different playstyles and drawbacks as well as advantages, there are no hard counters but some factions simply perform better than others.
Mordheim has high replayability due to its format – the game is based around the following areas;
Firstly, you have the warband management layer – You can train units, level them up, customise them, write biographies and hire warriors of different types here. There is also a shop to buy items for your warriors which replenishes every few days with different items.
The second layer is the economy layer – this layer is tied into both the game and warband management layer and serves as a pushing force to get you to take risks. The premise evolves around gathering Wyrdstone (Warpstone, a shiny green rock that is very valuable in the Warhammer universe) from the in-game battles, which are scattered around the map to be collected.
Once you have collected some and win the battle you can sell it for gold to 3 fixed factions which grants you gold based on supply and demand as well as a few minor improvements such as cost reduction for training specific skills.
Your main faction will demand a tribute of the Wyrdstone every few days, which you must keep up with or face consequences. I’ve personally never had issues with this as they are easy to fulfil without taking too many risks.
Each day you get a selection of missions to choose from, each has different optional objectives you can fulfil as well as a difficulty level (of which there are a lacking 3), so there are always different scenarios to play.
The third and final layer is the game is the battle layer, which you will compete for resources and use your warband to defeat another.
There are also a few story missions, but they are nothing of note.
Firstly, the interface is terrible. There are many hidden screens which can be only access by mashing the Ctrl or Alt keys several times to bring up the correct window, which slides in from the left or right of the screen and blocks a large portion of the display.
Secondly, this game is built to support widescreen monitors only. I only noticed this when temporarily playing on a vertical 19” monitor – normally I’m on a 20” widescreen. The change is aspect causes the UI to get mashed up and overlay with itself. I have scaled the UI down to the smallest size possible and I still get windows overlapping – the worst offender is the character skill menu which has a green arrow for rotating your character blocking some stats. I have no idea what the leadership values of my units are because of this. I must guess or look it up when I’m in an engagement by mashing Alt 3 times to bring up the stat sheet.
Thirdly the AI is stupid. I mean, bag of rocks stupid. It frequently passes it’s go, runs into walls, idles, buffs its self with non-stacking buffs 3 times a turn and in some situations, will even disengage from one of your units, and then instantly walk into them and thus re-engaging, at which point it will pass it’s turn. This not only breaks immersion but makes it stupidly easy to cheese the AI. It’s positively suicidal and will drip feed you units by throwing them at you with little care or regard.
This also makes the game horrible to play because you are trying to maintain a warband through not just this battle, but the many more to come. The AI doesn’t see it that way and just throws whatever at you because there are no consequences. The game to the AI is a sprint, for you it’s a marathon.
This brings me onto point four – you are always against stacked odds, even on the easiest difficulty.
One method Rogue Factor attempted to band aid the broken AI was to give it a passive buff based on the mission difficulty level. Even on the easiest difficulty every unit the enemy has does 10% more damage and has 10% more health than your units have. On the hardest difficulty, I believe it will be as high as 30%, maybe more. It’s changes like these that make me not want to support developers – make a half competent AI, not just give it huge buffs because you are too lazy to make one.
The fifth point is the lack of maps and map generation. There are very few maps in Mordheim – I can count 4 off the top of my head. Each of these maps is large but you will only use a fraction of it. The maps have randomly generated buildings, bridges, walkways, etc. you can use but overall the layout is the same. The maps after a few hours become very same-y and boring.
My sixth problem with Mordheim is the lack of both units and unit customisation – every faction has 3 types of hero unit, 1 type of leader, 2 types of basic unit and 1 impressive. That’s it. There is very little you can do with some of them as they come with different weapons and skills by default, so some of the unit types box you into a specific playstyle somewhat.
Furthermore, the customisation is one of the worst I’ve seen in a Warhammer game. The customisation is separated into “styles” and “models” styles are to do with colours and models change the item part itself. The styles range from 8 to 16 colour pallet swaps per model – many of these are darker versions or different colour trims so really there are only 4-6 colours you can choose overall.
Models have a range of 2-4 styles per body part. Sometimes nothing at all. What is even more of an insult is that by equipping armour such as plate mail, helmets and such you can reduce the amount of variation you can have in models. Most units you give a helmet to only get one style of helmet – the same for armour as well. The better you equip your units the more generic they become. WHY?
My final gripe is the Ironman mode. By default, you can only play ironman mode – for those who don’t know what ironman mode is, it is a playstyle where you cannot create manual saves and all your progress is permanent, you can’t back up a save or revert to a previous one. This doesn’t bother me much but it eliminates the casual experience from the game. Which I hate. And the main reason I’m giving this game a negative review.
To roll up the miscellaneous problems I have;
The voice acting is often forced and unbearable. Skaven is the worst for this since the guy doing it sounds more like a west country pirate than a rat man.
Animations are next to none, there’s basically one animation for everything and that’s it.
Good:
Strong world building
Faithful Aesthetic
Correct Lore
5 different factions with different playstyles
Replayability
Continuous progress
Bad:
Interface
AI
Unfair difficulty levels
Lack of maps
Map generation
Lack of optional objectives
Lacking army roster
Unit customisation
Forced ironman mode
Ugly:
Voice acting
Animations
Tacked on content that should’ve been in the game
Verdict: Not worth the end price, get heavily discounted (66% or more) or don’t get at all. The game is still patchy and hollow – the more you play the more issues you will find with it.

I didn't  know the existence of this gem. I'll be honest; I kinda found it because of the last Steam summer sale. I was browsing for cheap point-&-click games, since I'm saving money for a new desktop, and current using my old laptop from the year 2k04'ish.
So, after I've read the description of the game, and check the minimum system requirements, I knew I had to have it on my steam library.
...and what can I say about this Red Comrades Save the Galaxy: Reloaded?
It's a fun, irreverent point-&-click game full of crude humor, corny jokes, cheesy situations, sexual innuendos, and alot of Democratic socialist Vs Capitalist Vs Imperialist type of jokes mixed with some 80’s/90’s Eastern and Western pop culture references, and a large number of Rabinovich, Vasily Ivanovich type of characters. Since it’s a classic point-&-click game, the gameplay is “traditional” simple, you need to get some item to make some character satisfied, then that character will give you another item for you to combine with other item, that will make you able to get another item for other character, and so on. The story is equal simple, two stooges soldiers of the red guard found out their Bolshevik banner was stolen, and they need to find it before Lenin found out. On the way to find where the hell is the red banner, they got a huge help from their beloved neighbour Anka, a blonde comrade which is also a red army spy, working in Imperialist territory, in the process our two heroes found out their major problem isn’t the missing banner, but a grand alien invasion, and a conspiracy which may jeopordize the october revolution in the first place.
I recommend this game, if you like the Point-&-click genre, and want to play something different with some similarities with the game Leisure suit Larry. The animations are quite good, same for the environment, there’s a good “hint” system, alot of easter eggs, the music is simple and corny but quite enjoyable while you’re playing, and having the original russian audio is quite good.
The few cons I found, (ok, I never played the game outside the Steam), but I think the game needed more Steam achivements, there’s some situations in it crying out loud for an achievement, the other problem is some of the animations are quite long, specially in the Alien spaceship, where there’s a part with an escalator and we need to see the character climbing the slow escalator every frikkin’ time we want to go to the control panel, which could had a "Ground Control to Major Tom" achivement.
The other problem is how can I explain the game to my communist friends? Everytime I talk to them about the game they ask “why should I play it?” and my explanation quite doesn’t make any sense and that make me smile because Red Comrades: Save the Galaxy is a good old non-sensless point-&-click game.
and I definitely recommend it.

Alien Breed: Impact is the first episodes of the new Alien Breed trilogy which is the 21st century remake of the oldie, well known franchise of the same name. While the game is capable to grab the player from the beginning, its fast paced and has a story to tell, it has its faults which is coming out in the gameplay itself.
The controls are responsive, but if you ever played with Shadowgrounds, you would wish a similar controls instead of the one you have here, namely the camera and character control. Unlike in Shadowgrounds where you was able to attach the camera rotation to the character, here you have to rotate the camera independent from the character, which is a bit flustrating at few places, especially at one place where you have to escape from an enemy and the camera controls is very annoying.
The storyline is offering a mystery as your starship, the cruiser Leopold is crashing into a larger unknown craft. Right after that hell spreads all over your ship as aliens starts to decimate the surviving members of your crew. You, Chief Engineer Conrad have to find out what this space ship of alien origin is, while you also have to ensure the safety of the Leopold.
As Alien Breed is an episodic release, you'll get all your answers in the second and third episodes, but unfortunately as you step onboard the alien ship in the first episode, Impact, some of the textures of the alien ship is spoiling some twists from the later episodes.
The game itself is a simple fastpaced shooter, with five huge levels to discover and the episode ends with a cliffhanger (Each episodes have 5 levels, so the whole game is 15 levels long.). In the game you may gather credits to buy ammo and upgrade weapons, even sentry guns, while you have to repair critical elements of your space ship and fight your way through dozens of waves of alien hordes.
The atmosphere is good, the environment is detailed and beautiful for this game, but the game can be a bit repetative at times. It's a decent shooter, which is not great, but its still a good experience in the very rare sci-fi, top-down isometric survivor shooter genre. But if you loved the original series or if you ever loved Shadowgrounds, give a try for Alien Breed: Impact.

Microtransaction Simulator, also known as Crate opening simulator, is a brilliantly made action RPG city builder with elements of both FPS and open-world survival. It follows Ben Doverson, a simple gamer looking for his long-lost love through a harrowing adventure to reclaim the promised lands. It’s story and lore is well crafted, each word delicately placed to create a beautiful experience, a wonderful yet dark look at today’s societal fears and culture. You can really connect with each and every character as they go about their daily lives. Even the AI for little things such as ants will react to you. Fish will even swim away from you; such an amazing technical feat for our times.
Its graphics are simply astonishing for this era; each human looks realistic and hair from animal’s fur all seems to be placed individually. The physics took me completely off guard as well; compared to other games which pride themselves on the physics engine, they look false in comparison to Microtransaction Simulator.
The only real complaint I have is that you need an incredibly powerful computer simply to run it on 4K mode. It’s sad to think that even with today’s technology crafting such tear jerking master pieces such as Microtransaction simulator, we still do not have consoles powerful enough to run CPU heavy games like it.
I rate this a 9.5/10; for a beautiful story, amazing graphics, this truly is the game of 2017.

There are too many reasons why this game is THE BEST game that you could ever buy on steam.
There is so much that I can say about this game, but I will talk about the best aspects of the game.
The open world aspect of this game is incredible. From scene to scene, each area has something new to see and experience, from throwing pennies in a well to finding gold in the mines. It isn't a straightforward gaming experience, you can take your time and not be bugged by AI characters constantly telling to you move on with the game.
Along with the main storyline, there are THREE amazing minigames to play throughout The Land of Darkness:
1. The Brain Tickler: This minigame isn't much of a "minigame" as it is more of a game that you can experience along your way throughout the main in-depth storyline that is "Pajama Sam: No Need to Hide When It's Dark Outside". This game contains extremely hard multiple-choice questions such as "How is a star formed?", and even harder "What color is an orange?". These are extremely difficult questions that you will have to endure to be able to get to a certain area in the diverse open world of The Land of Darkness.
2. Cheese and Crackers: An extremely difficult minigame that consists of a 3x3 board where you play a toaster in a game of "Cheese and Crackers", a game where you must get 3 cheeses in a row before he gets 3 crackers in a row, taking turns placing down a cheese (you) and a cracker (the toaster). There are also other board sizes that you will be able to play on, but before you can even play the game, you must
There is no game in the world that can compare to this one.
3. Remote Mining Terminal: Quite possibly the best minigame within a game of all time. In this minigame, you take control of a minecart picking up gems in a grid, and each time you pick up a stone, the cart behind you increases. It is an extremely complex game to explain in text, you have to play it in the actual game.
The storyline goes as follows: Sam is about to go to bed for the first time without his big-boy night light, but gets scared of the dark, as we all do. You must then take it upon yourself to turn into...
You enter your closet to find that is The Land of Darkness, a magical land filled with toys and socks that Darkness lives in. However, you are stopped by the customs trees, which take your stuff that you must find to be able to defeat darkness. You go on a long and dangerous journey through The Land of Darkness, making lots of friends, such as a boat and a minecart, to help you find your extremely important items: a flashlight, a limited edition all metal Pajama Man lunchbox, and your mask. I will not spoil the difficult steps you must take to get said things, as each playthrough the items are in a different area, providing you replayability like there's no tomorrow.
In addition to all of this, the game comes at the price of only $6.99, an extremely low price for what you are earning in the end. I definitely recommend that you pick this game up, as there isn't another game like this with quite the content and replayability as this.

As of writing this review I've played 31 minutes of the game. I know that's not a lot, but I want to make one thing abundantly clear about the genius design of this game.
First, yes this is Double Dragon via Wayforward's goofy sense of humour. The moment you start the game up you are battered with screaming 80s nostalgia and Double Dragon injokes and a game which clearly refuses outright to take itself seriously. AND THIS IS IN NO WAY A BAD THING.
Let's be honest, Double Dragon is a product of its time. It has no business being a modern remake. If Ubisoft or EA or whoever did this, it'd be trash. It'd be like Duke Nukem Forever. Highly anticipated, woefully disappointing and a slap in the face to our memories. Wayforward KNOW this. So they jacked the game up to 11. Neon is in no way just a fun catchword. It is the SOUL of this game. Everything from the music to the character designs to the one-liners and the first boss (and probably bosses beyond that!) SMACKS of 80s ethos and design. It's nostalgic in the best way: It reminds you of all that was great when you look at the past with those rose tinted glasses, AND pokes fun at how bloody ridiculous it all actually is. It makes you laugh at it and yourself and also warms your heart with the reminder of how things used to be, and the ACTUALLY FUN things about it too.
The second most important thing about this game's genius design is how SLUGGISH everything feels. I remember playing the Streets of Rage and Final Fight series and marvelling at how quick and responsive everything was. Moves fired off nearly immediately and combat was straightforward but detailed enough to be entertaining, especially as both series expanded.
What struck me immediately upon playing this game was every movement has a lead-up time. Running, every attack, each attack feels slowed down and has a big tell, and more importantly, that it's GLOBAL. It affects EVERY character in the game, enemies included. Every attack still feels like it hits hard and has a lot of weight, mostly due to great sound design and the effects displayed, but everything was over the top and had huge tells to it. Then it struck me as to why this is a genius design decision. Because of the ducking/dodge mechanic, this means that you have time to counter-attack, time to know what's about to hit so you can react accordingly. Rather than it being a twitch-game, you actually get to think about how you're going to attack an opponent. You can learn their 'tells' and counter them effectively. It balances out the brutal difficulty with ACTUAL SKILL. You can no longer just face an enemy and hammer the attacks repeatedly and hope for the best. Now you can actually learn to dodge and counter opponents, stun them to lead up for throws which will topple other foes so they don't flank you, you learn new moves and special attacks which allow you to deal huge damage and counter other special attacks, weapons have their own unique abilities and are suitable in different situations...
These two points alone make Double Dragon Neon far more than just a cheeky, fun, silly remake, but turn it into a very well designed game IN ITS OWN RIGHT. If it wasn't Double Dragon, it would still be a fantastic sidescroller beat'em up. For this alone, despite the short amount of time I've played it, I recommend it.

LMB = fire the constantly overheating gun, RMB = hold/release to lock-on/fire the unreliable missiles, MMB = Hyper Speed (TM), ARROW KEYS TO MOVE, AND B OF ALL KEYS to refill missiles at the cost of score, which doesn't matter. Basically what you do is hold down MMB for the entire game to rush to the boss fights where you spam all your missiles and shoot it for a few seconds. With
, you can play a Choose Your Own Adventure Game in which you take on the role of a young Arthur or Arta, just having returned to your homeland of Britain after your education in Rome. Against your will, you get caught up in the war with the Saxons, and unwittingly become the Warleader of your people. Will you be able to gather enough allies to help you stand against the Saxons? And what kind of leader will you be -- a fearless warrior or a more peaceful diplomat? But the most important question of all: will you eventually take the crown for yourself?
+ The atmosphere is fantastic; it oozes mythic warriors of long-forgotten times
+ The author obviously knows a lot about Arthurian lore
+ The relationships between the characters were superb; I felt really invested in my protagonist's friendships
+ Despite it being shorter than most CoG games in length, it feels just as rich as the others
+ You actually get to pick choices that are not "canon" in Arthurian legend
- Despite the relationships feeling so real, there was no stat for them per character
- No save points
- Limited romance options (be warned of the famous incest relationship if that freaks you out)
Great game, and I was invested in my character and their relationships right from the start. Recommended for fans of interactive novels with Arthurian themes!
Note: choosing to play as either the male Arthur or the female Arta swaps all the main characters' genders around to match that of the protagonist (except for Morgan/Morgana). Playing as Arta, it was actually really cool to imagine all those massive armies of women marching through old Britain!

Ever get bored of promised graphic updates only to be disappointed? Fret not, for Pendragon Rising (And other games from Choice of Games) lets you use your imagination to power their stories. Pendragon Rising is a well written story that urges the reader to quickly come to grasp with the lore of the world, which there is quite a bit to learn on every playthrough. The romance system in the story isn't at all what you've seen in other CoG games, but personally I find it refreshing and a tad bit more relatable. My only complain about the game is how short it can be- it took me roughly 2.5 hours to finish it in my first run, shorter if I hadn't restarted it twice. But it does have high replayability if you're willing to read through some of the other mandatory texts.

Previous reviews have mentioned the good things about this game, so I will mention the bad.
1. My main gripe - No saves. There is literally no way to go back and see what a different choice would have done without doing ALL the choices over again. Which means in order to do everything, to see what your decisions do, you need to make your own flowchart, because you can make multiple saves to do divergent paths.
2. My second gripe - Achievements. The achievements are listed as not just being something you successfully did, but as having a "point value". This implies that those points could be used for something. They can't. Period.
3. While you *can* fail, it seems like you can only really fail at the end, or very close to it. Even intentionally making the stupidest of decisions will leave you alive for quite some time.
Don't take these things as me saying the game is horrible, it isn't. But these are the main issues I have with it.

-no checkpoint system
-does not appear to have a relationship system typical to the Choice of Games franchise, however, the story plays out so that it doesn’t matter
-limited romance options
-very strong story and equally well-written
-your decisions have great impact – if you fail to gain allies you will most likely fail
-stats matter – if you try a diplomatic option when you are known for taking the warrior route, there is a chance things will backfire
-interesting characters with many different scenes to increase replayability
-added religious element – if you so choose, you can honor the old gods or embrace the new Roman God
A fantastic title in the Choice of Games franchise, try it out if you enjoy choose-your-own-adventure text-based games and want to role-play as Arthur (or his female equivalent)
I recommend!

I'd like to say that i really enjoy this game and it does have issues i found to be very noticeable, but i still liked my play of it. So here is my long review and two cents, i hope you enjoy reading it
To begin with i'll mention the great -
The game is set in the warhammer universe and the atmosphere of the game perfectly captures the chaotic and ruined hellscape of the ruined city of mordheim, you play as one of four warbands in your quest to plunder the city's riches and satiate the lust of your contractor, whom you must regularly send shipments of treasure (Wyrdstone) to or you suffer severe consequences.
The city is tremendously pretty to adventure in, and by that i mean the maps are rather detailed and there are plenty of nods to warhammer lore.
The game is turn based with an RNG system and rather similar to xcom in that you have your little "Base" where you do all sorts of things such as customisation of your henchmen, buying equipment and so on, as well as the fact that you send your troops off to battles around the city to loot and otherwise stab the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of anyone that gets in your way. The game also contains permadeath, mutations, and permanent injuries too, to spice things up a bit. But they can also result in you wishing to fire a henchman as it is largely a hindrance when your tank darksoul gets his shield arm severed..
The battles are rather intense at times, always keeping you on your toes and rarely forgiving of mistakes, and the loot is absolutely worth it if you take those risks.
The game also contains a LOT of different weapons, each with their own benefits and drawbacks and so this allows you to tailor your warband to your tastes and play style, allowing for sneaky light armoured guys that run around shooting things from rooftops, heavily armoured guys that run around bonking things with big weapons, etc
The game has quite the "narrative" sort of system going for it as well, for example i have frequently conversed with my friends as to how their warbands are going and we will tell stories of how our henchmen only just barely made it out alive of battles with their lives intact, or how many people lost numerous limbs in one battle, or how even a single skaven went around on a luck streak beating the brains out of half an enemy warband.
Other times we will mourn the passing of our level 10 henchmen that we literally spent over a hundred hours playing with and have uncountable stories with.
This is further reinforced by the fact that you may rename your characters, and even add bios to them to make them feel more lifelike (and to make you cry more when they inevitably perish due to the city of the damned).
Now, positives aside... there are some things that bother me
Ok, so mordheim is typically described as a "hardcore" game, and while it could be said that it certainly is, the problem is that this comes from the fact that most scenarios you are put in are actually...rather unfair.
Now hear me out for a second - during all battles, even on easy as far as i know, the AI always brings more units than you, and with an increase in difficulty, the more units they bring than you. To make matters worse, their stats are also ALWAYS better than you, even on easy difficulty. And to further makes things harder, on any difficulty beyond hard (which is the second easiest difficulty ironically), Chaos Daemons show up on the map and rapetrain everything in sight. It's to the point where they either destroy your entire warband, perma killing half due to the level of♥♥♥♥♥♥and permanently injuring the other half of your warband OR the daemon turns on the AI warband and you run around looting every orifice of the map while the AI gets butchered helplessly.
If by some strange chance you do manage to take out the daemon as it flails it's arms around the map relentlessly, you typically won't have enough leftover soldiers to actually damage the opposing warband, it took my entire warband to take out a frickin daemon just to have an entire imperial warband rock up immediately after with their pockets stuffed with half of the city's treasure and then proceed to jam their swords into my moist chaos buttocks.
Further reinforcing how i feel about the game being unfair to a certain degree, is the campaign. The campaign missions are VERY hard. Very, very, hard. Even if i outclass the opponent's warband rating by 500 points.
So how does that work?
Well, the campaign levels are always unique to the mission and typically have lots of features you dont normally find in typical missions, such as opening doors, teleporters, weird♥♥♥♥♥daemon things, special abilities, even a unique character to come with you and so on. Mordheim: City Of The Damned
Based on the table-top game from Games Workshop. Turn based, stats based character development, Morale Tests etc
This game is very addictive and has loads of fun to offer. It is also very hard and challenging to begin with (do not expect a difficulty option to start your game). You need to play smart, be cautious and apply some forethought or tactics to your style of gameplay. Towards the endgame things become easier due to character development and your own game experience. Be warned - you can still lose and suffer for it!
You will find yourself frustrated and believe the 'die' are always cast against you but this is not the case - this is Mordheim. You win and lose, its how you come back that makes the game have more to offer.
4 Warbands are available to start the game - Mercenaries (Human), Skaven, Possessed and Sisterr of Sigmar. Perhaps more will become avaialble as time passes. Each faction has its own SIngle player campaign missions to complete as well as random battle encounters and missions for you to choose from, your overall goal being to keep your faction sponsor happy anf make timely Wyrdstone deliveries in the correct quantity. (You scavange these in mission whilst fighting off the enemy warband).
Next you have the whole mulitplayer aspect to the game. Play against real people and experience a real thinking and cunning oppenent as oppossed to game AI. All the while you can gain XP and still level up to use in the SP campaign.
Downsides to the game - people say it looks or feels rushed from EA to full release because the graphics are not perfect, if you zoom in and look around you can cut into characters' heads and walls will get sliced off partially. Visually the environment is very eerie and gloomy - well replicated Mordheim there. Yet there is no fine detail and polish. The characters clones, limited base models and are only cusromisable to a degree and can easily all end up looking drab and too similar.
There are also a lot of RNG complaints but again you have to make the odds favour you through attacking clever and using numbers where you can to force all alone tests and ensure you can stack attacks and debuffs etc.
It wasnt until my third warband that i grasped it and had a little luck go my way and i took them all the way to level 10 overall. Stick to Normal and Hard Missions and pick your tougher fights carefully to give a better chance.
Your choices in Mordheim are permanent. Death is eternal.
Dare you enter the City Of The Damned?

Release date: 22 march 2011

Mafia II is a complete masterpiece. From the best driving physics I've found in almost any game; certainly the best in any open-world, to an extremely interesting, attention-grabbing, and beautiful story, with all characters being likeable, memorable, and filled with personality.
The open-world itself is also filled with personality. Every corner you turn you will be hit with a completely new-looking neighborhood or block, and you will feel like you are in the game the whole time.
The character movement system is superb. You can run infinitely, fluidly cutting corners and hopping fences to break the lines of your pursuers and continue on to do whatever you want in the extremely interactive world.
The combat, also, is superb, with and impressive fighting system, and a wide arrange of guns that have advantages in all different situations.
The police notoriety system is extremely advanced too, with realistic chase times, normally brained cops (no AI cops predicting that you'd in an alley miles away from where you started), easy escape methods, and realistic reactions to your crimes. For example:
(1) If you hit a car and drive away immediately in front of a cop, he will chase you down and write you a ticket.
(2) If you fist fight a random ped on the sidewalk, and a cop is witnessing it, he will run over and break up your fight - no penalties at all.
(3) If you end up killing (knocking out) a ped and a cop witnesses it, he will want to arrest you. If he does catch up to you, you have the option to bribe him to clear your notoriety level, or run away, which will then encourage them to use lethal force.
(4) If you escape an active police chase, you will be "wanted" by the police. This means they will look for you in the clothes you were wearing when they last saw you, so an easy knock-up at a clothes store will completely clear your wanted status - or you could just buy the new clothes (boring ;p). Also, if you were in a car during the police chase, your license plate will be wanted, but a quick run to the many garages throughout town will let you change your plate number instantly, or you could just switch to another car. AND that's just a fraction of the whole system!
There's lockpicking, stick-up's, car deliveries etc. There's honestly too much to put into words, just buy the game, it may be the best purchase of your life.
Everything about this game is well over polished, and there are limitless ways to have fun - between - and after the story.
Mafia II will engage you immediately, pull you into a world of wonder, and probably until the day you die.
A true landmark of gaming history.

TL,DR: If you like early modern history, or RTS games, you should definitely buy this game.
REVIEW
Empire: Total War was released in 2009 and I've been playing it since. It's an 18th-century grand strategy game similar to other games in the Total War series. This title focuses on rifle combat and line infantry; naval battles and trade and colonialization. Empire: Total War is truly a global experience as the game takes place in Europe, India and the Americas. Large battles between thousands of soldiers on land, naval battles with dozens of ships at sea and an enormous grand campaign map are the hallmarks of this game.
PROS
-Great graphics, even for today's standards
-Balanced difficulty (Very Hard is quite a nearly impossible challenge; while Easy and Normal is not too difficult. I would recommend the "Hard" difficulty setting)
-Tactical gameplay is quite fun and engaging, especially at harder difficulties. The AI often notices your blunders and can counter them
-Expansive game map provides hours of conquest and city-micromanagement opportunities
-Diverse choice of countries to play as: For instance, Sweden and Spain provide completely different campaign experiences against different foes. The United Provinces (the Netherlands), for example, has a very strong navy and trade system but has only one province in Europe. The Ottoman Empire is probably the most fun to play as due to hardships in perhaps every category and the uniqueness of their units
CONS
-The AI is too stupid at times and they sometimes can't even respond to your attacks
-The AI loves to troll you by just standing still immediately outside your cannon range. You cannot approach them without taking losses
-Armed fortification battles can often be very buggy or against the player's favor, as the defending enemy will take very little losses unless you have a way to outsmart them
-Almost useless Diplomacy at times. Very few opposing states will ever accept any agreement if you are at war with them, even to make peace on terms beneficial to them

Red Comrades Save the Galaxy: Reloaded is the remastered version of Red Comrades Save the Galaxy which was released in 1998. It's a point'n'click game with the main story happening in Russia during a Civil War, where our characters go in a recovery mission for the lost flag, and they end up saving the world, at least for the moment. The main protagonist are Vasily Ivanovich Chapaev(in the subtitle Chapaev won't be mentioned) and Pete(like this his name is translated...I think in the old game he was called Petka) and for a short period even Anka.
The graphics are the original ones. The soundtrack is fitting with the environment. The only downside(if you can count it a downside) is the lack of the English voice over,English being present only as a subtitle. For the controls we have the clasic one and a new, simplified casual mode. There is an inventory system which is accesed by right click in casual mode or by selecting it from the menu in the clasic mode. Also there is a hint system which can help when you are stuck, sometimes the hints be vague and that can prologue the time required to figure what you need to do next. There are a lot of jokes and references in the game.
The game is divided in three sequences. Each one happening in another zone. First sequence is in the Red Base, second one in the White Base, where around half of the sequence Anka is the protagonist(as a spy with the name Anna), and the third one in the alien base on the moon.
If you are a big fan of achievements/trading cards no worry. Red Comrades Save the Galaxy: Reloaded have them both.

Been playing for a bit today. I have quite a bit of experience in fighter playing competition for over 15 years and in arcades since I could reach the stick. The game feels solid and has nice mechanics. This combines the kof type 4 button style with Third strike (3S) parries for 4 buttons.
Parrying in this game now has big consequences compared to 3S and are done with one of two buttone (high or low). On the ground if hit you take more damage and more hitstun, in the air a failed parry allows you to be juggled 5 more times for huge damage. Universal overhead give combos when hit on crouching opponent and mostly neutral on block. There are some commmand normals, such as the grappler must hit df+hk to sweep.
The animation has a 3S style and the game feels nice and responsive. You get to pick your super like 3S as well. This very much feels like its own game. The cast does have some influences from 3S and "clones" play nothing like each other.
I'll update this the more I play, but this is definitely solid so far. GGPO will be added later and many good players say the netcode is comparable to USF4 on a good connection. This will only get better with GGPO.
Give this game a chance.

PROS-
It's a fighting game that works! Holy cow!
Plays similar to oldschool fighting games, and can be pretty easy to pick up, but seems hard to master
Character variety in playstyles
Nice animations, even with the pixel design choices
Funny FGC related commentators
Music is pretty good
Online is functional and a lot better than a certain NRS game out there
Good fighting game for its price
Cons-
Anime style can be a bit offputting if you're not a fan
2 of the characters are legit clones outside of one being a charge character, and the other using fireball motions
UI looks awful and can definitely use some dumbing down
Relatively small cast, though this is hardly a con in my book
Arcade mode story is fairly mediocre, as expected from an indie fighting game
The game is to its core, OLD SCHOOL. Don't try to find some 50 hit 80 percent combos here, because they'll all be 5-7 and do tons of damage. The gameplay reminds me a lot of games like King of Fighters and Street fighter 3 Third strike, where the movement feels very similar to KOF, and the mechanics and fighting itself feels very 3s. The animations for the game are great, despite being pixelated. Some may be a bit offput by the design choice, with its pixely anime style, but overall I thought it was fine. The cast is also very diverse in play style. You have your charge characters, shotos, rekka characters, and grappler. The only complain in the cast I have is the two female young ladies who both have the same stance and animations, but one happens to be a charge character and the other happens to be a quartercircle character. Really wish there was more originality there, but overall, I'm not mad at that decision.
Outside of the gameplay, we have a decent training mode, relatively barebones story, online features that play pretty well so far, and a Ui that has to be the worst UI I've seen for a fighting game on steam so far. It's pretty ugly and way too big. Hopefully a patch or something can make this both look and feel way more user friendly. Controller support is all there. My Madcatz Fightstick pro was plugged in and worked no problem. You can assign your buttons pretty easily, and you should be fine. Layout for the game is fairly simple too.
If you're apart of the FGC, you'll be happy to know this does offer some pretty unique humor in highlighting some known FGC players, commentators, and content creators as chooseable commentators for your match. I tend to always pick Maximillian, usually always saying cornball but inspiring lines, or one of the japanese players, like Tokido.
Overall, I'm enjoying Yatagarasu so far. It's a game i'll stick with for some time. I definitely recommend it if you like oldschool fighting games, especially games like SF3 third strike. You'll fit right at home with it.

Will you strive to make peace via diplomacy wherever possible or be a revengeful ruler without mercy? An opportunistic coward or a true hero, who inspires your folk with brave speeches?

While I would have appreciated some depth to the puzzles there is some variety to keep them from getting stale and more importantly, no frustratingly obtuse puzzles that had me stuck for more than a couple of minutes. Graphics are excellent except for a few astoundingly low-res shadows in one outdoor sunlit section (which you may not even notice). Sound design is top-notch and the score is compelling yet subtle. Voice acting is also high quality. I was ultimately a little dissatisfied with the direction the story took and the pacing of the second half, but that's largely due to how intriguing the first five hours are. If you are a fan of old school Resident Evil games or even survival horror in general, this is a must-buy.
8.5/10
