This is a very nicely done point & click game, the graphics are really fitting for the game play. There are so many puzzles and things to explore in this game that you won't really get bored of it. The game itself is very good, although there are some things that aren't explained at all that makes this game fall a little but none the less it's a very good game,
This game is basically a point and click puzzle game with some very funny humour implemented into it as well. From what I have played so far it seems to be really fun, the puzzles are very nicely created. If you ever get stuck there is a nice help system that points you in the right direction so that you don't get stuck and so that you can progress with the storyline. This really helps you as some point & click games are way too hard with the puzzles that they have created, but this has very simple and easy puzzles to solve. There is a lot of things to look at and find in this game so exploring everything right from the start is very essential to this game. The humour that is used is very funny at times, trying to chat up other girls, and using a substitute as a scarecrow really got me in stitches. It doesn't over do the humour in a sense that it gets boring, it does it just enough to keep you laughing and smiling when a joke does happen. There are a few problems I have with this game though, and that is the controls for the game. There is absolutely no indication of what controls do what, for example I didn't realise that I had the suitcase with all my stuff in until about a hour and half into the game. You really need to add either a controls section in the settings menu, or add it at the start of the game. This also caused the problem as Vasily Ivanovich is sometimes in the way of the arrow so that you can exit out of the area. Such as the bridge that have the guards, if you didn't know that you can move Vasily Ivanovich then you might have some trouble finding the arrow as it's right under where he is standing. Another thing that I wasn't aware of while playing the game until later on was the fast travel system. If you have been to a area then you can go onto the map and click on that area to fast travel there. This would've been really helpful if I would've known that earlier.
The art style of this game is really nicely animated. It seems that there was a lot of time and dedication when it came to drawing out the backgrounds and the characters animations. I really don't really have anything to complain about this as it is just so well animated and drawn out. Although some of the art style seems to be a little blurry and don't fit in with the rest of them, but I guess that's just to help you with what you have to click on to explore and stuff.
The music is very fitting with the atmosphere as you walk around the areas, helping people out and solving puzzles. I would've liked to have some music in the background of the houses, as the music only comes on when your exploring the main area. The sounds are exceptionally good, I really liked all of the sounds that where played when certain things happened to characters.
This is defiantly a gem point & click game. It has some really nice puzzles that aren't too difficult to figure out, although I would've liked a small tutorial for what all the buttons are as I only figured out all the buttons after a hour and a half. The music and sounds are exceptionally good, and the art style is just superb. Along with the animations of the characters, I am really surprised of how well this game is for a drawn game. Would defiantly recommend this game to anyone.

If you're into turn based tactics or Warhammer, this game is really for you. The progression, with the injury system and levelling up your warband members so that they unlock more abilities and get stronger is really compelling. The theme is great, and the procedurally generated maps really make you feel like you're sending your team into Mordheim.
There are however a few things that make this game not quite as good as I had hoped. The progression system for units is un-necessarily complex, there are far too many abilities in comparison to the board game, with most of them giving tiny 5% boosts as passives or better abilities that end up being incredibly expensive. Leveling up your henchmen with XP also doesn't feel very impactful, with them again gaining 2% extra damage or 1% less chance of routing etc. In the board game, having a kitted out and experienced team makes a huge deal, with such things as 15% extra hit chance or an extra wound, which translates to being able to take twice as much damage before falling out of action.
The game also suffers from repetitive side missons, which are absolutely necessary to gaining enough Wyrdstone to pay your contracts off and leveling up your henchmen to complete the story missions. They all boil down to slowly inching forward, killing off your opponent one henchman at a time by outnumbering them as they come at you.
In the end, I've really enjoyed this game, for the time I've played it, but in the end, I just got burned out on it and it ended up just frustrating me as it comes sooo close to being the video game version of the tabletop game that I had hoped for. I'm hoping for a major update or a really good mod that will add better missons and make the progression system as good as Mordheim, Descent and any number of campaign based board games.

I love this game, but at time of writing this review I have to say that it is very deeply flawed.
For the most part a faithful and enjoyable adaption of Games Workshop's specialist squad-based combat system, City of the Damned is a wonderfully dark, gritty, tense and tactical experience...
... once you actually load the damn thing up. My PC is not exactly what you'd call slow, but it takes phenomenal amounts of time to get past the game's loading screens. Considering that you need to go through that ordeal every time you want to fight a battle, and that battles are practically the sole focus of the game, this detracts massively from the overall experience. And while I call the game "Tactical," this only really holds true playing against other human beings. The AI in this game is competent - clever, even - but nine games out of ten are almost guaranteed to have some kind of bug, whether that be running against a wall and never getting anywhere, not reliably counting as engaged in combat when fighting on or around stairs, or trying to get somewhere they simply will not fit.
Despite this, however, the management and progression systems are well polished, the skill and equipment mechanics deep and interesting enough that you can spend hours customising your fighters to fit the roles you want, the injuries show up in all their gory detail on the character models, and the array of mutations available to Chaos warbands is a thing of absolute twisted beauty. I feel entirely satisfied by the breadth of customisation available in this game, and overall it does a superlative job of capturing the essence and character of the Warhammer universe.
But when considering this game always bear in mind that I wrote this while waiting for a scenario to load.
Edit 09/02/16: It bears mentioning that loading times have now been much improved. I would say that it's even quite quick, now, often finishing before the excellent loading screen voiceovers finish doing their thing.

Disappointing and frustrating, but there is still promise.
I've been a fan of the Warhammer world for over 20 years, and that alone is enough to keep me playing this game, but I don't know if I can recommend it to others.  The missions and combat are incredibly repetitive, and the RNG and AI get frustrating at times with seeming like they are TRYING to screw you over.
Standard, non-story missions all have the same objective:  kill or rout the other warband.  There are optional objectives, but these are usually best ignored.  The problem is that the best strategy in every mission is to lump your people up as tight as possible and advance in a blob like toddlers playing soccer.  Sending warriors off alone or in pairs usually just ends up with them getting ganged up on by superior numbers and killed.  By keeping everyone together, especially in missions with no time limit, you can eventually come across less numerous opponents and gang up on them, killing enough to rout the band.  Also, you really should prioritize either ranged or melee combat for your warband.  Trying a balanced approach has, in my experience, been less effective than ganging up using a single strategy.  Hang back peppering approaching warriors with a warband full of bows, then pulling out melee weapons to finish off the stragglers that reach you, or give everyone a big axe, surround your target, and chop him apart.
More frustrating though are the penalties for failure.  One bad match can cripple your entire band, with the story missions being particularly punishing with a laundry list of mandatory objectives, and demanding you either complete them all or fight to the near last man.  I've played 3 of the story missions, and lost 2 of them thanks to either glitches or frustrating randomized spawning of the literally infinite reinforcements.  Using my Chaos band I fought into a Sigmarite temple to try and defile 11 different holy objects.  Once I'd killed the guards, defiled 10 of the 11, and fortified the entrances to the temple as best I could with my surviving warriors, creating cross-supporting zones of fire and ambush lanes, I sent the hero up to the belfry to get the last object, only to get ambushed on the roof by a randomly generated hero reinforcement, who charged and killed my wounded hero, generating an automatic failure condition.  Goodbye 45 minutes of work, hello injury rolls.  Another Imperial warband did not lose a single match until the story mission, then a glitch indicated I'd found 10 of the powder barrells I needed to use to blow up a location, but could only pick up 7.  I kept looping the map trying to find new barrells or respawn the old, and the infinite reinforcements wore me down until I ultimately lost, and then half my previously undefeated warband suffered permanent, debilitating injuries such as lost hands and arms.  Easier to just start over at that point, but there went all the days of progress.

Pajama Sam is a Humongous point and click adventure game released during the mid 90s. It was the third series Humongous made after Putt Putt and Freddi Fish, and proved to be one of the most successful. Today it's well regarded as one of the best games that the developer ever made, and for being one of the very first games Jeremy Soule of Elder Scrolls fame worked on.
The premise is Pajama Sam is a child who is afraid of the dark. Inspired by his favorite comic book hero Pajama Man, he decides to journey into his closet to combat "Darkness". He finds himself trapped in "the Lands of Darkness". Where he must find his belongings and finally confront Darkness. What I like about the story is it has this very epic feel to it but the entire story is framed as being part of a child's imagination. The "lands of darkness" resemble Mordor but are littered with things you'd find in a closet like socks and lunchboxes. Moreover Pajama Sam himself is a very likeable protagonist who grows as a character over the course of his journey and it has a very nice somber ending.
Much like other Humongous games Pajama Sam also contains random elements. The locations of all of Pajama Sam's missing gadgets are randomized every playthrough. Meaning what locations are mandatory varies from playthrough to playthrough. This makes the game much more replayable, albiet to compensate for the general short length of the game. Alongside that the game has collectables in the form of socks that you can locate throughout the game. This was so well recieved that Humongous would later create a puzzle game devoted to this.
Among all of Humongous's games the Pajama Sam trilogy remains one of my favorite. It's one of my favorite adventure games and I've replayed it several times. It has a blend of polish that is very rarely seen in games even today, and I dearly recommend it to fans of children's games and fans of games that tell a good story.

Sam is a little boy fan of a super-hero. However, tonight, it's the first time he'll sleep without the light. He really wants to do it but he's afraid of Darkness, a evil enemy. So, he turns into Pajama Sam, a super-hero and is resolved to capture his nemesis so that he can sleep without fear....
Pajama Sam: No Need to Hide When It's Dark Outside is a game aimed at children: it's a point-&-click adventure, with minigames in it, though they're not all needed to advance. The story can also speak for the little ones: it's showing Sam willing to sleep without light and getting over his fears. Kids can relate to him.
But to manage to do so, Sam is living an extraordinary adventure: he looses his flashlight, lunchbox and mask because trees are stealing them and before confronting Darkness, he needs to find them and retrieve them. Sam will have to show for example to Otto the boat that wood is floating, to oil the wheels of the wagon, etc..
What I realized is that the game is random: indeed, you have each time two possible locations for the items and so, a different solution for them (for example, the mask was with the carrot, I had to free the carrots in the fridge to get it - however, the mask would have been in the dance room, I would have made an invisibility potion). And I also liked the fact that you can choose your path in the mine. It means that you can find new locations, useful or not depending the "storyline" thrown at you. And as you're also in a quest to retrieve all socks in the game, some of them are there - be quick to click on them as Sam will not stop at them.
There is a minigame where you need to answer questions. And while one of them is tied to Darkness's domain, the others are about culture. However, I don't know if knowing how much fuel does a space shuttle need is pertinent. It's something very specific. Other questions were more general like the artist having paint Mona Lisa or the dinosaurs. There are also a Tic-Tac-Toe with crackers and cheese, a Snake-like game, a music room where you can hear several tunes, a laboratory where you can make many potions, ...
While I found the gameplay nice, Pajama Sam is also a testimony of its era: the '90. Indeed, in educational games or in children games, you tend to throw a lot of information. Big Thinkers, from the same developers/publishers, if you remember my review, were also full of items you can click and look at a special animation. Many easter eggs are also included: you can find Freddi Fish and Luther, Putt-Putt and Pep, characters from the same house.
Another thing is a testimony of the '90: the graphics themselves. However, contrary to Big Thinkers, Pajama Sam seems to have less aged. The soundtrack is also good.
The good surprise was the fact that the game is in French (and support other languages). It means that children will not need adults to translate or help them understand a foreign word. While the adults are still needed for anything else, it's a burden in less for them, particulary if they're not fluent at all with English.
But there is a little problem too: the inventory is showing itself by putting the cursor at the bottom of the screen. It's how you can find the menu too. There is no main menu, no tutorial about the keys to use, etc.. I had to search in a forum how to save, after having to exit the game and come back later - no progress was saved. I don't know if I was expecting it to be saved as in Big Thinkers but the lack of a profile was my first clue to that. So if you need to save and load, press S and L. It's apparently something related to the system used so that the game can run on recent machines.
Pajama Sam is really a good little moment for both children and adults. It may also be an help to get over fears. If I look into the second title, it's about thunders, so, I suppose that Pajama Sam was conceived to help children understand that some of their fears can be conquered. Anyway, if you search for a good children games, Pajama Sam should be considered to be in your list.

NEUTRAL:

Get used to seeing a lot of text over a bland square of white because that's exactly what the pause menus look like. There are translation errors everywhere. From cutscenes to the option menus, no one can escape the engrish. The controls can get messed up, going by the bugs forums. A disappointing fighter that I cannot foresee being substantially improved even after another development cycle. Sad to see this coming from some former King of Fighters developers, who probably shouldn't have gone indie - someone should tell them that SNKP is hiring for devs to work on KOF XIV right now. Note that I played the original doujin release of this for a good while before trying the Steam version, hoping that things would be improved after the Indiegogo campaign finished up.
The HUD elements besides the life and super meters, and the menus are bar none the most poorly designed and confusing I have ever seen in a commercially sold game. Right when you start up the game, you'll notice that Arcade Mode is listed TWICE...how the hell did this pass basic playtesting? There is no Steam integration whatsoever, and the online settings probably require some sort of computer science/engineering degree to use - a bit much to ask of fighting game freaks.
The graphics are okay, but uneven. Characters are generally well drawn and animated, but players who have more than a passing familiarity with Capcom and SNK fighters will notice some shameless sprite edits, especially with Jet inheriting several moves from SF's Dudley and KOF's Ralf Jones. The newer stages range from average to good-looking, but the ones made earlier in development all look like lazily photoshopped wallpapers, or even unfinished. The soundtrack varies from not terrible, to completely awful as in the vocal screamo song. There isn't a single song I'd remember or would listen to outside the game. There's no 16:9 support, but I wouldn't have used a stretch option with invisible walls (like in MvC2 on 360/PS3) anyway.
The characters and mechanics are rather unremarkable and derivative. Most of them are lazy clones of famous Street Fighters, and four of them are just palette swapped clones of each other. Yatagarasu makes no bones about its heavy Third Strike influences, with its selectable supers and parries, but completely lacks the finesse, production values and charm of that game. There's two parry buttons instead of needing to input a timed directional, which doesn't really work too well. There's a story mode (listed as a second arcade mode), but it's boring and bare-bones as crap, the translation is kinda off, and it fails at giving us any more of a reason to care about the doofus wannabes that make up the roster. Admittedly, the four characters added as a result of the Indiegogo funding are somewhat more original and well designed, though Hanzo's moveset is a complete mess.
The people promoting this made a big deal about the commentator feature, where canned clips of several well-known FGC personalities (or at least I think they're well known, I didn't recognize a single one) will play during the match in response to what's going on. I found this to be nothing but inane, annoying and immersion-destroying, especially with the real-life photographs popping out all the time. We don't need stream monster crap escaping Twitch and venturing into the world of the game itself. At least you can turn these off, but I don't think you can disable commentators used by online opponents.
I applied for a refund and probably won't be revisiting the game unless it gets hugely overhauled. Why would you ever want to settle for a vastly inferior clone of Third Strike? If you want an under-the-radar 2D fighter that's actually really cool, original and memorable, check out Chaos Code on PS3 (a Steam release has been hinted at).

Okay, there's no easy way to say this, but I kind of hate this game.
On a technical and graphical level, RE7 is pretty great: the entire game ran smooth as butter at 4K on some pretty high settings for me and will no doubt scale well for less powerful PCs. If nothing else, I can safely say that visually, the game is pretty damn incredible, and if the idea of a traditional Resident Evil experience that looks utterly gorgeous is enough to get you interested, then I predict you're going to have a good time.
Unfortunately, it seems I don't like the very fabric that makes the series tick.
The first and possibly worst element of the whole game is the awful movement and combat. Were this a more Outlast-style experience without any kind of weapons, then perhaps the game would be better, or by contrast, if the developers put more effort into making the gunplay meatier, then maybe I wouldn't have felt nothing but frustration throughout my playthrough.
As it is, however, basic control of the game feels like a nightmarish frankenmonster composed of World of Tanks and Cuphead.
Which is to say, you move around with all the speed and manoeuvrability of a Panzer, and your guns are about as effective as Cuphead's finger guns.
This results in a feeling that every single encounter in the game takes place at the pace of a leisurely stroll and that using your weapons is just an inconvenience for all involved. To be clear, it is entirely possible to have an effective horror experience and satisfying combat: Condemned managed it by giving you a surprisingly deep and effective melee combat system and made the guns you encounter both incredibly scarce and suitably effective, Alan Wake - in spite of its weird controls - managed to mete out supplies and weapons at a pace that made sure you were never helpless, but never felt truly confident, and FEAR even managed to serve up some quality scares whilst giving you assault rifles and bullet time.
And then, of course, there’s Dead space. All hail Dead Space and its pitch perfect juggling of firepower and vulnerability.
By comparison though, RE7 seems to try to attain that same feeling by simply nerfing all but the .44 Magnum and the shotgun into oblivion, which makes a whole lot of the early gameplay super frustrating because there’s a constant feeling that the game isn’t actually pitting you against horrific, all-powerful foes, but instead that it’s just being really, really cheap.
Oh, and then there’s melee combat… lord help you if you ever have to use that.
The game's story sadly also failed to do anything for me: perhaps had I not played Outlast 2 before this, I would have found the experience scarier, but as it is, everything in the game just feels like I've seen it all before.
Because after a literal room of dead children, there’s really not much this game can offer to match that in terms of sheer shock factor.
And that’s possibly the biggest problem with the scares RE7 tries to throw at you; where SOMA will stay with me for years to come for its harrowing and excruciatingly in-depth exploration of human consciousness and the very nature of being alive, RE7 will probably stay with me for as long as it takes me to get these gripes out of my system, because the scenarios I was faced with during my playthrough all seemed merely hum-drum.
It’s not like the game doesn’t try to do what it does well, and as many have pointed out, the Baker family are all a wonderful bunch of crazies, but unfortunately, none of them seem to be actually all that scary in and of themselves and the story behind them is woefully uninspiring.
Moreover, the game commits horror sin number one for me, which is that it gives you plenty of easy opportunities to AVOID THE HORROR yet forces you to go towards the obvious horror because a videogame has to happen.
Perhaps the most vexatious of these instances is really early, when the game has you rescue your wife from a basement dungeon (not as kinky as it sounds) then expects you NOT to want to go back the way you came, irrespective of the damaged - but still probably climbable - ladder, which is the only thing standing between you and getting away scot-free.
Or maybe the worst instance is the numerous completely working telephones in the house which the player character doesn’t use because… apparently Ethan can’t remember that 9-1-1 dials the emergency services?
Or could the worst offence be the fact I couldn’t shoot the big baddie until the very end of the game, despite the fact I knew that character would be trouble later and that I had a perfectly good shotgun right there?
And then of course, there’s the final nail in the coffin for me: the inventory system, and by extension, resources in the game in general.
While it’s nowhere near as complicated as previous games, RE7’s stripped-down inventory system still manages to make inventory Tetris a central and infuriating part of the experience.
Inventory Tetris isn’t fun. Inventory Tetris has never been fun. Inventory Tetris is to fun what the AK-47 is to world peace.
Where other games get by just fine without one or employ an inventory in some other less restrictive way, RE7 clings to the archaic combine-and-conquer inventory system that the series has always had and the flow of gameplay suffers for it.
The limited amount of inventory slots makes the earlier gameplay in particular extra frustrating because ammo, weapons and health items all take up vital inventory slots, leaving you with no choice but to get rid of important stuff on-the-fly, or trudge back to a magical teleport crate because the thing you need to progress takes up an inventory slot.
And - coming back to that melee bit I mentioned earlier - should you ever find yourself short on ammo or health items, the game never gives you any way to replenish those resources, meaning that the entire game can become literally impossible to beat because you simply don’t have enough ammunition to ever finish the fight, and never will have, because you either can’t possibly access it or used it all earlier.
It gives me no pleasure to say I don’t like this game. I tried my best to like it, I really did, but in the end I just found that there wasn’t an awful lot in the game that didn’t rub me the wrong way. Fans of the series may find this is the jolt they needed after the reportedly awful RE6, but I just can’t see the appeal here.
I’d heard so many great things about this; that it was crazy bonkers scary, that it was the series back on form, that it’s an absolute masterpiece, but instead I found a game that was neither satisfying to play, nor offered anything particularly scary or new for me. I only regret that I stuck with it in the hopes that it would get better long past the two-hour window, and didn’t refund it after the first hour or so.
I’m sorry.

The game is a mess and a huge disappointment.
I've been a long time fan of Rome and Medieval II and after a long break from Total War,  I bought this game hoping to get more of the same. They have significantly reworked elements of the Campagin map such as building etc and it works reasonably well. The ability to conduct diplomacy without having to send a diplomat is a nice improvement. The biggest problem with this game is the A.I and how it acts both on the campaign map and in the battle map.
The diplomacy ability of the Campaign A.I is to put if frankly laughable. Ridiculous demands and virtually no observance of alliances are the norm. Allies will stand by as you battle enemies with mutual borders. Colonial allies such as the 13 colonies when you are playing as the British, seem to have virtually no ability to train troops and fight even the smallest Native armies. The same natives will launch ridiculous three to four unit attacks on garrisoned towns, starting a war and then demand ridiculous concessions for peace. It is simply laughable how badly programmed the A.I is.
The Battle map A.I is equally bad, as is the interface. Troops cannot even be moved in formation across the map without ending up in a confused mess pointing anyway but forward.
Trying to get them to use cover such as walls (they can take cover against stone walls) is a frustrating experience. It is roughly 60/40 whether the troops will take up position on the right side of cover. It is literally that bad. Men will duck down behind walls with their backs to the enemey facing inward on their own lines.
Grouped units are almost impossible to use at times, particularly cavalry units. Ordering them to attack fleeing or exposed units usually results in them scattering across the map with maybe one or two units finding their target.
The drag feature that allows you to line up your units is equally a mess and not very intuitive and I have found the majority of the time it results in your units being lined up and facing the wrong direction. This wouldn't be so bad if the A.I had the ability to correct itself and face approaching enemies, but unfortunately it is so badly programmed units will just stand there as enemies melee or shoot them and surrounding units to bits.
I have found Canons to be virtually useless. The game seems to be programmed to make projectiles bounce and fly over or land short of their targets an unusually high percentage of the time. Even using cannister shot at almost point blank range does not seem to result in any great damage to the advancing enemies.
The only thing that the developers have really done a good job with is the naval battles, though the strength of pirate fleets is ridiculous with many of them outgunning the Royal Navy and Dutch navies right from the get go. They could also have done something more with the isloated naval areas where you can send trade fleets, maybe the ability to colonize some of the land there or fight native forces along the coast.
I would not recommend this game in its current state, I have heard of a fan made Mod called 'Darthmod' which apparently has resolved some of the A.I inconsitency and I am willing to give it a try if it makes the game a bit more playable. I will try and update this review if I download this mod.
I think it is disgraceful that any company could release a game in this state. Shame on you Sega.

I was honestly a bit baffled about the fact that this, Pendragon Rising, was sold as a game. In my eyes this is a book, not a game.
Well, terms aside, I really liked this one. The story, even if written hundreds of times already, was fairly well constructed. I don't know about the choices' effectiveness, or ineffectiveness, nor do I really care. It certainly doesn't feel like a game you'd be willing to play over and over again in short period of time.
It is a text-based adventure. What can you say about it? Story was good, extra points for option to lay with your sister. My only disappointment was the length. I wish it had been longer!

Pendragon Rising is a super fun, super engaging interative fantasy adventure where your choices have a very real sense of consquence - that is to say, the effects of your choices feel meaningful, subtle and consistent. The writing is very good, the characters memorable, and most noticably the story is paced very well with moments of, yes, conflict and magic, but also intimate spaces where you explore Arthur/Arta's place in the rapidly changing landscape of dark age Britain.
Choosing gender is also a matter of simply choosing which sex is the dominant one in Britain at that time. It is very well implemented, with consequences to being female that feel true to the nature of womanhood while also not diminishing it unecessarily. There are a few gender / name replacement typos, but they are little more than a distraction.
The game lasted only two or three hours long, but at £2 it's still a steal. I was gripped thoroughly and played it in one sitting. Also there is some sense in replaying it - how would a less diplomatic, more violent Arta turn out? Ultimately I don't want to because I have a very clear vision of my version of Arta, but the choice is still there.
One downside was the lack of sound. There isn't any sound at all - music or otherwise. I put on a Celtic music playlist and it sufficed, keeping in line with the lore.
Fans of dark age mythos and history, or even roleplayers, should really enjoy this. I sincerely hope that I can continue Arta's adventures in the future.

This is the first interactive novel I have ever played, and I can do nothing but praise it.
It adheres quite closely to the Celtic interpretation of Arthur, but still manages to incorporate familiar elements from medieval tradition. It conveys the atmosphere of a fractured, post-Roman Britain quite well, and although it has some fantastical elements, these are quite subdued for the most part and maintains a more realistic approach.
I found the writing to be engaging and enjoyable, and quite a few of the choices you make are recognized later on the in story, meaning that my decisions actually had some weight to them.
SPOILERS INCOMING!
I also greatly appreciated the fact that the game allowed you some flexibility in terms of the outcome. You do not have to stick to the classic Arthurian story. I actually deliberately avoided becoming king and prefered to work behind the scenes. You are not railroaded into taking the throne. You have the option of stepping down and supporting someone else instead, and this enhances the role-playing element.

Astoria: The Holders of Power is a commercial RPG made by GoldenUnicornGaming, using RPG Maker VX Ace. Being a commercial game I will be judging it on a higher standard than I do most indie games.
The low-down is this: Astoria is a game fraught with issues that stop it from becoming a gem of a game. The biggest of these issues is the large amount of default assets in the game. Now, when I say assets, I do not mean the RTP graphics or sounds. Indeed, anyone who knows me knows that I like RTP and I encourage its use. Yes, even commercially.
So what do I mean when I say that the biggest issue is its use of default assets? Why, only the laziest of excercises when it comes to creating a game - the constant use of sample maps.
For those who do not know of what I speak, some of the engines in the RPG Maker series came with a series of maps pre-installed for examples of how to use the tiles. It was expected that people would learn through looking at these maps in a more kinetic way. Astoria makes use of these maps, albeit with some minor editing here and there, which is, in a word, lazy.
It's one of the biggest things that I look out for when it comes to making game pages and something I notice straight away when playing a game. And it's a pity that this game does this because, apart from that, it's a pretty decent game.
Is it worthy of 5 stars? Hell no. Is it an average RPG with basic controls, story and gameplay? Yes. Is it sad to see that what could have been a pretty good game fall to being lazy? Very yes.
But let's break this down a bit more, shall we?
Story-wise the game is pretty good. There's a few spelling and grammar errors here and there, but the writing is quite solid and tells the tale of a group of people who are trying to stop an evil from taking over the land... and the consequences of failing. The start was a bit rocky but it soon picked up and the characters and story did a good job of keeping me playing. There were some tropes, but a lot of thought and care obviously went in to crafting interesting characters involved in interesting goings-on.
The gameplay was a bit of a mixed bag. You won't find anything really revolutionary going on - it's pretty much a bog-standard jRPG in how it handles things. Battles aren't too different to the typical genre, nothing really stands out, but it also doesn't do a bad job of fitting the pieces together to make a fairly coherent whole that wasn't boring, at least.
Battles kept you on your toes most of the time, providing perhaps a bit too much challenge sometimes. Trash mobs didn't give you much in the way of experience and if they got lucky, could wipe your party easily, especially in some dungeons where the amount of enemies outweighed your ability to handle them. I found myself having to leave in order to stay at an inn and rest up fairly often, as well as replenish supplies a lot.
This led to some issues. See, one of the balancing issues in this game revolved around money - you couldn't get enough. You'd try to grind up some levels and gold in order to get enough money to gird your loins and rest at an inn, but when enemies are doing so much damage that you have to heal all the time, it gets to be troublesome. At one point I was going back to trash mobs from the area before just to get enough money to buy some healing items... and those mobs weren't giving much in the way of gold, but I had little choice as they were the only ones I could reliably kill without worry that I'd be getting a game over after a battle or two.
On top of that, there were some dungeons where you could get screwed over big time - you would get locked into the dungeons (with no logical reason) and be stuck with only the goods you brought in with you. One dungeon I had to do three times because I kept dying at a boss. Each do-over I would grind for more money on mobs that paid a pittance just to get another potion added to the stockpile, just so I could last a bit longer in the locked dungeon. It made no sense when it would have been easy to just allow you to leave and come back (even thought that's annoying in and of itself to have to do) but that was not an option.
The game was relatively bug free, thankfully, though at one point I remember getting a crash that puzzled me. I can't recall the details exactly, but it was around the time of the fist big town getting taken over and I got stuck in an event which when interacted with, crashed the game. I wish I'd taken a note so I could tell you more about it.
Sound... was there. It wasn't anything I could recall, really, and nothing was memorable. It existed.
Graphics was something I touched on before but will do so again. I will say that there was some effort made to try and make the sample maps used look a little more spiced up, however this presented another issue - the over-use of decoration tiles. Sometimes you couldn't see where you were going due to the sheer amount of decoration tiles used all over the place. A few times I got stuck in dungeons because I couldn't figure out where I was supposed to go... thanks to decoration tiles making the way forward impossible to discern. There were just too many.
And this is the other issue - take away the decoration tiles and maps were bland empty rooms full of big space and nothingness. The decoration tiles were used as a bandaid fix to try and hide that mapping just wasn't all that great. It was serviceable enough and there were some areas that legitimately looked pretty good, but the overuse of certain tiles just made it into a jumble of colour instead of enhancing the map and guiding the players' eye as it should have done.
And let's not start on the complete mix and match of the various graphical styles used in the game. There are very few people who can do the old "I'll use this and this together and they'll look good because I'm editing them to fit each other" thing, and this game is not one of them.
Honestly, I do NOT recommend people play the game. Not only is the developer lazy, but they are also a cheat who tried to boost their game's image on other sites by making alternate accounts and posting high-scoring reviews under them. This is, quite frankly, despicable and I suggest that if you have a hankering for good RPGs of longer length, that you try searching google for RPG Maker websites where you can find better games for free... that don't try to cheat the system.

I highly recommend this game.
It has everything essential for a great RPG... engaging story, likable characters, strategic combat, and customization.  The design and feel are akin to classic SNES RPGs, with crisper graphics similar to some of the later remakes.  Overall, it easily rivals Final Fantasy 3/6, Chrono Trigger, and the Lufias, which would be my top-rated games from that era and in general for this specific style/genre.
Each character develops well alongside the primary plot.  Characters enter and leave your party somewhat often which can be a nuisance or a boon depending on your preference, but there is essentially a core cast that you will be pleased to see stick around for most of the game.  Their personalities can be extreme in serious and comedic ways, but I thoroughly enjoyed literally every main character, which is something I cannot say for some of my other favorite RPGs.  The overarching story has a fairly typical good versus evil feel to it, but it isn't without a few twists, and it certainly kept my interest piqued.  The combination of the story elements and the characters would make this game worthwhile even if the gameplay and combat were boring, which thankfully is not the case.  Astoria is not without its share of side quests either, which further develop the world, along with the characters' relationships and values.
The combat is a step higher than most in terms of preparation and strategy, but it is not overwhelming in my opinion.  Bursting down enemies with powerful spells, buffing and debuffing to gain an edge, playing defensive and restorative to grind out a long battle, and chopping straight through enemies are some of the various styles you will likely employ on your journey.  One facet I adored about the combat system was the actual usefulness of items, especially the various fruits, which give temporary bonuses to character attributes.  This game does not suffer from the annoyance of saving all magic for healing nor from fear of monotony in battles... cycling destructive magic in and out with defensive and support spells and skills in its memorization system encourages creative play and efficiency, especially with elemental weaknesses/strengths and status abnormalities/resistances.  It always felt great to wreck a mob of enemies with a powerful spell they are weak against, or to strengthen a character with luck and attack power to see how much damage a single critical hit can do.  The game’s difficulty seems to flow consistently… grinding out a few extra levels will make combat feel more casual, especially in the beginning parts of the game, while trying to essentially speedrun through would probably raise the challenge substantially.  In the dungeons, the enemies appear visible on the map and are permanently gone once defeated, and I personally felt that wiping out all active dungeon enemies felt rewarding and gave my party steady enough Experience and power to keep the fighting interesting.
Customization is a huge deal for me in RPGs, and Astoria delivers it in a few ways.  Level-ups yield immutable stat gains, but side quests, certain epic monsters, and weapon versatility give options to shape characters into more of what you want, whether that be to strengthen their strengths, cover their weaknesses, or balance them.  There is a sense that characters are designed to be built in certain ways, for example, for the mage it is far easier to raise intelligence for spellcasting rather than strength for attacking, but in a subsequent playthrough, I would be interested to see if you could stack magic and defense with a long list of memorized support spells, instead of going the glass-canon damage route for that character.  Those kinds of options make this game potentially worth multiple playthroughs, along with some alluring steam achievements if such things tickle your fancy.
Astoria’s world is very carefully done.  Every map is unique, from the towns, to the fields, to the dungeons.  There is obvious care in the detail each.  From vibrantly colored forests to dark and dreary caves, each location and situation captures the mood.  The game also offers a stellar soundtrack to accentuate the scenes even further.  Some of the tracks for the more iconic battles pumped me up from start, and added a nice boost to the gravity of each situation.  Don’t be surprised if a few tunes end up stuck in your head for a couple days, although I would have liked the general battle theme to cycle with one or two additional tracks at various progression points in the game.
In closing, this game should not run only $5, but hopefully that encourages more players to give it a shot.  It is easily one of the best games I have played in years, and the seemingly underwhelming popularity of the game despite such positive reviews and attention by the creator compelled me to write a review of my own.  Get this game!

I love this game.
This is my first RPG Maker game and I didn't know the difference.  The story line was involved and the characters were developed well.  I genuinely like the main characters and it reminded me of some of my favorites from the Tales series.  For a game with 16 bit art and not much in capabilities, some of the cutscenes were really heartfelt.
The dungeons are well done in that they only take about a half hour a piece and so the pace of the game goes by quicker than you'd think on a game advertised at 35 hours.  The way the creator did regular overworld encounters and balanced them with actual monsters that you see and kill in the dungeons was different and added more excitement and more going-on in each dungeon.
The soundtrack was plain great and each track fit the mood and tone of the levels.  Very well done.
Some of the quests were nice and quick and take seconds and some of them required writing notes, and those spanned the entire length of the game.  The longer quests, like the Lost Forest, kind of reminded me of playing Might and Magic games.
The battle system was typical first person, but I like some of the additional stats like counterattack that added an extra dynamic to combat.  The spells system was a bit unique as well because the buff and debuff spells did a percent change on the target and so were predictably weaker early game but then became essential later on.  I also really liked how the same spell doesn't stack (you can't stack Augment, for example), but you are allowed to stack similar spells and items to give massive bonuses to your party.  I thought the fruit items were really well done and they could seriously change the outcome of a fight, especially toward the end.  It's not often that I play an RPG where I regularly consider taking a turn to use non-healing items in combat.
Overall I think this game was well done.  I enjoyed it and you can't beat the price of $4.99 for so many hours of gameplay.  For me, it came out to pennies on the hour.  I've beaten this game 3 times already and I've still gone back to play it more, and I'm looking to get all of the Steam Achievements.  Pick this game up and add it to your library.

Great value for the money. For the asking price, this game has more than enough game play! It took me 48 hours of gameplay to complete the game and uncover all the secrets (I at least believe so...). The game does not have too much grinding, so it keeps you engaged by allowing the story to progress at all times. On the other hand, you may need to do some monster hunting at times if you want to grab the best and most expensive gear at the times and to get enough strength to kill all the bonus monsters.
The story was interesting but nothing really special. It includes all the typical elements: world in danger, you get a group of people that play the heroes that ultimately kill the most evil boss and save the world. Of course the adventure includes making many new friends, predictable love story, and lonely avengers that need others' help but at times take matters into their own hands because it's "my revenge". While the story could be of much higher standard, it is good enough and logical to keep the player in throughout the game.
The gameplay is for the most part typical old-school RPG gameplay you would expect from RPGMaker based games, including various locations and a world map. Interestingly, only the world map has random encounters and the enemies are based on the region and terrain. Other locations only have encounters with visible enemies, making it possible to avoid some battles altogether, or to safely retrace your steps in order to go back to safe place to rest and restore the party health. One very interesting element were a couple of assassination missions where you need to stealthily infiltrate locations, avoid being detected by the enemies, and assassinate your targets. Some locations also include light puzzles that are for the most part easy to solve, and some puzzles in the game require wits or combining knowledge from all around the game world. These large puzzles typically reward the player with some of the most powerful weapons or spells, making them worthwhile to pursue.
Music in the game gets quite repetitive, but it is not annoying (YMMV). Sound effects are indicative of reactions but nothing special. There aren't really any environmental sounds, the only effects are related to menu choices or battle actions.
At the time I played the game through it had already received several updates that fixed many bugs other players had reported. I only noticed a few occassions where ending a battle didn't work and the developer seems to be interested in fixing those. Other than those minor cases of the same non-game breaking bug, the technical execution of the game felt flawless.
So if you are after some classic RPG games but are weighing the options of tons of RPGMaker games on Steam, I would definitely recommend Astoria. Many of those games only have few hours worth of game play or otherwise seem like they were hastily put together with minimal effort. On the contrary, while ATHOPS appears to have quite much of the base RPGMaker content, the world and story really have seen some love and the game shows right from the start that it is seriously aimed to be a good game.

Most people don't understand how the RNG works in this game and it's sorta sad that this is the cause for several of the negative reviews. When one of your units goes to attack an enemy you get a % that indicates the chance to hit the target. This shows the difference between your units natural accuracy vs the enemy's resistance. Most weapons have a base hit chance of 80%, this can be raised by certain stats like weapon skill or skills that passively increase hit chance. This chance is then lowered by the enemy's resistance to attacks. So after all of that one may have a good chance, let's say 92% chance to hit. This is pretty good and 9 out of 10 times this should score a hit. However the enemy may be in dodge stance or parry stance which activates when a hit is registered. If your unit scores a hit but the enemy is in dodge stance, there is a SECOND roll strictly for dodges. If you have 92% hit to chance but the enemy has 75% dodge (this dodge chance is not shown in the predicted %) you have a much lower chance to hit that 92%.
If that didn't make sense feel free to ask me to explain it. Most people who struggle with the rng don't understand this part of the game. Honestly I didn't understand this for the first playthrough and failed attempt at playing. This is a great game and I'm streaming it for those who are interested in watching. I'm pretty sure I can play this game with 100% win rate against the AI.

This could quite possibly be my favorite game ever. It is in no way perfect, but man oh man did they capture the thrills AND frustrations of the table-top game, which I adore. The visuals are perfectly suited to Mordheim and look like they've been torn right from the rulebook and town cryers. The character design and development system is terrific. I love the fact that you have no idea who you're going into battle with beforehand, and I love how the game is played through the eyes of the characters.
Yes, it can be very aggravating when attacks are dodged multiple times in a row, even though your character has a 95% chance to hit. Yes, it's maddening to have a warband route just before you accomplish a secondary objective. Yes, it's insanely frustrating when a character with over a 70% chance just can't climb a wall. Yes, it's brutal when you have a few bad games and you have to disband and start again. But all these "problems" are absolutely how the table-top game plays out, too! Welcome to Mordheim! To all who worked so hard to make this game, THANK YOU! I can only hope there will be some future DLC with more warbands joining the mix!

If you like tabletop games, if you're an oldschool Warhammer (the GOOD one, not the Buzz Lightyear knockoff) fan, and if you want the difficulty of Dark Souls on a turn-based tactics game, play Mordheim.
If you want an easy game, try something else. Enough said.

Ahh, good ol Flatout. Where do i start? This game is insanely fun for the guys who grew up destroying ♥♥♥♥ as a little kid, thats for sure. Me being one of them, i was introduced to this series years ago thanks to a free demo on the Playstation Portable, and i fell in love with the game immediately. This is basically flatout 2 with updated graphics and much better features. I know i only have a few hours in but ive been playing this series for years, so i dont want any of the crybaby "you only have a few hours" guys. Anyway. For the people who dont want to read on, here are the "down to earth" pros and cons of this game:

Pros:
- Fast, intense gameplay
- Online play
- Graphics
- Physics
Cons:
- Games For Windows live (you may want to read further about this)
- Few online players
- AI is very hard to beat in some races
- Car always feels like youre going to lose control
Ok so, as you can tell there are good parts and bad parts to this game. The physics are realistic as an arcade racer can be, and they may just be the best racing physics ive felt before. Cars have weight to them, you cant hit that tight corner at 100mph, stuff like that. That being said, your car always feels like its just going to ♥♥♥♥ itself up and fly off the road. Realistic, yes. But still a little hard to drive unless you have an xbox controller to make fine adjustments while turning (i dont think gaming wheels are supported in this game). The one and only BIG issue with this game is the useless software called games for windows live. This game WILL NOT start unless it is installed. Many negative reviews are talking about this, and i will tell you how i fixed it. When you download this game, it has everything you need to run it. The GFWL is in the downloaded files, its just not installed. You need to go into your steam apps folder and go to this games folder, then run the "xliveredist" app in the support folder. That will install GFWL. Next you need to start your game up and either sign in using an existing xbox live account (needed to play online) or make a local account that will not be able to go online. Its insanely stupid, i know. Its not as hard as people make it out to be, however. Even after you do all of that, there arent very many people that go online anymore (side note, add me if youre down to play online).  The AI is hard to beat in most races and it will almost always keep you on the edge of your seat while racing, because every single AI racer has a chance to get first place and you arent "guarenteed" a win like most racing games, you actually have to earn it. The game states that it doesnt support integrated video cards, which isnt true as i can run it on my laptop with that. It runs like straight ♥♥♥♥ though unless i am on my desktop, as this game is somewhat graphically intensive. Anyway, this game is my favorite racing game and i will reccomend this game to anyone and everyone. Try it, it is great.

Double Dragon: Neon Review.
Introduction:
Chances are if you were born in the 80s your fully aware of what Double Dragon is, you’ve probably spent many a 10p on the arcade machine or had it on your NES. If your not a child of the 80s, chances areyou’ve never paid less than £1 on an arcade machine, don’t know what a NES is and never heard of Double Dragon.
Double Dragon was a side scrolling beat them up that took the arcades by storm, it helped invent a genre of games like Final Fight, Street Of Rage and even the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles to get in onit. Neon tries to recreate the 80s feel with a modern twist, but does it succeed? lets find out.
Story:
Now lets be frank, these games were never built on the base of a fantastic story. Generally anything that gives you a reason to punch someone in the street will do, neon is no different really. The gamewill see you travelling into space on a rocket powered Chonglou(Chinese layered house)for no apparent reason other than it gives you some cool backgrounds. There is no real story, but the game doesn’t need a story.
Gameplay:
Now this is where Neon gets difficult, see one of the modifications that WayForward has implemented is an entirely new control system. This means there are combos galore to be had but also that to just survive past the first level you will need to learn to dodge. This new dodge move makes the game very hard while mastering it and very easy once you have, maybe too easy in fact. These new controls, while appealing to more modern gamers will no doubt alienate the many fans of the originals. Its not that its a bad system, just too far removed from the classic method to sit well with fans.
Its funny how although they updated the controls they still don’t let you pick which brother you wish to be. It might have been nice to have a few secret characters too instead of the extra skins you can unlock.
As you progress you can unlock new special moves and stances, these don’t really change much. Stances give you a bonus in attack or defence, and special moves range from calling dragons onto the screen or even Bruce Lee’s one inch punch. These moves and stances are fine and dandy, but they don’t really add much. You don’t feel like your becoming more powerful or that your moving faster, like you would in a more traditional levelling up fair.
Its not bad, but its so far removed from the original and I’m not sure all this change really improved anything.
Presentation:
WayForward are known for there wonderful 2D graphics, so why they chose to use 3D graphic on a 2D plain confuses me. That’s not to say there bad graphics, just I feel 2D would have sat better. What they have done though is create an atmosphere that reeks of the 80s in every way. It really does create a feeling of nostalgia and makes you feel like a kid again. There’s nothing here that’s going to push your system here, but the models are nicely done and though not 2D they capture that feeling well.
Conclusion:
I would love to recommend this game as I really enjoyed playing it, even with its flaws. But I just feel WayForward tried to reinvent a wheel that was working fine before. There’s nothing wrong with updating a game and trying to modernise it, but nearly 20 years ago Treasure did reinvent this genre with Guardian Heroes very successfully and WayForwards offering to me isn’t nearly as accomplished or advanced as it was. Knowing that its really hard for me to tell you to get it if a game realised 20 years ago did it better, and the truth is I can’t. Its not a bad game, its just not good enough.

Approach this game with tempered expectations. Resident Evil 7 is not a groundbreaking, genre-redefining experience like RE4. There are some serious problems that need addressed.
1. The game starts out phenomenally. You feel like a dark, monstrous “something” could crawl out the shadows at any moment and drag you away. An overwhelming sense of vulnerability, of being hunted, of struggling for each minuscule victory permeates the first section of the game. But as you progress, you start to understand the pacing. You learn the game’s tricks. The wallpaper peels back, revealing something that is less terrifying than frustrating.  To put it bluntly, after the first couple of hours, there is no “horror” in this survival-horror game.
2. There are definite “rights” and “wrongs” in Resident Evil 7. For example, I never found the upgraded  handgun buried in an out-of-the-way wall behind a piece of siding. As such, my handgun was essentially useless for the rest of the game. This meant having to rely on the shotgun, which depleted my ammo and forced me to actually run from some enemies instead of fighting them. Running meant forfeiting valuable collectibles, which set me back even further. Missing one, hard-to-find secret can greatly affect the rest of the game. I recommend using a walkthrough. It will ruin the jump scares, but you might find yourself completely out of resources if you don’t seek out the right weapons at the right times.
3. There is almost no variety to be found. There are two – yes, two – types of enemies in the entire game. Boss battles help to spice things up, but there are only a handful of those, and some of them are incredibly formulaic. Gun variety is also sorely lacking. Players can choose between a handgun, a shotgun, a flamethrower that is only useful for forty-five minutes, a grenade launcher with maybe ten rounds of ammo total, a magnum you probably won’t unlock without a walkthrough, and a machine gun. Basically, you’re stuck with the shotgun for 80% of the game.
4. The combat is clunky. Shooting isn’t very accurate; the main character moves like he’s underwater, and the player is forced to use a blocking system, like an Elder Scrolls game with guns.
Overall, I wouldn’t call RE7 *bad*. It’s decently tense and offers a good challenge for anyone sick of hand-holding horror games like Layers of Fear. The problem is that it doesn’t have much in the “fun” department. It tries so hard to be survival-horror that some sections fall into the territory of “miserable.” With more enemies and less linear gameplay, it could have been a masterpiece. But as it sits, RE7 is a solid 6/10. Pick it up if you’re a fan of the series. Otherwise, wait for a hefty discount.

Alien Breed 1 Fails:
Camera system takes control away from the player, doesn't show enough, and is set at an angle that blocks much of the screen due to walls. Constant re-orientation screws up NSEW map memorization. One hit one kill monsters that you can't fight. Lots and lots and lots of backtracking, which makes the level BORING because you're not collecting powerups in areas you've already been through. There is WAY TOO MUCH ♥♥♥♥ING CAMERA SHAKING!!! The amount of environmental effects on screen is insanely stupid and annoying. Joystick controls are pretty meh, and your character has a tendency to lock aim in one of the 8 directions you might find in an older game. Far from increasing anxiety, the fact that you can run out of breath when running is really just annoying. There are entirely too many things that could be solved by blowing them up that the game does not allow you to do so. Grenades are worthless and dangerous.
Alien Breed 1 Success:
The radar is well instituted, the amount of inventory/weapons/powers in the game are well chosen and not overwhelming, weapons are somewhat balanced, collection is actually fun because there are optional areas and you need every bullet since you can't buy them in unlimited quantities. The maps are quite well designed for modular maps, the lighting is good and when you're not being spammed to death with them the atmospheric effects are well done. Background noise is eerie and non-repetitive, and is carefully layered to stay that way. Encounters are short but intense. Much more stable than it was when first released.
Alien Breed 1 WTF:
This is the WORST sci-fi game story I've seen in a long time. It's not that the premise is bad, but the writing is weak and the voice acting is ♥♥♥♥ing horrible. The comic segments are decent but noticably unfinished. I could give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about the character's background, oh look he's a super soldier and he's a double widower and he doesn't like artificial life forms because they killed his family boo hoo hoo. Missions seem very contrived. There are a surprising number of unarmed survivors on the ship.
Overall this is a fun little game to pick up on the cheap, but it's pretty clear that Team17 can't get past their 8-bit / 16-bit roots with their remakes. If they can embrace analog controls, learn how a camera should work and try not to trip over their own feet with the effects they could be a contender.

A solid fighting game of the old 2D fighting game era, that focuses on the basic strikes and give and take gameplay of games like King of Fighters. The game definitely has a reasonable cast of characters that feels appropriate for the genre and fight a bit differently without being overly different in their usage, and the paired down move list gives a more simple yet satisfying experience for the fighting game enthusiast. The game probably shouldn't have come out of early access in my opinion, as the polish around the edges especially with UI and in game inconsistency in elements is apparent after playing for a period of time, but that doesn't overlook the good solid fighting base here. It's no Skullgirls, but if you're looking for competitive fighting at a low cost, this may be up your alley.

Seems like a great online fighting game so far. Netcode is playable and smooth with anyone under 150 ping. There's a really robust training mode that lets you record a series of actions and play them back randomly to hone your reflexes. Not sure about the story mode.
Keys to the netcode are using the O and P keys on the character select screen to manually adjust delay until you can pick characters without lag. Also forward UDP 50055 through 50057 if you're having trouble connecting to people.
I think there are some issues with the implementation on PC. The UI is ugly (same as it was in the older version) and a little buggy. The lobby system is kinda awkward. There are few resolution options, just 1x (tiny window), 2x (big window), or fullscreen that stretches the 4:3 aspect ratio to your monitor. You may have external options to prevent it from doing that, but it will take a little research/setup. I like 2x windowed mode, fits on 1080 or 900 resolutions, but if you have a 720 monitor it might be too big. So it lacks some polish, hopefully they'll improve it, but once you're playing the actual game it's all good.

Astoria is a wonderful Epic RPG with a very interesting storyline and fun combat mechanics. Although the developer modestly says it's a 35+ hour RPG I played 106 hours and had a blast of a time. The 106 hours is for a single playthrough where I patiently did all the sidequest and every single achievement in the game. I am still highly enthusiastic about the game, and might played it again, but choosing to "build" my heroes differently.
There are many interesting things about this game which make it stands out. For example, it is just not forceful fighting all the way. There are also the stealth type missions, where you play a single assassin who accomplish various goals under the cover of darkness. Your party of regular NPC will also be joined by various other interesting NPCs that are event and story driven. This makes the fight interesting as you need to adapt your fighting mechanics to accomodate the skills and strengths of the other temporary team members that join you. The side quests and achievements are also varied and different. These include digging for treasures in the ground, walking on special invisible squares to trigger events like mermaids blessing, fighting epic monsters to get various weapons and armor enhancements, killing dragon hordes to get powerups for your team, finding unique relics and gears, cleansing shrines and searching for virtues of semi-godlike dead heroes. There are so many things to do in this game, and they are seemlessly intertwined into the storyline so that there are never dull moments. This is what drives me to play 1 more hour and 1 more hour until I reached 106 hours.
This is actually a kickstarter game which is already funded by many backers who are impressed by the quality of the game. Hence, this game is selling at a ridiculously low price of $4.99 on steam because the cost of this game is already "paid for" by previous backers and supporters.

Pros:
* Many games choose between random encounters and touch encounters. This game opted for random encounters on the world map and one-time touch encounters in dungeons. The former allows players to grind if they need to while the latter makes it less of a hassle to fully explore dungeons.
* I find the Dispel effect interesting, since it basically forces you to make a choice if your character has both good and bad statuses. Should they get rid of all their effects and recast the good ones later, or just endure it?
* I like how most of the human bosses aren't insanely durable damage sponges with high HP and instead use other tactics to make up for their lack of boss constitution. It feels more realistic for them to be only somewhat more durable than the average party member while being less durable than huge hulking beast and demon bosses.
* The story is horrifying at times without being too cynical and hopeless.
Cons
* The villains don't have much motive, backstory, or personality beyond being greedy and sadistic. The exception is the always-second-best traitor, who seems to have some regrets about his actions, but is too selfish and cowardly to own up to them. Though I do admit the human ones do an effective job at angering the player as much as possible.
* The final boss feels somewhat underwhelming compared to previous bosses due to how it only moves once per round if it uses a spell.
* Stunlocking (or weblocking from the spider enemies) from some enemies feels cheap, especially when the stun effect lasts for several turns
* The money drops are pretty low, even for a JRPG.
Tips
* Many story dungeons will lock you in once you enter, including the final one. Get used to carrying a lot of MP potions and using multiple save slots.
* Many of these story dungeons also can't be revisited, which means you should be extra thorough in looting and killing everything. Dungeon enemies tend to drop more EXP and gold, so killing them all is recommended unless you're severely lacking in items.
* Once you enter a friendly pirate's base, immediately buy the Magic Shovel. I don't think there's another opportunity to get it.
* In general, mobs containing human enemies will drop more gold.
* At the very least, you should complete the Chaos Lords sidequest to get a weapon that everything in the final dungeon is weak to.
* If a boss is fond of spamming multi-hit normal attacks, have Nolan use his taunt and counter buffs.
* Defeat all challenger bosses as soon as they appear. After some story events, they'll disappear and you won't be able to add them to your inventory.
* Be sure to do complete the initial part of the bestiary and talk to the NPC who is interested in it so you can get the remaining pages.
* The special gear in Bardstown just aren't worth it. They're too expensive and they'll become obsolete in the endgame.

This will be the first review I've written for a game on Steam. So bear with my rough assessment.
Pendragon Rising an old style text-based adventure where nearly, if not every decision you make matters in some way to the story. Unfortunately I missed the age of Text based games, so playing this as my first pure experience was quite fun.
As expected, the roughly 3 hours (per read-through) of gameplay consists solely of making decisions, leading to what kind of King Arthur/Queen Arta you will be. This consists of these main traits. Leadership, Diplomacy, Warrior, Compassion v. Ruthlessness, Bravado v. Cunning, and Old Religion v. Roman Christianity. But regardless of what kind of ruler you are, you are almost positive to get a rich story.
Pros:
+Great and immersive story.
+Fun experimentation with choices. Each one truly feels unique.
+Romances (Or flings) feel pleasantly tasteful.
+Writing is very strong, I don't recall seeing any spelling errors.
Cons:
-Personally wish the read length was longer.
-There was a choice or two I found were hard to understand what was meant in context.
Taking everything I've said I strongly recommend this game, with a solid 9/10. If you've got a few hours to spare, or even more for several read-throughs, it's definitely worth the humble price of $4. I'm looking forward to more stories from this developer!

A heavily atmospheric and dream-like game from the unusual perspective of a toddler. The elements of saturated colors, artistically created environments, and lush soundtrack are well harmonized for a unique experience. If you're tired of stereotypical horror games, this is something fresh.
PROS
* The visual design is striking. The bright colors and dark shadows play over strangely distorted landscapes. The child's perspective makes even common objects like swings or coats huge and menacing. This is a visual experience that will not soon be forgotten.
* The atmosphere is enhanced by the soundscape. There are bumps in the night, rumbling drones, and a haunting melody being hummed far off.
* Without spoiling anything, the subject matter is interesting and well paced.
* The voice acting of the teddy bear is another high point, being playful and surreal without becoming corny.
* This is a very imaginative experience. It felt like reading a storybook, in a similar vein as the movie The Babadook.
CONS
* The game is extremely linear. It almost felt like a straight line going through each area.
* When the monsters are introduced, it detracts greatly from the experience for me. The nightmarish environment lets your imagination run wild, so when the game becomes a hide-and-seek horror trope, the experience suffers.
* The monsters become constant by the end. Less really would have been more, both for scares and for letting the environment keep the spotlight.
* There's no story. There is a *situation* which you come to understand throughout the game. I feel that if the game developers were going to tackle this subject, there really should have been more depth given to both the "villain" and to the situation. Instead, the treatment feels shallow and even insensitive.

Story: One of the most well known aspects of Pajama Sam is it's story; it is simply unorthodox, as it does the process of not feeding all of the story the viewer; it drip-feeds it, giving the viewer only half the story, or sometimes giving scenes without any context. For some games, this would be a disaster waiting to happen, but in the case of Pajama Sam, this is done almost consistently masterfully, holding back information on such subjects such as the location of the flashlight or what color an orange is. Many have critisized the holding of frames later in the series, but taken into the context of the fact they were running out of money to make the game, is is understandable.
For many fans, their major criticism of the game is the handling of the ending, which many consider far too 'out there' and simply crap. I too, am not a huge fan of the ending, but taking the ending to the game, inside the context of the 'true' ending sequel, Pajama Sam 3: You are what you Eat from your Head to your Feet, the ending can make a lot more sense, and thus I enjoy it far, far more. To stop me from ranting on for ages, Pajama Sam's story is a master stroke in writing, one which has been a hard feat to replicate.
Art and Sound: I was introduced to Pajama Sam through the in-progress tetraology of games, The Rebuild of Pajama Sam; due to this, I became used to the cutting edge graphics employed for the higher-budget games. And to be honest, yes, the original game's art is beginning to show it's age 20 years on; however, this does not detract from the series in any major capcity, as the art compliments the anime extremely well.
The sound is also fantastic, and a very high-point for the show. Excellent music is employed to showcase the chaos of finding your lost socks, and for darker moments such as the internal struggles of the main cast of the game. Some of Beethoven's music is featured later in the series, which coupled with the emotional impact of the scene, produces one of the most excellent scenes in video game history.
Characters: By a massive leap, the highlight of the series. Pajama Sam features in it's story the struggles of the main characters, to devastatingly wonderful effect. Weak, timid, daddy-issues Sam, to powerful, arrogant, egotistical Mom, to the quiet, mysterious Boat, and the brooding, apparently agnostical Darkness, Pajama Sam develes into the mind and motivations of these characters, showcasing exactly what makes them tick, and this is what gives us some of gaming's most regonisable and wonderful characters.
I am certain entire essays have been written on why certain charcters tick, and that's another reason so many of these characters are so wonderful. Fans are so devoted to their favorite characters (personally I am partial to Mom and Boat), and this creates a wonderful feeling when learning about these characters and then discussing this with other fans. Generally, Pajama Sam employs some of the most human characters in games, showing us that the heroes of gaming aren't always strong, both mentally and physically, or not even in control of their lives.
In closing, Pajama Sam is one of the strongest games ever produced. It employs powerful characters, a deep, deep story, and art that has only just began to show it's age. What makes the game's longevity even more powerful is that even now on sites such as PJSamGeeks people are still analysing this series, trying to know everything about it. I hope Pajama Sam will live on in the hearts of it's fans, who'll continue to appreciate it's deep, metaphorical story. I hope that Pajama Sam will always remain an game that will be treasured, for all the ages.
